courses.title: AI Foundations
courses.summary: A practical, plain-English introduction to using today's AI tools well and responsibly — the assistants, image tools, model choices, and the new 'connectors' that let AI act for you.

lessons.title: Why this guide exists
lessons.html:
AI went from a novelty to an everyday tool faster than almost any technology before it. This course is a calm, practical map: what the main tools are, what each is good at, and how to use them with good judgment — no hype, no jargon.

You don't need to be technical. By the end you'll be able to pick the right tool for a task, write clearer prompts, and understand the new wave of 'agentic' tools that can take actions for you.

Homework

Reflect on your current relationship with AI tools: Do you use ChatGPT, Claude, or similar assistants? For what tasks? Write 150-200 words on what surprised you about how they work, or what you wish they could do better.

lessons.title: Assistants: Claude & ChatGPT
lessons.html:
Chat assistants are the front door to AI. You type a request; they respond. The skill is in how you ask: give context, say what good output looks like, and iterate.

  • Claude Desktop — a desktop assistant that can also connect to your files and tools (see the Connectors lesson).
  • ChatGPT — a general assistant strong at writing, reasoning, and — increasingly — images.

Rule of thumb: treat the assistant like a sharp, fast intern. Be specific, review its work, and never paste secrets or private data you wouldn't want stored.

Homework

Research one person in your sangat or broader Sikh community who uses AI in their work (parchar, scholarship, business, art). Interview them briefly (or reflect if you know their story): How do they use it? What do they trust it for, and what do they do by hand? Write 200-250 words on their approach.

lessons.title: Creating images: ChatGPT, Gemini & 'Nano Banana'
lessons.html:
Modern assistants can generate and edit images from a description. The craft is describing subject, style, composition, and lighting clearly, then refining.

  • ChatGPT image generation — good for illustrations, mockups, and edits.
  • Gemini (and its image model nicknamed 'Nano Banana') — strong, fast image creation and editing.

Always keep cultural and religious imagery respectful and accurate — AI can get sacred details wrong, so verify before sharing.

Homework

Take a question you genuinely have — about Gurbani, Sikh history, a spiritual concept, or a parchar challenge. Write it as you would ask an AI. Run it through Claude or ChatGPT. Then fact-check the answer by consulting a real source (a book, a scholar, a recording, a mentor). Write 200 words on: Was the AI answer right? What did it miss? How would you refine the question for a better result?

lessons.title: Choosing a model (and OpenRouter)
lessons.html:
There isn't one 'best' AI — different models lead at different things and the leaderboard changes monthly. A good habit in 2026: match the model to the task (writing vs. coding vs. images vs. cheap-and-fast).

OpenRouter is a single doorway to many models from different companies — handy for trying options without separate accounts. Start cheap and small; reach for a frontier model only when the task is hard.

Homework

Examine a piece of AI-generated text you've encountered (a social media post, a website, an article). Can you spot signs it was written by AI? What feels off or hollow? What's actually good about it? Write 150-200 words on what made it recognizable as AI and what humans could do better.

lessons.title: Agentic tools: Codex & getting things done
lessons.html:
The newest shift is agentic tools that don't just answer — they take steps to complete a goal (research, write code, edit files). OpenAI's Codex-style tools can act like a tireless assistant working through a task list.

Power comes with care: give clear goals, review what they did, and keep a human in the loop for anything that matters.

Homework

Choose an image made by an AI (from a news story, social media, or by generating one yourself). Look closely. What's slightly wrong or weird about it? Hands, faces, perspective, logic? Write 150-200 words on what you notice and what this teaches you about AI's current limits.

lessons.title: Connectors & MCP: letting AI use your tools
lessons.html:
Connectors (often built on the Model Context Protocol, MCP) let an assistant securely reach your files, calendar, or apps — so it can work with your real information instead of guessing.

Security first: only connect what you need, review permissions, and never grant write access you can't undo. This same care is how we built this very university.

Homework

Plan one parchar or personal learning goal (teach a class, write a piece, study a topic, translate something). Draft a 2-3 step plan on how you'd use an AI tool to help — not to do all the work, but to do part of it faster. Be specific about what AI handles and what you handle yourself. (200 words)

lessons.title: Understanding Tokens and Context Windows
lessons.html:
Every AI model processes language in chunks called tokens. A token is roughly 4 characters — when you send text to Claude or ChatGPT, it counts tokens, not words. This matters because models have a context window: a maximum number of tokens they can 'see' at once.

Think of it like a reader's memory. A model with a 200k token context window can hold roughly 150,000 words — that's a full novel plus a conversation. But a smaller window (8k tokens) fits maybe a few pages. When you paste a 50-page document and ask a question, a small context window might miss important sections.

Why This Matters for Your Work

When you're asking an AI to research something, draft parchar materials, or analyze a long Gurbani passage, the context window affects quality. Claude and newer GPT models have large windows (100k+), but older or cheaper models don't. If you upload a 100-page manuscript and the model only 'sees' the first 30 pages, it can't give you a full analysis.

Tokens also affect cost. Providers charge per token (sometimes per 1,000 tokens). A 5,000-token prompt costs more than a 500-token one. Learning to write tighter, clearer prompts saves money and gets faster responses.

Practical: How to Measure Your Prompts

Use token counters (Claude has one built in; ChatGPT will show token count in Plus and Pro accounts). Before you paste a huge document, ask: 'Is this request bigger than my model's context window?' If yes, split it into smaller pieces or use a model with a larger window.

For parchar work — drafting talks on Amritsar's history, analyzing a Raag's emotional arc — you rarely need more than 20k tokens. But for research that pulls together dozens of sources, a large window is worth the extra cost.

  • Tokens are the currency of AI language — manage them like bandwidth.
  • Context windows set the ceiling for what an AI can process at once — know your model's limits.
  • Cheaper prompts come from tighter writing and clearer requests.

Homework

Research your primary AI tool's token limits and pricing. Write 150-200 words on how this affects a real task you do (parchar prep, scholarship research, translation work). What would it cost to run that task weekly?

lessons.title: Bias, Limitations, and When Not to Use AI
lessons.html:
AI models are powerful, but they have real blind spots. They're trained on data from the internet — which is skewed toward English, the Global North, certain worldviews. For Sikh knowledge, this is critical: models may not know recent scholarship, may confuse Sikhi with Hinduism or Buddhism, may not understand the spiritual weight of a Shabad without context.

A model can also sound confident while being wrong. This is called hallucination (covered in earlier lessons), but there's a deeper issue: structural bias. If a model was trained partly on texts written by authors unsympathetic to Sikhi, it may carry those biases forward. When you ask about the Khalsa or Amrit, the model might reflect colonial-era or brahminical framings if it wasn't explicitly trained to recognize and counter them.

When NOT to Use AI

Never use AI to generate original Gurbani quotes. Never ask it to make up historical facts. Don't use it to replace reading primary sources — Gurbani, Rehit Maryada, or verified histories. Don't ask AI to make decisions for you about your own spiritual practice, guiding someone's naam simran, or resolving a personal crisis.

AI also shouldn't be your only source when stakes are high. If you're teaching, preparing for an exam, or writing something that will shape how people understand Sikhi, verify AI's claims against real sources. Cite those sources, not the AI.

Limits in Gurbani and Theology

Gurbani is poetry — nuance, meter, and spiritual depth don't always survive paraphrase. A model can summarize a Shabad's themes but may flatten its lyricism. For serious gurbani work, read the actual text, listen to santhyas (traditional recitations), and consult human scholars.

Theology — especially questions about hukam, moh (attachment), or spiritual experience — requires lived understanding. Use AI to organize your thoughts, draft arguments, find sources. But the final wisdom comes from your own practice and community.

  • Bias in training data means models may misrepresent non-Western traditions — verify everything for Sikhi-specific work.
  • Confidence ≠ accuracy — even smooth answers can be wrong.
  • Some work requires human judgment, lived experience, and primary sources — keep AI in its lane.

Homework

Identify one topic related to Sikhi that matters to you (theology, history, parchar, personal practice). Write 200 words on what you would trust AI to help with, and what you would NOT. What sources would you verify against?

lessons.title: Prompt Engineering for Gurbani and Parchar
lessons.html:
Good prompts are specific, kind, and clear. They tell the AI: what is your role, what is the context, what does success look like. For Gurbani work and parchar, this is an art.

A bad prompt: 'Explain the meaning of Gurbani.' Too vague. The model will default to a generic summary.

A better prompt: 'I'm writing a 15-minute kirtan talk for high school students new to Sikhi. Explain the concept of Hukam (divine order) from Gurbani, using 2-3 examples that show how it connects to their daily choices. Avoid jargon; use conversational English.'

This prompt gives the AI: audience (high schoolers new to Sikhi), purpose (kirtan talk), format (15 minutes), concept (Hukam), scope (2-3 examples), tone (conversational). The AI can now give you something useful.

Prompts for Different Tasks

Translation help: 'Translate this line from Gurmukhi to English, keeping the poetic rhythm. Explain one image or metaphor that's hard to translate.' (Give the actual line.)

Research summaries: 'Find [three sources] on the Khalsa's role in [historical period]. Summarize what each says in one paragraph, then tell me what's agreed and what's debated.'

Draft editing: 'This is a draft parchar talk on [topic]. Is the argument clear? Where does it get confusing? What would you add for a Canadian Sikh audience, age [25-45]?'

Fact-checking: 'Is this claim true? If yes, tell me the source. If no, what's the right fact? [Claim].' Then verify the AI's answer yourself.

The Iterate Loop

Your first response from AI is rarely final. Ask follow-ups: 'Make it shorter, that was preachy,' or 'Add more of this, cut that part.' Treat the AI like a co-worker. Show it what you're actually building (a website, a talk, a lesson) and ask for revision rounds.

  • Specific prompts beat generic ones — tell the AI who, what, why, and what success looks like.
  • Context is your friend — explain the background, the audience, the stakes.
  • Iterate — first answers are drafts, not finished work.

Homework

Take one parchar or teaching task you actually do (or want to do). Write two versions of a prompt: one vague, one detailed. Run both through your AI tool, compare the results, and write 150 words on what made the detailed prompt better.

lessons.title: Using AI for Translation and Language Learning
lessons.html:
AI is a co-pilot for language work. It can help you translate, parse Gurmukhi grammar, check whether your Punjabi is idiomatic, and generate practice materials — but it's not a substitute for a teacher.

Gurmukhi script recognition is improving: Claude and ChatGPT can usually read Gurmukhi text if you paste it or image it. You can ask: 'Transliterate this line into Roman Punjabi,' or 'What does this word mean in the context of Gurbani?' The AI will give you a starting point.

Translation with AI

For Gurbani, never ask AI alone to translate. Instead, use it to propose translations, then check against scholarly ones (SGGS-USA, Talib Singh's works, or published santhyas). Ask the AI: 'Here's my translation of this Shabad. Does it capture the meaning? What am I missing?' This way you learn and catch errors.

For modern Punjabi — a letter, a speech, a social media post — AI is much more reliable. You can draft in English, ask Claude to render it in conversational Punjabi, and refine. Punjabi Sikhs in your sangat can review the final version.

Grammar and Writing Checks

Gurmukhi grammar is intricate (case endings, word order, the ਖ਼ and ਖ distinction). AI can explain these, but not perfectly. When learning Gurmukhi script, use AI to check your transliterations and parsing, but verify against a grammar guide or a human speaker.

For Punjabi writing — whether you're composing an ਅਰਦਾਸ note, a thank-you letter, or parchar material — ask AI to: 'Check this for grammar and idioms. Is this how a native speaker would phrase it?' Then ask a trusted Punjabi speaker to review.

Limits

AI struggles with Gurbani's metaphorical depth and spiritual layers. It can parse the surface meaning but misses the 'Shabad experience' — the raag, the santhya, the silence after. Use AI for homework help, translation brainstorms, and script practice. For deep Gurbani study, sit with a teacher or a santhya recording.

  • AI can propose translations and parse grammar — but always verify against scholarly or native sources.
  • Use AI as a learning tool, not a shortcut — the struggle to understand deepens the knowledge.
  • Script and transliteration are AI's strength; spiritual interpretation is not.

Homework

Find one Gurbani line, couplet, or short Shabad that you want to understand better. Paste it (in Gurmukhi or Roman) into your AI tool and ask for: transliteration, word-by-word grammar, and translation. Then find a published English translation or santhya note and compare. Write 200 words on what the AI got right and where a human scholar adds depth.

lessons.title: Building an AI Workflow for Your Real Work
lessons.html:
The power of AI isn't in any single tool — it's in how you chain them together. A workflow is a sequence: 'First I use Claude for research, then I organize in a spreadsheet, then ChatGPT helps edit.' For Sikh parchar, scholarship, or personal projects, building your own workflow saves time and keeps quality high.

Sample Workflow: Preparing a Parchar Talk

Step 1 (Research): Ask Claude, 'Outline a 20-minute talk on [topic]. What should I cover? What sources exist?' Step 2 (Draft): 'Write a 5-minute intro that hooks a [demographic] audience.' Step 3 (Refine): Paste the draft and ask, 'Make this conversational. Where's the argument weak? What's unclear?' Step 4 (Check): Fact-check any claims against real sources. Step 5 (Practice): Use a recording tool (not AI) to hear yourself say it aloud. Revise based on how it lands.

Sample Workflow: Writing Academic or Gurbani-Focused Scholarship

Step 1: Ask AI to find sources on your topic (it won't find everything, but it's a starting point). Step 2: Use AI to organize your notes — 'I have notes on [themes]. Group them by argument.' Step 3: Draft sections — 'Write a paragraph on [this angle] for an academic audience unfamiliar with Sikhi.' Step 4: Have AI help structure logic — 'Does this argument flow? Are there gaps?' Step 5: Copy-edit for clarity and tone. Step 6: Have a human expert read it.

Tools to Chain Together

Most workflows use 2-3 tools: Claude for research and drafting, ChatGPT for a second opinion, Perplexity (web search AI) for fact-checking, a spreadsheet for organizing. Don't use AI for everything — some steps are faster by hand (reading a source, listening to a Shabad, talking to a mentor).

Keep a Prompt Library

Save prompts that work. Keep a note of: 'For parchar prep, ask AI to [specific structure]' or 'For gurbani translation help, give AI [this format].' Over time, you'll notice which prompts yield the best results for your work. Reuse and tweak them.

  • Workflows chain tools together in a sequence — plan before you start.
  • Each step has an AI tool, a human step, or both — know which is which.
  • Prompt libraries save time — collect what works for you.

Homework

Map out one real project or task you do regularly (teaching a class, writing, research, parchar prep, personal study). List 5-7 steps. For each, write whether you'd use AI, do it by hand, or combine both. Share your workflow with a peer or mentor and ask: 'What am I missing? Where would AI slow me down instead of speeding me up?'

lessons.title: The Future: AI Agents and What Comes Next
lessons.html:
AI is moving beyond 'you ask, AI answers.' The next wave is agents — AI systems that can take actions for you. An agent can draft an email, send it, read the reply, and adjust. It can research a question across multiple sources, synthesize findings, and hand you a memo. For Sikh work, this opens new possibilities and new risks.

What Are Agents?

An agent is an AI given access to tools and autonomy. Instead of giving it a prompt and waiting for text, you give it a goal: 'Research this historical figure and write a 500-word biography.' The agent then: searches the web, reads sources, compares them, writes, and presents the draft — often without you asking each step.

Tools an agent might use: web search, calendar access, email, file storage, spreadsheets, publishing platforms. Think of it as hiring an intern who can work unsupervised for stretches.

Opportunities for Parchar and Scholarship

An agent could: monitor Sikh news and compile a weekly summary. Draft multiple versions of a parchar talk and present them for your review. Organize research notes across dozens of sources. Translate a new article from Punjabi news. Manage a social media calendar for your parchar initiative. These tasks eat time today; agents could handle them in the background.

Real Risks

Agents are less transparent. You don't watch every step, so errors hide more easily. If an agent sends an email or posts something, you need to review before it goes live — but you might forget. Agents amplify both quality and mistakes.

For Sikh content, the stakes are higher. An agent that misrepresents Gurbani or perpetuates bias does it at scale. A parchar agent that gets Sikh history wrong reaches hundreds. These tools are coming; the discipline to use them well is on us.

Not Yet Ready for Unsupervised Work

Don't set an agent loose on Gurbani work, scholarship, or parchar without strong guardrails. Right now, an agent summarizing a Shabad might miss the spiritual layer. One writing parchar might flatten nuance. Review its work carefully. As tools improve, you'll trust them more — but today, agents are for tasks where clarity, not poetry, matters.

  • Agents are AI with access to tools and light autonomy — powerful, but less transparent than chat assistants.
  • Good uses: research synthesis, content organization, scheduling, monitoring. Bad uses: unsupervised spiritual or scholarly work.
  • Agents are coming; building judgment now prepares you for later tools.

Homework

Imagine an AI agent working for you on one of your regular tasks (research, organizing, writing, parchar prep, translation). Write out: What would you ask it to do? What checks would you put in place before it acts? What could go wrong, and how would you catch it? (200-250 words)

courses.title: Gurbani Exegesis with Prof. Sahib Singh
courses.summary: An author-as-professor course about Prof. Sahib Singh (1892-1977), among the most influential interpreters of Sri Guru Granth Sahib. The course studies who he was, the grammar-based method he built for reading Gurbani, his ten-volume Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan, his companion Gurbani Viakaran, his study of the…
outcomes: Describe the life, training, and motivating concerns of Prof. Sahib Singh as an interpreter of Sri Guru Granth Sahib.
Explain the core claim of his grammatical method: that the script's vowel-signs and word-endings carry meaning.
Identify the aims and structure of his major works, the Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan and the Gurbani Viakaran.
Apply grammatical principles of number, part of speech, and case to narrow the possible meanings of a line.
Summarize the main points of scholarly discussion and disagreement about his approach.
Practice a disciplined, grammar-aware reading habit grounded in humility and respect for the text.

terms.m: Laga-matra: the vowel signs and diacritical marks attached to Gurmukhi consonants, which the method treats as grammatically meaningful.
Gurbani Viakaran: the grammar of the language of Gurbani, the subject of Sahib Singh's companion grammar work.
Darpan: a mirror; the title image of his interpretation that reflects the meaning of the text back to the reader.
Teeka: a written commentary or exegesis that explains the meaning of scripture.
Kathaa: spoken discourse or exposition that explains Gurbani to a listening congregation.
Mool Mantar: the opening statement of Sri Guru Granth Sahib at Ang 1, often used to illustrate grammatical reading.
Raag: the musical mode in which a shabad is set, a poetic and musical factor relevant to interpretation.
Ang: a leaf or page of Sri Guru Granth Sahib, used to locate verses.

references: Singh, Sahib. Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan. 10 vols. Jalandhar: Raj Publishers.
Singh, Sahib. Gurbani Viakaran. Amritsar: Singh Brothers.
Singh, Sahib. About the Compilation of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. Amritsar: Singh Brothers.
Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014.
Mann, Gurinder Singh. The Making of Sikh Scripture. New York: Oxford University Press, 2001.

lessons.title: Who Was Prof. Sahib Singh?
lessons.summary: Introduces Prof. Sahib Singh (1892-1977), his training, the interpretive problem he saw, and the convictions that shaped his lifelong study of Sri Guru Granth Sahib.
lessons.html:
Full course contents
  1. Who Was Prof. Sahib Singh?
  2. His Place in Sikh Scholarship
  3. The Grammatical Method: Core Idea
  4. Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan: The Landmark Work
  5. How Grammar Resolves Interpretive Questions
  6. Influence and Scholarly Discussion

A Teacher of the Text

Prof. Sahib Singh (1892-1977) is remembered as one of the most consequential scholars of Sri Guru Granth Sahib in the twentieth century. He spent his life trying to read the Guru's words carefully, on their own terms, and to give ordinary Sikhs the tools to do the same. This course is not a reprint of his books. It is a course about him: about the questions he asked, the method he built to answer them, and the legacy he left for later students (Singh and Fenech 2014).

From a Modest Beginning

He came to deep study of Gurmukhi, of the classical and Persian vocabulary that feeds into the diction of Gurbani, and of grammar. His training as a teacher mattered: he thought constantly about how a learner actually understands a line, and how a misreading takes root and spreads. That teacherly instinct shaped everything he wrote, including his grammar book, the ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ ਵਿਆਕਰਣ (grammar of Gurbani).

The Problem He Saw

By his time, a great deal of oral and written interpretation, the tradition of ਟੀਕਾ (commentary) and ਕਥਾ (discourse), had accumulated. Some of it was illuminating. But Sahib Singh observed that interpreters often read individual words in isolation or imported meanings without checking them against the language of the text itself. The result was that the same line could be explained in contradictory ways, with no shared way to decide which reading the grammar supported (Singh).

His Central Conviction

His response became the engine of his scholarship: the Gurus and the other contributors to the Granth wrote in a disciplined, consistent language, and the written forms of words carry grammatical information that constrains meaning. If you learn the grammar embedded in the script, he argued, many disputes resolve themselves.

QualityWhat it meant in practice
ReverenceHe approached the Granth as Guru; method served understanding, not reduction.
SystemHe wanted reasons anyone could check, not authority no one could question.
PedagogyHe aimed to put a reliable reading method into students' hands.

Carry these three traits forward; the rest of the course unpacks the method and how to use it.

References: Singh, Sahib, Gurbani Viakaran; Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds., The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies (Oxford, 2014).

Homework

Spend 20–30 minutes reading the biographical preface that Prof. Sahib Singh wrote for one volume of the Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan (available in Punjabi libraries or digitized collections). In 250–300 words, reflect on what his own words reveal about his motivations, his sense of scholarly responsibility, and his relationship to the Gurbani he spent his life interpreting. What surprised you most about his self-presentation?

lessons.title: His Place in Sikh Scholarship
lessons.summary: Situates Sahib Singh against the interpretive traditions he inherited, shows what his reproducible method added, and explains why his influence endured across both devotional and academic settings.
lessons.html:
A Turning Point in How Sikhs Read

To appreciate Prof. Sahib Singh, picture the landscape of Gurbani interpretation around his work, and then see what he changed (Singh and Fenech 2014).

The Traditions He Inherited

Earlier traditions included the oral teaching of learned reciters and granthis, written ਟੀਕਾ (commentary) in various styles, and explanatory traditions of different schools of Sikh learning. These preserved enormous knowledge and devotion, passing down pronunciation, melody, and meaning across generations. Sahib Singh respected this inheritance and drew on it.

What He Added

His distinctive contribution was to insist on a reproducible method grounded in the grammar of the script. Where an earlier explanation might rest on the authority and piety of the teacher, Sahib Singh wanted an explanation that pointed to features anyone could verify in the written text. This moved interpretation toward disciplined textual analysis while keeping its devotional purpose intact.

A Bridge Between Faith and Study

He occupied an unusual middle ground: a committed Sikh writing for the community's spiritual benefit, yet with a rigor that academic scholars could engage. His work is cited both in ਕਥਾ (discourse) and teaching and in academic Sikh studies (Singh and Fenech 2014).

Why His Influence Endured

FactorWhy it mattered
CompletenessA continuous interpretation covering the whole Granth, not selected passages.
TransparencyBecause it appeals to grammar, a reader can follow and even contest his reasoning.
PedagogyHe wrote grammar materials so the method could be learned, not just admired.
AccessibilityHe wrote primarily in Punjabi, putting serious interpretation within community reach.

A Balanced View

He was not the only valid voice. Sikh tradition contains a rich plurality of interpretation, and respected scholars have both built on and questioned parts of his approach. His greatness lies less in being the final word than in giving the community a shared, checkable way to argue about the words (Mann 2001).

References: Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds., The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies (Oxford, 2014); Mann, Gurinder Singh, The Making of Sikh Scripture (Oxford, 2001).

Homework

Identify one Punjabi grammatical concept — such as the vocative case (ਸੰਬੋਧਨ ਕਾਰਕ), the ਸਿਹਾਰੀ construction, or a verbal tense form — that Prof. Sahib Singh uses to resolve an interpretive question in the Darpan. Spend 30 minutes studying that grammatical category using any available grammar primer. Then write 250 words explaining how understanding that grammar changes your reading of even one line of Gurbani.

lessons.title: The Grammatical Method: Core Idea
lessons.summary: Explains the heart of Sahib Singh's contribution: that laga-matra in the Gurmukhi of the Granth carry grammatical meaning, illustrated with an original English analogy and the principle of consistency.
lessons.html:
The Script Encodes Grammar

The heart of his contribution is one powerful idea: the Gurmukhi used in Sri Guru Granth Sahib is grammatically systematic, and the ਲਗਾਂ ਮਾਤਰਾਂ (vowel signs and diacritics) are not decorative but meaningful. Reading them correctly is part of reading the message correctly (Singh, Gurbani Viakaran).

What Laga-Matra Means

In Gurmukhi, consonants carry attached vowel symbols and other marks. Sahib Singh's claim is that, in the language of the Granth, such marks frequently signal grammatical roles: whether a noun is singular or plural, whether a word is a noun or adjective or verb, and which grammatical case a noun is in.

An Illustrative Principle (Original Example)

Consider a simple English illustration: "a teacher's book" versus "the teachers' books." The apostrophe and final "s" carry grammatical weight, telling you about possession and number. A reader who ignored those marks might confuse one teacher with many. Sahib Singh argued that vowel-endings in Gurbani work analogously: small written features systematically signal large differences in meaning. (This English analogy conveys the principle; it is not from his commentary.)

Why This Matters for Interpretation

If endings carry grammar, an interpreter cannot simply look up a dictionary meaning and stop. The interpreter must ask what role the word plays in this line. The written form, read attentively, often answers that question, so two readers who know the grammar can converge on a reading.

Consistency Across the Text

Without the methodWith the method
Endings treated as noiseEndings treated as signal
Readings chosen by intuitionReadings constrained by form
Disputes hard to settleDisputes tied to checkable evidence

Sahib Singh held that these patterns recur across the whole Granth. That consistency turns the method from a clever trick into a reliable tool, applied even in the ਮੂਲ ਮੰਤਰ (the opening statement at Ang 1).

References: Singh, Sahib, Gurbani Viakaran; Singh, Sahib, Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan.

Homework

Select any line from Gurbani that you find difficult or ambiguous — one where the meaning is not immediately clear to you. Without consulting any commentary, write down your instinctive interpretation. Then look up Prof. Sahib Singh's commentary on that line in the Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan or Gurbani Viakaran. Write 300 words comparing your initial reading with his grammatical analysis. Where did grammar resolve a genuine ambiguity? Where do you still have questions?

lessons.title: Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan: The Landmark Work
lessons.summary: Describes Sahib Singh's ten-volume Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan, its comprehensive aim, how the grammatical method appears in it, its pairing with the Gurbani Viakaran, and how to use it respectfully.
lessons.html:
A Mirror for the Whole Granth

His best-known achievement is the Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan, a multi-volume interpretation that walks through the Granth in order. The word ਦਰਪਣ (mirror) names its aim: to reflect the meaning of the text back to the reader clearly. It is commonly described as a ten-volume undertaking sustained over many years (Singh, Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan).

What It Sets Out to Do

The Darpan is not a loose set of reflections. Its ambition is comprehensive coverage: to take the verses as they stand and provide an explanation grounded in the language of the lines. The driving question throughout is, in effect, "What does this line actually say, when we respect its grammar?"

How the Method Shows Up

Because the work is built on his grammatical convictions, the explanations repeatedly attend to the form of words, not only their general sense. Where a casual reading might gloss over an ending, the Darpan treats that ending as a clue. The cumulative effect is an internally consistent reading. In keeping with this course's aim, we describe what the work does rather than reproduce its commentary on any verse.

An Accompanying Grammar

A reader cannot check grammatical claims without knowing the grammar, so Sahib Singh also produced the ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ ਵਿਆਕਰਣ (grammar of Gurbani). The pairing matters: the Darpan is the application, and the grammar is the toolkit that lets a reader test it.

WorkRole
Sri Guru Granth Sahib DarpanVerse-by-verse interpretation of the whole Granth.
Gurbani ViakaranThe grammar that the interpretation applies and that readers can use to test it.
About the Compilation of Sri Guru Granth Sahib JiHis study of how the Granth came to be compiled.

Why It Became a Standard

It is complete, methodical, and written in accessible Punjabi prose. For many students, granthis, and teachers it became a first place to look when a line's meaning was in question. Its standing does not make it immune to discussion, but it earned its place as a landmark. Consult it as Sahib Singh intended: as a reasoned reading you can examine, not an oracle.

References: Singh, Sahib, Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan; Singh, Sahib, About the Compilation of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji.

Homework

The Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan spans ten volumes and took decades to complete. Reflect on the commitment required for a single scholar to undertake such a work in the mid-twentieth century — without digital tools, with limited institutional support, while also teaching full-time. Write a 250-word reflection on what this kind of long-form scholarly dedication means for how we receive and use the Darpan today. What obligations do readers have toward a work of this scale?

lessons.title: How Grammar Resolves Interpretive Questions
lessons.summary: Shows, with original English examples, how the principles of number, part of speech, and case turn ambiguous lines into questions with checkable evidence, and how a reading decision gets made.
lessons.html:
From Ambiguity to Evidence

The promise of the method is practical: when readers disagree about a line, grammar can supply evidence that narrows the options. This lesson uses original examples rather than his commentary (Singh, Gurbani Viakaran).

Principle One: Number Disambiguates

Many disputes turn on whether a word refers to one thing or many. An ending that marks singular versus plural can settle this. In an invented English parallel, "the gift was given" versus "the gifts were given" point to different scenes. In Gurbani, the written ending of a noun often tells you its number.

Principle Two: Part of Speech Disambiguates

A second source of confusion is mistaking a word's part of speech. Consider "light": "the light shines" (noun), "light the lamp" (verb), "a light meal" (adjective). Fix the wrong part of speech and the whole sentence collapses. The forms in Gurbani carry signals that distinguish such roles.

Principle Three: Case and Relationship

Grammatical case expresses how a noun relates to the rest of the sentence. In English, "the disciple of the Guru" versus "the Guru of the disciple" reverse the relationship. Sahib Singh held that Gurbani's endings frequently mark these relationships directly.

AmbiguityGrammatical cluePayoff
One thing or many?Singular/plural endingCorrect referent count
Noun, verb, or adjective?Form of the wordCorrect sentence shape
Who relates to whom?Case markingCorrect relationships

How a Decision Gets Made

A reader meets a line with more than one possible meaning. Instead of choosing by intuition or a remembered story, the reader asks what the grammatical forms allow, sets aside readings incompatible with the forms, then weighs context among what remains. The grammar does not always force a single answer, but it reliably rules out unsupported readings, which is itself a major gain.

The Discipline Behind It

What makes this more than guesswork is consistency: the same signal is read the same way wherever it appears. This is why he paired interpretation with a full grammar (Singh, Gurbani Viakaran).

References: Singh, Sahib, Gurbani Viakaran; Singh, Sahib, Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan.

Homework

Find one example — from the Darpan, from secondary scholarship, or from your own reading — where grammatical analysis of a Gurbani line produces a meaning that differs significantly from a popular or traditional interpretation. Describe the line, the popular reading, and Prof. Sahib Singh's grammatical reading in 300 words. Reflect on how you personally navigate the tension between a technically rigorous reading and a devotionally received one.

lessons.title: Influence and Scholarly Discussion
lessons.summary: Presents the scope of Sahib Singh's influence alongside neutral scholarly questions about his method, how defenders respond, and the mature student's balanced stance of rigor with humility.
lessons.html:
A Method Debated, Not Frozen

A sign of an important scholar is that serious people engage the work seriously, including by questioning it. His method has been enormously influential and has also drawn thoughtful discussion (Singh and Fenech 2014).

The Scope of His Influence

His grammatical approach reshaped how a great many Sikhs read Gurbani. It influenced later commentators, teachers of ਕਥਾ (discourse), translators, and academic scholars. The idea that the ਲਗਾਂ ਮਾਤਰਾਂ (vowel-signs) carry grammatical meaning became, for many, a default starting assumption.

Points of Scholarly Discussion

Question raisedThe concern, stated neutrally
How fully systematic?The Granth's language spans centuries, regions, and voices, so one rigid system may not apply uniformly (Mann 2001).
Grammar vs. poetry and musicGurbani is sung in ਰਾਗ (musical mode); metrical and poetic factors may also shape word-forms.
Over-systematizingA powerful method can tempt interpreters to force every line into the system.
Relation to earlier traditionsHow to weigh long-standing community understanding against grammatical analysis.

How Defenders Respond

Those who champion the method reply that its consistency is its strength, that it reduces arbitrary readings, and that Sahib Singh attended to context rather than being mechanically rigid. Even where one disagrees with a reading, the method gives a shared basis for the disagreement.

The Mature Student's Stance

The aim is not to undermine his work but to model how to hold it. A mature student treats the grammatical method as an indispensable, clarifying tool, while remembering that scripture is rich, that poetry and music matter, and that reverent humility belongs alongside rigor. He gave the community a better way to argue about the words; honoring him includes continuing that careful conversation (Singh and Fenech 2014).

  • Use grammar to rule out unsupported readings.
  • Respect poetry, music, and inherited understanding.
  • State honest uncertainty where genuine ambiguity remains.
References: Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds., The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies (Oxford, 2014); Mann, Gurinder Singh, The Making of Sikh Scripture (Oxford, 2001).

Homework

Research one other major Gurbani scholar or commentator — such as Bhai Vir Singh, Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha, Giani Harbans Singh, or a contemporary academic — and compare their interpretive approach to Prof. Sahib Singh's grammar-first method. Write 300 words identifying at least two specific differences in method or emphasis, and reflect on what each approach offers that the other may not.

lessons.title: Gurbani Viakaran: The Grammar Primer and Its Pedagogy
lessons.html:
Table of Contents

  1. Introduction: Why a Grammar Primer?
  2. The Architecture of the Viakaran
  3. Key Grammatical Categories and Their Theological Stakes
  4. Pedagogy and the Ideal Student
  5. Key Terms
  6. Discussion Questions
  7. Further Reading

Keywords

Term (Unicode)Academic Context
ਵਿਆਕਰਣGrammar; the systematic study of language rules as applied to Gurbani.
ਕਾਰਕGrammatical case; the relational category that determines how a noun functions in a sentence.
ਸੰਬੋਧਨThe vocative case; direct address, theologically significant in devotional poetry.
ਮੁਕਤਾA vowel marker in Gurmukhi indicating the inherent 'a' sound; often misread in recitation.
ਪਦ-ਛੇਦWord-division; the parsing of continuous Gurmukhi script into discrete grammatical units.
ਧਾਤੂVerbal root; the base form of a verb from which conjugations derive.

Introduction: Why a Grammar Primer?

When Prof. Sahib Singh completed the ten volumes of the Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan, he recognized that his exegetical conclusions were only as useful as his readers' capacity to follow his reasoning. A commentary that resolves grammatical questions presupposes a reader who understands why grammar is in question in the first place. This recognition led him to produce the Gurbani Viakaran — a dedicated grammatical primer designed specifically for learners approaching the ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ as a linguistic text, not merely as a devotional object to be reverently recited.

The Viakaran is not a general Punjabi grammar. It is tailored entirely to the linguistic features that appear in Gurbani, drawing on early modern Punjabi, Braj Bhasha, Sanskrit, Persian, and Arabic elements that are woven into the scriptural text. Prof. Sahib Singh understood that a student equipped with general Punjabi grammar might still be helpless before a ਸ਼ਬਦ (shabad) composed in the idiom of fifteenth-century Braj or in the specialized theological vocabulary of Persian Sufi poetry. The Viakaran therefore teaches grammar contextually, always returning to scriptural examples.

This lecture examines the Gurbani Viakaran as both a pedagogical document and a theological statement. The choices Prof. Sahib Singh made about what to include, what to emphasize, and how to sequence the material reveal his understanding of what makes Gurbani difficult and what resources the student needs to meet that difficulty. In doing so, it also illuminates the broader scholarly project that the Darpan represents.

Students should approach this lecture with a copy of the Viakaran if possible. Reading the primary text alongside this analysis is essential for fully appreciating the methodological decisions that will be discussed. Where direct comparison with the Darpan is made, students are encouraged to cross-reference entries from both works to see how the grammar primer and the commentary function as a unified scholarly project (Sahib Singh, Gurbani Viakaran, 1939).

The Architecture of the Viakaran

The Gurbani Viakaran opens with a statement of purpose that is worth reading carefully. Prof. Sahib Singh does not frame grammar as an end in itself. He frames it as a form of service — ਸੇਵਾ — to the Guru's Word. The scholar who learns grammar is equipping himself to hear what the Guru actually said, rather than what tradition, sentiment, or casual recitation has led him to assume was said. This framing places the Viakaran squarely within the Sikh devotional tradition: it is an act of ਸ਼ਰਧਾ (shardha, reverence) expressed through intellectual discipline.

The primer proceeds through the major grammatical categories of Punjabi in a sequence designed for cumulative learning. It begins with the alphabet and phonology, emphasizing the precise sound values of Gurmukhi characters that are most frequently mispronounced in recitation. From there it moves to vowel markers, then to the noun system and its cases, then to verbs and their conjugations, and finally to syntax and the larger patterns of sentence construction. This sequence mirrors classical Sanskrit grammatical pedagogy, suggesting that Prof. Sahib Singh was conversant with the tradition of Paninian grammar even as he adapted it to a very different linguistic context (Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab, 1990).

One of the Viakaran's most important structural choices is its integration of scriptural examples at every stage. When Prof. Sahib Singh explains the ਕਾਰਕ (karak, case) system, he does not use invented examples. He draws directly from Gurbani, showing how lines from specific ਅੰਗ (ang, pages) of the ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ illustrate each grammatical category. This approach has a dual pedagogical effect: students learn grammar through Gurbani, and they simultaneously begin to develop the habit of reading Gurbani grammatically. The two forms of learning reinforce each other from the earliest stages.

The Viakaran also includes sections on the specific linguistic registers present in Gurbani. This is particularly significant given the multilingual character of the ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ, which contains compositions not only in early Punjabi but also in Braj Bhasha, Sindhi, Persian, Arabic, and several regional dialects. Prof. Sahib Singh addresses each of these registers with tailored grammatical notes, helping the student identify which linguistic conventions apply to any given passage. This feature alone makes the Viakaran an indispensable companion to serious Gurbani study (McLeod, Textual Sources for the Study of Sikhism, 1984).

Key Grammatical Categories and Their Theological Stakes

Not all grammatical categories are theologically neutral. In Gurbani, the choice of grammatical construction can determine whether a line is understood as a description, a command, a prayer, or an assertion — and these distinctions have profound consequences for how the teaching is received. Prof. Sahib Singh understood this with unusual clarity, and the Viakaran reflects sustained attention to the categories where grammatical analysis most significantly affects theological interpretation.

The vocative case — ਸੰਬੋਧਨ (sambodhana) — is perhaps the most theologically loaded category in devotional poetry. When a poet addresses the Divine directly, the grammatical form changes, and with it the entire relational register of the utterance. In Gurbani, the vocative is used with extraordinary frequency and subtlety. Prof. Sahib Singh's treatment of the vocative in the Viakaran is extensive, carefully distinguishing between vocatives addressed to the Divine, to the self (the poet addressing his own mind — ਮਨ), to the congregation (ਸੰਗਤ), and to the disciple. Misreading the vocative can turn a prayer into a statement, or an instruction to the self into a doctrine about others (Mandair, Religion and the Specter of the West, 2009).

Verbal tense and aspect present another theologically rich area of grammatical analysis. The ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ contains passages where the tense could be read as past, present, or timeless, and this ambiguity is not always accidental. The Gurus frequently used verbal forms that oscillate between historical narrative and eternal truth — describing the grace of the Divine in terms that apply simultaneously to a specific devotee in the past and to every devotee in the present. Prof. Sahib Singh's grammar primer carefully explains these verbal categories and illustrates how recognizing them prevents students from over-historicizing passages that are meant to be received as perpetually applicable teachings.

The gender system in Punjabi has also generated significant interpretive variation in Gurbani study. Because Punjabi grammatical gender does not always align with natural gender, and because Gurbani uses gender metaphorically in several extended passages — particularly in the tradition of the ਬਾਰਹ ਮਾਹਾ (Barah Maha, twelve-month poems) and the ਸੁਹਾਗਣਿ (Suhaagan, the blessed bride) metaphors — misreading grammatical gender can lead to theologically misleading conclusions. The Viakaran addresses these passages directly, providing grammatical grounding for readings that might otherwise seem arbitrary or culturally contingent (Kapur Singh, Parasharaprasna, 1959).

The ਪਦ-ਛੇਦ (pad-chhed), or word-division practice, is another area where the Viakaran makes a distinctive contribution. In Gurbani manuscripts and early printed editions, continuous script sometimes makes it difficult to determine where one word ends and another begins. Different word divisions can produce entirely different meanings. Prof. Sahib Singh systematically addresses the most contested instances of pad-chhed, using grammatical reasoning to determine the most defensible reading. His decisions in this area have been influential — though not universally accepted — and remain a reference point for subsequent scholars.

Pedagogy and the Ideal Student

The Gurbani Viakaran is not merely a reference tool. It is a pedagogical text with a vision of who its student is and what kind of learning it demands. Reading the Viakaran alongside the Darpan reveals a consistent understanding of what Prof. Sahib Singh believed a serious student of Gurbani needed to cultivate.

First, the ideal student must be willing to hold uncertainty. One of the most striking features of both the Viakaran and the Darpan is their willingness to acknowledge when multiple readings are grammatically possible, or when the evidence for a particular interpretation is strong but not conclusive. Prof. Sahib Singh does not present his conclusions as beyond question; he presents them as the best available reading given the grammatical evidence. This epistemic humility is itself a pedagogical model — the student learns not only the answers but the appropriate attitude toward the limits of knowledge (Barrier and Dusenbery, eds., The Sikh Diaspora, 1989).

Second, the ideal student must be prepared for cumulative learning. The Viakaran is not a reference dictionary to be consulted casually. It is a structured course of study to be worked through from beginning to end, with each section building on what came before. Prof. Sahib Singh's own life — he taught at Khalsa College for decades and spent evenings and holidays on the Darpan — models this commitment to sustained, patient scholarship as a form of spiritual discipline.

Third, and perhaps most importantly, the ideal student must hold grammar and devotion in productive tension. The danger of grammatical study is that it can create a distancing effect — the reader becomes an analyst rather than a devotee. Prof. Sahib Singh consistently resisted this outcome. In the Viakaran, grammatical analysis is always in service of deeper devotional understanding. The goal is not to reduce Gurbani to linguistic data but to clear away the misreadings that prevent the student from hearing what the Guru actually said. Grammar, in his pedagogy, is a form of listening.

This understanding connects the Viakaran to the broader tradition of ਗੁਰਮਤਿ (Gurmat, Guru's teaching) as it was developed in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, particularly through the Nirmala tradition's engagement with Sanskrit grammatical learning. Prof. Sahib Singh was not inventing a new approach; he was refining and applying a method that had deep roots in Sikh scholarly culture, and making it accessible to the educated Punjabi reader of the twentieth century (Oberoi, The Construction of Religious Boundaries, 1994).

Key Terms

  • ਵਿਆਕਰਣ — Grammar; the systematic analysis of language rules, here applied specifically to the multilingual text of the ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ.
  • ਕਾਰਕ — Grammatical case; the category indicating the syntactic role of a noun phrase, with theological implications for how devotional passages are understood.
  • ਸੰਬੋਧਨ ਕਾਰਕ — Vocative case; the form used in direct address, critically important in devotional poetry where the poet addresses the Divine, the self, or the congregation.
  • ਧਾਤੂ — Verbal root; the base from which all conjugated forms derive, essential for identifying the precise action or state described in a line of Gurbani.
  • ਪਦ-ਛੇਦ — Word-division; the practice of parsing continuous script into discrete units, with significant consequences for meaning in contested passages.
  • ਅੰਗ — Page of the ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ; the standard unit of reference in Gurbani citation.

Discussion Questions

  1. Prof. Sahib Singh framed the Gurbani Viakaran as an act of ਸੇਵਾ (seva, service). In what ways does grammatical scholarship qualify as a form of devotional service? Where might this framing be contested?
  2. The Viakaran integrates scriptural examples into grammatical instruction at every stage. What are the pedagogical advantages of this approach? What risks might arise from treating sacred text as grammatical illustration?
  3. Prof. Sahib Singh's treatment of the vocative case — ਸੰਬੋਧਨ — is extensive and theologically significant. Why might the distinction between self-address, divine address, and congregational address matter so much in a devotional context?
  4. The ideal student imagined by the Viakaran must hold grammar and devotion in tension without letting either collapse into the other. Do you find this balance achievable in practice? What personal experience — of Gurbani, of scripture study, or of sacred text in any tradition — informs your answer?
  5. How does the Viakaran's treatment of multilingual registers in Gurbani (Punjabi, Braj, Persian, Sanskrit) compare with how contemporary translation projects approach the same challenge? What does each approach preserve or lose?

Further Reading

  • Sahib Singh, Gurbani Viakaran (Amritsar: Singh Brothers, 1939) — the primary text; read alongside the Darpan for full context.
  • W. H. McLeod, Textual Sources for the Study of Sikhism (Manchester: Manchester University Press, 1984) — provides background on the multilingual character of the scriptural text.
  • Arvind Mandair, Religion and the Specter of the West: Sikhism, India, Postcoloniality, and the Politics of Translation (New York: Columbia University Press, 2009) — examines the broader politics of interpretation and translation in the Sikh tradition.
  • J. S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1990) — contextualizes the scholarly tradition within which Prof. Sahib Singh worked.
  • Key Takeaways
  • The Gurbani Viakaran is not a general Punjabi grammar but a purpose-built pedagogical tool for Gurbani study, integrating scriptural examples throughout.
  • Prof. Sahib Singh's treatment of the vocative case, verbal aspect, grammatical gender, and word-division reflects sustained attention to the categories where grammar most significantly affects theological interpretation.
  • The Viakaran models a pedagogy of epistemic humility — presenting conclusions as the best available reading rather than definitive truth.
  • The ideal student of the Viakaran holds grammar and devotion in productive tension, using linguistic precision to deepen rather than distance devotional understanding.
  • The Viakaran and the Darpan function as a unified scholarly project and are best studied together.

Homework

Obtain a copy of the Gurbani Viakaran (in print or digitized form) and spend 30 minutes working through the section on ਕਾਰਕ (grammatical cases). Identify one line of Gurbani where recognizing the case construction changes your understanding of the meaning. Write 250 words describing what you found and how this grammatical category functions as a tool for devotional clarity rather than mere academic analysis.

lessons.title: The Multilingual World of Gurbani: Navigating Multiple Languages
lessons.html:
Table of Contents

  1. Introduction: A Scripture Without a Single Language
  2. The Languages of Gurbani and Their Scholarly Challenges
  3. Prof. Sahib Singh's Multilingual Method
  4. Case Studies in Cross-Linguistic Interpretation
  5. Key Terms
  6. Discussion Questions
  7. Further Reading

Keywords

Term (Unicode)Academic Context
ਬ੍ਰਜ ਭਾਸ਼ਾBraj Bhasha; a literary dialect of Hindi widely used in devotional poetry across north India.
ਸਾਧ ਭਾਸ਼ਾSadh Bhasha; the composite devotional register used by the Sants and Bhagats whose compositions appear in Gurbani.
ਅਰਬੀArabic; present in Gurbani particularly in Islamic theological terminology.
ਫ਼ਾਰਸੀPersian; present in Gurbani through Sufi poetic vocabulary and administrative language.
ਤਤਸਮTatsama; Sanskrit loanwords retained in their original form within Punjabi or Braj.
ਰਾਗMusical mode; each shabad in the Guru Granth Sahib is assigned to a specific raga, which also carries linguistic and devotional associations.

Introduction: A Scripture Without a Single Language

The ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ is, among other things, a remarkable linguistic document. Its 1,430 ਅੰਗ (ang) contain compositions in early Punjabi, Braj Bhasha, Khariboli, Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic, Sindhi, and several regional dialects associated with the Bhagats whose compositions were incorporated into the scripture by Guru Arjan Dev Ji during the compilation of the Adi Granth in 1604. For any reader approaching the text expecting a single, consistent linguistic register, this diversity can be genuinely disorienting. For a commentator like Prof. Sahib Singh who sought to provide grammatically grounded readings of every passage, it represented a formidable scholarly challenge.

This lecture examines how Prof. Sahib Singh navigated the multilingual character of Gurbani in both the Darpan and the Viakaran. It asks what tools he brought to this task, how he distinguished between linguistic registers, and where his approach revealed its greatest strengths and its most significant limitations. It also situates his multilingual scholarship within the broader history of Gurbani exegesis, where different commentators have handled the same problem in strikingly different ways.

Understanding the multilingual landscape of Gurbani is not merely a matter of scholarly curiosity. It bears directly on the question of what Gurbani means — and by extension, on what Sikhi teaches about the Divine, the self, and the path of liberation (ਮੁਕਤੀ). When a single word can carry different meanings depending on whether it is read as Sanskrit, Braj, or Punjabi, the choice of linguistic frame is also a theological choice.

Students approaching this lecture should be aware that fluency in all of Gurbani's languages is not expected or required. What is required is an understanding of why the linguistic diversity matters, how Prof. Sahib Singh approached it, and what the consequences of different linguistic readings are for the interpretation of specific passages (McLeod, Textual Sources for the Study of Sikhism, 1984).

The Languages of Gurbani and Their Scholarly Challenges

The dominant language of the Sikh Gurus' own compositions is a form of early Punjabi that linguists sometimes call Old Punjabi or Medieval Punjabi. This language differs significantly from modern standard Punjabi in vocabulary, grammar, and phonology. Words that appear familiar to a modern Punjabi reader may carry different meanings in their medieval forms; grammatical constructions that have disappeared from contemporary usage appear with high frequency in Gurbani. Prof. Sahib Singh, trained in classical Punjabi scholarship and deeply familiar with historical Punjabi literature, was well equipped to navigate these diachronic differences.

Braj Bhasha presents a different set of challenges. This literary dialect of medieval Hindi was the prestige language of devotional poetry across north India from roughly the fourteenth to the eighteenth centuries. Many of the Bhagats whose compositions appear in the ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ — including Kabir Ji, Ravidas Ji, Namdev Ji, and Trilochan Ji — composed primarily in Braj. A reader trained only in Punjabi grammar will misread these compositions if they attempt to apply Punjabi grammatical rules to Braj constructions. Prof. Sahib Singh addresses this problem directly in the Viakaran, providing separate notes on Braj grammar and illustrating how Braj constructions appear in the scriptural text (Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab, 1990).

The Persian and Arabic elements in Gurbani reflect the deep engagement of the Sikh Gurus with the Islamicate world of Mughal India. Guru Nanak Dev Ji's compositions in the Bani include Persian and Arabic theological vocabulary — terms like ਖ਼ੁਦਾ (Khuda), ਅੱਲਾਹ (Allah), ਸ਼ਰਾ (Shara), ਇਬਾਦਤ (Ibadat) — which carry specific religious meanings in Islamic theology. A reader unfamiliar with these traditions might misread these terms as ornamental borrowings rather than as deliberate theological engagements. Prof. Sahib Singh was not a specialist in Persian or Arabic, but he brought careful attention to these terms and generally provided accurate contextual explanations of their theological weight (Mandair, Religion and the Specter of the West, 2009).

Sanskrit appears in Gurbani both as direct borrowings (ਤਤਸਮ, tatsama) and as older loan adaptations (ਤਦਭਵ, tadbhava). The Nirmala scholars who preceded Prof. Sahib Singh were particularly attentive to Sanskrit roots and often used Sanskrit etymology to resolve interpretive questions. Prof. Sahib Singh drew on this tradition selectively, accepting Sanskrit etymological reasoning where it shed genuine light on meaning while resisting the tendency — which he saw in some Nirmala commentaries — to over-Sanskritize Gurbani and assimilate it to the Brahmanical philosophical tradition.

Prof. Sahib Singh's Multilingual Method

Prof. Sahib Singh's approach to the multilingual character of Gurbani can be summarized in three principles that are visible throughout both the Viakaran and the Darpan.

The first principle is linguistic identification before interpretation. When approaching a line of Gurbani, Prof. Sahib Singh begins by identifying which linguistic register is operative. Is this Punjabi, Braj, Persian, or a mixed register? This identification determines which grammatical rules apply and which vocabulary sources are relevant. This sounds straightforward, but in practice it requires both linguistic knowledge and scholarly judgment, since Gurbani's languages blend and overlap in ways that resist rigid categorization.

The second principle is contextual semantics over etymological priority. When a word has different meanings in different languages, Prof. Sahib Singh does not automatically privilege the Sanskrit or Persian etymology. He asks what meaning fits the context of the shabad — its theological argument, its grammatical structure, its position within the larger composition. This contextual approach places him in productive tension with the more etymology-driven readings of Nirmala scholars and with the more experiential readings of oral traditions (Kapur Singh, Parasharaprasna, 1959).

The third principle is transparency about uncertainty. Throughout the Darpan, Prof. Sahib Singh acknowledges when a multilingual passage resists definitive reading — when the linguistic evidence supports multiple interpretations and the choice between them involves a degree of scholarly judgment that goes beyond what the text alone can settle. This transparency is both intellectually honest and pedagogically valuable: it invites the student into the interpretive process rather than presenting conclusions as beyond question.

These three principles together constitute what might be called a disciplined hermeneutic of linguistic humility. Prof. Sahib Singh does not pretend that the multilingual character of Gurbani can be fully resolved by any single scholarly method. He equips the student to navigate this complexity with the best available tools while remaining honest about the limits of those tools (Barrier and Dusenbery, eds., The Sikh Diaspora, 1989).

Case Studies in Cross-Linguistic Interpretation

Several specific passages in the ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ illustrate the stakes of multilingual interpretation in particularly vivid ways. Without inventing or misquoting specific Gurbani, we can identify the types of passages where Prof. Sahib Singh's multilingual method produces readings that differ significantly from earlier commentaries.

First, compositions of Bhagat Kabir Ji present some of the most challenging multilingual readings in the entire scripture. Kabir Ji's Braj compositions frequently employ vocabulary that had different meanings in his Varanasi context than similar-sounding Punjabi words have for modern readers. Prof. Sahib Singh's careful Braj analysis prevents several popular misreadings that arise from imposing Punjabi grammatical rules on Braj constructions.

Second, the ਸਾਧ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ (Sadh Bhasha) compositions — a composite register used by multiple Bhagats — present hybrid linguistic situations where Punjabi, Braj, and Sanskrit elements are simultaneously active. Prof. Sahib Singh's identification of which element governs a particular construction in any given line is one of the Darpan's most technically demanding and valuable contributions.

Third, the Persian-inflected vocabulary in several ਸ਼ਬਦ (shabad) of Guru Nanak Dev Ji at the beginning of the scripture — particularly those compositions that engage directly with Islamic theological concepts — requires familiarity with Sufi poetic tradition as well as standard Punjabi grammar. Prof. Sahib Singh's readings of these passages reflect his awareness of the Islamic theological context while maintaining Sikh theological priorities (Oberoi, The Construction of Religious Boundaries, 1994).

What these case studies reveal is that multilingual interpretation is not merely a technical problem. It is a hermeneutical and theological decision. When Prof. Sahib Singh chooses to read a contested word as Punjabi rather than Braj, or as Persian rather than Sanskrit, he is making a choice about how to understand the Guru's meaning — and by extension, about what the Guru was teaching. This is precisely why the multilingual dimension of Gurbani is not a peripheral concern for scholars but a central one.

Key Terms

  • ਬ੍ਰਜ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ — Braj Bhasha; the devotional literary dialect of medieval north India in which several Bhagats composed, requiring distinct grammatical rules from Punjabi.
  • ਸਾਧ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ — Sadh Bhasha; the composite devotional register characteristic of the Sant tradition, blending Punjabi, Braj, and Sanskrit elements.
  • ਅਰਬੀ — Arabic; present in Gurbani through Islamic theological vocabulary engaged by the Gurus in cross-religious dialogue.
  • ਫ਼ਾਰਸੀ — Persian; the prestige language of Mughal administration and Sufi poetry, engaged extensively by Guru Nanak Dev Ji.
  • ਤਤਸਮ — Tatsama; Sanskrit borrowings retained in their original form, requiring familiarity with Sanskrit grammar and philosophy to interpret accurately.
  • ਤਦਭਵ — Tadbhava; words derived from Sanskrit but phonologically adapted into Punjabi or Braj, sometimes creating new meanings distinct from their Sanskrit origins.

Discussion Questions

  1. Prof. Sahib Singh identifies which linguistic register governs a passage before applying grammatical rules. What risks arise when a commentator fails to make this identification first? Can you think of a reading from any tradition that seems to have gone wrong through this kind of linguistic misidentification?
  2. The presence of Persian and Arabic theological vocabulary in Gurbani reflects the Gurus' deep engagement with the Islamicate world of Mughal India. What does it mean for a religious scripture to contain the theological vocabulary of another tradition? How should a commentator handle such vocabulary?
  3. Prof. Sahib Singh resisted the Nirmala tendency to over-Sanskritize Gurbani. What is at stake — theologically and culturally — in this resistance? Is it possible to use Sanskrit etymology in Gurbani study without assimilating Gurbani to the Brahmanical tradition?
  4. The principle of contextual semantics over etymological priority means that Prof. Sahib Singh sometimes rejects a historically older meaning in favor of one that fits the context better. What are the methodological strengths and risks of this approach?
  5. If you were to study Gurbani in its original languages, which register would you prioritize first — early Punjabi, Braj, Persian, or Sanskrit — and why? What does your answer reveal about your understanding of Gurbani's primary audience and purpose?

Further Reading

  • W. H. McLeod, Textual Sources for the Study of Sikhism (Manchester: Manchester University Press, 1984) — essential background on the linguistic diversity of the Sikh scriptural text.
  • J. S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1990) — situates the Gurus' multilingual creativity within the cultural world of medieval Punjab.
  • Arvind Mandair, Religion and the Specter of the West (New York: Columbia University Press, 2009) — examines how translation and interpretation of Gurbani's multilingual character intersect with modern politics of religious identity.
  • Kapur Singh, Parasharaprasna (Amritsar: Sikh Publishing House, 1959) — a sophisticated engagement with the philosophical dimensions of Gurbani interpretation by a major twentieth-century Sikh thinker.
  • Key Takeaways
  • The ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ contains compositions in multiple languages — early Punjabi, Braj Bhasha, Persian, Arabic, Sanskrit, and regional dialects — each requiring distinct grammatical and contextual knowledge.
  • Prof. Sahib Singh's multilingual method rests on three principles: linguistic identification before interpretation, contextual semantics over etymological priority, and transparency about uncertainty.
  • The choice of linguistic frame in interpreting a contested word is also a theological choice with real consequences for how Gurbani's teaching is understood.
  • The Bhagat compositions present the most complex multilingual challenges in the scripture, requiring familiarity with Braj grammar and Sadh Bhasha conventions that differ significantly from Punjabi.
  • Prof. Sahib Singh's selective engagement with Sanskrit and Persian etymology reflects a deliberate methodological choice to resist assimilating Gurbani to other theological traditions.

Homework

Select a ਸ਼ਬਦ (shabad) from the Bhagat Bani section of the ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ — one composed by Kabir Ji, Ravidas Ji, Namdev Ji, or another Bhagat. Spend 30 minutes researching the linguistic register of that composition (Braj Bhasha, Sadh Bhasha, or other) and how that register differs from standard Punjabi. Write 300 words on what you discovered and how recognizing the language changes your understanding of the shabad's meaning.

lessons.title: Prof. Sahib Singh in Dialogue: Contemporary Scholarly Responses
lessons.html:
Table of Contents

  1. Introduction: The Darpan as an Ongoing Conversation
  2. Scholarly Affirmations and the Grammar-First Consensus
  3. Critical Engagements: Where Scholars Have Pushed Back
  4. Prof. Sahib Singh and Western Academic Sikh Studies
  5. Key Terms
  6. Discussion Questions
  7. Further Reading

Keywords

Term (Unicode)Academic Context
ਟੀਕਾਕਾਰCommentator; one who produces a tika (exegetical commentary) on sacred text.
ਵਿਵਾਦScholarly debate or controversy; a disagreement among interpreters about a textual or theological question.
ਸੰਪਰਦਾਈ ਵਿਆਖਿਆSectarian interpretation; a reading shaped by the specific theological commitments of a jatha or samprada.
ਇਤਿਹਾਸਕ ਆਲੋਚਨਾHistorical criticism; the academic method of reading texts in their historical context.
ਨਿਰਪੱਖਤਾImpartiality; a scholarly ideal that Prof. Sahib Singh claimed and that critics have questioned in specific cases.
ਅਨੁਵਾਦTranslation; the rendering of Gurbani into another language or contemporary idiom.

Introduction: The Darpan as an Ongoing Conversation

No scholarly work of the scale and influence of the Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan can remain unchallenged. In the decades since its completion, Prof. Sahib Singh's exegetical conclusions have been affirmed, refined, criticized, and sometimes directly contested by subsequent scholars — both within the Sikh tradition and in Western academic Sikh studies. Understanding where scholars agree and where they disagree with the Darpan's readings is essential not only for assessing Prof. Sahib Singh's contribution but for understanding the larger question of how Gurbani interpretation works and what standards it should meet.

This lecture maps the major lines of scholarly engagement with Prof. Sahib Singh's work. It examines the areas of broad scholarly consensus that his grammar-first method has generated, the specific readings that have attracted the most substantive criticism, and the relationship between his approach and the methodologies of Western academic Sikh studies. In doing so, it invites students to develop their own informed position on the Darpan's strengths and limitations — not as critics seeking to diminish a landmark achievement, but as thoughtful readers of a living interpretive tradition.

Students should approach this lecture with the understanding that scholarly debate about Gurbani interpretation is not a sign of crisis or weakness in the tradition. It is a sign of intellectual health. A tradition that cannot discuss its own interpretive history honestly is not a tradition that can continue to learn from its scripture. Prof. Sahib Singh himself modeled this openness, regularly acknowledging where his own readings were uncertain and where he had revised earlier positions (Mandair, Religion and the Specter of the West, 2009).

The goal of this lecture is not to produce a definitive verdict on the Darpan but to equip students to read the secondary literature on Prof. Sahib Singh with sufficient context to assess it critically. This is itself a form of the grammatical and hermeneutical discipline that the Darpan and Viakaran model.

Scholarly Affirmations and the Grammar-First Consensus

Among Punjabi-speaking scholars of Gurbani, Prof. Sahib Singh's grammar-first methodology has achieved something close to consensus status. The principle that Gurbani should be interpreted through the internal linguistic evidence of the text — rather than through external mythological, ritual, or sectarian filters — is now broadly accepted across the major institutions of Sikh learning, from Punjabi University Patiala to the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee's own educational programs.

Several major Punjabi scholars have built explicitly on the foundation of the Darpan. Giani Harbans Singh's work on Gurbani grammar extended and refined several of Prof. Sahib Singh's analyses, particularly in the area of verb morphology and the treatment of Persian and Arabic loanwords. Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's Mahan Kosh — the monumental Punjabi encyclopedia that preceded the Darpan and that Prof. Sahib Singh used extensively — has come to be seen as a complementary resource: where the Mahan Kosh provides lexical and historical breadth, the Darpan provides grammatical depth and exegetical application (Barrier and Dusenbery, eds., The Sikh Diaspora, 1989).

The Sikh Rehat Maryada's interpretive framework, codified in 1945-1950 through a process in which Professor Sahib Singh's textual expertise was influential, reflects the grammar-first approach in its insistence on reading Gurbani as it is written rather than as supplemented by oral tradition or popular devotional practice. This institutional endorsement has given Prof. Sahib Singh's method a normative status within mainstream Sikh religious life that few individual scholars achieve.

Contemporary Punjabi-medium educational curricula at the secondary and university levels in Punjab draw heavily on the Darpan. Students preparing for examinations in Gurbani study are typically introduced to Prof. Sahib Singh's readings as authoritative reference points. This educational institutionalization represents the deepest form of scholarly influence: when a scholar's conclusions become the baseline from which all subsequent teaching departs, their work has achieved a foundational status that transcends any individual debate (Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab, 1990).

Critical Engagements: Where Scholars Have Pushed Back

Substantial scholarly criticism has focused on several specific aspects of Prof. Sahib Singh's work. These critiques deserve careful attention precisely because they arise from within the tradition of rigorous Gurbani scholarship and do not represent attacks on the project of grammatical exegesis as such.

The first area of significant critique concerns Prof. Sahib Singh's treatment of ਅਦਵੈਤ ਵੇਦਾਂਤ (Advaita Vedanta) philosophical language in Gurbani. Some scholars in the Nirmala tradition have argued that his deliberate resistance to Sanskritic and Vedantic readings led him in certain cases to underread the philosophical depth of passages that engage — even if critically — with classical Indian philosophical categories. The argument is not that Gurbani endorses Vedanta but that some compositions can only be fully understood if the reader recognizes the philosophical system being engaged and addressed (Kapur Singh, Parasharaprasna, 1959).

A second area of critique involves his readings of certain devotional metaphors, particularly the ਬਾਰਹ ਮਾਹਾ (Barah Maha, twelve-month poem) and the extended ਸੁਹਾਗਣਿ-ਵਿਛੋੜੀ (Suhaagan-Vichhori, united and separated bride) metaphor. Some scholars feel that Prof. Sahib Singh's emphasis on grammatical precision at times fails to do full justice to the aesthetic and experiential dimensions of these compositions — that an overly grammatical reading can reduce the affective power of passages that depend on ambiguity, multiplicity of meaning, and devotional resonance for their theological effect.

A third and more recent line of critique comes from scholars influenced by postcolonial theory and translation studies. Arvind Mandair, Harjot Oberoi, and others have pointed out that any act of exegesis is embedded in a specific historical and political context. Prof. Sahib Singh was writing in the period of late colonialism and early Indian independence, a moment when the definition of Sikh identity was being actively contested by different political, religious, and scholarly formations. His claim to neutral, grammar-based objectivity may underestimate the extent to which his method itself reflected specific cultural and political assumptions about what counts as legitimate interpretation (Oberoi, The Construction of Religious Boundaries, 1994).

This postcolonial critique does not necessarily invalidate the Darpan's conclusions, but it invites readers to ask: Whose concerns does this interpretation serve? What assumptions does this method carry? What is made visible and what is made invisible by a grammar-first approach? These are difficult but important questions that serious students of Gurbani interpretation must engage.

Prof. Sahib Singh and Western Academic Sikh Studies

Western academic Sikh studies — particularly as developed in British and North American universities since the 1970s — has engaged with Prof. Sahib Singh's work in complex ways. W. H. McLeod, the most influential Western academic scholar of Sikhism of the twentieth century, relied on the Darpan for textual reference while developing an approach to Sikh history and scripture that departed significantly from the framework of traditional Gurbani scholarship.
