He wrote grammars of Punjabi, studies of Sikh history, biographical dictionaries of Sikh scholars, and polemical texts on questions of religious practice and identity. Each of these works fed into and drew upon the others. The Mahan Kosh is best understood not as a standalone achievement but as the central node in a broader scholarly network: it is the work in which the terminological decisions, historical judgments, and methodological commitments developed across Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's career are most fully and systematically expressed (Fenech and McLeod, 2014).

The scholar-activist dimension of Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's work raises important questions for contemporary readers. How do we evaluate scholarship that is simultaneously motivated by a commitment to a living religious community and aspiring to objective scholarly standards? This tension is not unique to Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha — it characterizes much of the greatest religious scholarship across traditions. What distinguishes the best such scholarship is precisely what distinguishes the Mahan Kosh: transparency about the commitments that animate the work, rigorous engagement with evidence and sources, and a willingness to acknowledge complexity and controversy rather than smoothing them over. These qualities make the Mahan Kosh not merely a document of its historical moment but an enduring model of engaged Sikh scholarship.

  • Key Takeaways:
  • The Mahan Kosh was produced in the context of profound social, religious, and political pressure on the Sikh community during British colonial rule in Punjab.
  • The Singh Sabha movement provided the institutional context, intellectual networks, and reform agenda that shaped Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's scholarly project.
  • Colonial-era census practices and missionary activity made the systematic definition of Sikh identity both urgent and politically consequential.
  • Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha was a scholar-activist whose lexicographical work was inseparable from his commitment to Sikh distinctiveness and the defense of ਗੁਰਮਤਿ.
  • The Mahan Kosh synthesizes indigenous Sanskrit, Persian, and Arabic scholarly traditions with awareness of Western orientalist methods, producing a distinctively modern Sikh reference work.

Key Terms

  • ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ — The Singh Sabha reform movement, active from 1873 onward, dedicated to Sikh education, publication, and identity articulation in response to colonial pressures.
  • ਹਮ ਹਿੰਦੂ ਨਹੀਂ — "We are not Hindus," the title of Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's 1899 polemical tract asserting the independent identity of Sikhism.
  • ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ — The script associated with the Gurus, in which ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ is written and which became central to Sikh scholarly identity in the Singh Sabha era.
  • ਦਰਬਾਰੀ ਵਿਦਵਾਨ — A court scholar attached to a princely or royal court; the institutional role that gave Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha the resources to pursue large-scale scholarship.
  • ਖਾਲਸਾ — The initiated Sikh community, whose boundaries and defining practices became a major subject of Singh Sabha debate and definition.
  • ਪ੍ਰਿੰਟ ਕਲਚਰ — Print culture; the new public sphere created by Punjabi-language printing in the colonial era, which enabled mass circulation of scholarly and reform literature.

Discussion Questions

  1. How did the British colonial practice of religious census-taking change the stakes of scholarly work on Sikh identity? Can you think of contemporary parallels in which administrative categorization shapes religious self-definition?
  2. The Singh Sabha movement was internally divided between groups with different visions of Sikh identity. How do internal reform debates typically shape the scholarship that emerges from them? Is such scholarship stronger or weaker for being produced in the context of controversy?
  3. Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha is described as a "scholar-activist." What obligations and risks does activist scholarship entail? How might commitment to a community both enable and constrain scholarly objectivity?
  4. The printing press is described as a transformative technology for Sikh scholarly production. In what ways does the current digital environment parallel the challenges and opportunities of the colonial-era print revolution?
  5. Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha engaged critically with Western orientalist scholarship on Sikhism while also absorbing some of its methods. How should scholars from within a tradition engage with external scholarly interpretations of that tradition — especially interpretations they find flawed or biased?

Further Reading

  • Harjot Oberoi, The Construction of Religious Boundaries: Culture, Identity, and Diversity in the Sikh Tradition (University of Chicago Press, 1994) — a foundational study of how Sikh identity was defined and contested in the colonial period.
  • Arvind-pal Singh Mandair, Religion and the Specter of the West: Sikhism, India, Postcoloniality, and the Politics of Translation (Columbia University Press, 2013) — a sophisticated analysis of how colonial and postcolonial conditions shaped Sikh religious thought.
  • Norman G. Barrier, The Sikhs and Their Literature (Manohar, 1970) — an early but still valuable survey of Singh Sabha publications and their role in Sikh reform.
  • Louis E. Fenech and W. H. McLeod, Historical Dictionary of Sikhism, 3rd ed. (Rowman and Littlefield, 2014) — provides concise, reliable entries on figures, institutions, and events relevant to this lecture.

Homework

Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha published ਹਮ ਹਿੰਦੂ ਨਹੀਂ in 1899 to argue that Sikhs are not Hindus. Research the historical context of that publication — what specific events or debates in the 1890s made that argument urgent — and write a 400-word reflection on how identity assertions made in times of pressure can shape how a community understands itself for generations. Consider whether the Singh Sabha's definition of Sikh identity has been a source of strength, constraint, or both for contemporary Sikh communities.

lessons.title: Philology and the Mahan Kosh: Reading Gurbani Through Etymology and Textual Criticism
lessons.html:
Table of Contents

  1. Introduction
  2. What Is Philology and Why Does It Matter for Sikh Studies?
  3. The Grammatical and Etymological Method of the Mahan Kosh
  4. Navigating Loan Words, Variant Spellings, and Contested Meanings
  5. Key Terms
  6. Discussion Questions
  7. Further Reading

Keywords

Term (Unicode)Academic Context
ਵਿਆਕਰਣGrammar; the systematic study of linguistic structure, central to classical Indian and Sikh scholarly traditions.
ਸ਼ਬਦ-ਵਿਉਤਪੱਤੀEtymology; the historical origin and development of a word's form and meaning.
ਤੱਦਭਵWords derived from Sanskrit through phonological change into vernacular forms; a major category in classical Indian lexicography.
ਤਤਸਮSanskrit words borrowed directly into a vernacular without phonological alteration.
ਲਿਪੀScript; the writing system used to represent a language, here specifically Gurmukhi.
ਪਾਠ-ਭੇਦTextual variant; a difference in wording between manuscript copies of the same text.

Introduction

A lexicon is not simply a list of words and their meanings. At its most rigorous, a lexicographical work is an exercise in philology — the discipline of studying language through its historical development, its textual transmission, and its relationship to the social and intellectual worlds in which it was used. The Mahan Kosh (ਮਹਾਨ ਕੋਸ਼) is, among other things, a work of philology: it traces the historical origins of Punjabi and ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ vocabulary, notes variant spellings across manuscripts, distinguishes authentic usages from scribal errors or later innovations, and situates each term in a network of related meanings. Understanding the philological dimension of the Mahan Kosh is essential for using the work intelligently and for appreciating what distinguishes it from simpler word lists or glossaries.

The philological tradition that Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha drew upon was ancient and multifaceted. Classical Sanskrit grammar, systematized most famously by Panini (approximately fourth century BCE), provided a rigorous framework for analyzing linguistic structure, deriving word forms from roots, and classifying vocabulary by origin. This grammatical tradition was deeply embedded in the education of any learned person in northern India during the period of Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's formation. Alongside it, the Persian and Arabic lexicographical traditions provided models for encyclopedic organization and the treatment of loan words. Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha synthesized these resources with his own careful reading of Sikh primary texts.

This lecture explores the philological method of the Mahan Kosh in depth. We will examine how Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha approached the etymological analysis of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ vocabulary, how he handled the complex linguistic situation of Punjabi as a language drawing on Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic, and vernacular sources, and how he dealt with the practical challenges of variant spellings, manuscript discrepancies, and contested meanings. These are not merely technical questions: they bear directly on the interpretation of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ and on the theological claims that different usages can support or undermine.

For students of Sikh scripture and theology, the philological questions raised by the Mahan Kosh are intimately practical. When a ਸ਼ਬਦ in the ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ uses a term that can be understood in multiple ways, the question of which understanding is most historically and linguistically grounded is not merely academic: it determines how the teaching is received, applied, and transmitted. The philological work of the Mahan Kosh thus operates at the intersection of scholarship and devotion, providing tools for the most careful possible engagement with the Gurus' words.

What Is Philology and Why Does It Matter for Sikh Studies?

Philology, broadly defined, is the study of texts in their historical context, with particular attention to language, transmission, and interpretation. In the Indian context, the equivalent discipline — sometimes called ਵਿਆਕਰਣ in its narrower form, or ਨਿਰੁਕਤ in a broader sense — had ancient roots in the Vedic commentary tradition and was regarded as one of the six auxiliary sciences necessary for understanding sacred texts (Shackle, 2004).

For Sikh Studies, philology matters for several interconnected reasons. First, the language of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ is historically distant from contemporary Punjabi: compositions in the ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ span more than two centuries and draw on multiple regional languages and dialects, including Punjabi, Braj Bhasha, Sanskrit, Persian, and Arabic. Reading these texts accurately requires knowledge of historical linguistics and awareness of how meanings have shifted over time. Second, the ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ was compiled from compositions by multiple authors across different periods, meaning that the same term may carry different semantic nuances in different contexts — a fundamentally philological challenge.

Third, the manuscript tradition of Sikh texts introduces significant variation. Early copies of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ, produced by hand before the standardization achieved through print, show variant spellings, different word divisions, and occasional scribal errors. Determining the most authentic reading requires the methods of textual criticism, which is itself a branch of philology. Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha was acutely aware of these manuscript variations and engaged with them systematically in the Mahan Kosh, noting cases where different manuscripts supported different readings and offering his judgment about which reading was most defensible (Mandair, 2013).

Fourth, the theological interpretation of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ has long been contested, and many of those contests turn on philological questions. When early colonial-era scholars like Ernst Trumpp produced translations of the ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ, their interpretive choices — including their etymological derivations and their handling of Sanskrit loan words — were controversial precisely because they had theological implications. Trumpp's reading of certain ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ terms as reflecting a "nihilistic" theology was challenged by Sikh scholars, including Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha, who argued that Trumpp's philological errors produced theological distortions. The Mahan Kosh can be read in part as a sustained counter-argument: a philologically grounded demonstration of what ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ vocabulary actually means when analyzed carefully and in context.

Finally, philology matters for Sikh Studies because it provides a shared methodological language for dialogue between Sikh scholars and scholars from other traditions. The Mahan Kosh's philological rigour is precisely what has made it a resource not only for Sikh readers but for Western academics working in Sikh Studies and adjacent fields.

The Grammatical and Etymological Method of the Mahan Kosh

Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's approach to etymology in the Mahan Kosh reflects his training in Sanskrit grammatical theory, adapted for the specific linguistic situation of Punjabi and ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ. In classical Sanskrit grammar, every word is ideally derivable from a verbal root (ਧਾਤੂ) through a series of well-defined morphological processes. This model of word formation, systematized by Panini and elaborated by subsequent grammarians, gives the grammatical tradition its characteristic precision. Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha applied this framework — with appropriate modifications — to Punjabi vocabulary (Singh, Harbans, 1994).

The classical Indian lexicographical tradition distinguished between two broad categories of vocabulary in vernacular languages. ਤਤਸਮ words are those borrowed directly from Sanskrit without phonological change. ਤੱਦਭਵ words are those derived from Sanskrit through the regular phonological processes of Prakrit and Apabhramsha, and which therefore look different from their Sanskrit originals but can be traced back to them through regular sound correspondences. This distinction is important for ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ because the Gurus used both types of vocabulary, and understanding whether a given word is ਤਤਸਮ or ਤੱਦਭਵ can have implications for how it should be interpreted.

Beyond these Sanskrit-derived categories, Punjabi contains a substantial layer of vocabulary borrowed from Persian and Arabic through the centuries of Islamic cultural influence in the Punjab. Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha was scrupulous in identifying these loan words and tracing them to their Persian or Arabic origins. When the Gurus used terms drawn from the Sufi and Islamic devotional tradition, they were making specific communicative choices whose significance the Mahan Kosh helps to illuminate. The etymological entries in the Mahan Kosh also engage with semantic shift — the way in which the meaning of a word changes over time or varies across contexts — providing multiple definitions organized by the textual context in which each meaning is operative (Shackle, 2004).

One of the distinctive features of the Mahan Kosh's etymological method is its treatment of folk etymologies — popular but philologically unsupported explanations of word origins that had accumulated in the oral tradition and in earlier less rigorous reference works. Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha consistently identified and corrected folk etymologies, explaining what the philological evidence actually supported. This critical stance sometimes brought him into conflict with more traditionally oriented scholars who preferred the authority of commentarial tradition over etymological analysis.

Navigating Loan Words, Variant Spellings, and Contested Meanings

The linguistic complexity of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ creates practical challenges for any lexicographer. The ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ contains compositions in at least seven distinct languages and dialects, including Punjabi, Braj Bhasha, Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic, Sindhi, and various regional vernaculars. When a ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ term is borrowed from one of these languages into the Punjabi context of the rest of the composition, it brings with it a web of associations that the original audience would have recognized but that later readers may miss. The Mahan Kosh attempts to provide this web of associations systematically (Fenech and McLeod, 2014).

The challenge of loan words is particularly acute for Persian and Arabic vocabulary in ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ. These terms were not merely borrowed as labels for unfamiliar concepts; they were chosen because they carried specific connotations within the Sufi and Islamic devotional tradition that the Gurus wished to engage. When the Gurus used a term from Sufi poetry, they were often deliberately engaging with or reframing the Sufi understanding of that concept in light of ਗੁਰਮਤਿ. Understanding the original Sufi context of such terms is therefore essential for understanding the theological move the Guru is making, and Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's knowledge of Persian literature equipped him to do exactly this.

Variant spellings present a different kind of challenge. The ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ script, as used in early Sikh manuscript tradition, did not have standardized orthographic conventions for all phonemes. When Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha compiled the Mahan Kosh, he had to decide which spelling to use as the primary entry for a given term and how to cross-reference variant spellings. His choices reflected both philological judgment about historical usage and practical decisions about usefulness. The orthographic conventions of the Mahan Kosh have themselves influenced subsequent Punjabi spelling practices, giving the work a normative as well as a descriptive function.

Contested meanings — cases in which different scholarly or devotional traditions have understood the same term differently — are perhaps the most delicate challenge Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha faced as a lexicographer. Nirmalas, Udasis, adherents of various sects, and mainstream ਖਾਲਸਾ Sikhs sometimes read the same ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ terms through quite different interpretive lenses. Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's approach was to state clearly what he regarded as the most defensible meaning on philological grounds while acknowledging that other readings existed. This transparent acknowledgment of interpretive plurality, combined with a clear statement of his own considered judgment, is one of the scholarly virtues that makes the Mahan Kosh a model of responsible lexicography.

  • Key Takeaways:
  • Philology — the historical study of language and texts — is essential for accurate reading of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ, which spans multiple centuries and draws on several distinct languages.
  • Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's etymological method combined classical Sanskrit grammatical theory with awareness of Persian and Arabic lexicography and modern critical philology.
  • The distinction between ਤਤਸਮ and ਤੱਦਭਵ vocabulary is a key analytical tool the Mahan Kosh applies to Punjabi and ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ terms.
  • The Mahan Kosh consistently corrects folk etymologies in favor of philologically defensible accounts of word origins.
  • Contested meanings in the Mahan Kosh reveal the intersection of philological method and theological commitment, making the work both a scholarly resource and a document of Singh Sabha interpretive priorities.

Key Terms

  • ਵਿਆਕਰਣ — Grammar; in classical Indian tradition, the systematic analysis of linguistic structure, used in the Mahan Kosh as the basis for etymological analysis.
  • ਸ਼ਬਦ-ਵਿਉਤਪੱਤੀ — Etymology; the tracing of a word's historical origin and development, a central method of the Mahan Kosh.
  • ਧਾਤੂ — Verbal root; in Sanskrit grammatical theory, the minimal unit from which words are derived, used in the Mahan Kosh to analyze ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ vocabulary.
  • ਤੱਦਭਵ — Words derived from Sanskrit through vernacular phonological change, a major lexical category in the Mahan Kosh.
  • ਪਾਠ-ਭੇਦ — Textual variant; differences in wording between manuscript copies, systematically noted in the Mahan Kosh to establish the most authentic reading.
  • ਨਿਰੁਕਤ — The classical Indian science of etymological interpretation, one of the six Vedanga disciplines, which provided a model for philological work in the Sikh scholarly tradition.

Discussion Questions

  1. Why is it significant that the ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ contains vocabulary from multiple languages including Sanskrit, Persian, and Arabic? What does this linguistic diversity suggest about the Gurus' communicative intentions?
  2. Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha distinguished between philologically defensible etymologies and folk etymologies that were popular but historically unsupported. When, if ever, might a folk etymology have value even if it is historically inaccurate?
  3. How might the same ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ term be interpreted differently by a Nirmala scholar trained in Sanskrit Vedanta versus a ਖਾਲਸਾ Singh Sabha scholar? What methodological resources would each bring to the interpretive task?
  4. The Mahan Kosh has influenced Punjabi spelling conventions — that is, it has had a normative as well as a descriptive effect. Is this kind of normative influence appropriate for a scholarly reference work, or should dictionaries simply describe rather than prescribe?
  5. Given that Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's theological commitments shaped his interpretive choices, how should contemporary scholars use the Mahan Kosh when studying ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ? What critical tools or supplementary sources would you recommend?

Further Reading

  • Christopher Shackle and Arvind-pal Singh Mandair, eds., Teachings of the Sikh Gurus: Selections from the Sikh Scriptures (Routledge, 2005) — provides translated selections with attention to the linguistic complexity of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ vocabulary.
  • Pashaura Singh, The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority (Oxford University Press, 2000) — a detailed study of the compilation, textual tradition, and canonical status of the Sikh scripture.
  • W. H. McLeod, Textual Sources for the Study of Sikhism (University of Chicago Press, 1990) — a selection of primary sources with scholarly introductions that address philological issues in Sikh texts.
  • Louis Renou, Sanskrit Grammar (Motilal Banarsidass, 1996) — for students wishing to understand the Sanskrit grammatical tradition that informed Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's etymological method.

Homework

Choose one ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ term that appears in multiple compositions in the ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ — good options include ਹਉਮੈ, ਨਾਮ, ਸਬਦ, ਭਾਣਾ, or ਸੰਤੋਖ. Look that term up in the Mahan Kosh or a reliable Sikh dictionary, paying close attention to the etymology given. Then find two or three compositions in the ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ where the term appears and read the surrounding context carefully. Write a 350–400 word reflection on how the etymological account in the Mahan Kosh does or does not capture the full range of meaning the term carries in different ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ contexts.

lessons.title: The Orientalist Encounter: Trumpp, Macauliffe, and the Mahan Kosh as Counter-Orientalist Archive
lessons.html:
Table of Contents

  1. Introduction
  2. The Orientalist Project and Its Sikh Critics
  3. Max Arthur Macauliffe and the Question of Collaboration
  4. The Mahan Kosh as a Counter-Orientalist Archive
  5. Key Terms
  6. Discussion Questions
  7. Further Reading

Keywords

Term (Unicode)Academic Context
ਪ੍ਰਾਚ੍ਯਵਾਦOrientalism; the Western scholarly tradition of studying and representing Asian cultures, critiqued for embedded power asymmetries.
ਅਨੁਵਾਦTranslation; a practice that involves interpretive choices with significant theological and political implications.
ਗਿਆਨ-ਸ਼ਕਤੀKnowledge-power; the relationship between scholarly authority and political authority, relevant to colonial-era scholarship.
ਵਿਆਖਿਆCommentary or interpretation; the tradition of explaining ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ that the Mahan Kosh both contributed to and evaluated critically.
ਸਵੈਮਾਣSelf-respect or self-representation; the aspiration of indigenous scholars to represent their own tradition on their own terms.
ਮੂਲ-ਪਾਠOriginal text or source text; the primary textual authority from which translations and commentaries derive.

Introduction

The production of knowledge about Asian religions and cultures by European scholars — what the Palestinian-American critic Edward Said famously termed "Orientalism" — was one of the defining intellectual phenomena of the colonial era. Western scholars of Sikhism, from the early nineteenth century onward, produced grammars, translations, historical surveys, and encyclopedic accounts of the Sikh tradition that circulated widely in European and American academic circles and that shaped the terms in which Sikhism was understood — and misunderstood — by non-Sikh audiences. The most important of these works for our purposes are the translation of the ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ by Ernst Trumpp (1877) and the multi-volume account of Sikh religion and history by Max Arthur Macauliffe (1909). These works bookend the period during which Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha was developing the scholarly project that would culminate in the Mahan Kosh.

The relationship between Western orientalist scholarship and Sikh scholarly production is not one of simple opposition. Sikh scholars engaged with orientalist works critically, sometimes angrily, but they also learned from them — absorbing methodological approaches, responding to interpretive challenges they posed, and sometimes collaborating directly with Western scholars. Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's engagement with orientalist scholarship illustrates this complexity: he was sharply critical of Trumpp's errors and what he saw as Macauliffe's limitations, but he also shared some methodological commitments with the Western philological tradition that informed orientalist Indology.

This lecture examines the orientalist scholarship on Sikhism, Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's response to it, and the ways in which the Mahan Kosh can be read as a counter-orientalist archive — a systematic, indigenous-authored reference work designed to establish Sikh scholarly authority over the interpretation of Sikh texts and traditions. This framing does not reduce the Mahan Kosh to a polemical document; it is far more than that. But understanding its counter-orientalist dimension is essential for appreciating why it was needed, what it accomplished, and why it continues to matter.

The questions raised by this lecture connect to broader debates in postcolonial studies, religious studies, and the history of scholarship about who has the authority to define and represent a religious tradition. These are not merely historical questions: they are live issues in contemporary Sikh Studies, where debates about methodology, representation, and community authority continue to shape the field.

The Orientalist Project and Its Sikh Critics

Ernst Trumpp's translation of the ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ, published in 1877 under the auspices of the India Office in London, was a landmark in Western Indological scholarship — and a landmark in the history of Sikh criticism of that scholarship. Trumpp, a German philologist and Protestant missionary, approached the Sikh scripture with formidable linguistic training in Sanskrit, Arabic, and Persian but with a theological framework that was deeply hostile to what he found. His introduction described the ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ in dismissive terms, characterized its theology as "indistinct and hazy," and made numerous philological errors that Sikh scholars identified and challenged. The translation was rejected by the Sikh community with unusual unanimity (Fenech and McLeod, 2014).

The critique of Trumpp's translation was not merely emotional or communal. Sikh scholars who engaged with it carefully identified specific philological errors — cases where Trumpp had misread ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ script, misunderstood Punjabi grammar, or failed to recognize the Sufi and Bhakti context of particular ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ usages. These errors had theological consequences: because Trumpp's translations of key terms were wrong, his characterization of Sikh theology was also wrong. The methodological lesson Sikh scholars drew from this experience was that philological precision and theological literacy were inseparable (Mandair, 2013).

The other major strand of the orientalist critique came from what we might call the political economy of knowledge production. Trumpp's project was commissioned by the India Office — the British government's administrative body for India — and was intended to serve administrative as well as scholarly purposes. Understanding Sikh religion was, for the colonial administration, a matter of governance. This entanglement of scholarship with administration meant that orientalist works were not neutral scholarly productions but were embedded in relations of power that shaped what questions were asked, how texts were read, and which Sikh voices were consulted or ignored (Oberoi, 1994).

Sikh critics of orientalism were alert to this political dimension. They understood that the authority to define Sikhism — to say what Sikh texts meant, what Sikh history had been, and what the essential features of Sikh identity were — was not merely an intellectual matter but a political one. The Singh Sabha scholars' insistence on producing their own reference works, their own translations, and their own historical accounts was thus a claim to political as well as intellectual authority — an assertion that the Sikh community had the right and the competence to represent itself on its own terms.

It is important not to romanticize this counter-orientalist impulse or to imagine that Sikh scholars were simply correct where Western scholars were simply wrong. The Singh Sabha scholars' own scholarly production was shaped by the same colonial conditions that shaped orientalist scholarship; they absorbed some orientalist assumptions even as they challenged others. The most nuanced contemporary scholarship, represented by historians like Harjot Oberoi and Arvind-pal Mandair, takes both the genuine contributions of Singh Sabha scholarship and its political entanglements seriously.

Max Arthur Macauliffe and the Question of Collaboration

If Trumpp represents the hostile pole of the orientalist encounter with Sikhism, Max Arthur Macauliffe represents its more sympathetic but still problematic counterpart. Macauliffe was a British civil servant in Punjab who became deeply interested in Sikh religion and history, learned Punjabi and ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ, collaborated extensively with Sikh scholars and priests, and eventually produced a six-volume work, The Sikh Religion: Its Gurus, Sacred Writings and Authors, published in 1909. Unlike Trumpp, Macauliffe sought to present Sikhism sympathetically (Singh, Pashaura, 2000).

Macauliffe's collaboration with Sikh scholars raises the "question of collaboration" in its most pointed form. On one hand, his reliance on Sikh informants and advisors — including significant figures in the Singh Sabha movement — meant that his account of Sikhism was in many respects shaped by Singh Sabha interpretive priorities. On the other hand, Macauliffe retained editorial control, wrote for a Western audience, and framed Sikhism within categories drawn from comparative religion that were not indigenous to the Sikh tradition. The result is a work of genuine value that is simultaneously a product of unequal power relations between Western scholar and Sikh collaborators (Barrier, 1970).

Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's relationship to Macauliffe was complex. He contributed to and consulted on Macauliffe's project, and he regarded The Sikh Religion as a significant improvement on Trumpp. But he was also critical of Macauliffe's limitations — his dependence on English-language secondary sources for historical context, his occasional misreadings of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ, and the ways in which the framework of comparative religion distorted the presentation of Sikh thought. The Mahan Kosh can be read in part as an implicit correction of Macauliffe: providing the kind of rigorous, philologically grounded, and theologically informed account of Sikh vocabulary and history that Macauliffe's work aspired to but did not fully achieve.

The question of collaboration has broader implications for the history of Sikh Studies. Much of the Western academic study of Sikhism has relied, directly or indirectly, on Sikh scholarly resources — manuscript collections, oral traditions, the interpretive frameworks developed by scholars like Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha himself. This reliance is not always acknowledged. Recognizing the Mahan Kosh as a foundational resource for the entire field of Sikh Studies — not merely as a Punjabi-language work relevant only to Punjabi readers — is an important act of intellectual restitution.

The Mahan Kosh as a Counter-Orientalist Archive

The concept of an "archive" in postcolonial scholarship refers not merely to a collection of documents but to a system that determines what knowledge is preserved, organized, and made accessible, and thereby shapes what questions can be asked and what answers are possible. The Mahan Kosh functions as an archive in this sense: it determines what counts as authoritative Sikh knowledge, which sources are cited, which interpretations are presented as mainstream and which as marginal, and what methodological standards govern scholarly claims about Sikhism (Mandair, 2013).

As a counter-orientalist archive, the Mahan Kosh performs several functions. First, it establishes an indigenous scholarly standard for the interpretation of Sikh texts — a standard rooted in the philological and theological traditions of the Sikh community itself, rather than in the academic frameworks developed for the study of other religious traditions. When Western scholars of Sikhism argue about how to interpret a particular ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ term or how to understand a moment in Sikh history, they are, whether they know it or not, operating in a landscape that the Mahan Kosh has fundamentally shaped.

Second, the Mahan Kosh makes Sikh knowledge accessible to Sikh readers in a way that orientalist scholarship, written in European languages for European audiences, could not. By producing a comprehensive reference work in Punjabi-ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ, Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha democratized access to sophisticated Sikh scholarship. This democratic orientation is itself a counter-orientalist gesture: it asserts that the Sikh community, not external scholars, is the primary audience for Sikh knowledge.

Third, the Mahan Kosh reframes the relationship between indigenous and foreign scholarly traditions. Rather than simply rejecting Western orientalist methods, Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha selectively engaged with them — absorbing what was methodologically useful while rejecting the theological and political assumptions that distorted orientalist readings. This selective engagement is a sophisticated intellectual strategy: it avoids both the uncritical acceptance of foreign frameworks and the wholesale rejection of methodological innovations that could strengthen indigenous scholarship. The counter-orientalist function of the Mahan Kosh continues to be relevant in the contemporary field of Sikh Studies, where debates about methodology and community accountability remain live issues.

  • Key Takeaways:
  • Western orientalist scholarship on Sikhism, particularly the translations by Ernst Trumpp and the historical account by Max Arthur Macauliffe, provided an important context for and challenge to Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's scholarly project.
  • Trumpp's 1877 translation was widely rejected by Sikh scholars, who identified specific philological errors with significant theological consequences.
  • The Mahan Kosh functions as a counter-orientalist archive — a systematic, indigenous-authored reference work that established Sikh scholarly authority over the interpretation of Sikh texts.
  • Macauliffe's collaborative relationship with Sikh scholars illustrates the complexity of the encounter between Western and Sikh scholarship in the colonial era.
  • The methodological questions raised by the orientalist encounter — about who has authority to represent a religious tradition and by what methods — remain live issues in contemporary Sikh Studies.

Key Terms

  • ਪ੍ਰਾਚ੍ਯਵਾਦ — Orientalism; the study and representation of Asian cultures and religions by Western scholars, often critiqued for its embeddedness in colonial power relations.
  • ਅਨੁਵਾਦ — Translation; a practice that involves interpretive choices about meaning, framing, and audience, with significant implications for how a religious tradition is understood.
  • ਵਿਆਖਿਆ — Commentary or interpretation; the tradition of explaining ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ that is central to Sikh scholarly practice and that the Mahan Kosh both exemplifies and evaluates.
  • ਸਵੈਮਾਣ — Self-respect; the aspiration of indigenous scholars and communities to represent their own tradition in their own terms, rather than through externally imposed frameworks.
  • ਗਿਆਨ-ਸ਼ਕਤੀ — Knowledge-power; the way in which scholarly authority and political authority are intertwined in the production of colonial knowledge.
  • ਮੂਲ-ਪਾਠ — Source text; the original textual authority from which translations and commentaries are derived, whose integrity the Mahan Kosh is dedicated to establishing and defending.

Discussion Questions

  1. Why did Ernst Trumpp's translation of the ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ provoke such a strong negative reaction from the Sikh community? What does this reaction tell us about the stakes of philological accuracy in religious scholarship?
  2. Macauliffe collaborated extensively with Sikh scholars while retaining Western editorial control over his final work. What are the ethical obligations of a scholar who uses community knowledge and assistance? How should such collaborations be credited?
  3. The Mahan Kosh is described as a "counter-orientalist archive." In what sense is an encyclopedic dictionary also a political document? Can scholarly reference works ever be politically neutral?
  4. Contemporary Sikh Studies continues to debate the role of community accountability in academic scholarship. Should scholars who are members of a religious community have different obligations than those who are not?
  5. How might a contemporary Sikh scholar build on the counter-orientalist project of the Mahan Kosh to engage with current Western academic discourse about Sikhism? What would a twenty-first century version of this project look like?

Further Reading

  • Arvind-pal Singh Mandair, Religion and the Specter of the West: Sikhism, India, Postcoloniality, and the Politics of Translation (Columbia University Press, 2013) — the most sophisticated analysis of how colonial and postcolonial conditions have shaped the study and self-understanding of Sikhism.
  • Edward Said, Orientalism (Pantheon Books, 1978) — the foundational text of postcolonial critique of Western representations of Asian cultures, essential background for understanding the counter-orientalist dimension of the Mahan Kosh.
  • Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion: Its Gurus, Sacred Writings and Authors, 6 vols. (Oxford University Press, 1909) — to be read critically as a primary source in the history of Western Sikh Studies, noting both its achievements and its limitations.
  • Pashaura Singh and Louis E. Fenech, eds., The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies (Oxford University Press, 2014) — contains several chapters on the history of Sikh Studies as a scholarly field, including its orientalist and post-orientalist phases.

Homework

Read a selection from Macauliffe's The Sikh Religion (volume one is the most accessible starting point — the biographical account of Guru Nanak Dev Ji). As you read, keep two lists: one of claims or interpretations that seem accurate and consistent with what you have learned about Sikh tradition, and one of claims or framings that seem distorted or that reflect European cultural assumptions rather than Sikh ones. Write a 400-word reflection analyzing what your two lists reveal about the strengths and limitations of sympathetic outside scholarship on a religious tradition.

lessons.title: History and the Mahan Kosh: Sources, Methods, and the Limits of Sikh Historical Memory
lessons.html:
Table of Contents

  1. Introduction
  2. The Architecture of Sikh Historical Memory
  3. The Mahan Kosh as a Historical Source
  4. Evaluating Historical Claims in the Mahan Kosh
  5. Key Terms
  6. Discussion Questions
  7. Further Reading

Keywords

Term (Unicode)Academic Context
ਇਤਿਹਾਸHistory; both the past events themselves and the discipline of recording and interpreting them.
ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀHagiographical narratives of the life of Guru Nanak Dev Ji, combining historical memory with devotional elaboration.
ਗੁਰ-ਬਿਲਾਸA genre of Sikh hagiographical literature celebrating the deeds and glory of the Gurus, with varied historical reliability.
ਸ੍ਰੋਤ-ਆਲੋਚਨਾSource criticism; the critical evaluation of the reliability, context, and bias of historical sources.
ਪਰੰਪਰਾTradition; the transmission of knowledge, practice, and identity across generations within a community.
ਗੁਰਦੁਆਰਾThe Sikh place of worship and community gathering, whose historical foundation and associated traditions are often documented in the Mahan Kosh.

Introduction

History and lexicography might seem like quite different scholarly enterprises: one concerned with events unfolding through time, the other with the synchronic mapping of meaning. Yet in the Mahan Kosh (ਮਹਾਨ ਕੋਸ਼), these two enterprises are deeply intertwined. A substantial proportion of the entries in the Mahan Kosh are not definitions of abstract terms but historical accounts — of Sikh Gurus and their lives, of historical figures who interacted with the Sikh community, of Gurdwaras and their founding contexts, of historical events and their significance. These historical entries make the Mahan Kosh a major repository of Sikh historical knowledge, and they require us to evaluate it as a historical source with the same critical attention we bring to any work of historical scholarship.

Sikh historical memory is a rich and complex field. The community has preserved its history through multiple channels: formal historical chronicles (ਇਤਿਹਾਸਕ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ), hagiographical narratives (ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀਆਂ, ਗੁਰ-ਬਿਲਾਸ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ), oral traditions maintained by hereditary scholars and reciters, architectural memory encoded in the placement and design of historical Gurdwaras, and the interpretive layers added by successive generations of commentators and historians. Each of these channels preserves genuine historical knowledge but also introduces its own forms of elaboration, legend, and ideological shaping. The historian's task — and the task Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha set himself in the historical entries of the Mahan Kosh — is to distinguish what these sources reliably record from what they embellish or reshape in the light of later concerns.

This lecture examines the historical dimensions of the Mahan Kosh, focusing on three interconnected questions. First, what sources did Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha draw on for his historical entries, and how did he evaluate their reliability? Second, what does the Mahan Kosh contribute to our understanding of specific historical periods and events in Sikh history? And third, how should contemporary scholars evaluate the historical claims made in the Mahan Kosh, given both its documentary strengths and its interpretive commitments?

Understanding the Mahan Kosh as a historical source also illuminates broader methodological questions in the study of Sikh history. The field of Sikh historiography has been marked by significant debates — about the relationship between hagiographical and critical historical methods, about the role of community perspectives in scholarly historical writing, and about the proper use of oral tradition alongside written documentation. The Mahan Kosh occupies a central position in these debates: it is simultaneously a product of the pre-critical hagiographical tradition and a pioneer of the critical-historical approach to the Sikh past.

The Architecture of Sikh Historical Memory

To understand what the Mahan Kosh does with Sikh history, we must first understand the landscape of historical sources that Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha inherited. The oldest stratum of Sikh historical memory is embedded in ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ itself: the compositions of the Gurus often contain autobiographical elements, references to historical events and persons, and implicit or explicit responses to the social and political context of the Gurus' lives. These internal textual references are the most authoritative historical evidence for the Sikh tradition, but they are often allusive and require careful contextual interpretation (Singh, Pashaura, 2000).

The ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀ literature — narrative accounts of the life of Guru Nanak Dev Ji — represents the next major stratum of historical memory. These texts, of which several distinct recensions survive, were composed from the sixteenth through the eighteenth centuries and preserve a mixture of authentic historical memory, legendary elaboration, and didactic narrative shaped by the devotional concerns of the communities that produced them. The critical study of the Janam-sakhis — determining which episodes can be dated early and which are later accretions, which details are historically plausible and which are hagiographical conventions — is one of the central projects of modern Sikh historiography (McLeod, 1990).

The ਗੁਰ-ਬਿਲਾਸ literature, composed primarily in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, celebrates the lives and deeds of the Gurus with an emphasis on their military, political, and miraculous dimensions. These texts were produced in a specific historical context — the Sikh community's experience of political conflict and military organization in the late Guru period — and they reflect the concerns and values of that context. Nevertheless, they preserve important information about Sikh institutions, social organization, and historical memory that is not available from other sources. Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha engaged extensively with the ਗੁਰ-ਬਿਲਾਸ texts, citing them frequently in the Mahan Kosh while also noting where their historical claims were unsupported or implausible (Singh, Harbans, 1994).

The Persian-language sources — accounts by Mughal court historians and other Muslim writers who documented the Sikh community from the outside — constitute a fourth important stratum. These sources often provide independent confirmation of events recorded in Sikh sources, and they sometimes preserve information not available in the Sikh tradition itself. Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's knowledge of Persian allowed him to draw on these sources directly, making the Mahan Kosh unusual among Sikh reference works of its era in its systematic engagement with non-Sikh historical documentation.

Finally, the tradition of Sikh historiography that emerged in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries — represented by major works like Ratan Singh Bhangu's ਪ੍ਰਾਚੀਨ ਪੰਥ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ (1841) and Giani Gian Singh's ਪੰਥ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ (1880) — provides the most recent stratum of historical source material that Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha inherited. Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha was deeply familiar with this literature and consistently evaluated its claims against earlier sources, noting discrepancies and assessing the relative reliability of different accounts.

The Mahan Kosh as a Historical Source

The historical entries in the Mahan Kosh cover an enormous range of subjects. The lives of the ten Sikh Gurus are documented in substantial biographical entries that draw on multiple source traditions and attempt to reconcile discrepant accounts. Historical figures associated with the Sikh tradition — Bhai Mardana, Mata Gujri Ji, Banda Singh Bahadur, and many others — receive detailed entries. Major Gurdwaras are documented with accounts of their historical foundations. The cumulative effect of these entries is to make the Mahan Kosh a comprehensive historical reference for the Sikh tradition, providing the kind of synthesized and source-critical account that no earlier work had attempted at this scale.

Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's method in the historical entries reflects his commitment to ਸ੍ਰੋਤ-ਆਲੋਚਨਾ. He consistently identifies the sources on which each claim rests, notes cases where sources disagree, and offers his assessment of which account is most reliable. This critical apparatus — unusual in Sikh reference works of the period — transforms the historical entries from mere summaries of received tradition into exercises in historical reasoning. A reader who engages carefully with the Mahan Kosh's historical entries is not simply receiving information; they are being educated in how to evaluate historical claims about the Sikh tradition (Fenech and McLeod, 2014).

The Mahan Kosh's historical entries are particularly valuable for periods and subjects that are poorly documented in other sources. The early eighteenth century — the period between the end of Guru Gobind Singh Ji's life and the emergence of the Sikh Misl confederacies — is one of the most historically obscure periods in Sikh history, and the Mahan Kosh preserves information about this period drawn from sources that are no longer easily accessible. Similarly, the history of specific Gurdwaras, the biographies of lesser-known Sikh scholars and martyrs, and the historical background of regional Sikh traditions are documented in the Mahan Kosh with a thoroughness not available elsewhere.

At the same time, the Mahan Kosh's historical entries reflect the interpretive commitments of its author and its historical moment. Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's Singh Sabha framework inclined him toward particular readings of contested historical questions — about the boundary between Sikh and Hindu practice, about the theological significance of specific historical events, and about the identity and legacy of figures who stand at the boundary between different religious communities. These interpretive inclinations do not render the historical entries unreliable, but they do mean that the entries should be evaluated as interpretations in dialogue with other scholarly perspectives.

Evaluating Historical Claims in the Mahan Kosh

The critical evaluation of historical claims in the Mahan Kosh requires a set of tools and habits of mind that go beyond simply accepting or rejecting what Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha says. The first tool is source comparison: identifying the sources that Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha himself cites and comparing his use of them with the original texts. In some cases, this comparison reveals that he has cited sources accurately and that his interpretation is sound. In other cases, it reveals that he has selected particular elements of a source while omitting others. Both types of finding are valuable: they help the reader understand both the quality of the Mahan Kosh's scholarship and the interpretive choices it embeds (Barrier, 1970).

The second tool is chronological analysis. Many disputed questions in Sikh history turn on chronology — which events happened when, and what the temporal relationship between events was. The Mahan Kosh makes numerous chronological claims, some of which are well supported by multiple independent sources and some of which rest on single sources or on inference. Comparing the Mahan Kosh's chronological claims with those of other historical works — including non-Sikh Persian and British sources — allows the reader to assess their reliability and to identify where greater uncertainty exists than the confident tone of the entries might suggest.

The third tool is genre awareness. The Mahan Kosh draws on sources from multiple genres — ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀ narratives, ਗੁਰ-ਬਿਲਾਸ texts, formal chronicles, Persian administrative documents, and oral traditions — each of which has its own conventions, purposes, and modes of historical claim-making. Understanding the genre of a source is essential for evaluating what kind of historical information it can reliably provide. A ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀ episode may preserve authentic memory of the broad outlines of Guru Nanak Dev Ji's travels while embellishing specific events; a Mughal court document may provide reliable dates and names while misrepresenting the significance of events.

The fourth tool is what we might call historical imagination: the capacity to place the events and persons described in the Mahan Kosh in the fullness of their historical context, to understand what pressures and possibilities shaped their choices, and to recognize the distance between their world and ours. The Mahan Kosh was written by a man who was himself a historical actor, embedded in the specific conditions of colonial Punjab, committed to a specific vision of Sikh identity, and drawing on the scholarly resources available to him in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Reading it with historical imagination means understanding it as a product of that specific moment while recognizing that its achievements transcend that moment.

  • Key Takeaways:
  • The Mahan Kosh contains a substantial body of historical entries covering the Sikh Gurus, historical figures, Gurdwaras, and events, making it a major repository of Sikh historical knowledge.
  • Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha drew on multiple strands of Sikh historical memory — ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀ literature, ਗੁਰ-ਬਿਲਾਸ texts, formal chronicles, and Persian sources — and evaluated their reliability critically.
  • The Mahan Kosh's method of source citation and ਸ੍ਰੋਤ-ਆਲੋਚਨਾ distinguishes it from earlier hagiographical reference works and makes it a pioneer of critical Sikh historiography.
  • The historical entries reflect Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's Singh Sabha interpretive commitments and should be read critically in dialogue with other scholarly perspectives.
  • Evaluating the Mahan Kosh as a historical source requires tools of source comparison, chronological analysis, genre awareness, and historical imagination.

Key Terms

  • ਇਤਿਹਾਸ — History; both the events of the past and the discipline of documenting and interpreting them, a central concern of the Mahan Kosh's non-lexical entries.
  • ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀ — Hagiographical narratives of the life of Guru Nanak Dev Ji, combining historical memory with devotional elaboration; a major source tradition for the Mahan Kosh.
  • ਗੁਰ-ਬਿਲਾਸ — A genre of Sikh literature celebrating the deeds and glory of the Gurus, composed primarily in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries; used but critically evaluated in the Mahan Kosh.
  • ਸ੍ਰੋਤ-ਆਲੋਚਨਾ — Source criticism; the methodological practice of evaluating the reliability, context, and bias of historical sources, a central method of the Mahan Kosh's historical entries.
  • ਪਰੰਪਰਾ — Tradition; the transmission of knowledge, practice, and identity across generations, which the Mahan Kosh both preserves and evaluates critically.
  • ਗੁਰ-ਇਤਿਹਾਸ — The history of the Sikh Gurus; a body of historical knowledge central to Sikh identity and the subject of sustained engagement in the Mahan Kosh.

Discussion Questions

  1. The ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀ texts combine authentic historical memory with devotional elaboration. What criteria would you use to distinguish which elements of such texts are historically reliable and which are later additions?
  2. Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha drew on Persian administrative sources alongside Sikh hagiographical texts. What are the advantages and limitations of each type of source for understanding Sikh history? How should a historian balance them?
  3. The Mahan Kosh is simultaneously a document of Sikh historical memory and a contribution to critical historiography. Can these two functions coexist without tension, or do they inevitably come into conflict?
  4. Some historical questions about the Sikh past remain genuinely uncertain even after careful critical analysis. How should scholars communicate this uncertainty to community readers who may prefer confident answers?
  5. If you were to write a new encyclopedic entry about a figure or event in Sikh history following the Mahan Kosh's critical method, what sources would you consult? How would you signal uncertainty and acknowledge interpretive choices?

Further Reading

  • W. H. McLeod, The Evolution of the Sikh Community (Oxford University Press, 1976) — a foundational work in critical Sikh historiography that engages directly with the methodological questions raised in this lecture.
  • Giani Gian Singh, Panth Parkash (1880; various modern editions) — one of the major nineteenth-century Sikh historical chronicles that Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha drew on; to be read as a primary source with awareness of its genre.
  • Kavi Santokh Singh, Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth (1843; various modern editions) — the most comprehensive pre-Mahan Kosh treatment of Sikh history and hagiography in Punjabi, an essential source for understanding Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's historical context.
  • Pashaura Singh and Louis E. Fenech, eds., The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies (Oxford University Press, 2014) — contains several chapters on Sikh historiography and the critical study of Sikh historical sources.

Homework

Select one historical figure documented in the Mahan Kosh — not one of the ten Gurus, but a Sikh scholar, saint, martyr, or political figure from the eighteenth or nineteenth century — and look up that person's entry. Then find at least one other scholarly source that discusses the same person (a historical dictionary, an academic article, or a chapter in a book on Sikh history). Write a 350–400 word comparison: where do the Mahan Kosh and your other source agree? Where do they differ, and what might explain the difference? What does the comparison reveal about the interpretive choices each work makes?

lessons.title: The Legacy and Reception of the Mahan Kosh: From Print to the Digital Age
lessons.html:
Table of Contents

  1. Introduction
  2. The Mahan Kosh in the Twentieth-Century Sikh Scholarly Tradition
  3. Critiques, Corrections, and Continuations
  4. Digital Futures and the Encyclopedic Legacy
  5. Key Terms
  6. Discussion Questions
  7. Further Reading

Keywords

Term (Unicode)Academic Context
ਵਿਰਾਸਤHeritage or legacy; the accumulated intellectual and cultural inheritance of a tradition passed to subsequent generations.
ਸੋਧCorrection or revision; the scholarly process of updating earlier work in light of new evidence or improved methods.
ਡਿਜੀਟਲ ਵਿਦਵਤਾDigital scholarship; the use of computational and digital tools in the production and dissemination of academic knowledge.
ਕੋਸ਼ਕਾਰੀLexicography; the practice and theory of dictionary-making, a field in which the Mahan Kosh established a model for subsequent Punjabi and Sikh reference works.
ਅੰਤਰ-ਵਿਸ਼ੇInterdisciplinary; approaches that cross traditional academic boundaries, characteristic of contemporary Sikh Studies scholarship.
ਪਹੁੰਚਯੋਗਤਾAccessibility; the capacity of knowledge resources to be used by a wide range of users, a central value in the open educational mission of platforms like this one.

Introduction

Scholarly works have afterlives. The Mahan Kosh (ਮਹਾਨ ਕੋਸ਼), published in its final form in 1930, did not remain static in the decades that followed. It was cited, questioned, corrected, and built upon by successive generations of Sikh scholars; it was translated, excerpted, and digitized; it became the foundation for new reference works and the starting point for scholarly debates about methodology, interpretation, and community authority. Understanding the reception history of the Mahan Kosh — how it has been used, valued, criticized, and extended since its publication — is essential for understanding its place in the living intellectual tradition of Sikhism.

The twentieth century brought profound changes to the conditions of Sikh scholarship. The partition of Punjab in 1947, which divided the Sikh homeland between India and Pakistan, displaced communities, separated scholars from their manuscript collections, and created new demographic and political contexts for Sikh intellectual life. The emergence of academic Sikh Studies in Western universities from the 1960s onward introduced new methods, new debates, and new audiences for scholarship on Sikhism. The digital revolution of the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries transformed the production, distribution, and searchability of reference works, raising new questions about what an encyclopedia or lexicon should look like in the digital age.

This lecture examines the reception and legacy of the Mahan Kosh across three dimensions. First, we consider how the work was received and used within the twentieth-century Sikh scholarly tradition. Second, we examine the critiques and corrections that subsequent scholars have offered, and what these reveal about both the limitations and the durability of Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's achievement. Third, we consider the digital future of the encyclopedic tradition — how digital tools are transforming the possibilities for reference work in Sikh Studies.

The legacy of the Mahan Kosh also raises questions about how intellectual traditions are transmitted and renewed. What does it mean to "use" a reference work produced in a specific historical context when that context has changed fundamentally? How do we distinguish the enduring contributions of the Mahan Kosh from the interpretive choices that reflected its specific moment? And how can contemporary scholars honor the achievement of Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha while also subjecting his work to the critical scrutiny that genuine engagement requires?

The Mahan Kosh in the Twentieth-Century Sikh Scholarly Tradition

The immediate reception of the Mahan Kosh within the Sikh community was overwhelmingly positive. Scholars, educators, and religious leaders recognized it as a landmark achievement — a work that had no predecessor of comparable scope in the Punjabi-ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ tradition and that would define the standards of Sikh reference scholarship for generations. The Sikh Educational Conference, the ਸ਼੍ਰੋਮਣੀ ਗੁਰਦੁਆਰਾ ਪ੍ਰਬੰਧਕ ਕਮੇਟੀ, and various academic institutions promoted its use as the authoritative reference for questions of Sikh vocabulary, history, and theology. This institutional endorsement helped to establish the Mahan Kosh's normative authority (Mandair, 2013).

The establishment of Punjabi University at Patiala in 1962 marked a significant development in the institutionalization of Punjabi and Sikh scholarship in India. The university's commitment to Punjabi-medium scholarship created new institutional support for the kind of reference scholarship that the Mahan Kosh represented. Scholars at Punjabi University produced bibliographies, reference works, and critical editions that built on the foundations laid by the Mahan Kosh, and the university's Encyclopaedia of Sikhism project — a multi-volume reference work in English — explicitly acknowledged the Mahan Kosh as its primary model and source (Singh, Harbans, 1994).

The relationship between the Mahan Kosh and the emerging English-language academic study of Sikhism was more complex. W. H. McLeod, whose critical historical work on Sikhism from the 1960s onward was both enormously influential and deeply controversial within the Sikh community, drew extensively on the Mahan Kosh — both as a source of information and as a benchmark against which to measure his own critical findings. McLeod's use of the Mahan Kosh as a starting point for historical-critical analysis, while simultaneously questioning some of its historical claims, illustrates the paradox of the work's authority: it was both the standard reference and the object of critical scrutiny, functioning simultaneously as a foundation and as a challenge.

Western academic publishers also engaged with the Mahan Kosh's legacy. The production of English-language dictionaries, encyclopedias, and historical handbooks for Sikhism — including the Historical Dictionary of Sikhism by Fenech and McLeod and the Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies — all positions itself in relation to the Mahan Kosh. The measure of a reference work's enduring influence is its capacity to generate further scholarship, and by that measure the Mahan Kosh has been extraordinarily influential (Fenech and McLeod, 2014).

Critiques, Corrections, and Continuations

No scholarly work, however foundational, is beyond critique. The Mahan Kosh has been subject to several significant lines of scholarly criticism that illuminate both its limitations and the evolution of Sikh Studies as a field. Understanding these critiques does not diminish the work; it is precisely the mark of a serious scholarly contribution that it generates productive critical engagement rather than either uncritical acceptance or dismissal.

The most substantive historical critiques have focused on the Mahan Kosh's treatment of the early Sikh period — the lives and teachings of the Gurus before Guru Gobind Singh Ji — where the historical evidence is thinnest and the temptation to rely on hagiographical sources is greatest. Scholars in the critical tradition of Sikh historiography, most prominently McLeod, have argued that Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha sometimes accepted hagiographical claims without adequate critical scrutiny, particularly in the ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀ narratives. These critics do not accuse Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha of dishonesty; they suggest that the critical-historical methods needed to interrogate hagiographical sources were not yet fully developed in his era (McLeod, 1990).

A different line of critique comes from scholars working in gender studies and the history of women in Sikhism. The Mahan Kosh was written in a period and a scholarly culture that paid relatively little attention to women's roles in Sikh history and community life. Entries on female figures are relatively sparse, and the analytical frameworks used to discuss them often reflect the patriarchal assumptions of their era. Contemporary scholars who seek to recover and document women's contributions to Sikh history, theology, and community life have found the Mahan Kosh less useful than they might wish (Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur, 1993).

A third critique concerns the Mahan Kosh's treatment of traditions within the broader Sikh universe that were marginalized by the Singh Sabha reform agenda. Sects, lineages, and interpretive traditions that did not fit neatly within the Singh Sabha's vision of a unified, ਖਾਲਸਾ-centered Sikhism — including Udasi sadhus, Nirmala scholars, and the followers of various Sant figures — are sometimes treated dismissively in the Mahan Kosh. Contemporary scholars who seek to understand the full diversity of Sikh religious practice and thought have noted this bias and have worked to recover the perspectives of these marginalized traditions (Oberoi, 1994).

These critiques have generated a body of corrective and supplementary scholarship that constitutes, in effect, a continuation of the Mahan Kosh project by other means. Critical editions of major Sikh historical texts, new biographical dictionaries that include women and marginalized figures, specialized studies of Sikh sectarian traditions, and comparative studies that situate Sikh thought in the broader context of South Asian religion — all of these can be understood as extensions of the encyclopedic project that the Mahan Kosh inaugurated.

Digital Futures and the Encyclopedic Legacy

The digitization of the Mahan Kosh has been one of the most significant developments in its recent reception history. Several initiatives have made the full text of the Mahan Kosh available online in searchable digital form, vastly expanding its accessibility to readers who might not have access to physical copies of the work. This digitization has transformed the Mahan Kosh from a reference work that required physical proximity to a library into a resource that can be accessed from anywhere in the world — a development that would certainly have pleased Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha, whose commitment to the broad dissemination of Sikh knowledge was evident throughout his career.

Digital tools also open new possibilities for engaging with the Mahan Kosh analytically. Computational methods allow scholars to map the network of cross-references within the work, identifying clusters of related terms and tracing the conceptual architectures that Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha built across thousands of entries. Natural language processing tools can identify patterns in how certain terms are defined, what sources are cited most frequently, and how the work's vocabulary relates to that of the primary texts it documents. These computational approaches do not replace close reading, but they can supplement it in ways that reveal patterns not visible to any single reader working through the text sequentially.

The digital environment also raises new questions about what a twenty-first century successor to the Mahan Kosh might look like. A digital encyclopedic resource for Sikh Studies would have capabilities unavailable to Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha: hyperlinked cross-references, searchable databases of quotations and sources, multimedia content including audio recordings of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ recitation, and the capacity for collaborative authorship that could draw on the expertise of scholars across multiple disciplines and institutions. At the same time, a digital resource would face challenges: maintaining scholarly quality control in an environment of easy and rapid publication, preserving a large digital resource over time, and ensuring that the resource remains accessible to Punjabi and Sikh readers who may have varying levels of English and digital literacy.

Open educational platforms like the one you are now using represent one vision of the digital future for Sikh knowledge. The commitment to free, accessible, and rigorous scholarship that animated the Mahan Kosh's creation finds new expression in digital resources that can reach global Sikh communities without the barriers of cost, geography, or institutional affiliation. The challenge facing such platforms is precisely the challenge that Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha faced: how to combine accessibility with scholarly rigour, how to serve a community's immediate needs while maintaining the standards that will make the resource trustworthy over time.

  • Key Takeaways:
  • The Mahan Kosh was received enthusiastically within the Sikh scholarly community and quickly became the normative reference for questions of Sikh vocabulary, history, and theology.
  • Subsequent scholars have offered significant critiques of the Mahan Kosh's historical method, its treatment of women, and its marginalization of non-ਖਾਲਸਾ Sikh traditions.
  • The digitization of the Mahan Kosh has transformed its accessibility and opened new possibilities for computational engagement with its content.
  • Digital tools raise new questions about what a twenty-first century successor to the Mahan Kosh might look like and what challenges it would face.
  • The enduring value of the Mahan Kosh lies not only in its specific content but in its model of committed, rigorous, and transparent scholarly engagement with the Sikh tradition.

Key Terms

  • ਵਿਰਾਸਤ — Legacy or heritage; the intellectual inheritance that the Mahan Kosh represents for subsequent Sikh scholarship and for the broader field of Sikh Studies.
  • ਸੋਧ — Revision or correction; the scholarly process by which later scholars have updated, corrected, and extended the work of the Mahan Kosh in light of new evidence and methods.
  • ਕੋਸ਼ਕਾਰੀ — Lexicography; the theory and practice of dictionary-making, a field in which the Mahan Kosh established a standard for Punjabi and Sikh reference works.
  • ਡਿਜੀਟਲ ਵਿਦਵਤਾ — Digital scholarship; the use of computational tools to produce, analyze, and disseminate scholarly knowledge, opening new possibilities for engagement with the Mahan Kosh.
  • ਪਹੁੰਚਯੋਗਤਾ — Accessibility; a central value in both the original Mahan Kosh project and in the digital open-education initiatives that continue its spirit.
  • ਅੰਤਰ-ਵਿਸ਼ੇ — Interdisciplinary; the crossing of traditional academic boundaries characteristic of the most productive contemporary scholarship in Sikh Studies.

Discussion Questions

  1. How has the digitization of the Mahan Kosh changed how it is used and by whom? What possibilities does digital access open for readers who could not previously engage with the work?
  2. The critiques of the Mahan Kosh — regarding its historical method, its treatment of women, and its bias toward ਖਾਲਸਾ-centric Sikhism — have generated valuable corrective scholarship. How should a reader balance their use of the Mahan Kosh with awareness of these critiques?
  3. What would a twenty-first century successor to the Mahan Kosh look like? What subjects, perspectives, and methodological approaches would it need to incorporate that were absent or underdeveloped in the original work?
  4. The Mahan Kosh was a product of a specific historical moment — colonial Punjab in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. In what ways does this historical situatedness limit its usefulness for contemporary scholarship? In what ways does it make it more valuable as a historical document?
  5. Open educational platforms aim to combine accessibility with scholarly rigor. What tensions arise between these two goals, and how can they be navigated?

Further Reading

  • Pashaura Singh and Louis E. Fenech, eds., The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies (Oxford University Press, 2014) — the most comprehensive current survey of the field, which implicitly models what a twenty-first century successor to the Mahan Kosh's encyclopedic project might look like.
  • Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, The Feminine Principle in the Sikh Vision of the Transcendent (Cambridge University Press, 1993) — a major contribution to recovering women's perspectives in Sikh theology, addressing one of the Mahan Kosh's significant gaps.
  • Harjot Oberoi, The Construction of Religious Boundaries: Culture, Identity, and Diversity in the Sikh Tradition (University of Chicago Press, 1994) — essential for understanding the diversity of Sikh religious practice that the Mahan Kosh's Singh Sabha framework tended to minimize.
  • Gurinder Singh Mann, The Making of Sikh Scripture (Oxford University Press, 2001) — a detailed study of the compilation and manuscript tradition of the ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ that supplements and in places corrects the Mahan Kosh's treatment of the same subject.

Homework

The Mahan Kosh has been criticized for paying insufficient attention to women's roles in Sikh history and theology. Identify one woman who played a significant role in Sikh history — such as Mata Khivi Ji, Mata Gujri Ji, Bibi Bhani Ji, or Mata Sahib Kaur Ji — and spend 30 minutes researching her contributions using at least two sources. Write a 400-word entry as you might write it for a twenty-first century successor to the Mahan Kosh: factual, source-cited, and attentive to her specific contributions and historical context.

lessons.title: The Ethics and Practice of Sikh Scholarship: Learning, Humility, and Living the Encyclopedic Legacy
lessons.html:
Table of Contents

  1. Introduction
  2. The Ethics of Sikh Scholarship
  3. Integrating the Mahan Kosh into Scholarly and Devotional Practice
  4. The Encyclopedic Tradition as Living Legacy
  5. Key Terms
  6. Discussion Questions
  7. Further Reading

Keywords

Term (Unicode)Academic Context
ਵਿਦਿਆKnowledge or learning; in the Sikh tradition, understood as a means of liberation rather than an end in itself.
ਨਿਮਰਤਾHumility; a central Sikh virtue that the tradition insists must accompany all learning to prevent it from reinforcing ego.
ਸੇਵਾSelfless service; the orientation toward scholarship as service to the community and the tradition, not personal aggrandizement.
ਸਤਿਗੁਰThe True Guru; in Sikh theology, the source of authentic knowledge and the authority that grounds all valid learning.
ਸਿਮਰਨRemembrance of the Divine; a practice that the Sikh tradition places at the center of authentic spiritual and intellectual engagement.
ਗਿਆਨWisdom or true knowledge; distinguished in Sikh thought from mere information or intellectual cleverness.

Introduction

We have arrived, in this final lecture, at a question that has been implicit throughout this course: What does it mean to engage seriously with a work like the Mahan Kosh (ਮਹਾਨ ਕੋਸ਼) as a Sikh student or scholar? The preceding lectures have equipped you with the historical, philological, and methodological tools needed to understand the Mahan Kosh in its context and to use it critically. This lecture asks a different kind of question: not how to use the Mahan Kosh technically, but how to inhabit the intellectual and spiritual tradition it represents — how to become, in some sense, a worthy inheritor of the encyclopedic legacy of Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha.

This question is not merely inspirational. It has practical dimensions that bear directly on how scholarship is conducted, how communities transmit knowledge, and how individuals integrate learning into a life of faith and service. The Sikh tradition has always insisted that ਵਿਦਿਆ is not an end in itself: it is valuable insofar as it deepens one's understanding of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ, strengthens one's commitment to the ਪੰਥ, and ultimately serves the goal of coming closer to ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ. Scholarship conducted without this orientation, the tradition warns, risks becoming a form of pride — another manifestation of the ਹਉਮੈ that the Gurus identified as the central obstacle to spiritual liberation.

This lecture examines three interrelated themes. First, the ethics of Sikh scholarship — the values and virtues that should guide those who undertake serious study of the tradition. Second, the practical integration of the Mahan Kosh and the broader encyclopedic tradition into scholarly and devotional life. Third, the encyclopedic tradition as a living legacy — not a museum piece to be admired from a distance, but a continuing project to which each generation of Sikh scholars contributes and which each generation is responsible for renewing.

The course began with the encyclopedist and his project; it ends with you and your project. The Mahan Kosh was written for readers like you — people who take seriously their responsibility to understand the Sikh tradition deeply, accurately, and humbly. Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha spent decades of his life in the service of that project because he believed that careful scholarship was itself a form of ਸੇਵਾ — an act of service to the Guru and the ਸੰਗਤ. That conviction, perhaps more than any specific entry in the Mahan Kosh, is the most important thing this course has to transmit.

The Ethics of Sikh Scholarship

The Sikh tradition does not separate the intellectual life from the ethical and spiritual life. For the Gurus, knowledge divorced from virtue was worse than ignorance, because it produced pride without wisdom. The scholar who accumulates vast learning but fails to internalize the teachings — who can explain ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ without living by it — is, in the tradition's view, missing the point entirely. This integration of intellectual and spiritual development is not unique to Sikhism; it characterizes the great scholarly traditions of most religious communities. But it takes specific forms in the Sikh context that bear directly on how scholarship should be conducted.

The first ethical principle of Sikh scholarship is ਨਿਮਰਤਾ — humility. The vastness of the Sikh literary and theological tradition, and the depth of the ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ's inexhaustible meaning, should cultivate in the scholar a posture of permanent learnership rather than confident mastery. Every answer genuinely pursued in Sikh scholarship opens onto further questions; every term carefully analyzed reveals further layers of meaning.
