A skilled poet builds a mood gradually, then lets it peak. The same event can be told in different moods depending on the poet's aim. Reading for rasa means asking not only what happened but how the poem wants us to feel about it (Pashaura Singh and Fenech 2014).

Homework

Spend 20 minutes reading one section of a Sikh literary text — this can be a passage from Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth in translation, from the Braj poetry of the Dasam Granth in translation, or from any kavya-style historical account you have access to. As you read, make a list of every emotional atmosphere or rasa-quality you notice. Then write 350 words arguing whether the text succeeds in evoking the rasa the author likely intended, and what textual choices produce that effect.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: The Heroic Ballad — Vaar
lessons.summary: Describes the vaar form and its role in carrying history and ethics.
lessons.html:
The Heroic Ballad: ਵਾਰ

The ਵਾਰ (vaar) is a heroic ballad or ode, traditionally meant to be sung. The form has deep roots in Punjabi oral culture, where bards praised brave deeds and kept the memory of important events alive.

The vaar usually carries the heroic mood, ਬੀਰ ਰਸ, but in Sikh literature it does more than celebrate fighting. It frames courage as a moral and spiritual quality. A vaar can praise steadfastness in faith, sacrifice for justice, or loyalty to the Guru's path.

Because the vaar was sung in community settings, it served as a form of shared memory. The rhythm and repetition that suit singing also make the verses easy to recall, so the values they carry spread and endure (Oberoi 1994). When we study a vaar, we study not only a poem but a way that a community taught itself who it wanted to be.

Homework

Find a recorded performance of a Vaar — either a traditional ragis' rendition or a Dhadi Jatha performance — and listen to it at least twice. Write a 400-word analysis comparing the live musical or oral performance to what you would expect from reading the Vaar as written text. Consider: Does the music emphasise the heroic (veer) rasa? Does the performer add dramatic pauses or vocal ornamentation? What does the oral dimension add that the written form cannot?

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Form and Meaning Together
lessons.summary: Brings metre, figures, mood, and the vaar together to read poetry as a whole.
lessons.html:
Reading Form and Meaning Together

We have studied four tools: metre (ਛੰਦ), figures of speech (ਅਲੰਕਾਰ), mood (ਰਸ), and the heroic ballad (ਵਾਰ). In real poetry these never work alone. A poet may choose a fast metre, fill it with vivid similes, aim for a heroic mood, and cast the whole passage as a vaar.

This is the heart of Santokh Singh's craft in the Suraj Prakash and the Nanak Prakash. He matched form to content so closely that the shape of a passage becomes part of its message. A scene of awe sounds different from a scene of teaching, and that difference is built from the tools we have learned (Gurinder Singh Mann 2001).

As a reader, your task is to hold both halves at once: ask what the poem says, and ask how its form makes you receive that saying. When you can do both, you read Sikh classical poetry not as decoration on doctrine but as meaning made audible.

References

  • Pashaura Singh and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014.
  • Christopher Shackle and Arvind-Pal Singh Mandair, eds. Teachings of the Sikh Gurus. London: Routledge, 2005.
  • Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh. The Birth of the Khalsa. Albany: SUNY Press, 2005.
  • Gurinder Singh Mann. The Making of Sikh Scripture. New York: Oxford University Press, 2001.
  • Harjot Oberoi. The Construction of Religious Boundaries. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1994.

Homework

Choose any single kavya work — from Sikh tradition or any classical literary tradition you know — and write a 400-word close reading of a passage no longer than ten lines. Your goal is to demonstrate how form and meaning work together: identify at least one metrical feature, one figure of speech, and one emotional atmosphere (rasa) in the passage, and explain how each of those elements reinforces the passage's central idea. This exercise is a rehearsal of the kind of integrated reading that advanced poetics demands.

lessons.title: Kavi Santokh Singh — Life, Formation, and Literary Mission
lessons.html:
Introduction

Of all the poets who gave literary form to the Sikh tradition in the post-Guru era, Kavi (Bhai) Santokh Singh stands in a class of his own. His monumental Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth — known simply as Suraj Prakash — is the most extensive biographical and theological poem in Punjabi literary history, running to more than fifty thousand verses and organized across six great sections called ruts (seasons). Before we can interpret his poetic choices, appreciate his metrical sophistication, or trace the figures of speech he deploys, we need to understand who this poet was: where he came from, what traditions formed him, what mission he understood himself to be carrying out, and how the historical moment shaped his ambitions.

Santokh Singh was born in the late eighteenth century, at a time when the Sikh Panth had won military and political ascendancy across the Punjab but was simultaneously navigating the challenge of consolidating its cultural and theological identity in literary form. The Guru Granth Sahib Ji stood as the eternal Guru and as the supreme literary monument of the tradition. But the vast body of hagiographic, theological, and narrative memory that surrounded the lives of the ten Gurus existed in scattered, often oral, and frequently inconsistent form. Santokh Singh's project was, in the deepest sense, an act of synthesis: to gather, evaluate, organize, and above all beautify this body of knowledge through the highest available literary art.

Understanding his formation therefore means understanding three overlapping traditions: the Sanskrit-derived classical kavya tradition in which he was educated, the Braj Bhasha literary world that was the prestige medium of North Indian court poetry in his era, and the specifically Sikh literary lineage that stretched from the compositions within the Guru Granth Sahib Ji through the Gurbilases and Janamsakhis that preceded him. He was not writing naively or intuitively — he was a conscious artist working with sophisticated tools acquired through rigorous study.

This lesson traces Santokh Singh's biography as far as the historical record allows, examines the intellectual and literary context that produced him, and establishes why his choices of form, language, and structure were not incidental but were themselves theological and pedagogical acts. Every decision about metre, every invocation of a rasa, every deployment of an alankaar was a statement about what kind of text the Sikh tradition deserved and required.

Biography and Historical Context

The historical details of Santokh Singh's life are known primarily through references embedded within his own works and through later Sikh biographical literature. He was born around 1787 CE (some sources give slightly different dates) in the village of Nuurpur in the Amritsar region, into a Sikh family with strong connections to Gurbani study and kirtan. His early education followed the traditional dera model — study under a learned Sikh scholar, immersion in Gurbani, and parallel training in the Sanskrit grammatical and literary sciences that any serious poet of the era would have needed.

The period of his maturity — roughly 1800 to 1843, when he died — coincided with the reign of Maharaja Ranjit Singh, whose Lahore Durbar created the conditions for a remarkable flourishing of Punjabi, Braj, and Persian literary culture simultaneously. Ranjit Singh was himself a devout Sikh who patronized scholars and poets, maintained an elaborate court culture, and oversaw what historians have called the last great flowering of pre-colonial North Indian court literature. Santokh Singh spent years at Kaithal under the patronage of Sardar Udai Singh, a Sikh chief who was also a serious literary patron, and it was under this patronage that the bulk of the Suraj Prakash was composed.

The patronage relationship mattered enormously for the literary character of the work. Santokh Singh was not composing privately or for a small community of disciples — he was producing a work that would be recited in darbars, read aloud in deras, and eventually disseminated as the authoritative literary account of the Gurus' lives and teachings. This public, performative context shaped his choices: the metres he selected needed to be suitable for extended oral recitation; the rasas he cultivated needed to sustain attention across thousands of verses; the language needed to be learned enough to command respect but accessible enough to move non-specialist audiences.

His main completed works are the Suraj Prakash (completed 1843), the Nanak Prakash (an earlier and in some ways more experimental work covering the life of Guru Nanak Dev Ji), and the Garab Ganjani Tika — a Punjabi commentary on selected compositions from the Guru Granth Sahib Ji. Each of these represents a different literary mode: the Suraj Prakash is primarily mahakavya in its ambition; the Nanak Prakash shows greater lyrical variety; the Tika places him in the classical commentarial tradition. Together they establish him as among the most technically accomplished literary figures in the Sikh tradition.

His death in 1843, just two years before the first Anglo-Sikh War, marks a historical boundary. The literature he produced belongs to a pre-colonial world of patronage, oral performance, and classical learning. The scholars who came after him would increasingly work in a print culture, in dialogue with colonial philology, and with a very different sense of audience. To read Santokh Singh well is to enter a world that is now irretrievably past — but also to encounter a set of literary values and ambitions that continue to shape how the Sikh tradition understands its own history.

Intellectual Formation: Sanskrit, Braj, and Sikh Literary Heritage

To write a mahakavya — a great classical poem — in the tradition of Sanskrit literary aesthetics, a poet needed more than talent. He needed systematic training in at least four bodies of knowledge: grammar (ਵਿਆਕਰਣ, vyakaran), prosody (ਛੰਦ-ਸ਼ਾਸਤ੍ਰ, chhand-shastra), poetics (ਅਲੰਕਾਰ-ਸ਼ਾਸਤ੍ਰ, alankaar-shastra), and rasa theory (ਰਸ-ਸ਼ਾਸਤ੍ਰ, rasa-shastra). Santokh Singh acquired all four, and evidence of that training is visible throughout his work in the precision with which he handles complex metres, the density of his alankaar usage, and the deliberateness with which he moves between emotional registers.

The Sanskrit side of his formation connected him to a tradition stretching back to Valmiki's Ramayana and Vyasa's Mahabharata, through the court poets Kalidasa, Bharavi, and Magha, and through the theoretical works of Bharata (Natyashastra), Anandavardhana (Dhvanyaloka), and Mammata (Kavyaprakasha). The concept of dhvani — poetic resonance or suggestion, the idea that a poem's deepest meaning is not stated but evoked — was central to the most sophisticated strand of Sanskrit poetics, and Santokh Singh's awareness of it is visible in the way his narrative passages often carry a theological suggestion that goes beyond their surface story.

Equally important was the Braj Bhasha literary tradition. By the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, Braj — a dialect of Old Hindi associated with the Mathura-Vrindavan region and the devotional poetry of the Krishna bhaktas — had become the dominant prestige medium for poetry across North India, used by poets of every religious tradition at virtually every court. The Guru Granth Sahib Ji itself contains compositions in Braj, and Guru Gobind Singh Ji's literary circle at Anandpur produced extensive Braj-medium kavya. Santokh Singh worked primarily in Braj (with Punjabi admixture), which meant he was positioning his work within this broader North Indian literary world, not only within the narrower Punjabi vernacular tradition.

The specifically Sikh literary heritage he inherited included the Janamsakhis (hagiographic accounts of Guru Nanak's life), several Gurbilases (accounts of the Gurus' courts and exploits, varying considerably in literary quality and historical reliability), devotional compositions in various vernaculars, and the growing tradition of katha — oral exegesis of Gurbani. Santokh Singh approached this heritage critically. He was explicit about his desire to supersede or correct earlier accounts he considered unreliable or literarily inadequate. His ambition was not merely to retell familiar stories but to provide their definitive literary form.

What is remarkable about this triple formation is the synthesis it enabled. Santokh Singh could move in a single passage from a highly Sanskritized metre and alankaar usage to a Punjabi folk idiom, from a rasa appropriate to Sanskrit court poetry to one appropriate to the Sikh congregation gathered for katha. This range was not eclecticism — it was a considered literary strategy. The Sikh Panth's audience included both learned scholars and unlettered village sangat, and a poem that aspired to serve as the tradition's authoritative narrative needed to speak to both.

The Literary Mission of Suraj Prakash

The full title of Santokh Singh's masterwork — Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth — is itself a statement of intent. Pratap means glory, radiance, power; Suraj means the sun. The text understands itself as the sun — the source of illuminating light — and the Gurus as its subject are understood as the radiant source that the sun merely reflects and describes. The cosmological metaphor embedded in the title is not decorative; it announces a theology of revelation in which the Guru's glory, properly described through the highest literary art, becomes itself a vehicle of spiritual illumination for the reader or listener.

The organizational structure of the Suraj Prakash reinforces this cosmological ambition. The six ruts (seasons) into which it is divided map the lives and gurgaddi (Guruship) of the ten Gurus onto the cycle of the year, suggesting that the Gurus' presence in history is as natural, as cyclically renewing, and as cosmically necessary as the seasons themselves. This is a theological argument made through literary structure — a point we will return to throughout this course.

Within each rut, the text is divided into ansus (rays of light — another solar metaphor), and within each ansu the narrative moves through episodes, dialogues, miracles, teachings, and battles. The range of content demanded an equally wide range of literary tools. Battle sequences required the veer rasa and the appropriate high-energy metres. Dialogues between the Guru and a seeker required the quieter registers of shanta or sringara bhakti. Descriptions of the Guru's court required the language and imagery of royal panegyric. Accounts of miracles required the adbhuta rasa and its associated astonishment effects.

Santokh Singh's literary mission was therefore simultaneously an act of devotion (bhakti), an act of scholarship (academic mastery of classical poetics), and an act of institutional service (providing the Panth with a reliable, authoritative, and aesthetically worthy account of its founding figures). These three dimensions are inseparable in the text, and any reading that reduces the Suraj Prakash to merely one of them — devotional literature, historical chronicle, or literary performance — will miss what makes it extraordinary.

Key Terms

  • ਮਹਾਕਾਵਿ (mahakavya) — The Sanskrit genre of the "great poem": a long narrative poem on a heroic or divine subject, composed according to the full rules of classical poetics. Santokh Singh's Suraj Prakash aspires to this status.
  • ਰੁਤ (rut) — Season; also the name for the major structural divisions of the Suraj Prakash, each associated with a different Guru or phase of Sikh history.
  • ਅੰਸੁ (ansu) — Ray (of light); the sub-divisions within each rut, functioning like chapters. The term is a deliberate extension of the solar metaphor in the text's title.
  • ਧੁਨਿ (dhvani) — Poetic resonance or suggestion; in Sanskrit aesthetics, the principle that a poem's deepest meaning is suggested or resonated rather than stated directly. Associated with the theorist Anandavardhana.
  • ਬ੍ਰਿਜ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ (Braj Bhasha) — The prestige literary dialect of medieval North India, associated with Krishna bhakti poetry and used by Santokh Singh as his primary medium.
  • ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ (Gurbilasa) — "Sport/delight of the Guru": a genre of Sikh hagiographic literature describing the deeds and courts of the Gurus, a predecessor genre to Santokh Singh's own works.

Discussion Questions

  1. Santokh Singh described his work as providing the definitive literary account of the Gurus' lives, implying that earlier accounts were inadequate. What are the ethical and theological risks of a single poet claiming this kind of authority over a community's founding narratives? How might the Sikh Panth as a community evaluate such a claim?
  2. The Suraj Prakash was composed under royal patronage at a court. How might patronage relationships shape the literary choices a poet makes — and specifically, how might Santokh Singh's relationship to Sardar Udai Singh at Kaithal have influenced which stories he told and how he told them?
  3. Santokh Singh worked in three overlapping traditions simultaneously: Sanskrit classical poetics, Braj Bhasha court poetry, and Sikh vernacular/devotional literature. Can you think of other examples from any tradition where a writer successfully synthesized multiple literary heritages? What are the characteristic strengths and tensions of such synthesis?
  4. The title Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth embeds a cosmological claim: the text is a sun illuminating the Gurus' glory. How does this metaphorical self-understanding differ from how a modern academic historian might frame the same project? What does the difference reveal about the relationship between literary art and historical knowledge in pre-colonial Sikh culture?
  5. The lesson argues that Santokh Singh's literary choices — of metre, rasa, alankaar — were themselves theological acts, not merely aesthetic ones. Can you think of a specific example from any literature you know where a formal or structural decision carries theological or philosophical weight beyond its surface aesthetic function?

Further Reading

  • Surjit Hans, A Reconstruction of Sikh History from Sikh Literature — for the broader literary and historiographic context of Sikh textual production in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.
  • Harbans Singh (ed.), The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, entry on "Santokh Singh" and "Suraj Prakash" — for a concise overview of biographical data and textual scope.
  • Christopher Shackle and Arvind Mandair (eds.), Teachings of the Sikh Gurus — for the broader literary heritage within which Santokh Singh worked, with attention to Braj and Punjabi compositional traditions.
  • A. A. Macdonell, A History of Sanskrit Literature — for the Sanskrit kavya tradition (mahakavya genre, alankaar theory, rasa doctrine) that provided Santokh Singh's technical framework.
  • Key Takeaways:
  • Santokh Singh was born around 1787 and worked at the court of Kaithal under Sardar Udai Singh during the era of Maharaja Ranjit Singh — a context of political ascendancy and cultural consolidation for the Sikh Panth.
  • His formation drew on three simultaneous traditions: Sanskrit classical kavya, Braj Bhasha court poetry, and Sikh hagiographic and devotional literature — a synthesis that gave him an exceptionally wide range of literary tools.
  • The Suraj Prakash was a consciously ambitious project: to provide the Panth with a single, authoritative, and aesthetically worthy literary account of the ten Gurus' lives and teachings.
  • The organizational structure of the text — six ruts (seasons) subdivided into ansus (rays of light) — is itself a theological argument, mapping the Gurus onto cosmic cycles of renewal.
  • Every formal decision in the text — of metre, rasa, language register, alankaar — must be read as simultaneously an aesthetic and a theological choice, not as decoration added to a pre-existing narrative.

Homework

Select a passage of at least twenty verses from Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth in any available translation. Read the passage twice — first for narrative content (what happens), then a second time attending only to tone, atmosphere, and emotional register. Write 350 words identifying the dominant rasa you detect, explaining which specific word choices or images produce that rasa, and reflecting on why you think Santokh Singh chose that emotional register for this particular episode in the Guru's life.

lessons.title: The Mahakavya Tradition and the Structure of Suraj Prakash
lessons.html:
Introduction

The Sanskrit literary tradition classified poetry into two great categories: muktaka (independent, self-contained compositions) and prabandha (bound or structured compositions that sustain a narrative or argument across many units). Within prabandha, the highest achievement was the mahakavya — the great poem — a genre with specific formal requirements that distinguished it from shorter narrative works (khandakavya) and from prose romances (akhyayika and katha). To understand Santokh Singh's Suraj Prakash as a literary achievement, we must first understand what a mahakavya is, what it aspires to, and how Santokh Singh adapted, extended, and ultimately transformed the genre for Sikh theological purposes.

The formal requirements of the mahakavya were codified in treatises like Dandin's Kavyadarsha and discussed in Mammata's Kavyaprakasha. A mahakavya must: deal with a subject of great importance (typically a hero of divine lineage or a king whose deeds carry cosmic significance); begin with an auspicious invocation (mangalacharana); maintain formal dignity through the selection of appropriate metres; include set-piece descriptive passages on canonical topics (the rising sun, the seasons, love in its various stages, the hero's court, the battle, the journey); use figures of speech with variety and skill; and sustain a unified emotional arc (the dominant rasa) across its entire length, while allowing subsidiary rasas in individual sections.

What Santokh Singh did with this tradition was both deeply faithful to it and radically innovative. He fulfilled its formal requirements with conspicuous skill — the set-piece descriptions, the metrical variety, the alankaar density, the rasa structure are all present and accomplished. But he redirected the genre's heroic and cosmic ambitions toward a specifically Sikh theological understanding of the Guru: not as a warrior-king in the Sanskrit epic sense, but as the embodiment of Waheguru's light (jyot) moving through ten human forms, each illuminating the world in a way appropriate to its historical moment. The mahakavya form was not incidental to this theology — it was chosen precisely because the genre's capacity to hold cosmic significance and human particularity simultaneously made it the appropriate vehicle.

This lesson examines the mahakavya tradition in its classical form, traces how Santokh Singh fulfilled and innovated upon its requirements in the Suraj Prakash, and explores the organizational logic of the text's major structural divisions. Understanding this structure is essential for reading any individual passage well — a battle scene in the Suraj Prakash carries different weight than a battle scene in the Ramayana, because it is positioned within a different theological architecture.

Classical Mahakavya: Form and Requirements

The earliest and most influential definitions of the mahakavya appear in Dandin's Kavyadarsha (roughly seventh century CE), which lists the genre's requirements in systematic form. Dandin specifies that a mahakavya must open with an auspicious invocation (ਮੰਗਲਾਚਰਣ, mangalacharana) — a benediction that establishes the poem's devotional orientation and its cosmic stakes. This invocation typically names the deity or hero who is the poem's subject, establishes the poet's humble position as a vessel rather than an independent creator, and requests divine assistance for the poem's completion. The mangalacharana is not mere convention; it is a formal statement of the poem's theology.

The subject of a mahakavya must be a figure of great consequence — a king, hero, or divine being whose actions have cosmic significance. The poem must be divided into cantos (sargas in Sanskrit; equivalent divisions in later vernacular mahakavyas), each with a relatively unified focus and each ending in a different metre than the body of the canto — a formal device for signaling transitions and for providing metrical variety. Each canto should include at least one of the canonical descriptive set-pieces: the prabhata (dawn description), the nagar (description of a city), the samudriya (description of the sea or a river), the ritu (description of a season), the vipralambha (description of love in separation), the sangrama (battle description), and the nagara-pravesa (description of the hero's triumphal entry into a city).

These set-pieces were not merely decorative — they were occasions for the display of the poet's alankaar mastery and his ability to sustain a rasa through extended description. The prabhata, for example, required images of nature awakening, light replacing darkness, and the world renewing itself — a structure that could carry both aesthetic pleasure and theological suggestion. In the Sikh theological context, the dawn description becomes implicitly a meditation on the Guru as the source of spiritual light, independent of whatever story it nominally describes.

The dominant (ਅੰਗੀ, angi) rasa of a mahakavya was traditionally the veer (heroic) or shringara (love/devotion) rasa, with the remaining rasas appearing as subordinate (ਅੰਗ, anga) moods in individual passages. Bharata's analysis in the Natyashastra emphasized that only one rasa could be the dominant of any complete work — the others necessarily served and supported it. This requirement placed a significant organizational demand on a poet attempting to sustain a unified emotional arc across fifty thousand verses covering ten different lives spanning more than two centuries.

The language of a mahakavya was expected to be elevated — neither too colloquial nor obscure to the point of incomprehensibility. The ideal was what Sanskrit critics called prasada (clarity, luminosity) combined with ojas (energy, force) — a style that was simultaneously powerful and accessible. This balance was difficult to maintain across a very long work, and one of the critical assessments a scholar can make of Santokh Singh is precisely how well he sustains this balance across the Suraj Prakash.

Structural Architecture of Suraj Prakash

The Suraj Prakash is organized into six ruts (seasons): Raini (night, covering the period before the Gurus' manifestation), Grishma (summer), Varsha (monsoon), Sharad (autumn), Hemanta (the cool season), and Shishira (winter). The assignment of particular Gurus to particular seasons is itself an interpretive and literary act. Guru Nanak Dev Ji is associated with the morning light that ends the Raini — the night of ignorance and separation. The middle Gurus occupy seasons of growth, abundance, and culmination. Guru Gobind Singh Ji, whose life and legacy occupy the final and most extensive sections, is associated with the season of full harvest and its aftermath — a time of completion, consolidation, and the laying of foundations that will survive the winter.

Within each rut, the text is subdivided into ansus — rays of light. The ansu functions as the equivalent of the Sanskrit mahakavya's sarga or canto. Each ansu typically focuses on a single episode, dialogue, or set-piece descriptive passage. Some ansus are quite brief (fifty to one hundred verses); others extend to several hundred. The variation in length is itself significant — episodes of great theological importance tend to receive more extensive treatment, regardless of whether they involve dramatic external action.

The metrical variety across and within ansus is one of the most technically impressive features of the text. Santokh Singh commands dozens of metres — from the stately and slow-moving metres appropriate to theological exposition, to the rapid and energetic metres appropriate to battle and chase sequences, to the lyrical metres appropriate to description and devotional address. The ability to shift metres fluidly and to match metre to mood and content is a hallmark of classical kavya mastery, and Santokh Singh demonstrates it throughout.

The text also includes formal set-piece passages that are explicitly modeled on the mahakavya convention. Dawn descriptions appear repeatedly, each slightly different in its imagery and in the theological suggestion it carries. Descriptions of the Guru's court — its splendor, the assembly of devotees, the atmosphere of Naam — function as the Sikh equivalent of the Sanskrit nagar or sabha descriptions. Battle sequences, particularly in the sections covering the period of armed conflict during the life of Guru Gobind Singh Ji, deploy the sangrama conventions with notable skill, including the canonical imagery of the two armies, the description of weapons, the role of divine intervention, and the aftermath of the field.

Innovation: The Guru as Mahakavya Hero

The most significant and theologically complex aspect of Santokh Singh's use of the mahakavya form is his handling of the genre's central requirement: a hero of cosmic significance. In classical Sanskrit mahakavyas, the hero is typically a king or warrior whose deeds establish or restore cosmic and social order — Rama in the Ramayana, Arjuna and Krishna in the Mahabharata as epic predecessors. The hero's greatness is demonstrated through external action, through conquest, through the winning of a destined consort, and through the proper performance of royal duty (dharma).

Santokh Singh's Guru-hero operates according to an entirely different logic. The Sikh Gurus are not primarily warriors or kings (though some led armies and held royal courts). Their heroism is primarily the heroism of spiritual illumination — the conquering of the ego (haumai), the demonstration of divine grace (nadar), the instruction of seekers, the establishment of sangat, and the deepening of the Panth's theological understanding. This is a fundamentally different kind of greatness than the Sanskrit epic tradition was designed to celebrate.

Santokh Singh navigates this tension in several ways. He does deploy conventional heroic imagery when describing episodes of armed conflict — the battles with Mughal forces, the Blue Horse, the martyrdoms. But he consistently frames the Guru's heroism theologically: the Guru's courage is presented not as military prowess for its own sake but as the expression of nirbhau (fearlessness) — one of the divine qualities enumerated in the Mool Mantar. The true battle being fought throughout the Suraj Prakash is not military but theological: the battle against ego, ignorance, and the forces that separate the human soul from Waheguru.

This reframing of the mahakavya's heroic logic is Santokh Singh's most profound literary innovation. He took a genre designed to celebrate worldly heroism and adapted it to celebrate a fundamentally different kind of greatness — one that is invisible to conventional eyes, that does not culminate in territorial conquest or dynastic succession, and that achieves its ultimate expression not in triumph over external enemies but in the dissolution of the self into Waheguru's will (ਭਾਣੇ ਵਿੱਚ, bhaane vich). To sustain this reframing across fifty thousand verses, while still fulfilling the genre's formal requirements, required both literary mastery and theological clarity.

Key Terms

  • ਪ੍ਰਬੰਧ (prabandha) — Bound or structured composition; contrasted with independent (muktaka) compositions. Mahakavya is the highest form of prabandha.
  • ਮੰਗਲਾਚਰਣ (mangalacharana) — Auspicious invocation at the opening of a classical poem; establishes the poet's devotional stance and the text's cosmic stakes.
  • ਸਰਗ (sarga) — Canto; the major structural division of a Sanskrit mahakavya. Santokh Singh's equivalent structural unit is the ਅੰਸੁ (ansu).
  • ਅੰਗੀ ਰਸ (angi rasa) — The dominant or primary rasa of a complete literary work, which all subsidiary rasas serve and support.
  • ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦ (prasada) — Luminosity, clarity; a highly valued quality of classical literary style, referring to language that is elevated but not obscure.
  • ਭਾਣਾ (bhaana) — God's will, divine pleasure; in Sikh theology, the ultimate orientation of a spiritually realized being. Santokh Singh's Guru-heroes are characterized by perfect bhaana-consciousness rather than conventional heroic self-assertion.

Discussion Questions

  1. The classical mahakavya tradition required a hero of cosmic significance whose greatness was demonstrated through external action. Santokh Singh reframed Sikh Guru-heroism as spiritual rather than military greatness. Do you think this reframing succeeds on its own literary terms? What would a critic of Santokh Singh's approach argue?
  2. The set-piece descriptive passages of the classical mahakavya (dawn, seasons, the city, the battle) were opportunities for poets to display technical skill. How might Santokh Singh transform these conventional topics to carry specifically Sikh theological content? Can you imagine what a Sikh "dawn description" in his style might emphasize?
  3. The structural division of the Suraj Prakash into six ruts (seasons) maps the Gurus' lives onto a cosmological cycle. What theological argument does this structure make? Is the argument compelling or does it impose an artificial pattern onto complex historical events?
  4. Santokh Singh's decision to work in a long-form, highly structured genre meant that individual passages can only be fully understood in relation to the whole text's structure and theological arc. How does this compare to the experience of reading shorter, independent compositions like individual shabads from the Guru Granth Sahib Ji? What does each mode offer that the other cannot?
  5. Scholars have debated whether the Suraj Prakash is primarily a work of theology, of history, or of literature — and whether these categories are even meaningful distinctions in the context of pre-colonial Sikh culture. Where do you position yourself in this debate, and why?

Further Reading

  • Adi Shakya Dandin, Kavyadarsha (available in modern scholarly editions and translations) — the foundational classical statement of mahakavya requirements and theory.
  • Edwin Gerow, A Glossary of Indian Figures of Speech — for technical vocabulary of Sanskrit poetics applicable to understanding Santokh Singh's formal choices.
  • W. H. McLeod, Textual Sources for the Study of Sikhism — for context on the Sikh hagiographic tradition (Janamsakhis, Gurbilases) that Santokh Singh was working within and against.
  • Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, The Name of My Beloved: Verses of the Sikh Gurus — for comparative reading of how lyrical and narrative registers operate differently across Sikh literary forms.
  • Key Takeaways:
  • The mahakavya is the highest genre of classical Sanskrit literature, with codified requirements for subject matter, structure, metrical variety, descriptive set-pieces, and dominant rasa.
  • Santokh Singh fulfilled these requirements with conspicuous skill while simultaneously redirecting the genre's heroic logic toward a Sikh theological understanding of Guru-greatness as spiritual illumination rather than military conquest.
  • The Suraj Prakash's six-rut structure maps the ten Gurus onto a cosmological seasonal cycle, making a theological argument through form itself.
  • Individual ansus (cantos) fulfill the mahakavya requirement for set-piece descriptive passages, but each is transformed by Sikh theological content into something more than conventional display.
  • The tension between classical form and Sikh theological content is the productive creative space in which Santokh Singh's literary innovation operates.

Homework

Read the opening invocation (mangalacharana) of the Suraj Prakash in any available translation. Then write a 350-word analysis of what Santokh Singh is claiming in that opening — who he invokes, how he positions himself as a poet, and what theological relationship between poet, text, and audience he establishes. Compare his opening moves to the opening of any other long poem you know (religious or secular) and note what is similar and what is distinctly Sikh about Santokh Singh's approach.

lessons.title: Language and Register — Braj, Punjabi, and Sanskrit in Sikh Kavya
lessons.html:
Introduction

One of the most immediately striking features of Santokh Singh's poetry, for any reader approaching it from a modern Punjabi perspective, is that it is not primarily written in contemporary Punjabi. The language of the Suraj Prakash is predominantly Braj Bhasha — the medieval literary dialect of North India associated with the Krishna devotional tradition — laced with Sanskrit vocabulary, Sanskrit-derived grammatical forms, and, at intervals, passages that shift into a more distinctly Punjabi register. This multilingual texture is not a defect or an inconsistency; it is a deliberate literary strategy with deep historical roots and significant theological implications.

Understanding why Santokh Singh made these linguistic choices requires understanding what language itself meant in the literary culture of eighteenth and nineteenth century North India. Language was not merely a practical medium of communication; it carried prestige, theological associations, social markers, and aesthetic qualities. Sanskrit was the language of the sacred cosmos, of eternal knowledge. Braj was the language of bhakti, of Krishna's divine sport, of the heart's longing and devotion. Punjabi was the language of the community, the everyday, the gurdwara congregation. Persian was the language of courts, of administrative power, of the great Islamic literary tradition. A poet composing at the intersection of these worlds was making constant choices about which linguistic register to deploy — and those choices were legible to educated audiences in ways that are often invisible to modern readers.

This lesson examines the three primary linguistic registers of classical Sikh kavya — Braj, Punjabi, and Sanskrit — and traces how Santokh Singh moves between them in the Suraj Prakash. We will consider how each register carries distinct aesthetic and theological associations, how register shifts signal changes in content and emotional tone, and what the multi-register texture of classical Sikh kavya tells us about the literary culture in which it was produced. We will also consider the implications for contemporary readers and translators who must navigate these distinctions.

The broader context for this discussion is the question of literary diglossia — the coexistence of multiple language varieties in a single literary culture, with distinct social and aesthetic functions assigned to each. Classical Sikh kavya is a particularly rich example of this phenomenon, and understanding it illuminates not only Santokh Singh's specific choices but also the linguistic landscape of the entire Guru Granth Sahib Ji, which itself moves through multiple language registers with evident intentionality.

Braj Bhasha as the Prestige Literary Medium

By the seventeenth century, Braj Bhasha had become the dominant literary language of North India — used by poets, scholars, and court composers of virtually every religious tradition. Its prestige derived primarily from its association with the Sursagar of Surdas, the Ramacharitmanas of Tulsidas, and the vast body of Krishna devotional poetry produced at the courts and temples of Mathura and Vrindavan. When a poet chose to write in Braj, he was positioning his work within this prestigious tradition, claiming its aesthetic values (the primacy of devotional love, the beauty of separation and union, the capacity of poetry to carry the listener into divine experience) and its technical conventions (specific metres, specific imagery, specific alankaar preferences).

The Guru Granth Sahib Ji itself contains extensive Braj-medium compositions — including many of the compositions of Guru Nanak Dev Ji himself, as well as compositions by the Bhagats whose works were included in the canonical scripture. The choice of Braj for these compositions was not incidental: it placed them in dialogue with the broader bhakti tradition while simultaneously transforming that tradition's theological assumptions. Similarly, the Dasam Granth — the collection of compositions associated with Guru Gobind Singh Ji — contains extensive Braj-medium poetry, including highly sophisticated kavya-style narrative compositions.

Santokh Singh's use of Braj therefore connected him to this entire lineage. When he composed a descriptive passage or a dialogue in Braj, he was not merely using a convenient medium; he was invoking a set of aesthetic associations — the bhakti tradition's emphasis on longing and love, the classical kavya tradition's emphasis on formal beauty, the devotional tradition's understanding of the poem as a vehicle of spiritual experience. These associations enriched the semantic content of individual passages in ways that a reader steeped in the tradition would immediately feel, even without consciously analyzing them.

At the same time, the choice of Braj carried limitations. It was not the daily speech of the Punjabi sangat; it was a learned literary medium requiring education to access fully. This meant that the Suraj Prakash was always, to some degree, a text for the educated listener, requiring a mediating figure — the kathavachak or the scholar — to make its full meaning accessible to a general congregation. The tension between the learned literary register and the community's everyday language is itself significant, and Santokh Singh navigates it by allowing Punjabi passages to surface at moments of particular community intimacy or urgency.

Sanskrit Vocabulary and the Claim to Sacred Authority

Running through the Braj medium of the Suraj Prakash is a dense Sanskritic vocabulary — technical terms from philosophy, theology, mythology, and poetics, as well as Sanskrit-derived epithets, compound constructions, and grammatical forms. This Sanskritic layer serves multiple functions simultaneously.

First, it marks the text as a work of shastra — of learned, authoritative knowledge — not merely of devotional poetry. The Sanskritic vocabulary signals that Santokh Singh is not simply telling stories but making theological arguments, drawing on the full weight of the classical intellectual tradition to support his account of the Gurus' significance. A passage about the Guru's enlightenment that deploys Sanskrit philosophical vocabulary — terms like brahma-jnana, turiya, ananda — is making a claim about the universality and transhistorical depth of that enlightenment, connecting it to a conceptual tradition with millennia of credibility.

Second, the Sanskritic vocabulary provides access to the vast storehouse of Hindu mythological imagery. The Suraj Prakash draws extensively on this imagery — references to the avatars, to the cosmic elements, to the devas and their attributes — not to endorse Hindu theological frameworks uncritically but to use them as a shared cultural vocabulary for conveying the Gurus' spiritual stature. When Santokh Singh compares the Guru to the sun, the moon, or a cosmic ocean, he is drawing on associations that his readers would have absorbed from the broader Sanskrit literary tradition, redirecting them toward Sikh theological purposes.

Third, Sanskrit serves a ritual and devotional function in the text. Certain passages — particularly the mangalacharana, the benedictions, and the formal descriptions of the Guru's form and attributes — are intensely Sanskritic in a way that signals their ritual character. These passages are not primarily narrative or argumentative; they are acts of devotional praise, and the Sanskrit register gives them the elevated, sacred quality that such praise requires. This is the same principle that governs the use of Sanskrit in liturgical Hindu contexts: the language itself is understood to carry sacred power (ਸ਼ਕਤਿ, shakti) beyond its semantic content.

Punjabi as the Register of Community and Authenticity

Alongside the dominant Braj-Sanskrit register, the Suraj Prakash contains passages of more distinctly Punjabi character — direct speech in Punjabi idiom, proverbial expressions, folk imagery, and the everyday language of the Punjabi community's religious life. These passages typically appear at moments of particular immediacy: in dialogue between ordinary characters and the Guru, in descriptions of the community at worship, in moments of humour or pathos that require a human scale rather than the elevated scale of the literary Braj register.

The function of these Punjabi passages is not merely stylistic variety; it is a statement about the nature of the Guru's accessibility. The Guru appears in the text at the level of Sanskrit-cosmic authority (the Sanskritic passages) and at the level of Braj literary beauty (the dominant register) but also at the level of the ordinary Punjabi seeker's daily life (the vernacular passages). This structural arrangement embeds a theological claim: the Guru's grace operates across all levels of human existence and requires no particular learning or cultural preparation to receive.

The Punjabi passages also function as anchor points for audiences whose primary language is Punjabi and who might find the extended Braj-Sanskrit passages difficult to follow in live oral performance. A skillful kathavachak reading the Suraj Prakash aloud would modulate his voice and pace at these moments, using the Punjabi passages as opportunities to reconnect the audience's emotional attention before returning to the elevated literary register.

From a historical linguistics perspective, the Punjabi of the Suraj Prakash is itself a distinctive variety — eighteenth and early nineteenth century literary Punjabi, not identical to any modern spoken form. Tracing its specific features — its vocabulary, its grammatical forms, its relationship to Guru Granth Sahib Ji's Punjabi — is an area of ongoing scholarly interest, and students of classical Sikh poetics who wish to read the original text need some preparation in the history of the Punjabi language alongside their training in Braj and Sanskrit.

Key Terms

  • ਦਿਗਲੋਸੀਆ (diglossia) — The coexistence of two or more language varieties in a single literary culture, with distinct social and aesthetic functions assigned to each. Classical Sikh kavya is a multilingual diglossic system.
  • ਭਾਖਾ (bhakha) — Vernacular language; contrasted with Sanskrit (samskrita, the refined language). In Sikh literary discourse, Guru Nanak Dev Ji's choice of bhakha over Sanskrit was theologically significant.
  • ਰਜਿਸਟਰ (register) — A variety of language used for a specific purpose or in a specific social context; in literary terms, the level of formality, vocabulary, and stylistic choice that signals what kind of text this is and who it is for.
  • ਤਤਸਮ (tatsama) — Sanskrit-derived word adopted unchanged into a vernacular language; contrasted with ਤਦਭਵ (tadbhava), words that have evolved from Sanskrit through phonological change. Santokh Singh uses both, often simultaneously for stylistic effect.
  • ਕਾਵਿਭਾਸ਼ਾ (kavibhasha) — Poet's language; the characteristic mixed literary idiom of a particular poetic tradition, which may not correspond exactly to any spoken dialect.
  • ਸ਼ਾਸਤ੍ਰੀ (shastri) — Pertaining to shastra (authoritative learned text); the Sanskritic register of the Suraj Prakash aligns it with this tradition of systematic sacred knowledge.

Discussion Questions

  1. Guru Nanak Dev Ji's choice to compose in the vernacular rather than Sanskrit was understood as a deliberate theological act — making sacred knowledge accessible to all regardless of social position. How does Santokh Singh's use of the learned Braj-Sanskrit register stand in relation to that founding commitment? Is it in tension with it, or can it be understood as continuous with it?
  2. Modern readers of the Suraj Prakash in Punjabi translation necessarily lose the texture of the original's multilingual register. What specific dimensions of meaning are lost when a multilingual classical text is rendered into a single modern language? How might translators compensate for this loss?
  3. The Sanskritic vocabulary in the Suraj Prakash connects Santokh Singh's descriptions of the Gurus to Hindu mythological and philosophical frameworks. Contemporary scholars debate whether this connection is theologically appropriate or whether it risks misrepresenting Sikh theological distinctiveness. Where do you stand on this debate?
  4. The Guru Granth Sahib Ji itself uses multiple language registers (Punjabi, Braj, Sanskrit, Persian, and others). How does this compare to Santokh Singh's multilingual approach? Are the functions of language-switching similar in the two texts, or fundamentally different?
  5. If you were to compose a Sikh literary work in the twenty-first century that aimed at the same combination of learned authority and community accessibility that Santokh Singh achieved, what linguistic registers would you use and why? What would be the modern equivalent of the Braj-Sanskrit-Punjabi combination?

Further Reading

  • Christopher Shackle, An Introduction to the Sacred Language of the Sikhs — the foundational linguistic introduction to the multilingual register of Guru Granth Sahib Ji, essential background for understanding Santokh Singh's language choices.
  • Ronald Stuart McGregor, Hindi Literature from its Beginnings to the Nineteenth Century — for the history and literary culture of Braj Bhasha from its origins through Santokh Singh's era.
  • Harjot Oberoi, The Construction of Religious Boundaries — for the broader context of language, identity, and religious demarcation in nineteenth-century Punjab.
  • Gurinder Singh Mann, The Making of Sikh Scripture — for the linguistic and editorial decisions embedded in the compilation of Guru Granth Sahib Ji, which provides essential comparative context.
  • Key Takeaways:
  • Classical Sikh kavya, including the Suraj Prakash, operates in a multilingual register combining Braj Bhasha, Sanskrit vocabulary, and Punjabi vernacular elements — each carrying distinct aesthetic and theological associations.
  • Braj was the prestige literary medium of pre-colonial North India, connecting Santokh Singh's work to the bhakti tradition and classical kavya conventions.
  • Sanskrit vocabulary in the text signals learned authority, invokes classical theological frameworks, and carries ritual sacred power.
  • Punjabi passages signal community accessibility and the Guru's presence at the level of everyday human life, functioning as emotional anchor points in extended oral performance.
  • The multilingual texture of the Suraj Prakash is a literary strategy, not a linguistic inconsistency — and reading it well requires sensitivity to what each register contributes.

Homework

Choose a passage from any multilingual classical text you have access to — this could be from the Guru Granth Sahib Ji (which includes multiple language registers), from a translation of the Suraj Prakash, or from any comparable work where you can detect shifts in linguistic register. Write 350 words identifying at least two distinct registers in the passage, explaining what markers (vocabulary, tone, imagery, grammatical forms) allow you to recognize them as distinct, and reflecting on what each register contributes to the passage's overall meaning and emotional effect.

lessons.title: Set-Piece Description — Prabhata, Nagar, and Sangrama in Sikh Context
lessons.html:
Introduction

Classical kavya poetry was organized not only by narrative progression but by a set of recognized descriptive occasions — moments in the story when the poet was expected to pause, dilate, and produce an extended, technically accomplished description of a canonical topic. These descriptive set-pieces (chitra or varnana) were the occasions for the most concentrated display of poetic skill: alankaar, metrical variety, rasa evocation, and the capacity to find original expression for familiar subjects. The poet who could describe the dawn or the monsoon in a genuinely new and beautiful way — while fulfilling the tradition's expectations for what such a description should include — was demonstrating mastery that audiences and critics recognized and celebrated.

The most important set-pieces in the mahakavya tradition include the prabhata (dawn description), the ritu-varnana (seasonal description, particularly the monsoon), the nagar-varnana (description of a city or royal court), the sangrama-varnana (battle description), the nagara-pravesa (triumphal entry into a city), and various descriptions of natural landscape. Each of these had established conventions — canonical topics, expected imagery, and recognized rasa registers. A poet could fulfill these conventions faithfully (demonstrating learning), vary them cleverly (demonstrating originality), or subvert them deliberately (making a theological or argumentative point). The most accomplished poets did all three simultaneously.

Santokh Singh inherits these conventions and deploys them throughout the Suraj Prakash, but always with a Sikh theological inflection that transforms their meaning. A dawn description in the Suraj Prakash is never only a dawn description; it is simultaneously an account of the Guru's light dispelling the darkness of ignorance, an occasion for devotional praise, and a demonstration of poetic mastery. A battle description is simultaneously an account of historical events, a meditation on the nature of fearlessness (nirbhau) and righteous conflict (dharam yudh), and a deployment of the veer rasa in its specifically Sikh understanding.

This lesson examines three of the most important set-piece conventions — prabhata, nagar-varnana, and sangrama-varnana — in their classical forms and then traces how Santokh Singh transforms them in the Suraj Prakash. Understanding these transformations is essential for reading individual passages well and for appreciating how formal literary choices become vehicles of theological argument.

Prabhata — The Dawn Description and Spiritual Awakening

The prabhata (dawn) is one of the most frequently recurring set-pieces in classical North Indian poetry. Its canonical imagery includes: the fading of stars, the first light on the horizon, the lotus opening, the birds beginning to sing, the sleeping world awakening, the smoke of morning fires, the call to prayer or ritual, and the renewal of human activity. These images carry a consistent emotional register — the transition from darkness to light, from sleep to wakefulness, from unconsciousness to conscious engagement with the world. In the Sanskrit aesthetic tradition, the dawn was associated with the rasa of the quiet wonder (adbhuta) at natural beauty, and also with the sringara rasa of the parted lovers reuniting or reluctantly separating in the morning.

In the context of bhakti poetry more broadly, the prabhata acquired an additional layer of meaning: the dawn was the auspicious time of amrit vela (the ambrosial hours before sunrise), the ideal time for meditation, Naam recitation, and communion with the divine. This tradition is deeply embedded in the Guru Granth Sahib Ji, which contains multiple references to the amrit vela as the optimal time for spiritual practice. When Santokh Singh writes a dawn passage, he is therefore activating both the classical literary convention and this devotional-liturgical association simultaneously.

In the Suraj Prakash, prabhata passages appear at structurally significant moments: at the opening of the text, at the beginning of new ruts (seasonal divisions), at the birth or awakening of Gurus, and at the dawn of historically significant days. Each such passage fulfills the formal requirements — the images of light, birds, lotus, awakening — while simultaneously carrying the Sikh theological suggestion that the specific dawn being described is not merely a natural phenomenon but a moment of divine grace (nadar) made manifest in the world.

The alankaar most favored in prabhata passages is rupak (metaphor of complete identification) and upama (simile): the rising sun is identified with the Guru; the fading darkness is identified with ignorance and ego; the opening lotus is identified with the opening heart of the devotee. These identifications are sustained across multiple lines, creating the kind of extended metaphorical consistency (ekavali) that Sanskrit critics particularly admired. A reader who knows both the classical conventions and the Sikh theological framework reads these passages at two levels simultaneously — as formal poetic achievement and as devotional theology.

Nagar-Varnana — Describing the Guru's Court and Community

The nagar-varnana or city description was a canonical set-piece in which the poet described the physical splendor, administrative order, commercial activity, aesthetic beauty, and human vitality of a royal capital. In Sanskrit mahakavyas like Kalidasa's Raghuvamsha, these descriptions established the hero-king's legitimacy by demonstrating that his realm was prosperous, well-ordered, and aesthetically pleasing — a physical reflection of his dharmic governance. The nagar-varnana was therefore both an aesthetic display and a political argument: this king is righteous because his city is beautiful and flourishing.

Santokh Singh inherits this convention but redirects it toward the Guru's community (ਸੰਗਤ, sangat) and the Guru's court (darbar). His descriptions of the Guru's gathering places — Kartarpur, Amritsar, Anandpur — function as nagar-varnanas in formal terms, deploying the canonical imagery of prosperity, beauty, and orderly vitality, but with a crucial theological transformation. What makes the Guru's community beautiful and flourishing is not royal power or wealth but the presence of Naam — the divine Name — and the atmosphere of devotion, equality, and spiritual service that the Guru's grace creates.

The canonical topics of the nagar-varnana thus acquire Sikh inflections: instead of the marketplace's commercial bustle, Santokh Singh describes the flow of sangat arriving from distant places, drawn by the Guru's spiritual magnetism; instead of the city's fortifications and military strength, he describes the spiritual impregability of a community grounded in Naam; instead of the aesthetic beauty of architecture and gardens, he describes the beauty of kirtan, seva (selfless service), and the langar (community kitchen) that embodies equality. Each transformation is formally recognizable as a variant of the classical set-piece while simultaneously making a distinctly Sikh theological argument.

The rasa of these passages is typically a mixture of adbhuta (wonder at the community's spiritual vitality), shanta (the tranquility of a place of genuine devotion), and a form of bhakti-sringara (devotional love and longing awakened by the Guru's presence). This combination — wonder, peace, and devotional longing — is characteristic of the Sikh aesthetic experience of the gurdwara as a sacred space, and Santokh Singh's nagar-varnanas are among the most evocative literary representations of that experience in the tradition.

Sangrama-Varnana — Battle Description and Dharam Yudh

The sangrama-varnana (battle description) was one of the most technically demanding set-pieces in classical kavya, and also among the most conventionalized. Its canonical elements included: the assembly of the two armies, the sound of drums, conches, and battle-cries, the description of warriors and their weapons, the chaos of the battle itself (with its characteristic imagery of elephants, horses, and infantry in confusion), the role of divine intervention or supernatural figures, the descriptions of the fallen and the wounded, and the aftermath — the lamentation of the defeated and the triumph of the victor.

The rasa of the sangrama-varnana was primarily veer (heroic) — the emotion of courage, martial energy, and righteous strength — typically combined with bhayanaka (terror at the carnage) and raudra (fury and ferocity). The challenge for a classical poet was to sustain the veer rasa as dominant while allowing the others to amplify and contrast with it, creating a textured emotional experience rather than a monotonous celebration of violence. The metres used in sangrama passages were characteristically rapid and energetic — Bhujangaprayata, Totak, Geetika — metres that carry the listener forward with the momentum of the battle itself.

Santokh Singh's sangrama passages in the sections of the Suraj Prakash covering the battles of Guru Gobind Singh Ji's era are formally accomplished deployments of the classical convention. They include the canonical elements — the two armies, the weapons, the chaos, the role of divine grace — and deploy appropriate high-energy metres with skill. But they are also systematically inflected by the Sikh theological concept of dharam yudh (righteous warfare) — the understanding that the battles described were not fought for territorial or dynastic motives but as an expression of Waheguru's will to protect the righteous and resist tyranny.

This theological inflection transforms the sangrama's meaning at every level. The hero's courage in these passages is not the courage of personal glory-seeking but the courage of nirbhau (fearlessness rooted in Waheguru-consciousness) — one of the divine qualities of the Mul Mantar. The battle's outcome is not determined by military skill alone but by divine grace (kirpa) and the community's collective spiritual state. The fallen warriors are not merely soldiers but singhs who have offered their lives as seva — a form of devotion rather than a military transaction. These theological transformations are not imposed artificially on the battle descriptions; they are woven into the imagery, the metaphors, and the rasa structure of the passages themselves.

Key Terms

  • ਵਰਣਨ (varnana) — Description; the general term for descriptive passages in classical kavya. Set-piece descriptions are standardized varnana occasions.
  • ਪ੍ਰਭਾਤ (prabhata) — Dawn; both a natural phenomenon and a literary convention for describing the transition from darkness to light, carrying devotional associations with the amrit vela.
  • ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਵੇਲਾ (amrit vela) — The ambrosial hours before dawn; in Sikh tradition, the optimal time for Naam simran and devotional practice. The prabhata literary convention carries this devotional weight in Sikh kavya.
  • ਧਰਮ ਯੁੱਧ (dharam yudh) — Righteous warfare; in Sikh theological understanding, conflict undertaken for the protection of the righteous and the resistance of oppression, at Waheguru's command rather than for personal gain.
  • ਚਿਤ੍ਰ (chitra) — Picture, image; in poetic terms, the vivid descriptive passage that creates a visual impression in the listener's mind. A mark of accomplished kavya.
  • ਏਕਾਵਲੀ (ekavali) — A chain or sequence in which each link builds on the last; in alankaar terms, an extended metaphor or simile sustained across multiple verses.

Discussion Questions

  1. The classical battle description (sangrama-varnana) celebrates heroic courage and martial energy. How does the Sikh theological concept of dharam yudh change the ethical meaning of these same formal elements? Can a battle description that deploys conventional veer rasa imagery carry a genuinely different theology?
  2. The nagar-varnana convention was designed to celebrate royal power and legitimacy. Santokh Singh redirects it to describe the Guru's community and the spiritual atmosphere of sangat. What are the implications of using a form associated with royal ideology to describe a religious community that explicitly challenged certain forms of hierarchical power?
  3. The prabhata (dawn) is one of the oldest literary conventions in the world, appearing in traditions from ancient Mesopotamia to Elizabethan England. Why do you think the transition from darkness to light is such a universal poetic subject? What does this universality tell us about the relationship between natural phenomena and human spiritual experience?
  4. Classical kavya criticism valued the poet who could find new expression for familiar topics — who could describe the dawn or the monsoon in a way that felt both true to convention and genuinely original. Is this a different kind of creativity than the kind we tend to value in modern literature, which typically prizes novelty and the breaking of convention? Which model do you find more compelling?
  5. If you were to write a contemporary Sikh literary work that used the set-piece convention, what contemporary occasions and topics might serve the function that prabhata, nagar, and sangrama served in the classical tradition? What are the canonical descriptive occasions of twenty-first century Sikh communal life?

Further Reading

  • Kalidasa, Raghuvamsha (translation by M. R. Kale or Romesh Chunder Dutt) — for the classical model of mahakavya set-piece descriptions against which Santokh Singh's innovations can be measured.
  • Barbara Stoler Miller (ed.), The Powers of Art: Patronage in Indian Culture — for the social and political contexts of classical descriptive conventions and their ideological functions.
  • Pashaura Singh, The Bhagats of the Guru Granth Sahib — for the devotional and theological context of the amrit vela and sangat imagery that Santokh Singh draws on.
  • Doris Jakobsh, Relocating Gender in Sikh History — for alternative perspectives on the martial and communal imagery of classical Sikh literature, including feminist critiques of the battle-description tradition.
  • Key Takeaways:
  • Classical kavya required extended descriptive set-pieces (prabhata, nagar-varnana, sangrama-varnana) at canonical moments in the narrative — occasions for demonstrating technical mastery and rasa evocation.
  • Santokh Singh fulfills these conventions while systematically inflecting them with Sikh theological content, transforming their meaning without abandoning their formal structure.
  • The prabhata activates the devotional association of amrit vela; the nagar-varnana describes sangat rather than royal power; the sangrama-varnana embeds dharam yudh theology in heroic battle imagery.
  • Reading these passages well requires knowing both the classical convention (what is being fulfilled) and the Sikh theological inflection (what is being transformed).
  • The set-piece convention demonstrates that formal poetic requirements and theological argument can reinforce each other — form and meaning are not separate dimensions of the text.

Homework

Find a description of a physical space in any work of devotional literature you are familiar with — this could be a description of a gurdwara, a temple, a mosque, a church, a natural sacred site, or a community gathering. Write 400 words analyzing how the description works: what does the writer choose to emphasize, what sensory details appear, what emotional atmosphere is evoked, and what theological claim about that space is being made through the description? Then compare this to what you have learned about the nagar-varnana convention and note what is similar in approach, even if the traditions are very different.

lessons.title: Theological Poetics — How Sikh Kavya Teaches Theology
lessons.html:
Introduction

Throughout this course we have examined the formal tools of classical Sikh poetics — metre, figures of speech, rasa, set-piece description, structural architecture. We have seen how Santokh Singh deploys these tools with extraordinary skill in the Suraj Prakash. But we have not yet asked the most fundamental question about this body of literature: what is it for? Not in the shallow sense of "what story does it tell" or "what audience does it address" — but in the deepest sense: what does this kind of poetry do that could not be done by prose? What specific functions does poetic form serve in the transmission of Sikh theological understanding? And what does the existence of a sophisticated tradition of theological poetics tell us about how the Sikh tradition has understood the relationship between beauty, knowledge, and spiritual transformation?

These questions take us into the field of what scholars have called theological poetics — the study of how literary forms carry, transmit, and in some cases constitute theological knowledge. The basic claim of theological poetics is that certain kinds of religious understanding cannot be adequately expressed in propositional prose — that they require the resources of poetry, narrative, and image to reach their full articulation. This is not a modern claim; it is embedded in the most ancient traditions of religious literature worldwide. The Psalms of the Hebrew Bible, the Homeric hymns of Greece, the Sanskrit Vedas, the Persian ghazals of Rumi and Hafiz — all of these attest to a persistent intuition that poetry is not merely a beautiful way of saying what could be said plainly; it is a different mode of knowing and transmitting.

In the Sikh tradition, this intuition is foundational. The Guru Granth Sahib Ji is itself the supreme expression of theological poetics: its compositions are simultaneously hymns for congregational singing, texts for individual contemplation, and theological arguments presented through image, metaphor, and emotional modulation. The tradition of kavya poetry that grew alongside and in response to the Guru Granth Sahib Ji — including Santokh Singh's Suraj Prakash — extended this theological-poetic project into the domain of narrative, biography, and history.

This lesson asks what specific theological functions poetic form serves in the Sikh kavya tradition, drawing primarily on the Suraj Prakash for examples while connecting to the broader theological-poetic tradition of the Guru Granth Sahib Ji. We will examine four distinct functions: the evocation of devotional experience (bhakti), the transmission of theological concepts through image rather than proposition, the cultivation of moral formation through narrative identification, and the creation of community through shared aesthetic experience.

Poetry as Bhakti — Devotion Through Aesthetic Experience

The oldest and most fundamental theological function of poetry in the Sikh tradition is its role in producing and deepening bhakti — devotional love for Waheguru and the Guru. This function is explicitly discussed in the Guru Granth Sahib Ji itself: numerous compositions describe the devotee as a poet (kavi) whose highest aspiration is to praise the divine with true words (sacha shabda), and the act of praising through beautiful language is understood as itself a form of devotion, not merely a vehicle for describing devotion from outside.

The theoretical basis for this understanding draws on the rasa doctrine examined in Lesson 4. If the highest rasa in Sikh theological aesthetics is what some scholars have called bhakti-rasa — the rasa of devotional love and longing — then a poem that successfully evokes this rasa in its audience is not merely describing devotion; it is facilitating it. The reader or listener who is genuinely moved by the beauty of a kirtan composition, who feels the pull of devotion awakened by a well-crafted metaphor or a perfectly placed pause, is not simply learning about bhakti intellectually; they are having a bhakti experience that the poem has created.

This understanding has important implications for how we evaluate Santokh Singh's literary choices. When he deploys an elaborate and beautiful description of the Guru's form or presence, the purpose is not to convey information that could be stated more efficiently in prose. The purpose is to produce in the reader a specific quality of attention and emotional opening — a moment of surati (focused inner awareness) in which the Guru's reality becomes experientially present rather than merely conceptually known. The beauty of the poetry is not separate from its theological function; it is the mechanism through which that function operates.

This is why the classical tradition placed such emphasis on the aesthetic quality of devotional poetry. A mediocre poem about the Guru does not merely fail aesthetically; it fails theologically, because it cannot produce the experiential opening that constitutes its purpose. Conversely, a poem of genuine beauty and power succeeds not only as art but as a vehicle of grace (kirpa) — it becomes one of the means through which Waheguru's grace reaches the seeker. The Sanskrit aesthetic tradition's concept of sahridaya — the cultivated, sympathetic reader or listener capable of genuine aesthetic response — maps onto the Sikh concept of the prepared devotee, whose simran and sangat practice has made them capable of receiving what the poem offers.

Theology Through Image — Conceptual Knowledge via Poetry

A second theological function of Sikh kavya is the transmission of theological concepts through image, metaphor, and narrative rather than through propositional statement. This function is particularly important for the most profound and paradoxical aspects of Sikh theology — concepts that resist direct definition precisely because they describe realities that exceed the ordinary categories of language and thought.

Consider the theological concept of hukam — the divine order or will that governs all existence. This concept can be stated propositionally: Waheguru's hukam governs everything; nothing happens outside it; the spiritually realized being accepts hukam willingly; resistance to hukam is the root of suffering. These propositions are true and important. But they convey the concept at the level of intellectual understanding, which is a necessary but not sufficient level for genuine spiritual transformation. A person can understand hukam intellectually while continuing to resist it in daily life — the gap between knowing and living is the basic problem that spiritual practice addresses.

Poetry approaches this gap differently. A poem that embeds the reality of hukam in a vivid narrative image — the flow of a river that cannot be diverted from the sea, the tree that cannot prevent its fruit from ripening and falling, the soldier who fights valiantly in a battle whose outcome has already been determined — does not merely convey information about hukam; it creates an experiential encounter with the quality of hukam in the reader's imagination. This experiential encounter may do more to close the gap between knowing and living than any number of propositional statements.

Santokh Singh's use of extended metaphor (rupak) and simile (upama) in the Suraj Prakash frequently serves this function. When he compares the Guru's presence to the sun, he is not making a simple decorative comparison; he is systematically developing an image of unearned, non-judgmental, universally available radiance that creates in the reader an experiential sense of what the Guru's grace is like — an experience that the proposition "the Guru's grace is universal and unconditional" could not produce on its own. The image does theological work that the proposition cannot do.

Moral Formation Through Narrative Identification

A third theological function of Sikh kavya is its role in moral and spiritual formation through narrative identification. The Suraj Prakash is, among other things, a vast collection of narratives about figures who either draw close to the Guru through devotion and service, or who resist the Guru through ego, greed, or worldly attachment. These narratives do not merely describe moral choices; they invite the reader to identify with particular figures, to inhabit their perspectives emotionally, and through that imaginative inhabiting to develop the moral and spiritual intuitions that the tradition regards as essential to a Sikh life.

The classical theory of this function draws on Aristotle's concept of catharsis (the emotional purification produced by dramatic narrative) as well as the Sanskrit concept of lila — divine play that invites the devotee's imaginative participation. In the Sikh context, the narratives of the Gurus' lives and of the seekers who came to them are not merely historical accounts or moral exemplars; they are occasions for the reader's own spiritual development. To read about a devotee who overcame ego and approached the Guru in humility is to have one's own ego examined and one's own capacity for humility cultivated — if the narrative is well-crafted enough to produce genuine identification rather than merely intellectual acknowledgment.

This is one reason why the quality of character portrayal matters so much in the Suraj Prakash, and why Santokh Singh's psychological acuity is one of his most important literary achievements. His major characters are not simple moral types — not purely virtuous seekers or purely villainous opponents — but complex figures whose struggles with ego, fear, longing, and pride are recognizable to any reader examining their own interior life. This complexity produces stronger identification, and stronger identification produces more effective moral and spiritual formation.

Key Terms

  • ਸਹਿਰਦਯ (sahridaya) — The cultivated, sympathetic reader or listener; in Sanskrit aesthetics, the person who has developed the emotional and aesthetic sensitivity to receive what a work of art offers. In Sikh terms, analogous to the prepared devotee.
  • ਸੁਰਤਿ (surati) — Focused inner awareness; in Sikh theology, the faculty through which the soul attends to and receives the divine. Theological poetry aims to activate surati in the listener.
  • ਹੁਕਮ (hukam) — Divine order, God's will; one of the most theologically central concepts in Sikh thought. Poetry can transmit the experiential sense of hukam in ways that propositional statement cannot.
  • ਲੀਲਾ (lila) — Divine play; the understanding of divine action in the world as a form of creative, loving play in which devotees are invited to participate imaginatively.
  • ਸ਼ਬਦ (shabad) — Word, divine Word; in Sikh theology, both the specific compositions of the Gurus and the divine resonance that those compositions carry. Theological poetry participates in and extends the shabad.
  • ਭਾਵਨਾ (bhavana) — Devotional feeling or intention; the emotional-spiritual orientation of the reader or listener that allows theological poetry to do its transformative work.

Discussion Questions

  1. The lesson argues that poetic beauty is not separate from theological function in the Sikh tradition — that a beautiful poem about the Guru is simultaneously a vehicle of grace. Do you find this claim compelling? What would a skeptic say about it, and how would you respond?
  2. We have seen that poetry can transmit theological concepts through image and metaphor in ways that propositional statement cannot. Can you think of a theological concept from Sikh or any other tradition that you understand better through a poem or story than through a direct explanation? What does that example tell you about the limits of propositional religious language?
