The pairing of meaningful words with disciplined sound is the foundation on which the whole tradition of Gurmat Sangeet, the music of the Guru's wisdom, is built. Everything that follows in this course unfolds from this simple idea: that singing the sacred word is itself an act of devotion.

Homework

After studying what kirtan is and its place in Sikh worship, attend or listen to a full recorded kirtan session of at least 30 minutes — this could be from a Gurdwara livestream, a YouTube recording of Hazoori Ragis, or a community program. As you listen, keep a journal open and write down three specific moments where the music seemed to shift your mental state or emotional awareness. In 250–300 words, reflect on what you personally experienced: Did the sound feel contemplative, uplifting, or devotional? How did the congregation's participation (if any) change the atmosphere? This is not an analytical exercise — write honestly about your inner experience.

lessons.title: Raag and the Structure of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji
lessons.html:
What a Raag Is

A Raag is a melodic framework in the classical music of the Indian subcontinent. It is more than a scale and less than a fixed song. A Raag defines which notes are used, how they are approached and left, which notes are emphasized, and the characteristic phrases that give the Raag its identity. Within these guidelines a musician improvises and arranges, so two performances of the same Raag can sound quite different while still being recognizably the same.

Each Raag is traditionally associated with a particular mood or emotional color, and often with a time of day or a season. One Raag may evoke calm and longing, another joy, another deep seriousness. This association between melody and feeling is essential to understanding why Raag matters in Sikh music.

How the Scripture Is Organized

One of the most distinctive features of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji is that its main body is arranged by Raag. After an opening section of daily prayers, the compositions are gathered into chapters, each devoted to a single Raag. Within each Raag, the verses are ordered in a careful sequence, generally moving through the contributing authors in a fixed pattern. This means the scripture is, in its very structure, a musical anthology as much as a written text.

This arrangement was a conscious choice. By placing each composition under a specific Raag, the Gurus indicated the emotional setting in which the verse was meant to be sung. The mood of the Raag and the meaning of the words are intended to reinforce one another, so that the music becomes a partner to the message rather than a decoration added afterward.

Why This Matters for Kirtan

Because the scripture is organized this way, a singer who follows the tradition closely will perform a given verse in the Raag under which it appears. Singing a composition in its prescribed Raag is considered the most faithful way to present it, honoring the intention behind its placement. While many beautiful renderings exist outside the strict Raag framework, returning to the prescribed Raags is a central goal of those who study Gurmat Sangeet seriously. The Raag, then, is not a technical detail for specialists alone; it is woven into the design of the scripture itself.

Homework

Select any one of the six main seasonal or time-based raags mentioned in your study of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji (for example, Raag Basant, Raag Bilawal, or Raag Sarang). Without needing any musical training, research what that raag is said to evoke emotionally — its mood (ras), the time of day or season traditionally associated with it, and any general descriptions you can find from musicians or scholars. Write a 300–400 word reflection connecting that raag's emotional character to the type of spiritual state you imagine it might cultivate in a listener. Include one question the topic raises for you that you'd like to explore further.

lessons.title: An Overview of the Thirty-One Main Raags
lessons.html:
The Count of Raags

The main body of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji is organized under thirty-one principal Raags. In addition to these, a number of related forms and combinations appear, so the total variety of melodic settings is larger, but the thirty-one main Raags form the backbone of the structure. Learning their names and characters is a natural early step for any student of the tradition.

A Sense of Their Range

The thirty-one Raags were chosen to cover a wide emotional and seasonal range. Some are gentle and devotional, suited to quiet contemplation. Some carry a heroic or weighty feeling. Others are bright and celebratory, and several are tied to particular seasons such as the rains or the spring. Taken together, they offer a melodic palette broad enough to match the full sweep of human experience that the verses address, from sorrow and separation to peace and joy.

Among the Raags that appear early and prominently is one associated with the dawn and with a serious, searching mood, fitting for the opening of the collection. Others are linked to the close of day, to the rainy season, or to longing and union. A student does not need to master all of these at once; the point is to appreciate that each Raag brings its own atmosphere, deliberately matched to the verses placed within it.

Order and Purpose

The Raags do not appear at random. They follow a deliberate sequence through the scripture, and within each Raag chapter the compositions are themselves ordered by form and by author. This layered organization reflects the care with which the collection was compiled. For the beginner, the practical takeaway is simple: the thirty-one Raags are the organizing principle of the scripture's music, and growing familiar with even a few of them deepens one's appreciation of how words and melody are joined.

How to Approach Them

Rather than memorizing the entire list at the outset, learners are usually encouraged to become acquainted with a handful of Raags through listening. Hearing the same Raag in several compositions trains the ear to recognize its characteristic phrases and mood. Over time, the thirty-one Raags become familiar landmarks, and the structure of the scripture comes alive as a sequence of distinct musical worlds.

Homework

From the thirty-one main raags of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, choose one raag that is less commonly performed today (avoid the popular ones like Raag Yaman Kalyan or Raag Bhairavi). Using any available resources — books, recordings, interviews with musicians — find at least one audio or video example of that raag being performed in the Gurmat Sangeet tradition, even if brief. In 300–350 words, describe what you heard: the melodic character, the pace, the emotional quality, and how the Shabad being sung seemed to interact with the raag's atmosphere. If you cannot find a recording, research the raag's classical origins and write about what the tradition says about its character.

lessons.title: Traditional Instruments and the Rababi Tradition
lessons.html:
The Instruments of Gurmat Sangeet

The traditional instruments of Sikh sacred music were chosen to support the human voice without overpowering it. Each has a distinct role, and several are closely associated with the early history of the tradition.

The rabab is a plucked, stringed instrument with a deep, warm tone. It holds a special place because it is linked with the very beginnings of Kirtan in the Sikh tradition. The taus is a bowed string instrument whose body is shaped to resemble a peacock; it produces a rich, sustained sound well suited to following the curves of a melody. The dilruba is a smaller bowed instrument, lighter and more portable than the taus, developed so that musicians could carry it more easily while keeping a similar sweetness of tone.

The tabla is a pair of hand drums that provide the rhythmic foundation, marking the cycles of beats that structure a performance. The harmonium is a hand-pumped keyboard instrument that became widely used for its ability to sustain notes and support the singer's pitch. While the harmonium is now extremely common, the older bowed and plucked string instruments are central to the classical approach that the revival movement seeks to restore.

The Rababi Tradition

From the earliest days of the Sikh path, the singing of sacred verse was often performed by skilled musicians who played the rabab, and from this the term Rababi came into use. The Rababis were hereditary musician families, many of them from a Muslim background, who served as Kirtan performers across generations. They carried the practice of singing Gurbani in its Raags with great refinement, preserving melodies and styles through oral transmission from teacher to student and parent to child.

For centuries the Rababi families were among the principal custodians of Sikh musical practice, performing in places of worship and passing down a living knowledge of how the compositions were meant to sound. Their contribution is a remarkable example of a shared heritage, in which musicians of one community devoted their art to the sacred music of another.

A Disruption and Its Legacy

The continuity of the Rababi tradition was severely disrupted by the upheavals of the twentieth century, particularly the partition of the region in 1947, which separated many of these families from the congregations they had long served. The loss of this living link was deeply felt and is one of the reasons that later generations placed such emphasis on reviving the classical forms. The instruments and the memory of the Rababi masters remain touchstones for anyone seeking to understand the authentic sound of Gurmat Sangeet.

Homework

Research one instrument from the traditional kirtan ensemble beyond the harmonium and tabla — for example, the sarangi, dilruba, taus, or rabab. Find information about its physical construction, how it is played, and its historical role in Sikh kirtan specifically. Then write a 350–400 word essay exploring why this instrument's role may have diminished in modern kirtan practice and what, if anything, is being done to revive it. Draw on at least two sources (books, documentaries, or credible online resources) and note them at the end of your response.

lessons.title: The Shabad and Its Musical Setting
lessons.html:
What a Shabad Is

The word Shabad means the sacred word or utterance. In the context of Sikh music, a Shabad is a single composition of Gurbani that is sung as a unit, a hymn complete in itself. When people speak of attending Kirtan, they are usually describing the singing of one Shabad after another. The Shabad is therefore the basic building block of a Kirtan performance.

A Shabad carries meaning on two levels at once. There is the literal sense of the words, and there is the deeper spiritual teaching they point toward. The musician's task is to render the Shabad so that both levels come through, allowing the listener to follow the words and also to feel their import. This is why faithful pronunciation and a fitting melody are valued so highly.

How a Shabad Is Set to Music

Setting a Shabad to music begins with the Raag prescribed for it in the scripture, which establishes the emotional frame. Within that Raag, the musician shapes a melody for the verses and chooses a rhythmic cycle, marked by the drums, to carry the performance forward. A short refrain line, often the opening or a central line of the composition, is typically returned to again and again as an anchor, while the other lines unfold around it.

The pace and intensity are usually built gradually. A Shabad may begin slowly and meditatively, giving the words room to be absorbed, and then grow in energy. Throughout, the melody is meant to serve the meaning. Ornaments and elaborations are welcome when they deepen the feeling of the verse, but the tradition cautions against musical display that draws attention away from the message.

The Union of Word and Sound

The ideal in Gurmat Sangeet is a seamless union of word and sound, in which the listener cannot easily separate the beauty of the music from the truth of the words because the two have become one experience. When a Shabad is sung well in its proper Raag, the melody seems to arise naturally from the meaning, and the meaning seems to flower through the melody. Achieving this union is the lifelong aim of the dedicated Kirtan musician, and recognizing it is one of the great rewards of attentive listening.

Homework

Choose one Shabad from Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji that you are already familiar with — perhaps from childhood, from Gurdwara, or from your own practice. Without needing musical expertise, listen to two different musical renditions of the same Shabad: one traditional Gurmat Sangeet performance and one more contemporary or devotional style. In 300–400 words, compare how the two settings affected your experience of the Shabad's meaning. Did one version draw your attention more to the words? Did one feel more meditative? What does this exercise reveal to you about the relationship between music and meaning in Gurbani?

lessons.title: The Revival of Gurmat Sangeet
lessons.html:
A Tradition Under Strain

Over the course of the twentieth century, the classical practice of Sikh sacred music faced serious challenges. The disruption of the hereditary Rababi families, the increasing dominance of the harmonium over the older string instruments, and the spread of simpler, popular tunes detached from the prescribed Raags all contributed to a gradual loss of the classical heritage. Many compositions came to be sung in general melodies rather than in the specific Raags under which they appear in the scripture, and knowledge of the older instruments grew rare.

The Movement to Restore

In response, a movement arose to revive Gurmat Sangeet in its classical form. Scholars, musicians, and institutions began to research the original Raags, to recover the prescribed melodic settings, and to teach the older string instruments such as the taus and dilruba once again. The goal was not to reject all later developments but to reconnect the practice with its roots, restoring the link between each composition and the Raag intended for it.

This revival has taken many forms. Schools and academies devoted to Gurmat Sangeet have been established to train new generations of musicians in the classical method. Researchers have worked to document the Raags and to clarify how the compositions were traditionally rendered. Workshops, recordings, and public performances have helped reintroduce the older sound to congregations that had grown unfamiliar with it. Crafts-people have revived the making of the traditional string instruments, ensuring that students have authentic instruments to learn on.

Where Things Stand

Today there is a growing community of musicians and listeners committed to the classical tradition, alongside the more popular styles that remain widespread. The two coexist, and many congregations now hear both. The revival has given the classical heritage a renewed presence and has inspired younger students to take up the discipline of Raag-based Kirtan. For a beginner, this is encouraging news: the resources, teachers, and recordings needed to learn the tradition in its fuller form are more available now than they were a generation ago. The work of restoration continues, carried forward by those who believe that the proper marriage of word and Raag is worth preserving.

Homework

Research one figure or institution that has played a meaningful role in the modern revival of Gurmat Sangeet — for example, Bhai Avtar Singh Ji, Bhai Gurcharan Singh Ji, or the work of institutions like Gurmat Sangeet Akademi or Jawaddi Taksal. Write a 350–400 word biographical or institutional profile covering: their background and training, what specific aspect of Gurmat Sangeet they worked to preserve or transmit, and the impact of their work on the broader community. Conclude with one sentence about what their example means to you personally.

lessons.title: How to Begin Learning Gurmat Sangeet
lessons.html:
Start by Listening

The first and most accessible step is attentive listening. Before learning to play or sing, spend time hearing Kirtan, ideally performances rooted in the classical tradition. Listen to the same Shabad rendered in its prescribed Raag, and over repeated hearings begin to notice the characteristic mood and recurring phrases. This trains the ear, which is the foundation of all the music that follows. Listening in the sangat, where Kirtan is sung in the presence of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, adds a devotional dimension that recordings alone cannot provide.

Learn the Words and Their Meaning

Because Gurmat Sangeet is the singing of sacred verse, understanding the words is essential. A beginner benefits greatly from learning to read the script of the scripture and from studying the meaning of the compositions being sung. When the meaning is clear, the musical setting makes far more sense, and the singer can shape the melody to serve the words. Many learners pursue language and scripture study alongside their musical training for this reason.

Find a Teacher and an Instrument

Traditional Indian music, including Gurmat Sangeet, has long been passed from teacher to student through close personal instruction. Finding a qualified teacher is the surest path, whether in person at a Gurdwara or academy or, increasingly, through structured online programs. A teacher can correct pronunciation, demonstrate the subtleties of a Raag, and guide the development of the voice.

For an instrument, many beginners start with the harmonium because it is widely available and helps with learning pitch. Students who wish to enter the classical tradition more deeply may take up a bowed string instrument such as the dilruba, which is more portable than the taus and well suited to following a vocal melody. Whatever the instrument, steady daily practice matters far more than the amount of time spent in any single session.

Practice with Patience and Devotion

Progress in this tradition is gradual, and patience is part of the discipline. Begin with one or two Raags and a few Shabads, learning them thoroughly rather than rushing to cover many. Practice the basics of voice and rhythm regularly. Above all, remember that Gurmat Sangeet is a form of worship; the aim is not performance for its own sake but the sincere offering of the sacred word through music. Approached in this spirit, the study itself becomes a meaningful practice, and skill grows naturally over time.

Homework

Based on what you have studied about beginning to learn Gurmat Sangeet, design a personal 30-day learning intention — not a rigid schedule, but a thoughtful plan. In 300–350 words, describe: what aspect of Gurmat Sangeet you most want to deepen (listening, understanding raag, learning an instrument, or memorizing Shabads), what specific resources or people you would draw on, what one small daily practice you could realistically sustain, and how you would know at the end of 30 days that you had made progress. Be honest about the obstacles you anticipate and how you might work with them.

lessons.title: Raag Identification by Ear: Listening Deeply to Gurmat Sangeet
lessons.html:
Introduction

One of the most transformative skills a student of Gurmat Sangeet can develop is the ability to recognize a raag by ear — to hear the opening phrases of a performance and identify the melodic grammar underlying it. This may sound like an advanced musicological skill reserved for trained classical musicians, but the tradition of Gurmat Sangeet has always placed listening at its center. The Gurus themselves composed within specific raags, and the Sangat historically developed a felt familiarity with these melodic frameworks through decades of immersive participation in kirtan. Before notation systems, before formal pedagogy, the ear was the primary instrument of transmission.

This lesson bridges theory and practice. In earlier lessons we surveyed the thirty-one main raags of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji and explored the relationship between raag and shabad. Now we go deeper, asking: what does a raag actually sound like? What are its characteristic phrases (mukhya ang), its forbidden notes (varjit swar), and its particular emotional coloring (ras)? How does a trained or even an attentive untrained listener begin to distinguish Raag Bilawal from Raag Bhairav, or Raag Tilang from Raag Bihagra?

This is also a lesson in epistemology — in how we know what we know through sound rather than through text. Much of what makes Gurmat Sangeet distinct from academic musicology is that its transmission has always been primarily oral-aural, from teacher to student, from ragi to Sangat, in the living sonic environment of the Gurdwara. Reading about raags in a textbook develops only a partial understanding; hearing them, and hearing them repeatedly with attentive ears, develops the deeper kind of knowing the tradition calls ਸੁਣਿਆ (suniaa) — listening that transforms.

In this lesson we will study the listening process systematically: the structural features that make each raag identifiable, the practice of comparative listening, and the way regular engagement with Gurmat Sangeet recordings can develop genuine raag-recognition skills over time. We will focus on a handful of raags as case studies, drawing attention to the specific musical features that a careful listener can learn to notice.

The Anatomy of a Raag: What the Ear Must Learn to Hear

To listen intelligently to a raag, a student must first understand what features define it. A raag is not simply a scale — that misunderstanding is common and leads to frustration when two raags that share nearly identical notes sound entirely different in performance. What distinguishes a raag is a combination of several interlocking elements, and learning to hear each of them separately before integrating them is the key to developing genuine listening comprehension.

The most basic element is the set of notes (ਸੁਰ, swar) the raag uses in its ascent (ਆਰੋਹ, aroha) and descent (ਅਵਰੋਹ, avaroha). Some raags use all seven notes (called ਸੰਪੂਰਨ, sampuran) in both directions; others use six (ਖਾੜਵ, khadav) or five (ਔੜਵ, audav) in one or both directions. Learning to count the notes in a performance — to notice when a performer skips directly from one note to another without passing through the one in between — is a foundational listening skill. The ear quickly learns that certain raags feel like they leap across intervals while others move in stepwise, conjunct motion.

Beyond the note set, each raag has characteristic melodic phrases called ਪਕੜ (pakad) — literally, a grip or catch. These are short motifs of three to six notes that instantly signal which raag a performer is in, even to a relatively untrained listener who has heard the raag many times. The pakad functions somewhat like a musical signature. For example, listeners familiar with Raag Bhairav often recognize it not from a systematic analysis of its notes but from the distinctive way it hovers around the komal Re (flattened second) in the lower register. This hovering creates an unmistakable gravity and solemnity that is recognizable even before the intellectual identification occurs.

A third element is the vadi and samvadi — the most important and second-most important note of the raag, respectively. These notes are emphasized throughout a performance; phrases return to them, rest on them, and orbit around them. Learning to identify which note a performer keeps returning to — which note functions as a kind of home base — trains the ear to orient within the raag's internal hierarchy. This is a skill that develops with patient listening over months and years, not hours.

Finally, each raag has a time and season of performance (समां, samaa) that is part of its character. While modern Gurmat Sangeet performances do not always observe these restrictions strictly, understanding them helps the listener contextualize the emotional quality of the raag. Morning raags like Raag Bhairav and Raag Bilawal carry an quality of freshness and aspiration. Evening raags like Raag Yaman Kalyan and Raag Bihagra evoke longing, transition, and the approaching night. These associations are not arbitrary — they reflect centuries of observation about how human emotional states interact with time, light, and the body's rhythms.

Practically speaking, a student developing listening skills should approach raag-recognition the way one approaches learning to identify bird calls or to distinguish wine varietals by taste: not through memorization alone, but through repeated, attentive, pleasurable exposure. The goal is not to interrupt the experience of kirtan with anxious identification exercises, but to develop a background familiarity that deepens appreciation and connection over time.

Case Studies in Listening: Three Contrasting Raags

Rather than surveying all thirty-one raags superficially, this section offers three detailed case studies that illustrate contrasting listening profiles. These three raags — Raag Bhairav, Raag Yaman Kalyan, and Raag Asa — appear frequently in Gurmat Sangeet and represent three quite different emotional and sonic territories.

Raag Bhairav is one of the oldest and most revered raags in the Hindustani classical tradition, and it holds an important place in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. Its defining characteristic to the ear is the use of komal (flattened) Re and komal Dha — the second and sixth degrees of the scale are lowered by a half step. This creates a soundscape of unusual gravity and interiority. The flattened second gives the raag its characteristic quality of pressed, inward longing rather than outward exuberance. Listeners often describe Bhairav as feeling like early dawn — the darkness before sunrise, the stillness before the world wakes. When Gurbani compositions in Raag Bhairav are sung, the music reinforces themes of humility, divine presence in silence, and the soul's early-morning orientation toward the Divine.

Raag Yaman Kalyan presents an entirely different sonic personality. Sometimes called simply Raag Yaman, it is characterized by the use of tivra (sharp) Ma — the fourth degree of the scale is raised by a half step, creating an openness and lift that is immediately perceptible to even an untrained ear. Where Bhairav feels inward and heavy, Yaman Kalyan feels expansive and luminous. It is traditionally associated with the early evening, and the raised Ma gives it a quality of gentle yearning that is neither sorrowful nor ecstatic but somewhere in between — a kind of serene longing. In Gurmat Sangeet performances, Shabads in this raag often feel like they open the heart to devotion gently, without urgency or demand.

Raag Asa, the raag in which the well-known Asa di Var is sung, is a raag of the early morning hours and is among the most commonly heard in Gurdwaras worldwide. Its note set and characteristic phrases create a sound that is active, forthright, and alert rather than contemplative. The Asa di Var tradition has its own specific melodic setting (ਵਾਰ, vaar) that is itself a learnable piece of musical heritage, and many Sikhs who have never formally studied Gurmat Sangeet can nonetheless recognize Asa di Var's distinctive opening because they have absorbed it through years of Sangat. This is itself a profound example of aural transmission at work.

Comparing these three raags in listening sessions — ideally using recorded performances by recognized Hazoori Ragis or masters of Gurmat Sangeet — reveals how dramatically the raag shapes the listener's emotional and physiological state. The same theological concept, sung in these three different raags, produces three entirely different inner experiences. This is not incidental — the Gurus selected raags with profound intentionality, matching the raag's emotional character to the content and spiritual purpose of each composition.

Comparative Listening as a Spiritual Practice

The tradition of Gurmat Sangeet does not separate musical education from spiritual development. In the classical Gurmat Sangeet pedagogy, learning to listen is not merely an academic exercise — it is a form of ਸੇਵਾ (sevaa) and ਭਗਤੀ (bhagti). The student who trains the ear to recognize a raag is also training the mind to become attentive, receptive, and present. The two processes reinforce each other in ways that purely theoretical study cannot replicate.

Comparative listening — the practice of intentionally placing two performances side by side for close listening — is a powerful pedagogical method that both develops raag-recognition skills and deepens spiritual sensitivity. When a student listens to the same Shabad in two different raag settings, or listens to two different Shabads in the same raag, patterns emerge that would otherwise remain invisible. The raag's personality becomes clearer when contrasted with another raag's personality. The Shabad's meaning seems to shift and deepen when the musical frame around it changes.

A recommended listening exercise for this lesson is the following: select any Shabad that you know well and search for performances of it in its assigned raag. Then listen to any other performance — perhaps the same Shabad sung in a contemporary style without strict raag adherence — and notice what changes. This is not an exercise in raag purism or in judging which is better. It is an exercise in noticing: noticing what the raag adds, what it emphasizes, what emotional dimensions of the Shabad it brings forward, and what might be lost when the raag is not the organizing frame.

Many students of Gurmat Sangeet report that developing listening skills changes their experience of Gurdwara kirtan permanently and profoundly. Where once they heard music as a pleasant ambient backdrop to prayer, they begin to hear structure, intention, and depth. The Ragi's choices — which note to hold, where to place an ornament (ਮੀੰਡ, meend), how long to dwell on a particular phrase before resolving it — become legible. The Sangat's collective emotional response begins to make sense not just as devotion but as a sophisticated musical-spiritual engagement that has been refined over five centuries.

This deepened listening also generates a particular kind of humility. The more one learns about the complexity and depth of Gurmat Sangeet, the more one appreciates how much there is yet to know. Master ragis speak of spending their entire lives studying a single raag and still finding new dimensions in it. For a student at the beginning of this journey, that humility is itself a gift — an orientation of perpetual openness and learning that aligns well with the broader Sikh spiritual disposition of ਨਿਮਰਤਾ (nimrata), humility before the infinite.

Key Terms

  • ਪਕੜ (Pakad) — The characteristic catch-phrase or identifying motif of a raag; a short melodic phrase that signals which raag is being performed.
  • ਵਾਦੀ (Vadi) — The most important or dominant note of a raag, to which phrases repeatedly return and on which they often rest.
  • ਆਰੋਹ / ਅਵਰੋਹ (Aroha / Avaroha) — The ascending and descending note sequences of a raag, which may differ from each other and may not include all seven notes.
  • ਕੋਮਲ (Komal) — Literally "soft"; refers to a flattened note (lowered by a half step) used in certain raags, giving them a characteristic gravity or interiority.
  • ਤੀਵਰ (Tivra) — Literally "sharp" or "intense"; refers to a raised note (raised by a half step), most commonly the Ma, that gives certain raags like Yaman Kalyan their characteristic openness and lift.
  • ਸੁਣਿਆ (Suniaa) — The act of deep, transformative listening; a spiritual concept in Gurmat emphasized in Gurbani, referring to listening that changes the listener's inner state.

Discussion Questions

  1. The tradition holds that listening to the right raag at the right time of day produces a particular emotional and spiritual effect. Do you find this idea intuitive or strange? What does your own experience of music at different times of day suggest to you about this claim?
  2. In your own listening experience — in Gurdwara, at home, or at special programs — have you ever noticed a piece of kirtan affecting you more powerfully than you expected? Looking back, what musical or contextual factors might have contributed to that experience?
  3. The pakad of a raag functions like a musical signature that the ear learns to recognize before the mind can articulate why. What does this suggest about the relationship between conscious analysis and embodied knowing in musical learning?
  4. Many contemporary kirtan performances do not observe strict raag discipline. As a student of Gurmat Sangeet, how do you think about this? Is strict raag adherence essential to the spiritual function of kirtan, or can devotion and musical beauty achieve similar ends through other means?
  5. The concept of ਸੁਣਿਆ (suniaa) in Gurbani points to a quality of listening that goes beyond hearing sound — it implies a transformation of the listener. How might developing raag-recognition skills serve or interfere with this kind of deep listening?

Further Reading

  • Joep Bor (ed.), The Raga Guide — A comprehensive multi-volume resource with recorded examples covering major Hindustani raags; essential for developing aural familiarity alongside theoretical knowledge.
  • Surinder Singh Kohli, A Critical Study of Adi Granth — Contains analysis of the raag assignments in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji and discussion of their musical-theological significance.
  • Bhai Gurcharan Singh, lectures and demonstrations available through various Sikh educational archives — The late master's recorded teaching sessions on individual raags are among the most accessible entry points for aural learning of Gurmat Sangeet raags.
  • Vikram Sampath, My Name is Gauhar Jaan — While not about Gurmat Sangeet specifically, this biography of one of the early twentieth century's greatest Hindustani vocalists provides vivid context for the world of raag performance into which Sikh musicians were also embedded.
  • Key Takeaways
  • A raag is identified not by its note set alone but by its pakad (characteristic phrases), vadi (dominant note), and emotional coloring — all features the ear can learn to recognize with attentive practice.
  • Comparative listening — placing different raags or different settings of the same Shabad side by side — is one of the most effective methods for developing genuine raag-recognition skills.
  • The Gurus' assignment of specific Shabads to specific raags was intentional: the raag's emotional character was chosen to match and amplify the shabad's spiritual content.
  • Learning to listen deeply to Gurmat Sangeet is itself a spiritual practice rooted in the Gurbani concept of ਸੁਣਿਆ (suniaa) — the kind of transformative listening that changes the listener from the inside.
  • Raag-recognition skills develop over months and years of pleasurable, attentive exposure — not through memorization exercises alone, but through immersive engagement with the living tradition of kirtan.

Homework

Choose two raags from those discussed in this lesson — Raag Bhairav, Raag Yaman Kalyan, and Raag Asa — and find at least one recorded Gurmat Sangeet performance for each. Listen to both recordings in a quiet setting, without multitasking, for their full duration. In 300–350 words, describe what you heard: the mood or emotional quality each raag created, any musical features you could identify (a note that felt emphasized, a phrase that kept returning, a quality of the scale), and how the raag's character seemed to interact with the Shabad being sung. Conclude with a sentence about which experience surprised you most and why.

lessons.title: The Aesthetics of Devotion: Rasa Theory and Gurmat Sangeet
lessons.html:
Introduction

Every musical tradition that serves a religious or spiritual function grapples, explicitly or implicitly, with a central question: what is the relationship between beauty and truth? Can a piece of music be aesthetically powerful and spiritually effective at the same time? And if so, how does aesthetic experience serve — rather than distract from — the pursuit of the Divine? In the Sikh tradition, this question is not left abstract or unresolved. The philosophical framework that underlies Gurmat Sangeet offers a sophisticated and deeply considered answer, rooted in both the classical Indian theory of aesthetic experience (rasa) and the unique theological vision of the Gurus.

Classical Indian aesthetic theory, codified most influentially in the Natyashastra of Bharata Muni, identified eight primary aesthetic emotions or rasas — from the Sanskrit root meaning "juice" or "essence" — that great art could evoke in a prepared audience. These rasas ranged from ਸ਼ਿੰਗਾਰ (shringar, romantic love or beauty) to ਕਰੁਣ (karuna, compassion or grief) to ਵੀਰ (veer, heroism or courage) to ਸ਼ਾਂਤ (shant, peace or serenity). The theory held that when an artist successfully evoked a rasa in an audience, the audience experienced a form of aesthetic pleasure that was simultaneously emotional, cognitive, and, in its highest form, spiritually illuminating.

Gurmat Sangeet's relationship with rasa theory is both inherited and transformed. The classical tradition of Indian music from which Gurmat Sangeet drew was deeply shaped by rasa thinking, and the Gurus composed within this aesthetic world. But the Gurus also reoriented the aesthetic framework: in Gurmat Sangeet, the ultimate purpose of all aesthetic experience — of all the rasas — is the cultivation of one supreme rasa, the rasa of ਭਗਤੀ (bhagti), devotional love for the Divine. This transformation of classical aesthetic theory into a devotional framework is one of the most intellectually significant contributions of the Sikh musical tradition.

This lesson explores rasa theory as it applies to Gurmat Sangeet, examining how the Gurus employed and reoriented classical aesthetics, how specific raags map onto specific rasas, and what this framework implies for both performers and listeners of Sikh sacred music. Understanding rasa theory does not require musical training — it requires only attentive reflection on your own experience of great art and a willingness to think carefully about why beauty moves us.

Classical Rasa Theory and Its Indian Musical Context

The word ਰਸ (rasa) is one of the richest and most contested terms in the entire vocabulary of classical Indian aesthetics. At its most literal, it means "juice" — the juice of a fruit, the essential liquid that nourishes and delights. Applied to art and music, it came to mean the essential emotional flavor or essence of a work — the thing that makes a performance not merely technically correct but truly alive and moving. Rasa is what differentiates a great performance from a merely competent one; it is what the audience receives when a performer has not only mastered technique but has also achieved genuine emotional truth in the moment of performance.

Bharata Muni's Natyashastra, composed sometime between the second century BCE and the second century CE, is the foundational text of this tradition, though the theory it articulates was certainly older. Bharata enumerated eight rasas: shringar (beauty and love), hasya (humor and joy), karuna (compassion and grief), raudra (fury and passion), veer (heroism and courage), bhayanak (terror and awe), bibhatsa (disgust), and adbhuta (wonder and amazement). Each rasa had a corresponding bhava (emotion) in the performer, a dominant color, a presiding deity, and specific performative techniques associated with evoking it. Later theorists added shant (peace and serenity) as a ninth rasa, and this addition proved particularly important for devotional music traditions.

Within Hindustani classical music — the tradition from which Gurmat Sangeet developed — each raag came to be associated with specific rasas. This association was not always systematic or universally agreed upon, and different gharanas (musical lineages) sometimes held different views. But certain associations became culturally stable: Raag Bhairav was associated with shant and karuna; Raag Bhairavi with karuna and shringar (in its aspect of longing rather than fulfillment); Raag Darbari Kannada with veer and the dignity of courts; Raag Malkauns with a deep, introspective gravity. These associations became part of the raag's identity, shaping how performers approached them and what audiences expected.

Understanding this classical context matters because it was the aesthetic world the Gurus inhabited. Guru Nanak Dev Ji, Guru Amar Das Ji, and the other Guru-composers were not composing in a cultural vacuum — they were composing for audiences that understood and felt these aesthetic associations. When the Gurus assigned a Shabad to a particular raag, they were drawing on a shared aesthetic vocabulary that their Sangat could feel, even if they could not articulate the theory. The choice of raag was itself a theological act: it communicated something about the Shabad's emotional register and spiritual purpose before a single word was heard.

The Gurmat Transformation: From Rasa to Bhagti Rasa

While the Gurus drew on classical rasa theory, they did not simply adopt it unchanged. The most significant transformation in Gurmat aesthetics is the subordination of all individual rasas to what may be called ਭਗਤੀ ਰਸ (bhagti rasa) — the rasa of devotional love and spiritual longing. In Gurmat Sangeet, every other emotional flavor is not eliminated but reoriented: shringar becomes the longing of the soul for the Divine; karuna becomes grief at separation from Waheguru; veer becomes the courage of the saint-warrior who faces the ego's attachments with fearlessness; shant becomes the stillness of a mind that has found its resting place in Naam.

This reorientation is visible throughout Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. Gurbani regularly uses the imagery of shringar — the adorning of a bride for her beloved, the longing of the virahini (the woman separated from her beloved) — as a metaphor for the soul's relationship with the Divine. This is not incidental or merely decorative. The Gurus understood that the most powerful human experiences of longing, love, and devotion could become vehicles for spiritual awakening if properly reoriented. The aesthetic experience of shringar rasa in a kirtan context is not designed to produce romantic sentiment but to use the full force of that sentiment to open the heart toward the Divine.

Similarly, the raag associated with karuna (grief and compassion) becomes, in Gurmat Sangeet, an opportunity to feel the pathos of the jivatma (individual soul) caught in the web of haumai (ego-driven existence), separated from its source. Gurbani compositions in raags associated with karuna often speak of this separation — the pain of viog (separation from the Beloved) — and the music amplifies this feeling in a way that is not merely sorrowful but ultimately redemptive. The grief itself becomes a doorway: to feel the separation deeply is to begin longing for reunion, and that longing is the beginning of bhagti.

The philosophical implications of this framework are significant. Gurmat aesthetics holds that art — including music — is not a morally neutral activity. It has a direction: toward or away from the Divine. Music that produces rasa without spiritual orientation may provide temporary pleasure, but it does not serve the soul's deepest need. Music that produces rasa within the framework of bhagti — that uses aesthetic experience to open the heart toward ਪ੍ਰਭੂ (Prabhu, the Divine) — becomes a form of worship in itself. This is why kirtan is not background music in a Gurdwara but the central devotional act: it is the moment when aesthetic experience and spiritual practice become one.

Contemporary scholars have noted that this Gurmat transformation of rasa theory has parallels in other South Asian devotional traditions — particularly in the Vaishnava bhakti movements that developed bhakti rasa theory, and in Sufi musical traditions that use sama (sacred listening) as a path to divine proximity. Comparative study of these traditions enriches our understanding of Gurmat Sangeet without reducing it to merely one instance of a general type. The Sikh tradition's specific theological commitments — its rejection of polytheism, its insistence on the Nirgun (formless) nature of the Divine, its emphasis on the householder's path over renunciation — shape its aesthetics in distinctive ways that deserve to be studied on their own terms.

Practical Aesthetics: How Ragis Embody Rasa in Performance

The theory of rasa in Gurmat Sangeet is not merely an intellectual framework — it has direct practical implications for how ragis approach performance. A ragi who understands that the goal of kirtan is to evoke bhagti rasa in the Sangat approaches their preparation differently than a performer whose only goal is technical correctness. The preparation includes not only practice of notes and rhythms but also ਨਿਮਰਤਾ (nimrata, humility), ਅਰਦਾਸ (ardas, prayer), and personal engagement with the Shabad's meaning.

Master ragis in the Gurmat Sangeet tradition consistently emphasize that rasa cannot be manufactured — it must be genuinely felt by the performer if it is to be transmitted to the listener. A ragi who sings about the soul's longing for the Divine without having that longing in their own heart may produce technically beautiful music but will not produce rasa. This is why the great masters of Gurmat Sangeet have always insisted that musical training is incomplete without spiritual practice, and that spiritual practice deepens musical expression. The two are not separate tracks — they are one path.

For the listener or member of Sangat, the corresponding practice is ਧਿਆਨ (dhiaan, attention or meditation). Rasa theory holds that the audience's receptivity is itself a condition for the communication of rasa. A Sangat that is present, attentive, and spiritually oriented provides a different kind of listening environment than one that is distracted or disengaged. The collective attention of a deeply focused Sangat actually enables the ragi to reach greater depths in the performance — a feedback loop of mutual elevation that experienced participants in kirtan programs recognize immediately.

This has practical implications for how we attend kirtan. If rasa theory is correct, then our preparation for listening to kirtan matters. Coming to the Gurdwara having read or reflected on the Shabad beforehand, having done some ਸਿਮਰਨ (simran) to settle the mind, having let go — at least provisionally — of the day's preoccupations creates the conditions for genuine rasa experience. The Sangat that arrives ready to receive will receive more. This is not a passive process but an active spiritual engagement in which the listener plays a crucial role.

Key Terms

  • ਰਸ (Rasa) — Literally "juice" or "essence"; in classical Indian aesthetics, the emotional flavor or felt quality evoked by great art; in Gurmat Sangeet, the rasas are all ultimately oriented toward bhagti rasa.
  • ਭਾਵ (Bhava) — The underlying emotional state or feeling that gives rise to rasa; the authentic emotion in the performer that enables rasa to be transmitted to the audience.
  • ਭਗਤੀ ਰਸ (Bhagti Rasa) — The supreme rasa in Gurmat aesthetics: the rasa of devotional love and spiritual longing for the Divine, toward which all other rasas are ultimately directed.
  • ਵਿਯੋਗ (Viyog) — Separation; in Gurmat poetry and music, the pathos of the soul separated from the Divine, whose feeling is itself a doorway to longing and devotion.
  • ਧਿਆਨ (Dhiaan) — Focused attention or meditative awareness; in the context of kirtan listening, the quality of receptive presence that enables the audience to receive rasa.
  • ਸ਼ਾਂਤ ਰਸ (Shant Rasa) — The rasa of peace, serenity, and transcendent stillness; often considered the highest rasa in devotional music traditions, associated with the deep inner calm of spiritual realization.

Discussion Questions

  1. Can you recall a piece of music — from any tradition — that moved you in a way you could not fully explain? Reflecting back on that experience through the lens of rasa theory, what rasa do you think was evoked, and what conditions (your state of mind, the performance context, your familiarity with the music) contributed to its effectiveness?
  2. The Gurmat transformation of rasa theory holds that all emotional experiences can be reoriented toward the Divine. Do you find this framework spiritually compelling, or does it feel like it risks instrumentalizing genuine human emotions (grief, joy, longing) by making them always serve a further purpose?
  3. Rasa theory suggests that the audience's preparation and receptivity are conditions for the communication of rasa. What does this imply about the responsibilities of the Sangat in a kirtan program? How does this compare with your usual experience of attending kirtan?
  4. The concept of viyog — separation from the Divine — is used in Gurbani as a source of intense spiritual longing. How do you personally relate to this framework? Is spiritual longing something you recognize in your own experience, and does music seem to have a role in evoking or deepening it?
  5. Scholars have noted parallels between Gurmat bhagti rasa and Sufi sama traditions, as well as Vaishnava bhakti rasa. What might comparative study of these traditions reveal about the universal human need for devotional music, and what might it reveal about the distinctiveness of the Sikh tradition's approach?

Further Reading

  • Kapila Vatsyayan, Bharata: The Natyashastra — A scholarly translation and commentary on the foundational text of rasa theory; provides essential background for understanding the classical framework from which Gurmat aesthetics developed.
  • Pashaura Singh, The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority — Includes analysis of the aesthetic and devotional frameworks underlying Gurbani composition and its musical settings.
  • Regula Qureshi, Sufi Music of India and Pakistan — A detailed ethnomusicological study of sama in the Qawwali tradition; invaluable for comparative understanding of devotional music's aesthetics in the South Asian context.
  • Daljeet Singh, Essentials of Sikhism — Contains accessible discussion of Gurmat philosophy as it relates to art, beauty, and devotional practice.
  • Key Takeaways
  • Classical Indian rasa theory identifies eight primary aesthetic emotions (rasas) that great art can evoke; Gurmat Sangeet inherited this framework and transformed it by making bhagti rasa — devotional love — the ultimate orientation of all aesthetic experience.
  • The Gurus' assignment of Shabads to specific raags was not arbitrary: it drew on stable cultural associations between raags and rasas to amplify the shabad's theological and emotional content.
  • In Gurmat aesthetics, rasa cannot be produced by technical skill alone — the ragi's authentic bhava (emotional truth) and spiritual preparation are understood as essential conditions for genuine rasa transmission.
  • The Sangat's attentive presence and spiritual preparation (dhiaan) are themselves conditions for the communication of rasa; listening to kirtan is an active spiritual engagement, not a passive reception.
  • The concept of viyog (separation from the Divine) is a key aesthetic-theological concept in Gurmat Sangeet, transforming the classical karuna rasa into a specifically devotional longing that is itself the beginning of spiritual awakening.

Homework

Select a Shabad from Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji that you have heard in kirtan and that you feel has a specific emotional quality — perhaps one that feels peaceful, or sorrowful, or joyful and expansive. Without needing to know the technical raag name, describe in 300–350 words the emotional flavor or rasa of the music as you have experienced it. Then reflect: does that emotional quality seem to match or deepen the meaning of the Shabad's words as you understand them? Using the vocabulary of rasa introduced in this lesson (shringar, karuna, shant, bhagti rasa), try to name what you experienced. Conclude with a reflection on whether knowing this framework changes how you want to listen to kirtan in the future.

lessons.title: Women in Gurmat Sangeet: History, Erasure, and Revival
lessons.html:
Introduction

Any serious study of Gurmat Sangeet must eventually confront a difficult historical question: where are the women? The classical tradition of Sikh sacred music, as it is most commonly narrated, centers predominantly on male figures — the Gurus themselves, the Rababi accompanists, the great lineages of Hazoori Ragis, the modern masters of revival. Women appear in this narrative mainly at the margins: as members of Sangat, as learners in family lineages, occasionally as exceptional individual performers whose names are recalled with admiration but whose stories are rarely told in depth.

This marginalization is not a feature of the Gurus' original vision. The theology of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji is strikingly egalitarian with respect to gender — Gurbani speaks consistently of the soul as feminine in relation to the masculine Divine, dissolving earthly gender distinctions in the ocean of devotional metaphor. Guru Nanak Dev Ji explicitly challenged gender-based restrictions on spiritual participation. Women were present in early Sikh Sangats as singers, learners, and participants in kirtan. The subsequent historical narrowing of women's formal roles in Gurmat Sangeet performance is a product of cultural and institutional forces that the tradition itself, at its theological core, does not endorse.

This lesson takes that narrowing seriously — tracing its historical causes, identifying the women who nevertheless managed to practice and transmit Gurmat Sangeet across the centuries, and examining the vibrant contemporary revival of women's participation in Gurmat Sangeet that has gathered extraordinary momentum in the early twenty-first century. Understanding this history enriches our picture of the tradition and challenges us to think carefully about the difference between what a tradition teaches and how institutions have sometimes practiced it.

This is also a lesson in historical recovery — in the work of finding figures, stories, and lineages that have been underdocumented and bringing them into clearer view. Such recovery work is itself an act of fidelity to the tradition's deepest values.

Theological Foundations: Gender, Soul, and the Divine in Gurmat

Before examining historical patterns, it is essential to understand what the Gurmat theological tradition itself says about women's spiritual and musical participation. This foundation matters because it establishes a standard against which historical practice can be evaluated — and often found wanting.

Gurbani's position on the spiritual equality of women is unambiguous and was radical in the historical context of sixteenth-century South Asia. Guru Nanak Dev Ji's verses on this subject are among the most forthright in any religious scripture of the period. The Guru critiqued social practices that assigned women a subordinate spiritual status and affirmed that the Divine is equally accessible to all regardless of gender, caste, or social station.

Equally significant is Gurbani's pervasive use of feminine imagery for the spiritual aspirant. Throughout Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, the soul (ਜੀਵਾਤਮਾ, jivatma) is figured as a bride (ਸੁਹਾਗਣ, suhagan) or as a woman longing for her Beloved (ਵਿਰਹਣ, virahin). The Divine is the husband or Beloved. This is not a patriarchal framing — it is a devotional inversion that places all human beings, regardless of their earthly gender, in the position of the feminine, receptive, longing soul before the Divine. The implication is that women's emotional and spiritual experience — particularly the experience of love, longing, and devotion — is not a deficit but a model for what every soul must cultivate.

The Gurus also institutionalized women's participation in practical ways. Mata Khivi Ji, the wife of Guru Angad Dev Ji, is mentioned by name in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji itself — an extraordinary honor — in recognition of her role in nurturing the Sangat through the institution of ਲੰਗਰ (langar). Bibi Bhani Ji, daughter of Guru Amar Das Ji and mother of Guru Ram Das Ji, was renowned for her devotion and spiritual attainment. These figures were not ornamental — they were central to the institutional and spiritual life of the early Sikh community.

The historical constriction of women's formal roles in Gurmat Sangeet performance therefore represents a deviation from the tradition's own founding principles — a deviation driven primarily by the surrounding culture's gender norms being imported into Sikh institutional practice, particularly after the social disruptions and political pressures of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Recognizing this is not an anachronistic imposition of modern values but a recovery of the tradition's own stated commitments.

Historical Patterns: Women as Performers and Transmitters

Despite the historical marginalization of women in formal Gurmat Sangeet lineages, women have always been present in the tradition as performers, learners, and transmitters — often in the domestic and community spheres that formal institutional histories have tended to overlook.

In the early Sikh community, there is evidence that women participated in kirtan programs both as performers and as composers. The tradition of ਕੀਰਤਨ ਸੋਹਿਲਾ (Kirtan Sohila) and other liturgical compositions being sung in household settings by women kept the musical tradition alive across generations in ways that formal ragi lineages alone could not have done. Families who maintained kirtan as a domestic practice — with women teaching children, learning from elders, and gathering for collective singing — were crucial nodes in the informal transmission network of Gurmat Sangeet.

The nineteenth and early twentieth centuries present a more complex picture. As Gurmat Sangeet became more formally institutionalized — with trained ragi jathas performing at major Gurdwaras, with competitions and festivals organized, with recording technologies beginning to capture performances — the formal spaces of performance became increasingly male-dominated. The same period saw, however, exceptional individual women who broke through these norms. Some came from family lineages where musical training was transmitted to daughters as well as sons. Others were encouraged by reform-minded Sikh institutions that took seriously the theological equality of women's participation.

The Singh Sabha movement of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, which sought to reform and revitalize Sikh practice, had a complicated relationship with women's musical participation. On one hand, Singh Sabha reformers were often progressive on questions of women's education and literacy. On the other hand, the reformers' emphasis on formal institutional structures and trained professional ragis tended to favor male performers who had access to formal training. Women who could not access institutional training were effectively excluded from formal performance spaces, regardless of their talent or devotion.

The postcolonial period brought new opportunities and new constraints. The partition of Punjab in 1947 was catastrophic for many musical lineages, disrupting family networks and uprooting communities. In the rebuilding of Sikh institutions in India, Pakistan, and across the diaspora, the reconstruction of Gurmat Sangeet traditions was often led by male performers who had survived and whose lineages were documented. Women's roles in this reconstruction have been systematically underdocumented, a gap that contemporary scholars and musicians are beginning to address.

Contemporary Revival: Women Reclaiming the Tradition

The late twentieth and especially the early twenty-first century have witnessed a remarkable revival of women's participation in formal Gurmat Sangeet performance. This revival has several distinct dimensions: the growing presence of women as Hazoori Ragis at major Gurdwaras, the formation of all-women ragi jathas, the growth of women's Gurmat Sangeet education programs, and a generational shift in which young women are pursuing serious, formal training in classical Gurmat Sangeet in unprecedented numbers.

The debate around women serving as Hazoori Ragis at Harmandir Sahib (the Golden Temple) in Amritsar is perhaps the most high-profile expression of this revival — and also of the resistance it has encountered. Hazoori Ragis perform kirtan within the inner sanctum of Harmandir Sahib continuously, maintaining the tradition of ਅਖੰਡ ਕੀਰਤਨ (akhand kirtan, unbroken kirtan). Whether women should serve in this formal capacity has been a subject of significant controversy. Supporters point to the foundational theological equality in Gurbani; opponents cite institutional tradition and practical considerations. This debate is ongoing and reflects broader questions about the relationship between theological principle and institutional practice in the Sikh community.

Beyond the specific controversy at Harmandir Sahib, the broader landscape of women's Gurmat Sangeet practice has transformed significantly. Female ragi jathas now perform at Gurdwaras around the world, at akhand path programs, at major Sikh celebrations, and at increasingly prominent platforms. Institutions offering Gurmat Sangeet training — including residential programs, university courses, and community academies — have enrolled women in growing numbers, and some of the most technically accomplished young Gurmat Sangeet performers of the current generation are women whose rigorous training rivals that of any male counterpart.

The diaspora has played a particularly important role in this revival. Communities in North America, the United Kingdom, and Australia have often been more open to women's formal participation in kirtan programs than some more traditional institutions in Punjab. Diaspora Gurdwaras have provided platforms for female ragi jathas and have supported women's musical training in ways that have had a feedback effect on the broader tradition. Young women who grow up attending kirtan programs where women perform professionally come to see such participation as natural and expected rather than exceptional.

This contemporary revival is not without tensions and debates within the community. Questions about appropriate dress, the role of the Rehat Maryada (Sikh code of conduct), the relationship between local Gurdwara customs and Panthic (community-wide) decisions, and the politics of who speaks authoritatively for Sikh tradition all intersect with questions about women's musical participation. Engaging these questions thoughtfully — without dismissing the concerns of traditionalists or minimizing the legitimate claims of women seeking full participation — is itself a form of theological and communal work that the tradition requires of its members.

Key Terms

  • ਸੁਹਾਗਣ (Suhagan) — A married woman whose husband is alive and present; in Gurbani, a metaphor for the soul that has found union with the Divine, as contrasted with the virahin who remains in separation.
  • ਵਿਰਹਣ (Virahin) — A woman separated from her beloved; in Gurbani, a pervasive metaphor for the soul in a state of longing and separation from the Divine, whose anguish is itself a form of devotion.
  • ਹਜ਼ੂਰੀ ਰਾਗੀ (Hazoori Ragi) — A ragi who performs kirtan in the direct presence (hazoori) of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji at a major Gurdwara, particularly at Harmandir Sahib; the highest formal designation for a practicing Gurmat Sangeet performer.
  • ਰਹਿਤ ਮਰਿਆਦਾ (Rehat Maryada) — The Sikh code of conduct ratified by the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee; the primary institutional document governing formal Sikh practice, whose interpretation in relation to women's kirtan is a subject of ongoing discussion.
  • ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ (Singh Sabha) — The reform movement of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries that sought to revitalize and codify Sikh practice; its institutional legacy continues to shape formal Gurmat Sangeet structures today.
  • ਅਖੰਡ ਕੀਰਤਨ (Akhand Kirtan) — Unbroken or continuous kirtan; a practice associated particularly with Harmandir Sahib, where kirtan is performed continuously during the Gurdwara's open hours by formally designated Hazoori Ragis.

Discussion Questions

  1. The theological foundation of Gurmat affirms women's full spiritual equality, yet institutional practice has historically restricted their formal participation in kirtan. How do you account for this gap between principle and practice? What factors — historical, social, institutional — helped create and sustain it?
  2. The debate about women serving as Hazoori Ragis at Harmandir Sahib is both a theological debate and a political one. What do you think are the strongest arguments on each side? Where do you stand, and why?
  3. Historical recovery work — finding and telling the stories of women who practiced and transmitted Gurmat Sangeet despite institutional barriers — is itself an act of fidelity to the tradition's values. What other historical erasures in the Gurmat Sangeet tradition might benefit from similar recovery work?
  4. The diaspora has often been more open to women's formal participation in kirtan than some institutions in Punjab. What does this suggest about the relationship between geography, community norms, and the evolution of religious practice? Is diaspora-driven change in Sikh practice authentic, or does it risk losing connection with the tradition's roots?
  5. Gurbani's use of feminine imagery for the soul's relationship with the Divine is one of its most distinctive aesthetic features. How does understanding this imagery change the way you hear or read Gurbani? What does it suggest about the tradition's fundamental orientation toward gender?

Further Reading

  • Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, The Feminine Principle in the Sikh Vision of the Transcendent — A landmark scholarly study of feminist theology in the Sikh tradition; essential reading for understanding Gurbani's gender theology and its implications for practice.
  • Doris Jakobsh, Relocating Gender in Sikh History: Transformation, Meaning and Identity — A rigorous historical examination of how gender roles in Sikhism have changed over time, with important implications for understanding women's musical participation.
  • Pashaura Singh and Louis E. Fenech (eds.), The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies — Contains several chapters relevant to women's roles in Sikh institutional life and devotional practice.
  • Recordings of prominent contemporary female ragi jathas available through various Sikh media platforms — Engaging directly with the living voices of women performing Gurmat Sangeet today is itself a form of study that no text alone can replace.
  • Key Takeaways
  • Gurbani's theology consistently affirms women's spiritual equality and uses feminine imagery for the soul's relationship with the Divine — a foundation that makes women's exclusion from formal Gurmat Sangeet performance a deviation from the tradition's own principles.
  • Women have always been present in Gurmat Sangeet as performers and transmitters, particularly in domestic and community spheres that formal institutional histories have underrepresented.
  • Historical constrictions on women's formal roles in Gurmat Sangeet were driven primarily by surrounding cultural norms rather than by Gurmat theology, and were intensified by institutional formalization during the Singh Sabha period and the disruptions of partition.
  • A significant revival of women's formal participation in Gurmat Sangeet has gathered momentum in the early twenty-first century, with the diaspora playing a particularly important enabling role.
  • Ongoing debates about women's participation in formal kirtan spaces reflect broader questions about institutional authority, theological interpretation, and the relationship between principle and practice in contemporary Sikh communities.

Homework

Research one contemporary female ragi jatha or individual female Gurmat Sangeet performer — look for recorded performances, interviews, or biographical profiles through Sikh media platforms, YouTube channels dedicated to Gurmat Sangeet, or Sikh news sources. Watch or listen to at least one full performance. In 300–400 words, write a profile that covers: who they are and their musical background or training, what their performance reveals about their mastery of Gurmat Sangeet, and what their work contributes to the tradition. Conclude with a reflection on what this artist's presence in the tradition means to you personally as a student of Gurmat Sangeet.

lessons.title: Gurmat Sangeet Across the Diaspora: Transmission, Transformation, and Identity
lessons.html:
Introduction

Gurmat Sangeet has always traveled with the Sikh people. From the time of Guru Nanak Dev Ji's udaasis (journeys) across South Asia, Central Asia, the Middle East, and beyond, kirtan has been carried by Sikhs as an essential expression of their faith, their identity, and their community. The twentieth century brought the largest dispersal of Sikh communities in history — first through the partition of Punjab in 1947, then through labor migration to the United Kingdom in the 1950s and 1960s, then through professional migration to North America, Australia, and Europe from the 1960s onward, and subsequently through refugee flows, educational migration, and chain migration that has created significant Sikh communities in dozens of countries.

In each of these new contexts, Gurmat Sangeet has had to navigate a fundamental tension: how does a classical musical tradition, deeply embedded in a specific cultural, linguistic, and institutional world, survive and flourish when transplanted into radically different environments? How do communities maintain musical fidelity to the tradition when teachers are scarce, instruments are expensive, learning resources are limited, and the surrounding culture offers constant alternative musical stimuli? And what happens when the tradition, in adapting to survive, also changes — when diaspora communities develop distinctive local styles, pedagogical innovations, and institutional forms that differ from those in Punjab?

These questions are not merely academic. For Sikh communities in the diaspora, Gurmat Sangeet is not just music — it is one of the primary vehicles through which Sikh identity, memory, and belonging are transmitted to the next generation. The Gurdwara kirtan program is often the central communal gathering that binds a dispersed community together, and the quality, character, and continuity of that kirtan directly shapes the community's spiritual and cultural life. How kirtan sounds, who performs it, in what languages it is explained, and what pedagogical resources exist to teach it to young people — these practical questions have profound consequences for the tradition's future.

This lesson examines Gurmat Sangeet in the global diaspora: the challenges of transmission in new environments, the innovations and adaptations that have emerged, the role of digital technology in both preserving and transforming the tradition, and the complex questions of authenticity and identity that diaspora communities must constantly navigate. We will draw on examples from the United Kingdom, North America, and Australia — the three largest diaspora Sikh communities outside South Asia — while acknowledging that significant Sikh communities exist in many other parts of the world as well.

The Challenges of Transmission in Diaspora Contexts

The transmission of Gurmat Sangeet in diaspora contexts faces challenges that are both practical and cultural. On the practical side, the traditional model of transmission — a student (ਸ਼ਾਗਿਰਦ, shagird) living with or studying closely under a master (ਉਸਤਾਦ, ustaad) for years or decades — is extremely difficult to maintain in communities where trained masters are few, where students have competing educational and professional demands, and where the economic and social conditions that supported extended musical apprenticeships in Punjab do not exist.

The early diaspora communities of the 1950s and 1960s in the United Kingdom faced particularly acute challenges. Many Sikh immigrants arrived from agricultural backgrounds in Punjab with limited formal Gurmat Sangeet training, though many had absorbed a folk kirtan tradition through family and community practice. The first Gurdwaras in the UK were often converted houses or community centers with minimal resources, and the recruitment of trained ragis from Punjab was both expensive and logistically difficult. The result was that kirtan in many early diaspora Gurdwaras was performed by community members with varying levels of training — a democratization of participation that maintained the practice but sometimes at the cost of musical depth and classical fidelity.

The arrival of more formally trained ragis in subsequent decades, often through family sponsorship or Gurdwara invitation, introduced higher levels of classical Gurmat Sangeet into diaspora settings. But these ragis often found themselves in a pedagogical bind: the demand for kirtan performance was constant and time-consuming, leaving little opportunity for the sustained teaching relationships through which the tradition had been transmitted in Punjab. The ragi who performs for five or six hours of kirtan a day has limited energy for the slow, methodical teaching that classical Gurmat Sangeet transmission requires.

Cultural challenges compounded the practical ones. Young Sikhs growing up in Western countries were surrounded by Western popular music, and many found classical Gurmat Sangeet initially difficult to access — not because they lacked devotion but because the aesthetic framework of the tradition was unfamiliar. The pentatonic and heptatonic scales of Western popular music, the chord-based harmonic framework, the dominant role of percussion and bass — these created a default musical aesthetic in young people's ears that made the modal, melodically rich, rhythmically subtle world of classical Gurmat Sangeet feel, at least initially, remote and difficult.

The response of diaspora communities to these challenges has been creative and varied. Some communities invested heavily in bringing master teachers from Punjab for extended residencies. Others developed local teaching programs — afternoon classes, weekend workshops, holiday camps — that provided structured introduction to Gurmat Sangeet for young people. Others experimented with adapting the tradition's presentation, using English-language explanations of Shabad meanings, simplified instrumental approaches, and contemporary audiovisual materials to make the tradition more accessible without (in their view) compromising its core.

Innovation, Adaptation, and Questions of Authenticity

The adaptations that diaspora communities have made to Gurmat Sangeet performance and pedagogy have been productive and controversial in roughly equal measure. This section examines several specific areas of adaptation and the debates they have generated.

The most pervasive and debated adaptation has been the growing use of electronic instruments, particularly the electronic keyboard and electronic harmonium, alongside or instead of the traditional harmonium and tabla. In some diaspora Gurdwaras, kirtan programs incorporate synthesizers, drum machines, and amplification systems that would be entirely alien to traditional Gurmat Sangeet practice. Defenders of these adaptations argue that they make kirtan more accessible to contemporary ears and enable smaller communities with fewer trained musicians to maintain regular kirtan programs. Critics argue that these electronic adaptations fundamentally alter the sonic texture and emotional quality of Gurmat Sangeet in ways that may feel like kirtan but do not function as classical Gurmat Sangeet.

A different kind of adaptation has been the growth of what might be called ਕੀਰਤਨ ਸਿੱਖਿਆ (kirtan sikhia, kirtan education) programs that teach the basics of shabad singing and harmonium playing to large numbers of young people, prioritizing breadth of participation over depth of classical training. These programs — often run by Gurdwaras, Sikh camps, or community organizations — have produced a generation of diaspora Sikhs who can participate actively in kirtan rather than merely observing. The question is whether this breadth-first approach serves or hinders the long-term health of the classical tradition. Proponents point to the hundreds of young Sikhs who would otherwise have no musical connection to kirtan at all; critics note that very few participants in these programs go on to develop the deep classical training that traditional Gurmat Sangeet requires.

The concept of ਸ਼ੁੱਧਤਾ (shuddhata, purity or correctness) is central to debates about diaspora adaptations. Traditionalists in the Gurmat Sangeet world sometimes use the language of purity to argue for strict adherence to classical forms, correct raag singing, proper taal (rhythmic cycle) discipline, and the avoidance of non-traditional instruments. This is a legitimate concern rooted in real understanding of what the tradition requires at its highest levels. But the language of purity can also become a gatekeeping mechanism that excludes practitioners who do not have access to classical training — often through no fault of their own — and effectively reserves the tradition for an elite. Finding a middle path between authentic classical depth and genuine inclusivity is one of the defining challenges of Gurmat Sangeet in the diaspora.

Perhaps the most interesting innovations have come from musicians who combine deep classical Gurmat Sangeet training with serious engagement with Western musical traditions. A small but growing number of diaspora Sikh musicians are exploring the intersections between Gurmat Sangeet's modal and melodic world and Western classical music, jazz, and contemporary composition. These experiments — which include arrangements for string quartets, collaborations with jazz ensembles, and original compositions that draw on both traditions — raise profound questions about cross-cultural musical dialogue that the tradition has not previously had to navigate. Whether these explorations represent an enrichment of Gurmat Sangeet or a departure from it is a question the tradition will continue to work through.

The Digital Transformation: Technology, Preservation, and Access

The digital revolution of the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries has had a profound and ambivalent impact on Gurmat Sangeet in the diaspora. On one hand, digital technology has created an unprecedented resource for preservation, access, and learning. On the other hand, it has changed the conditions of musical transmission in ways that may have significant long-term consequences for how the tradition is experienced and learned.

The preservation benefits are immense. Recordings of great Gurmat Sangeet masters who performed in the mid-twentieth century — figures whose live performances could once be heard only by those present at specific Gurdwaras — are now available through digital archives, YouTube channels, and streaming platforms. A student in Vancouver, London, or Singapore can listen to the same recordings as a student in Amritsar.
