lessons.title: Guru Nanak Sahib and the Founding of Sikhi
lessons.summary: The birth and message of Guru Nanak Sahib, the three core principles of practice, the community at Kartarpur, and the choosing of a successor by merit.
lessons.html:
Full course contents
  1. Guru Nanak Sahib and the Founding of Sikhi
  2. The Early Gurus and the Building of Institutions
  3. Sacrifice and Conscience: The Martyrdoms
  4. Guru Hargobind Sahib and the Doctrine of Miri-Piri
  5. Guru Gobind Singh Sahib and the Founding of the Khalsa
  6. The Eighteenth Century, the Misls, and the Rise of Ranjit Singh

How we begin

This course studies Sikh history the way the historian Dr. Ganda Singh studied it: from sources, with care, and without exaggeration. Where tradition and evidence agree, we say so plainly. Where details differ across sources, we note it (Singh and Singh 1950).

Guru Nanak Sahib

Guru Nanak Sahib was born in 1469 near Talwandi, a village in the Punjab now called Nankana Sahib in present-day Pakistan. He is revered as the first of the Ten Gurus and the founder of the Sikh faith, known as ਸਿੱਖੀ. The word Sikh means a learner or disciple, and the heart of his message was the call to learn, to remember the Divine, and to live truthfully.

Guru Nanak Sahib taught the oneness of God. He rejected the idea that any one community, ritual, or caste held a monopoly on the sacred. According to widely shared tradition, after a profound spiritual experience he taught that outward labels matter far less than sincere devotion and ethical living (McLeod 1989).

Three principles of practice

  • Naam Japna — remembering and meditating on the Divine Name.
  • Kirat Karni — earning an honest living through one's own labor.
  • Vand Chakna — sharing with and serving others, especially those in need.

Kartarpur and succession

Guru Nanak Sahib is traditionally described as undertaking long journeys, the Udasis, to engage people of many backgrounds in dialogue. Toward the end of his life he settled at Kartarpur, where he established a community organized around collective worship, honest work, and the shared meal. One of his most consequential acts was the institution of succession: rather than passing leadership to a family member, he chose a devoted disciple, Bhai Lehna, for his humility and service, renaming him Guru Angad Sahib (Singh and Singh 1950).

References: Singh, Teja, and Ganda Singh. A Short History of the Sikhs. Bombay: Orient Longmans, 1950. McLeod, W. H. The Sikhs. New York: Columbia University Press, 1989.

Homework

Spend 20-30 minutes reflecting on why knowing history matters to your own spiritual practice and understanding of Sikhi. What questions about our past do you most want answered? Journal your thoughts.

lessons.title: The Early Gurus and the Building of Institutions
lessons.summary: Guru Angad Sahib through Guru Arjan Sahib gave the community Gurmukhi, Langar, the Manji system, the city of Amritsar, and the Adi Granth.
lessons.html:
Lasting institutions

The Gurus who followed Guru Nanak Sahib gave the young community lasting institutions. Some details are recorded differently across traditional sources; the outlines below reflect mainstream understanding (Singh and Singh 1950).

From Guru Angad Sahib to Guru Ram Das Sahib

Guru Angad Sahib (Guru from 1539) is closely associated with the development and promotion of the ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ script, in which Sikh scripture is written. He also strengthened the practice of ਲੰਗਰ, the free community kitchen where all sit together as equals.

Guru Amar Das Sahib (Guru from 1552) further institutionalized equality, reportedly requiring even visiting dignitaries to first sit in the Langar before meeting him. He organized the growing community through the Manji system, appointing local representatives to teach and guide Sikhs across regions. He is also remembered for advocating the dignity of women.

Guru Ram Das Sahib (Guru from 1574) founded the city that would become Amritsar, centered on a sacred pool, which grew into the spiritual heart of the Sikh world.

Guru Arjan Sahib and the Adi Granth

Guru Arjan Sahib (Guru from 1581), the fifth Guru, completed the great complex at Amritsar, the site now known as the Harmandir Sahib. His most enduring scholarly achievement was the compilation of the ਆਦਿ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ around 1604, gathering the hymns of the Gurus together with the verses of other revered saints and poets from diverse backgrounds (Grewal 1998).

Timeline of the early Guru period

Approx. yearGuruKey institution or event
1539Guru Angad SahibGurmukhi script, strengthening of Langar
1552Guru Amar Das SahibManji system, dignity of women
1574Guru Ram Das SahibFounding of Amritsar
1604Guru Arjan SahibCompilation of the Adi Granth
References: Singh, Teja, and Ganda Singh. A Short History of the Sikhs. Bombay: Orient Longmans, 1950. Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998.

Homework

Locate the Punjab on a map and research its geography: major rivers, cities, and neighboring regions during the time of Guru Nanak. Write a 250-word reflection on how geography might have shaped the Gurus' teachings and the flow of ideas in that region.

lessons.title: Sacrifice and Conscience: The Martyrdoms
lessons.summary: The martyrdoms of Guru Arjan Sahib (1606) and Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib (1675), and how they shaped Sikh ideas of conscience and fearlessness.
lessons.html:
Two martyrdoms at the center of memory

Two martyrdoms stand at the center of Sikh historical memory. Dr. Ganda Singh stressed that such events should be told from the earliest reliable sources, with neutral care for what can and cannot be confirmed (Singh and Singh 1950).

Guru Arjan Sahib, 1606

Guru Arjan Sahib was martyred in 1606. The historical context involved the politics of the Mughal court of the period and concerns among some authorities about the growing influence and independence of the Sikh community. According to Sikh tradition, the Guru remained serene and steadfast, accepting his fate as the Divine Will. His martyrdom is widely understood as a turning point that influenced his successors' approach to protecting the community (Grewal 1998).

Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib, 1675

Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib, the ninth Guru, was martyred in Delhi in 1675. The most widely transmitted account holds that he stood in defense of the freedom of conscience of others, including a community facing forced religious conversion under the policies of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb. Tradition relates that he chose to give his life rather than abandon the principle that people should be free to follow their own faith (McLeod 1989).

Why these events matter

  • They affirmed that religious freedom and the defense of the persecuted were core moral commitments, even at the cost of one's life.
  • They reinforced the Sikh value of fearlessness in the face of oppression while remaining spiritually centered.
  • They directly shaped the responses of the later Gurus and the community's readiness to defend itself and others.

These events are remembered not as celebrations of conflict but as testimonies to standing firm for truth and the rights of all people.

References: Singh, Teja, and Ganda Singh. A Short History of the Sikhs. Bombay: Orient Longmans, 1950. Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998. McLeod, W. H. The Sikhs. New York: Columbia University Press, 1989.

Homework

Research one aspect of pre-Guru Nanak Punjab: the Bhakti movement, Sufi traditions, or the caste system of that era. Write 250-300 words on what spiritual or social challenges Guru Nanak was responding to in his teachings.

lessons.title: Guru Hargobind Sahib and the Doctrine of Miri-Piri
lessons.summary: The sixth Guru joined spiritual and temporal authority through the principle of Miri-Piri and the founding of the Akal Takht.
lessons.html:
A new dimension

Following the martyrdom of his father Guru Arjan Sahib, Guru Hargobind Sahib, the sixth Guru (Guru from 1606), articulated the principle of ਮੀਰੀ ਪੀਰੀ — the teaching that spiritual authority and temporal responsibility are joined rather than separate.

Two swords

Tradition relates that Guru Hargobind Sahib wore two swords, symbolizing these two domains: Piri, representing spiritual sovereignty and devotion, and Miri, representing worldly authority and the duty to uphold justice and defend the community. This was not a turn away from Guru Nanak Sahib's spiritual message but an extension of it into the social and political realities of the age (Grewal 1998).

The Akal Takht

He is also associated with the establishment of the Akal Takht at Amritsar, a seat representing temporal authority that stands facing the Harmandir Sahib. The pairing of these two centers physically embodied the balance of Miri and Piri — the temporal and the spiritual standing together.

Militarization in context

The militarization of this period must be understood in context. It was a defensive and protective response to the political pressures and persecution the community had experienced, including the martyrdom of Guru Arjan Sahib. The Guru is traditionally remembered for maintaining a body of trained followers and horses and for engaging in defensive conflicts, while continuing to emphasize spiritual devotion. The aim, as understood in mainstream Sikh tradition, was not conquest but the capacity to protect the innocent and resist tyranny (Singh and Singh 1950).

References: Singh, Teja, and Ganda Singh. A Short History of the Sikhs. Bombay: Orient Longmans, 1950. Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998.

Homework

Read or listen to a teaching of Guru Nanak on the theme of equality before the Divine (such as rejecting caste distinctions). Reflect on what was revolutionary about this message in the sixteenth century and how it applies to justice and inclusion today. Write 250-300 words.

lessons.title: Guru Gobind Singh Sahib and the Founding of the Khalsa
lessons.summary: The founding of the Khalsa in 1699, the Panj Pyare, the shared identity of Singh and Kaur, and the conferral of eternal Guruship on Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji in 1708.
lessons.html:
Vaisakhi, 1699

Guru Gobind Singh Sahib, the tenth Guru (Guru from 1675), founded the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ in 1699, traditionally on the festival of Vaisakhi at Anandpur.

The Panj Pyare

According to the widely transmitted account, the Guru called upon the assembled congregation and asked who was willing to give their head for their faith. One by one, five devotees stepped forward, drawn from different regions and social backgrounds. These five became known as the ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ, the Five Beloved Ones. The Guru initiated them through a ceremony involving Amrit (sweetened, consecrated water stirred with a double-edged sword), inaugurating the Khalsa. In a striking gesture of equality, the Guru then asked the Panj Pyare to initiate him in turn (Singh and Singh 1950).

The meaning of the Khalsa

  • It bound Sikhs to a code of ethical conduct, devotion, courage, and service.
  • It dissolved distinctions of caste; men commonly took the name Singh (lion) and women the name Kaur (princess), affirming a shared identity and the dignity of all.
  • It established a visible, committed community ready to uphold justice and defend the oppressed.

Eternal Guruship, 1708

Guru Gobind Singh Sahib lived through immense hardship in defense of the community, and several members of his own family gave their lives during this era. Before his passing in 1708, he declared that there would be no further human Guru. Instead, he conferred eternal Guruship upon the sacred scripture, thereafter revered as Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, the supreme spiritual authority guiding the community for all time (Grewal 1998).

References: Singh, Teja, and Ganda Singh. A Short History of the Sikhs. Bombay: Orient Longmans, 1950. Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998.

Homework

Create a timeline of the Ten Gurus with key accomplishments or teachings of each (e.g., institutions founded, scriptures compiled, martyrdoms). Then choose one Guru whose life and work particularly moves you and write 250-300 words about why their example resonates with you.

lessons.title: The Eighteenth Century, the Misls, and the Rise of Ranjit Singh
lessons.summary: Struggle and resilience after the Gurus, Banda Singh Bahadur and the Misls, the Sikh Empire of Maharaja Ranjit Singh, and the path to colonial rule, with attention to historical method.
lessons.html:
Struggle and resilience

The eighteenth century was a period of severe hardship and remarkable resilience. Following the era of the Gurus, Sikhs faced repeated persecution under regional Mughal authorities and during invasions of the Punjab. Dr. Ganda Singh devoted a careful study to one of the great figures of armed resistance in his book on Banda Singh Bahadur, built closely from primary sources (Singh 1935).

The Misls

Over time, as central authority weakened, Sikh fighting bands consolidated into confederacies known as the Misls. Each Misl was a semi-independent group controlling territory in the Punjab, cooperating at times for common defense, particularly against external invasions, while managing their own affairs. The Misls represented a decentralized form of Sikh power and laid the groundwork for later unity (Grewal 1998).

The Sikh Empire

By the end of the eighteenth century, Maharaja Ranjit Singh rose to prominence. Beginning from the base of one Misl, he united the various factions and established the Sikh Empire in 1801, with Lahore as his capital.

  • He built a powerful, modernized army, drawing on European-style training and artillery alongside traditional Sikh forces.
  • His state was notable for relative pluralism: people of different faiths served in his administration and army.
  • He is associated with the adornment of the Harmandir Sahib, contributing to the gold work that gave rise to the popular name Golden Temple.

A note on method and sources

Dr. Ganda Singh also showed how much can be learned from outside observers. In his edited collection of early European accounts, he gathered the writings of travelers and officials who described the Sikhs of this period, comparing them carefully against Sikh sources to test what was reliable (Singh 1962).

Approx. yearDevelopment
1708Passing of Guru Gobind Singh Sahib; eternal Guruship of the scripture
1700sPersecution, resistance, and the rise of the Misls
1801Maharaja Ranjit Singh establishes the Sikh Empire at Lahore
1839Death of Maharaja Ranjit Singh; growing instability
1849Annexation of the Punjab and the start of British colonial rule

Toward the colonial period

Maharaja Ranjit Singh died in 1839. After his death, internal instability weakened the empire, and within roughly a decade it came into conflict with the expanding British East India Company. The Punjab was annexed and brought under British colonial rule by 1849, ending Sikh sovereignty. The later nineteenth and twentieth centuries saw reform movements such as the Singh Sabha, the Gurdwara reform of the 1920s, the Partition of 1947, and the growth of a worldwide Sikh community whose history continues to unfold while remaining rooted in the teachings of the Gurus (Singh and Singh 1950).

References: Singh, Ganda. Banda Singh Bahadur. Amritsar: Khalsa College, 1935. Singh, Ganda, ed. Early European Accounts of the Sikhs. Calcutta: Indian Studies Past and Present, 1962. Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998. Singh, Teja, and Ganda Singh. A Short History of the Sikhs. Bombay: Orient Longmans, 1950.

Homework

Research one aspect of Khalsa identity and practice: the Panj Ks (five articles of faith), the Rehat Maryada (code of conduct), or the role of the Panj Pyare. Write 250-300 words on how these practices maintain Sikh identity and values across generations.

lessons.title: The Colonial Period and the Singh Sabha Movement
lessons.html:
A new era: British rule and Sikh adaptation

The annexation of the Punjab in 1849 brought the Sikh homeland under British colonial rule, ending nearly two centuries of Sikh political independence. This period, stretching roughly from 1849 to 1947, was one of profound transformation. While the Sikhs lost temporal sovereignty, this era also witnessed remarkable intellectual and spiritual renewal, particularly through the Singh Sabha movement (Grewal 1998).

The British colonial system introduced new educational institutions, administrative structures, and ways of thinking about history, community, and religious authority. Many Sikhs adopted English education and took positions in the colonial bureaucracy, military, and commerce. At the same time, Sikh thinkers and leaders began to ask: How do we preserve and strengthen our faith and community in this new context?

The Singh Sabha and reform

The Singh Sabha, a Sikh reform movement that emerged in the late nineteenth century, represents one of the most important internal developments in modern Sikh history. Singh Sabhas were organizations dedicated to the study of scripture, the education of youth, and the assertion of Sikh identity and autonomy (McLeod 1989).

Key themes of the Singh Sabha included scriptural authority, with scholars emphasizing the primacy of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji and the teachings of the Gurus as the fountainhead of Sikh belief and practice. Education became central; they founded schools and colleges to teach Sikh youth in both Punjabi and English, and to cultivate pride in Sikh identity. The printing press became a tool of renewal; Singh Sabha scholars printed and distributed the Adi Granth, theological works, and histories (Singh and Singh 1950).

The Gurdwara Reformation and the SGPC

Building on Singh Sabha foundations, the early twentieth century saw the Gurdwara Reformation movement, which sought to return control of Sikh shrines from mahants (custodians of mixed loyalties) to the Sikh community itself. This culminated in the formation of the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (SGPC) in 1925, which unified the management of major Sikh gurdwaras and became the highest temporal authority in Sikhdom (Grewal 1998).

A note on agency and adaptation

The colonial period is sometimes narrated as pure loss or pure victimhood. But Sikh historians like Ganda Singh recognized that Sikhs also exercised considerable agency. They adapted to new circumstances while maintaining theological continuity. They used the tools of the colonial world—printing, English education, organizational structure—to strengthen their community. This is a complex historical reality that neither romanticizes the past nor denies the real hardships and losses of the era.

Key takeaways:
  • The Singh Sabha movement was a Sikh-led effort to preserve and strengthen faith and identity under colonial rule through education, scriptural study, and community organization.
  • The Gurdwara Reformation of the early twentieth century brought Sikh shrines and institutions under collective community control.
  • Sikhs exercised agency in adapting to colonial rule while maintaining theological and historical continuity with the Guru period.

Homework

Research one figure associated with the Singh Sabha movement (such as Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha or Pandit Teja Singh) and write 250-300 words about their contributions to Sikh theology or education during this period. What problems were they trying to solve?

lessons.title: The Partition and the Global Sikh Diaspora
lessons.html:
August 1947: Independence and division

The Partition of the Indian subcontinent in August 1947 was a rupture with profound consequences for Sikhs. The Punjab, the heartland of Sikhdom, was divided between India and the newly created nation of Pakistan. This was not a clean geographical line; it meant the uprooting of millions. Many Sikhs whose homes lay in what became West Punjab migrated eastward; similarly, many Muslims moved westward (Grewal 1998).

The violence surrounding Partition was severe. While estimates of overall deaths across the subcontinent vary, the upheaval was immense. The Golden Temple, Harmandir Sahib, and many other sacred sites remained in India, but millions of Sikhs suddenly found themselves citizens of a newly independent India rather than the unified Punjab they had known. The loss of a Sikh-majority homeland was a defining moment in modern Sikh consciousness (McLeod 1989).

Migration and the global diaspora

In the decades following Partition, Sikhs began migrating in significant numbers to North America, the United Kingdom, Malaysia, Singapore, and other parts of the world. These migrations were driven by economic opportunity, political instability, and sometimes the search for a place where Sikh identity could flourish openly.

The diaspora communities rebuilt Sikh institutions in new lands. The first North American gurdwaras were established in the early twentieth century, but expansion accelerated after 1947. Sikhs built gurdwaras, established educational institutions, and created formal organizations to preserve Sikh teachings and culture among their children. The Sikh Student Federation and other youth organizations emerged to address the challenge of maintaining identity across generations in pluralistic societies (Nesbitt 2005).

The 1984 crisis and its aftermath

In June 1984, the Indian government ordered a military operation at the Golden Temple in Amritsar, resulting in significant loss of life and deep trauma within the global Sikh community. This event galvanized diaspora Sikhs and sparked renewed engagement with Sikh history, theology, and politics. It also brought urgent attention to Sikh human rights concerns and elevated Sikh visibility in Western countries (Tatla 1999).

A global faith rooted in a particular place

The twentieth-century diaspora created a paradox: Sikhism became a truly global faith with vibrant communities on every continent, yet remained deeply connected to the Punjab and its sacred geography. Today, Sikhs navigate the relationship between a diaspora identity and roots in the Guru's land. This tension has become part of modern Sikh history and consciousness (McLeod 1989).

Key takeaways:
  • Partition in 1947 divided the Punjab and catalyzed global migration of Sikh communities to North America, the UK, and other regions.
  • Diaspora Sikhs rebuilt gurdwaras and institutions abroad while maintaining theological and historical connection to the Guru period and the Punjab.
  • Major events like 1984 intensified diaspora engagement with Sikh identity and human rights concerns.

Homework

Interview a Sikh family member or community member about their personal or family history during Partition or emigration. Write 250-300 words on what you learned about how Sikhs adapted to displacement and built new communities. What sacrifices or losses do they recall?

lessons.title: Women in Sikh History and Leadership
lessons.html:
Equality in principle and practice

One of the defining teachings of Guru Nanak Sahib was the radical equality of all people before the Divine. The Adi Granth explicitly rejects the idea that women are spiritually inferior or should be excluded from religious practice. Yet like all traditions, Sikhism has also experienced tension between its egalitarian theology and historical social practices shaped by the patriarchal contexts in which it developed (Kaur 2005).

Guru Amar Das Sahib is specifically remembered in Sikh tradition for advocating the dignity and education of women. He reportedly required widows to remarry rather than practice sati (self-immolation on a husband's pyre), and he appointed women as teachers in the Manji system. This was countercultural in sixteenth-century Punjab (Singh and Singh 1950).

Women in the Khalsa and beyond

When Guru Gobind Singh Sahib founded the Khalsa in 1699, women were initiated alongside men and given the surname Kaur (princess), just as men received Singh (lion). In principle, this established shared spiritual status. However, the subsequent history of women's participation in Khalsa structures and leadership has been uneven. Some periods and communities emphasized women's roles; others marginalized them (Nesbitt 2005).

The twentieth-century reform movements, especially the Singh Sabha, brought questions of women's education and participation to the fore. Female literacy became a priority, and women became teachers, organizers, and custodians of Sikh tradition in families and communities. In the diaspora, Sikh women have been particularly active in maintaining gurdwaras and passing on teachings to younger generations (Tatla 1999).

Contemporary voices and ongoing work

Modern Sikh movements for women's leadership address historical exclusions in decision-making structures, liturgical roles (such as reading the Guru Granth Sahib in gurdwaras), and family law. These movements invoke the theology of the Gurus while questioning practices that later accumulated in Sikh tradition. The recovery and study of women's voices in Sikh history—including the writings of Sikh women scholars and historians—is an ongoing project of contemporary Sikh communities (Kaur 2005).

Why this matters to understanding history

The history of women in Sikhi reminds us that understanding a tradition requires looking not only at its theology but at how actual people lived, struggled, and advocated for change. It shows that Sikh history is not a closed narrative but a living conversation between principle and practice, past and present.

Key takeaways:
  • Sikh theology affirms the spiritual equality of all people, including women, but historical practice has been more varied.
  • Women have always played crucial roles in Sikh communities—as teachers, organizers, and guardians of tradition—though their contributions are sometimes overlooked in standard histories.
  • Contemporary Sikh movements continue to engage with gender equality as both a scriptural principle and a living ethical commitment.

Homework

Read or listen to a shabad by Guru Nanak that speaks to the dignity and worth of all people regardless of gender or status. Reflect on how this principle was revolutionary in the sixteenth century and what it might mean to live out this teaching fully today. Write 250-300 words on your reflection.

lessons.title: The Eighteenth-Century Martyrs: Stories of Conscience and Courage
lessons.html:
A century of trial

The eighteenth century was one of the most difficult periods in Sikh history. Following the passing of Guru Gobind Singh Sahib in 1708 and the end of the Guru period, Sikhs faced sustained persecution, military campaigns, and a struggle for survival. Yet this century also produced some of the most celebrated figures in Sikh memory—individuals who chose principle over safety and whose stories became foundational to Sikh identity (Singh and Singh 1950).

Banda Singh Bahadur: Armed resistance and justice

One of the most significant but also most historically contested figures of this era is Banda Singh Bahadur. Guru Gobind Singh Sahib reportedly granted him authority to lead Sikh forces in resistance against persecution. Banda Singh rose to prominence in the early eighteenth century, building a powerful armed movement that challenged Mughal authority in the Punjab and redistributed land and resources to the poor and oppressed.

Historical sources differ on details of Banda Singh's rule and methods. Dr. Ganda Singh devoted careful scholarly attention to primary sources regarding Banda Singh, recognizing both his importance and the need for caution in separating fact from later romanticization (Singh 1935). What is clear is that Banda Singh became a symbol of Sikh resistance and the principle that defending the weak and challenging injustice were sacred duties.

The Great Sikh Holocaust and collective martyrdom

In the 1740s, Mughal authorities launched intensified campaigns against Sikhs. Thousands were captured, imprisoned, and executed. This period, sometimes called the Chota Ghallughara and later the Wadda Ghallughara (the great massacre), remains vivid in Sikh memory as a time of immense suffering. Yet Sikh sources record that many Sikhs faced this persecution with spiritual composure, refusing to renounce their faith (Grewal 1998).

These collective experiences reinforced a particular understanding within Sikhi: that standing firm for truth and justice, even at great personal cost, is a measure of spiritual maturity and conscience. The Khalsa forged through persecution was not merely a military order but a spiritual body unified by shared commitment to dharma—righteous duty.

From persecution to power

By the mid-eighteenth century, as Mughal central authority weakened, Sikhs gradually shifted from a purely persecuted minority to the Misls—competing but eventually consolidating confederacies that would lay the groundwork for the Sikh Empire. This transition, from martyr-consciousness to political power, is a crucial inflection point in Sikh history and raises enduring questions: What are the ethics of power? How do communities maintain their spiritual principles when they acquire temporal authority?

Key takeaways:
  • The eighteenth century saw intense persecution of Sikhs and produced celebrated figures like Banda Singh Bahadur whose stories became central to Sikh identity.
  • The experience of collective martyrdom reinforced the Sikh principle of standing firm for justice and righteousness, regardless of personal cost.
  • The transition from persecution to power through the Misls raised enduring questions about how faith communities maintain their spiritual values when they gain temporal authority.

Homework

Research one specific Sikh martyr from the eighteenth century (such as someone from the Chota Ghallughara period). Write 250-300 words about what drew them to this path of resistance and what their sacrifice meant to the Sikh community. Consider: What principles were they defending?

lessons.title: The Sacred Landscape: Harmandir Sahib and Sikh Places of Pilgrimage
lessons.html:
Sacred geography and spiritual centers

Sikhism is a faith deeply rooted in particular places. While the teachings of the Gurus can be practiced anywhere, certain locations have become spiritually significant through history, miracle, and collective memory. The study of these sacred sites is not merely antiquarian; it reveals how communities understand their identity and transmit their values across generations (McLeod 1989).

The Harmandir Sahib and Amritsar

The Harmandir Sahib, commonly called the Golden Temple for its gilded dome, stands at the center of Sikh spiritual geography. Founded by Guru Ram Das Sahib in the late sixteenth century on the site of a sacred pool, it was further developed under Guru Arjan Sahib. The Adi Granth was installed there, making it the repository of Sikh scripture and the focal point of Sikh worship (Grewal 1998).

The city of Amritsar grew around this spiritual center. The pool itself, the Amrit Sarovar (Pool of Nectar), became a place of pilgrimage and spiritual purification. Over centuries, the Harmandir Sahib has been destroyed and rebuilt, rebuilt with marble and decorated with gold, and has witnessed both profound devotion and historical trauma. Yet it remains the supreme symbol of Sikhdom, the destination of millions of pilgrims each year (Singh and Singh 1950).

Anandpur Sahib and the Khalsa creation

Anandpur Sahib, in the foothills of the Himalayas, is where Guru Gobind Singh Sahib founded the Khalsa in 1699 and where much of his spiritual work was accomplished. For Sikhs, this site carries the memory of the moment when a new form of Sikh identity was created. The city has become a major pilgrimage destination, especially during the Holla Mohalla festival celebrating the founding of the Khalsa (Tatla 1999).

Nankana Sahib and the diaspora connection

Nankana Sahib, the birthplace of Guru Nanak Sahib in present-day Pakistan, has remained symbolically central even though it lies outside the borders of India. For diaspora Sikhs unable to visit regularly, the name itself carries spiritual weight. It represents the Gurus' roots and the continuity of the faith from its origin point. Many Sikhs in the diaspora maintain a spiritual connection to the Punjab through these sacred names and places.

Pilgrimage and theology

In Sikhism, pilgrimage (tirth) to these sites is not understood as magically efficacious in itself; rather, it is a practice of devotion and remembrance. Visiting the Harmandir Sahib or Anandpur Sahib is an opportunity to meditate on the teachings of the Gurus associated with those places, to encounter the Sangat (congregation) in worship, and to participate in the lived continuity of faith across centuries.

Key takeaways:
  • The Harmandir Sahib and the city of Amritsar are the supreme spiritual center of Sikhdom, housing the Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji and drawing millions of pilgrims.
  • Anandpur Sahib commemorates the founding of the Khalsa and remains a major pilgrimage site celebrating Sikh courage and identity.
  • Sacred sites connect Sikhs emotionally and spiritually to the teachings and legacy of the Gurus, serving as anchors of faith and community across the diaspora.

Homework

If you have visited a gurdwara or sacred Sikh site, reflect on your experience: What did you notice about how people engaged spiritually in that space? What teachings were being reinforced? If you have not visited a gurdwara, research one major Sikh pilgrimage site and write 250-300 words about its historical significance and what draws Sikhs to it today.

lessons.title: Sikh History in Sources: Learning the Historian's Method
lessons.html:
Dr. Ganda Singh and the study of sources

Throughout this course, we have referenced Dr. Ganda Singh, a foundational historian of Sikhism. Why? Because learning history is not just about memorizing events and dates—it is about learning to think like a historian, to ask critical questions, and to distinguish between what we can know with confidence from sources and what remains contested or uncertain (Singh and Singh 1950).

Dr. Ganda Singh showed that Sikh history can be studied rigorously. He collected and analyzed primary sources: ਹੁਕਮਨਾਮੇ (Hukamnamas, letters of command issued by Gurus), early manuscripts, eyewitness accounts, and official records. He compared these sources against each other, noted where they agreed and where they differed, and drew careful conclusions (Singh 1962).

Types of historical sources

Understanding where our historical knowledge comes from is essential. Sikh history draws on several types of sources, each with strengths and limitations:

  • Religious texts: The Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji is the supreme scripture but contains teachings and poetry, not a straightforward historical narrative. Gur Bilas texts and the Suraj Prakash are later compositions recounting Guru histories, written down generations after the events.
  • Administrative records: Mughal court records, land deeds, and tax documents sometimes mention Sikh communities, providing non-partisan evidence about dates, locations, and interactions.
  • Eyewitness accounts: Letters, travel narratives, and accounts by people who saw events directly are invaluable but must be read critically, noting the observer's perspective and potential biases.
  • Later oral tradition: Stories passed down through generations often contain kernels of historical truth but can also include embellishment or legendary material. Historians must ask: What does this story tell us about what people believed and valued, even if some details are uncertain?

The problem of hagiography and legend

Much early Sikh literature is devotional or hagiographical—written to inspire faith and celebrate the virtues of the Gurus. This is valuable for understanding what Sikhs believed, but it is not the same as a neutral historical record. A modern historian must learn to read such texts with both reverence for their spiritual importance and critical attention to distinguishing layers of tradition (McLeod 1989).

Contested questions in Sikh history

Even after careful source work, some questions remain contested among scholars. When did certain institutions develop? Exactly how did the Khalsa ceremony work in 1699? What motivated particular policies of the Gurus? Responsible historians acknowledge uncertainty and show their work, laying out the evidence and the reasoning rather than claiming false certainty.

Why this matters for us

Learning to read sources critically, to distinguish primary evidence from later retelling, to recognize the perspectives of those who wrote, and to acknowledge what we do not know—these skills allow us to inherit our history with both deep reverence and clear eyes. This is the gift that historians like Dr. Ganda Singh gave us: a method for understanding our past truthfully.

Key takeaways:
  • Sikh history can be studied using rigorous methods of source analysis, comparing primary evidence and testing claims against multiple perspectives.
  • Different types of sources—religious texts, administrative records, eyewitness accounts, and oral tradition—each offer different kinds of knowledge and must be read with attention to their context and limitations.
  • Responsible historical study means acknowledging what we know with confidence, what remains contested, and what we cannot yet determine from available evidence.

Homework

Choose one episode or claim from Sikh history that you encountered in this course (such as a detail about a Guru or an event). Try to identify at least two different sources that discuss this claim: a scriptural or devotional source, and a scholarly or external historical source. Write 250-300 words comparing what each source says and what you notice about their different purposes, perspectives, or levels of detail.

courses.title: Introduction to Gurmat (Sikh Theology)
courses.summary: A rigorous yet accessible introduction to Gurmat, the theology of the Guru's teachings, covering the nature of the Divine, the Shabad Guru, the path of devotion, grace and effort, ethics and equality, and the meaning of liberation.
outcomes: You will be able to define Gurmat and explain how it differs from manmat (the self-centered way).
You will be able to describe the Sikh view of the Divine, including Ik Onkar and the Nirgun and Sargun aspects.
You will be able to explain the idea of the Shabad Guru and the status of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji as the living Guru.
You will be able to outline the path of devotion through Naam, Shabad, and Simran.
You will be able to relate divine grace (Nadar/Kirpa) to human effort within the order of Hukam.
You will be able to compare the Gurmukh and the Manmukh and explain Gurmat's view of liberation (Mukti).

terms.m: The wisdom, mind, or way of the Guru; the whole vision of Sikh teaching.
There is one Reality; the opening statement of Sikh scripture (Ang 1).
The divine Word; the true Guru that awakens the soul.
The presence and self-disclosure of the Divine made available to awareness.
Loving, attentive remembrance of the Divine.
The divine Order, Command, or Will within which all things unfold.
Egoism or 'I-am-ness'; the root sense of a separate, self-important self.
Liberation; loving union with the Divine and freedom from the bondage of ego.

references: Sahib Singh. Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan. Jalandhar: Raj Publishers, 1962.
Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998.
McLeod, W. H. The Sikhs: History, Religion, and Society. New York: Columbia University Press, 1989.
