    • The Jat peasant social structure — rooted in village clan (ਪੱਤੀ) organization and seasonal agricultural rhythms — provided both the manpower and the material base of Khalsa military power.
    • Merchant communities, especially Khatri and Arora families, were essential economic partners who provided credit, commercial networks, and logistical support to the Misls.
    • The moral economy of the Khalsa — expressed through dasvandh, langar, and redistributive norms — shaped how leaders managed resources and built loyalty, creating a system where piety and political reputation reinforced each other.
    • Amritsar's dual identity as sacred center and commercial hub exemplifies the inseparability of religious and economic life in 18th-century Sikh civilization.

Homework

Visit a map of 18th-century Punjab — the Punjab Digital Library (punjabidigitallibrary.com) or the maps section of J.S. Grewal's The Sikhs of the Punjab contain good examples. Identify two major trade routes that passed through the territory controlled by Sikh Misls. Write a 350-word reflection on how geography and commerce shaped the political possibilities available to the Khalsa. Consider: how did control of trade routes translate into military and political leverage? How might economic power have supported or complicated the spiritual ideals of the Panth?

lessons.title: Women of the Eighteenth-Century Khalsa: Agency, Sacrifice, and Leadership
lessons.html:
Introduction

The history of the eighteenth-century Khalsa, as it has most often been told, is a history of men. The sardars of the Misls, the warriors of the ਜਥੇ (jathas), the martyrs of the Ghallugharas — these figures dominate the narrative, and they are predominantly male. Yet this gendered framing obscures a more complex reality. Women of the Sikh Panth were present throughout the eighteenth century as witnesses, participants, organizers, and — in certain documented cases — as military leaders and political actors in their own right. To write women out of this history is not only to do them an injustice; it is to misunderstand how the Khalsa community actually functioned.

Sikh theology, from the time of Guru Nanak, had consistently affirmed the spiritual equality of women and men. The concept of the soul (ਆਤਮਾ) as the bride seeking union with the divine Groom (ਪ੍ਰਭੂ) is one of the central metaphors of Gurbani, and it positions all human beings — regardless of gender — in the same devotional relationship with Waheguru. The early Gurus had spoken explicitly against practices of female infanticide (ਕੁੜੀਮਾਰ), sati, and purdah. The Khalsa ਰਹਿਤ (rahit, code of conduct) admitted women to the Amrit Sanchar and made them members of the Panth with full spiritual standing. These theological commitments did not eliminate patriarchy from Sikh social life, but they created ideological resources that women could and did invoke.

This lecture examines the roles of women in the eighteenth-century Khalsa, drawing on the historical record — admittedly incomplete and androcentric in its primary sources — to recover what can be known. We look at women as spiritual practitioners, as preservers of Gurbani and oral tradition, as managers of households and communities during the prolonged absences of male warriors, as participants in military campaigns, and as political actors in the later Misl period. We also attend to scholarly debates about how to read sources that rarely foreground women's perspectives directly.

This is not a simple story of liberation. The eighteenth century imposed extraordinary burdens on Sikh women: the trauma of the Ghallugharas, the disruption of settled family life by constant warfare, the threat of capture and enslavement during Afghan raids, and the structural constraints of a patrilineal social system. Yet within and despite those constraints, women exercised agency in ways that shaped the destiny of the Panth.

Theological Foundations: Women in Sikh Teaching

Any discussion of women in 18th-century Sikh practice must begin with the theological foundation laid by the Gurus. Guru Nanak's teachings, preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib (ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ), included pointed critiques of the social devaluation of women. He asked why women — who give birth to kings, saints, and warriors — should be considered inferior. This affirmation was not merely rhetorical; it was embedded in a theology that understood all souls (regardless of the body they inhabited) as equally capable of union with the divine.

The institution of the langar (ਲੰਗਰ), which Guru Nanak established and Guru Amar Das formalized, was a site where gender hierarchy was symbolically suspended: men and women ate together, sat together in sangat (ਸੰਗਤ), and served together in seva. Guru Amar Das is particularly noted for his active encouragement of women's participation in community life, reportedly appointing women as preachers (ਪ੍ਰਚਾਰਕ) and deploying them as manjidars to spread the Sikh faith in different regions.

Guru Gobind Singh's establishment of the Khalsa in 1699 included women as initiates. The Amrit Sanchar was not closed to women, and the ਸਿੰਘਣੀ (Singhni) — the female Khalsa — carried the same obligations and spiritual standing as the ਸਿੰਘ. The Panj Kakars were required of initiated Sikh women as well as men. In practice, the degree to which women participated in the Amrit ceremony varied by region, family, and circumstance, but the theological door was open. This distinguishes the Khalsa from many contemporary religious traditions that maintained strict gender segregation in initiation and ritual.

These theological commitments created an ideological framework within which exceptional women could claim authority and be recognized by their communities. When Mai Bhago (ਮਾਈ ਭਾਗੋ) rallied the deserters of Anandpur and led them back to Guru Gobind Singh — fighting at the Battle of Khidrana (1705) alongside the forty who would become the ਚਾਲੀ ਮੁਕਤੇ (Chali Mukte, Forty Liberated Ones) — she was not acting outside Sikh norms. She was enacting them. Her story became a touchstone that later Sikh women and communities could invoke to affirm women's capacity for martial and spiritual courage.

Women's Roles in the Misl Period: Household, Community, and Politics

The most common roles of women in the eighteenth-century Khalsa were invisible to the historical record precisely because they were domestic and communal rather than military or political. Women managed households during the long absences of male warriors, maintained the religious observances of the family (ਪਾਠ, ਨਿਤਨੇਮ), instructed children in Gurbani, organized the local sangat, and managed the agricultural and economic activities that sustained the community. These roles were not passive; they required initiative, judgment, and leadership. They were also essential to the survival of the Panth during periods of intense persecution, when dispersal and concealment meant that women were often the primary preservers of Sikh identity and practice.

The Afghan invasions of the mid-eighteenth century imposed particular burdens and horrors on Sikh women. Ahmad Shah Durrani's campaigns included the capture and sale of enslaved women and children, and the liberation of such captives became one of the Khalsa's most celebrated moral commitments. The sardars made the rescue of enslaved Punjabi women — Hindu, Muslim, and Sikh alike — a stated priority, and there are accounts of Sikh jathas intercepting slave caravans to free captives. This practice was both a humanitarian impulse and a community solidarity statement: the Khalsa presented itself as the protector of the Punjab's people in contrast to the Afghan raiders and the failing Mughal state.

Among the most significant political women of the Misl period was Sada Kaur (ਸਦਾ ਕੌਰ, c. 1762–1832), the leader of the Kanhaiya Misl after her husband's death. Sada Kaur was not merely a regent holding power on behalf of a male heir; she was an active military and political leader who negotiated alliances, commanded armies, and made consequential strategic decisions. Her alliance with Ranjit Singh — and her role in his rise to prominence — was motivated by calculated political interest as much as family loyalty. She eventually clashed with Ranjit Singh as he consolidated power, illustrating both the agency she exercised and the limits imposed by the emerging centralized state.

Sada Kaur's career is exceptional in its documentation and scope, but she was not entirely alone. Other Misl households included women who managed estates, negotiated with rivals, and maintained family coalitions during periods when male leadership was absent, incapacitated, or in conflict. The structure of the Misl — which was partly a family enterprise, with territory and authority passing through kinship networks — created spaces in which women with the requisite character and intelligence could exercise power, particularly in the interstitial moments between male successions.

Scholarship, Memory, and the Recovery of Women's History

The historical recovery of women's roles in the 18th-century Khalsa faces significant source challenges. The primary chronicles of the period — Ratan Singh Bhangu's Prachin Panth Parkash (ਪ੍ਰਾਚੀਨ ਪੰਥ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼), the Suraj Parkash of Bhai Santokh Singh, and Persian-language Mughal and Afghan sources — were written by men, for male audiences, and focused predominantly on the actions of male leaders. Women appear in these texts most often as objects of events rather than subjects — as captives to be rescued, as mothers of great men, or as exceptional individuals whose martial valor is noted as remarkable precisely because it departs from expected gender norms.

Modern Sikh historians and scholars of gender have begun to read these sources against the grain. Scholars such as Doris Jakobsh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, and Purnima Dhavan have examined the ways in which gender was constructed in Sikh religious and historical literature, raising important questions about how women's agency was represented, celebrated, or suppressed. Jakobsh's work in particular has shown that the consolidation of Sikh institutional identity in the 19th and early 20th centuries involved decisions — about the Rahit Maryada, about women's participation in certain rituals — that sometimes narrowed the spaces that the 18th-century tradition had left open.

Oral traditions preserved within Sikh families and communities sometimes provide richer accounts of women's lives than written chronicles. The songs (ਵਾਰਾਂ, ਬੋਲੀਆਂ) sung by Punjabi women at weddings and seasonal festivals often preserved memories of the Misl period, including memories of women's experiences during the Ghallugharas and Afghan invasions. These oral traditions are imperfectly preserved and resist easy scholarly analysis, but they represent a genuine layer of historical memory that deserves attention alongside the written record.

The recovery of 18th-century women's history is not merely an academic exercise. It has contemporary significance for debates within the Sikh community about women's roles in institutions such as the Akal Takht, the Panj Pyare, and the governance of historic Gurdwaras. When these debates invoke history, they invoke a contested and incompletely recovered history. The scholarly project of reconstructing women's roles in the 18th-century Khalsa is thus both an intellectual necessity and a contribution to ongoing conversations about identity, authority, and justice within the Panth.

Key Terms

  • ਸਿੰਘਣੀ (Singhni) — A female member of the Khalsa Panth who has received Amrit initiation; carries the same spiritual obligations as the Singh, including the Panj Kakars.
  • ਕੁੜੀਮਾਰ (Kurimar) — The practice of female infanticide, condemned by Sikh Gurus and explicitly prohibited in the Khalsa Rahit.
  • ਚਾਲੀ ਮੁਕਤੇ (Chali Mukte) — The Forty Liberated Ones who returned to fight at the Battle of Khidrana in 1705; Mai Bhago's role in rallying them is one of the most celebrated examples of women's martial leadership in Sikh history.
  • ਵਾਰਾਂ (Varan) — Heroic ballads in Punjabi literary tradition; oral compositions that celebrated martial valor and sometimes preserved memories of historical events, including women's experiences.
  • ਰਹਿਤ (Rahit) — The code of conduct for initiated Khalsa Sikhs; its application to women has been a site of both inclusion (equal initiation) and ongoing debate about specific ceremonial roles.
  • ਮਨਜੀਦਾਰ (Manjidari) — A system of regional preaching representatives established by Guru Amar Das; reportedly included women among its appointees, establishing an early precedent for women's public religious leadership.

Discussion Questions

  1. Sikh theology affirmed women's spiritual equality from the time of Guru Nanak, yet 18th-century historical sources rarely foreground women's experiences. How do you explain this gap between theological ideal and historical record?
  2. Mai Bhago's story has become iconic in Sikh tradition. What does the way her story is told — and which details are emphasized — reveal about the values the Khalsa community has wanted to project about gender and martial virtue?
  3. Sada Kaur exercised real political and military leadership within the Misl system. What structural features of Misl organization made her leadership possible? Would the same have been possible in a more centralized state?
  4. Scholars like Doris Jakobsh have argued that 19th-century Sikh institutional consolidation sometimes narrowed spaces for women that were more open in the 18th century. Do you find this argument persuasive, and what evidence would you want to examine to evaluate it?
  5. How can historians recover women's experiences from sources that were created almost entirely by men and that treat women as marginal? What methods and cautions are appropriate?

Further Reading

  • Doris Jakobsh, Relocating Gender in Sikh History: Transformation, Meaning and Identity — the most comprehensive academic study of gender in Sikh history and institution-building.
  • Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, The Feminine Principle in the Sikh Vision of the Transcendent — examines the role of feminine imagery and theology in Gurbani and its implications for gender in Sikh practice.
  • Purnima Dhavan, When Sparrows Became Hawks: The Making of the Sikh Warrior Tradition, 1699–1799 — includes discussion of women's roles within the broader argument about how Khalsa warrior identity was constructed.
  • Ratan Singh Bhangu, Prachin Panth Parkash (trans. Kulwant Singh) — the primary 19th-century chronicle of the Misl period, which contains some of the earliest accounts of figures like Mai Bhago.
  • Key Takeaways
    • Sikh theology consistently affirmed women's spiritual equality, and the Khalsa Rahit admitted women to Amrit initiation — but these commitments coexisted with patrilineal social structures that limited most women's public roles.
    • Women's contributions to the 18th-century Khalsa were most often invisible to the historical record: managing households, preserving Gurbani, sustaining community life during male warriors' absences.
    • Mai Bhago's leadership at the Battle of Khidrana and Sada Kaur's leadership of the Kanhaiya Misl represent documented cases of women exercising military and political authority within the Khalsa framework.
    • The recovery of 18th-century women's history requires reading existing sources against the grain and attending to oral traditions alongside written chronicles.
    • Scholarly debates about gender in Sikh history have contemporary significance for ongoing conversations about women's roles in Sikh institutions and governance.

Homework

Research one woman from 18th-century Sikh history not covered in detail in the lesson — for example, Mai Bhago's later life as a guardian at Nanded, or Sada Kaur's role in Sikh politics after her alliance with Ranjit Singh. Write a 400-word profile drawing on at least one academic source. Then add a 150-word reflection: What does this woman's story reveal about the possibilities and constraints facing Sikh women in the 18th century? Avoid romanticizing — engage with both her agency and the structural limits she faced.

lessons.title: The Ghallugharas: Memory, Martyrdom, and Sikh Historical Consciousness
lessons.html:
Introduction

In the Sikh liturgical and historical calendar, certain events carry a weight that transcends their immediate historical significance. The two Ghallugharas (ਘੱਲੂਘਾਰੇ) — the Chhota Ghallughara (small catastrophe) of 1746 and the Vadda Ghallughara (great catastrophe) of 1762 — belong to this category. These massacres, in which thousands of Khalsa Sikhs were killed in concentrated military operations aimed at the elimination of the Panth, are not merely tragic episodes in an otherwise triumphant narrative. They are defining moments whose memory has shaped Sikh historical consciousness, collective identity, and theological reflection in ways that persist to the present day.

The word ਘੱਲੂਘਾਰਾ itself is significant. Derived from a root meaning dispersal or scattering, it conveys not just killing but attempted annihilation — the effort to destroy a community so thoroughly that nothing remains. The choice of this term in Sikh historical memory signals that the Ghallugharas were understood not as military defeats in the ordinary sense but as existential assaults on the Panth's very existence. That the Khalsa survived, regrouped, and ultimately prevailed is presented in Sikh historiography as evidence of divine protection (ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ ਦੀ ਰਜ਼ਾ) and of the community's extraordinary resilience.

This lecture examines the two Ghallugharas in their historical context, explores how they were understood and commemorated by the Sikh community in their immediate aftermath, and considers the longer arc of their role in Sikh historical consciousness. We draw on primary chronicle sources — particularly Ratan Singh Bhangu's Prachin Panth Parkash and the accounts embedded in Sikh rahitnamas (ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ) — as well as modern scholarly analysis by historians such as Surjit Singh Gandhi, Hari Ram Gupta, and J.S. Grewal. We also engage with the theological dimensions of Sikh responses to mass suffering, including the concepts of ਚੜ੍ਹਦੀ ਕਲਾ (charhdi kala, ascending spirit) and ਭਾਣਾ ਮੰਨਣਾ (acceptance of divine will).

Understanding the Ghallugharas is essential to understanding why the Khalsa fought as it did in the later eighteenth century and why the eventual establishment of Sikh sovereignty carried the emotional and spiritual weight it did. These events were not incidental tragedies in a success story; they were constitutive of the Sikh identity that carried that success story forward.

The Chhota Ghallughara, 1746: Context and Events

The background to the Chhota Ghallughara (ਛੋਟਾ ਘੱਲੂਘਾਰਾ) lies in the political crisis that followed the execution of Banda Singh Bahadur in 1716. After Banda's death, the Khalsa lost its organizational center and reverted to dispersed guerrilla operations from the forests and hills of the Shivalik range and the marshes (ਝਾੜੀਆਂ) along the Ravi and Beas rivers. Mughal provincial authorities, under pressure from Delhi to suppress the Sikh movement, pursued periodic campaigns of extermination. The appointment of Yahiya Khan as governor of Lahore in 1745 inaugurated a particularly intense phase of these operations.

Yahiya Khan dispatched a large military force under Diwan Lakhpat Rai in early 1746. Lakhpat Rai had a personal motive beyond politics: his brother had been killed in a recent Sikh raid. The military operation he led in the spring of 1746 drove a large concentration of Khalsa fighters and their families — estimates in the sources range widely, and modern historians treat them with appropriate caution — into the wetlands and forested terrain north of Lahore. Over several days of pursuit and combat, several thousand Sikhs were killed, and hundreds more were captured and subsequently executed in Lahore. The event is known in Sikh sources as the Chhota Ghallughara — the small catastrophe — small not because it was minor but because it was later overshadowed by the Vadda Ghallughara sixteen years later.

The community's response to the Chhota Ghallughara reveals much about how the Khalsa processed collective trauma. Rather than abandoning their identity — which the executions in Lahore were designed to compel — survivors intensified their commitment. Ratan Singh Bhangu and other chroniclers describe the period immediately following 1746 as one of the most spiritually concentrated in the Panth's history: dispersed in forests and hills, denied access to their shrines, hunted by Mughal forces, the Khalsa maintained their ਨਿਤਨੇਮ (daily prayer discipline), their Gurpurabs (ਗੁਰਪੁਰਬ), and their connection to each other through informal networks of communication. The Sarbat Khalsa continued to meet at Amritsar, at significant risk to all who attended, demonstrating the depth of institutional commitment to collective governance even under extreme persecution.

The theological resources the community deployed in this period were not abstract consolations. The concept of ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ (shaheedi, martyrdom) gave meaning to deaths that would otherwise have been simply losses. Those who died rather than apostatize were incorporated into the sacred memory of the Panth alongside the earlier martyrs — Guru Arjan Dev Ji, Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji, Bhai Mati Das Ji — creating a continuous tradition of sacrifice that linked the present suffering to the deepest theological commitments of Sikhi. This incorporation of new martyrs into an already-existing martyrology gave each death a significance beyond its immediate tragedy.

The Vadda Ghallughara, 1762: Ahmad Shah Durrani and the Attempted Annihilation

The Vadda Ghallughara (ਵੱਡਾ ਘੱਲੂਘਾਰਾ) of February 1762 was quantitatively and qualitatively different from its predecessor. Ahmad Shah Durrani, returning from his fifth invasion of India, received intelligence that a large body of Khalsa fighters — estimated by various sources at between 30,000 and 50,000 warriors and their families, including non-combatants — was moving through the Punjab. Durrani executed a rapid flanking maneuver that brought his seasoned Afghan cavalry in contact with the Sikh column near the village of Kup Rahira in the Malwa region. The Sikhs, unable to form an effective defensive perimeter while encumbered by civilians, suffered catastrophic losses over a single day of fighting.

Contemporary and near-contemporary estimates of the dead range from 10,000 to 25,000 or more, though modern historians urge caution about accepting these figures at face value. Even allowing for significant exaggeration in the sources, the Vadda Ghallughara was an unprecedented catastrophe for the Khalsa — a single engagement that killed more Sikhs than any previous event in the Panth's history. The scale of the losses and the circumstance — the attempted extermination of a community that included women, children, and elderly non-combatants as well as fighters — gave this event its distinctive character in Sikh historical memory.

What followed is equally significant for understanding the Khalsa's resilience. Within months of the Vadda Ghallughara, the survivors regrouped, reconvened the Sarbat Khalsa, and launched a counteroffensive. The Sikh forces attacked and sacked Sirhind in January 1764, killing its governor Zain Khan who had collaborated with Durrani. By the mid-1760s the Misls were expanding their territorial control across central Punjab, and the Afghan grip on the region was beginning to loosen. The speed of this recovery — from near-annihilation to territorial expansion within two years — is one of the most striking facts of 18th-century Sikh history and goes to the heart of what made the Khalsa movement so extraordinary.

Ahmad Shah Durrani was reportedly shaken by the Sikhs' refusal to be destroyed. Persian and Afghan sources record his bewilderment at a community that could suffer such losses and still fight. The famous remark attributed to him — that Sikhs are a people who grow stronger through persecution — may be apocryphal, but it captures a real pattern that confounded his expectations and those of the Mughal provincial governors before him. Understanding why the Khalsa proved so resilient requires understanding both the military and logistical factors (mobility, local intelligence, terrain familiarity) and the ideological and spiritual ones (the theology of martyrdom, the institutions of the Sarbat Khalsa and langar, the distributed leadership of the Misl system).

Memory, Commemoration, and Historical Consciousness

The Ghallugharas entered Sikh collective memory almost immediately. Ratan Singh Bhangu, writing in the early 19th century but drawing on oral traditions from survivors and their descendants, provides detailed accounts of both events that emphasize the heroism of the fallen and the providential survival of the community. His framing is explicitly theological: the Ghallugharas are tests of faith that the Khalsa passed, demonstrations that ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ (the Timeless One) had not abandoned the Panth even in its darkest hours. This theological framing — suffering as test rather than punishment, survival as divine evidence — became the dominant mode of Sikh historical consciousness regarding these events.

The vocabulary of the Ardas (ਅਰਦਾਸ), the Sikh congregational prayer, incorporates the Ghallugharas into the community's liturgical memory. The Ardas recalls those who were sawed, those who were scalped, those who were broken on the wheel — a litany of martyrdom that locates contemporary Sikh worshippers within a continuous tradition of sacrifice. This liturgical incorporation means that the Ghallugharas are not merely historical facts but living presences in the devotional life of the community, invoked in every formal act of congregational prayer.

The concept of ਚੜ੍ਹਦੀ ਕਲਾ (charhdi kala, ascending or buoyant spirit) is the theological counterpart to the memory of suffering. Rather than allowing the Ghallugharas to produce a culture of victimhood or despair, the Khalsa tradition insists on a posture of spiritual elevation even in the face of catastrophe. This is not a denial of suffering but a transformation of its meaning: the martyrs died in the service of truth (ਸੱਚ), and their deaths are therefore occasions for inspiration rather than lamentation. The phrase that closes the Ardas — ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ ਜੀ ਕਾ ਖਾਲਸਾ, ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ ਜੀ ਕੀ ਫ਼ਤਿਹ (the Khalsa belongs to Waheguru, victory belongs to Waheguru) — encapsulates this theological stance.

Modern Sikh communities commemorate the Ghallugharas through annual observances, educational programs, and the incorporation of these events into the Sikh curriculum taught to children in Gurdwaras around the world. The diaspora Sikh community has been particularly active in ensuring that these events are known and commemorated beyond South Asia. At the same time, scholars have begun to examine the politics of Ghallughara commemoration — noting that different Sikh political communities emphasize different aspects of these events and draw different conclusions from them about the nature of Sikh identity and the relationship between the Panth and political authority.

Key Terms

  • ਘੱਲੂਘਾਰਾ (Ghallughara) — Literally a scattering or dispersal; used in Sikh historical vocabulary to denote the two great massacres of 1746 and 1762 in which large numbers of Khalsa Sikhs were killed in concentrated operations aimed at the elimination of the Panth.
  • ਛੋਟਾ ਘੱਲੂਘਾਰਾ (Chhota Ghallughara) — The small catastrophe of 1746, in which Mughal forces under Lakhpat Rai killed thousands of Khalsa Sikhs and captured hundreds more who were subsequently executed in Lahore.
  • ਵੱਡਾ ਘੱਲੂਘਾਰਾ (Vadda Ghallughara) — The great catastrophe of February 1762, in which Ahmad Shah Durrani's forces inflicted catastrophic losses on a large Sikh column at Kup Rahira.
  • ਚੜ੍ਹਦੀ ਕਲਾ (Charhdi Kala) — The Sikh concept of ascending or buoyant spirit; the theological posture of spiritual elevation maintained even in the face of suffering, disaster, or persecution.
  • ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ (Shaheedi) — Martyrdom; the death of a Sikh who refuses to abandon their faith under coercion; a concept that gives sacred meaning to violent death in defense of religious identity.
  • ਅਰਦਾਸ (Ardas) — The congregational supplicatory prayer of the Sikhs, which incorporates a litany of historical martyrs and events — including the Ghallugharas — into the liturgical memory of the community.

Discussion Questions

  1. How does the concept of ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ (shaheedi) function differently from secular understandings of heroic death? What theological work does it do for the community that remembers the Ghallugharas?
  2. The Khalsa recovered from the Vadda Ghallughara with remarkable speed, launching major military campaigns within months. What factors — military, logistical, ideological — best explain this resilience?
  3. The Ardas incorporates the Ghallugharas into weekly congregational worship. What are the benefits and potential risks of liturgically remembering collective trauma? How might this shape community psychology across generations?
  4. Compare the Sikh theology of ਚੜ੍ਹਦੀ ਕਲਾ (charhdi kala) as a response to the Ghallugharas with how another religious or ethnic community has theologically processed collective catastrophe. What is distinctive about the Sikh approach?
  5. Ratan Singh Bhangu frames the Ghallugharas as divine tests that the Khalsa passed. Is this a satisfying historical explanation? What does this framing reveal about how the Sikh tradition approaches the problem of innocent suffering?

Further Reading

  • Hari Ram Gupta, History of the Sikhs, Volume III: The Sikh Lion of Lahore — provides detailed military histories of both Ghallugharas with analysis of sources and casualty estimates.
  • Ratan Singh Bhangu, Prachin Panth Parkash (trans. Kulwant Singh) — the essential primary source for 18th-century Sikh history, containing firsthand oral accounts of the Ghallugharas.
  • Surjit Singh Gandhi, History of the Sikh Gurus Retold — contextualizes the Ghallugharas within the broader narrative of Khalsa history and theology.
  • Anne Murphy, The Materiality of the Past: History and Representation in Sikh Tradition — sophisticated analysis of how Sikh communities construct and use historical memory, with attention to the politics of commemoration.
  • Key Takeaways
    • The two Ghallugharas — Chhota (1746) and Vadda (1762) — were not incidental tragedies but defining events that shaped Sikh historical consciousness, collective identity, and theological reflection.
    • The Khalsa's response to these catastrophes drew on theological resources including the concept of ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ (shaheedi), ਚੜ੍ਹਦੀ ਕਲਾ (charhdi kala), and the liturgical incorporation of martyrs into the Ardas.
    • The speed of the Khalsa's recovery from the Vadda Ghallughara — from near-annihilation to territorial expansion within two years — reflects both military-logistical factors and the ideological resilience of the Panth's distributed institutional structure.
    • The Ghallugharas are incorporated into Sikh liturgical memory through the Ardas, making them living presences in contemporary Sikh devotional life rather than merely historical facts.
    • The politics of Ghallughara commemoration remain contested, with different Sikh communities emphasizing different aspects of these events in relation to contemporary questions of identity and political authority.

Homework

The Vadda Ghallughara (1762) is commemorated in the Sikh calendar alongside other major events of persecution and resilience. Research how this event is remembered in contemporary Sikh practice — look at the Sikh Research Institute's resources, the Sikh Coalition's educational materials, or any scholarly article on Sikh commemoration. Write a 400-word reflection on the relationship between historical memory and community identity: How does remembering the Ghallugharas shape how Sikhs understand their identity today? What are the risks of over-emphasizing suffering as the foundation of identity, and what resources within Sikhi offer a counterbalance?

lessons.title: Ahmad Shah Durrani and the Khalsa: Conflict, Resilience, and the Afghan Invasions
lessons.html:
Introduction

Between 1747 and 1769, Ahmad Shah Durrani (ਅਹਿਮਦ ਸ਼ਾਹ ਦੁੱਰਾਨੀ) launched nine major invasions of the Indian subcontinent, passing through the Punjab on every campaign. He defeated the Marathas at the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761, temporarily reasserting Afghan dominance over north India, and he inflicted the Vadda Ghallughara on the Khalsa in 1762. By any conventional military calculus, he should have destroyed the Sikh movement. He commanded larger, better-equipped armies than the Misls. He had the resources of an empire behind him. He was one of the most able commanders of the eighteenth century. Yet the Khalsa not only survived his campaigns but emerged stronger after each one. The story of the Khalsa's encounter with Ahmad Shah Durrani is one of the most instructive episodes in the history of asymmetric warfare and ideological resilience.

The Durrani invasions forced the Khalsa into a crucible that tested every aspect of its organizational, ideological, and military character. The responses the community developed — mobile warfare, forest sanctuaries, rapid dispersal and regroupment, the cultivation of local intelligence networks, and the theological resources of ਚੜ੍ਹਦੀ ਕਲਾ (charhdi kala) — were not merely tactical improvisations. They were expressions of a community that had been shaped by decades of persecution into an extraordinarily resilient form. Understanding how the Khalsa survived and responded to Durrani illuminates the deeper dynamics of the entire 18th-century Sikh experience.

This lecture examines the Afghan invasions from multiple angles: the political context of Durrani's empire and his objectives in the Punjab, the military dynamics of Khalsa resistance, the specific engagements of 1746–1764 including the two Ghallugharas, and the Khalsa's remarkable counteroffensive that led to the sacking of Sirhind in 1764 and the effective end of sustained Afghan control over the Punjab. We also consider the broader implications of this conflict for understanding how ideologically committed movements sustain themselves against superior conventional military force.

The Durrani period is not simply a chapter of suffering to be gotten through on the way to Sikh victory. It is the forge in which the Khalsa's distinctive character was formed. The institutions, tactics, and theological orientations that enabled the Sikh Empire of the 19th century were developed and tested during these decades of existential pressure.

Ahmad Shah Durrani: Empire, Strategy, and the Punjab

Ahmad Shah Durrani — also known as Ahmad Shah Abdali — founded the Durrani Empire in 1747 following the assassination of Nadir Shah of Persia, under whom he had served as a military commander. He was elected Shah by a Pashtun loya jirga at Kandahar and spent the first decade of his reign consolidating his control over Afghanistan and extending it into Khorasan, Kashmir, and the Punjab. His invasions of India were motivated by a combination of factors: the desire for the enormous wealth of the subcontinent's fertile plains, the weakening of Mughal authority that made Indian territory suddenly vulnerable, the need to pay his troops and reward his tribal allies, and a genuine sense of Islamic mission in relation to what he regarded as the declining standards of Mughal governance.

The Punjab was both a target and a corridor for Durrani. Its agricultural wealth — the grain, cotton, and pastoral resources of the five-river plain — was itself valuable. But the Punjab also lay on the route to Delhi, where the greatest prizes of Mughal wealth were concentrated. Durrani's strategy was to extract maximal resources from the Punjab with each passage, to appoint reliable governors in Lahore, and to use the threat of return to ensure compliance. This strategy worked adequately against sedentary populations with fixed assets and leaders who had something to lose by resistance. Against the Khalsa, it failed consistently.

The Mughal successor state in Lahore — governed after 1752 by Durrani-appointed governors — was too weak to suppress the Sikh guerrilla movement on its own and too unreliable as a coalition partner for Durrani. The governors of Lahore oscillated between attempting to suppress the Khalsa (as Yahiya Khan and his son-in-law Mir Mannu did in the 1740s and early 1750s) and attempting to use them as mercenary auxiliaries against other threats. This inconsistency reflected the fundamental strategic problem: the Khalsa controlled the countryside and the communication routes of central Punjab in ways that no urban-based governor could effectively counter.

Durrani attempted several different approaches to the Sikh problem. Direct military assault — exemplified by the Vadda Ghallughara — could inflict catastrophic losses but could not prevent regroupment. Economic pressure through destroying crops and cutting off access to Amritsar could be temporarily effective but could not be sustained between invasions. Political negotiation — offering the Sikhs recognized territorial status in exchange for submission — was attempted but ran against the Khalsa's fundamental refusal to accept subordination to a non-Sikh sovereign. None of these approaches solved the strategic problem.

Military Dynamics: Guerrilla Warfare and the Khalsa Method

The military methods that the Khalsa developed against Durrani were not formally theorized but were practically sophisticated. The core Khalsa military approach was based on mobility, local intelligence, and the avoidance of set-piece battle against superior forces — combined with the willingness to fight ferociously when the terrain and circumstances favored it. The Misls maintained large cavalry forces (ਘੋੜਸਵਾਰੀ) that could disperse rapidly when Afghan heavy forces appeared and concentrate with equal speed when a vulnerable target presented itself.

The forests and wetlands of the Punjab — the ਜੰਗਲਾਂ along the river banks, the ਝਾੜੀਆਂ (scrublands), and the Shivalik foothills to the northeast — served as refuges during Afghan campaigns. The Khalsa had developed intimate knowledge of these terrains over decades of persecution, and they used them with considerable tactical skill. Durrani's cavalry was formidable on open plains but lost much of its effectiveness in dense scrub and forested terrain. The Khalsa exploited this differential with considerable success.

The Khalsa also maintained an intelligence network of remarkable effectiveness. Village headmen, merchants, horse traders, and travelling bards (ਢਾਢੀ) provided information about Afghan movements that allowed the Sikh forces to anticipate and avoid encounters they could not win while preparing ambushes for those they could. The relationship between the Khalsa and the Punjabi rural population — built through the ਰਾਖੀ system, through langar, and through shared religious and ethnic identity — gave the Sikh fighters an intelligence advantage that Durrani's forces could never fully overcome.

The Khalsa's willingness to absorb catastrophic losses — as at the Vadda Ghallughara — and continue fighting was perhaps the most militarily significant aspect of its character. Most political and military organizations of the 18th century had threshold losses beyond which they would negotiate or submit. The Khalsa did not. This was not because Sikh fighters were indifferent to death but because the theological framework of ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ (shaheedi) meant that death in the service of the Panth was not a loss but a fulfillment. An enemy that cannot achieve submission through the threat of death faces a fundamental strategic problem, and Durrani faced it acutely in his dealings with the Khalsa.

The Counteroffensive: Sirhind and the Turning of the Tide

The Khalsa's counteroffensive after the Vadda Ghallughara demonstrates the movement's resilience most dramatically. Within months of suffering losses that would have destroyed most military organizations, the Sikh Misls were raiding as far as Delhi — the famous incident in which Sikh horsemen reportedly bathed their horses in the Yamuna — and planning major operations against the collaborationist administration of Sirhind.

The sacking of Sirhind in January 1764 was one of the most symbolically charged events of the eighteenth century for the Sikh community. Sirhind (ਸਰਹਿੰਦ) had been the seat of the governor who ordered the execution of Guru Gobind Singh's younger sons — the Sahibzade — in 1705. Its destruction was thus simultaneously a military operation, an act of political assertion, and an act of historical justice within the Sikh theological framework. The killing of Zain Khan, Sirhind's governor and a Durrani collaborator, satisfied both immediate military objectives and deeper communal imperatives.

Following Sirhind, the Misls rapidly extended their territorial control across the Punjab. By 1765 the Sikh Misls had expelled Durrani's appointees from Lahore and were minting their own coins in the name of the Guru. The coin inscriptions — invoking ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ and Guru Gobind Singh — were not merely monetary but theological declarations: sovereignty over the Punjab now rested with the Khalsa, not with the Mughal Emperor or the Afghan Shah. The speed of this transition from the Vadda Ghallughara to territorial sovereignty — roughly two years — is remarkable and speaks to the depth of the Khalsa's organizational and ideological resources.

Durrani's ninth and final invasion in 1769 found a very different Punjab from the one he had entered in 1747. The Misls were now organized territorial powers with fixed revenues, standing forces, and administrative infrastructure. They were no longer a guerrilla movement dependent on mobility and evasion; they were governing entities with the capacity for conventional military defense. Durrani extracted what tribute he could and withdrew. He would not return. The Khalsa had, in effect, outlasted him.

Key Terms

  • ਅਹਿਮਦ ਸ਼ਾਹ ਦੁੱਰਾਨੀ (Ahmad Shah Durrani) — Founder of the Durrani Empire (1747) and the most formidable external military threat faced by the 18th-century Khalsa; his nine invasions of India tested and ultimately failed to suppress the Sikh movement.
  • ਘੋੜਸਵਾਰੀ (Ghorhsavari) — Horsemanship and cavalry; the military arm on which both the Durrani forces and the Khalsa Misls relied, and the focus of intense investment by both sides.
  • ਸਰਹਿੰਦ (Sirhind) — The Mughal administrative center in the Punjab, sacked by the Khalsa in January 1764; its destruction carried both military and profound symbolic significance related to the martyrdom of Guru Gobind Singh's sons.
  • ਢਾਢੀ (Dhadi) — Hereditary bards in Punjabi tradition who sang ballads of heroism and history; they served as carriers of oral historical tradition and, in the Misl period, as informal intelligence networks.
  • ਜੰਗਲ (Jangal) — Wilderness, forest; the forests and scrublands of the Punjab served as critical refuges for the Khalsa during Durrani campaigns, providing cover that negated Afghan cavalry superiority.
  • ਫ਼ਤਿਹ (Fatih) — Victory; the Sikh greeting ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ ਜੀ ਕੀ ਫ਼ਤਿਹ (Victory belongs to Waheguru) expressed the theological conviction that ultimate sovereignty belongs to the divine, not to any earthly power including the Afghan Shah.

Discussion Questions

  1. Ahmad Shah Durrani was arguably the most militarily capable commander the Khalsa ever faced, yet he failed repeatedly to suppress the movement. What does this failure reveal about the limits of conventional military power against ideologically committed insurgencies?
  2. The sacking of Sirhind in 1764 served both military and theological purposes. Can you think of other historical events where military action simultaneously satisfied practical objectives and deep communal-symbolic imperatives? What are the advantages and dangers of this conflation?
  3. The Khalsa's intelligence network — built through the ਰਾਖੀ system, langar, and shared identity with the Punjabi rural population — gave it significant advantages over Durrani. What does this tell us about the relationship between a military movement and the civilian population it claims to protect?
  4. Durrani's ninth invasion in 1769 found a Khalsa that had transformed from a guerrilla movement into a collection of territorial governing entities. How does the transition from resistance to governance typically challenge the ideological commitments of a movement? Do you see evidence of such tensions in the Misl period?
  5. The Khalsa's theological framework — ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ, ਚੜ੍ਹਦੀ ਕਲਾ, ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ ਜੀ ਕੀ ਫ਼ਤਿਹ — meant that death in battle was not a deterrent but a fulfillment. How does this complicate conventional strategic thinking about how to defeat an adversary through force?

Further Reading

  • Ganda Singh, Ahmad Shah Durrani: Father of Modern Afghanistan — an authoritative biography of Durrani that provides the Afghan perspective on the Punjab campaigns and helps contextualize the Khalsa conflict within his broader imperial project.
  • Hari Ram Gupta, History of the Sikhs, Volume III — detailed military histories of the Durrani-Khalsa conflicts with analysis of the major engagements.
  • Fauja Singh, ed., Historians and Historiography of the Sikhs — contains essays on how different historiographical traditions have narrated the Khalsa-Durrani conflict.
  • Purnima Dhavan, When Sparrows Became Hawks: The Making of the Sikh Warrior Tradition, 1699–1799 — situates the Durrani conflict within the broader argument about how the Khalsa warrior identity was constructed and maintained.
  • Key Takeaways
    • Ahmad Shah Durrani's nine invasions of India posed an existential threat to the Khalsa, yet consistently failed to suppress the Sikh movement despite Durrani's overwhelming conventional military superiority.
    • The Khalsa's military effectiveness rested on mobility, local intelligence networks, terrain knowledge, and the theological refusal to accept defeat as final — factors that nullified many of Durrani's advantages.
    • The sacking of Sirhind in January 1764, carried out within months of the Vadda Ghallughara, represented both a military counteroffensive and a profound act of historical and theological justice.
    • By 1765, the Misls had expelled Durrani's appointees from Lahore and were minting coins in the Guru's name — a transformation from guerrilla resistance to territorial sovereignty accomplished in roughly two years after near-annihilation.
    • The Khalsa-Durrani conflict is a case study in how ideologically committed movements can outlast militarily superior adversaries, with implications for the study of asymmetric warfare far beyond the 18th-century Punjab.

Homework

Read Chapter 4 or 5 of J.S. Grewal's The Sikhs of the Punjab, or the relevant sections of Hari Ram Gupta's History of the Sikhs, focusing on the Durrani invasions. Write a 400-word analytical essay on the following question: Was Ahmad Shah Durrani's repeated failure to suppress the Khalsa primarily a result of military factors, political factors, or the ideological resilience of the Sikh movement? Use specific events and evidence from your reading to support your argument, and acknowledge the strongest counterargument to your position.

lessons.title: Sikh Law, Ethics, and the Rahit in the Eighteenth Century
lessons.html:
Introduction

Every religious community that endures over time must address the question of how its members should live — what practices define belonging, what behaviors transgress the community's norms, and how violations should be handled. For the eighteenth-century Khalsa, this question was urgent in a distinctive way. The community was simultaneously under existential military pressure and undergoing rapid expansion, absorbing new members from diverse backgrounds with varying degrees of prior Sikh formation. Maintaining coherence of identity and practice while fighting for survival and growing in numbers was a challenge that required practical institutional responses.

The primary institutional response was the rahitnama (ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ) — literally a text of conduct or code of discipline. The rahitnamas are a genre of Sikh literature that flourished particularly in the eighteenth century, consisting of texts that specified what initiated Khalsa Sikhs were required to do, what they were forbidden from doing, and what consequences attached to violations of the code. Attributed in many cases to Guru Gobind Singh himself or to his close companions (though the actual compilation and elaboration of these texts continued well into the 18th century), the rahitnamas were the primary vehicles through which the Khalsa ਰਹਿਤ (discipline, code of conduct) was defined and transmitted.

This lecture examines the rahitnamas as historical documents that reveal both the ideals and the anxieties of the eighteenth-century Khalsa community. We look at what the texts specify — the required practices (ਕਰਨੀ, what must be done) and the prohibitions (ਕੁਰਹਿਤ, what must not be done) — and consider what these specifications reveal about the social and religious environment the compilers were navigating. We also examine the tensions between different rahitnamas, the scholarly debates about their dating and authority, and the long-term significance of this 18th-century codification effort for Sikh religious law.

Understanding the rahitnamas is essential for understanding how the Khalsa maintained its distinctive identity under the pressures of the 18th century. They are not merely rulebooks; they are windows into the community's deepest concerns about who it was and what it stood for in the face of persecution, internal diversity, and the temptations of assimilation.

The Rahit Tradition: Origins, Texts, and Authority

The concept of ਰਹਿਤ (rahit, discipline or code of conduct) predates the formal establishment of the Khalsa in 1699 but becomes dramatically more concrete after that event. Guru Gobind Singh's creation of the Khalsa through the Amrit Sanchar ceremony established a initiated community with specific visible markers (the Panj Kakars — ਪੰਜ ਕਕਾਰ: ਕੇਸ, ਕੰਘਾ, ਕੜਾ, ਕਛਹਿਰਾ, ਕ੍ਰਿਪਾਨ) and specific behavioral expectations. The earliest rahitnamas attempted to specify and elaborate these expectations in written form.

The most significant surviving rahitnamas from the 18th century include the text attributed to Chaupa Singh Chhivar (ਚੌਪਾ ਸਿੰਘ), who served as a retainer of Guru Gobind Singh; the Rahitnama attributed to Desa Singh; the texts associated with Bhai Nand Lal (ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ), one of Guru Gobind Singh's most celebrated Persian-language poets; and several shorter texts attributed to various companions of the Guru. W.H. McLeod's scholarly analysis of these texts, published in his Textual Sources for the Study of Sikhism and his monograph The Chaupa Singh Rahit-Nama, provides the most rigorous academic treatment, noting the textual complexity and the evidence of later interpolation in several of these works.

The question of authority was central to the rahitnama tradition. Because the texts were often attributed to Guru Gobind Singh directly, their prescriptions carried a weight that mere community custom could not. Yet the diversity of the surviving texts — sometimes contradicting each other on specific points — indicated that the rahitnama tradition was not a single authoritative code but a contested field in which different factions within the Khalsa advanced their particular views of what Sikh practice should entail. This diversity was itself an expression of the decentralized, multi-centered character of the Misl-era Panth.

The major categories of rahit prescription include: daily spiritual practice (ਨਿਤਨੇਮ, morning and evening prayers); maintenance of the Panj Kakars; dietary regulations (prohibition on ਕੁੱਠਾ — meat slaughtered according to Muslim rite); prohibitions on tobacco and other intoxicants; requirements regarding the worship of Gurus' scripture and the Gurdwara; and social regulations regarding marriage, caste, and relations with non-Sikhs. The relative weight given to different categories varies among texts, and some rahitnamas include prescriptions regarding specific occupations, trading practices, and relationships with political authorities that reflect the particular social environment of their composition.

Kurahits: Violations, Discipline, and Community Identity

Perhaps the most revealing sections of the rahitnamas are those specifying the ਕੁਰਹਿਤ (kurahit, major violations) — the acts that, if committed by an initiated Sikh, required public confession before the Panj Pyare (ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ) and the performance of penance (ਤਨਖ਼ਾਹ, tankha). The four major kurahits that became standard — cutting hair, using tobacco, eating meat slaughtered according to Muslim rite, and committing adultery — reflect specific anxieties about the boundaries of Khalsa identity in the 18th-century context.

The prohibition on cutting hair was fundamental to the visual distinctiveness of the Khalsa and hence to its identity. In a context where apostasy under persecution was an ever-present temptation, and where cutting one's hair and adopting Muslim or Hindu dress could mean the difference between life and death, the insistence on maintaining ਕੇਸ (uncut hair) was a declaration of non-negotiable commitment. The stories of Sikhs who maintained their ਕੇਸ even under torture — and became ਸ਼ਹੀਦ (martyrs) as a result — were celebrated precisely because they demonstrated the community's collective commitment to this visible marker over even survival.

The prohibition on tobacco (ਤੰਬਾਕੂ, tambaku) has puzzled some scholars because tobacco does not appear to have been specifically addressed in the early teachings of the Gurus. The rahitnama tradition traces it to a specific incident involving Guru Gobind Singh, but the historical accuracy of this account is debated. What is clear is that by the mid-18th century the prohibition on tobacco had become one of the most consistent and emphatic prescriptions in the rahitnama literature. Its inclusion among the four major kurahits may reflect the association of tobacco with Mughal and Afghan court culture — smoking the hookah (ਹੁੱਕਾ) being a marker of accommodation to a social world that the Khalsa was committed to rejecting.

The prohibition on ਕੁੱਠਾ (kuttha) meat reflected both theological concerns about taking life carelessly and socio-political concerns about the boundary between Sikh and Muslim practice. In a context where Mughal and Afghan political authority was associated with Islam, the rejection of halal meat was a marker of non-submission to that authority as much as a dietary regulation. The parallel prohibition on consuming meat from animals killed by gradual suffocation (ਜ਼ਟਕਾ vs. ਕੁੱਠਾ) embedded a specific Sikh position within an existing debate about ritual slaughter that had political as well as religious dimensions.

The handling of kurahit violations through the institution of the Panj Pyare and tankha penance was significant as a form of community governance. It meant that disciplinary authority rested not with any individual sardar or religious specialist but with a collective of five initiated Sikhs — replicating the founding structure of the Khalsa itself. This decentralization of disciplinary authority was consistent with the broader Misl-era commitment to distributed governance and resistant to the kind of hierarchical concentration of power that characterized Mughal and Afghan political structures.

The Rahit and Contemporary Debates

The 18th-century rahitnamas cast a long shadow over subsequent Sikh history. When the Singh Sabha reform movement of the late 19th century sought to purify and systematize Sikh practice, it drew heavily on the rahitnama tradition — particularly on those texts that presented the Khalsa as a sharply bounded community distinguished from Hinduism as well as from Islam. The resulting Sikh Rahit Maryada (ਸਿੱਖ ਰਹਿਤ ਮਰਯਾਦਾ), finalized by the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (SGPC) in 1950, represented an attempt to create a single authoritative code for the entire Panth — something the diverse 18th-century texts had never achieved.

Scholarly debates about the rahitnamas are closely connected to contemporary debates about Sikh identity. W.H. McLeod's critical analysis of the rahitnama tradition — which traced some features to 19th-century interpolation rather than to Guru Gobind Singh's time — generated intense controversy within the Sikh community and remains a flashpoint in discussions about the appropriate relationship between historical scholarship and religious tradition. The stakes of these debates are not merely academic: they bear on the question of which version of Sikh practice is normative and authoritative.

The 18th-century rahitnama tradition also reveals important information about what the Khalsa was trying to be in a period of existential pressure. The emphasis on visible identity markers (ਕੇਸ, ਕੜਾ, ਕਛਹਿਰਾ), on prohibition of substances associated with Mughal-Afghan culture (tobacco, ਕੁੱਠਾ), and on daily spiritual practice (ਨਿਤਨੇਮ) tells us that the Khalsa understood its survival as depending on the maintenance of a distinctive, practiced, embodied identity — an identity that was expressed in daily life and visible in public, not merely held as a private belief. This insistence on embodied, visible, practiced Sikh identity is one of the 18th-century Khalsa's most durable legacies.

Key Terms

  • ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ (Rahitnama) — A text of conduct; the genre of 18th-century Sikh literature that specified required practices and prohibitions for initiated Khalsa Sikhs, providing the institutional framework for Khalsa identity maintenance.
  • ਕੁਰਹਿਤ (Kurahit) — Major violations of the Khalsa code of conduct, requiring public confession before the Panj Pyare and the performance of tankha (penance); the four major kurahits became the cardinal prohibitions of initiated Sikh life.
  • ਤਨਖ਼ਾਹ (Tankha) — Penance or punishment assigned by the Panj Pyare to a Sikh who has committed a kurahit; the process of confession and penance through which a violator could be restored to full standing in the Khalsa community.
  • ਕੁੱਠਾ (Kuttha) — Meat slaughtered according to the Muslim halal method; its prohibition in the Khalsa rahit served both theological and socio-political functions in the 18th-century context.
  • ਪੰਜ ਕਕਾਰ (Panj Kakar) — The five K's (ਕੇਸ, ਕੰਘਾ, ਕੜਾ, ਕਛਹਿਰਾ, ਕ੍ਰਿਪਾਨ): the five articles of faith required of all initiated Khalsa Sikhs, which formed the most visible markers of Khalsa identity.
  • ਸਿੱਖ ਰਹਿਤ ਮਰਯਾਦਾ (Sikh Rahit Maryada) — The standardized Sikh code of conduct finalized by the SGPC in 1950, drawing on the 18th-century rahitnama tradition and the 19th-century Singh Sabha reform movement; the primary contemporary reference point for normative Sikh practice.

Discussion Questions

  1. The 18th-century rahitnamas were produced in a context of existential threat. How might the specific prescriptions they contain — particularly the major kurahits — reflect the particular anxieties and challenges of that historical moment? Do any of these prescriptions make less sense outside that context?
  2. The prohibition on tobacco became one of the four major kurahits even though tobacco is not explicitly addressed in the teachings of the early Gurus. What does the process by which this prohibition was established reveal about how the Khalsa community developed its normative standards?
  3. W.H. McLeod's scholarly analysis of the rahitnamas, which questioned their dating and attributed some features to later interpolation, generated significant controversy. How should a religious community relate to scholarly criticism of its foundational texts? What methods and attitudes seem most appropriate?
  4. The rahitnama tradition emphasized embodied, visible, practiced identity — not merely private belief. How does this emphasis on embodied religious identity differ from the approaches of other religious traditions? What are its strengths and potential drawbacks as a strategy for community maintenance?
  5. The 18th-century rahitnama tradition was diverse and sometimes contradictory. The 1950 Sikh Rahit Maryada attempted to create a single authoritative code. What was gained and what may have been lost in this move from diversity to standardization?

Further Reading

  • W.H. McLeod, The Chaupa Singh Rahit-Nama — the most detailed scholarly analysis of a single rahitnama text, with extensive historical and textual commentary.
  • W.H. McLeod, Textual Sources for the Study of Sikhism — includes translations of key rahitnama passages alongside other primary sources; an essential reference for advanced students.
  • J.S. Grewal and S.S. Bal, eds., Guru Gobind Singh: A Biographical Study — contextualizes the rahitnama tradition within the life and thought of the Guru who founded the Khalsa.
  • Pashaura Singh and Louis E. Fenech, eds., The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies — the chapter on the Khalsa Rahit provides an accessible scholarly overview of the rahitnama tradition and contemporary debates.
  • Key Takeaways
    • The rahitnamas were the primary institutional mechanism through which the 18th-century Khalsa maintained coherence of identity and practice under conditions of persecution, rapid expansion, and organizational decentralization.
    • The four major kurahits — cutting hair, using tobacco, eating kuttha meat, and adultery — reflect specific anxieties about boundary maintenance in the 18th-century context of Mughal-Afghan political and cultural pressure.
    • The diversity and occasional contradictions among surviving rahitnamas indicate that the Khalsa rahit was a contested field rather than a single authoritative code throughout the 18th century.
    • Disciplinary authority through the Panj Pyare and tankha system reflected the Khalsa's broader commitment to decentralized, collective governance rather than individual or hierarchical authority.
    • The 18th-century rahitnama tradition laid the foundation for the 1950 Sikh Rahit Maryada and continues to shape contemporary debates about Sikh identity, practice, and the relationship between historical scholarship and religious authority.

Homework

Obtain and read a translation of one of the 18th-century Sikh rahitnamas — Chaupa Singh's Rahitnama, Desa Singh's Rahitnama, or Bhai Nand Lal's Rahitnama are all available in W.H. McLeod's Textual Sources for the Study of Sikhism or in dedicated translations. Write a 350-word response: What does this text reveal about what the compilers considered the most important threats to Sikh identity in the 18th century? What continuities and tensions do you see between the concerns of this 18th-century text and contemporary discussions of Sikh practice and identity?

lessons.title: Legacy of the Eighteenth Century: The Khalsa's Transformation and the Foundations of the Sikh Empire
lessons.html:
Introduction

By the final decade of the eighteenth century, the landscape of the Punjab had been transformed beyond recognition from what it had been when Banda Singh Bahadur died in 1716. The Mughal Empire that had executed Banda no longer existed as a meaningful political force. The Afghan power that had inflicted the Ghallugharas was receding from the Punjab. The twelve Misls that had fought for survival in the forests and marshes of the Punjab were now governing entities controlling millions of acres of agricultural land, minting coins in the Guru's name, and administering territories from which they collected taxes, maintained armies, and exercised the functions of sovereignty. The conditions were in place for the consolidation that would produce the Sikh Empire under Maharaja Ranjit Singh.

This final lecture of the course asks what the eighteenth century as a whole means — both as a chapter of history and as a foundation for subsequent Sikh civilization. We examine the specific institutional, military, economic, and ideological legacies that the Misl period bequeathed to the Sikh Empire. We consider the tensions and contradictions embedded in those legacies — the ways in which the transition from resistance movement to governing power inevitably transformed the character of the Khalsa. And we reflect on the question that the eighteenth century poses to subsequent generations of Sikhs: what is the relationship between the founding ideals of 1699 and the forms that Sikh power actually took?

The story of the eighteenth-century Khalsa is, in one reading, a story of triumph: a community facing elimination in 1716 became the sovereign power of one of the Indian subcontinent's richest regions by 1799. But it is also a story of transformation under pressure — a transformation in which something important about the original Khalsa vision was both preserved and altered by the demands of governance, warfare, and power. Engaging honestly with both dimensions of this legacy is the task of serious historical scholarship and of genuine engagement with the Sikh tradition.

This lecture is also an invitation to synthesis. Students who have followed the full arc of this course — from the Amrit Sanchar of 1699 through the Ghallugharas, the Misl period, and the economic and social dimensions of Khalsa life — are now in a position to integrate those perspectives into a coherent understanding of one of the most remarkable chapters in South Asian and world history.

Institutional Legacies: From Misls to Empire

The Misl system bequeathed to the Sikh Empire a set of institutional legacies that were both enabling and constraining. On the enabling side: the Misls had developed functional systems of land tenure and revenue extraction (built on ਰਾਖੀ and later on more formalized jagir arrangements), cavalry-based military organization, and the integration of religious institutions (Gurdwaras, langar, Harmandir Sahib) into the fabric of governance. Ranjit Singh could build on these existing structures rather than creating political institutions from scratch.

The Sarbat Khalsa and Gurmata system, which had served as the Khalsa's collective decision-making body during the Misl period, did not survive the transition to centralized monarchy. Ranjit Singh convened the last significant Sarbat Khalsa in the 1800s; thereafter, his consolidation of power under a single sovereign rendered the old consensus mechanism obsolete. This was a genuine institutional break — the substitution of monarchical authority for the decentralized, collective governance that had characterized the Khalsa during the Misl era. Scholars debate whether this represented a betrayal of the Khalsa's founding principles or an inevitable adaptation to the requirements of governing a large, multi-religious state.

The Akal Takht (ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ) in Amritsar survived the transition and maintained its symbolic authority as the seat of Khalsa temporal sovereignty, even as actual political power shifted to Lahore under Ranjit Singh. The continued existence and reverence of the Akal Takht — and the complex relationship between Ranjit Singh and the religious authority it represented — illustrates the way in which 18th-century institutional forms were preserved in modified and sometimes subordinated forms within the new imperial structure.

The administrative arrangements of the Sikh Empire also reflected Misl-era practices. The sardars of the major Misls were incorporated into the imperial structure as governors, generals, and court nobles, bringing with them the networks of land tenure, military obligation, and family alliance that they had built during the 18th century. This incorporation was not always smooth — several major sardars resisted Ranjit Singh's consolidation and were eventually subordinated or dispossessed — but it meant that the imperial state had a ready-made administrative class with deep roots in the Punjabi countryside.

Ideological Legacies: Sovereignty, Identity, and the Meaning of Raj Karega Khalsa

The ideological legacy of the eighteenth century for the Sikh Empire was complex and sometimes contradictory. The concept of ਰਾਜ ਕਰੇਗਾ ਖਾਲਸਾ (Raj Karega Khalsa, the Khalsa shall rule) had animated the resistance movement through the darkest periods of persecution, providing theological justification for the claim to sovereignty. When that sovereignty was achieved under Ranjit Singh, the slogan's meaning became more ambiguous: whose khalsa? Ruling in whose interest? By what standards of justice?

Ranjit Singh's Sikh Empire was notably multi-religious in its composition and governance. His court included Sikh, Muslim, and Hindu nobles. His armies employed European officers (most famously the French general Allard and the Italian Ventura) alongside Sikh, Muslim, and Hindu soldiers. His administration collected revenue from a population that was predominantly Muslim in the western Punjab and mixed in the central and eastern districts. The Sikh Empire governed in the name of the Guru but did not govern as a theocracy in any simple sense — it governed as a pragmatic multi-ethnic state in which Sikh religious identity held the symbolic center while political and administrative reality was considerably more diverse.

This pragmatic pluralism was both a strength and a source of tension. It allowed the empire to administer a large, diverse population more effectively than a rigidly sectarian state could have. But it also created anxiety within the Khalsa community about whether the ideals of 1699 — the vision of a community of equal, initiated, practicing Khalsa Sikhs governed by the Guru's word — were being honored or subordinated to the demands of imperial power. The tension between the founding vision and the governing reality is a permanent feature of all religious polities, and it characterized the Sikh Empire from its earliest days.

The eighteenth century's ideological legacy also included the deep imprint of ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ (martyrdom tradition) on Sikh collective identity. By the end of the century, the Khalsa had produced a remarkable martyrology — from Banda Singh Bahadur and the thousands killed in the Ghallugharas to the countless unnamed fighters who chose death over apostasy. This martyrology was not merely a source of historical pride; it was a living moral standard that shaped how Sikhs in subsequent generations understood courage, commitment, and the proper relationship between individual and community. The willingness to die for the Panth became a defining characteristic of the Sikh warrior ideal, with both inspiring and sometimes problematic implications for how Sikh communities understood sacrifice and resistance.

The Eighteenth Century in Sikh Historical Memory and Modern Significance

The eighteenth century occupies a privileged place in Sikh historical memory. It is the period in which the Khalsa proved itself — not in the relatively sheltered environment of a Guru's court or the early community's growth, but in the crucible of existential threat. The survival of the Panth against the combined forces of Mughal persecution and Afghan invasion, and its emergence as the sovereign power of the Punjab, has become the foundational narrative of Sikh resilience — the proof that ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ ਜੀ ਕੀ ਫ਼ਤਿਹ (victory belongs to Waheguru) is not merely a greeting but a theological claim confirmed by historical experience.

This narrative serves important functions for contemporary Sikh communities worldwide. It provides a model of perseverance under extreme adversity, a reminder that institutions built on genuine commitment can outlast apparently overwhelming opposition, and a source of pride in the distinctiveness and resilience of the Sikh identity. For Sikh diaspora communities navigating majority cultures that sometimes misunderstand or misrepresent their traditions, the eighteenth-century narrative provides both historical grounding and practical inspiration.

At the same time, historians urge caution about the ways in which this narrative can be simplified or distorted in its popular transmission. The eighteenth century was not a simple story of good versus evil, or of inevitable Sikh triumph. It involved real moral complexity: Khalsa sardars who collaborated with Afghan invaders when convenient, inter-Misl violence that imposed heavy burdens on the Punjabi population, and the gradual social and economic stratification of a community that had been founded on the ideal of equality. Engaging with this complexity honestly, rather than papering over it with triumphalist narrative, is essential for both scholarly integrity and spiritual maturity.

The eighteenth century's relevance extends beyond the Sikh community. It is a case study in how a minority religious community under existential pressure can develop the institutional, ideological, and social resources to not merely survive but transform the political landscape around it. The specific resources the Khalsa deployed — distributed governance, embodied identity markers, theological frameworks for processing suffering, the integration of religious and political authority — are of broad comparative and theoretical interest for scholars of religion, politics, and social movements.

Key Terms

  • ਰਾਜ ਕਰੇਗਾ ਖਾਲਸਾ (Raj Karega Khalsa) — The Khalsa shall rule; a phrase from the Sikh Ardas expressing the theological conviction that sovereign authority ultimately belongs to the Khalsa Panth; its meaning became contested when Sikh sovereignty was actually achieved under Ranjit Singh.
  • ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ (Akal Takht) — The Throne of the Timeless One; the institutional seat of Khalsa temporal sovereignty established by Guru Hargobind at Amritsar, which maintained its symbolic authority through the Misl period and into the Sikh Empire.
  • ਮਹਾਰਾਜਾ ਰਣਜੀਤ ਸਿੰਘ (Maharaja Ranjit Singh) — The Lion of the Punjab (1780–1839); founder of the Sikh Empire who consolidated the Misl territories under a single sovereignty in the first decade of the 19th century, marking the culmination of the 18th-century Khalsa's trajectory.
  • ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ ਪਰੰਪਰਾ (Shaheedi Parampara) — The martyrdom tradition; the accumulated tradition of Sikh martyrology that gave theological meaning to violent death in defense of faith and community, forming one of the most powerful ideological legacies of the 18th century.
  • ਸ਼ਾਹੀ ਦਰਬਾਰ (Shahi Darbar) — Royal court; the court culture of the Sikh Empire under Ranjit Singh, which combined Khalsa symbols and Sikh religious forms with the Persian-language courtly traditions of the Mughal successor states.
  • ਮਿਸਲਦਾਰ (Misaldar) — The leader of a Misl; collectively, the Misaldars of the twelve Sikh Misls formed the political and military elite that Ranjit Singh incorporated into (or displaced by) the imperial structure of the Sikh Empire.

Discussion Questions

  1. Ranjit Singh's consolidation of the Misl territories into a single empire required subordinating the Sarbat Khalsa system of collective governance to monarchical authority. Was this an inevitable result of the transition from resistance movement to governing state, or was it a choice that betrayed the founding principles of the Khalsa?
  2. The Sikh Empire was multi-religious in its composition and governance, employing Muslim and Hindu nobles and European officers alongside Sikh leaders. How should we evaluate this pragmatic pluralism in light of the Khalsa's founding ideals? Is it a fulfillment or a compromise of those ideals?
  3. The eighteenth century produced a powerful martyrdom tradition (ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ ਪਰੰਪਰਾ) that became central to Sikh collective identity. What are the long-term effects on a community when sacrifice and suffering become central to its self-understanding? What are the risks, and how does the Sikh tradition attempt to address them through concepts like ਚੜ੍ਹਦੀ ਕਲਾ?
  4. The eighteenth-century Khalsa provides a historical case study in how a minority religious community can survive and ultimately transform the political landscape against apparently overwhelming odds. What lessons, if any, do you think are transferable to other communities facing existential pressure? What cautions would you add?
  5. Having completed this course, what aspects of the eighteenth-century Khalsa's experience do you find most inspiring, most troubling, and most relevant to contemporary Sikh life? Try to be specific and to avoid both uncritical celebration and unfair criticism.

Further Reading

  • J.S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab — Chapter 6 covers the transition from Misl confederation to Sikh Empire and provides the most authoritative scholarly overview.
  • Khushwant Singh, A History of the Sikhs, Volume I: 1469–1839 — includes a detailed narrative of the Misl period and the reign of Ranjit Singh, accessible to a general academic audience.
  • Rattan Singh Bhangu, Prachin Panth Parkash (trans. Kulwant Singh) — the essential primary source for understanding how contemporaries and near-contemporaries understood the 18th-century transformation.
  • Patwant Singh, The Sikhs — a broader cultural and historical survey that contextualizes the 18th century within the full sweep of Sikh history and civilization.
  • Key Takeaways
    • The eighteenth century bequeathed to the Sikh Empire a set of institutional, military, economic, and ideological resources built through decades of persecution and guerrilla governance under the Misl system.
    • The transition from the decentralized Sarbat Khalsa system to Ranjit Singh's consolidated monarchy represented a genuine institutional transformation that raises ongoing questions about the relationship between the Khalsa's founding ideals and the exercise of state power.
    • The martyrdom tradition (ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ ਪਰੰਪਰਾ) became one of the eighteenth century's most powerful and enduring legacies, shaping Sikh collective identity and self-understanding in ways that persist to the present day.
    • The Sikh Empire's pragmatic multi-religious governance reflected the Misl period's experience of building coalitions across religious and ethnic lines while maintaining Khalsa symbolic authority at the center.
    • The eighteenth-century Khalsa is of broad comparative interest as a case study in how ideologically committed minority communities can develop the institutional, spiritual, and social resources to survive and transform under extreme adversity.

Homework

The 18th century ended with the Khalsa on the verge of consolidated sovereignty under Ranjit Singh. Write a 400-word essay on the following question: What were the two or three most important factors — whether military, ideological, institutional, economic, or spiritual — that enabled the Khalsa to move from a persecuted minority in 1716 to the rulers of the Punjab by 1799? Rank your factors in order of importance and justify your ranking. Then add a 100-word reflection on what you personally find most remarkable about this transformation.

With such a dress there was no need for him to advertise his arrival. At Kurkshetra, during a solar eclipse, he began to cook venison which a disciple had presented to him.
