Guru Nanak Sahib Ji, who lived and taught in conversation with both Hindu and Muslim traditions as well as the Nath yogis, directed sustained critique at the religious failures of his day — not from outside religion, but from within a deep commitment to genuine spiritual reality. This critical tradition is not an incidental feature of ਗੁਰਮਤਿ; it is structurally essential to it. ਗੁਰਮਤਿ defines itself partly through what it is not.

Bhai Gurdas inherits this critical tradition and amplifies it with extraordinary literary skill. His Vaaran are among the most sustained and sophisticated exercises in religious polemic in the Punjabi literary tradition. He critiques Brahmanical ritualism, caste hierarchy, ascetic withdrawal, idol worship, self-serving clergy, and what he calls ਪਾਖੰਡ (pakhand) — the hypocrisy of outward religious display without inner transformation. These critiques are not incidental; they are central to his positive vision of what ਗੁਰਮਤਿ offers and demands.

This lesson examines the polemical dimension of Bhai Gurdas's work in depth. We ask not only what he criticized but how: What literary and rhetorical strategies does he employ? How does he distinguish genuine critique from mere contempt? And how does his polemic serve the positive theological purpose of making ਗੁਰਮਤਿ intelligible as a distinct and superior path to liberation? These questions matter not only historically but for students of Sikhi today, who must understand why this tradition insists so emphatically on distinguishing genuine from false religion (Oberoi, The Construction of Religious Boundaries, 1994).

It is important to note at the outset that Bhai Gurdas's critique is not an expression of contempt for persons; it is an expression of grief for human beings trapped in systems that cannot liberate them. His polemic has a pastoral dimension that distinguishes it from mere sectarian rivalry. He criticizes because he cares, and his caring is shaped by the ਗੁਰਮਤਿ conviction that every human being has the capacity and the right to encounter the Divine directly, without the mediation of ritual, caste, or priestly privilege (Pashaura Singh, The Guru Granth Sahib, 2000).

Targets of Critique: Brahmanical Ritualism, Caste, and Asceticism

The primary targets of Bhai Gurdas's critique can be organized into three broad categories. The first is Brahmanical ritualism — the system of ਕਰਮਕਾਂਡ (karmakand) in which elaborate ritual performance substitutes for genuine spiritual transformation. Bhai Gurdas observes that the priest who performs rituals for payment, the householder who makes offerings for worldly benefit, and the devotee who attends temples out of social obligation rather than genuine longing are all engaged in forms of religious practice that cannot produce liberation. His critique of ritualism does not mean that all ritual is wrong; it means that ritual divorced from inner sincerity and the Guru's grace is spiritually empty.

What makes Bhai Gurdas's critique of ritualism distinctively Sikh rather than merely Bhakti is its theological grounding. He does not simply say that ritual is useless; he explains why: liberation (ਮੁਕਤੀ, mukti) is not a product of correct procedure. It is not achieved by the performance of rites but by the transformation of the ਮਨ (man, mind-heart) through encounter with ਨਾਮ. The Guru Granth Sahib Ji, on Ang 12, teaches that the Name of the Lord is the highest of all; through the Guru's grace, it is understood by the rare devotee. This theological framework — ਨਾਮ as the only genuine path and the Guru as its source — underpins all of Bhai Gurdas's critique of ritual substitutes.

The second target is caste hierarchy, or ਵਰਨ-ਭੇਦ (varan-bhed). This is perhaps the most politically charged dimension of Bhai Gurdas's polemic, and it is expressed with remarkable consistency across the Vaaran. He repeatedly affirms that in the ਸੰਗਤ (sangat) of the Guru, birth-based hierarchy has no place. The ਗੁਰਮੁਖ (Gurmukh) is not distinguished by caste or lineage but by their relationship to ਨਾਮ and the Guru. Bhai Gurdas describes the sangat as a space where distinctions of high and low birth are dissolved in the shared experience of ਨਾਮ-ਸਿਮਰਨ (Nam-Simran) and ਸੇਵਾ (seva). This is not merely a social ideal but a theological statement: ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ (Waheguru) does not recognize human distinctions of rank, and a community that claims to orient itself toward the Divine must reflect that recognition.

The third major target is what might loosely be called asceticism or world-renunciation — ਤਿਆਗ (tyag) pursued as an end in itself. The Nath yogis, certain Sufi orders, and various Hindu renunciants of Bhai Gurdas's day practiced withdrawal from worldly life as a spiritual path. Bhai Gurdas's critique of this approach is subtle: he does not deny the value of inner discipline or the cultivation of detachment. What he critiques is the assumption that physical withdrawal from the world, without the Guru's grace and the company of the ਸੰਗਤ (sangat), can produce liberation. The ਗੁਰਮੁਖ lives in the world, works, maintains family relationships, and engages in ਸੇਵਾ — but does so in a state of inner detachment rooted in ਨਾਮ rather than in geographic or social separation (Giani Gian Singh, Panth Parkash, 1880).

The Polemical Method: How Bhai Gurdas Argues

Bhai Gurdas is not a polemicist in the sense of a debater who scores points; he is a poet-theologian who uses literary craft to make theological arguments. His polemical method is therefore worth studying closely, because it reveals as much about Sikh intellectual style as it does about the specific content of his arguments. Several distinct rhetorical strategies appear consistently across the Vaaran.

The first strategy is the use of vivid contrast between the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ and the ਮਨਮੁਖ (manmukh). Almost every Vaar that includes critique sets up this contrast: the person who lives oriented toward the Guru and the person who lives oriented toward the ego and its desires. By presenting the alternative models side by side, Bhai Gurdas invites the reader to choose — not through abstract argument but through imaginative identification. Which life do you want? Which person do you recognize yourself as being? This method of contrast as invitation is one of his most effective pedagogical tools.

The second strategy is the extended metaphor or simile drawn from nature and daily life. When Bhai Gurdas wants to describe the futility of religious ritual without inner transformation, he does not offer a philosophical argument; he offers an image: the lamp that is lit but gives no light, the field that is watered but yields no crop, the mirror that is polished but shows no reflection. These images work because they are concrete and immediately recognizable. The reader understands before they can articulate why they understand, and this experiential understanding is more durable than abstract argument.

The third strategy is the appeal to historical example. Bhai Gurdas draws on the stories of the Gurus' own lives, on figures from the Puranas and Bhagavata tradition (read through a ਗੁਰਮਤਿ lens), and on the examples of contemporary saints and charlatans. When he wants to illustrate ਪਾਖੰਡ (pakhand), he does not merely define it; he shows it in action through a recognizable character type: the pandit who recites scripture for payment without understanding it, the yogi who performs austerities for public admiration rather than genuine renunciation. These character sketches have the sharpness of satire and the weight of theological argument simultaneously.

Fourth, Bhai Gurdas consistently returns to the positive alternative even in his most critical passages. His critique is never merely negative. When he attacks ਕਰਮਕਾਂਡ (karmakand), he simultaneously describes what genuine devotion looks like. When he critiques caste hierarchy, he simultaneously celebrates the egalitarian ਸੰਗਤ. This structural pattern — critique followed immediately by positive vision — reflects the ਗੁਰਮਤਿ conviction that the purpose of critique is liberation, not condemnation. The goal is to free the reader from false paths so that they can find the true one (Mandair, Religion and the Specter of the West, 2009).

Critique as Compassion: The Pastoral Dimension of Polemic

Perhaps the most distinctive and misunderstood aspect of Bhai Gurdas's polemic is that it is fundamentally an expression of ਦਇਆ (daia, compassion). This might seem paradoxical: How can sharp criticism be compassionate? The answer lies in the theological anthropology of ਗੁਰਮਤਿ. Human beings are understood as fundamentally capable of liberation — every person carries the ਨਾਮ within them, like a seed waiting for the conditions in which it can germinate. The tragedy of false religion, from a ਗੁਰਮਤਿ perspective, is not that it corrupts basically evil people but that it prevents basically capable people from actualizing their spiritual potential.

When Bhai Gurdas criticizes the ਬ੍ਰਾਹਮਣ (Brahman) who performs empty rituals, he is not expressing contempt for Brahmans as persons. He is expressing grief for a community that has inherited a tradition of genuine spiritual power — the Sanskrit learning, the ritual expertise, the connection to sacred knowledge — and has allowed that tradition to degenerate into a system of social privilege and commercial transaction. The critique is sharp precisely because the potential is great. If there were nothing there to criticize, there would be nothing to grieve.

Similarly, when Bhai Gurdas critiques yogis who display their austerities for public admiration, he is not denying that discipline and renunciation have spiritual value. He is arguing that the misdirection of genuine spiritual power — toward the cultivation of personal reputation rather than genuine encounter with the Divine — is a particularly acute form of spiritual loss. The yogi who could be a ਗੁਰਮੁਖ (Gurmukh) but instead performs for an audience has not merely failed to progress; they have actively corrupted what could have been a genuine spiritual path.

This pastoral dimension of polemic has implications for how students of Bhai Gurdas should read his critical passages today. They are not invitations to look down on members of other traditions or to feel superior as Sikhs. They are invitations to look inward: Am I performing religious identity for social approval? Am I substituting ritual habit for genuine encounter with ਨਾਮ? Am I allowing caste, class, or community prejudice to corrupt my practice of ਸੰਗਤ? Bhai Gurdas's critique, rightly understood, is always first a mirror held up to the reader (Kapur Singh, Parasaraprasna, 1959).

Discussion Questions

  1. Bhai Gurdas's critique of ਕਰਮਕਾਂਡ (ritual formalism) is central to several of his Vaaran. Can you identify any forms of ritual formalism in contemporary Sikh life that his critique might address? How should communities engage this critique without becoming dismissive of all ritual practice?
  2. How does Bhai Gurdas's critique of caste hierarchy compare with his positive vision of the ਸੰਗਤ (sangat)? In what ways has the Sikh Panth succeeded in embodying this vision, and in what ways has it fallen short?
  3. The lesson argues that critique in Bhai Gurdas's writing is an expression of compassion rather than contempt. Do you find this interpretation convincing? What distinguishes compassionate critique from contempt in practice?
  4. Bhai Gurdas critiques asceticism or world-renunciation as a path. How does this relate to the ਗੁਰਮਤਿ ideal of the ਗ੍ਰਿਹਸਤੀ (grihasthi, householder) life? What does it mean to be spiritually detached while remaining fully engaged in the world?
  5. The lesson describes three main rhetorical strategies Bhai Gurdas uses in his polemical writing. Which of these do you find most persuasive, and why? Are there rhetorical strategies you think he should have used that he does not employ?

Further Reading

  • Harjot Oberoi, The Construction of Religious Boundaries: Culture, Identity, and Diversity in the Sikh Tradition (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1994) — situates the Sikh critique of rival religious systems in its historical and sociological context.
  • Pashaura Singh, The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority (New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2000) — explores the theological framework within which Bhai Gurdas's polemic operates.
  • Giani Gian Singh, Panth Parkash (Amritsar, 1880) — a classic Punjabi historical work that provides the traditional Sikh context for understanding the polemical dimension of early Sikh writing.
  • Kapur Singh, Parasaraprasna (Amritsar: Sikh Missionary College, 1959) — contains substantive engagement with the theological foundations of Bhai Gurdas's critique of false religion.
  • Key Takeaways
  • Bhai Gurdas's polemic against false religion is not incidental but structurally essential to ਗੁਰਮਤਿ, which defines itself partly through contrast with inadequate alternatives.
  • His three primary targets — ਕਰਮਕਾਂਡ, ਵਰਨ-ਭੇਦ, and ਤਿਆਗ as ends in themselves — are critiqued not from contempt but from the theological conviction that human beings deserve genuine liberation rather than its substitutes.
  • His rhetorical method — contrast, metaphor, historical example, and positive vision — makes his polemic pedagogically effective for communities seeking to understand their own practice more deeply.
  • Read rightly, Bhai Gurdas's critique functions as a mirror for the Sikh community itself, inviting ongoing self-examination rather than complacent comparison with others.

Works Cited

Giani Gian Singh. Panth Parkash. Amritsar, 1880.

Kapur Singh. Parasaraprasna. Amritsar: Sikh Missionary College, 1959.

Mandair, Arvind-pal Singh. Religion and the Specter of the West. New York: Columbia University Press, 2009.

Oberoi, Harjot. The Construction of Religious Boundaries: Culture, Identity, and Diversity in the Sikh Tradition. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1994.

Pashaura Singh. The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2000.

Homework

Choose one category of religious practice that Bhai Gurdas critiques in his Vaaran — such as empty ritualism, the caste system, ascetic withdrawal, or idol worship. Spend 20-25 minutes reading any available English or Punjabi commentary on a Vaar that addresses this theme (Bhai Vir Singh's edition of the Vaaran or the Sikh Research Institute's translations are helpful starting points). Then write a 300-word reflection: Does Bhai Gurdas's critique still apply to any practices you observe in contemporary Sikh or religious life? How do you evaluate the balance between critique and compassion in his writing?

lessons.title: Bhai Gurdas and the Sikh Community: Building Sangat through Poetry
lessons.html:
Table of Contents

  • Introduction: Poetry as Community-Building
  • The Theological Vision of ਸੰਗਤ in the Vaaran
  • Social Structures of the Early Sikh Community: Langar, Seva, and Sangat
  • ਸੰਗਤ as Spiritual Environment: How Community Enables Liberation
  • Key Terms
  • Discussion Questions
  • Further Reading
  • Key Takeaways
  • Works Cited
Term (Unicode)Academic Context
ਸੰਗਤThe gathered community of Sikh practitioners; both a social reality and a theological concept in Bhai Gurdas's writing.
ਲੰਗਰThe community kitchen; the practice of free, shared meals that embodies the egalitarian ethic of ਗੁਰਮਤਿ.
ਸੇਵਾSelfless service; a spiritual practice and social ethic in which the ego is dissolved through dedicated action for others.
ਸਤਿਸੰਗThe community of truth-seekers; a term Bhai Gurdas uses to describe the ideal ਸੰਗਤ oriented fully toward the Guru and ਨਾਮ.
ਪਰਉਪਕਾਰBeneficence toward others; the outward-directed dimension of Sikh ethics, rooted in recognizing the Divine in every person.
ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿThe company of the holy; a term in Gurbani and in Bhai Gurdas's writing for the community of practitioners who mutually support one another's spiritual development.

Introduction: Poetry as Community-Building

When we think of poetry, we tend to think of individual expression — the lyric voice speaking from personal experience to a solitary reader. But in many premodern traditions, poetry served an entirely different function: it was the medium through which communities understood themselves, transmitted their values, and performed their collective identity. The Homeric epics created the Greek world's self-understanding. The Mahabharata provided the ethical and cosmological framework for South Asian civilization. The Psalms built the worshipping community of ancient Israel. Bhai Gurdas's Vaaran belong in this tradition of community-building poetry: they are not expressions of private feeling but architectural texts, constructing the imaginative, theological, and social space within which the Sikh ਸੰਗਤ (sangat) lives.

This understanding changes how we read the Vaaran. When Bhai Gurdas describes the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ (Gurmukh) in vivid and idealized terms, he is not merely expressing an ideal; he is creating a model for the community to aspire toward and measure itself against. When he describes the social practices of the ਸੰਗਤ — the ਲੰਗਰ (langar), the ਕੀਰਤਨ (kirtan), the ਸੇਵਾ (seva) — he is encoding these practices with theological meaning, explaining not just what Sikhs do but why they do it and what it accomplishes spiritually. His poetry is, in this sense, a form of practical theology: it tells the community who it is by telling it what to do and why.

This lesson examines the community-building dimension of Bhai Gurdas's work. We focus on three interlocking themes: his theological vision of what ਸੰਗਤ is and should be; the specific social structures and practices he describes as essential to authentic Sikh community life; and the spiritual logic that makes ਸੰਗਤ not merely a social arrangement but a condition for liberation. Understanding these dimensions of his work helps explain why Bhai Gurdas has remained so central to Sikh community life for over four centuries (Mann, The Making of Sikh Scripture, 2001).

There is also a contemporary urgency to these questions. In an era when individualism pervades spiritual life — when many people describe themselves as spiritual but not religious, preferring private practice to communal commitment — Bhai Gurdas offers a profound and sustained argument for why community is not an optional supplement to spiritual life but its very ground. His argument, rooted in ਗੁਰਮਤਿ theology, remains one of the most compelling defenses of communal spirituality in the world's religious literature (Pashaura Singh, Life and Work of Guru Arjan, 2006).

The Theological Vision of ਸੰਗਤ in the Vaaran

For Bhai Gurdas, ਸੰਗਤ (sangat) is not simply a gathering of people who share a religious identity. It is a theologically loaded reality: the space in which the transformative encounter with ਨਾਮ (Naam) becomes possible for ordinary human beings who are otherwise trapped in the isolation of ਹਉਮੈ (haumai). The ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ (Guru Granth Sahib Ji) describes the ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ (sadhsangat, company of the holy) on Ang 72 as the place where the Divine Name is celebrated and liberation becomes accessible — teachings that Bhai Gurdas takes up and develops with characteristic vividness in the Vaaran.

The theological vision of ਸੰਗਤ in the Vaaran has several key dimensions. First, it is a space of equality. In the ਸੰਗਤ of the Guru, the distinctions that organize the social world — caste, gender, wealth, scholarship — are suspended in the common orientation toward ਨਾਮ. Bhai Gurdas is emphatic on this point: the ਸੰਗਤ is not a gathering of the already-pure; it is a gathering of seekers who come from all conditions of life. What unifies them is not their social identity but their orientation toward the Guru and their willingness to engage in ਨਾਮ-ਸਿਮਰਨ and ਸੇਵਾ together.

Second, ਸੰਗਤ is described as a transformative environment. Bhai Gurdas uses several extended metaphors to make this point. Just as iron placed in fire takes on the fire's heat, or as a fragrant flower imparts its scent to cloth that wraps it, so the person who enters the ਸੰਗਤ of genuine ਗੁਰਮੁਖ (Gurmukh) practitioners is gradually transformed by the spiritual environment. This transformation is not automatic; it requires sincere engagement and ਸੇਵਾ. But the environment itself creates conditions that make transformation possible in ways that isolated practice cannot.

Third, the ਸੰਗਤ is understood as the presence of the Guru in a community form. The Guru Granth Sahib Ji's teaching that the Guru is always with the ਸੰਗਤ, and the sangat always with the Guru, points to a theology of corporate presence: the Guru is not only encountered in the text or in the inner experience of meditation but in the gathered community itself, particularly when it gathers with genuine devotion. Bhai Gurdas amplifies this understanding by consistently describing the marks of authentic ਸੰਗਤ: shared ਕੀਰਤਨ, mutual ਸੇਵਾ, shared ਲੰਗਰ, and the practice of ਨਾਮ-ਸਿਮਰਨ (Kapur Singh, Parasaraprasna, 1959).

Social Structures of the Early Sikh Community: Langar, Seva, and Sangat

Bhai Gurdas writes about the social structures of the early Sikh community not as a sociologist describing external arrangements but as a theologian describing the embodiment of ਗੁਰਮਤਿ in concrete practice. The ਲੰਗਰ (langar), the ਕੀਰਤਨ divan, and the practice of ਸੇਵਾ are, for him, not organizational decisions but theological necessities: the forms that ਨਾਮ-ਸਿਮਰਨ and the Guru's grace take in the social world.

The ਲੰਗਰ deserves particular attention. Established by Guru Nanak Sahib Ji and institutionalized by Mata Khivi (wife of Guru Angad Dev Ji), the community kitchen is described in Gurbani itself — on Ang 967 of the Guru Granth Sahib Ji — as a practice that honors the Guru's teaching of equality and care. Bhai Gurdas understands the ਲੰਗਰ as the social expression of the theological claim that every human being is equally a child of ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ (Waheguru) and equally deserving of nourishment and dignity. The act of sharing food across caste, class, and community lines is not merely a charitable gesture; it is a concrete enactment of the ਗੁਰਮਤਿ understanding of reality.

ਸੇਵਾ (seva) — selfless service — occupies a similarly central place in Bhai Gurdas's account of community life. He describes ਸੇਵਾ as the practical school in which the ਮਨ (man, mind-heart) learns to release its attachment to its own agenda. When a person sweeps the gurdwara floor, serves in the ਲੰਗਰ, or performs any task in the ਸੰਗਤ without thought of personal benefit or recognition, they are practicing the dissolution of ਹਉਮੈ (haumai) not through meditation alone but through action. ਸੇਵਾ is, in Bhai Gurdas's vision, a form of active ਨਾਮ-ਸਿਮਰਨ: the mind that is genuinely absorbed in serving others is not simultaneously generating the ego-narratives that sustain ਹਉਮੈ.

The gathering for ਕੀਰਤਨ — the communal singing of Gurbani in prescribed musical modes (ਰਾਗ, raag) — is the third major structural practice Bhai Gurdas describes. He writes about the ਕੀਰਤਨ divan with obvious love and theological precision: the gathering of voices in praise of ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ creates a sonic environment in which the individual's experience of ਨਾਮ is amplified and sustained by the community's collective intention. The ਸੰਗਤ in ਕੀਰਤਨ is not merely a collection of individuals having simultaneous private experiences; it is a corporate body whose collective practice creates something that individual practice alone cannot (McLeod, Sikhism, 1997).

ਸੰਗਤ as Spiritual Environment: How Community Enables Liberation

The deepest theological argument Bhai Gurdas makes about ਸੰਗਤ is that it is not an optional supplement to the individual spiritual life but a necessary condition for liberation in the ਗੁਰਮਤਿ understanding. This argument runs counter to the dominant Western spiritual assumption that authentic religious life is fundamentally private — a matter between the individual soul and God. Bhai Gurdas, drawing on the Guru's own teaching, argues something more radical: the isolated individual seeking liberation without ਸੰਗਤ is structurally disadvantaged, because ਹਉਮੈ (haumai) cannot be dissolved by the ਹਉਮੈ's own efforts.

The spiritual logic here is subtle. ਹਉਮੈ is defined as the tendency of the ਮਨ (mind-heart) to make itself the center of its own universe, interpreting all experience in terms of its own needs, fears, and desires. The problem with attempting to overcome ਹਉਮੈ through solitary practice is that even the practice of overcoming ਹਉਮੈ can become a project of the ਹਉਮੈ itself — an effort to achieve spiritual status, purity, or liberation that feeds the ego even as it appears to deny it. The ਸੰਗਤ, by placing the practitioner in a community where they must actually serve others, listen to others, and subordinate their preferences to the community's collective practice, creates conditions in which ਹਉਮੈ is challenged in ways that pure individual practice cannot replicate.

Bhai Gurdas also understands ਸੰਗਤ as the medium through which the Guru's grace (ਕਿਰਪਾ, kirpa) operates in the social world. The Guru Granth Sahib Ji on Ang 74 describes the Guru's grace as flowing through the ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ. Bhai Gurdas amplifies this by describing the ਸੰਗਤ as a spiritual force field in which the grace that individuals could not generate for themselves becomes available through the collective orientation of the community toward ਨਾਮ. The ਗੁਰਮੁਖ does not achieve liberation alone; they are carried toward liberation by the current of ਨਾਮ that flows through the assembled ਸੰਗਤ.

This teaching has implications for how we understand the failures of Sikh community life. When ਸੰਗਤ becomes merely social — when people gather out of habit, community obligation, or cultural identity rather than genuine orientation toward ਨਾਮ — it loses its transformative power. Bhai Gurdas is clear-eyed about this possibility and warns against it in several Vaaran: the gathering that looks like ਸੰਗਤ but lacks ਨਾਮ-ਸਿਮਰਨ and genuine ਸੇਵਾ is an external form without its spiritual content. True ਸੰਗਤ is distinguished not by its size, its regularity, or its social organization but by the quality of its collective orientation toward the Guru's word (Mandair, Religion and the Specter of the West, 2009).

Discussion Questions

  1. Bhai Gurdas argues that ਸੰਗਤ is a necessary condition for liberation, not just a helpful supplement to individual practice. Do you find this argument convincing? How does it compare with views of community in other religious traditions you know?
  2. The lesson describes three core practices of ਸੰਗਤ: ਲੰਗਰ, ਸੇਵਾ, and ਕੀਰਤਨ. How does each of these practices address the problem of ਹਉਮੈ? Which do you find most spiritually challenging, and why?
  3. Bhai Gurdas's vision of ਸੰਗਤ is egalitarian — a space where caste, gender, and social distinctions are suspended. To what extent does contemporary Sikh community life embody this vision? Where do you see gaps between ideal and reality?
  4. The lesson argues that poetry itself is a form of community-building. How does reading or hearing the Vaaran create community among people who may be separated by time and geography? What does this suggest about the role of shared texts in religious identity?
  5. Bhai Gurdas warns that ਸੰਗਤ that lacks genuine ਨਾਮ-ਸਿਮਰਨ loses its transformative power and becomes merely social. How can a community assess whether it has genuine ਸੰਗਤ or merely the appearance of it? What practices or disciplines might help a community cultivate authentic orientation toward ਨਾਮ?

Further Reading

  • Gurinder Singh Mann, The Making of Sikh Scripture (New York: Oxford University Press, 2001) — contains important discussion of how the early Sikh community's practices shaped the formation of its scripture and commentary tradition.
  • Pashaura Singh, Life and Work of Guru Arjan (New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2006) — provides historical context for the social structures of the early Sikh community, including ਲੰਗਰ and ਸੰਗਤ as institutional practices.
  • Arvind-pal Singh Mandair, Religion and the Specter of the West (New York: Columbia University Press, 2009) — offers philosophical analysis of the ਗੁਰਮਤਿ understanding of community and individuality.
  • Kapur Singh, Parasaraprasna (Amritsar: Sikh Missionary College, 1959) — discusses the theological relationship between ਸੰਗਤ and ਨਾਮ as understood in the classical Sikh tradition.
  • Key Takeaways
  • Bhai Gurdas's Vaaran function as community-building poetry: they create the imaginative, theological, and social space within which the Sikh ਸੰਗਤ understands and practices its identity.
  • His theological vision of ਸੰਗਤ is not merely social but soteriological: community is a necessary condition for liberation because ਹਉਮੈ cannot dissolve itself through isolated effort.
  • The core practices of ਸੰਗਤ — ਲੰਗਰ, ਸੇਵਾ, and ਕੀਰਤਨ — are for Bhai Gurdas embodiments of ਗੁਰਮਤਿ theology in social form, not merely organizational decisions.
  • Authentic ਸੰਗਤ is distinguished by genuine collective orientation toward ਨਾਮ, not by size, regularity, or social organization alone.

Works Cited

Kapur Singh. Parasaraprasna. Amritsar: Sikh Missionary College, 1959.

Mandair, Arvind-pal Singh. Religion and the Specter of the West. New York: Columbia University Press, 2009.

Mann, Gurinder Singh. The Making of Sikh Scripture. New York: Oxford University Press, 2001.

McLeod, W.H. Sikhism. London: Penguin, 1997.

Pashaura Singh. Life and Work of Guru Arjan. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2006.

Homework

This week, attend a sangat gathering — whether a gurdwara divaan, a community kirtan, an online satsang, or a study circle. As you participate, observe with the lens of this lesson: In what ways does the gathering reflect the ideals of ਸੰਗਤ that Bhai Gurdas describes — equality, mutual service, shared orientation toward the Guru, the dissolution of ego? In what ways does it fall short of or diverge from that ideal? Write a 300-word honest reflection on what you observed and what it made you think about the gap between ideal and practice in Sikh community life.

lessons.title: Reading Bhai Gurdas Today: Scholarly Debates and Interpretive Challenges
lessons.html:
Table of Contents

  • Introduction: Why Interpretation Is Always a Contemporary Act
  • Major Scholarly Debates: Canon, Authenticity, and Translation
  • The Colonial Encounter and Its Legacy for Bhai Gurdas Scholarship
  • Reading Bhai Gurdas in the Twenty-First Century: New Approaches
  • Key Terms
  • Discussion Questions
  • Further Reading
  • Key Takeaways
  • Works Cited
Term (Unicode)Academic Context
ਵਿਆਖਿਆInterpretation or commentary; the scholarly and devotional practice of explaining the meaning of a text.
ਨਿਰਣਾDetermination or critical judgment; the scholarly activity of establishing the authentic text and its correct reading.
ਸੰਪਾਦਨEditorial work; the critical editing and preparation of a text for publication and study.
ਅਨੁਵਾਦTranslation; the practice of rendering a text from one language into another, always involving interpretive choices.
ਪੋਸਟਕੋਲੋਨੀਅਲPostcolonial; describing the scholarly approach that examines how colonial history shapes the interpretation of non-Western texts and traditions.
ਹਰਮੇਨੀਉਟਿਕਸHermeneutics; the theory and method of textual interpretation, including the philosophical questions of what interpretation is and how meaning is produced.

Introduction: Why Interpretation Is Always a Contemporary Act

Every generation reads its foundational texts anew. The questions it brings to those texts, the methods it uses to interpret them, and the concerns it sees them as addressing are shaped by the intellectual, social, and political world of the reader's own time. This is not a defect of reading; it is its nature. The illusion that a text can be read with no interpretive perspective — that a reader can simply extract the text's pure meaning without bringing anything of themselves to the encounter — is precisely that: an illusion. What varies is not whether readers bring their own concerns to a text but how self-aware they are about doing so and how rigorously they subject their interpretive assumptions to examination.

This principle applies with full force to the reading of Bhai Gurdas's Vaaran. The devotional tradition has read them as theological guides to Gurbani, as practical manuals for Sikh community life, and as expressions of the early Sikh community's self-understanding. The colonial-era British scholars read them through the lens of comparative religion and Orientalist assumptions about South Asian religion. The post-independence nationalist scholars read them as evidence of a distinctively Punjabi cultural heritage and as resources for Sikh self-determination. Contemporary academic scholars read them through frameworks drawn from postcolonial theory, gender studies, literary theory, and religious studies. Each of these readings has yielded genuine insights; none has been simply wrong; and each has reflected the concerns and assumptions of its own moment.

This final lecture in the course asks: What does it mean to read Bhai Gurdas's Vaaran responsibly in the twenty-first century? We examine the major scholarly debates that surround his work, consider how the colonial encounter shaped Bhai Gurdas scholarship in ways that still affect us, and explore new approaches that are being developed by contemporary scholars. Our goal is not to arrive at the definitive reading — that goal is itself a colonial fantasy — but to equip students with the critical tools to engage the Vaaran with both scholarly rigor and spiritual humility (Mandair, Religion and the Specter of the West, 2009).

This self-awareness about interpretation is, ironically, one of the things Bhai Gurdas himself models. He was not simply a passive transmitter of Gurbani; he was an active interpreter, and he made interpretive choices that reflected his own context, his own concerns, and his own theological commitments. Reading him well requires us to appreciate both his interpretive achievement and its historical particularity — to honor what he saw and to acknowledge what he may not have seen (Mann, The Making of Sikh Scripture, 2001).

Major Scholarly Debates: Canon, Authenticity, and Translation

Several significant scholarly debates surround the Vaaran of Bhai Gurdas, and engaging with these debates is essential preparation for serious study of the texts. The first concerns questions of authorship and textual integrity. The tradition attributes thirty-nine Vaaran to Bhai Gurdas, and this attribution is strong in the manuscript tradition. However, scholars have noted variations in theological emphasis, literary style, and theological vocabulary across the corpus that raise questions about whether all thirty-nine were composed by the same author or whether some were later additions attributed to him. This is not a question unique to Bhai Gurdas; debates about textual authenticity surround virtually every major religious corpus. But it has implications for how the Vaaran are used as evidence for Bhai Gurdas's theology.

Gurinder Singh Mann's research on the manuscript tradition of early Sikh texts has been particularly important in this area. His work demonstrates the remarkable consistency of the Bhai Gurdas Vaaran manuscript tradition compared with some other early Sikh texts, suggesting that the corpus is substantially intact and represents Bhai Gurdas's actual composition rather than later editorial accretion (Mann, The Making of Sikh Scripture, 2001). However, specific questions about individual Vaaran remain open, and students of the texts should approach them with awareness that the text they read has passed through centuries of manuscript transmission, printing, and editorial decision-making.

The second major debate concerns translation. The Vaaran are in classical Punjabi, a language whose vocabulary, idiom, and poetic conventions are substantially different from contemporary spoken Punjabi. Several major translation projects exist, including the editions prepared by Bhai Vir Singh (early twentieth century) and by the Sikh Missionary Society; more recent English translations have been produced by scholars including Dr. Jodh Singh and others associated with the Sikh Research Institute. Each translation reflects interpretive choices — about the meaning of specific terms, about the register of the translation, about how to handle theologically loaded vocabulary — and comparing translations reveals as much about the history of Sikh interpretation as it does about the text itself.

The question of how to translate key theological terms is particularly contested. Should ਨਾਮ (Naam) be rendered as Name, as Word, as the Divine Reality, or left untranslated? Each choice carries theological implications. Should ਹਉਮੈ (haumai) be rendered as ego, as self-will, as pride, or as something for which there is no adequate English equivalent? The choices translators make reflect their understanding of what ਗੁਰਮਤਿ essentially is and what audience the translation serves. Students who read Bhai Gurdas in translation should be aware that they are reading not only Bhai Gurdas but also the translator's interpretive tradition (Pashaura Singh, The Guru Granth Sahib, 2000).

The Colonial Encounter and Its Legacy for Bhai Gurdas Scholarship

The British colonial encounter with Punjab in the nineteenth century had profound and lasting effects on Sikh self-understanding and on the scholarship of Sikh texts including the Vaaran. The colonial administration's effort to classify, understand, and administer the diverse religious communities of Punjab generated a large body of scholarship — much of it conducted by British officials and missionaries — that categorized Sikhism in ways that reflected colonial assumptions as much as Sikh self-understanding.

Several features of this colonial encounter are particularly relevant for understanding how Bhai Gurdas has been read. First, the colonial period coincided with the Singh Sabha movement (1870s-1920s), a reform movement within Sikhism that sought to define Sikh identity clearly against both Hinduism and Islam, partly in response to colonial census categories that required firm religious classification. This reform context shaped how Bhai Gurdas's critique of Brahmanical ritualism and caste hierarchy was read: it was read not simply as theological teaching but as evidence that Sikhism is essentially distinct from Hinduism. The political context of this reading shaped how it was deployed, sometimes in ways that simplified the actual complexity of Bhai Gurdas's relationship to the Indic intellectual tradition.

Harjot Oberoi's controversial work, The Construction of Religious Boundaries (1994), argued that the rigid boundaries between Sikh, Hindu, and Muslim religious identity in Punjab were partly a colonial and reform-era construction, and that pre-colonial Sikh practice was more fluid and overlapping than the Singh Sabha reformers (and their colonial interlocutors) acknowledged. This argument has important implications for reading Bhai Gurdas: if his critique of Brahmanical ritualism is read in its seventeenth-century context rather than through the lens of nineteenth-century reformism, it may look somewhat different — more as an internal critique of religious formalism within a shared Punjabi religious world than as a clear declaration of Sikh separateness from Hinduism.

This is not to say that Bhai Gurdas was not making genuine theological distinctions; he clearly was. It is to say that how those distinctions have been read and used is itself a historical question that requires critical attention. Postcolonial scholarship on Sikhism, particularly the work of Arvind-pal Singh Mandair, has developed sophisticated tools for disentangling Bhai Gurdas's actual theological contribution from the colonial and nationalist overlays that have accumulated on his work. Engaging with this scholarship is essential for any serious student of the Vaaran who wants to understand not just what Bhai Gurdas wrote but how it has been interpreted and why (Mandair, Religion and the Specter of the West, 2009).

Reading Bhai Gurdas in the Twenty-First Century: New Approaches

Contemporary scholars bring several new approaches to the Vaaran that open dimensions of the texts not previously emphasized. Gender studies perspectives, for instance, ask how Bhai Gurdas represents women and female experience in his poetry, and what his representations suggest about the gender assumptions of early Sikh community life. Some scholars have noted that while the theological egalitarianism of ਗੁਰਮਤਿ is clear in his writing, the specific social roles he describes for women in the ਸੰਗਤ sometimes reflect the gender conventions of his own era. Critical engagement with these dimensions of the text is not a rejection of Bhai Gurdas's authority but an application of his own critical method — the insistence on seeing clearly rather than settling for comfortable assumptions.

Comparative religious studies approaches have also opened productive new perspectives. Scholars including Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh have brought feminist theology and comparative mysticism to bear on Sikh texts, finding in the Vaaran resources for understanding ਗੁਰਮਤਿ in conversation with global religious thought. This comparative approach differs from the colonial comparativist project, which often measured Sikhism against Western religious categories and found it wanting or confusing; instead, it allows ਗੁਰਮਤਿ to contribute its distinctive voice to global theological conversations as an equal partner.

Literary studies approaches have also enriched understanding of the Vaaran's aesthetic achievement. Scholars with expertise in Punjabi literary history have examined how Bhai Gurdas transforms the classical Punjabi Vaar form, what literary conventions he inherits and which he innovates, and how the specific features of his poetic style serve his theological purposes. This attention to form and craft is not separate from theological understanding; it reveals how Bhai Gurdas's theology is inseparable from his art, and why the Vaaran cannot be fully understood when reduced to paraphrase or doctrinal summary (Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, The Feminine Principle in the Sikh Vision of the Transcendent, 1993).

Perhaps most importantly for students of Sikhi today, there is a growing recognition that the most valuable reading of Bhai Gurdas combines scholarly rigor with genuine spiritual engagement. The scholar who reads the Vaaran purely as historical documents misses their living theological force. The devotee who reads them without critical awareness risks missing the interpretive choices embedded in every translation and traditional commentary. The ideal reader — which this course has tried to cultivate — is both: someone who can ask critical questions about the text's history, transmission, and interpretation while remaining genuinely open to its transformative power as a guide to ਗੁਰਮਤਿ living.

Discussion Questions

  1. The lesson argues that every generation reads foundational texts through its own concerns and assumptions. Reflecting on your own position as a student of Bhai Gurdas's work: What concerns, assumptions, or questions do you bring to the Vaaran that might shape what you see in them? How might someone from a different background read the same texts differently?
  2. The colonial encounter shaped how Bhai Gurdas's critique of Brahmanical ritualism was read and used in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. How should contemporary readers relate to this history? Is it possible to read Bhai Gurdas independently of the interpretive history that surrounds his work, or must we always engage that history?
  3. The lesson describes debates about translation of key terms like ਨਾਮ (Naam) and ਹਉਮੈ (haumai). Why do these translation choices matter? Have you encountered examples where an English translation of a Sikh concept seemed to miss or distort something important? What was it, and why did it matter?
  4. Contemporary scholars bring gender studies, comparative religion, and literary studies approaches to the Vaaran. Do you think these approaches enrich understanding of Bhai Gurdas's work, or do they risk distorting it by imposing modern categories on a seventeenth-century text? How should the community navigate the relationship between devotional and academic reading?
  5. Having completed this course, what do you now see as the single most important contribution Bhai Gurdas made to Sikh tradition and thought? And what question about his work do you most want to pursue further?

Further Reading

  • Gurinder Singh Mann, The Making of Sikh Scripture (New York: Oxford University Press, 2001) — the essential starting point for understanding the scholarly debates about the formation and transmission of early Sikh texts including the Vaaran.
  • Arvind-pal Singh Mandair, Religion and the Specter of the West (New York: Columbia University Press, 2009) — the most sophisticated account of how the colonial encounter shaped Sikh self-understanding and the scholarly study of Sikh tradition.
  • Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, The Feminine Principle in the Sikh Vision of the Transcendent (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1993) — brings feminist theological and literary perspectives to Sikh texts in ways that model the integrated scholarly-devotional reading this course advocates.
  • Harjot Oberoi, The Construction of Religious Boundaries: Culture, Identity, and Diversity in the Sikh Tradition (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1994) — essential and controversial; challenges readers to think critically about how Sikh identity boundaries were constructed historically.
  • Key Takeaways
  • Interpretation of the Vaaran is always a contemporary act, shaped by the reader's own context, concerns, and assumptions — and acknowledging this is the beginning of responsible reading rather than its abandonment.
  • Major scholarly debates about the Vaaran — concerning textual authenticity, translation, and the legacy of the colonial encounter — are not peripheral but central to understanding how the texts have functioned and continue to function in Sikh life.
  • New approaches from gender studies, comparative religion, and literary studies enrich understanding of the Vaaran without replacing the devotional engagement for which Bhai Gurdas composed them.
  • The ideal reader of Bhai Gurdas today is both critically aware and genuinely open: bringing scholarly rigor to questions of history and interpretation while remaining open to the transformative power of his theological vision.

Works Cited

Mandair, Arvind-pal Singh. Religion and the Specter of the West. New York: Columbia University Press, 2009.

Mann, Gurinder Singh. The Making of Sikh Scripture. New York: Oxford University Press, 2001.

Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh. The Feminine Principle in the Sikh Vision of the Transcendent. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1993.

Oberoi, Harjot. The Construction of Religious Boundaries: Culture, Identity, and Diversity in the Sikh Tradition. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1994.

Pashaura Singh. The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2000.

Homework

Identify one specific interpretive debate or scholarly disagreement about Bhai Gurdas's work that you find most interesting or challenging — for example, debates about his relationship to Brahmanical learning, questions about the authenticity of all thirty-nine Vaaran, or disagreements about how to translate key theological terms. Spend 20-25 minutes researching this debate using any available scholarly sources. Then write a 300-word reflection: What is at stake in this debate? Why does it matter how we resolve it? Where do you currently stand, and why?

courses.title: The Colonial Era & the Singh Sabha Movement
courses.summary: This upper-level course traces the Sikh experience from the British annexation of Punjab in 1849 through the colonial period and the Singh Sabha renaissance to the Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925. Students study key reformers, institutions, the Tat Khalsa and Sanatan debates, and the Gurdwara Reform movement, with…
outcomes: Explain the political consequences of the British annexation of Punjab in 1849 and the place of Sikhs under colonial rule.
Identify the external and internal pressures on Sikh identity during the colonial period.
Trace the origins, aims, and growth of the Singh Sabha movement from 1873.
Describe the leading figures and institutions of the Sikh reform era, including Khalsa College and the Chief Khalsa Diwan.
Compare the Tat Khalsa and Sanatan tendencies in a balanced and fair-minded way.
Outline the Gurdwara Reform (Akali) movement and the significance of the Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925.

lessons.title: Course Overview and Contents
lessons.summary: An orientation to the colonial era and the Singh Sabha movement, with a map of the six lessons that follow.
lessons.html:
This course studies one of the most formative periods in modern Sikh history: the years from the British annexation of the Punjab in 1849 through the Singh Sabha renaissance to the Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925. It explains how foreign rule and rapid social change placed Sikh identity under strain, and how reformers responded with a movement of education, publishing, and institution-building. Throughout, approximate dates are flagged and contested interpretations are presented neutrally (Grewal 1998).

The lessons proceed in order from political annexation, through the pressures on Sikh identity and the rise of the ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ (Singh Sabha), to the internal debates, the print and education renaissance, and finally the Gurdwara Reform movement and its legislative outcome.

LessonTitleFocus
1Course Overview and ContentsOrientation and table of contents
2Annexation and Sikhs Under British Rule1849 and colonial administration
3Pressures on Sikh IdentityMissions, Arya Samaj, internal concerns
4The Rise of the Singh Sabha1873 onward; aims and growth
5Figures, Institutions, and DebatesLeaders, colleges, Tat Khalsa and Sanatan
6Gurdwara Reform and the Act of 1925Akali movement and its legacy

Learners should read each lesson in sequence and consult the references for fuller treatment (Singh and Fenech 2014).

Homework

Select one event from 1849—the year of annexation—and research how it was recorded differently by British colonial sources versus Sikh oral and literary traditions of the same period. Write a 400-word comparison noting what each account emphasizes, what it omits, and what that reveals about the nature of historical memory. Conclude with a sentence on which account you find more complete and why.

lessons.title: The Annexation of Punjab and Sikhs Under British Rule
lessons.summary: How the British annexation of 1849 ended Sikh sovereignty and reshaped Punjab through new administration and army recruitment.
lessons.html:
The Sikh empire founded by Maharaja Ranjit Singh reached its height in the early nineteenth century. After his death in 1839, succession struggles weakened the Lahore Darbar. Two Anglo-Sikh wars followed, and in 1849 the British East India Company annexed the Punjab, ending Sikh political sovereignty (Grewal 1998).

British rule brought new systems of land revenue, law courts, railways, the telegraph, and a cash economy. The colonial army recruited Sikhs in large numbers, often emphasizing visible markers of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ (Khalsa), such as unshorn hair. The loss of self-rule also removed patronage that had supported gurdwaras and scholarship, opening the way for missionary activity and Western-style schools.

  • 1849: Annexation of the Punjab by the British.
  • Key shifts: new revenue and legal systems, infrastructure, and a cash economy.
  • Army recruitment: Sikhs enlisted in large numbers, often with emphasis on Khalsa identity markers.

Homework

The colonial period introduced new systems of land revenue, courts, and education that reshaped daily Sikh life. Choose one of these systems and research how it affected a specific community or region in the Punjab. Write 350 words describing the change, its immediate impact on Sikhs, and any form of resistance or adaptation you find documented. Reflect on what this tells you about the relationship between political power and religious identity.

lessons.title: Pressures on Sikh Identity in the Colonial Period
lessons.summary: External and internal forces that strained Sikh identity, and the central question of who counts as a Sikh.
lessons.html:
The decades after annexation brought intense pressure on Sikh practice. Christian missionary activity expanded across the Punjab, and a few high-profile conversions alarmed many Sikhs. At the same time the Arya Samaj, a Hindu reform movement founded in the 1870s, grew rapidly and at times criticized Sikh practices (Jones 1989).

Internally, reformers worried about idols and Brahminical rituals in some gurdwaras, the management of shrines by hereditary ਮਹੰਤ (mahants), and low literacy in Punjabi and ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ (Gurmukhi). A central question of the age was deceptively simple yet deeply contested: who is a Sikh, and what defines Sikh practice (Oberoi 1994)?

  • External pressures: Christian missions and Hindu reform movements such as the Arya Samaj.
  • Internal concerns: ritual practices in gurdwaras, hereditary shrine management, and low literacy.
  • Core debate: the definition and boundaries of Sikh identity.

Homework

The question 'Who is a Sikh?' was fiercely debated during the colonial era. Spend 20 minutes writing a personal journal entry from the perspective of an educated Sikh man or woman living in Lahore circa 1880. Describe the pressures you feel from Christian missionaries, the Arya Samaj, and internal reformers. What pulls at your identity? What do you hold onto? Aim for 350–400 words and write in first person.

lessons.title: The Rise of the Singh Sabha Movement
lessons.summary: The founding and aims of the Singh Sabha from 1873, pursued mainly through scholarship, education, and publishing.
lessons.html:
In response to these pressures, Sikh leaders organized to defend and renew their faith. The first ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ (Singh Sabha) was established at Amritsar in 1873, and a second prominent society followed at Lahore in 1879 (Grewal 1998).

The movement sought to restore the teachings of the Gurus and the scriptures, to remove practices considered foreign to the faith, to promote modern education while strengthening Gurmukhi and Punjabi, and to publish religious and historical literature widely. In its early decades it worked largely through persuasion, scholarship, and institution-building rather than political agitation, and local Singh Sabhas multiplied across towns and villages (Singh and Fenech 2014).

  • 1873: First Singh Sabha founded at Amritsar.
  • 1879: Singh Sabha established at Lahore.
  • Aims: religious reform, education, publishing, and community uplift, pursued mainly through peaceful means.

Homework

The first Singh Sabha was founded in Amritsar in 1873. Research the specific circumstances that triggered its founding—particularly the conversion incidents and the missionary presence—and write a 400-word narrative account of those founding months. Include at least two named individuals involved, what goals were articulated at the first meeting, and how the community responded. Cite at least one secondary source by name.

lessons.title: Figures, Institutions, and the Tat Khalsa and Sanatan Debates
lessons.summary: Leading reformers and institutions of the era, and a balanced account of the Tat Khalsa and Sanatan tendencies.
lessons.html:
The Singh Sabha era produced a remarkable generation of scholars and organizers. Among the most influential were Bhai Vir Singh (1872 to 1957), a foundational figure of modern Punjabi literature, and Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha, whose encyclopedia of Sikh tradition became a standard reference. Earlier reformers such as Giani Ditt Singh (1850 to 1901), editor of the Khalsa Akhbar, contributed energetic preaching and journalism in service of the cause (Singh and Fenech 2014).

Institution-building was central. Khalsa College, Amritsar (commonly dated to 1892) became a flagship of Sikh higher education, and the Chief Khalsa Diwan, founded in 1902, coordinated many local Singh Sabhas. The movement also contained two broad internal currents. The ਤੱਤ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ (Tat Khalsa) emphasized a distinct Sikh identity centered on the Guru Granth Sahib and the Khalsa, while the ਸਨਾਤਨ (Sanatan) tendency held a more inclusive view that accommodated long-standing devotional practices. Both reflected sincere devotion; over time the Tat Khalsa perspective broadly shaped mainstream modern practice (Oberoi 1994).

  • Scholars: Bhai Vir Singh, Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha, and Giani Ditt Singh.
  • Institutions: Khalsa College, Amritsar (1892) and the Chief Khalsa Diwan (1902).
  • Debates: Tat Khalsa and Sanatan tendencies, presented neutrally.

Homework

Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's Hum Hindu Nahin (1898) was one of the most consequential pamphlets of the Singh Sabha era. Research its core argument and the immediate reactions it provoked from Sanatan Sikhs. Write a 400-word critical summary: What was the central claim? What evidence did Nabha use? Who opposed it and on what grounds? How did it shift the Tat Khalsa–Sanatan debate? Reflect on why definitional questions about religious identity carry such high stakes.

lessons.title: The Gurdwara Reform (Akali) Movement and the Act of 1925
lessons.summary: The nonviolent campaign to reform gurdwara management and the landmark Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925.
lessons.html:
The reforming energy of the Singh Sabha period eventually turned to the management of the gurdwaras themselves. Many historic shrines remained under hereditary ਮਹੰਤ (mahants), some accused of mismanagement. From around 1920 a broad campaign, known as the Gurdwara Reform or ਅਕਾਲੀ (Akali) movement, arose to place gurdwaras under representative community control (Grewal 1998).

To coordinate the effort, the ਸ਼੍ਰੋਮਣੀ ਗੁਰਦੁਆਰਾ ਪ੍ਰਬੰਧਕ ਕਮੇਟੀ (SGPC) was formed in 1920, and the Akali Dal led the campaigns. The movement was marked by nonviolent, disciplined agitation; the events at Nankana Sahib in 1921 and the protest at Guru ka Bagh in 1922 became symbols of peaceful sacrifice. After years of struggle, the Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925 placed many historic gurdwaras under elected community control, a lasting framework for democratic shrine administration (McLeod 1989).

  • From about 1920: a nonviolent campaign to reform gurdwara management.
  • 1920: formation of the SGPC; the Akali Dal led the agitation.
  • 1921 to 1922: Nankana Sahib and Guru ka Bagh became symbols of peaceful sacrifice.
  • 1925: the Sikh Gurdwaras Act placed many historic shrines under elected community control.

References

  • Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Rev. ed. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998.
  • Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014.
  • Oberoi, Harjot. The Construction of Religious Boundaries. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1994.
  • McLeod, W. H. The Sikhs: History, Religion, and Society. New York: Columbia University Press, 1989.
  • Jones, Kenneth W. Socio-Religious Reform Movements in British India. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1989.

Homework

The Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925 created the SGPC as the elected body overseeing historic Sikh shrines. Research the SGPC's structure as established by the Act and evaluate how well it fulfilled the reformers' original goals. Write 400 words covering: what powers the Act granted, which gurdwaras fell under its jurisdiction, how elections were structured, and what compromises were made to secure British agreement. Conclude with your assessment of whether the 1925 settlement was a victory, a compromise, or both.

lessons.title: The Print Revolution and the Punjabi Literary Renaissance
lessons.html:
Introduction

Among the most consequential—and often underestimated—forces of the Singh Sabha era was the printing press. The introduction of lithographic and later letterpress technology into the Punjab from the 1860s onward created an entirely new public sphere: one in which ideas about Sikh identity, scripture, history, and practice could be debated, standardized, and disseminated on a scale previously impossible. Reformers who had once reached dozens through oral preaching could now reach thousands through a weekly newspaper or a cheaply printed tract. The print revolution did not merely amplify existing voices; it helped constitute new audiences, new communities of readers, and new norms for what authoritative Sikh discourse looked like (Barrier 1966).

This lecture explores how the Singh Sabha movement harnessed print technology to prosecute its reform agenda. We examine the major periodicals and publishing houses of the era, the standardization of Gurmukhi script and Punjabi prose, the role of Bhai Vir Singh as a literary and religious visionary, and the debates that print helped ignite—including contentious pamphlet wars over Sikh identity and practice. We also consider the social dimension of literacy: who could read these publications, and how did the literate minority transmit their content to the wider community?

Print culture intersected deeply with the question of religious authority. Before the Singh Sabha press, much religious knowledge was transmitted orally by ਗ੍ਰੰਥੀ (granthis), ਢਾਡੀ (dhadis), and ਭਾਈ (bhais) trained within hereditary traditions. Print introduced a new kind of authority: the scholar-editor who could compile, annotate, and publish versions of texts, potentially displacing older custodians of knowledge. This tension between oral-traditional and print-mediated religion is a recurring theme in the history of reform movements, and the Punjab provides one of its richest case studies.

By the end of this lecture, students will understand why Sikh historians regard the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries not just as a period of religious reform but as a genuine intellectual renaissance—a ਨਵਜਾਗ੍ਰਣ (navjagran, awakening)—in which Punjabi became a vehicle for modern scholarship, fiction, poetry, and journalism simultaneously.

The Technology of Reform: Printing Presses and Publishing Houses

The first printing presses in Punjab were established by Christian missionaries in the 1830s and 1840s, and their success in producing vernacular religious literature was not lost on Sikh and Hindu observers. By the 1860s and 1870s, Indian-owned presses had begun to proliferate in Lahore, Amritsar, and smaller towns. The cost of setting up a small press fell considerably over this period, and the colonial postal system—one of the genuine infrastructural legacies of British rule—allowed publications to reach subscribers across the Punjab and beyond (Barrier 1966).

For the Singh Sabha movement, the press became an instrument of systematic religious education. The Khalsa Tract Society, established in Amritsar in 1894, was among the most prolific publishers of reformist religious literature in Punjabi. It produced cheap pamphlets on theology, history, and ethics, specifically designed for wide distribution and accessible reading. The society's catalogues reveal the range of topics considered pressing: the distinctiveness of Sikh ਰਹਿਤ (rehat, conduct and discipline) from Hindu practice, the biographies of the Gurus, explanations of ਨਿਤਨੇਮ (nitnem, the daily prayers), and critiques of superstition and ritual corruption.

The Wazir-i-Hind Press in Amritsar, founded by Bhai Vir Singh's family, became arguably the single most influential Sikh publishing enterprise of the colonial period. It produced Bhai Vir Singh's novels, poetry, and scholarly works, as well as the weekly newspaper Khalsa Samachar. The press's output exemplified a conscious editorial philosophy: Punjabi prose should be cultivated as a literary medium capable of conveying both devotional depth and modern analytical rigor. This was not merely a commercial venture; it was, as Bhai Vir Singh's biographers have noted, a form of seva (service) to the Panth.

Regional printing networks grew through the 1890s and 1900s, with Singh Sabhas in smaller towns such as Rawalpindi, Ferozepur, and Gujranwala establishing their own presses or acting as distribution points for Amritsar and Lahore publications. Subscription lists for papers like the Khalsa Akhbar reveal a readership that extended beyond urban elites to include village schoolteachers, granthi families, army pensioners, and prosperous farmers—a far broader constituency than reformers might have reached through platform oratory alone.

Colonial administrators monitored Punjabi-language publications carefully. The Vernacular Press Act of 1878, though repealed in 1882, demonstrated British awareness of print's political potential. Singh Sabha publications walked a careful line: they were reformist and community-focused, but largely avoided direct political confrontation with the Raj in this early period. This restraint would shift dramatically in the Gurdwara Reform era, when newspapers such as the Akali openly challenged colonial authority. The print infrastructure built during the Singh Sabha decades would prove indispensable for that later mobilization.

Bhai Vir Singh and the Creation of Modern Punjabi Literature

No figure better embodies the synthesis of literary creativity and religious reform in this period than Bhai Vir Singh (1872–1957). Born in Amritsar into a family with deep connections to Sikh scholarship, he began writing in his twenties and produced a body of work spanning novels, epic poetry, lyric verse, biography, and scholarly commentary that transformed Punjabi as a literary language (Kohli 1987).

His novels—Sundri (1898), Bijay Singh (1899), and Satwant Kaur (1900)—were among the first historical novels in Punjabi and served an explicitly reformist purpose. Set during the eighteenth-century period of Sikh persecution and resilience, they depicted idealized Khalsa characters who embodied virtues the Tat Khalsa wished to see in contemporary Sikhs: uncompromising identity, scriptural devotion, martial courage, and moral purity. The novels were consumed eagerly by a reading public hungry for heroic Sikh narratives at a time when the political sovereignty symbolized by such heroes had been extinguished by British annexation.

Bhai Vir Singh's poetry, particularly the epic Rana Surat Singh (1905) and later the lyric collections gathered under the title Meray Sayian Jio, introduced a new register into Punjabi verse: one that could hold together intense personal devotion to the ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ (Waheguru) and self-conscious aesthetic craft. Scholars of Punjabi literature have called him the father of modern Punjabi poetry, and the Sahitya Akademi of India awarded him its highest honor in 1955—recognition that reached beyond the Sikh community to acknowledge his contribution to Indian letters.

Less celebrated but equally significant was Bhai Vir Singh's scholarly work. His multivolume commentary on Gurbani, the Santhya Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, represented a major undertaking in making the scriptural language accessible to readers educated in modern Punjabi rather than trained through the traditional gurmat transmission. His encyclopedic dictionary Gurbani Kosh standardized interpretations of key Gurbani terms. These works were inseparable from the Singh Sabha project of centering the Guru Granth Sahib Ji as the sole and authoritative guide for Sikh practice and identity (Kohli 1987).

It would be a mistake, however, to read Bhai Vir Singh simply as a propagandist for the Tat Khalsa position. His devotional poetry in particular reveals a sensibility that resists easy categorization: rooted in the Gurbani tradition, deeply personal, and at times mystical in a way that sits uneasily with the rationalist reform impulse that characterized some of his Singh Sabha contemporaries. This complexity is a reminder that the Singh Sabha era produced individuals of genuine spiritual depth, not only institutional architects.

The Pamphlet Wars: Print, Debate, and the Definition of Sikh Identity

The most intellectually charged use of the Sikh press was arguably in the genre of the religious pamphlet and the polemical essay. The question that animated these exchanges—what distinguishes Sikh practice from Hindu practice, and who has authority to define that distinction—was not merely academic. It determined who would control gurdwaras, how life-cycle rituals would be conducted, what would be taught in schools, and ultimately what the community of the Panth meant.

The Tat Khalsa position, associated with reformers centered on the Lahore Singh Sabha, insisted on a sharp demarcation: Sikhism was a distinct religion, not a sect of Hinduism. The Guru Granth Sahib Ji was the sole scripture. Idols had no place in gurdwaras. Sikh life-cycle rituals—naming, marriage, death—should follow Sikh rites, not Brahminical ones. This position was elaborated in pamphlets and newspaper columns throughout the 1880s and 1890s, and it received its most famous expression in Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's Hum Hindu Nahin (We Are Not Hindus, 1898) (Singh and Fenech 2014).

The Sanatan Sikh position, defended by figures such as Pandit Tara Singh Narotam and associated with the older Amritsar Singh Sabha, argued for continuity between Sikh and broader Indic tradition. The Gurus had not rejected the Vedic heritage; they had reformed and transcended it. Gurdwaras had historically accommodated images of Hindu deities without contradiction. The Sanatan position drew on genuine historical evidence of syncretic practice and resisted what its defenders saw as an artificial and politically motivated narrowing of the Sikh tradition.

These debates were conducted in Punjabi newspapers, in printed pamphlets that sold for a few annas, and in public lectures that were then transcribed and published. The sheer volume of text produced in this controversy is striking: dozens of pamphlets appeared in the 1890s alone. Print gave both sides the ability to make their arguments precisely, to quote sources, to respond to opponents point by point, and to reach audiences across a vast geography simultaneously. It also raised the stakes: a position once published could be quoted, refuted, and held up for scrutiny in ways that oral debate did not permit.

The pamphlet wars had lasting consequences. They accelerated the institutionalization of a normative Tat Khalsa position—what scholars such as Harjot Oberoi (1994) and J.S. Grewal (1998) have analyzed as the construction of a bounded Sikh identity through discourse and print. By the time of the Gurdwara Reform movement, the Tat Khalsa framework had effectively won the institutional debate, even as Sanatan practices persisted in many communities. Understanding this print-mediated controversy is essential for understanding both the energy of the Singh Sabha movement and the internal diversity that it sought—with only partial success—to resolve.

Literacy, Language, and the Social Reach of the Press

A critical question for historians of the Singh Sabha print culture is: who actually read these publications? Literacy rates in late nineteenth-century Punjab were low by modern standards, and Gurmukhi literacy—as opposed to Persian or Urdu literacy, which remained important in administrative and commercial life—was concentrated in certain communities and occupational groups. Village-level literacy was limited, and women's literacy was lower still, though not negligible (Fox 1985).

The social reach of the print medium was therefore significantly greater than literacy rates alone would suggest. In the gurdwara, in the school, and in the village gathering, literate individuals read aloud from newspapers and pamphlets to audiences who could not read themselves. The Khalsa Akhbar, the Khalsa Samachar, and other publications were read collectively, discussed, argued over, and remembered by communities whose relationship to the written word was primarily mediated through such public readings. This oral-print hybrid was the normal mode of reception for much of the Sikh rural population.

Gurmukhi script itself became a political marker. The Singh Sabha movement's insistence on Gurmukhi as the script of Sikh identity—and its efforts to establish schools where Punjabi in Gurmukhi was the primary medium—positioned script choice as a religious and communal decision. This had consequences in the colonial educational bureaucracy, which was more comfortable with Urdu (in the Nastaliq script) as the administrative language of the Punjab. The demand for Gurmukhi-medium education was not merely pedagogical; it was an assertion of communal distinctiveness against both the colonial administration and neighboring communities that associated themselves with different scripts and languages.

Women's access to print culture was constrained but not absent. Bhai Vir Singh wrote specifically for female readers—his novel Sundri features a female protagonist of exemplary Khalsa virtue—and some Singh Sabha publications addressed women's education and domestic practice explicitly. The Singh Sabha movement established a number of schools for girls, and literacy among upper-caste Sikh women in urban areas grew through this period. However, the scholarly and polemical pamphlet culture was largely a male domain, reflecting the broader gender dynamics of colonial Punjab (Fox 1985).

  • Key Takeaways
  • The printing press transformed the Singh Sabha movement from a local reform effort into a Punjab-wide intellectual and religious renaissance, enabling new forms of public debate and community formation.
  • Bhai Vir Singh's literary output—novels, poetry, commentary, and lexicography—constitutes the founding moment of modern Punjabi literature and was inseparable from his religious and reformist commitments.
  • The pamphlet wars between Tat Khalsa and Sanatan positions were the primary arena in which the definition of Sikh identity was contested, and print gave both sides new tools of precision and reach.
  • The social reach of print extended well beyond the literate minority through practices of communal reading, and Gurmukhi itself became a symbol of Sikh communal identity in relation to both the colonial state and neighboring communities.
  • The print infrastructure built during the Singh Sabha era became the communications backbone of the later Gurdwara Reform movement, demonstrating the long-term political significance of cultural investment.

Key Terms

  • ਨਵਜਾਗ੍ਰਣ (Navjagran) — 'Awakening' or renaissance; used to describe the intellectual and cultural renewal associated with the Singh Sabha period, including the literary flourishing in Punjabi.
  • ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ (Gurmukhi) — The script in which the Guru Granth Sahib Ji is written and in which Punjabi is traditionally expressed in the Sikh tradition; became a marker of communal identity during the Singh Sabha era.
  • ਸੇਵਾ (Seva) — Selfless service; the framing used by Singh Sabha publishers and writers to describe their literary and editorial work as spiritual practice in service of the community.
  • ਰਹਿਤ (Rehat) — Conduct and discipline; the code of Sikh practice that Singh Sabha pamphlets worked to define and standardize against what reformers saw as corrupted customs.
  • ਗ੍ਰੰਥੀ (Granthi) — The custodian and reader of the Guru Granth Sahib Ji in a gurdwara; a figure whose traditional authority over scriptural interpretation was both challenged and reconstituted by the print era.

Discussion Questions

  1. How did the printing press change the nature of religious authority in the Sikh community? In what ways did it democratize access to knowledge, and in what ways did it create new forms of elite gatekeeping?
  2. Bhai Vir Singh used historical fiction as a vehicle for religious and social reform. What are the advantages and risks of conveying religious ideals through fictional characters rather than direct theological argument?
  3. The Tat Khalsa–Sanatan debate was largely conducted in print. How might the medium itself—the permanence and precision of print versus the flexibility of oral tradition—have shaped the outcome of that debate?
  4. The Singh Sabha movement insisted on Gurmukhi as the script of Sikh identity. In a multilingual, multi-script colonial environment, what was at stake in that insistence? Are there parallels in other religious or national communities you can identify?
  5. Women's access to the Singh Sabha print culture was limited but growing. How does the gendering of literacy and print access shape which ideas and communities get represented in the historical record?

Further Reading

  • Norman G. Barrier, The Sikhs and Their Literature (1970) — the foundational study of Punjabi print culture and the Singh Sabha publishing networks.
  • Surinder Singh Kohli, studies on Bhai Vir Singh's literary and religious contributions — essential for understanding the literary renaissance dimension of the movement.
  • Harjot Oberoi, The Construction of Religious Boundaries (1994) — analyzes the print-mediated discourse through which Sikh identity was contested and redefined.
  • Richard G. Fox, Lions of the Punjab (1985) — examines the social and political dimensions of Sikh communal mobilization, including the role of literacy and print.

Homework

Select one Punjabi-language newspaper or periodical from the Singh Sabha era—such as the Khalsa Akhbar, the Khalsa Samachar, or the Gurmat Prakash—and research its founding, editorial voice, and readership. Write a 400-word profile of the publication: who founded it, what issues it championed, how it engaged with the Tat Khalsa–Sanatan debate, and what audience it sought to reach. Reflect in a closing paragraph on how access to print media shapes the way a community understands itself.

lessons.title: Sikh Education, Khalsa Colleges, and the Colonial Knowledge System
lessons.html:
Introduction

Education was, alongside print, the primary institutional instrument through which the Singh Sabha movement pursued its goals. Reformers understood that unless Sikh children received an education that combined modern skills with grounding in Gurbani, Punjabi, and Sikh history, the next generation would be shaped entirely by colonial schools whose curricula were indifferent or actively hostile to Sikh religious formation. The establishment of Khalsa schools and colleges was therefore not simply a philanthropic or pedagogical enterprise; it was a deliberate act of cultural survival and community reproduction (Fox 1985).

This lecture examines the Sikh educational movement of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries: the founding of Khalsa schools across the Punjab, the establishment of Khalsa College, Amritsar as a flagship institution, the debates over curriculum and medium of instruction, and the complex relationship between Sikh educational institutions and the colonial university system. We also examine what this educational enterprise meant for different segments of the community—urban elites, rural communities, and women—and how it interacted with the broader colonial knowledge economy.

The question of education in colonial India was never merely technical. It was, as the historian Gyan Pandey and others have argued, a site of contest over authority, identity, and the future shape of the community. Who decided what was worth knowing? Whose texts counted as scripture, whose as literature, whose as history? The Singh Sabha's investment in education was simultaneously an answer to these questions and a site of ongoing disagreement about them.
