The tensions between modern scientific education and traditional scriptural learning, between Punjabi and English as media of instruction, and between accommodation with the colonial system and resistance to it, ran through every institutional founding of this era.

By engaging with this lecture, students will understand how colonized communities negotiate with dominant educational systems—accepting some elements, resisting others, and transforming still others—in the service of cultural and religious continuity. The Sikh case offers rich material for comparison with analogous projects among Muslim, Hindu, and other communities in colonial South Asia.

The Colonial Education System and its Impact on Sikh Communities

The colonial education system in the Punjab was not designed with Sikh religious or cultural formation in mind. The educational reforms following the 1857 uprising, particularly the formal organization of universities at Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras in 1857 and the subsequent spread of affiliated colleges, created a system in which English was the language of higher education and advancement in government service. The Punjab University, established at Lahore in 1882, became the institutional framework within which Sikh higher education had to operate if its graduates were to access colonial employment and professional life (Fox 1985).

Mission schools, run by various Christian denominations, had established themselves in major Punjab towns by the 1860s and 1870s. They offered high-quality English-language education and, in some cases, scholarships for conversion. For Sikh families ambitious for their sons' advancement, these schools presented a genuine dilemma: accept an education that provided real material advantages but in an environment potentially corrosive to religious identity, or hold out for Sikh institutions that might offer weaker academic preparation. The establishment of Khalsa schools was in part a response to exactly this dilemma.

Government schools (run by the colonial educational bureaucracy) taught in Urdu and English and were largely indifferent to Sikh religious content. Gurmukhi literacy was not part of the government school curriculum, and Punjabi was accorded low status in the colonial linguistic hierarchy. Reformers observed with alarm that Sikh students educated in government schools could emerge fluent in Urdu and English but unable to read the Guru Granth Sahib Ji in its original Gurmukhi script. The implications for intergenerational transmission of the faith were obvious.

The colonial army's large Sikh recruitment also intersected with educational policy. The military valued the Khalsa's distinctive identity—unshorn hair, turban, the five ਕਕਾਰ (Kakars)—as markers of the 'martial races' it preferred for recruitment. This created an odd alignment of interests: colonial officials who valued Khalsa distinctiveness as a military asset had some reason to support institutions that maintained it. Yet army service also pulled young men out of village communities and into an environment shaped by imperial values and inter-community mixing. The relationship between military service and religious identity was complex and not uniformly corrosive of Sikh practice (Rand and Wagner 2012).

The Khalsa School Network: Founding, Funding, and Curriculum

From the 1880s onward, local Singh Sabhas across the Punjab began establishing ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ (Khalsa) schools. These ranged from small village primary schools, often housed in or near gurdwaras, to larger urban secondary institutions. By 1900, the number of schools associated with the Singh Sabha movement had grown into the dozens; by 1920, they numbered in the hundreds. This expansion represented a sustained community investment of funds, time, and organizational energy that is remarkable by any measure.

Funding came from multiple sources: individual donors (often prosperous merchants, army officers, or landowners), gurdwara endowments, and small subscriptions from wider communities. The Chief Khalsa Diwan, founded in 1902 as the umbrella coordinating body for Singh Sabha activities, played an important role in standardizing school management and advocating for Sikh educational interests with the colonial government. It published model curricula, trained teachers, and lobbied for Gurmukhi to be recognized in government examinations (Grewal 1998).

The curriculum question was deeply contested. Reformers agreed that Sikh students needed grounding in Gurbani and Punjabi; they disagreed about how much of the curriculum should be devoted to religious content versus the secular academic subjects—mathematics, science, English, history—that colonial employers and universities required. A school that emphasized Gurbani at the expense of English might produce devout graduates unable to compete in colonial professional life. A school modeled too closely on government schools might produce the opposite. Most Khalsa schools attempted a hybrid, but the proportions varied considerably by institution and by the class of students served.

Teacher training was a significant bottleneck. Traditional ਗੁਰਮਤ (Gurmat) education had been transmitted through guru-disciple relationships in informal settings, not through a standardized professional training system. The Singh Sabha institutions needed teachers who could deliver both religious and secular content in a school setting, a combination for which no existing training pathway prepared candidates. The movement's response included the establishment of training schools (normal schools, in colonial terminology) and the reform of gurmat teaching to include preparation for classroom delivery.

Khalsa College, Amritsar: Flagship Institution and its Contradictions

The founding of Khalsa College, Amritsar, commonly dated to 1892, represented the apex of the Singh Sabha educational effort. The college was intended to provide Sikh students with higher education of quality equivalent to—and in affiliation with—Punjab University, while grounding them in Sikh studies, Punjabi, and the values of the Khalsa tradition. Its establishment required negotiation between Singh Sabha leaders, the colonial government, and the Punjab University, and the result reflected the compromises inherent in that triangular relationship (Singh and Fenech 2014).

The college's founding committee included some of the most prominent Sikh leaders of the day, and its early decades saw genuine tension between the Tat Khalsa and Sanatan factions that were simultaneously contesting the direction of the wider Singh Sabha movement. Questions about whether Sikh studies or secular subjects should dominate, about the role of English in instruction, and about the religious atmosphere of the institution were debated intensely. The colonial government's financial support—welcome but not unconditional—gave authorities leverage over the college's institutional direction.

Khalsa College produced a first generation of graduates who went on to careers in the colonial civil service, the professions, the military officer corps, and—crucially—the leadership of the Gurdwara Reform movement. The college became a seedbed of educated Sikh leadership, men who combined modern analytical training with a Sikh educational formation. Several leading figures of the Akali movement of the 1920s were Khalsa College alumni, and the college's alumni networks proved politically important in the organizational work of that movement.

The institution's contradictions were real, however. It was affiliated with a colonial university system that privileged English. Its curriculum necessarily accommodated the examination requirements of Punjab University rather than being structured purely by religious or community priorities. The financial dependence on colonial government grants created vulnerabilities that reformers recognized but could not wholly avoid. Khalsa College is thus a case study in the ambivalence of institution-building under colonial conditions: an achievement of considerable significance, but one shaped by and embedded within the very system it sought to supplement and resist.

Women's Education and the Limits of the Reform Vision

The Singh Sabha movement's educational enterprise was largely male-focused, reflecting the broader gender dynamics of colonial Punjab. However, it was not entirely indifferent to women's education. Several Singh Sabha organizations established schools for girls, and reformers including Bhai Vir Singh wrote and published materials specifically for female readers. The argument for women's education was typically framed in terms of mothers' roles in transmitting religious values to the next generation rather than women's own intellectual or professional development—a framing shared with many reform movements of the colonial era across South Asia (Grewal 1998).

Girls' Khalsa schools were established in Amritsar and several other towns from the 1890s onward. Enrollment was initially small and concentrated among the families of reformers and educated elites. Curriculum focused on Punjabi literacy, domestic skills, and religious knowledge rather than the secular academic subjects offered in boys' schools. The gap between male and female educational provision within the Singh Sabha network reflected and reinforced existing social hierarchies, even as it represented a genuine expansion of educational opportunity for women who had previously had access to almost none.

The question of widow remarriage, women's property rights, and the conduct of Sikh life-cycle rituals for women also surfaced in Singh Sabha educational discourse. Reformers who sought to replace Brahminical rituals with distinctively Sikh ਅਨੰਦ ਕਾਰਜ (Anand Karaj) marriage ceremonies and other rites implicitly involved women as participants in religious practice, not merely as objects of it. But the full implications of this for women's agency and education were not drawn out in this period; they would become more explicit in later decades.

  • Key Takeaways
  • The Sikh educational movement was a strategic response to the colonial school system's indifference to Sikh religious and cultural formation, seeking to offer modern skills alongside grounding in Gurbani and Sikh history.
  • Khalsa College, Amritsar, embodied the achievements and contradictions of Singh Sabha institution-building: a genuine educational advance made possible only through accommodation with the colonial university and funding system.
  • The curriculum debate—between religious content and secular subjects, between Punjabi and English—was never fully resolved and reflected deeper tensions about what kind of community the reformers were trying to produce.
  • Women's education was a secondary priority within the Singh Sabha educational enterprise, framed primarily through the lens of maternal and domestic roles rather than women's independent development.
  • The graduates of Khalsa educational institutions became the leadership cadre of the Gurdwara Reform movement, demonstrating the long-term political return on the earlier generation's educational investment.

Key Terms

  • ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ (Khalsa) — The community of initiated Sikhs who have taken ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ (Amrit); also used as an adjective for institutions, schools, and publications identified with and serving the Sikh community.
  • ਕਕਾਰ (Kakar) — The five articles of Khalsa discipline: ਕੇਸ (Kes, uncut hair), ਕੜਾ (Kara, steel bracelet), ਕੰਘਾ (Kangha, wooden comb), ਕਛਹਿਰਾ (Kachera, undergarment), and ਕਿਰਪਾਨ (Kirpan, steel sword); maintenance of the Kakars was a marker of Khalsa identity that Singh Sabha reformers worked to standardize and defend.
  • ਗੁਰਮਤ (Gurmat) — 'The Guru's teaching'; used to refer to the body of Sikh religious instruction and, by extension, to traditional forms of religious education centered on scripture and gurmat discourse.
  • ਅਨੰਦ ਕਾਰਜ (Anand Karaj) — The distinctively Sikh marriage ceremony, centered on the reading of ਲਾਵਾਂ (Lavan) from the Guru Granth Sahib Ji; its promotion over Brahminical wedding rites was a key reform priority of the Tat Khalsa.
  • ਨਿਤਨੇਮ (Nitnem) — The daily regimen of scriptural prayers; Singh Sabha educational materials frequently included instruction in nitnem as a foundational element of Sikh religious formation.

Discussion Questions

  1. The Singh Sabha's educational institutions were built within and in affiliation with a colonial university system. What does this case tell us about the possibilities and limits of using the 'master's tools' to resist the master's house?
  2. The curriculum debate in Khalsa schools—religious content versus secular subjects, Punjabi versus English—mirrors debates in many colonized communities. How should a community prioritize between educational strategies that serve immediate economic survival and those that serve long-term cultural continuity?
  3. Women's education within the Singh Sabha movement was framed primarily around maternal and domestic roles. How does this framing both enable and constrain women's participation in public and religious life? What would a more expansive vision of women's education have looked like in 1890s Punjab?
  4. Khalsa College alumni became leaders of the Gurdwara Reform movement. What does this tell us about the relationship between formal education and political mobilization within colonized communities?
  5. Compare the Singh Sabha's educational strategy with that of another religious or national community facing colonial education systems (for example, Muslim communities and the Aligarh movement, or Jewish communities in Eastern Europe). What similarities and differences do you find?

Further Reading

  • J.S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab (1998) — covers the educational and institutional dimensions of the Singh Sabha movement with scholarly precision.
  • Richard G. Fox, Lions of the Punjab (1985) — examines the social base of Sikh reform, including the class dimensions of educational mobilization.
  • Gail Minault, Secluded Scholars: Women's Education and Muslim Social Reform in Colonial India (1998) — a useful comparative framework for understanding women's education in colonial reform movements.
  • Gurpreet Bal, scholarship on gender and education in colonial Punjab — addresses the specific experiences of Sikh women within the reform era's educational enterprises.

Homework

Khalsa College, Amritsar was founded in the 1890s as a flagship institution of Sikh higher education. Research its founding history, the debates among Singh Sabha leaders about its curriculum and relationship to the colonial university system, and the first generation of graduates it produced. Write a 400-word account of what the college represented to the Sikh community and what compromises were made to secure colonial government cooperation. Conclude with a reflection on what it means for a colonized community to build a school within a system designed by the colonizing power.

lessons.title: Sikh Historical Consciousness and the Recovery of the Past
lessons.html:
Introduction

Every reform movement requires a usable past. The Singh Sabha reformers were acutely aware that their claims about authentic Sikh identity—that Sikhi was a distinct religion with its own theology, ethics, and practice—needed to be grounded in historical evidence as well as theological argument. They therefore invested heavily in the recovery, editing, and popularization of Sikh history: the lives of the Gurus, the history of the Khalsa, the biographies of martyrs and scholars, and the narrative of the community's survival through persecution and adversity. This engagement with the past was not antiquarian; it was profoundly present-oriented, designed to inspire, to define, and to mobilize (Singh and Fenech 2014).

This lecture examines how the Singh Sabha movement developed a distinctive historical consciousness and why historical writing mattered so much to the reform project. We look at the major works of Sikh historical writing produced in this period, the scholars who produced them, the debates about historical method and interpretation that shaped their work, and the ways in which historical narrative was mobilized for contemporary religious and political purposes. We also consider the limitations and blind spots of this historical project: whose stories were told, and whose were marginalized?

The relationship between historical writing and religious reform is a recurring theme across South Asian religious modernism. The Arya Samaj, the Ahmadiyya movement, the Brahmo Samaj, and the Deoband movement all developed characteristic forms of historical consciousness that served their specific reform agendas. The Singh Sabha's historical project shared features with these contemporaries while also expressing something specific to the Sikh situation: the recent memory of a great empire lost, the vivid tradition of Guru-biography (ਜਨਮ ਸਾਖੀ, janamsakhis), and the intimate relationship between historical narrative and the practice of commemorative devotion at gurdwaras.

By the end of this lecture, students will understand how historical narrative functions as a form of religious and communal argument, why the Singh Sabha's investment in historical recovery was integral to rather than separate from its religious reform agenda, and how the historical works produced in this period continue to shape Sikh self-understanding today.

The Janamsakhi Tradition and its Singh Sabha Reception

The primary genre of traditional Sikh historical writing was the ਜਨਮ ਸਾਖੀ (janamsakhi), the life-stories of Guru Nanak Dev Ji and other Gurus. The janamsakhis were composed from the sixteenth century onward in a hagiographic mode, combining verified biographical episodes with legendary and miraculous narratives that conveyed theological truths about the Guru's divine nature and mission. Multiple janamsakhi traditions existed, sometimes with significant variations in the stories they told and the theological emphases they made (McLeod 1980).

For the Singh Sabha reformers, the janamsakhis presented a challenge as well as a resource. The miracle stories and legendary elements in many janamsakhi accounts seemed, to reformers influenced by modern historical criticism, to obscure rather than illuminate the Gurus' genuine historical greatness. At the same time, the Gurus' lives were the primary narrative of Sikh identity, and the reformers had no wish to undermine devotion to them. The response was a form of selective rationalization: retelling the Gurus' lives in ways that emphasized their moral courage, their social teachings, and their opposition to caste and superstition while either rationalizing or gently setting aside the more overtly miraculous elements.

Bhai Vir Singh's biographies of the Gurus, written in a fluid modern Punjabi prose, exemplify this approach. His Guru Nanak Chamatkaar and Guru Kalgidhar Chamatkaar (the latter on Guru Gobind Singh Ji) present the Gurus as heroic and spiritually luminous figures whose greatness is grounded in their teaching, their character, and their service to humanity—while the miraculous elements are handled with a literary deftness that neither dismisses them nor presents them as literal historical fact. The effect was a form of Sikh historical narrative that could be read as spiritually inspiring by the devout and as rationally defensible by the Western-educated.

The colonial encounter also brought new tools of historical criticism. Western scholars, beginning with missionaries and then professional Orientalists, had begun to study Sikh texts and history using philological and historical methods developed in European classical and biblical scholarship. Some of this scholarship was valuable and genuinely enriched understanding of Sikh texts; some was hostile or dismissive. Singh Sabha scholars engaged with Western Orientalist scholarship selectively: accepting methods of textual criticism and source comparison while contesting many of the Orientalists' interpretive conclusions (Mandair 2009).

Encyclopedic Scholarship: Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha and the Mahan Kosh

Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha (1861–1938) represents the scholarly dimension of the Singh Sabha movement at its most impressive. His life's work was the systematic compilation and interpretation of Sikh tradition in forms that made it available for modern readers, scholars, and reformers. His most celebrated achievement, the Gurushabad Ratnakar Mahan Kosh (1930), is a multivolume encyclopedia of Sikh terminology and tradition—one of the most ambitious reference works produced in any Indian language in the colonial period.

The Mahan Kosh covers the vocabulary of the Guru Granth Sahib Ji and the wider Sikh literary tradition, with entries that are simultaneously philological, theological, and encyclopedic. Nabha drew on Sanskrit, Persian, Braj Bhasha, and Punjabi sources, situating Sikh terms in their broader literary and religious context while always returning to Gurbani as the primary authority. The work took decades to compile and represents a scholarly achievement by any standard—not least because it was produced by a single scholar working without modern research infrastructure (Singh and Fenech 2014).

The Mahan Kosh was also, unmistakably, a reformist document. Its entries on disputed religious practices, its definitions of key Sikh terms, and its citations of Gurbani as the arbiter of correct interpretation all embedded the Tat Khalsa perspective within what appeared to be neutral encyclopedic reference. When Nabha defined a term, he was not merely reporting historical usage; he was adjudicating a debate about contemporary practice. The form of the encyclopedia—authoritative, comprehensive, systematically organized—lent a scholarly weight to positions that were in fact contested within the community.

Nabha's smaller polemical work, Hum Hindu Nahin (We Are Not Hindus, 1898), was more explicitly argumentative. Written in response to the claim—made by some Arya Samaj leaders and accepted by some colonial administrators—that Sikhs were simply a variety of Hindu, it marshaled historical, theological, and sociological evidence for the distinctiveness of Sikh identity. The pamphlet's arguments were influential in shaping the Tat Khalsa position and in framing the terms of later debates about Sikh political and legal status under colonial and post-colonial law (Singh and Fenech 2014).

Max Arthur Macauliffe and the Anglo-Sikh Historical Encounter

Among the most significant historical works on Sikhism produced in the colonial period was Max Arthur Macauliffe's The Sikh Religion: Its Gurus, Sacred Writings and Authors (1909), a six-volume work produced by a British colonial official who devoted decades to learning Punjabi and Gurmukhi and to working with Singh Sabha scholars. Macauliffe's work was deeply unusual: a Western administrator who approached Sikh tradition with genuine respect and who worked collaboratively with figures such as Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha and others in the Singh Sabha network.

The Sikh Religion offered Western readers—and English-educated Indians—a systematic account of Sikh theology, Guru biography, and scriptural teaching. Macauliffe was explicit that his work was intended to counter both Christian missionary dismissals of Sikhism and Arya Samaj claims about Sikh identity. His sympathetic portrayal of the Gurus, his translations of Gurbani (made with scholarly assistance from Singh Sabha experts), and his defense of Sikhism's distinctiveness as a world religion aligned closely with the Tat Khalsa position.

The collaboration between Macauliffe and Singh Sabha scholars illustrates the complex traffic between colonial and indigenous knowledge systems in this period. Macauliffe needed Singh Sabha scholars for linguistic and textual expertise; Singh Sabha reformers valued Macauliffe's ability to produce and disseminate an English-language account of Sikhism that could reach both Western audiences and English-educated Indians who might otherwise depend on less sympathetic sources. The result was a joint product that cannot be cleanly attributed to either partner—a reminder that colonial-era knowledge production was often collaborative and complicated even when it appears to come from a single author (Mandair 2009).

Macauliffe's work raised methodological questions that Sikh historians continue to engage with: How should Gurbani be translated? What is the relationship between devotional engagement and scholarly analysis of a religious tradition? To what extent can a non-Sikh scholar access and represent Sikh religious experience authentically? These questions were not resolved by the Singh Sabha encounter with Macauliffe, but they were posed with a clarity and urgency that shaped subsequent scholarship in Sikh Studies as an academic field.

Commemoration, Martyrdom, and the Uses of the Past

Sikh historical consciousness in the Singh Sabha period was not limited to scholarly publication. It was also expressed through practices of commemoration: the celebration of Gurpurabs (anniversaries of the Gurus' births and deaths), the annual commemoration of martyrdoms such as that of Guru Arjan Dev Ji and Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji, and the practice of ਕੀਰਤਨ ਦਰਬਾਰ (kirtan darbar) events at which historical narratives were sung as well as recited. These commemorative practices linked the historical past directly to present devotional life in ways that no book could replicate (Mandair 2009).

The figure of the Sikh martyr was particularly important for the Singh Sabha's historical imagination. The tradition of ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ (shaheedi, martyrdom) in Sikh history—from Guru Arjan Dev Ji in 1606 through Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji in 1675 to the countless figures of the eighteenth-century period of persecution—provided a narrative of steadfastness, sacrifice, and divine protection that resonated powerfully with the community's sense of itself as besieged but indestructible. Singh Sabha reformers drew on this tradition explicitly, framing the struggle to maintain Sikh identity under colonial pressure as a continuation of the martyrs' witness.

The Gurdwara Reform movement of the 1920s would activate this martyrdom tradition even more intensely: the Sikhs who died at Nankana Sahib in 1921 were immediately commemorated as ਸ਼ਹੀਦ (shaheed, martyrs), and the broader Akali agitation was framed in the language of sacrifice and divine testing. Understanding the Singh Sabha's cultivation of historical consciousness is therefore essential for understanding how, two generations later, nonviolent protesters could walk into lethal violence with extraordinary composure—they understood themselves to be enacting a story whose shape and meaning the community had been rehearsing for centuries.

  • Key Takeaways
  • The Singh Sabha movement invested heavily in historical recovery and writing because historical narrative was essential to its claim that Sikhism was a distinct religion with its own authoritative tradition—not a variety of Hinduism or a colonial-era invention.
  • Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's encyclopedic scholarship embedded the Tat Khalsa's interpretive positions within the authoritative form of reference works, giving reform perspectives the appearance of neutral scholarly consensus.
  • Macauliffe's collaboration with Singh Sabha scholars produced the most influential early English-language account of Sikhism, illustrating the complex and often collaborative nature of colonial-era knowledge production.
  • The janamsakhi tradition was selectively rationalized by Singh Sabha writers like Bhai Vir Singh, who preserved its devotional power while adapting its narrative form to modern historical sensibilities.
  • Sikh commemorative practice—Gurpurabs, martyrdom anniversaries, kirtan darbars—anchored historical consciousness in living devotional practice, preparing the community for the heightened martyrdom culture of the Gurdwara Reform era.

Key Terms

  • ਜਨਮ ਸਾਖੀ (Janamsakhi) — Traditional life-story literature about Guru Nanak Dev Ji and other Gurus; hagiographic in form and theological in purpose; engaged selectively and critically by Singh Sabha historical writers.
  • ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ (Shaheedi) — Martyrdom; the tradition of dying for one's faith, central to Sikh historical consciousness and activated politically during the Gurdwara Reform movement.
  • ਗੁਰਪੁਰਬ (Gurpurab) — The anniversary of a Guru's birth or death; commemorative occasions that connected historical memory to living devotional practice in the Singh Sabha era and beyond.
  • ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ ਪੰਥ (Khalsa Panth) — The community of initiated Sikhs, understood historically and spiritually; the Singh Sabha's historical writing sought to define and defend the Panth's boundaries and distinctiveness.
  • ਕੀਰਤਨ (Kirtan) — The singing of Gurbani in musical performance; a devotional and communal practice that carried historical narrative as well as scriptural content in Singh Sabha-era gatherings.

Discussion Questions

  1. The Singh Sabha reformers both respected and selectively modified the janamsakhi tradition. What criteria should scholars and communities use when deciding which elements of a received tradition to preserve, rationalize, or set aside?
  2. Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's encyclopedic works appear authoritative and neutral but embedded specific theological and reformist positions. How can readers of reference works become more alert to the interpretive choices embedded in apparently neutral scholarly formats?
  3. Macauliffe was a British colonial official who produced sympathetic and influential scholarship on Sikhism. Does the origin of a scholar in a colonial administration compromise the scholarship they produce? How should we read such work today?
  4. The Singh Sabha's historical consciousness centered on martyrdom and resilience as core themes. What are the spiritual and psychological benefits of such a historical narrative? What are its potential risks or distortions?
  5. How does historical writing function as a form of religious argument? Can you identify a parallel in another tradition where the recovery of history served primarily to support a contemporary theological or communal claim?

Further Reading

  • W.H. McLeod, Early Sikh Tradition (1980) — the foundational critical study of the janamsakhi literature and its historical value.
  • Arvind-Pal Singh Mandair, Religion and the Specter of the West (2009) — examines the philosophical dimensions of Sikh engagement with Western scholarship and colonial epistemology.
  • J.S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab (1998) — provides a rigorous historical overview of the Singh Sabha movement's scholarly and institutional achievements.
  • Harjot Oberoi, The Construction of Religious Boundaries (1994) — analyzes the discursive construction of Sikh identity in the colonial period, including the role of historical writing.

Homework

Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's Mahan Kosh (1930) is described as an encyclopedia of Sikh tradition. Research this work: What was its scope and method? How long did it take to compile? What sources did Nabha draw on? Write a 350-word account of the Mahan Kosh's significance as a scholarly achievement and as a tool of the Singh Sabha reform agenda. Reflect on how the act of encyclopedic compilation itself performs a claim about what a tradition is and who defines it.

lessons.title: Sikh Political Thought, the Chief Khalsa Diwan, and Colonial Governance
lessons.html:
Introduction

The Singh Sabha movement is most often remembered as a religious and educational reform movement, and that characterization is accurate as far as it goes. But the movement also produced a distinctive form of Sikh political thought—a set of ideas about community representation, relations with the colonial state, and the meaning of Sikh political interests that shaped the later Gurdwara Reform movement and the Sikh engagements with Indian nationalism. Understanding this political dimension requires moving beyond accounts that treat the Singh Sabha as purely a spiritual or cultural phenomenon (Oberoi 1994).

This lecture examines the political thought and practice of the Singh Sabha era through three lenses: the organizational politics of the Chief Khalsa Diwan (CKD) and its approach to colonial governance; the early Sikh engagement with the Indian National Congress and the question of nationalism; and the emergence of a distinctively Sikh understanding of communal representation and political rights that would crystallize in the Gurdwara Reform movement. We pay particular attention to the tensions between accommodation and resistance in Sikh political strategy—a tension that was never fully resolved in this period and that generated significant internal controversy.

The Singh Sabha's political inheritance was complex. The memory of Sikh political sovereignty under Maharaja Ranjit Singh remained vivid, but the possibility of its restoration was not practically on the agenda. The movement's leaders were operating within a colonial system that permitted limited forms of representation and petition while firmly excluding any challenge to British paramountcy. Navigating this space required pragmatism, but pragmatism could shade into collaboration, and collaboration raised questions about the integrity of the reform project.

By engaging with this lecture, students will understand how the Singh Sabha movement developed political skills and institutions that proved essential in the more confrontational Gurdwara Reform era, and will be able to evaluate the strategic choices made by CKD leaders with appropriate historical sympathy and critical distance.

The Chief Khalsa Diwan: Organization, Strategy, and Limitations

The ਚੀਫ਼ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ ਦੀਵਾਨ (Chief Khalsa Diwan, CKD), established in Amritsar in 1902, represented the institutional culmination of the Singh Sabha movement's organizational phase. It was created to coordinate the activities of the dozens of local Singh Sabhas that had proliferated across Punjab, to speak on behalf of the Sikh community in dealings with the colonial government, and to manage the educational and social welfare institutions the movement had established. Its leadership overlapped significantly with the educated, often professionally employed Sikh elite that had benefited most from colonial educational opportunities (Grewal 1998).

The CKD's political strategy was, in retrospect, one of loyal petitioning within the colonial system. It presented Sikh concerns and interests to the Lieutenant-Governor of Punjab and to the Viceroy through formal memorials and deputations, emphasizing the community's loyalty to the Crown—particularly through military service—while requesting specific accommodations: recognition of Gurmukhi in education, representation on provincial councils, protection of Sikh religious sites. This strategy was not without results: the colonial government did make some concessions to Sikh educational and religious interests, partly because it valued the Sikh community's military contribution.

The CKD's relationship with the Indian National Congress was ambivalent. Some Sikh leaders were early Congress supporters; others were suspicious that a Congress-dominated India would privilege Hindu majoritarian interests at Sikh expense. The CKD's official position tended toward caution: it did not endorse the Congress's nationalist program, but neither did it actively oppose it. This positioning reflected both the ideological diversity within the Sikh educated elite and a genuine strategic uncertainty about where Sikh interests lay in the evolving landscape of Indian colonial politics (Grewal 1998).

The CKD's limitations became increasingly visible as the Gurdwara Reform crisis developed in the late 1910s and early 1920s. Its strategy of polite petition was manifestly inadequate in the face of mahant resistance and British hesitation to act against entrenched hereditary rights in gurdwaras. The CKD's cautious leadership was effectively superseded by the more confrontational Akali Dal and SGPC, whose willingness to organize mass nonviolent action proved far more effective than petitioning. The transition from CKD to Akali leadership is a case study in the limits of accommodationist strategies when the stakes are high enough.

Sikh Communal Representation and the Colonial Legal Framework

A key dimension of Singh Sabha political thought was the claim to communal representation—the idea that Sikhs constituted a distinct community with interests that required formal recognition in the colonial political system. This claim was not unique to Sikhs; Muslim leaders had been making analogous arguments, and the colonial government had responded with the Morley-Minto reforms of 1909, which introduced separate Muslim electorates. The Sikh case for communal representation drew on the Tat Khalsa argument for Sikh religious distinctiveness: if Sikhs were a distinct religion, not a Hindu sect, they had legitimate grounds for distinct political recognition (Fox 1985).

The legal definition of who counted as a Sikh for electoral and representational purposes was thus not merely an administrative question; it was a direct extension of the Tat Khalsa–Sanatan theological debate into the domain of colonial law. The Singh Sabha reformers' insistence on a bounded, definitionally clear Sikh identity—centered on ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ (Amrit) initiation and the five Kakars—was partly motivated by the need to produce a legally recognizable community that could make coherent claims on the colonial state. The fuzzier, more inclusive Sanatan vision of Sikh identity did not translate well into the bureaucratic categories that colonial governance required.

The Lucknow Pact of 1916, negotiated between the Indian National Congress and the All India Muslim League, illustrated the stakes of communal representation. Sikh leaders watched anxiously as Hindus and Muslims negotiated their political shares in a future representative India, and they pressed for Sikh interests to be recognized in any such settlement. The concern that Sikhs might be absorbed into a Hindu majority—or reduced to a tiny minority in a system dominated by Hindu-Muslim dyad—motivated much of the CKD's political activity in the 1910s and early 1920s.

The Montagu-Chelmsford reforms of 1919, which introduced elected provincial councils under the system known as dyarchy, required the Punjab government to determine communal voter categories and reserved seats. The classification of Sikhs as a separate category in this system was a significant political achievement for the CKD, and it established a precedent for Sikh communal representation that would carry forward through the negotiations over Indian independence and partition in the 1940s. The foundations of this legal recognition were laid by the patient political work of the Singh Sabha era.

The Emergence of Akali Political Thought: From Reform to Resistance

The political thought that animated the Gurdwara Reform movement represented a significant departure from the CKD's accommodationist approach. The ਅਕਾਲੀ (Akali) movement developed a theology of political action rooted in the Sikh doctrine of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ (Miri-Piri)—the inseparability of temporal and spiritual sovereignty. Drawing on the tradition established by Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji, who wore two swords symbolizing spiritual and temporal authority, Akali leaders argued that Sikh religion could not be separated from Sikh political self-governance. Gurdwara control was not merely an administrative question; it was a question of ਸਵੈ-ਸ਼ਾਸਨ (sway-shaasan, self-rule) in the spiritual domain (Singh and Fenech 2014).

This framework had significant implications. It meant that the Akali movement could not accept a situation in which Sikh shrines were administered either by hereditary mahants beholden to no community body or by colonial officials exercising governmental oversight. Sikh sovereignty over Sikh sacred space was, in this view, a matter of religious principle, not merely practical administration. This gave the Akali movement a moral intensity and a willingness to accept sacrifice that purely administrative reform would not have generated.

The relationship between Akali political thought and Indian nationalism was complicated. Some Akali leaders were sympathetic to Mahatma Gandhi and the Congress; the Congress provided crucial moral support during the Gurdwara agitation, and Gandhi's endorsement of nonviolent resistance as a tactic aligned with the Akali movement's disciplined approach. But the Congress's conception of Indian nationalism as essentially Hindu in cultural character remained a source of deep Sikh suspicion. The Akali movement was simultaneously nationalist (in its resistance to British imperialism) and communalist (in its insistence on distinct Sikh political interests)—a combination that defies the simple categories often applied to colonial-era movements.

  • Key Takeaways
  • The Chief Khalsa Diwan's accommodationist political strategy achieved significant gains within the colonial system—particularly in educational and representational matters—but proved insufficient for the more confrontational demands of the Gurdwara Reform crisis.
  • The Singh Sabha's insistence on a bounded, legally recognizable Sikh identity was driven partly by the requirements of communal representation in the colonial political system, linking the theological debate about Sikh identity directly to political strategy.
  • The Akali movement's political theology, grounded in the Miri-Piri doctrine, provided a framework for claiming spiritual sovereignty over sacred spaces that was genuinely distinct from both Congress nationalism and Muslim League communalism.
  • The Sikh community's political positioning in the colonial period—loyal to the Crown but insistent on distinct communal recognition—produced a complicated legacy that shaped Sikh politics through partition and independence.
  • The transition from CKD petitioning to Akali mass mobilization illustrates a broader pattern in colonial-era politics: the conditions under which gradualist reform strategies give way to more confrontational ones.

Key Terms

  • ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ (Miri-Piri) — The Sikh doctrine of the inseparability of temporal (Miri) and spiritual (Piri) authority, established by Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji; used by Akali leaders to ground their claim to spiritual sovereignty over gurdwaras.
  • ਅਕਾਲੀ (Akali) — 'Servant of the Timeless One (Akal Purakh)'; the name adopted by the Gurdwara Reform movement's activists and its political arm, the Akali Dal.
  • ਪੰਥ (Panth) — The Sikh community understood as a religious-political body; central to Singh Sabha and Akali claims about communal self-governance.
  • ਚੀਫ਼ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ ਦੀਵਾਨ (Chief Khalsa Diwan) — The umbrella organization founded in 1902 to coordinate Singh Sabha activities and represent Sikh interests to the colonial government; its accommodationist strategy was later superseded by the Akali movement.
  • ਸ਼੍ਰੋਮਣੀ ਗੁਰਦੁਆਰਾ ਪ੍ਰਬੰਧਕ ਕਮੇਟੀ (SGPC) — The Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, established in 1920 to manage major Sikh gurdwaras; the organizational expression of the Akali movement's claim to community self-governance over sacred spaces.

Discussion Questions

  1. The Chief Khalsa Diwan pursued a strategy of loyal petitioning within the colonial system. Under what conditions is accommodation with a dominant power a wise strategy, and under what conditions does it become complicity? How would you evaluate the CKD's choices?
  2. The Sikh claim to communal representation in the colonial political system was partly driven by the theological argument that Sikhs were a distinct religion. What does this tell us about the relationship between religious claims and political interests? Can religious identity claims be purely theological, or are they always also political?
  3. The Akali movement used the Miri-Piri doctrine to ground its claim to gurdwara control. How does a religious community translate theological concepts into political programs? What is gained and what is risked in that translation?
  4. The Sikh political position in the colonial period was simultaneously loyal to the Crown, insistent on communal recognition, and suspicious of Hindu-dominated nationalism. Is this combination coherent, or does it involve irresolvable tensions? How did it shape Sikh politics in the independence and partition period?
  5. The transition from CKD gradualism to Akali mass mobilization suggests that the conditions matter for which political strategy is appropriate. What changed between 1902 and 1920 that made the Akali approach both possible and necessary?

Further Reading

  • J.S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab (1998) — the best single-volume scholarly history of Sikh political development in the colonial period.
  • Richard G. Fox, Lions of the Punjab (1985) — examines the class and social base of Sikh political mobilization, with attention to the CKD and Akali eras.
  • Mohinder Singh, The Akali Movement — an important study of Akali political thought and the Gurdwara Reform agitation.
  • Tony Ballantyne, Between Colonialism and Diaspora: Sikh Cultural Formations in an Imperial World (2006) — broadens the frame to include global Sikh communities and their relationship to Singh Sabha and Akali politics.

Homework

The Chief Khalsa Diwan (CKD) was founded in 1902 as the umbrella coordinating body for Singh Sabha activities. Research the CKD's relationship with the colonial government: What was its approach to political loyalty and petition? How did it respond to the partition of Bengal in 1905 or the Morley-Minto reforms of 1909? Write a 400-word account of the CKD's political strategy and evaluate whether its accommodation of colonial authority was wise, necessary, or a betrayal of the reform movement's deeper goals.

lessons.title: Nonviolent Resistance, Martyrdom, and the Shahidi Legacy in the Gurdwara Agitation
lessons.html:
Introduction

The Gurdwara Reform movement of the early 1920s was not simply a legal and administrative campaign for control of historic shrines. It was, at its moral and spiritual core, a movement shaped by the Sikh tradition of martyrdom and sacrifice—ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ (shaheedi)—deployed as a form of disciplined nonviolent resistance against both mahant power and British colonial authority. The willingness of Akali jathas (bands of activists) to walk into violence without retaliation, and of communities to send their members knowing they might not return, drew on centuries of Sikh experience and narrative in ways that startled British administrators and inspired Indian nationalists including Mahatma Gandhi.

This lecture examines the nonviolent ethics and practices of the Gurdwara Reform agitation, the specific incidents—Nankana Sahib (1921), Guru ka Bagh (1922), and Jaito (1923–1924)—that defined its moral character, the role of the Sikh martyrdom tradition in shaping the movement's self-understanding, and the complex relationship between Akali nonviolence and the Gandhian nonviolence of the Congress movement. We also consider what the movement's conduct reveals about the relationship between spiritual formation and political action—how decades of Singh Sabha emphasis on Gurbani, Sikh history, and the Khalsa discipline prepared ordinary Sikhs for extraordinary acts of courage.

The Gurdwara Reform agitation has attracted comparisons to the American civil rights movement, to Gandhian satyagraha, and to other traditions of disciplined nonviolent resistance. These comparisons are illuminating but require care: the Akali movement drew on specifically Sikh theological and historical resources that gave it a character distinct from these parallels. Understanding that distinctiveness is the central task of this lecture.

Students engaging with this material should be prepared to think carefully about the relationship between religious conviction and political strategy in movements of nonviolent resistance. The question of whether Akali nonviolence was primarily strategic (chosen because it worked) or principled (chosen because the Sikh tradition demanded it) is an important one, and the evidence suggests that for most participants, the distinction between strategy and principle was not meaningful—their spiritual formation made principled nonviolence their natural strategic response.

The Theology of Sikh Martyrdom and its Political Activation

The Sikh tradition of martyrdom is not incidental to the faith; it is inscribed in some of its most sacred narratives. Guru Arjan Dev Ji, the fifth Guru, was executed on the orders of Mughal Emperor Jahangir in 1606, refusing to convert or compromise his teachings. Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji, the ninth Guru, gave his life in 1675 to defend the right of Kashmiri Pandits to practice their own faith—an act of interfaith solidarity as much as personal witness. The eighteenth-century Khalsa survived repeated genocidal assaults, and the tradition commemorates this survival through the concept of ਘੱਲੂਘਾਰਾ (Ghallughara, the great massacres), honoring those who died defending the community (Singh and Fenech 2014).

This tradition was not merely historical memory; it was actively maintained through ritual, narrative, and commemorative practice throughout the Singh Sabha period. The ਸ਼ਹੀਦ (shaheed, martyr) was understood not as a tragic victim but as a heroic witness whose death testified to the truth of the faith and whose sacrifice sustained the community. This understanding of martyrdom—as spiritually meritorious, communally generative, and historically vindicated—meant that the Akali movement could draw on a reservoir of prepared meaning when its activists faced violence and death.

The Akali jathas of the early 1920s were organized in explicit imitation of historical Khalsa bands, and their discipline was modeled on the Khalsa's rehat (code of conduct). Volunteers took oaths not to retaliate if attacked. They carried no weapons. They marched singing Gurbani. Their dress and bearing were those of the Khalsa. When violence came, they absorbed it without responding in kind—and the communities that watched understood immediately what they were witnessing: a reenactment of the martyrdom tradition in a modern political key (Singh and Fenech 2014).

British administrators who encountered this disciplined nonviolence found it deeply disorienting. Their previous experience of political agitation involved either armed resistance (which they could suppress militarily) or legal petition (which they could manage bureaucratically). A movement whose members walked toward death singing Gurbani while making no aggressive move fell outside their repertoire of responses. The moral authority this generated—in India and internationally—was a political resource the Akalis had not entirely anticipated but quickly learned to deploy.

Nankana Sahib, Guru ka Bagh, and Jaito: Three Defining Moments

Three events above all others defined the moral character of the Gurdwara Reform agitation and determined its outcome. Each demonstrated the collision between Akali nonviolence and the violence of those who opposed gurdwara reform; each generated national and international attention; and each served as a kind of proof—to the movement itself and to outside observers—of the righteousness of the Akali cause.

Nankana Sahib, February 1921: The gurdwara complex at Nankana Sahib, the birthplace of Guru Nanak Dev Ji, was controlled by Mahant Narain Das, who had accumulated considerable wealth from its endowments and whose management was the subject of serious grievances. When a jatha of around 150 Sikhs led by Bhai Lachhman Singh arrived to take peaceful possession, the mahant's hired men attacked them, killing most of the jatha. The death toll and the circumstances—the burning of bodies, the desecration of a supremely sacred site—shocked the Sikh community and Indian public opinion. The massacre transformed the Gurdwara Reform movement from a local administrative dispute into a national cause (Grewal 1998).

Guru ka Bagh, August–November 1922: The dispute at Guru ka Bagh, near Amritsar, concerned Sikhs' right to cut wood from a garden attached to a gurdwara whose mahant had called in British police support. For months, daily jathas marched to the disputed site, were beaten by police, and returned without retaliating. The sight of unarmed men absorbing police beatings while reciting Gurbani attracted enormous press coverage, including from foreign correspondents. Gandhi himself sent a delegation to observe, and his movement provided both moral support and practical assistance. The Colonial government ultimately capitulated to Sikh demands, and the event is studied as a model of successful nonviolent resistance.

Jaito, 1923–1924: The Jaito agitation arose in connection with the deposition of the Maharaja of Nabha, a Sikh ruler who had supported the Gurdwara Reform movement. A religious ceremony (ਅਖੰਡ ਪਾਠ, Akhand Path, continuous reading of the Guru Granth Sahib Ji) that had been interrupted at Jaito became the focus of protest. A series of five large jathas marched toward Jaito over several months, being arrested before reaching their destination. The movement's willingness to send five hundred volunteers at a time knowing they would be arrested demonstrated a depth of organizational capacity and community support that colonial authorities found impossible to dismiss.

Akali Nonviolence and its Relationship to Gandhian Satyagraha

The relationship between Akali nonviolence and Mahatma Gandhi's satyagraha is complex and has been the subject of scholarly debate. There are obvious structural similarities: disciplined refusal to use violence, acceptance of arrest and suffering as a moral witness, the use of nonviolent tactics to generate moral authority and political pressure. Gandhi publicly praised the Akali jathas, and Congress volunteers participated in some of the agitations in a supporting role.

However, the differences are as significant as the similarities. Gandhian satyagraha was grounded philosophically in ahimsa (nonviolence as an absolute moral principle derived from Hindu and Jain thought) and in Gandhi's specific theory of truth-force (satyagraha, holding to truth). Akali nonviolence was grounded in the Sikh martyrdom tradition—not in ahimsa as an absolute but in the specific Khalsa discipline of fighting without fear and, when necessary, dying without resistance when strategic nonviolence served the cause. The Sikh tradition also has a robust tradition of armed resistance when circumstances warranted, and Akali leaders did not foreclose that option in principle (Fox 1985).

This theological difference had practical implications. The Akali movement was less invested than the Congress in nonviolence as a permanent strategic commitment and more willing to consider its limits as a tactic if the community's fundamental interests were at stake. The later history of Sikh political action—including the armed resistance movements of the 1980s—cannot be understood without acknowledging this distinction between Gandhian nonviolence as principle and Sikh nonviolence as discipline appropriate to specific circumstances.

  • Key Takeaways
  • The Akali movement's disciplined nonviolence drew on specifically Sikh theological resources—particularly the martyrdom tradition—rather than on Gandhian ahimsa, giving it a distinct moral character that combined courage with composure.
  • The three major confrontations of the Gurdwara Reform agitation—Nankana Sahib, Guru ka Bagh, and Jaito—each demonstrated the moral power of nonviolent resistance and helped generate the public support that ultimately forced British agreement to the Sikh Gurdwaras Act.
  • British administrators found Akali nonviolence strategically disorienting precisely because it fell outside their repertoire of responses to political challenge, illustrating how disciplined nonviolence can be a highly effective political weapon.
  • The relationship between Akali and Gandhian nonviolence was one of alignment and cooperation on tactics combined with significant theological and strategic differences on the nature and limits of the nonviolent commitment.
  • The Singh Sabha era's emphasis on Sikh history, martyrdom, and Khalsa discipline was the essential preparation for the Gurdwara Reform movement's capacity to sustain its nonviolent witness under pressure.

Key Terms

  • ਸ਼ਹੀਦ (Shaheed) — A martyr who dies for the faith; the highest form of sacrifice in the Sikh tradition, distinguished from mere death by the intention and context of the death.
  • ਜਥਾ (Jatha) — A band or group of Sikhs organized for a specific purpose; in the Gurdwara Reform era, the organized bands of nonviolent activists who marched to disputed gurdwaras.
  • ਘੱਲੂਘਾਰਾ (Ghallughara) — The great massacres; specifically the major catastrophes suffered by the Khalsa in the eighteenth century; a term of historical commemoration that anchored the community's understanding of collective suffering and survival.
  • ਅਖੰਡ ਪਾਠ (Akhand Path) — The uninterrupted continuous reading of the entire Guru Granth Sahib Ji; the interrupted Akhand Path at Jaito became the symbolic focal point of a major phase of the Gurdwara Reform agitation.
  • ਰਹਿਤ (Rehat) — The code of Khalsa discipline; the ethical and behavioral framework that shaped the conduct of Akali jathas and grounded their nonviolent discipline in a religious rather than merely strategic commitment.

Discussion Questions

  1. The Akali jathas absorbed violence without retaliating while singing Gurbani. What does this tell us about the relationship between spiritual practice and political courage? Can political courage be cultivated without a spiritual framework?
  2. How does the Sikh martyrdom tradition differ from traditions of martyrdom in Christianity or Islam? What are the specifically Sikh theological ideas that shape the meaning of dying for one's faith?
  3. Gandhi praised the Akali jathas but his philosophical foundation for nonviolence differed significantly from theirs. Does it matter whether two movements share the same philosophical basis for nonviolence if they achieve similar tactical results?
  4. The Nankana Sahib massacre of 1921 transformed the Gurdwara Reform movement. How do acts of violence against nonviolent protesters typically affect political movements? What conditions determine whether violence by opponents accelerates or defeats a nonviolent campaign?
  5. The Akali movement did not embrace nonviolence as a permanent commitment but as a discipline appropriate to its circumstances. How do you evaluate this position compared to absolute nonviolence as a moral principle?

Further Reading

  • Mohinder Singh, The Akali Movement — the most detailed single study of the Gurdwara Reform agitation, covering all three major confrontations in depth.
  • J.S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab (1998) — essential context for the Gurdwara Reform period.
  • Louis E. Fenech, Martyrdom in the Sikh Tradition (2000) — the definitive scholarly study of the Sikh martyrdom tradition and its role in community identity and political action.
  • Gene Sharp, The Politics of Nonviolent Action (1973) — a comparative framework for understanding the mechanisms through which nonviolent resistance generates political pressure, applicable to the Akali case.

Homework

The Nankana Sahib massacre of February 1921 was a pivotal moment in the Gurdwara Reform movement. Research this event in detail: Who was Mahant Narain Das, and what were the grievances against him? What happened on February 20, 1921? How did the colonial government respond? How did Sikh organizations respond? Write a 450-word narrative account of the event and its immediate aftermath, and reflect on how a single violent incident can transform the character and pace of a political movement.

lessons.title: The Legacy of the Colonial Era for Modern Sikh Identity and Global Community
lessons.html:
Introduction

Every historical period leaves a legacy, but the colonial era and the Singh Sabha movement left a legacy of unusual breadth and depth in the Sikh world. The institutions, texts, debates, and norms produced in the decades from 1849 to 1925 continue to shape how Sikhs understand themselves, organize their communities, govern their gurdwaras, debate contested questions of practice and identity, and engage with the wider world. This lecture examines that legacy with the dual purpose of consolidating what has been learned in this course and of equipping students to read contemporary Sikh life with historically informed eyes.

We examine four dimensions of the colonial era's legacy: the institutional legacy (particularly the SGPC and the structures established by the 1925 Act); the theological and normative legacy (the Tat Khalsa position on Sikh identity as it was codified in the ਸਿੱਖ ਰਹਿਤ ਮਰਯਾਦਾ, Sikh Rehat Maryada); the literary and intellectual legacy (the scholarly and literary works of the Singh Sabha era as the foundation of modern Punjabi culture); and the diaspora dimension (how Sikh communities outside the Punjab have engaged with, adapted, and contested this legacy in a global context).

Legacies are not simply received; they are actively interpreted, contested, and remade by each generation. The Singh Sabha's answers to the questions 'Who is a Sikh?' and 'What is authentic Sikh practice?' were not final answers—they were persuasive interventions in an ongoing debate that continues today. Contemporary Sikh communities around the world—in the Punjab, in the United Kingdom, in North America, and beyond—engage with the legacy of the colonial era in ways that are simultaneously respectful and creative, honoring the reformers' achievements while recognizing that their historical context was very different from the present.

By the end of this lecture and course, students will be able to connect the historical developments of the 1849–1925 period to contemporary Sikh life, to identify where the debates of the colonial era are still active in the present, and to appreciate the Singh Sabha's achievement as one of the most remarkable religious reform movements in modern South Asian history.

The Institutional Legacy: SGPC, the 1925 Act, and its Long Shadow

The ਸ਼੍ਰੋਮਣੀ ਗੁਰਦੁਆਰਾ ਪ੍ਰਬੰਧਕ ਕਮੇਟੀ (SGPC) established by the Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925 remains one of the most significant institutions in Sikh public life a century after its founding. As the elected body responsible for the management of the historic gurdwaras in Punjab, Haryana, and Himachal Pradesh (and through related legislation, in other Indian states), it controls substantial financial resources, employs thousands of granthi and support staff, and shapes the practice of Sikhi at the most sacred sites of the tradition (Grewal 1998).

The SGPC's institutional design reflected the specific concerns of 1925: above all, the need to replace hereditary mahant control with representative community governance. It achieved this goal. But the democratic framework it established has also created its own pathologies: the SGPC has become a prize in Punjabi and Sikh politics, with the Akali Dal and its rivals competing intensely for control of its elected board. Critics across the political and theological spectrum have argued that this politicization has corrupted the institution's original purpose, using its resources for partisan political ends rather than purely for the service of the Panth.

The definitional question of who is eligible to vote in SGPC elections has continued to require ongoing adjudication. The 1925 Act's definition of a Sikh voter essentially adopted the Tat Khalsa position: a Sikh is someone who professes the Sikh faith, observes its rites, and does not profess any other religion. This definition excluded many people who considered themselves part of a broadly Sikh cultural community while including others who identified primarily by ethnicity or family tradition. The debates that the Tat Khalsa and Sanatan factions conducted in the 1890s thus continue to have practical electoral consequences a century later.

The partition of India in 1947 had devastating consequences for the Sikh community and restructured the institutional landscape. The transfer of Nankana Sahib, Panja Sahib, and other historic gurdwaras to Pakistani territory removed major sacred sites from SGPC jurisdiction. The SGPC's geographic scope became limited to Indian Punjab, while the management of gurdwaras in Pakistan, the United Kingdom, North America, and elsewhere developed through separate institutional frameworks. The global diaspora of Sikh communities from the 1960s onward created a situation in which the SGPC's institutional authority is geographically specific even as its symbolic authority as custodian of the most historic shrines gives it a claim to pan-Sikh influence.

The Sikh Rehat Maryada: Codifying the Tat Khalsa Vision

The most consequential normative document produced in the aftermath of the Singh Sabha movement is the ਸਿੱਖ ਰਹਿਤ ਮਰਯਾਦਾ (Sikh Rehat Maryada, SRM), the official code of Sikh conduct approved by the SGPC. Its development was a long process, beginning in the 1920s and reaching its definitive form only in 1945. The SRM codified the Tat Khalsa position on virtually every major question of Sikh practice: the definition of a Sikh, the ceremony of Amrit initiation, the content of daily prayer (nitnem), the conduct of life-cycle rituals (birth, marriage, death), and the management of gurdwara worship.

The SRM's significance can hardly be overstated. It represents the institutional crystallization of the Singh Sabha reform agenda: the Tat Khalsa's vision of a uniformly observant, distinctively Sikh community governed by authoritative norms derived from Gurbani rather than local custom or Brahminical tradition. It has provided a common standard of reference for Sikh communities around the world, facilitating a degree of ritual and normative consistency across vastly different geographic and cultural contexts (Singh and Fenech 2014).

The SRM has also been a source of controversy. Critics from within the Sikh community—including those representing traditions that the Singh Sabha reformers marginalized (such as the Namdharis and Nirankaris) and those who argue that the SRM represents a specific, historically contingent reading of Sikhism that should not be accorded absolute authority—have contested its status as the definitive expression of Sikh practice. The question of whether and how the SRM should be revised to address contemporary situations—including questions about gender, sexuality, and Sikh practice in diaspora contexts—is one of the most active sites of contemporary Sikh theological debate.

The Diaspora and the Global Transformation of Singh Sabha's Legacy

The largest Sikh diaspora communities—in the United Kingdom, Canada, and the United States—have engaged with the Singh Sabha legacy in ways that reflect both the vitality and the complexity of that inheritance. The gurdwaras established in Birmingham, Southall, Vancouver, Toronto, and dozens of other cities around the world have drawn on the organizational forms, liturgical practices, and normative frameworks developed in the Singh Sabha era. The insistence on the Guru Granth Sahib Ji as the supreme and sole authority, the centrality of kirtan and Gurbani in worship, the maintenance of the langar (community kitchen serving all visitors regardless of background)—these are the Singh Sabha movement's gifts to global Sikh practice.

At the same time, diaspora communities have encountered questions that the 1925 framework did not anticipate and cannot straightforwardly resolve. How should gurdwara management bodies be structured in countries with no equivalent to the SGPC? What is the status of Sikh practice that diverges from the SRM in diaspora communities where enforcement is impossible and social pressure works differently than in Punjab? How should Sikh institutions engage with issues of gender equality, interfaith marriage, and LGBTQ+ inclusion in contexts where civil law and social norms differ fundamentally from those of colonial Punjab? (Jakobsh 2003).

These contemporary questions are not departures from the Singh Sabha legacy; they are its continuation. The reformers of the 1870s–1920s asked, with great urgency: What does authentic Sikh identity look like in a changed world? Their answer—grounded in Gurbani, organized around reformed institutions, and shaped by modern scholarship and print culture—was a creative and historically specific response to their circumstances. The Sikh communities of the twenty-first century face analogous challenges in circumstances that are different in detail but similar in structure: the need to maintain a distinctive identity while engaging fully with a world that presses from without and transforms from within.

  • Key Takeaways
  • The SGPC, established by the 1925 Act, remains the most significant Sikh institution a century after its founding, but its politicization has generated persistent criticism from across the Sikh theological and political spectrum.
  • The Sikh Rehat Maryada codified the Tat Khalsa's reform agenda and provided a common normative standard for Sikh practice globally, but its status as the definitive expression of Sikhism is contested both from within the Sikh world and in academic scholarship.
  • The partition of 1947 restructured the institutional landscape of Sikhism, removing historic gurdwaras from SGPC jurisdiction and accelerating the development of independent institutional frameworks in the diaspora.
  • Diaspora Sikh communities around the world have both preserved and transformed the Singh Sabha legacy, adapting its organizational and normative frameworks to radically different social and legal contexts while maintaining the doctrinal core.
  • The fundamental questions posed by the Singh Sabha movement—Who is a Sikh? What is authentic Sikh practice? How should the community govern itself?—remain live questions in Sikh communities worldwide, testimony to the enduring relevance of the colonial era's debates.

Key Terms

  • ਸਿੱਖ ਰਹਿਤ ਮਰਯਾਦਾ (Sikh Rehat Maryada) — The official SGPC code of Sikh conduct, developed 1925–1945; the most comprehensive codification of Tat Khalsa norms for Sikh practice worldwide.
  • ਲੰਗਰ (Langar) — The community kitchen and shared meal served free to all in the gurdwara, regardless of caste, religion, or background; a central expression of Sikh egalitarianism maintained and emphasized by Singh Sabha reformers.
  • ਗੁਰਦੁਆਰਾ (Gurdwara) — 'Gateway to the Guru'; the Sikh place of worship and community assembly; the institutional management of gurdwaras was the central stake of the Gurdwara Reform movement and remains central to Sikh institutional life.
  • ਪ੍ਰਵਾਸੀ ਸਿੱਖ (Pravasi Sikh) — Diaspora Sikh; Sikh communities living outside of the Punjab and South Asia; their engagement with the Singh Sabha legacy has both preserved and productively transformed the forms of Sikh institutional and devotional life.
  • ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ (Amrit) — The sacred water of Khalsa initiation; the ceremony of Amrit initiation (ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਸੰਚਾਰ, Amrit Sanchar) was codified in the Sikh Rehat Maryada as the definitive rite of Khalsa membership.

Discussion Questions

  1. The SGPC was created to remove hereditary mahant control and replace it with democratic community governance. Has this goal been achieved? What new problems has democratic control of gurdwaras created, and how might the original reformers have assessed the institution a century on?
  2. The Sikh Rehat Maryada codified a specific vision of Sikh identity and practice. Is a codified, authoritative code of conduct necessary for a religious community's integrity and coherence? What is gained and what is lost when religious practice is standardized?
  3. Diaspora Sikh communities face questions—about gender, interfaith marriage, LGBTQ+ inclusion—that the 1925 framework did not address. How should communities use the legacy of a reform movement to address situations the reformers never anticipated?
  4. The Singh Sabha movement defined Sikhism in sharp distinction from Hinduism and Islam. In a twenty-first-century context of religious pluralism and interfaith dialogue, how should Sikh communities maintain their distinctive identity without fostering unnecessary division?
  5. This course has traced Sikh experience through a period of colonial pressure, institutional innovation, and communal mobilization. What lessons from this history do you find most relevant to a Sikh community—or any religious minority community—navigating pressure from a dominant culture today?

Further Reading

  • Doris Jakobsh, Relocating Gender in Sikh History (2003) — examines how the Singh Sabha movement's gender assumptions were codified in the SRM and their implications for Sikh women's religious roles.
  • Pashaura Singh and Louis Fenech, eds., The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies (2014) — comprehensive coverage of contemporary Sikh studies, including diaspora communities and ongoing debates about the Singh Sabha legacy.
  • Tony Ballantyne, Between Colonialism and Diaspora (2006) — traces Sikh cultural formations across the British Empire and into the diaspora, with attention to the Singh Sabha movement's global dimensions.
  • Gurharpal Singh and Giorgio Shani, Sikh Nationalism (2011) — examines how Singh Sabha–era political thought evolved into the various forms of Sikh political identity and nationalism in the post-colonial period.

Homework

The SGPC established by the Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925 has governed major Sikh shrines for a century. Research one significant decision, controversy, or policy made by the SGPC in the post-1947 period and write a 400-word analysis of it. How does this contemporary decision connect to the debates and principles of the Singh Sabha and Gurdwara Reform era? What unresolved questions from the 1920s continue to shape how the SGPC operates today? Conclude with your assessment of whether the 1925 framework has served the Sikh community well a century later.

sourceText.english: The second reason is suitability (yogta), which means that the object of the action must be capable of being acted upon. For example, there is suitability in the phrase "bring a pot," but if one says "bring a mountain" or "bring the moon," the action of "bringing" is physically possible in a general sense, but the object itself is not suitable for such an action. Therefore, a definitive and certain understanding of the word cannot be achieved. If someone is told to bring the moon or a mountain, they will laugh and consider it absurd. Thus, suitability must exist within the words or sentences. The third is proximity (sannidhi), meaning the words should be without delay or gap, so that the structure of the words and the meaning can be clearly understood.

courses.title: Haumai, the Self, and Liberation
courses.summary: An upper-division study of one of the central problems in Sikh philosophy: Haumai, the deep-rooted sense of a separate, self-asserting 'I' that the Gurus identify as the root of human bondage. Drawing on the reverent expository tradition of katha exemplified by Giani Sant Singh Maskeen (1934-2005), a renowned…
outcomes: Explain Haumai as the egoic sense of a separate, self-asserting 'I' and 'mine,' and why Gurmat treats it as the root of bondage rather than one fault among many.
Analyze how Haumai, Maya, and attachment reinforce one another, while distinguishing enslaving attachment from the affirmed householder's engagement in the world.
Demonstrate how the five thieves are expressions of one underlying egoic condition rather than independent enemies.
Contrast the Manmukh and Gurmukh orientations and explain why becoming a Gurmukh depends on grace as well as effort.
Describe the roles of Naam, Shabad, and grace in dissolving the ego, and articulate the mainstream view that liberation is ultimately a gift.
Evaluate Jivan Mukti as embodied liberation and situate the Sikh view of the self respectfully alongside other traditions.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Haumai as the Core Human Predicament
lessons.summary: Defines Haumai as the egoic 'I' and 'mine,' explains why it binds, and frames it as a curable misdirection of the self.
lessons.html:
Full course contents
  1. Haumai as the Core Human Predicament
  2. The Self, Maya, and the Glue of Attachment
  3. The Five Thieves and the Root of Haumai
  4. Manmukh and Gurmukh: Two Orientations
  5. Naam, Shabad, and Grace: The Dissolving of Ego
  6. Jivan Mukti and the Sikh Self in Wider Conversation

The Word and the Problem

The term ਹਉਮੈ (ego, the self-asserting "I") is often rendered in English as egoism or self-centredness, but those words capture only part of its meaning. The word is usually read as a compound of hau (I) and mai (me, mine), so that ਹਉਮੈ names the relentless saying of "I" and "mine." In ਗੁਰਮਤਿ (the teaching of the Gurus) it is not mere vanity but the basic structuring of experience around a separate self that takes itself to be the centre and the agent of all it does (McLeod 1989).

This makes ਹਉਮੈ the core human predicament rather than one fault among many. The Gurus diagnose suffering first as a problem of mistaken self-understanding. When a person lives as though the small, bounded "I" is the ultimate reality, every perception, desire, and relationship is coloured by that error, and the result is restlessness, comparison, and separation from the divine Source.

A Disease That Carries Its Own Cure

A well-known passage in the Asa di Var section of the Guru Granth Sahib describes ਹਉਮੈ as a deep, chronic affliction, yet adds a striking turn: within the malady lies its own remedy. The faculty that, when misdirected, produces egoism is also what can, when reoriented toward the divine, become the means of healing. ਹਉਮੈ is therefore not a foreign invader to be destroyed by force but a misdirection of the self that must be transformed. (The teaching is described here rather than reproduced as a quotation.)

This framing rules out two extremes. On one side is the view that the self is simply evil and must be annihilated; on the other, that the ego is harmless. ਗੁਰਮਤਿ holds a middle position: the assertive "I" is real in its effects and genuinely binding, yet curable, and its cure is available within ordinary human life (Sahib Singh).

Why Haumai Binds

ਹਉਮੈ binds because it generates a cycle. Acting from a sense of separate selfhood produces consequences; those consequences reinforce the sense of being a separate doer; and that reinforced self acts again. In the vocabulary the Gurus reworked, this is tied to action and reaction and to repeated birth and death. The person caught in ਹਉਮੈ is described as coming and going, never at rest.

AspectCommon misreadingGurmat understanding
ਹਉਮੈ (ego)Ordinary pride or vanityRoot structuring of the self as a separate "I" and "mine"
Having a personalityThe self is the problemThe problem is the claim that the finite self is sovereign
The remedyDestroy the self by forceTransform a misdirected self through the divine

The Gurus do not teach that having a name or responsibilities is the problem. The problem is the inner claim that this finite self is self-sufficient, the author of its own existence (Kahn Singh Nabha).

References
  • Kahn Singh Nabha, Bhai. Mahan Kosh.
  • McLeod, W. H. The Sikhs. New York: Columbia University Press, 1989.
  • Sahib Singh. Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan.
  • Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014.

Homework
