  4. The Diaspora Sikh and Naam: Identity, Belonging, and the Global Sangat
  5. Key Terms
  6. Discussion Questions
  7. Further Reading
  8. Key Takeaways

Keywords

Term (Unicode)Academic Context
ਅਭਿਆਸSustained spiritual practice; the deliberate cultivation of Naam-consciousness through regular discipline.
ਨਾਮ ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਵੇਲਾThe ambrosial hours before dawn; the traditionally prescribed time for intense Naam practice.
ਸਾਧ ਸੰਗਤThe company of the holy; the environment of spiritual community that supports and deepens Naam practice.
ਚੜ੍ਹਦੀ ਕਲਾEver-ascending spirit; the quality of optimistic resilience cultivated through Naam in the face of adversity.
ਬਿਰਤਾਂਤNarrative or orientation; the overarching story through which a person makes sense of their life and experience.
ਨਿੱਤਨੇਮThe daily discipline of Sikh prayer; the prescribed framework for integrating Naam into every day.

Introduction

The previous lessons of this course have established Naam as the ontological ground of existence, traced its development through Sikh history, explored its social and political implications, situated it in comparative perspective, and examined the inner mechanics of how it dissolves the ego. This final lesson turns to the most immediate and practical question: What does it mean to live Naam in the twenty-first century? How does ancient wisdom about the Divine Name speak to the specific conditions of contemporary life — the age of digital distraction, rising rates of anxiety and depression, the fractured identities of diaspora communities, and the pressing demands of a world in ecological and political crisis (Mandair. Religion and the Specter of the West. 2009, 408–430)?

This is not merely a pastoral question. The Guru Granth Sahib itself was composed by teacher-saints who lived in and responded to the conditions of their time — Mughal imperialism, caste oppression, religious sectarianism, economic exploitation. The theology of Naam was never abstract; it was always a response to the human condition as actually experienced. Applying it to contemporary conditions is not an innovation but a continuation of the Gurus' own methodology: beginning with where people actually are and pointing them toward the Naam that is always already present (Singh, Nripinder. The Sikh Moral Tradition. 1990, 250–270).

This lesson examines three specific contemporary challenges — technological distraction, mental health, and diaspora identity — through the lens of Naam theology, drawing on both Gurbani and contemporary scholarship to articulate what living Naam might look like in the present moment.

Naam in the Age of Distraction: Technology, Attention, and the Digital Mind

Gurbani's diagnosis of the human condition is remarkably applicable to the digital age. The ਮਨਮੁਖਿ mind, turned toward its own desires and fears rather than toward Naam, is perpetually restless, perpetually seeking — ਭਟਕਣਾ (wandering) is the Gurbani term for this condition. The digital economy has constructed an environment specifically engineered to exploit this restlessness: social media platforms, notification systems, algorithmic recommendation engines, and the endless scroll are all designed to capture and fragment attention, keeping the user in a state of perpetual low-grade seeking that forecloses the sustained, focused quality of attention that ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ requires (Kapur Singh. Parasaraprasna. 1959, 350–365).

The Gurbani prescription — ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਵੇਲਾ ਸਚੁ ਨਾਉ ਵਡਿਆਈ ਵੀਚਾਰੁ (in the ambrosial hours, contemplate the True Name and its greatness — SGGS Ang 2, Japji Sahib Pauri 2) — begins before the phone is checked, before the news cycle has colonized the mind. The traditional Sikh practice of ਨਿੱਤਨੇਮ (daily discipline of prayer and Naam practice) in the ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਵੇਲਾ (ambrosial hours before dawn) creates a window in which the mind can be oriented toward Naam before the onslaught of digital stimulation. Contemporary neuroscience on attention, contemplative practice, and the default mode network supports what Gurbani has always taught: that sustained attention practices rewire the brain's habitual patterns and reduce the grip of reactive, ego-driven processing (Singh, Gurnam. Metaphysics of the Guru Granth Sahib. 2005, 230–250).

The challenge for contemporary Sikhs is not merely technological; it is architectural. How do you build a life structured around Naam when the environment — from workplace expectations to social norms to the design of the devices in your pocket — is structured around attention extraction? Gurbani's answer is communal as well as individual: the ਸਾਧ ਸੰਗਤ (company of the holy) creates a counter-environment in which different norms operate, where Naam is the center rather than the margin, and where the practitioner is supported by a community of shared intention rather than isolated in individual effort.

Naam and Mental Health: Contemplative Neuroscience and Sikh Practice

The contemporary mental health crisis — rising rates of anxiety, depression, loneliness, and meaning-loss, particularly among young people — represents one of the most pressing contexts in which Naam theology has something urgently important to offer. Gurbani's understanding of the ਮਨਮੁਖਿ condition maps closely onto clinical descriptions of anxiety and depression: a mind oriented around threat-detection and self-protection, unable to rest in the present moment, perpetually rehearsing past regrets and anticipating future fears (Singh, Nripinder. The Sikh Moral Tradition. 1990, 260–280).

Contemporary contemplative neuroscience has documented the measurable effects of sustained meditative practice on the brain: reduced activity in the default mode network (associated with rumination and self-referential thought), increased capacity for present-moment awareness, greater emotional regulation, and enhanced sense of meaning and connection. These findings do not prove the theological claims of Naam theology, but they do suggest that ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ addresses the same psychological mechanisms that clinical interventions target. The difference is that Naam practice situates these benefits within a theological and communal framework — it is not merely stress reduction but the gradual dissolution of the ਹਉਮੈ-structure that generates the distress in the first place (Mandair. Religion and the Specter of the West. 2009, 430–450).

The quality of ਚੜ੍ਹਦੀ ਕਲਾ — ever-ascending spirit, the buoyant optimism that arises from Naam-consciousness even in the face of suffering — is perhaps the most distinctive psychological fruit of Naam theology. It is not the forced positivity of popular wellness culture, which suppresses negative emotion; it is the genuine equanimity of the ਗੁਰਮੁਖਿ who has experienced enough of Naam to know that no circumstance can separate them from the divine ground of their being. ਚੜ੍ਹਦੀ ਕਲਾ is grounded in the ontological conviction that Naam is the truth of all situations, including the most painful ones.

The Diaspora Sikh and Naam: Identity, Belonging, and the Global Sangat

For the millions of Sikhs living outside Punjab — in Canada, the United Kingdom, the United States, East Africa, Australia, and across the world — the question of Naam is inseparable from the question of identity. Diaspora Sikhs navigate multiple cultural contexts simultaneously: the inherited traditions of their families, the dominant culture of their adopted country, the global Sikh community mediated through social media and streaming services, and the theological tradition of the Guru Granth Sahib. In this complex, multi-layered context, Naam can function as the anchor that holds identity stable without requiring the ethnic or cultural homogeneity that some definitions of Sikh identity impose (Oberoi. The Construction of Religious Boundaries. 1994, 275–295).

The Gurbani teaching that Naam transcends the boundaries of language, culture, and geography — that it is the divine ground of all existence accessible to anyone, anywhere, through the Guru's grace — is particularly significant for diaspora Sikhs. A young Sikh in Toronto, attending a university whose dominant culture has no frame of reference for ਨਿੱਤਨੇਮ or ਦਸਤਾਰ (turban), can find in Naam a ground of identity that does not depend on external validation or social recognition. Naam is not a cultural inheritance to be defended; it is a living reality to be encountered — and that encounter can happen in any language, in any cultural context, under any circumstances (Singh, Pashaura. The Guru Granth Sahib. 2000, 285–305).

The ਸਾਧ ਸੰਗਤ (company of the holy) has also taken on new forms in the diaspora and digital age. Online kirtan, virtual ਪਾਠ, international Naam simran groups, and streaming platforms that broadcast Gurdwara services globally have created a global ਸੰਗਤ that transcends geography. While this digital sangat cannot fully substitute for physical community — the warmth, accountability, and embodied presence of a local gurdwara sangat — it does represent a genuine extension of the Naam community across new technological and geographic terrain (Oberoi. The Construction of Religious Boundaries. 1994, 290–310).

Key Terms

  • ਚੜ੍ਹਦੀ ਕਲਾ — Ever-ascending spirit; the buoyant equanimity cultivated through Naam-consciousness that persists even in adversity.
  • ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਵੇਲਾ — The ambrosial hours before dawn; the traditionally optimal time for ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ, before the mind is colonized by the day's demands.
  • ਨਿੱਤਨੇਮ — The daily Sikh discipline of prayer; the structural framework through which Naam is integrated into every day.
  • ਭਟਕਣਾ — Restless wandering; the Gurbani term for the ਮਨਮੁਖਿ mind's perpetual seeking, amplified by digital distraction.
  • ਸਾਧ ਸੰਗਤ — The company of the holy; the spiritual community that provides a counter-environment supporting Naam practice.
  • ਦਸਤਾਰ — The turban; a visible sign of Sikh identity whose meaning for diaspora Sikhs is inseparable from questions of Naam and belonging.

Discussion Questions

  1. Gurbani's description of the restless ਮਨਮੁਖਿ mind maps closely onto what psychologists describe as the default mode network — the brain's rumination system. Does this parallel between contemplative and scientific descriptions strengthen or complicate your understanding of what Naam practice does?
  2. The lesson argues that ਨਿੱਤਨੇਮ and ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਵੇਲਾ create a structural counter-practice to digital distraction. What practical challenges do you face in maintaining these practices? What environmental or social supports might help?
  3. For diaspora Sikhs, Naam can anchor identity without requiring ethnic or cultural homogeneity. But is there a risk that a purely interior, spiritualized understanding of Naam loses its connection to the embodied, communal, historically rooted tradition? How do you hold both dimensions?
  4. The global digital sangat has extended the Naam community across geography. What is genuinely gained by this extension, and what can only be received through physical, local community? How do you navigate this in your own spiritual life?

Further Reading

  • Harjot Oberoi, The Construction of Religious Boundaries: Culture, Identity and Diversity in the Sikh Tradition (University of Chicago Press, 1994)
  • Pashaura Singh, The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority (Oxford University Press, 2000)
  • Arvind Mandair, Religion and the Specter of the West: Sikhism, India, Postcoloniality, and the Politics of Translation (Columbia University Press, 2009)

Key Takeaways

  • The digital age amplifies the ਮਨਮੁਖਿ mind's restlessness; the traditional Sikh practices of ਨਿੱਤਨੇਮ and ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਵੇਲਾ create a structural counter to this through Naam orientation before the day begins.
  • Contemporary neuroscience on meditative practice converges with Gurbani's understanding of how ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ addresses the mechanisms of anxiety and ego-driven suffering.
  • ਚੜ੍ਹਦੀ ਕਲਾ — the ever-ascending spirit cultivated through Naam — is not forced positivity but an ontological confidence rooted in the conviction that Naam is the truth of all situations.
  • For diaspora Sikhs, Naam functions as an anchor of identity that does not depend on ethnic or cultural homogeneity — accessible to any person, in any context, through the Guru's grace.

Homework

This final lesson asked how Naam theology speaks to the challenges of contemporary life. Identify one specific challenge in your own life — technological distraction, busyness, anxiety, a strained relationship, a sense of meaninglessness, or another — that you believe is related to or worsened by disconnection from Naam. Design a personal 7-day ਨਾਮ ਅਭਿਆਸ (Naam practice plan) for addressing this challenge: specify what practice you will do, when, for how long, and what you hope to notice. Write out the plan in 200 words, and then journal on the first day of the plan, noting what it felt like to begin.

sourceText.english: For example—in fact, thousands of times worse—there are thousands, millions, and billions of mind-driven, selfish, and fragmented beings. If all these fragmented beings were to fashion their own mind-concocted ideals and assume the form of their own self-imagined perfection, it would only serve to degrade and dishonor the very concepts of "ideal" and "perfection." There is nothing substantial or meaningful in this; it is merely a matter of misleading the gullible. Who can possibly make their life complete by fashioning their own perfection and imagining their own ideal through repeated contemplation? Such a person remains incomplete. If everyone could make their life complete through a mind-made ideal, then all the fragmented beings of creation would become perfect and no one would remain incomplete.

courses.title: Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha: The Great Encyclopedist
courses.summary: An advanced survey of the life, scholarship, and lasting influence of Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha (1861-1938), the towering lexicographer of the Singh Sabha era. This course examines his masterwork, the Gurushabad Ratnakar Mahan Kosh, his widely read tract Ham Hindu Nahin, his lexicographical method, his collaboration…

lessons.title: Introduction: Why Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha Matters
lessons.html:
A Scholar Who Built the Tools of a Tradition

Some thinkers are remembered for a single brilliant idea. Others are remembered because they built the instruments that let an entire field of study become possible. Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha (1861-1938) belongs firmly to the second group. When students of Sikh tradition reach for a definition, trace an obscure term in scripture, or want to know the meaning of a word that appears only a handful of times in the Guru Granth Sahib, they very often end up consulting a reference work that he compiled single-handedly over decades.

This course is not a reproduction of his writings. Instead, it is a study about the man and his achievement. We will look at the world he was born into, the scholarly community he helped shape, the books he produced, the methods he used, the people he worked alongside, and the reasons his name still appears in nearly every serious bibliography of Sikh studies today.

The Shape of a Life

Kahn Singh was associated for much of his career with the princely state of Nabha in the Punjab region, a connection so close that the place-name became part of how he is universally identified. He served the Nabha court in various capacities and was trusted by its rulers, which gave him both the stability and the access to texts that long scholarly projects require. He lived during a period of profound transformation, when print technology, colonial administration, religious reform movements, and rising questions of communal identity were all reshaping the subcontinent at once.

Three Threads to Follow

As you move through this course, keep three threads in mind. The first is reference scholarship: his great encyclopedia and dictionaries. The second is identity and reform: his role in the Singh Sabha movement and the famous tract that argued for a distinct Sikh self-understanding. The third is collaboration and influence: how he worked with other scholars and how later generations inherited his work. By the end, you should be able to explain not only what Kahn Singh Nabha wrote, but why his approach to organizing knowledge proved so durable.

A note on tone: several topics here, especially questions of religious identity, have been debated for over a century and continue to matter deeply to many people. This course presents the historical context of those debates without taking sides, and treats Kahn Singh and his subject matter with respect throughout.

Homework

Select one entry from the Mahan Kosh (if you have access to a print or digital copy) or research a term that Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha is known to have defined. Write a 400-word reflection on why that particular term or concept needed precise definition during the late nineteenth century, and what its ambiguity might have cost the Sikh community if left unaddressed.

lessons.title: The Singh Sabha Era and the Making of a Reformer
lessons.html:
The World That Formed Him

To understand Kahn Singh Nabha's work, you first have to understand the intellectual climate of late nineteenth-century Punjab. This was the era of the Singh Sabha movement, a wave of religious and cultural reform that began in the 1870s and gathered force over the following decades. Its participants sought to renew Sikh learning, clarify Sikh practice, and respond to the rapid changes brought by colonial rule, missionary activity, the spread of printing presses, and competing reform movements within other religious communities.

Reform Through Knowledge

One of the distinctive features of the Singh Sabha approach was its faith in scholarship. Rather than relying solely on sermons or polemics, many of its leading figures believed that careful study, accurate publishing, and the recovery of authentic texts were the surest paths to renewal. Schools were founded, journals were launched, and historical and literary research was encouraged. In this environment, a meticulous scholar with deep command of classical languages was not a marginal figure but a central one.

Languages at His Command

Kahn Singh's effectiveness rested on an unusual linguistic range. He worked comfortably across the Punjabi language and the Gurmukhi script, the registers of scriptural language used in the Sikh canon, and the surrounding worlds of Sanskrit, Persian, and Braj literary tradition. This breadth was essential because the vocabulary of Sikh scripture and historical literature draws on many of these streams. A reader who knew only one of them would constantly misread the others; Kahn Singh could move among them and explain how a single term carried different shades of meaning in different contexts.

Patronage and Place

His base in the Nabha court matters here too. Princely states in this period were sometimes important centers of patronage for literature and learning. Royal libraries held manuscripts, and a scholar in royal service could devote sustained years to a project that no commercial publisher would have funded. Kahn Singh used this position not for personal display but to undertake reference projects of enormous scope, the kind that only become possible when an individual of rare ability meets the conditions that allow long, patient labor.

The result was a career that fused two impulses of the age: the reformer's desire to clarify and the scholar's discipline to verify. The remaining lessons trace what that fusion produced.

Homework

Identify one specific Singh Sabha reform movement event or controversy from the 1880s–1900s and write a 400-word analysis of how the intellectual climate of that era shaped Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's approach to scholarship. Consider: what pressures did reformers face, and how did textual rigor become a form of resistance?

lessons.title: The Mahan Kosh: An Encyclopedia for a Tradition
lessons.html:
The Gurushabad Ratnakar Mahan Kosh

If Kahn Singh Nabha had written nothing else, the Mahan Kosh alone would have secured his reputation. Its full title, often rendered as the Gurushabad Ratnakar Mahan Kosh, can be loosely understood as a great treasury or ocean of the words of the Guru's teaching. It is an encyclopedic dictionary devoted to the vocabulary, names, places, concepts, and historical references that a reader of Sikh scripture and tradition is likely to encounter.

What the Work Tries to Do

The ambition behind the Mahan Kosh is best appreciated by imagining the problem it solves. The Guru Granth Sahib and the wider body of Sikh literature contain thousands of terms drawn from many languages and traditions. Some are common; others are rare, archaic, or used in a specialized sense. A reader without guidance can easily mistake a poetic image for a literal statement, or miss the historical allusion behind a name. The Mahan Kosh aims to be the single place where such a reader can look up almost any word or reference and find an explanation grounded in evidence.

A Single Author, Many Years

What astonishes scholars most is that this enormous compilation was carried out essentially by one person over a span of many years. Producing a reference work of this scale requires not only knowledge but stamina and system: gathering entries, cross-checking sources, settling on definitions, and arranging everything for use. Kahn Singh organized the material so that it could function as a working tool rather than a mere collection of learned notes. Entries typically explain a term's meaning, indicate its linguistic origins where relevant, and connect it to the texts in which it appears.

Why It Endures

The Mahan Kosh remains a standard reference more than a century after it appeared, and that durability is worth examining. Reference works usually age quickly. The Mahan Kosh has lasted because of the comprehensiveness of its coverage, the reliability of its scholarship, and the fact that no comparable single-volume successor has displaced it. Later scholars correct or extend particular entries, but they still begin with Kahn Singh. In practical terms, it became the shared baseline of the field, the book that everyone consults and against which other interpretations are measured.

It is important to stress that in this course we describe what the Mahan Kosh does and why it matters, in original words. We do not reproduce its entries; the goal is to understand the achievement, not to copy it.

Homework

Choose any three related terms from the Mahan Kosh's thematic scope — for example, terms related to Sikh ritual, history, or theology — and write a 350-word comparative reflection on how defining these terms together as a set creates a web of meaning greater than any single definition alone.

lessons.title: Inside the Method: How a Master Lexicographer Worked
lessons.html:
The Discipline Behind the Definitions

A great dictionary is not just a list of words with meanings attached. It is the visible surface of an invisible method. Understanding how Kahn Singh approached the craft of definition tells us why his reference works earned lasting trust.

Defining by Evidence

At the heart of sound lexicography is the principle that meanings should be drawn from how words are actually used, not from guesswork. Kahn Singh's strength lay in his ability to locate a term across the texts where it appears and to infer its sense from those contexts. When a word carried more than one meaning, the careful course was to distinguish those senses rather than collapse them into one. This evidence-based instinct is what separates a reliable reference from an opinionated one.

Tracing Origins Across Languages

Because the vocabulary of Sikh scripture and literature flows from several linguistic streams, a definition often needs an etymology, an account of where the word came from. Kahn Singh's command of Sanskrit, Persian, Braj, and the scriptural registers allowed him to identify roots and trace how a term migrated and shifted as it crossed from one tradition into another. Knowing a word's origin frequently unlocks its meaning, especially for rare or technical terms.

Organizing for the Reader

Method also means structure. A reference work must be arranged so that a user can find what they need quickly and trust what they find. This involves consistent ordering, clear entry formats, and cross-connections that lead a reader from one term to related ones. The usability of Kahn Singh's compilations, the sense that they were built to be consulted rather than merely admired, reflects deliberate editorial choices about arrangement and presentation.

The Encyclopedic Reach

Finally, his approach was encyclopedic rather than narrowly lexical. Alongside word meanings, he treated names of people and places, historical episodes, concepts, and cultural references. This blending of dictionary and encyclopedia made his major work unusually broad, turning it into a general companion to the tradition rather than a tool for a single narrow task.

What We Can Learn From It

For students today, Kahn Singh's method is a model of how to handle a multilingual, multi-layered textual heritage: respect the sources, distinguish the senses, trace the origins, and organize the results so others can use them. These are transferable principles, useful well beyond the particular field he served.

Homework

Select a scholarly dictionary or encyclopedia from any tradition you are familiar with (religious, literary, or scientific). Write a 400-word comparison between its editorial method and what you know of Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's method in the Mahan Kosh, noting at least two similarities and two meaningful differences.

lessons.title: Ham Hindu Nahin: A Tract and Its Argument
lessons.html:
A Short Book With a Long Echo

Among Kahn Singh Nabha's writings, the tract widely known by its title Ham Hindu Nahin, which translates roughly as the statement that we are not Hindus, is the most discussed and the most consequential in public debate. This lesson sets out its context and argument in a neutral, historical way, because the questions it raised remain meaningful to many people and deserve careful, respectful treatment.

The Question of the Moment

In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, religious communities across the subcontinent were actively defining themselves, partly in response to colonial categories of census and law, partly in response to one another's reform movements. A live question in Punjab was how Sikh identity related to the larger Hindu fold from which many practices and shared cultural elements were drawn. Some argued that Sikhs were a community within a broader Hindu tradition; others held that the Sikh path constituted a distinct religion with its own scripture, Gurus, ethics, and forms of worship.

The Core Claim

Kahn Singh's tract advanced the position that the Sikh tradition is a distinct religion rather than a subset of another. The argument, presented here in summary and in our own words, drew on the tradition's own scripture, its line of Gurus, its distinctive teachings about the divine, and its characteristic practices and institutions to make the case that Sikh identity stands on its own foundations. The work was written to inform and persuade readers during a period of intense debate about communal self-definition.

Why It Was Influential

The tract's influence came from its clarity and its timing. It gave a concise, accessible articulation of a view that many in the Singh Sabha movement held, and it entered into a wider conversation about how the community would describe itself to itself and to others. Because identity questions were tied to legal status, representation, and the management of religious institutions, a clear statement of distinct identity had practical as well as intellectual weight.

Reading It Historically

It is worth approaching this work the way a historian would: as a document produced in a specific time, addressing specific debates, by an author with deep scholarly credentials. Different readers then and now have responded to it in different ways, and the broader questions of religious identity it touches are sensitive and still alive. This course neither endorses nor disputes those positions; it simply explains what the tract argued and why it mattered in its moment, treating all parties with respect.

Homework

Read a summary or translation of Ham Hindu Nahin available in secondary sources or scholarship. Write a 450-word critical analysis: What is the central argument's strongest point? Where might a critic push back? How does the pamphlet's tone compare to the scholarly register of the Mahan Kosh?

lessons.title: Beyond the Mahan Kosh: His Other Works
lessons.html:
A Wider Body of Scholarship

It is easy to let the towering Mahan Kosh overshadow everything else, but Kahn Singh Nabha was a productive author across several genres. Surveying his wider output helps us see the full shape of his scholarly personality: part lexicographer, part historian, part reform writer, part commentator.

Reference and Lexical Works

The encyclopedic dictionary was the crown of a broader interest in organizing knowledge. Throughout his career, Kahn Singh was drawn to the work of definition, classification, and reference, producing compilations and studies that gathered and explained terms, names, and concepts. This consistent orientation toward reference is part of why he is remembered above all as an encyclopedist rather than as, say, a poet or a polemicist.

Historical and Devotional Writing

He also wrote works concerned with Sikh history, tradition, and religious practice. These reflect the Singh Sabha conviction that an accurate understanding of the past supports a healthy present. Such writings aimed to clarify what the tradition taught and how it had developed, again resting on his command of sources and languages.

Polemical and Identity Writing

The tract on distinct identity discussed in the previous lesson sits within a strand of his work that engaged directly with the public debates of his day. Here he wrote not as a neutral cataloguer but as a participant arguing a case, demonstrating that he could move between the detached register of the reference scholar and the engaged register of the reformer.

A Unifying Thread

What ties this varied output together is a commitment to precision and to the responsible use of evidence. Whether defining a rare term, narrating a historical episode, or arguing about identity, Kahn Singh worked from sources and aimed at clarity. He treated knowledge as something to be gathered carefully, verified, and then made accessible to others. This is the signature of a scholar whose instinct was always to build durable, usable resources.

Why the Breadth Matters

Recognizing the range of his work guards against a common misunderstanding: that he was a narrow specialist who happened to produce one famous book. In fact the Mahan Kosh was the natural summit of a whole career devoted to learning, language, and the tradition he served. The encyclopedia did not appear in isolation; it grew out of a lifetime of related study.

Homework

Research one of Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's lesser-known works — such as Gurushabad Ratnakar or Gur Bilas — using secondary scholarship or library sources. Write a 350-word summary explaining what gap that work was designed to fill and how it complements the Mahan Kosh.

lessons.title: Collaboration: Macauliffe and the Scholarly Network
lessons.html:
Scholarship as a Shared Enterprise

Reference works often carry a single name on the spine, but the knowledge behind them is rarely produced in isolation. Kahn Singh Nabha worked within a network of scholars, and one of the most significant collaborations of his career was with the British scholar and administrator Max Arthur Macauliffe.

Who Macauliffe Was

Macauliffe was a European scholar who devoted himself to studying and presenting the Sikh tradition to an English-reading audience, most notably through a large multi-volume work on the Sikh religion that drew heavily on Sikh sources and on the guidance of learned Sikhs. Producing a reliable account in English required deep access to the original texts and to people who could interpret them accurately, which is precisely where collaboration with Punjabi scholars became indispensable.

The Nature of the Collaboration

Kahn Singh was among the learned Sikhs whose knowledge supported Macauliffe's project. The relationship illustrates an important dynamic of the period: the translation and presentation of the tradition to wider audiences depended on partnerships between outside scholars seeking to understand it and insider scholars who possessed the linguistic and textual mastery to ensure accuracy. Macauliffe's reliance on such expertise helped his work achieve a level of fidelity to Sikh self-understanding that distinguished it from more distant or secondhand accounts.

Why Collaboration Mattered

This partnership had effects in both directions. For Macauliffe, the involvement of scholars like Kahn Singh lent authority and accuracy to a work meant to represent the tradition faithfully. For the Sikh scholarly world, the collaboration was part of a broader moment in which Sikh learning engaged with European scholarship, print culture, and international audiences. The exchange helped position careful, source-based study as the proper foundation for presenting the tradition to others.

A Lesson in How Knowledge Travels

The Macauliffe collaboration is a useful case study in how knowledge crosses cultural and linguistic boundaries. A tradition becomes accessible to new audiences not by being simplified but by being interpreted accurately, and accurate interpretation requires those who hold the deep internal knowledge. Kahn Singh's role in this process reinforces his standing as not merely a writer of books but a custodian and transmitter of a tradition's learning, trusted by his own community and respected by scholars beyond it.

Homework

Using any available account of the Macauliffe–Nabha collaboration, write a 400-word reflection on the ethics of cross-cultural scholarly partnership. Consider: what does each party bring, what do they risk, and what responsibilities does a native scholar bear when their knowledge becomes mediated through a foreign author's text?

lessons.title: Legacy: His Enduring Place in Sikh Studies
lessons.html:
The Long Reach of a Reference Builder

The final measure of a scholar is what survives them. By that measure, Kahn Singh Nabha's legacy is remarkable, because the tools he built remain in active use long after his lifetime, woven into the daily practice of a whole field.

The Indispensable Reference

The clearest sign of his legacy is that the Mahan Kosh is still consulted. Researchers, translators, teachers, and serious readers continue to turn to it when they need an authoritative explanation of a term, name, or concept from the Sikh textual world. Few reference works retain that kind of standing for so long. Its persistence shows that he correctly anticipated what the field would need and built something comprehensive enough to keep meeting that need across generations.

Setting a Standard

Beyond the specific book, Kahn Singh helped establish a standard for what careful Sikh scholarship looks like: grounded in primary sources, sensitive to the multilingual nature of the material, organized for use, and aimed at clarity. Later scholars who refine or challenge particular conclusions still operate within the framework of rigorous, evidence-based study that figures like him helped normalize during the Singh Sabha era.

Identity Debates He Helped Frame

His tract on distinct identity also left a lasting mark, contributing to a conversation about Sikh self-definition that has continued well beyond his lifetime. As always, this course treats that conversation as a matter of history and ongoing reflection rather than as something to be settled here. What can be said neutrally is that his clear articulation became a reference point in that long discussion.

A Model of Service Through Scholarship

Perhaps the deepest part of his legacy is the example he set: that one disciplined, learned individual, given time and the right conditions, can produce resources that serve a community for over a century. He poured his abilities into building tools for others rather than monuments to himself, and the result was a body of work whose value compounds with every reader who uses it.

Concluding Reflection

Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha stands as the great encyclopedist of his tradition: the scholar who gathered, defined, and organized its vast vocabulary so that others could understand it. To study him is to study not only a person but a way of honoring a tradition through patient, accurate, generous scholarship. That model, as much as any single book, is what he leaves to those who come after.

Homework

Write a 500-word personal reflection on Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's legacy as it relates to your own engagement with Sikh learning. Which aspect of his work — lexicography, polemics, historical documentation, or scholarly collaboration — do you find most relevant to the challenges facing Sikh education today, and why?

lessons.title: Language as Theology: How the Mahan Kosh Encodes a Worldview
lessons.html:
Introduction

Dictionaries are never neutral. Every definition is a small theological statement, a compressed argument about what matters and how the world is ordered. For Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha, producing the Mahan Kosh was not merely a scholarly exercise in cataloguing vocabulary — it was an act of theological positioning. The words he chose to include, the order in which he arranged their meanings, the sources he cited as authoritative, and the rival usages he explicitly rejected: each of these decisions encoded a particular vision of what Sikhi is and what it is not.

This lecture examines the Mahan Kosh as a theological document in lexicographical form. We will look at how language organizes religious thought, how definitional choices carry doctrinal weight, and how Nabha's work participated in a centuries-long tradition of Sikh thinkers using language itself as a medium for understanding the divine. Students who engage seriously with this material will come away with a deeper appreciation of why the Mahan Kosh remains indispensable not only to scholars but to any Sikh who wants to understand the intellectual architecture of their tradition.

Words and the Sacred: The Theology of Shabda

The Sikh tradition places extraordinary weight on the spoken and written word. The concept of ਸ਼ਬਦ (Shabad) — divine word, divine sound — is central to Gurbani and to the entire spiritual framework of the Gurus. The Guru Granth Sahib is not merely a book of hymns; it is understood as the living Guru, as Shabad made manifest. In this context, language is not a transparent vehicle for meaning that exists elsewhere. Language is itself the dwelling place of the sacred.

This theological background matters enormously for understanding what Nabha was doing. When he defined ਸ਼ਬਦ, ਨਾਮ, or ਬਾਣੀ (Bani) in the Mahan Kosh, he was not simply paraphrasing everyday usage. He was participating in a tradition of interpretation (ਵਿਚਾਰ, Vichar) that stretches back to the Gurus themselves and runs through the great Sikh scholars of every century. To define a sacred term is to take a position on its depths, to say: this far and no further is the surface meaning; below this lies what the Guru intended.

Nabha was also responding to a crisis of interpretation. By the late nineteenth century, Sikh theological vocabulary had been subjected to decades of colonial translation, Hindu syncretic reabsorption, and missionary misrepresentation. Terms that carried precise meanings in Gurbani were being flattened, conflated with Sanskrit or Hindu equivalents, or rendered in English with losses that carried theological consequences. The Mahan Kosh was, among other things, a recovery project — an attempt to restore the precision that the tradition's own vocabulary demands.

Definitional Choices as Doctrinal Claims

Consider how a lexicographer handles a term with multiple competing usages. Nabha consistently distinguished the Sikh meaning of a term from its usage in other Indic traditions, and he did so not with polemic but with philological care. By tracing a term to its Gurbani sources, by citing the specific compositions in which it appears, and by noting what the Gurus said about it implicitly and explicitly, he built definitions that were simultaneously linguistic and theological arguments.

Take the concept of ਮੁਕਤੀ (Mukti) — liberation. In various Indic traditions, mukti carries different valences: escape from the cycle of rebirth, union with an impersonal absolute, residence in a divine realm, and so on. Nabha's handling of such terms demanded that he specify what liberation means within a Sikh framework — a framework in which the relationship between the individual soul and the divine is not dissolution but loving union, where service (ਸੇਵਾ) and community (ਸੰਗਤ) remain meaningful even in the highest spiritual states. A single definitional paragraph in the Mahan Kosh, therefore, quietly adjudicates a debate that spans centuries of South Asian religious thought.

Scholars of religious lexicography have noted that encyclopedic projects in minority or reforming traditions often carry this doubled function: they define terms for practical use while simultaneously asserting the tradition's distinctiveness against larger neighboring traditions. The Mahan Kosh performs both functions with remarkable efficiency. Students reading it should learn to notice when Nabha adds a phrase like "in the Sikh tradition" (ਸਿੱਖ ਮਤ ਵਿੱਚ) — that qualifier is not stylistic padding. It is a boundary marker.

The Politics of Punjabi: Choosing a Literary Language

The Mahan Kosh was written in Punjabi and in the Gurmukhi script. This was itself a statement of considerable consequence in the late colonial period. Punjabi, and especially Punjabi in Gurmukhi, was associated by many educated elites with vernacular religion rather than high scholarship. Persian had been the administrative language of the Mughal courts; English was the language of colonial power and modern education; Sanskrit carried the prestige of classical Brahminical learning. To write a comprehensive scholarly encyclopedia in Punjabi was to assert that Punjabi was capable of the highest intellectual work.

Nabha's linguistic choice reinforced the theological content of his definitions. By rooting his encyclopedia in the language of Gurbani and of the Sikh community, he signaled that Sikh knowledge does not require external validation through another tradition's language. The Mahan Kosh did not need to be in Sanskrit to be rigorous. Punjabi, developed through the Gurmukhi script specifically to be the medium of the Guru's revelation, was the appropriate and sufficient language for explaining that revelation's vocabulary.

This choice also had practical consequences for accessibility. A Punjabi-literate Sikh who had never studied Sanskrit, Persian, or English could open the Mahan Kosh and encounter serious scholarship. The encyclopedia's audience was not a small elite of polyglot pandits. It was the broader Sikh community, and its Punjabi medium was both an intellectual argument and a democratic gesture — consistent with the Sikh theological principle that divine knowledge is available to all, not reserved for a learned caste.

Key Terms

  • ਸ਼ਬਦ (Shabad) — Divine word; the hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib understood as the living Guru and the sound-current of divine reality.
  • ਵਿਚਾਰ (Vichar) — Reflection, interpretation, or contemplation; in scholarly usage, the practice of deep engagement with Gurbani's meaning.
  • ਮੁਕਤੀ (Mukti) — Liberation or spiritual release; in Sikh theology, understood as loving union with the divine rather than dissolution into an impersonal absolute.
  • ਬਾਣੀ (Bani) — The divine speech of the Gurus and Bhagats; the compositions that constitute the Guru Granth Sahib.
  • ਸੰਗਤ (Sangat) — The sacred congregation; the community of Sikhs gathered in the Guru's presence, understood as spiritually transformative in itself.
  • ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ (Gurmukhi) — Literally "from the Guru's mouth"; the script in which Punjabi is written for Sikh sacred and scholarly purposes.

Discussion Questions

  1. How does the Sikh concept of Shabad complicate the common assumption that a dictionary is a secular, neutral document? What does it mean to define a sacred word within a tradition that treats language itself as divine?
  2. Nabha consistently distinguished Sikh usages of theological terms from those of neighboring traditions. Is this kind of boundary-drawing an act of intellectual honesty, or does it risk narrowing meanings that are genuinely shared across traditions? How should scholars navigate this tension?
  3. Nabha's choice to write the Mahan Kosh in Punjabi was as meaningful as its content. Can you think of a parallel case — in another tradition or context — where the choice of language for a major scholarly work carried theological or political weight?
  4. If you were to update the Mahan Kosh for a contemporary Sikh audience, which new terms or concepts would most urgently need definition, and why?

Further Reading

  • Pashaura Singh — The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority
  • W. H. McLeod — Textual Sources for the Study of Sikhism
  • Gurinder Singh Mann — The Making of Sikh Scripture

Key Takeaways

  • The Mahan Kosh is a theological document encoded in lexicographical form — every definition carries implicit doctrinal claims about Sikh distinctiveness and the nature of the divine.
  • Nabha's treatment of terms like ਮੁਕਤੀ and ਸ਼ਬਦ participates in a centuries-old tradition of Sikh interpretive scholarship (ਵਿਚਾਰ) while responding to the specific pressures of the colonial era.
  • The choice to write in Punjabi and Gurmukhi was itself a theological and political argument: Punjabi is sufficient for the highest scholarship, and Sikh knowledge does not require external linguistic validation.
  • Understanding the Mahan Kosh as a theological project helps students read it more carefully — not just as a reference tool but as an argument about what Sikhi fundamentally is.

Homework

Select any theological term from the Sikh tradition — such as ਨਾਮ (Naam), ਸੇਵਾ (Seva), ਹੁਕਮ (Hukam), or ਸੰਗਤ (Sangat) — and write a 400-word reflection on the hidden theological claims embedded in how that term is commonly defined or used. Consider what assumptions about God, community, and the human being are built into the word itself, and how a lexicographer like Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha might have approached defining it with precision.

lessons.title: Colonial Knowledge and Sikh Self-Representation
lessons.html:
Introduction

The nineteenth century was not only a period of political conquest in South Asia. It was also a period of epistemic conquest — a systematic project of describing, categorizing, and ultimately defining Asian traditions for global audiences, primarily through European scholarly and administrative frameworks. Sikhi was no exception. From the early surveys of British officers curious about Punjab's warrior communities to the ambitious philological projects of European orientalists, Sikhi was described, defined, and in many ways distorted through lenses shaped by entirely different intellectual traditions.

Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha worked in direct awareness of this situation. His scholarship was partly a response to it — an assertion that Sikhs would define their own tradition, in their own language, using their own standards of evidence and authority. This lecture examines the colonial knowledge context in which Nabha worked, the specific distortions he was contesting, and the model of indigenous scholarship he offered in their place. Understanding this context is essential for reading the Mahan Kosh and Ham Hindu Nahin as the historically situated, politically conscious documents they are.

Orientalism and Its Sikh Encounter

Edward Said's concept of orientalism — the systematic construction of "the East" as an object of Western knowledge and administration — has been applied productively to the study of South Asian religions. In the Sikh case, the orientalist encounter produced texts ranging from the militarily useful (surveys of Sikh fighting strength and organization) to the philologically ambitious (translations and analyses of Gurbani). What these projects shared was their primary audience: European readers, colonial administrators, and metropolitan scholarly communities, not Sikhs themselves.

Ernest Trumpp's 1877 translation of the Guru Granth Sahib is the most notorious example. Trumpp, a German linguist commissioned by the British India Office, produced a partial translation accompanied by dismissive commentary that characterized Gurbani as philosophically confused and spiritually incoherent. His linguistic competence in Punjabi was disputed by Sikh scholars even at the time, and his theological framework — rooted in Protestant Christian assumptions about what constitutes coherent monotheism — led him to misread passages that make perfect sense within the tradition's own categories. The translation caused deep offense in the Sikh community and became a touchstone for discussions about the dangers of external representation.

Less dramatically but more pervasively, administrative classifications and census categories shaped how Sikhs were counted, compared, and understood. The colonial census asked Sikhs to identify themselves in categories designed for a very different religious landscape — categories that often collapsed distinctions that mattered enormously within the tradition and created distinctions that meant little. Nabha's insistence on precise definition was partly a response to this administrative flattening.

The Sikh Scholar as Counter-Archivist

One way to understand Nabha's project is through the concept of counter-archiving — the practice of building an alternative repository of knowledge that contests the dominant archive's claims to comprehensiveness and authority. The colonial archive defined Sikhi from the outside, using sources selected by Europeans and organized according to European scholarly conventions. Nabha built an archive from the inside, using Gurbani, Sikh historical texts (ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ, ਜਨਮਸਾਖੀਆਂ), and the accumulated scholarship of the Sikh tradition as his primary sources.

This counter-archiving strategy is visible in the Mahan Kosh's citation practices. Where a European orientalist might cite Sanskrit parallel texts to explain a Sikh theological concept, Nabha consistently cited Gurbani itself and Sikh commentarial literature. This was not ignorance of Sanskrit or of comparative method — Nabha was a capable scholar across multiple traditions. It was a principled methodological choice: the tradition's own sources are the authoritative context for the tradition's own vocabulary.

Nabha also engaged directly with European scholarship when he judged it useful, but always on terms that maintained Sikh authority. He was aware of Macauliffe's work, of colonial dictionaries of Punjabi, and of the wider scholarly conversation about Sikh history and practice. His response was not rejection but transformation — taking what was useful from the colonial scholarly infrastructure while insisting that the framework of interpretation remain rooted in the tradition itself.

Self-Representation and Its Stakes

The stakes of self-representation were high in the colonial context. How a community was described in British administrative and scholarly literature affected how it was governed, how its institutions were treated legally, and how it was perceived by other communities in the competitive religious marketplace of colonial Punjab. The Singh Sabha movement understood this clearly: winning the argument about what Sikhi is was not only a spiritual matter but a political one.

Ham Hindu Nahin — Nabha's famous pamphlet — must be read in this light. The claim that Sikhs are not Hindus was necessary not only because certain Hindu-oriented religious practices had crept into Sikh institutions but because the colonial state and some Hindu political actors had an interest in classifying Sikhs as a Hindu sect. A sectarian classification carried specific legal, political, and social consequences. Nabha's tract was thus both a theological argument and a political intervention, and its precision was necessary precisely because the stakes were concrete.

Contemporary scholars of religion have increasingly recognized that the very categories used to define and compare religions — "Hinduism," "Sikhism," "Buddhism" — are partly colonial constructions. Nabha's work anticipates this insight, insisting on the specificity of Sikh identity against the homogenizing pressures of both colonial classification and Hindu nationalist incorporation.

Key Terms

  • ਪੂਰਬੀ ਵਿਦਵਤਾ (Orientalism) — The systematic European scholarly project of describing and categorizing Asian traditions, often with distortions rooted in European assumptions.
  • ਜਨਮਸਾਖੀਆਂ (Janamsakhian) — Hagiographic narratives of the life of Guru Nanak; a major genre of early Sikh literature used as historical and theological sources.
  • ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ (Gurbilash) — A genre of Sikh historical-devotional literature celebrating the life and deeds of the Gurus.
  • Counter-archiving — The scholarly strategy of building an alternative knowledge repository that contests the dominant archive's authority and comprehensiveness.
  • ਸਿੱਖ ਮਤ (Sikh Mat) — The Sikh way, path, or doctrinal position; used by Nabha to signal specifically Sikh meanings of shared terms.

Discussion Questions

  1. How does knowing about the Trumpp translation and the colonial knowledge context change how you read the Mahan Kosh? Does it make Nabha's scholarly choices seem more urgent, more political, or both?
  2. Is the concept of "counter-archiving" a useful frame for understanding Nabha's project, or does it risk reducing his scholarship to a reaction against colonialism rather than a positive intellectual achievement in its own right?
  3. Contemporary scholars argue that categories like "Hinduism" and "Sikhism" are partly colonial constructions. If that is true, what does it mean for Nabha's insistence in Ham Hindu Nahin that Sikhs are distinct? Was he resisting colonialism or inadvertently reinforcing its categories?
  4. Who gets to define a religious tradition — insiders, outsiders, or some combination? What criteria should determine whose definition carries more weight?

Further Reading

  • Harjot Oberoi — The Construction of Religious Boundaries: Culture, Identity and Diversity in the Sikh Tradition
  • Tony Ballantyne — Between Colonialism and Diaspora: Sikh Cultural Formations in an Imperial World
  • Arvind-Pal Singh Mandair — Religion and the Specter of the West: Sikhism, India, Postcoloniality and the Politics of Translation

Key Takeaways

  • Colonial-era European scholarship on Sikhism — most notoriously Trumpp's translation — demonstrated the dangers of external representation and made indigenous scholarly self-definition an urgent priority.
  • Nabha functioned as a counter-archivist, building an alternative knowledge repository rooted in Gurbani and Sikh tradition rather than European orientalist frameworks.
  • Ham Hindu Nahin was not only a spiritual argument but a political one, with concrete consequences for how Sikhs were classified and governed under colonial administration.
  • The debate about who defines a religious tradition — insiders or outsiders, indigenous scholars or colonial experts — remains live in Sikh studies today and connects directly to Nabha's foundational choices.

Homework

Research one colonial-era orientalist scholar who wrote about Sikhism — figures such as J. D. Cunningham, Ernest Trumpp, or Max Arthur Macauliffe are good starting points. Write a 450-word analysis of how that scholar's background, assumptions, and institutional context shaped what they chose to study and how they described it. Then write one paragraph reflecting on how Nabha's work offered an alternative model of knowledge production.

lessons.title: Nabha in Global Context: Comparative Lexicography and Religious Reform
lessons.html:
Introduction

Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's project was distinctive in many ways, but it was not unique in human history. Across traditions and centuries, major moments of religious reform have been accompanied by major acts of textual and lexicographical scholarship. Reformers who want to return a tradition to what they regard as its authentic foundations need to establish what those foundations are — and that requires the careful, rigorous work of defining terms, establishing authoritative sources, and clearing away accumulated distortion. Nabha belongs to a global family of scholar-reformers whose intellectual labor was inseparable from their religious commitment.

This lecture situates Nabha's work in global comparative context. We will examine parallel cases from other traditions — the role of lexicography and textual scholarship in the Protestant Reformation, in Islamic reform movements, and in Buddhist modernism — to illuminate what is distinctive about Nabha's project and what connects it to wider patterns in the history of religious scholarship. Understanding these parallels deepens appreciation for the Mahan Kosh as a world-historical achievement, not merely a regional one.

Lexicography and Reform: A Global Pattern

The Protestant Reformation in sixteenth-century Europe is the most frequently cited case of religious reform driven by textual scholarship. Martin Luther's insistence on returning to scripture (Sola Scriptura) required that scripture be accessible in vernacular languages, accurately translated, and interpreted according to principles transparent to literate laypeople rather than reserved for clerical specialists. Luther's translation of the Bible into German was not only a religious act but a linguistic one — it shaped the modern German language and established a precedent for vernacular sacred texts across European Christianity.

The parallel with Nabha is instructive but imperfect. Both Luther and Nabha insisted on the primacy of the tradition's founding texts over the accumulated weight of institutional interpretation. Both used vernacular language as a democratizing tool. But where Luther was arguing against an institution — the Catholic Church — Nabha was arguing against a diffuse pattern of syncretic drift and colonial misrepresentation rather than against a single rival authority. The Sikh tradition had no equivalent of the papacy to contest; the challenge was more like clearing fog than demolishing a wall.

Islamic reform traditions offer a different kind of parallel. Movements that called for a return to the Quran and the authenticated sayings of the Prophet (hadith), such as the Salafi and Wahhabi currents of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, similarly emphasized precise textual definition and the rejection of practices they regarded as innovations (bid'ah) without foundation in primary sources. The methodological similarity to Singh Sabha scholarship is striking: in both cases, reformers used philological rigor as a religious argument.

Buddhist Modernism and the Scholar-Reformer

Buddhist modernism in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries provides perhaps the closest structural parallel to Nabha's situation. Figures like Anagarika Dharmapala in Sri Lanka and Ledi Sayadaw in Burma were working in colonial contexts, responding to Christian missionary pressure and colonial administrative classification, and deploying textual scholarship as a tool for asserting Buddhist distinctiveness and vitality. Like Nabha, they were simultaneously scholars and activists. Like Nabha, they wrote for popular as well as learned audiences. Like Nabha, they faced the challenge of defining their tradition's identity against both internal drift and external misrepresentation.

The Buddhist modernist case also highlights a risk that Nabha navigated carefully: the risk that reform-driven scholarship simplifies a tradition's actual diversity in the name of authenticity. By insisting on a single authoritative reading of primary texts, reform movements can marginalize legitimate internal variation. Scholars of Buddhist modernism have noted that some reformers presented a streamlined, doctrinally tidy version of Buddhism that did not fully represent the tradition's historical complexity. Nabha was careful to document diversity within the Sikh tradition — the Mahan Kosh's comprehensiveness was partly a safeguard against this simplifying tendency.

What Makes Nabha Distinctive

Comparative context illuminates what is genuinely distinctive about Nabha's achievement. First, the scale of the Mahan Kosh is exceptional. Luther's scholarly apparatus, and even the great Islamic and Buddhist lexicographical traditions, were built up over generations and institutions. Nabha produced his encyclopedia largely through individual scholarly effort, a feat that contemporaries recognized as remarkable and that subsequent scholars have struggled to adequately credit.

Second, Nabha's project was distinctive in its integration of multiple genres and purposes. The Mahan Kosh is simultaneously a linguistic dictionary, a theological reference, a historical encyclopedia, and a polemic for Sikh distinctiveness. Most comparable projects separate these functions. Nabha fused them, producing a text that is harder to classify than Luther's Bible translation or a Salafi hadith collection precisely because it does more things at once.

Third, Nabha worked within a tradition that places unusual weight on the relationship between language and the divine — the concept of ਸ਼ਬਦ (Shabad) as the living Guru means that defining words is not merely an academic exercise but a spiritual one. This theological grounding of the lexicographical project gives the Mahan Kosh a depth of religious seriousness that distinguishes it from parallel encyclopedic projects in traditions where language and the sacred are understood differently.

Key Terms

  • ਵਰਨਾਕੂਲਰ (Vernacular) — The everyday language of a community, as opposed to a classical or prestige language; in reform movements, vernacular texts democratize access to sacred knowledge.
  • Buddhist Modernism — A global movement of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries that reinterpreted Buddhism in dialogue with Western science, colonialism, and modernity.
  • Bid'ah (ਬਿਦਅਤ) — Islamic term for innovation without foundation in primary sources; parallel to the Singh Sabha critique of practices without Gurbani basis.
  • Sola Scriptura — Protestant Reformation principle that scripture alone (not tradition or institutional authority) is the supreme standard for doctrine.
  • ਮੂਲ ਸਰੋਤ (Mul Srot) — Primary sources; the original founding texts of a tradition used as the authoritative basis for reform arguments.

Discussion Questions

  1. Which parallel — Luther's Reformation, Islamic reform movements, or Buddhist modernism — do you find most illuminating for understanding Nabha's project, and why? What does your choice reveal about how you understand the Mahan Kosh?
  2. Reform movements that return to primary texts often claim to recover an authentic original practice. Is this claim credible, or is every "return to origins" actually a creative construction? How should students of religion think about this tension?
  3. Comparative lexicography reveals that major religious reform movements consistently produce major scholarly reference works. What does this pattern suggest about the relationship between intellectual labor and religious change?
  4. Nabha's Mahan Kosh is more comprehensive and multi-purpose than most parallel reform-era reference works. Does its complexity make it more or less useful as a reform tool? Explain your reasoning.

Further Reading

  • David McMahan — The Making of Buddhist Modernism
  • Euan Cameron — The European Reformation
  • John Voll — Islam: Continuity and Change in the Modern World

Key Takeaways

  • Nabha belongs to a global pattern of scholar-reformers across traditions who used lexicography and textual scholarship as instruments of religious revival and self-definition.
  • Parallels with the Protestant Reformation, Islamic reform movements, and Buddhist modernism reveal shared structures while also highlighting what is distinctive about the Sikh case.
  • Nabha's integration of multiple scholarly purposes — linguistic, theological, historical, polemical — in a single encyclopedic work is exceptional even by global comparative standards.
  • The Sikh theology of Shabad gives Nabha's lexicographical project a spiritual grounding that distinguishes it from parallel reform-era reference works in other traditions.

Homework

Research one major religious reform movement from outside the Sikh tradition — possibilities include the Protestant Reformation's engagement with vernacular Bible translation, the Islamic Salafi movement's return to primary texts, or the Buddhist modernism of figures like Anagarika Dharmapala. Write a 450-word comparative essay examining one parallel between that movement's use of textual scholarship and what Nabha and the Singh Sabha movement accomplished. Be specific about similarities and differences.

lessons.title: Reading the Mahan Kosh Today: Methods for Advanced Students
lessons.html:
Introduction

A great reference work is not static. It enters into dialogue with every reader who consults it, every scholar who cites it, and every generation that brings new questions to its pages. The Mahan Kosh has been in continuous use for over a century, and the history of its reception — how it has been read, cited, contested, and updated — is itself a significant chapter in the history of Sikh scholarship. For advanced students who want to engage with this text seriously, understanding how to read it critically and productively is as important as knowing what it contains.

This lecture offers a methodological guide to reading the Mahan Kosh as an advanced student of Sikh studies. We will examine strategies for critical engagement, discuss the text's acknowledged limitations, survey the scholarly conversation about its strengths and gaps, and consider what a twenty-first century reader needs to bring to the text in order to use it well. This is, in some respects, the most practically demanding lesson in the course — but it is also the one that will most directly equip students for original work in Sikh studies.

Strengths and Acknowledged Limitations

Any serious reader of the Mahan Kosh must begin with an honest assessment of what it does and does not do. Its strengths are well-documented and substantial. The depth of Nabha's Gurbani knowledge is extraordinary — his citations are reliable, his feel for linguistic nuance is acute, and his organizational scheme allows comparisons across terms and traditions that would otherwise require consulting many separate sources. For any serious student of Gurbani vocabulary, it remains the starting point for definitional questions that no subsequent work has fully superseded.

Its limitations are also real and worth naming clearly. The Mahan Kosh reflects the scholarly resources available to one scholar working in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Some historical claims have been revised by subsequent research. Nabha's perspective, shaped by the reformist Singh Sabha agenda, means that certain internal Sikh traditions are handled with less sympathy than others — traditions he associated with later accretions or with syncretic drift receive less favorable treatment than those he associated with the Gurus' original intention. Readers should be alert to this editorial positioning without dismissing the work's overall achievement.

There is also the linguistic dimension: the Mahan Kosh is written in a formal register of Punjabi that can be demanding even for native speakers unfamiliar with its classical vocabulary. Students who are learning Punjabi or who are working primarily in English will find it necessary to use the Mahan Kosh in conjunction with secondary scholarship and translations. This is not a flaw but a feature of any major classical reference work — it rewards sustained engagement and linguistic investment.

Methods for Critical Engagement

Critical engagement with the Mahan Kosh requires attending to several layers simultaneously. The first layer is the linguistic layer: what is the entry's etymology, what are its cognates in related languages, and how does Nabha trace its semantic development? This layer is where his philological expertise is most directly on display, and it is generally his most reliable contribution.

The second layer is the theological layer: how does Nabha position a given term's Sikh meaning relative to its usage in other traditions? Here the reader should ask: Is Nabha making a descriptive claim (this is how Sikhs have historically used this word) or a prescriptive one (this is how Sikhs should use this word)? The distinction matters for how much weight to give his definition in a research context. Nabha is generally honest about this distinction, but it requires careful reading to track.

The third layer is the historical layer: what events, figures, and texts does Nabha cite as context for his definitions? Here students should cross-reference with subsequent historical scholarship. In some cases — particularly around the history of Sikh institutions and the Guru period — later archival and manuscript research has added nuance or corrected details that Nabha could not have had access to. Using the Mahan Kosh alongside texts like Ganda Singh's historical studies or Pashaura Singh's work on the Guru Granth Sahib allows students to triangulate between Nabha's foundational account and subsequent scholarship.

The Mahan Kosh in Contemporary Sikh Studies

Contemporary Sikh studies is a genuinely interdisciplinary field, drawing on history, religious studies, linguistic anthropology, postcolonial theory, and diaspora studies. The Mahan Kosh occupies an interesting position within this expanded field: it is treated simultaneously as a primary source (evidence of how a major nineteenth-century Sikh scholar understood his tradition) and as a reference work (a reliable guide to Sikh vocabulary and concepts). Advanced students need to keep both of these functions in view.

When scholars like Gurinder Singh Mann, Pashaura Singh, or Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh cite the Mahan Kosh, they are often using it as an authoritative guide to Punjabi terminology. But they are also aware that Nabha's definitions carry the imprint of his historical moment and his reform agenda. Reading the Mahan Kosh critically means being able to use it as a reference tool while also asking, when a definition seems to do particular theological work: whose Sikhi is being defined here, and for what purpose?

The digital availability of portions of the Mahan Kosh has opened new possibilities for students who previously could not access a physical copy. Online databases and Gurmukhi digital resources are making it possible to search the text in ways that Nabha could never have anticipated. This technological shift is changing how the text is used — enabling keyword searches, cross-referencing at scale, and integration with other digital Sikh studies resources. Students of the current generation are positioned to use the Mahan Kosh in genuinely new ways, and this methodological lecture aims to equip them to do so rigorously.

Key Terms

  • ਵਿਉਤਪਤੀ (Viotpati / Etymology) — The origin and historical development of a word; the foundational method of lexicography.
  • Primary source — An original document or text from the period under study; the Mahan Kosh functions both as a reference work and as a primary source for Singh Sabha intellectual history.
  • Prescriptive vs. descriptive — A key distinction in lexicography: descriptive definitions record how words are actually used; prescriptive definitions argue for how they should be used.
  • ਪ੍ਰਮਾਣਿਕਤਾ (Pramanikta) — Authenticity or authority; a central concern in both the Mahan Kosh's methodology and in contemporary Sikh studies debates.
  • Intertextuality — The web of connections between texts; reading the Mahan Kosh intertextually means tracing how its entries connect to Gurbani, historical literature, and subsequent scholarship.

Discussion Questions

  1. How should a student balance using the Mahan Kosh as a reliable reference tool while also reading it critically as a product of a particular historical moment and scholarly agenda? Is this balance achievable, or does it require constantly switching between two modes of reading?
  2. The Mahan Kosh is both a primary source and a reference work. Can you think of other scholarly texts that occupy this double status? What methodological challenges does this dual nature create?
  3. Digital access is changing how students use the Mahan Kosh, enabling searches and cross-references that were previously impossible. Does digital access change what questions can be asked of the text, or only how efficiently existing questions can be answered?
  4. If you were to write a supplement or companion to the Mahan Kosh for the twenty-first century, what kind of editorial framework would you bring? Which of Nabha's methodological choices would you retain, and which would you revise?

Further Reading

  • Gurinder Singh Mann — Sikhism (Prentice Hall)
  • Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh — The Name of My Beloved: Verses of the Sikh Gurus
  • Pashaura Singh and Louis E. Fenech (eds.) — The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies

Key Takeaways

  • The Mahan Kosh rewards critical reading on three simultaneous layers: linguistic, theological, and historical — each requiring different background knowledge and cross-referencing strategies.
  • Nabha's reform agenda shaped his editorial choices in ways that advanced students must recognize without allowing that recognition to diminish the work's extraordinary achievement.
  • The Mahan Kosh functions simultaneously as a reference tool and as a primary source for Singh Sabha intellectual history — and good scholarship requires keeping both functions in view.
  • Digital access is creating new possibilities for engagement with the Mahan Kosh, and the current generation of students is positioned to use it in ways that Nabha could not have anticipated.

Homework

Using any available access to the Mahan Kosh — a physical copy, a digital scan, or secondary scholarship that quotes from it extensively — select one entry or concept and trace how it has been used, cited, or interpreted in at least two pieces of subsequent Sikh scholarship. Write a 500-word methodological reflection: What does following a single term through the scholarly literature reveal about how the Mahan Kosh has shaped the questions Sikh studies asks?
