lessons.title: What a Teeka Is and Why One Was Needed
lessons.summary: Defines the teeka as a genre and explains why a complete commentary on Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji became necessary.
lessons.html:
Full course contents
  1. What a Teeka Is and Why One Was Needed
  2. The Story of the Faridkot Teeka and Its Patronage
  3. The Nirmala Method and Braj Bhasha
  4. Strengths and Limits of the Faridkot Teeka
  5. Revision, Publication, and Lasting Influence
  6. Using the Faridkot Teeka as a Modern Student

What is a teeka?

A ਟੀਕਾ (commentary) is a traditional, line-by-line explanation of a sacred text. Across Indian scholarship, a teeka takes a verse, gives the meaning of difficult words, and then explains the fuller sense. For Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, a teeka helps a reader understand ਬਾਣੀ (the sacred word) when the language, imagery, or context is not obvious.

Why was one needed?

The language of Gurbani draws on many tongues and poetic forms, and over time fewer readers could follow every word without help. A complete written commentary made the meaning of the whole scripture available in one consistent work, rather than relying only on oral teaching passed within a ਸੰਪਰਦਾਇ (teaching tradition). Scholars note that the demand for accessible scriptural understanding grew in the nineteenth century (Pashaura Singh and Fenech 2014).

The shape of a teeka

  • It often gives ਪਦ ਅਰਥ (word-by-word meaning) first.
  • It then offers a fuller ਵਿਆਖਿਆ (explanation) of the passage.
  • It aims at a single, readable ਅਰਥ (meaning) for each line.

This course studies the Faridkot Teeka, widely regarded as the first complete traditional commentary on the whole of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji (Pashaura Singh and Fenech 2014).

Pashaura Singh and Louis E. Fenech, eds., The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies (Oxford, 2014).

Homework

Select any single shabad from Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji that you find personally meaningful. Without consulting any commentary, write 300–400 words explaining what the shabad means to you based on your own understanding. Then reflect in 2–3 sentences on what questions remain unanswered for you — questions a teeka might help resolve. This exercise prepares you to appreciate what traditional commentary actually offers.

lessons.title: The Story of the Faridkot Teeka and Its Patronage
lessons.summary: Tells how the Faridkot Teeka came to be written, who wrote it, and the royal patronage behind it.
lessons.html:
The author

The Faridkot Wala Teeka (ਫ਼ਰੀਦਕੋਟ ਵਾਲਾ ਟੀਕਾ) was written by Sant Giani Badan Singh of Dera Sekhwan. He worked within a classical scholarly Sikh tradition and produced a ਟੀਕਾ (commentary) covering the whole of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji.

The patron

The work was written at the request and encouragement of Maharaja Bikram Singh of Faridkot. Such royal patronage gave the author the time and support needed for so large a task. The commentary took about six and a half years and was completed in 1883 (Pashaura Singh and Fenech 2014).

A timeline

EventDate
Commentary completed by Giani Badan Singh1883
First edition published (Wazir Hind Press, Amritsar)1906

Why patronage mattered

The Sikh kingdoms and chiefships of Punjab often supported religious scholarship, and the involvement of the Faridkot court placed this commentary within that wider pattern of princely support for Sikh learning (Grewal 1998).

  • The patron set the task and supported the author.
  • The author gave years of careful work to the whole scripture.
  • The result was a single complete commentary, not a partial one.
Pashaura Singh and Louis E. Fenech, eds., The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies (Oxford, 2014); J. S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab (Cambridge, 1998).

Homework

Research the life and patronage of Raja Bikram Singh of Faridkot using any reliable historical source (books, academic articles, or reputable Sikh historical websites). Write a 400-word profile focusing on his relationship to Sikh scholarship and what motivated his support for the teeka project. Conclude with one paragraph reflecting on the role of wealthy patrons in preserving religious knowledge across traditions.

lessons.title: The Nirmala Method and Braj Bhasha
lessons.summary: Explains the Nirmala tradition of exegesis and the Braj Bhasha mixed with Punjabi in which the teeka is written.
lessons.html:
A Nirmala-tradition work

The Faridkot Teeka is a classical exegesis in the manner of the ਨਿਰਮਲਾ (a scholarly Sikh order). This tradition was known for its training in Sanskrit learning and its careful methods of reading scripture. Its scholars handed down a ਸੰਪਰਦਾਇ (teaching tradition) of how to explain bani (Pashaura Singh and Fenech 2014).

The language of the commentary

The commentary is written largely in Braj Bhasha mixed with Punjabi. Braj was a respected literary language for religious and poetic writing in north India, so using it placed the teeka within an established scholarly style. The body explains Gurbani written in ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ (the script of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji).

How the method works

  • It treats the text line by line, giving an ਅਰਥ (meaning) for each.
  • It draws on the wider Indian commentarial style familiar to its tradition.
  • It offers a long, continuous ਵਿਆਖਿਆ (explanation) across several thousand pages.

Scale of the work

Because it covers the entire scripture in this detailed manner, the teeka runs to several thousand pages. This scale was part of what made it a landmark: a complete reading of the whole text in one tradition's voice.

Pashaura Singh and Louis E. Fenech, eds., The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies (Oxford, 2014).

Homework

Find one example of a Nirmala scholar or a Braj Bhasha text from Sikh history (other than the Faridkot Teeka itself). Write 300 words describing who the author was, what they wrote, and why the Nirmala tradition valued classical Sanskrit-adjacent learning. Reflect briefly on how this linguistic approach shaped how Sikhi was explained to educated audiences of that era.

lessons.title: Strengths and Limits of the Faridkot Teeka
lessons.summary: Weighs the strengths of the teeka and notes, neutrally, the points where later scholars read differently.
lessons.html:
Strengths

The Faridkot Teeka was the first to give a complete ਟੀਕਾ (commentary) on the whole of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. For the first time, readers had a single consistent explanation of the entire scripture. Its careful, line-by-line method made the ਅਰਥ (meaning) of each passage available in writing.

  • It was complete, covering the whole text.
  • It was rooted in a trained scholarly ਸੰਪਰਦਾਇ (teaching tradition).
  • It set a model others could follow.

Limits

Every commentary reflects the time and tradition in which it was written. Because the Faridkot Teeka uses the Nirmala style and Braj Bhasha, some of its readings carry that tradition's assumptions. Later scholars, working with different methods, sometimes reached different conclusions.

Where later scholars differed

For example, Professor Sahib Singh, in his later work Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan, would differ on some readings, approaching the text through grammar and a close study of Gurbani's own language (Sahib Singh). These differences are part of normal scholarly study; stated neutrally, they show that interpretation can develop over time without any one work replacing the value of another.

  • A teeka is a guide, not the final word.
  • Different methods can yield different ਵਿਆਖਿਆ (explanation).
  • Comparing works deepens understanding.
Sahib Singh, Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan (Jalandhar); Pashaura Singh and Louis E. Fenech, eds., The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies (Oxford, 2014).

Homework

Choose one shabad from Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji that deals with a concept you find complex — such as the nature of the Divine, the state of the liberated soul, or the relationship between the Guru and the disciple. Read it in its original Gurmukhi without any commentary. Then write 400 words honestly identifying where you felt confident in your understanding and where you felt uncertainty. This exercise grounds the theoretical discussion of the teeka's strengths and limits in your own reading experience.

lessons.title: Revision, Publication, and Lasting Influence
lessons.summary: Covers the synod that revised the teeka, its 1906 publication, and its role as a model for later commentary.
lessons.html:
Revision by a synod

After Giani Badan Singh completed the commentary, it was later revised by a synod of Sikh scholars. This synod was chaired by Mahant Sumer Singh of Patna Sahib. The revision prepared the large work for wider use and publication (Pashaura Singh and Fenech 2014).

Publication

The first edition was published in 1906, funded by Maharaja Balbir Singh of Faridkot, and printed at the Wazir Hind Press in Amritsar. Printing made the teeka available far beyond a single dera or court.

StageDetailDate
Written and completedBy Giani Badan Singh, about six and a half years of work1883
RevisedSynod chaired by Mahant Sumer Singh of Patna Sahibbefore publication
PublishedFunded by Maharaja Balbir Singh; Wazir Hind Press, Amritsar1906

Lasting influence

The Faridkot Teeka became a prototype and model for later teekas. Commentators who followed could build on, respond to, or differ from it, but they worked in a field it had helped to open. Its influence shows how one complete ਟੀਕਾ (commentary) can shape a whole tradition of reading ਬਾਣੀ (the sacred word).

Pashaura Singh and Louis E. Fenech, eds., The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies (Oxford, 2014).

Homework

Locate a secondary source — an academic article, book chapter, or encyclopedia entry — that discusses the publication history of Sikh religious texts in the 19th or early 20th century. Write a 350-word summary of what you find, connecting it to what you have learned about the Faridkot Teeka's own journey from manuscript to print. Note any parallels or contrasts with how other major religious traditions have managed the publication of their canonical commentaries.

lessons.title: Using the Faridkot Teeka as a Modern Student
lessons.summary: Shows how a modern reader uses this classical commentary carefully and alongside later works.
lessons.html:
Read it as a window into a tradition

A modern student can read the Faridkot Teeka to hear how a trained ਨਿਰਮਲਾ (scholarly Sikh order) explained Gurbani in the nineteenth century. Its ਅਰਥ (meaning) for each line shows one careful tradition's understanding.

Read it carefully

  • Remember it is written in Braj Bhasha mixed with Punjabi, so some words need patience.
  • Treat its readings as informed guidance, not as the only possible ਵਿਆਖਿਆ (explanation).
  • Stay reverent toward ਬਾਣੀ (the sacred word) itself, which the commentary serves.

Read it alongside other works

A good practice is to compare the Faridkot Teeka with later commentaries, such as Professor Sahib Singh's Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan, noting where they agree and where they differ (Sahib Singh). Comparing helps a student see why a reading is given, not just what it is.

A simple method

  • Read the line of bani in ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ (the script of the scripture) first.
  • Check the ਪਦ ਅਰਥ (word-by-word meaning).
  • Read the fuller explanation, then compare with another teeka.

Used this way, the Faridkot Teeka remains a valuable companion for study, honoring both its historical importance and the ongoing growth of understanding (Pashaura Singh and Fenech 2014).

Sahib Singh, Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan (Jalandhar); Pashaura Singh and Louis E. Fenech, eds., The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies (Oxford, 2014).

Homework

Spend one study session (at least 45 minutes) actually opening the Faridkot Teeka — either a physical copy, a scanned PDF from SikhiToTheMax or a Punjabi university digital archive, or a reputable online rendering. Select any one page or passage and read it slowly. Write 300–400 words describing the experience: What did you understand easily? What was difficult? What tools or knowledge would have helped? How does the experience compare to your expectations from this course?

lessons.title: The Language of the Teeka: Braj Bhasha, Sanskrit Roots, and the Question of Access
lessons.html:
Introduction

Every act of interpretation is also an act of translation — not merely between languages, but between worlds of meaning. The Faridkot Teeka was composed primarily in Braj Bhasha, a literary language of North India with deep roots in Sanskrit-influenced poetic tradition. For the Nirmala scholars who undertook this monumental project, Braj Bhasha was not an arbitrary choice. It represented the most prestigious vehicle for philosophical and devotional commentary available to them in the late nineteenth century. Understanding why they chose this medium, and what that choice cost in terms of accessibility, is essential to evaluating the teeka on its own terms.

This lecture examines the linguistic architecture of the Faridkot Teeka in detail. We will explore the relationship between Braj Bhasha and Sanskrit, consider how the teeka handles the multilingual reality of Gurbani itself — which draws on Punjabi, Sant Bhasha, Persian, Arabic, and Sanskrit registers — and reflect on the ongoing scholarly debate about whether the teeka's language empowered or restricted the community it was meant to serve. By the end of this lecture, students will have a nuanced appreciation of how language choices in religious commentary are never neutral.

Braj Bhasha as a Scholarly Medium

Braj Bhasha emerged as a major literary language in North India roughly between the fourteenth and eighteenth centuries. It was the language of the Bhakti poets, of Tulsidas and Surdas, and it carried enormous cultural prestige precisely because of its associations with devotional poetry and Sanskrit learning. For educated audiences in the nineteenth century — the pandits, the aristocracy, and the clergy of multiple traditions — Braj Bhasha signaled seriousness and scholarship. A commentary written in colloquial Punjabi might have been understood by more people, but it would not have commanded the same intellectual respect in the circles where the teeka was meant to circulate.

The Nirmala scholars who formed the backbone of the Faridkot project were trained in this tradition. Their education involved close study of Sanskrit grammatical texts, Vedantic philosophy, and classical Braj poetry. When they sat down to explain a shabad, they naturally reached for the conceptual vocabulary and syntactic patterns they had spent years mastering. The result is a commentary that reads, in places, almost like a Sanskrit philosophical treatise that happens to be written in Braj Bhasha — dense with compound constructions, technical philosophical terms, and allusions to classical Indian thought.

This was both a strength and a limitation. On one hand, it meant that the teeka could engage seriously with the philosophical depth of Gurbani, using established Sanskrit categories to articulate concepts that might otherwise resist precise definition. On the other hand, it created a significant barrier for the ordinary Sikh of the Punjab, for whom Braj Bhasha was not a native language and whose education did not include Sanskrit philosophy. The teeka was, in a real sense, written for scholars by scholars.

Modern researchers who work with the text often note that reading it fluently requires simultaneous competence in Braj Bhasha grammar, Sanskrit philosophical vocabulary, and Gurmukhi script — a combination that is exceedingly rare today, and was not common even in the nineteenth century outside specialist circles.

The Multilingual Reality of Gurbani

One of the most intellectually demanding aspects of writing any commentary on Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji is confronting its extraordinary linguistic diversity. The Gurus composed in what scholars sometimes call Sant Bhasha — a fluid, literary language drawing on Punjabi, Hindi dialects, and Persian/Arabic loanwords — but they also incorporated words and entire phrases from Sanskrit, Prakrit, Sindhi, and regional dialects. The Bhagats whose compositions are included in SGGS wrote in their own regional languages: Kabir Ji's Purbi-inflected vernacular, Namdev Ji's Marathi-influenced Sant Bhasha, Farid Ji's Punjabi with Persian undertones. The linguistic landscape is genuinely vast.

The Faridkot Teeka navigates this complexity by treating Braj Bhasha as a unifying metalanguage — a consistent medium through which all of these diverse linguistic strands can be explained and harmonized. When the teeka encounters a Persian or Arabic term in Gurbani, it typically renders an explanation in Braj Bhasha that draws on Sanskrit philosophical equivalents. This has the effect of systematizing Gurbani within a broadly Sanskrit-inflected worldview, which some later scholars have argued distorts the more pluralistic and vernacular spirit of the original compositions.

This is not a trivial criticism. When Bhagat Kabir Ji uses an image drawn from the weaver's craft, or when Guru Nanak Dev Ji employs a term from Sufi devotional vocabulary, these are not accidents. They are deliberate choices that carry specific cultural and spiritual resonances. A commentary that translates these terms into Sanskrit philosophical equivalents risks smoothing over precisely the creative friction that gives Gurbani its distinctive power. The Faridkot scholars were aware of this tension, and they handled it with varying degrees of success across the many thousands of pages of the teeka.

Later commentators — particularly those writing in the twentieth century in simple Punjabi — often positioned their work explicitly as a correction to this aspect of the Faridkot approach, arguing that Gurbani's meanings are better served by staying close to the vernacular spirit of the original.

Key Terms

  • ਬ੍ਰਜ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ (Braj Bhasha) — a classical North Indian literary language with Sanskrit influence, used as the primary medium of the Faridkot Teeka
  • ਸੰਤ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ (Sant Bhasha) — the fluid devotional vernacular used by the Bhakti and Sikh poet-saints, blending regional languages
  • ਟੀਕਾ (Teeka) — a traditional commentary that explains a sacred text word by word or verse by verse
  • ਮੇਟਾ-ਲੈਂਗੁਏਜ (metalanguage) — a language used to describe or explain another language; here, Braj Bhasha serves this function for the multilingual Gurbani
  • ਭਗਤ ਬਾਣੀ (Bhagat Bani) — the compositions of the Bhakti saints included in SGGS, written in various regional languages and dialects

Discussion Questions

  1. The Nirmala scholars chose Braj Bhasha over colloquial Punjabi for this commentary. What does this choice reveal about their intended audience and their understanding of scholarly authority? Is there a parallel in other religious traditions where elite languages have been used for sacred commentary?
  2. When a commentary translates Persian Sufi terms from Gurbani into Sanskrit philosophical equivalents, does it explain the text or transform it? Where do you think the line between clarification and distortion lies?
  3. Given that Gurbani is itself multilingual and draws from diverse cultural traditions, what would an ideal commentary language look like? Is there any single language adequate to the task?
  4. The teeka was accessible primarily to educated scholars rather than ordinary Sikhs. How does this affect how we evaluate it as a work of religious service versus scholarly production?

Further Reading

Gurinder Singh Mann, The Making of Sikh Scripture

Harjot Oberoi, The Construction of Religious Boundaries: Culture, Identity and Diversity in the Sikh Tradition

Pashaura Singh, The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority

Key Takeaways

  • Braj Bhasha was chosen for the Faridkot Teeka because it carried scholarly prestige and suited the Nirmala educational tradition, not because it was widely accessible.
  • Gurbani's own multilingual texture — drawing on Punjabi, Persian, Arabic, Sanskrit, and regional dialects — poses a fundamental challenge for any single-language commentary.
  • Using Sanskrit philosophical categories to explain Gurbani terms risks both clarifying and subtly distorting the original meanings, a tension that later commentators explicitly addressed.
  • The language of a commentary is never neutral: it encodes assumptions about audience, authority, and the nature of the text being explained.

Homework

Take any one shabad from Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji that you know contains words from a non-Punjabi source — for example, a Persian/Arabic term or a Sanskrit compound. Write 350 words identifying the non-Punjabi element, what you think it means in its original cultural context, and how that meaning relates to the spiritual teaching of the shabad. Do not consult the Faridkot Teeka for this exercise; rely on your own research and reflection. The goal is to feel the linguistic challenge firsthand before studying how the teeka addresses it.

lessons.title: Vedantic Frameworks in the Teeka: Interpreting Sikh Theology Through Classical Indian Categories
lessons.html:
Introduction

One of the most debated aspects of the Faridkot Teeka is its consistent use of Vedantic philosophical categories to interpret Gurbani. The Nirmala scholars who authored the commentary were deeply trained in Advaita Vedanta — the non-dualistic philosophy associated with Adi Shankaracharya — and they drew on its conceptual framework extensively when explaining the theology of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. Terms like Brahman, Maya, Atman, and Moksha appear throughout the teeka as interpretive lenses through which the teachings of the Gurus are filtered.

This is not a peripheral feature of the commentary — it shapes the teeka's entire theological architecture. For some scholars, this Vedantic framing represents the Nirmala tradition at its most intellectually sophisticated: bridging Sikh Gurbani and classical Indian philosophy to demonstrate the universal depth of the Guru's teachings. For others, it represents a fundamental misreading that obscures the distinctly Sikh theological contribution of the Gurus, which departed in significant ways from Vedantic premises. This lecture explores this debate with care, examining specific conceptual areas where the Vedantic and Sikh frameworks align, where they diverge, and what is gained or lost when one is used to explain the other.

Advaita Vedanta and Its Core Claims

Advaita Vedanta, as systematized by Shankaracharya in the eighth century CE, rests on the claim that ultimate reality is a single, undivided consciousness — Brahman — and that the apparent multiplicity of the world is the product of Maya, a kind of cosmic illusion or superimposition. The individual self (Jiva) is ultimately identical with Brahman; the experience of separation is itself the fundamental ignorance (Avidya) from which liberation (Moksha) consists in awakening. In this system, devotion (Bhakti) is typically treated as a lower rung on the ladder toward the highest non-dual realization.

The Nirmala scholars found much in Gurbani that seemed compatible with this framework. Gurbani does speak of the One (ਇੱਕ, Ikk) as the ground of all existence, describes the world of appearances as transient and deceptive, and frames liberation in terms of union with the Divine. It was natural for scholars trained in Advaita to read these themes through the conceptual vocabulary they knew best. The teeka thus frequently uses Brahman as a gloss for ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ (Waheguru) or ਪਰਮਾਤਮਾ (Parmatma), and interprets passages about divine unity in rigorously non-dualistic terms.

Where this interpretive strategy works well is in passages where Gurbani describes the nature of the Absolute — its formlessness, its pervasiveness, its transcendence of ordinary categories. The Vedantic vocabulary of Nirguna (without attributes) maps usefully onto Gurbani's own language of the formless Divine. The teeka's explanations in these areas are often philosophically rich and genuinely illuminating.

Where Sikh and Vedantic Theologies Diverge

The difficulties arise at the points where Sikh theology makes moves that Vedanta does not. Perhaps the most significant of these is the concept of ਨਾਮ (Naam). In Gurbani, Naam is not simply a name or label for the Divine — it is the dynamic, creative, sustaining presence of the Divine in the world, accessible through the Guru's grace and internalized through devotional practice. This is a relational, personal, and ethical concept that does not reduce neatly to Vedantic categories of Brahman or Maya.

The Faridkot Teeka's handling of Naam has been criticized by scholars including Bhai Vir Singh and later by Gurbachan Singh Talib for flattening this concept into something resembling the Vedantic Brahman — the undifferentiated Absolute — thereby stripping away the relational and devotional character that is central to the Gurmat understanding. Similarly, the concept of the Guru in Gurbani is not simply a teacher who transmits knowledge of Brahman; the Guru is understood as the living presence of the Divine Word, a concept that has no precise Vedantic equivalent.

These divergences matter because they affect how students and worshippers understand what Gurbani is actually teaching. If a reader comes to Gurbani primarily through the Faridkot Teeka, they may come away with a picture of Sikh theology that is philosophically sophisticated but subtly Vedanticized — more concerned with non-dual realization than with the distinctly Sikh themes of seva (service), sangat (congregation), and the transformative relationship with the living Word.

This is not to say the teeka is wrong — it is to say that it represents one philosophical tradition's reading of Gurbani, and that awareness of this framing is essential for any critical engagement with the text.

The Legacy of This Interpretive Approach

The debate over Vedantic interpretation of Gurbani did not end with the Faridkot Teeka — it defined much of Sikh intellectual life in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. The Singh Sabha movement, which was developing at roughly the same time the teeka was being finalized and published, pushed back explicitly against what its leaders saw as the Hinduization of Sikh theology. Scholars like Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha argued vigorously that Sikhi was a distinct revelation with its own theological categories, and that using Vedantic frameworks to interpret Gurbani produced distortion rather than clarity.

This tension gave rise to the tradition of Gurbani commentary that became dominant in the twentieth century — commentaries written in simple Punjabi, explicitly rejecting Vedantic glosses, and emphasizing the distinctly Gurmat character of each theological concept. Works by scholars such as Bhai Vir Singh, Principal Teja Singh, and later Gurbachan Singh Talib all define themselves, implicitly or explicitly, against the Faridkot Teeka's Vedantic approach.

Understanding this history allows students of the teeka to appreciate it as a product of a specific intellectual moment — the late nineteenth century, when Nirmala scholarship represented the most systematic and learned engagement with Gurbani available — while also recognizing why subsequent generations found it necessary to develop alternative approaches.

Key Terms

  • ਅਦਵੈਤ ਵੇਦਾਂਤ (Advaita Vedanta) — non-dualistic Hindu philosophy holding that ultimate reality is a single undivided consciousness; a major framework used in the Faridkot Teeka
  • ਨਾਮ (Naam) — in Gurmat, the dynamic divine presence accessible through the Guru's grace, not merely a label or abstract Absolute
  • ਨਿਰਗੁਣ / ਸਰਗੁਣ (Nirguna / Sarguna) — Gurbani terms for the Divine beyond attributes versus the Divine with attributes; also used in Vedantic discourse but with different implications
  • ਗੁਰਮਤਿ (Gurmat) — the teaching or philosophy of the Guru; the distinctly Sikh theological framework grounded in Gurbani
  • ਮਾਇਆ (Maya) — in Vedanta, cosmic illusion; in Gurbani, the attachment and delusion that separates the soul from the Divine — related but not identical concepts

Discussion Questions

  1. Is it possible to use a foreign philosophical framework to illuminate a religious text without distorting it? Where would you draw the line between helpful comparison and interpretive imposition?
  2. The Singh Sabha movement argued that Vedantic interpretation obscured Sikh distinctiveness. Do you think distinctiveness and philosophical dialogue with other traditions are necessarily in tension?
  3. How should a modern student of Gurbani use the Faridkot Teeka given its Vedantic framing? What safeguards or supplementary sources would help maintain a balanced understanding?
  4. Consider the concept of Naam as described in this lecture. Can you think of another religious tradition's concept that is similarly difficult to translate without distortion into another tradition's categories?

Further Reading

W.H. McLeod, Guru Nanak and the Sikh Religion

Bhai Jodh Singh, Gurmat Nirnay

Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, The Name of My Beloved: Verses of the Sikh Gurus

Key Takeaways

  • The Faridkot Teeka consistently interprets Gurbani through Advaita Vedanta, reflecting the Nirmala scholars' training rather than a neutral reading of the text.
  • Vedantic categories such as Brahman and Maya have partial but imperfect overlap with Gurbani concepts like Waheguru and Naam.
  • The teeka's Vedantic approach was a direct catalyst for the Singh Sabha movement's project of defining distinctly Gurmat theological categories.
  • Critical engagement with the teeka requires awareness of its philosophical presuppositions and supplementary reading in Gurmat-centred commentary traditions.

Homework

Read about the concept of Naam in any reliable Gurmat-centered source — such as the writings of Bhai Vir Singh, Principal Teja Singh, or a modern Sikh theological text. Write 400 words comparing that source's explanation of Naam with what you might expect from a Vedanta-influenced explanation (using what you have learned in this lecture). Where do the two approaches agree? Where do they diverge, and what are the spiritual consequences of those divergences?

lessons.title: Parallel Commentary Traditions: How Other Religions Have Explained Their Scriptures
lessons.html:
Introduction

The Faridkot Teeka did not emerge in a vacuum. The impulse to write systematic, comprehensive commentary on sacred scripture is one of the most consistent features of the world's major religious traditions. Jewish rabbis compiled the Talmud and Midrash; Christian theologians produced vast patristic commentaries; Islamic scholars developed the science of Tafsir; Hindu pandits wrote bhashyas on the Upanishads and Brahma Sutras. In every case, the act of commentary was both an act of devotion and an act of intellectual power — defining, for the community, what the scripture meant and how it should be read.

Placing the Faridkot Teeka within this global context enriches our understanding of it in two ways. First, it reveals the universal human need to mediate between sacred text and living community — a need that the teeka was directly responding to. Second, it highlights the distinctive features of Sikh commentary practice: the particular challenges posed by Gurbani's form, the role of the Guru lineage, and the historical moment in which the teeka was produced. This lecture surveys several major commentary traditions with the explicit goal of illuminating the Faridkot project by contrast and comparison.

The Jewish and Islamic Commentary Traditions

The Jewish tradition of scriptural commentary is arguably the oldest continuous commentary tradition in any religion. The Mishnah and Talmud, compiled between approximately 200 CE and 600 CE, are essentially layered commentaries on the Torah, recording debates among rabbis across generations. What is remarkable about the Talmudic tradition is its explicit preservation of disagreement: minority opinions are recorded alongside majority ones, and the process of interpretation is itself treated as spiritually significant. The text does not pretend to deliver a single definitive meaning; it models ongoing interpretive community as a religious practice.

Islamic Tafsir literature developed with similar thoroughness but with a different emphasis. The classical Tafsir tradition — represented by works like those of Al-Tabari, Al-Zamakhshari, and Ibn Kathir — proceeds verse by verse through the Quran, drawing on Hadith (sayings and actions of the Prophet), Arabic linguistic analysis, and theological reasoning. Like the Faridkot Teeka, classical Tafsir is a work of extraordinary scale and erudition, requiring mastery of multiple disciplines. And like the teeka, the classical Tafsir tradition has been critiqued in the modern period for inaccessibility and for encoding particular theological positions as if they were neutral readings of the text.

Both the Talmudic and Tafsir traditions suggest a pattern that also appears in the Faridkot context: the most authoritative early commentaries tend to be produced by scholarly elites, written in prestigious classical languages (Hebrew/Aramaic, classical Arabic), and later criticized by reformers who argue for vernacular, accessible interpretation. The parallel with the Singh Sabha critique of the Faridkot Teeka is striking and instructive.

Hindu Bhashya Tradition and Its Influence on the Nirmala Scholars

The bhashya (commentary) tradition in Hindu philosophy is the most direct ancestor of the approach taken in the Faridkot Teeka. A bhashya, in classical Indian scholarship, is a systematic word-by-word or phrase-by-phrase explanation of a foundational text (prakarana or sutra), typically drawing on the author's broader philosophical commitments. Shankaracharya's bhashyas on the Brahma Sutras, the principal Upanishads, and the Bhagavad Gita are the most celebrated examples, and they are explicitly philosophical works that use the sacred texts as occasions to articulate a comprehensive theological vision.

The Nirmala scholars were trained in this tradition. Their education in Sanskrit texts, philosophical debate, and the bhashya method meant that when they approached Gurbani, they naturally adopted a bhashya-like methodology: working through the text systematically, explaining each word and phrase, and situating individual passages within a larger philosophical framework. The very structure of the Faridkot Teeka — its word-by-word attention, its philosophical digressions, its use of classical categories — reflects this inheritance.

This is not a criticism but a historical observation. Every commentator brings a methodology to their work, and methodology shapes interpretation. The Nirmala scholars brought the bhashya methodology — and recognizing this helps us read the teeka more critically and more appreciatively at the same time. We can appreciate its systematic rigor while remaining alert to the ways in which bhashya conventions may not map perfectly onto Gurbani's distinctive form and spirit.

Key Terms

  • ਤਫ਼ਸੀਰ (Tafsir) — the Islamic tradition of Quranic commentary, notable for its linguistic, historical, and theological thoroughness
  • ਭਾਸ਼ਿਆ (Bhashya) — a Sanskrit philosophical commentary tradition; the most direct methodological ancestor of the Faridkot Teeka's approach
  • ਮਿਦ੍ਰਾਸ਼ (Midrash) — Jewish interpretive literature that expands on and explores the meanings of scriptural narratives
  • ਟੀਕਾ (Teeka) — the Sikh/Indian term for scriptural commentary, related to but distinct from the bhashya form in its devotional context
  • ਵਿਆਖਿਆ (Viakhya) — explanation or elucidation; a broader Punjabi/Sanskrit term for the act of scriptural commentary

Discussion Questions

  1. The Jewish Talmud preserves minority opinions alongside majority ones, treating interpretive disagreement as spiritually valuable. How does this approach compare to the Faridkot Teeka's generally unified philosophical voice? What are the advantages and risks of each approach?
  2. Reform movements in both Islam and Judaism have called for vernacular, accessible commentaries to replace classical elite ones. The Singh Sabha movement made a similar call in Sikhism. What does this recurring pattern tell us about the relationship between knowledge, power, and community in religion?
  3. The Nirmala scholars adopted bhashya methodology from Hindu philosophy. Does the use of an interpretive methodology from another tradition compromise the integrity of a Sikh commentary, or is methodology value-neutral? Defend your view.
  4. If you were designing a commentary tradition for Gurbani from scratch today, what features would you borrow from the traditions discussed in this lecture, and what would you deliberately avoid?

Further Reading

Jane Dammen McAuliffe (ed.), The Cambridge Companion to the Qur'an

Daniel Boyarin, Intertextuality and the Reading of Midrash

Francis X. Clooney, Comparative Theology: Deep Learning Across Religious Borders

Key Takeaways

  • Every major religion has developed systematic commentary traditions to mediate between sacred text and living community — a universal religious impulse that the Faridkot Teeka participated in.
  • The bhashya tradition of classical Hindu philosophy was the most direct methodological influence on the Nirmala scholars who produced the teeka.
  • Patterns of elite scholarly commentary followed by vernacular reform movements appear across Judaism, Islam, and Sikhism, suggesting deep structural similarities in how religious communities manage scriptural authority.
  • Comparative study of commentary traditions illuminates the Faridkot Teeka not as an isolated achievement but as part of a global human effort to keep sacred meaning alive across generations.

Homework

Choose one commentary tradition discussed in this lecture — Jewish Midrash/Talmud, Islamic Tafsir, or Hindu Bhashya — and research it further using any reliable academic source. Write 400 words comparing that tradition's approach to its scripture with the Faridkot Teeka's approach to Gurbani. Focus on three specific points of comparison: the language used, the methodology (word-by-word, thematic, etc.), and the intended audience. Conclude with one paragraph on what the Sikh commentary tradition can learn from — or teach — the tradition you studied.

lessons.title: The Singh Sabha Movement and Its Challenge to the Teeka's Authority
lessons.html:
Introduction

The publication of the Faridkot Teeka in the late nineteenth century coincided with one of the most turbulent periods of intellectual and religious reform in Sikh history. The Singh Sabha movement, which began in Amritsar in 1873 and rapidly spread across the Punjab, was not merely a social reform effort — it was a comprehensive project of Sikh identity definition, scriptural reclamation, and institutional building. Its leaders were convinced that Sikh distinctiveness was being eroded by syncretistic practices and, crucially, by commentarial traditions that read Gurbani through Hindu philosophical lenses.

This lecture examines the relationship between the Faridkot Teeka and the Singh Sabha movement as a study in intellectual conflict and productive tension. The two projects overlapped chronologically but diverged sharply in their assumptions about what Gurbani was, who was authorized to interpret it, and in what language and framework that interpretation should proceed. Understanding this tension is essential not only for evaluating the teeka but for understanding the entire trajectory of modern Sikh scholarship and education.

Singh Sabha's Critique of Nirmala Interpretation

The Singh Sabha reformers, particularly the Tat Khalsa faction led by figures like Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha and Principal Teja Singh, argued that the Nirmala approach to Gurbani commentary was fundamentally flawed at the level of presupposition. Their critique had several distinct components. First, they argued that the Nirmala scholars had treated Gurbani as if it were a text within the Hindu philosophical tradition, to be explained by the same categories used to explain the Vedas and Upanishads. This, in their view, denied Gurbani's status as a distinct and complete revelation that transcended and, in important ways, critiqued Brahmanical philosophy.

Second, Singh Sabha scholars objected to the inaccessibility of the Braj Bhasha medium. Their vision of Sikh revival was explicitly democratic and populist: they wanted ordinary Sikhs — farmers, merchants, women, and children — to be able to read and understand Gurbani without years of classical education. Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's monumental Mahankosh (the Encyclopaedia of the Sikh Literature), while itself a work of formidable scholarship, was written with the clear goal of making Gurbani's vocabulary accessible to educated but non-specialist Punjabi readers.

Third, and most foundationally, the Singh Sabha reformers argued that the Gurmat tradition had its own distinct theological categories — Naam, Seva, Sangat, Pangat, the Guru's grace — and that interpreting these through Vedantic lenses actively distorted what the Gurus were teaching. This argument anticipated by several decades the modern academic debate about the distinctiveness of Sikh theology vis-à-vis Hindu and Islamic traditions.

The Institutional Consequences of This Debate

The intellectual debate between Nirmala commentarial tradition and Singh Sabha reformism had direct and lasting institutional consequences. The establishment of the Chief Khalsa Diwan, the Singh Sabha's apex organizational body, channeled energy into creating new educational institutions — Khalsa schools and colleges — that taught Gurbani in a distinctly Gurmat framework. These institutions produced generations of Sikh scholars and teachers who were trained in the Singh Sabha interpretive tradition rather than the Nirmala one.

The founding of the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (SGPC) in 1925, following the Gurdwara Reform Movement, effectively transferred custodianship of major historical gurdwaras from groups that included Nirmala and Udasi clergy to elected Sikh bodies. This had direct implications for which commentary traditions would be promoted and disseminated in gurdwara contexts. The SGPC has generally favored Gurmat-centered, Punjabi-medium commentaries over the Faridkot Teeka's Braj Bhasha approach, reflecting the long-term triumph of Singh Sabha values in institutional Sikhism.

At the same time, it would be a mistake to present this as a simple story of the Singh Sabha defeating the Nirmala tradition. The Faridkot Teeka has never stopped being used. It remains a reference work for serious Sikh scholars, and its value as a record of traditional Nirmala learning is widely recognized even by those who disagree with its theological framing. The debate produced not a winner and a loser but a richer, more contested commentarial landscape within which students of Gurbani must now find their way.

Key Terms

  • ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ (Singh Sabha) — Sikh reform movement begun in 1873, advocating for Sikh distinctiveness, vernacular education, and Gurmat-centered interpretation
  • ਤੱਤ ਖਾਲਸਾ (Tat Khalsa) — the more reformist faction of the Singh Sabha that took strong positions on Sikh distinctiveness from Hinduism
  • ਮਹਾਨਕੋਸ਼ (Mahankosh) — Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's encyclopaedic Punjabi dictionary of Sikh literature, a foundational Singh Sabha scholarly achievement
  • ਐਸ.ਜੀ.ਪੀ.ਸੀ. (SGPC) — Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee; the elected body that manages major Sikh gurdwaras and has shaped institutional Sikh scholarship
  • ਗੁਰਮਤਿ (Gurmat) — the teaching of the Guru; used by Singh Sabha reformers to designate distinctly Sikh theological categories as opposed to Vedantic or Sufi ones

Discussion Questions

  1. The Singh Sabha argued that Gurbani commentary in Braj Bhasha and Vedantic categories was an act of cultural colonization of Sikh thought by Hindu philosophy. Do you find this argument persuasive? What would make it stronger or weaker?
  2. How should a religious community balance respect for its classical scholarly heritage (such as the Faridkot Teeka) with the need to reclaim and protect its distinct identity?
  3. The SGPC's institutional dominance has shaped which Gurbani interpretations reach most Sikhs today. What are the benefits and risks of having a single institution exercise this kind of influence over scriptural interpretation?
  4. The Singh Sabha movement is often described as a reform movement, but it was also a conservative one in some respects — seeking to recover what it saw as authentic Sikh identity. How do you distinguish between reform and restoration in religious movements?

Further Reading

Harjot Oberoi, The Construction of Religious Boundaries: Culture, Identity and Diversity in the Sikh Tradition

Gurdarshan Singh Dhillon, Singh Sabha Movement: A Revival

J.S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab

Key Takeaways

  • The Singh Sabha movement directly challenged the Faridkot Teeka's authority by arguing that its Vedantic framing distorted Sikh theology and its Braj Bhasha medium excluded ordinary Sikhs.
  • Singh Sabha scholars like Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha developed alternative scholarly tools — such as the Mahankosh — that embodied a different vision of accessible, Gurmat-centered learning.
  • The institutional triumph of Singh Sabha values through the SGPC shaped which commentary traditions became dominant in Sikh religious life, but did not eliminate the Faridkot Teeka from serious scholarly use.
  • The debate between the Nirmala and Singh Sabha approaches produced a richer Sikh commentarial landscape rather than a simple victory for one side.

Homework

Research Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha — his life, his major works, and his vision for Sikh scholarship — using any reliable historical source. Write a 400-word profile that specifically addresses: (1) what he found inadequate about existing Gurbani commentary traditions; (2) what alternative approach he advocated; and (3) how his work has shaped the Sikh scholarly tradition down to the present day. End with a brief personal reflection on what his career suggests about the relationship between scholarship and religious community.

lessons.title: Twentieth-Century Commentaries: What Came After the Faridkot Teeka
lessons.html:
Introduction

The Faridkot Teeka did not mark the end of Gurbani commentary — it marked the beginning of a new era in which the task of explaining Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji to a changing world became more urgent and more contested than ever. The twentieth century saw an explosion of commentary writing in Sikhism, driven by rising literacy rates, the spread of printing, the partition of 1947, the Sikh diaspora, and the growing demand from English-educated Sikhs who needed access to Gurbani's teachings in modern formats. Each major commentary of the twentieth century was, in some sense, in dialogue with the Faridkot Teeka — accepting some of its interpretive moves, rejecting others, and charting new paths through the inexhaustible richness of Gurbani.

This lecture surveys the most significant Gurbani commentaries produced after the Faridkot Teeka, examining their methodological choices, their intended audiences, and their theological commitments. By understanding the arc of commentary writing across the twentieth century, students gain both a clearer picture of the teeka's lasting influence and a practical guide to the resources available to them as modern students of Gurbani.

Major Commentaries of the Early to Mid Twentieth Century

The most celebrated Sikh scholar-poet of the early twentieth century, Bhai Vir Singh, produced commentary work that stands as a direct response to the Faridkot Teeka's approach. His explanations of Gurbani — expressed partly through creative writing, poetry, and editorial work — consistently emphasized the living, devotional character of Gurbani over its philosophical systematization. Where the Faridkot Teeka might situate a shabad within Advaita categories, Bhai Vir Singh would draw out its emotional and devotional texture, its image of the longing soul reaching toward the Divine. His approach was in literary Punjabi — lyrical, accessible, and deeply personal in tone.

Principal Teja Singh's English-language introductions and translations of SGGS sections represented a different response: the effort to make Gurbani intelligible to the English-educated Sikh elite of colonial and early post-colonial India. His work did not attempt to be a full commentary on the scale of the Faridkot Teeka, but it modeled a way of engaging Gurbani analytically and accessibly in the medium of a world language. This tradition would eventually lead to Gurbachan Singh Talib's monumental four-volume Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji: Translation and Explication — an English-medium academic commentary that remains one of the most used reference works for English-speaking scholars of Sikhism.

The mid-twentieth century also saw the production of the Shabdarth Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, published by the SGPC — a Punjabi-medium commentary that became the institutional standard for gurdwara education across India and the diaspora. Its authorship was collective and its approach deliberately moderate: avoiding both the Vedantic framing of the Faridkot Teeka and the highly personal literary style of Bhai Vir Singh, it aimed for clear, accessible, theologically conservative explanation of each shabad in simple Punjabi.

Digital Age Commentaries and the Democratization of Access

The digital revolution transformed the landscape of Gurbani commentary in ways that would have been unimaginable to the scholars of Faridkot. Platforms such as SikhiToTheMax, Gurbani.org, and the Sikh Research Institute's educational resources now make multiple English and Punjabi translations and explanations available simultaneously for any given shabad. A student today can, with a few clicks, compare the Faridkot Teeka's Braj Bhasha explanation with the SGPC's Punjabi Shabdarth, Gurbachan Singh Talib's English rendering, and several contemporary translations — all in real time.

This democratization of access is an extraordinary development. It means that no single commentary can claim exclusive interpretive authority in the way the Faridkot Teeka once did for scholars who had access to it. But it also creates new challenges: when all interpretations are equally accessible, how does a student develop the critical skills to evaluate them? How does one recognize when a translation has made a significant theological choice, or when a commentary is reading its own presuppositions into the text?

These are the skills this course aims to develop. The existence of the Faridkot Teeka as a reference point — a known quantity with known strengths and limitations — is invaluable in this context. A student who understands the teeka's methodology is far better equipped to read any other commentary critically than one who approaches each translation fresh, without a framework for evaluation.

Key Terms

  • ਸ਼ਬਦਅਰਥ (Shabdarth) — meaning of the word; the name of the SGPC's official Punjabi-medium commentary on SGGS, widely used in Sikh education
  • ਅਨੁਵਾਦ (Anuvad) — translation; the act of rendering a text from one language to another, distinct from but related to commentary
  • ਵਿਆਖਿਆ (Viakhya) — explanation or explication; a broader term for the interpretive act that can encompass both translation and commentary
  • ਡਿਜੀਟਲ ਸੰਸਾਧਨ (Digital Sansadhan) — digital resources; the online platforms now making multiple Gurbani commentaries simultaneously accessible
  • ਸਿੱਖੀਟੂਦਮੈਕਸ (SikhiToTheMax) — one of the most widely used digital platforms for accessing Gurbani texts, translations, and commentaries

Discussion Questions

  1. Bhai Vir Singh and the SGPC's Shabdarth represent two very different visions of what a Gurbani commentary should do — one personal and literary, the other institutional and conservative. Which approach do you find more valuable for your own spiritual development, and why?
  2. The availability of multiple simultaneous commentaries online could be a gift or a trap. What habits of mind and skills of evaluation does a student need to benefit from this abundance rather than being confused by it?
  3. Each commentary of the twentieth century was partly a response to the Faridkot Teeka. Does this mean the teeka has more influence on modern Sikh scholarly thought than it might appear, even when that influence takes the form of reaction against it?
  4. If you were to write a Gurbani commentary today for a global Sikh diaspora audience, what language or languages would you use, what methodology would you follow, and what existing commentaries would most inform your approach?

Further Reading

Gurbachan Singh Talib, Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji: Translation and Explication (4 vols.)

Bhai Vir Singh, Santhya Sri Guru Granth Sahib

Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, Sikhism: An Introduction

Key Takeaways

  • The twentieth century saw an explosion of Gurbani commentary in Punjabi and English, each in dialogue with the Faridkot Teeka — some continuing its approach, others deliberately departing from it.
  • The SGPC's Shabdarth became the institutional standard commentary for Sikh religious education, while scholars like Bhai Vir Singh pursued more personal and literary approaches.
  • Digital platforms have democratized access to multiple simultaneous commentaries, making critical evaluation skills more important than ever.
  • Understanding the Faridkot Teeka's methodology provides a foundation for reading all subsequent Gurbani commentaries more critically and effectively.

Homework

Spend a study session using SikhiToTheMax or a similar digital platform to look up any one shabad of your choosing. Read at least three different English translations or commentaries of that shabad side by side. Write 400 words identifying: (1) one significant theological or interpretive difference you notice between the translations; (2) which translation you find most illuminating and why; and (3) what questions remain unanswered that you would want a full commentary to address. This exercise develops the comparative reading skills that the digital age requires.

lessons.title: Reading the Teeka Today: A Practical Workshop for Advanced Students
lessons.html:
Introduction

This final lecture shifts register from historical and analytical to practical. Throughout this course, we have studied the Faridkot Teeka from the outside — examining its origins, its methodology, its theological presuppositions, and its place in the history of Sikh scholarship. Now we turn to the question that should drive any serious student: how do you actually use this text? What does a productive session with the Faridkot Teeka look like in practice, and how do you integrate what it offers with the other resources available to a modern student of Gurbani?

This lecture is designed as a practical workshop. It will walk through concrete strategies for approaching the teeka, address common difficulties that students encounter, and provide a framework for integrating the teeka's insights with those of other commentaries. It will also reflect on the deeper question of why a modern student, surrounded by accessible English translations and digital tools, would invest the significant effort required to engage with this classical Braj Bhasha text at all — and what the answer to that question reveals about the nature of serious Gurbani study.

Practical Strategies for Engaging the Teeka

The first and most important practical point is to enter the Faridkot Teeka with a specific question or passage in mind, rather than attempting to read it linearly from beginning to end. The teeka is over seven thousand pages in its printed form; no student reads it cover to cover. It is a reference work, and like all great reference works, it rewards purposeful consultation. Before opening the teeka, identify a specific shabad or concept you want to understand more deeply. This gives your reading a focus and allows you to evaluate what the teeka offers against what you already know.

The second strategy is to read the original Gurbani passage first — in Gurmukhi, aloud if possible — before consulting the teeka. This keeps the primary text central and prevents the commentary from becoming a substitute for direct engagement with Gurbani. Write down your initial understanding, your questions, and the words or phrases that puzzle you. Then open the teeka and see which of your questions it addresses, which it ignores, and whether it raises new questions you had not considered. This dialogue between your own reading and the commentary is the heart of productive scholarly engagement.

Third, when you encounter the teeka's Braj Bhasha explanations, do not try to understand every word before moving forward. Get the overall sense of the explanation first, identify the key interpretive move the teeka is making, and then work backward to the specific vocabulary. Many students make the mistake of getting lost in linguistic details and losing the thread of the theological argument. The argument is what matters most; the linguistic details support it.

Integrating the Teeka with Other Commentaries

No single commentary should be used in isolation, and this is especially true of the Faridkot Teeka given its specific Vedantic orientation. The most productive approach is to consult the teeka alongside at least one other major commentary — most practically, the SGPC's Punjabi Shabdarth — and to note where they agree and where they diverge. Agreement across commentaries usually signals that an interpretation has strong traditional grounding. Divergence signals a genuine interpretive choice point, and these are the most intellectually valuable moments in commentary study.

When you find a divergence, ask yourself: what is each commentary emphasizing? What theological commitment drives each reading? Which reading is more consistent with the overall arc of the shabad and the teachings of Gurbani as a whole? You will not always be able to resolve the question definitively, and that is fine. The goal of advanced Gurbani study is not to achieve certainty about every interpretive question but to develop a nuanced, informed, and spiritually engaged understanding that can hold complexity without collapsing it.

English-speaking students have one additional resource that earlier generations did not: the growing body of academic scholarship on Gurbani and Sikh theology. Works by scholars such as Pashaura Singh, Gurinder Singh Mann, and Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh can provide historical and theological context that no traditional commentary — however comprehensive — was designed to offer. Using academic scholarship alongside traditional commentary gives you a stereoscopic view of the text: close-up, devotional depth from the teeka, and wider historical and comparative perspective from modern scholarship.

Key Terms

  • ਪਾਠ (Path) — recitation of Gurbani; reading the sacred text aloud, a fundamental practice of Sikh devotional life and a natural companion to commentary study
  • ਵਿਚਾਰ (Vichar) — reflection, contemplation; the act of pondering Gurbani's meaning deeply, which commentary is designed to support
  • ਸੰਦਰਭ (Sandarbh) — context; understanding a shabad in its full textual and historical context is essential to avoiding misreading
  • ਤੁਲਨਾਤਮਕ ਅਧਿਐਨ (Tulnatmak Adhiain) — comparative study; reading multiple commentaries alongside each other to identify interpretive choices and debates
  • ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤ (Sadh Sangat) — the community of seekers; studying Gurbani with others remains one of the most time-honoured approaches to deepening understanding

Discussion Questions

  1. This lecture recommends entering the Faridkot Teeka with a specific question rather than reading it linearly. How does your usual approach to studying religious texts compare to this strategy? What would you need to change about your study habits?
  2. When two commentaries offer divergent interpretations of the same shabad, you face a genuine interpretive choice. What criteria would you use to evaluate which reading is more convincing?
  3. Is it possible to study Gurbani purely academically — as a scholarly exercise — without it affecting your spiritual life? Is this desirable, or does the most valuable scholarship always involve personal transformation?
  4. At the end of this course, how has your understanding of what a teeka is and does changed? If you were to recommend the Faridkot Teeka to a fellow student, what would you say about both its value and its limitations?

Further Reading

Pashaura Singh and Louis E. Fenech (eds.), The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies

Gurinder Singh Mann, The Making of Sikh Scripture

Sikh Research Institute, Sojhi Curriculum (accessible online)

Key Takeaways

  • Productive engagement with the Faridkot Teeka requires purposeful consultation — coming with specific questions — rather than linear reading from beginning to end.
  • Reading Gurbani aloud before consulting any commentary keeps the primary text central and prevents commentary from substituting for direct devotional engagement.
  • Comparing the teeka with at least one other commentary — such as the SGPC Shabdarth — reveals the interpretive choices each makes and sharpens your own theological thinking.
  • The most rewarding Gurbani study integrates traditional commentary, modern academic scholarship, and personal devotional practice into a unified, ongoing discipline.

Homework

As a capstone exercise for this course, choose a shabad from Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji that you wish to understand more deeply. Spend at least one full hour in the following structured activity: (1) read the shabad aloud in Gurmukhi three times; (2) write 200 words on your initial understanding; (3) consult at least two different commentaries or translations and note where they agree and diverge; (4) write a final 200-word reflection on how your understanding changed through this process, and what questions you still carry. Submit the full written record — your initial understanding, your comparative notes, and your final reflection — as your course capstone.

quiz.q: What is a teeka?
options: A musical setting of bani
A traditional line-by-line commentary or explanation of a text
A handwritten copy of scripture
A pilgrimage route

quiz.q: Why is the Faridkot Wala Teeka historically important?
options: It was the shortest commentary ever written
It is widely regarded as the first complete traditional commentary on the whole of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji
It replaced Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji
It was written in English

quiz.q: Who wrote the Faridkot Teeka?
