courses.title: The Garab Ganjani Teeka: A Commentary on Japji Sahib
courses.summary: This course studies the Garab Ganjani Teeka, a prose commentary on Japji Sahib written by Kavi (Bhai) Santokh Singh in the Nirmala tradition of Sikh exegesis. Students learn what a teeka is, who Santokh Singh was, why this particular commentary was written, and the interpretive debate it addressed. The course…
outcomes: Define what a teeka (commentary) is and explain its role in the Sikh tradition of reading Gurbani.
Identify Kavi Santokh Singh and situate the Garab Ganjani Teeka within his larger body of work.
Explain, neutrally, why the Garab Ganjani Teeka was written and the interpretive debate it sought to address.
Describe how the teeka reads key ideas of Japji Sahib through a Gurmat lens.
Summarize the Nirmala method of commentary and evaluate its strengths and limits.
Apply a teeka responsibly as one tool among several when studying Gurbani as a modern student.

terms.m: a written commentary or exegesis that explains a sacred text
the opening composition of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, composed by Guru Nanak Dev Ji
the teaching or wisdom of the Gurus; the Sikh worldview
an order of Sikh scholars known for textual study and exegesis
the scholarly literary register used in much traditional commentary
pride or ego, the quality the teeka's title says it shatters
the sacred utterance or revealed word of the Gurus
a school of Indian philosophy whose reading the teeka responds to

references: Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998.
Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014.
Singh, Sahib. Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan. Jalandhar: Raj Publishers, n.d.
Singh, Santokh. Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth. Amritsar: traditional Nirmala scholarship, 19th century.
Singh, Santokh. Garab Ganjani Teeka. Commentary on Japji Sahib, Nirmala tradition, 19th century.

lessons.title: What a Teeka Is and Why It Matters
lessons.summary: Introduces the idea of a teeka as a commentary on a sacred text and explains why such works are valued in the Sikh tradition.
lessons.html:
Full course contents
  1. What a Teeka Is and Why It Matters
  2. Kavi Santokh Singh: The Author and His World
  3. Why the Garab Ganjani Teeka Was Written
  4. How the Teeka Reads Japji Sahib
  5. The Nirmala Method: Strengths and Limits
  6. Using a Teeka as a Modern Student

The word and the work

A ਟੀਕਾ (commentary) is a written explanation that walks a reader through a sacred text line by line. In the Sikh tradition, the central text is ਬਾਣੀ (the revealed word of the Gurus), and a teeka tries to open its meaning for students who may not share the original language, idiom, or background of the verses.

Why commentaries arise

Sacred poetry is dense. A single line can hold several layers of meaning. A teeka slows the reading down, defines hard words, and connects ideas across a composition. Scholars have long noted that exegesis is a normal part of how living religious communities pass on their texts (Singh and Fenech 2014).

ElementWhat it does
Word glossDefines difficult or archaic terms
ParaphraseRestates a verse in plainer language
Cross-referenceLinks a line to related ideas elsewhere
InterpretationArgues for a particular meaning

A note of humility

A teeka is a human aid, not the bani itself. The best commentaries point the reader back to the source rather than replacing it.

  • A teeka explains, it does not substitute for the text.
  • Commentaries reflect the time and school of their author.
  • Reading several teekas together gives a fuller picture.
References: Singh and Fenech 2014; Grewal 1998.

Homework

Select one term from the Mool Mantar (such as ਸਤਿ, ਕਰਤਾ, ਨਿਰਭਉ, or ਨਿਰਵੈਰੁ) and spend 20 minutes sitting quietly with that single word. Afterward, write a 300-word reflection on what the word evokes for you — emotionally, philosophically, and practically. Then find one place in your daily life where that quality is either present or absent, and describe what it would look like to embody it more fully.

lessons.title: Kavi Santokh Singh: The Author and His World
lessons.summary: Introduces Kavi Santokh Singh, the scholar-poet who wrote the Garab Ganjani Teeka, and places him among his major works.
lessons.html:
The scholar-poet

Kavi (Bhai) Santokh Singh (1787-1843) was one of the most productive scholars of his era. He is best known for the ਬਾਣੀ-adjacent historical epics Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth and Nanak Prakash, which retell the lives of the Gurus at great length (Grewal 1998).

His training

Santokh Singh worked within the ਨਿਰਮਲਾ (an order of Sikh scholars known for textual study). This order placed a strong emphasis on careful reading, classical learning, and the explanation of texts, which made commentary a natural part of its work.

His language

Much of his writing, including the Garab Ganjani Teeka, uses ਸਾਧ ਭਾਖਾ (the scholarly literary register). This register drew on a learned vocabulary that signaled seriousness and depth to its intended readers.

WorkType
Sri Gur Pratap Suraj GranthHistorical epic of the Gurus
Nanak PrakashLife of Guru Nanak Dev Ji
Garab Ganjani TeekaCommentary on Japji Sahib

Why he matters here

Knowing who the author was helps a student read the teeka fairly. A commentary always carries the voice, training, and concerns of its writer.

References: Grewal 1998; Singh and Fenech 2014.

Homework

Choose one feature of Bhai Santokh Singh's writing style mentioned in this lesson — his use of Sanskrit vocabulary, his narrative framing, or his appeal to Vedantic parallels — and write a 350-word reflection on why that approach might help or hinder a modern student of Gurbani. Draw on at least one concrete example from your own experience learning religious or philosophical texts.

lessons.title: Why the Garab Ganjani Teeka Was Written
lessons.summary: Explains, neutrally, the purpose of the Garab Ganjani Teeka and the interpretive debate it set out to address.
lessons.html:
The meaning of the name

The title Garab Ganjani roughly means pride-shatterer. The key word is ਗਰਬ (pride or ego), and the work presents itself as humbling a reading the author believed had gone astray.

The debate, stated neutrally

The teeka was written to respond to an earlier interpretation of ਜਪੁਜੀ ਸਾਹਿਬ (the opening composition of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji). That earlier reading is commonly described as leaning toward ਵੇਦਾਂਤ (a school of Indian philosophy). Santokh Singh's aim was to reassert a ਗੁਰਮਤਿ (the teaching of the Gurus) understanding of the text.

Students should hold this history with care. Different communities have remembered the debate in different ways, and this course presents it as a documented disagreement over interpretation rather than as a settled verdict.

PositionCore concern
Earlier readingRead Japji through a philosophical lens
Garab Ganjani TeekaRead Japji on the terms of Gurmat

Why purpose shapes meaning

  • A polemical aim focuses attention on disputed verses.
  • The author argues, not merely paraphrases.
  • Knowing the target of a commentary clarifies its choices.
References: Singh and Fenech 2014; Grewal 1998.

Homework

In 300–400 words, reflect on the historical and social circumstances that shaped the Garab Ganjani Teeka. Consider: what pressures does a scholar face when writing for a specific patron or community? How might those pressures shape the interpretation of sacred text? Compare this to a modern situation where context shapes how a religious or philosophical teaching is presented.

lessons.title: How the Teeka Reads Japji Sahib
lessons.summary: Surveys the way the teeka approaches the central ideas of Japji Sahib through a Gurmat lens.
lessons.html:
Starting at the beginning

ਜਪੁਜੀ ਸਾਹਿਬ (the composition of Guru Nanak Dev Ji) opens Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji at Ang 1. Because it stands first, its reading shapes how a student approaches the whole scripture, which is part of why its interpretation mattered so much to the teeka's author.

A Gurmat lens

The teeka consistently reads Japji Sahib in line with ਗੁਰਮਤਿ (the teaching of the Gurus). Where a verse could be pulled toward an outside philosophy, the commentary works to anchor it in the Gurus' own framework of the One Creator, divine command, and loving devotion.

Method in practice

StepWhat the teeka does
DefineGlosses a key word of the verse
RestateOffers a plain paraphrase
DefendArgues against a rival reading where one exists

What to take away

The point of the teeka is not to add new doctrine but to keep the reader's attention on what the Gurus taught. This course does not quote specific lines or assign new Ang numbers; students should read Japji Sahib itself alongside the commentary.

  • The teeka prioritizes the text's own framework.
  • It treats interpretation as a responsibility, not a free exercise.
References: Singh, Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan; Singh and Fenech 2014.

Homework

Select one pauri (stanza) from Japji Sahib that you know well. Without looking at any commentary, write your own 200-word interpretation of its central teaching. Then write a second 150-word paragraph reflecting on what questions a commentator like Santokh Singh might have asked about the same passage — and what tools (linguistic, philosophical, scriptural) he would have used to answer them.

lessons.title: The Nirmala Method: Strengths and Limits
lessons.summary: Describes the Nirmala approach to commentary and weighs its strengths against its limits.
lessons.html:
The Nirmala approach

The ਨਿਰਮਲਾ (scholarly order) brought classical learning to the study of ਬਾਣੀ (the revealed word). Their teekas tend to be careful, systematic, and rich in cross-reference, and they often write in ਸਾਧ ਭਾਖਾ (the scholarly register).

Strengths

  • Deep attention to individual words and grammar.
  • A long memory of earlier interpretive traditions.
  • A disciplined, line-by-line method.

Limits

  • The learned register can be hard for modern readers.
  • Classical philosophical vocabulary can color the reading.
  • The author's purpose may sharpen some verses more than others.
FeatureStrengthLimit
Scholarly registerPrecision and depthAccessibility
Classical learningRich contextOutside frameworks may intrude
Polemical aimClear argumentSelective emphasis

Reading with balance

Recognizing both sides lets a student gain from the method's rigor while staying alert to its tendencies (Singh and Fenech 2014).

References: Singh and Fenech 2014; Grewal 1998.

Homework

The Nirmala tradition drew on Sanskrit learning as a bridge between Sikh and Hindu intellectual worlds. In 350 words, reflect on the following: What are the benefits and risks of using one tradition's philosophical vocabulary to explain another tradition's sacred text? Use a specific example from a tradition you are familiar with — Sikh, Hindu, Christian, Islamic, or otherwise — to ground your argument.

lessons.title: Using a Teeka as a Modern Student
lessons.summary: Offers practical guidance on how a present-day student can use the Garab Ganjani Teeka and similar works responsibly.
lessons.html:
Start with the bani

The first step is always to read ਜਪੁਜੀ ਸਾਹਿਬ (the composition of Guru Nanak Dev Ji) itself. A ਟੀਕਾ (commentary) is a guide to the text, not a replacement for it.

Read more than one commentary

Comparing the Garab Ganjani Teeka with a modern reference such as the Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan helps a student see where commentators agree and where they differ (Singh, Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan).

A simple workflow

StepAction
1Read the verse of Japji Sahib first
2Note your own questions
3Read the teeka's gloss and paraphrase
4Compare with another commentary
5Return to the bani with fresh understanding

Stay grounded

  • Keep a ਗੁਰਮਤਿ (the teaching of the Gurus) frame at the center.
  • Treat historical debates with respect and neutrality.
  • Let the commentary deepen, not crowd out, your own reading.

Used this way, a teeka becomes a doorway back into the bani rather than a detour around it.

References: Singh, Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan; Singh and Fenech 2014; Grewal 1998.

Homework

Identify one teaching from Japji Sahib whose meaning you have found difficult to fully grasp. Write a 300-word reflection on what has made it difficult — is it linguistic, conceptual, experiential, or cultural? Then describe two concrete strategies you will use going forward: one involving a Teeka or commentary, and one involving personal practice or community engagement. Conclude with a single sentence naming what you hope to understand more deeply by the end of this course.

lessons.title: The Mool Mantar: Theology in Miniature
lessons.html:
Introduction

Japji Sahib opens not with a pauri (stanza) but with a theological statement so compact and so dense that commentators across centuries have devoted entire volumes to its unpacking. The Mool Mantar — literally the 'root formula' or 'seed mantra' — precedes the composition proper and functions as both a creed and an invitation. Before the Guru sings, he declares. Before the student listens, they are asked to orient themselves toward a specific understanding of ultimate reality.

The Garab Ganjani Teeka, following the Nirmala interpretive tradition, treats the Mool Mantar as a philosophical thesis statement: every teaching that follows in Japji Sahib is, in some sense, an elaboration of what is compressed into these opening words. Kavi Santokh Singh does not rush past the Mool Mantar as a preamble; he reads it as the key that unlocks the entire composition. Understanding his approach requires us to slow down and examine what each term carries — linguistically, theologically, and experientially.

This lesson works through the major theological claims of the Mool Mantar, examining how the Garab Ganjani Teeka reads each term and what intellectual tradition it draws on to do so. We will also explore why the sequence of these attributes matters — and what the Teeka says about the relationship between naming the Divine and knowing the Divine.

One Being: The Claim of ੴ

The Mool Mantar begins with ੴ (Ik Oankaar), a symbol rather than a word — a numeral and a sound fused into a single written form. Commentators in every era have wrestled with how to translate it. Santokh Singh, writing in the Nirmala tradition saturated in Vedantic thought, reads ੴ as an assertion of non-dual oneness: there is one Being, and all that exists participates in that Being rather than standing apart from it.

What makes this reading significant is not just the philosophical claim but its implication for the rest of the Teeka. If the foundational assertion is radical oneness, then every subsequent description of the Divine — creator, fearless, without enmity, beyond time — must be read in light of that oneness. The attributes are not separate divine functions but facets of a single, undivided reality. The Teeka uses terms from Advaita Vedanta to elaborate this point, drawing on concepts like निर्गुण (nirgun — beyond qualities) and सगुण (sagun — with qualities) to argue that ੴ encompasses both.

Students should note an important tension here: the Sikh tradition is not straightforwardly Advaita, and Santokh Singh's borrowing of Vedantic vocabulary has been debated by later scholars. Some Sikh theologians argue that the Guru's vision of the Divine preserves a relational dimension — a Waheguru who responds, who is encountered, who graces — that strict non-dualism cannot accommodate. The Garab Ganjani Teeka navigates this tension, but not always with full resolution, and recognizing that navigation is part of reading the Teeka critically.

The symbol ੴ itself has a visual theology. The numeral '1' asserts singularity; the Oankaar curve below it gestures toward the unending, unclosed nature of the divine. Santokh Singh, true to his Nirmala formation, connects this to the Sanskrit Aum — but also insists that the Guru's ੴ carries a distinct register, asserting not just cosmic unity but the personal accessibility of that unity to the ordinary devotee through Naam.

The Attributes: Fearless, Without Enmity, Beyond Time

The Mool Mantar proceeds to name a series of divine attributes: ਸਤਿ ਨਾਮੁ (True is the Name), ਕਰਤਾ ਪੁਰਖੁ (Creator Being), ਨਿਰਭਉ (Without Fear), ਨਿਰਵੈਰੁ (Without Enmity), ਅਕਾਲ ਮੂਰਤਿ (Form Beyond Time), ਅਜੂਨੀ (Unborn), ਸੈਭੰ (Self-Existent), and ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ (By the Guru's Grace). The Garab Ganjani Teeka gives extended attention to each, and the pattern of its analysis reveals what Santokh Singh considers theologically primary.

ਨਿਰਭਉ (Nirbhau — without fear) and ਨਿਰਵੈਰੁ (Nirvair — without enmity) are treated as a complementary pair that defines the moral character of the Divine. The Teeka argues that because the Creator has no rival and no need, there is nothing from which to fear and no ground for enmity. This is not merely a negative definition (God lacks these things) but a positive one: the Divine is the ground of security and the source of reconciliation. For Santokh Singh, these attributes carry ethical consequence: a devotee who increasingly realizes the Divine in themselves will also shed their own fear and enmity.

ਅਕਾਲ ਮੂਰਤਿ (Akaal Moorat — the form that is beyond time) receives particularly rich treatment in the Teeka. This phrase is deliberately paradoxical: a 'form' is usually something visible and bounded in time, yet here it is described as timeless. Santokh Singh reads this as a deliberate tension: the Divine is not formless in an abstract sense but is the very source of all form, a living presence that cannot be exhausted by any single manifestation. This reading protects against both idol-worship (no single form is final) and pure abstraction (the Divine is not an empty concept but a living presence).

ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ (Gur Prasaad — by the Guru's Grace) closes the Mool Mantar and, for Santokh Singh, is arguably its most important line. All the philosophical attributes that precede it would remain inaccessible without grace. The Teeka is explicit: knowledge of the Divine is not achieved through intellectual effort alone but is received as a gift mediated through the Guru. This is the point at which the Garab Ganjani Teeka most clearly diverges from pure philosophical rationalism and anchors its interpretation in the lived devotional tradition.

Naming the Divine and Knowing the Divine

One of the deepest questions the Mool Mantar raises — and one that the Garab Ganjani Teeka takes seriously — is whether naming the Divine brings us closer to knowing the Divine or whether language always falls short. This is not merely an academic question; it shapes how we read every line of Japji Sahib that follows.

Santokh Singh's position, drawn from both Nirmala learning and Gurbani itself, is that Naam (Name) is not merely a label but a participatory reality. When the text says ਸਤਿ ਨਾਮੁ (True is the Name), it does not mean that the word 'Waheguru' accurately describes an object called God. It means that the Name — when engaged through devotion, recitation, and surrender — actually brings the devotee into contact with the reality it points toward. Language, properly understood and properly practiced, is a vehicle of encounter.

This has major implications for how the Teeka functions as a genre. A commentary on Gurbani is itself a sustained act of naming — of using more words to illuminate words already given. Santokh Singh is aware of the risk: that elaboration can substitute for encounter, that explanation can produce intellectual satisfaction without spiritual transformation. The Garab Ganjani Teeka hedges against this risk by consistently returning the reader to the practice of Naam Simran (ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ) as the irreducible foundation of Sikh life. No amount of commentary, he implies, replaces the direct engagement with the Naam itself.

Modern students of the Teeka are therefore invited into a double practice: analytical reading of the commentary's theological arguments, and contemplative engagement with the Gurbani that underlies it. These two modes are not opposites — the Garab Ganjani Teeka insists they are mutually reinforcing — but they require different kinds of attention, and developing both is the work of this course.

Key Terms

  • ੴ (Ik Oankaar) — The opening symbol of the Mool Mantar, asserting the oneness of the Divine Being; both numeral and sound combined.
  • ਮੂਲ ਮੰਤਰ (Mool Mantar) — The 'root formula' opening Japji Sahib; the foundational theological statement of the Sikh scriptures.
  • ਅਕਾਲ ਮੂਰਤਿ (Akaal Moorat) — 'Form beyond time'; a paradoxical name for the Divine that holds together presence and transcendence.
  • ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ (Gur Prasaad) — 'By the Guru's Grace'; the closing phrase of the Mool Mantar indicating that divine knowledge is received, not achieved.
  • ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ (Naam Simran) — Remembrance and recitation of the Divine Name; the foundational devotional practice of the Sikh tradition.
  • ਨਿਰਗੁਣ / ਸਰਗੁਣ (Nirgun / Sargun) — The Divine beyond qualities (transcendent) and the Divine within qualities (immanent); a paired concept central to Gurbani theology.

Discussion Questions

  1. The Mool Mantar both names the Divine and insists that the Divine exceeds all naming. How does the Garab Ganjani Teeka hold this tension, and is its resolution satisfying to you as a modern reader?
  2. Santokh Singh draws on Vedantic concepts like nirgun and sargun to explain the Mool Mantar. What does this borrowing gain for a student of Gurbani — and what might it obscure?
  3. The phrase ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ places grace at the center of theological knowledge. How does this change the way you approach studying a text like Japji Sahib?
  4. If you were writing your own Teeka of the Mool Mantar for a twenty-first century audience, which attribute would you spend the most time on, and why?

Further Reading

Gurinder Singh Mann, The Making of Sikh Scripture — for the textual and theological formation of the SGGS.

Bhai Vir Singh, Santhya Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji — a modern Punjabi commentary that frequently engages the same passages as Santokh Singh.

Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, The Name of My Beloved: Verses of the Sikh Gurus — for accessible theological reflection on Gurbani's core concepts including the Mool Mantar.

Key Takeaways

  • The Garab Ganjani Teeka treats the Mool Mantar not as a preface but as the theological thesis of the entire Japji Sahib.
  • Santokh Singh uses Vedantic vocabulary (nirgun/sargun) to elaborate the Mool Mantar's attributes, which enriches but also complicates the reading.
  • The phrase ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ anchors the Teeka's entire approach: theological knowledge is ultimately a gift of grace, not an intellectual achievement.
  • The Mool Mantar's treatment of Naam suggests that language is not merely descriptive but participatory — engaging the Name draws the devotee into the reality it names.

Homework

Choose one attribute in the Mool Mantar — such as ਅਕਾਲ ਮੂਰਤਿ (beyond time) or ਅਜੂਨੀ (unborn) — and spend 15 minutes in quiet reflection on what that quality means for how you relate to the Divine in daily life. Then write a 350-word journal entry exploring: How does this attribute challenge or confirm your existing understanding of God? Where do you notice this quality — or its absence — in the world around you?

lessons.title: Haumai and the Human Condition: The Teeka's Anthropology
lessons.html:
Introduction

Every religious tradition has an account of what is wrong with the human being and what must change for liberation or flourishing to become possible. In Japji Sahib and across Gurbani, that account centers on a single Punjabi word: ਹਉਮੈ (haumai). Often translated as ego, pride, or self-will, haumai names something more specific and more pervasive than any of these English approximations suggest. The Garab Ganjani Teeka gives sustained attention to haumai as the central obstacle to ਮੁਕਤੀ (mukti — liberation) and as the lens through which the human condition must be understood.

What makes the Teeka's treatment of haumai distinctive is its integration of philosophical analysis and practical diagnosis. Santokh Singh does not merely define haumai as a theological concept; he traces how it operates at every level of human experience — in the impulse to claim authorship of good deeds, in the attachment to social standing, in the subtle pride that can accompany even religious practice. For students approaching this material, the Teeka's analysis of haumai offers both a philosophical framework and an invitation to honest self-examination.

This lesson explores the Garab Ganjani Teeka's account of haumai: what it is, how it works, how the Teeka's Nirmala framework shapes its reading, and what Japji Sahib proposes as its remedy. We will see that understanding haumai is inseparable from understanding what the Sikh tradition means by grace, Naam, and the Guru's role in human transformation.

Defining Haumai: More Than Ego

The word ਹਉਮੈ (haumai) is built from two Punjabi/Sanskrit roots: 'hau' (I) and 'mai' (also I or mine). The doubling is deliberate and revealing: haumai is not simply having a sense of self but the compulsive, repetitive insistence on that self at the center of all experience. It is the mind that cannot encounter anything — a person, a situation, a teaching, even the Divine — without immediately asking 'What does this mean for me?'

Santokh Singh, drawing on the Nirmala tradition's Vedantic literacy, connects haumai to the concept of अहंकार (ahankar — ego-sense) in Indian philosophical systems. But the Gurbani usage, he is careful to note, carries a more specific moral and spiritual weight. Haumai is not merely the philosophical problem of mistaking the individual self for the ultimate self (as in Advaita Vedanta); it is the practical problem of a will that has turned away from the Divine will and substituted its own agenda.

This distinction matters for how the Teeka reads the remedy. In Vedantic philosophy, the solution to ahankar is primarily cognitive: realize that the individual self is not ultimately real, and the problem dissolves. In Gurbani as read by Santokh Singh, the solution is not primarily cognitive but relational and devotional: the haumai-ridden person must turn toward the Guru, engage the Naam, and submit to ਨਾਦਰ (nadar — the divine glance of grace). Intellectual understanding of haumai, while useful, does not by itself dissolve it.

The Teeka also notes that haumai is self-concealing: the very mind afflicted by haumai is the same mind that tries to analyze and overcome haumai. This is why, for Santokh Singh, the Guru's intervention from outside the self — mediated through Gurbani, through Sangat (holy community), through the practice of Simran — is not optional but structurally necessary.

Haumai in the Pauris of Japji Sahib

The Garab Ganjani Teeka does not treat haumai as an abstract concept but traces it through specific pauris (stanzas) of Japji Sahib. Several pauris address the predicament of the person who performs religious acts — ritual bathing, pilgrimage, fasting, scholarship — but remains trapped in self-referential pride. The Teeka reads these pauris as a systematic dismantling of the assumption that haumai can be resolved through religious effort directed by the ego itself.

This is one of the most theologically searching aspects of the Garab Ganjani Teeka's reading of Japji Sahib. Santokh Singh points out that haumai is subtle enough to inhabit even devotion: the person who recites Gurbani while quietly taking pride in their recitation, the scholar who studies the Teeka while congratulating themselves on their learning, the practitioner who meditates while savoring their own spiritual progress. In each case, haumai has colonized the very activity meant to dissolve it.

The pauris that describe the khandas (realms or planes) — Dharam Khand, Gyan Khand, Saram Khand, Karam Khand, and Sach Khand — are read by the Teeka partly as a map of how haumai progressively loosens its grip as the devotee advances. At the level of Dharam Khand (realm of righteous action), haumai is still strongly operative; action is directed by the self toward divine reward. By Sach Khand (realm of truth), the self has been so thoroughly oriented toward the Divine that individual will and divine will are no longer experienced as separate. The Teeka is careful, however, to insist that this is not the erasure of the person but the fulfillment of the person in the Divine.

The Remedy: Naam, Sangat, and Sevaa

If haumai is the diagnosis, the Garab Ganjani Teeka is clear that the prescription involves three interconnected practices: Naam Simran (ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ — remembrance of the Divine Name), Sangat (ਸੰਗਤ — the holy community), and Sevaa (ਸੇਵਾ — selfless service). Each of these operates as a counterforce to haumai's logic in a specific way.

Naam Simran works against haumai by re-centering attention. The mind habituated to haumai moves perpetually toward self-reference; Simran trains the mind to move toward the Divine. This is not a one-time redirection but a gradual, repeated practice of return — every time the mind wanders back to 'I, me, mine,' Simran redirects it toward 'Waheguru.' Santokh Singh, citing the Nirmala emphasis on the transformative power of sacred sound, argues that this practice is not merely psychological but ontological: the Naam itself carries a purifying power that acts on the devotee's inner state.

Sangat works against haumai by placing the individual in a community of practice where self-assertion is constantly checked by the presence of others walking the same path. The Teeka draws on Gurbani's consistent praise of the Sadh Sangat (ਸਾਧ ਸੰਗਤ) to argue that community is not merely supportive but therapeutically necessary: haumai thrives in isolation and diminishes in the company of those equally committed to the Divine.

Sevaa works against haumai most directly, by training the body and will toward action that produces no personal credit. When one serves the Sangat anonymously — preparing food, cleaning the Gurdwara, caring for the sick — the ego's hunger for recognition finds nothing to feed on. Over time, Santokh Singh suggests, the very habit of self-donation begins to reshape the inner landscape, creating spaces where the Naam can take root.

Key Terms

  • ਹਉਮੈ (Haumai) — Ego-will; the compulsive self-referencing that the Sikh tradition identifies as the root of human suffering and separation from the Divine.
  • ਮੁਕਤੀ (Mukti) — Liberation; freedom from the cycle of suffering and rebirth, achieved through grace and Naam in the Sikh tradition.
  • ਨਾਦਰ (Nadar) — The divine glance of grace; the unearned gift of divine attention that initiates or sustains the devotee's spiritual journey.
  • ਸਾਧ ਸੰਗਤ (Sadh Sangat) — The holy congregation; the community of practitioners whose company is held in Gurbani to be a vehicle of purification.
  • ਸੇਵਾ (Sevaa) — Selfless service; a central Sikh practice that counteracts haumai by directing effort toward others without expectation of reward.
  • ਅਹੰਕਾਰ (Ahankar) — Sanskrit/Punjabi term for ego-sense; used in Indian philosophy broadly but given a specific devotional-ethical meaning in Gurbani.

Discussion Questions

  1. Santokh Singh argues that haumai can inhabit even religious practice — devotion, scholarship, and service can all become vehicles for ego. Do you find this claim convincing? What safeguards does the Sikh tradition offer against this subtle form of haumai?
  2. How does the Garab Ganjani Teeka's reading of haumai compare with how the concept of ego is addressed in another tradition you are familiar with — Buddhist, Christian, Islamic, or secular psychological?
  3. The Teeka suggests that intellectual understanding of haumai does not dissolve it — only Naam, Sangat, and Sevaa can do that. What does this imply about the limits and proper place of a Teeka (commentary) in Sikh learning?

Further Reading

W.H. McLeod, Guru Nanak and the Sikh Religion — contains careful analysis of the theological anthropology in early Sikh thought including haumai.

Daljeet Singh, Essentials of Sikhism — a concise account of Sikh theological anthropology including the role of haumai and grace.

Arvind-Pal Singh Mandair, Religion and the Specter of the West — for a critical philosophical analysis of concepts like selfhood and ego in the Sikh tradition.

Key Takeaways

  • Haumai (ਹਉਮੈ) names not mere pride but the pervasive self-referencing that the Sikh tradition sees as the root of human separation from the Divine.
  • The Garab Ganjani Teeka reads haumai as subtler than ego in the ordinary sense — it can inhabit even devotional and scholarly activity.
  • The remedy proposed by the Teeka involves Naam Simran, Sangat, and Sevaa as structurally necessary — not optional supplements — to spiritual transformation.
  • Santokh Singh's Nirmala framework connects haumai to Vedantic ahankar but insists that Gurbani's remedy is relational and devotional rather than primarily cognitive.

Homework

Sit quietly for 10 minutes and observe, without judgment, the moments during that time when your mind asserts 'I want,' 'I think,' or 'I know.' Afterward, write a 350-word reflection on what you noticed. Where does ਹਉਮੈ (haumai) show up most persistently for you — in relationships, in work, in learning? Then describe one specific daily practice — it need not be religious — that you believe could gently loosen that grip over time.

lessons.title: The Five Khandas: Mapping the Spiritual Journey
lessons.html:
Introduction

Among the most remarkable passages in Japji Sahib are the pauris that describe five progressively elevated realms or planes of spiritual existence: Dharam Khand, Gyan Khand, Saram Khand, Karam Khand, and Sach Khand. These five khandas (ਖੰਡ — realms or domains) have fascinated commentators, practitioners, and scholars alike because they offer something relatively rare in the Sikh scriptural tradition: a structured map of the spiritual journey. Understanding how the Garab Ganjani Teeka interprets these realms is central to understanding Santokh Singh's overall theological vision.

The Nirmala tradition in which Santokh Singh was trained had extensive exposure to Indian philosophical frameworks — including the cosmological and soteriological hierarchies found in Vedanta, Yoga, and Tantric literature. The question of how much these frameworks shaped his reading of the khandas is one of the most contested in the scholarly study of his Teeka. This lesson examines his interpretation carefully, noting where it illuminates the Gurbani and where it may import categories that sit uneasily with Guru Nanak's own formulations.

Students should approach this lesson with dual attention: absorbing Santokh Singh's rich philosophical elaboration of the khandas while also developing their own critical sensibility about the interpretive choices he makes. The five khandas are not merely an intellectual map — they are also a devotional invitation, and the Teeka at its best holds both registers simultaneously.

Dharam Khand and Gyan Khand: Earth and Cosmos

Dharam Khand (ਧਰਮ ਖੰਡ — the realm of righteousness or duty) is the starting point of the journey mapped in Japji Sahib. The Garab Ganjani Teeka reads this realm as the domain in which the soul first awakens to the existence of moral order — the recognition that actions have consequences, that the created world operates according to divine law (ਧਰਮ), and that the human being is accountable within that order. Santokh Singh connects this to the concept of karma, but in a distinctively Gurbani-inflected way: karma here is not an impersonal mechanical law but operates within a universe watched over by a living, gracious Creator.

The description of Dharam Khand in Japji Sahib includes a vision of the cosmos — countless worlds, suns, moons, and living beings — that the Teeka reads as an invitation to awe. For Santokh Singh, the sheer vastness of creation described in this pauri is itself a spiritual argument: confronted with this immensity, the haumai-driven assumption that the individual self is the center of reality becomes untenable. The cosmos is the first classroom in which the soul learns its actual proportion.

Gyan Khand (ਗਿਆਨ ਖੰਡ — the realm of knowledge) is described in Japji Sahib through an even more expansive cosmic vision — winds, waters, fires, and living beings in their innumerable varieties, all sustained by the Creator. The Teeka reads Gyan Khand as the realm in which the soul begins to perceive the divine intelligence woven through all creation. This is not book-learning but experiential insight: the devotee begins to see that every creature, every element, every process is an expression of the same divine creativity declared in the Mool Mantar.

Santokh Singh's elaboration of Gyan Khand draws heavily on Vedantic descriptions of cosmic consciousness, and here the student must exercise some critical awareness. While the Nirmala framework enriches the philosophical texture of the commentary, it can sometimes shift the emphasis from the relational encounter with a personal Divine (which Gurbani consistently emphasizes) toward a more impersonal vision of cosmic intelligence. The Teeka's best moments in this section are those where Santokh Singh returns to the Gurbani's own language of loving encounter with Waheguru.

Saram Khand and Karam Khand: Beauty and Power

Saram Khand (ਸਰਮ ਖੰਡ — the realm of effort or beauty) represents a significant shift in register. The Japji Sahib describes this realm in terms of the shaping and refining of the devotee's inner being — the ਮਨ (man — mind), ਬੁਧਿ (budh — intellect), and ਸੁਰਤਿ (surat — awareness) are all described as being 'fashioned' or 'crafted' in Saram Khand. The Teeka reads this as the stage of spiritual formation in which the divine grace actively works on the interior life of the practitioner, reshaping the capacities through which the soul perceives and responds to reality.

This is one of the most theologically rich passages in the Garab Ganjani Teeka's treatment of the khandas. Santokh Singh insists that the shaping that occurs in Saram Khand is not the product of the devotee's own discipline alone — it is the work of grace acting through practice. The practitioner engages seriously with Naam Simran, Gurbani recitation, and Sevaa, but the transformative result is a divine gift, not an achievement. This keeps the Teeka's account of spiritual progress from becoming a self-improvement program and roots it firmly in Sikh theology's insistence on ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ (prasaad — grace).

Karam Khand (ਕਰਮ ਖੰਡ — the realm of grace or divine action) is where the language of Japji Sahib becomes most explicitly devotional. The Teeka describes this realm as populated by the great devotees — warriors of spiritual strength, beings saturated with divine praise — and reads this as pointing toward the transformation of the devotee into someone whose entire being has become an instrument of divine expression. The 'warriors' of Karam Khand are not military figures but souls whose inner battles against haumai have been won through grace.

Santokh Singh's commentary here draws on the tradition of Bhakti — the path of loving devotion — and connects the great devotees of Karam Khand to historical and legendary figures of intense divine love. This is one of the places where the Nirmala tradition's broad education enriches rather than distorts the commentary: by locating Sikh devotion within the larger river of Indian bhakti, the Teeka helps readers see the distinctiveness of Guru Nanak's formulation precisely by contrast with what came before.

Sach Khand: The Realm of Truth

Sach Khand (ਸੱਚ ਖੰਡ — the realm of truth) is the culminating realm described in Japji Sahib, and Santokh Singh's treatment of it in the Garab Ganjani Teeka is among the most carefully composed sections of the entire commentary. The language of Japji Sahib in describing Sach Khand becomes both more vivid and more resistant to systematic paraphrase — the text speaks of the ਨਿਰੰਕਾਰ (Nirankaar — the Formless One) dwelling there, of countless beings in their many forms living in divine presence, of something that can only be described in its effects, not its substance.

The Teeka's challenge in this section is significant: how does one write prose commentary on a passage that explicitly exceeds the capacity of language? Santokh Singh's response is to allow the commentary to thin out at exactly this point — he provides philosophical scaffolding up to the threshold of Sach Khand, then acknowledges that the threshold itself cannot be crossed by any scholarly apparatus. The devotee must be led to the edge; the entry is by grace alone. This self-aware restraint is one of the most mature moments in the Garab Ganjani Teeka as a piece of religious writing.

Sach Khand in the Teeka is not a distant heavenly realm but the ground of all being — the state in which the soul rests in unobstructed awareness of its unity with the Divine. Importantly, Santokh Singh does not describe this as the annihilation of individuality but as its fulfillment. The devotee in Sach Khand is not dissolved but perfected — fully themselves because fully aligned with the One who created them. This nuance distinguishes the Garab Ganjani Teeka's soteriology from purely non-dualist accounts and reflects the distinctively Sikh insistence that the creation (and the creature) remain real even in divine union.

Key Terms

  • ਖੰਡ (Khand) — Realm or domain; the five khandas in Japji Sahib describe progressive stages of spiritual development.
  • ਧਰਮ ਖੰਡ (Dharam Khand) — Realm of righteousness; the stage of moral awakening and awareness of divine law.
  • ਸਰਮ ਖੰਡ (Saram Khand) — Realm of effort/beauty; the stage of interior spiritual formation by divine grace.
  • ਸੱਚ ਖੰਡ (Sach Khand) — Realm of truth; the culminating state of union with the Divine, described as the dwelling of the Formless One.
  • ਨਿਰੰਕਾਰ (Nirankaar) — The Formless One; a name for the Divine emphasizing transcendence beyond any fixed form.
  • ਸੁਰਤਿ (Surat) — Spiritual awareness or consciousness; one of the inner faculties described as being refined in Saram Khand.

Discussion Questions

  1. The five khandas offer a hierarchical map of spiritual progress. Does a hierarchical framework fit comfortably with the Sikh teaching of the equality of all souls? How might the Teeka address this tension?
  2. Santokh Singh's commentary becomes more restrained and less systematic as it approaches Sach Khand. What does this tell us about the relationship between language and spiritual experience in the Nirmala tradition?
  3. Compare the khandas framework with a spiritual map from another tradition you know — the Sufi maqamat (stations), the Buddhist bhumis (grounds), or the Christian mystical ladder. What do the similarities and differences reveal?
  4. If the entry into Sach Khand is entirely by grace and cannot be earned, what is the purpose of the long process of practice described in the preceding khandas?

Further Reading

Sher Singh, The Philosophy of Sikhism — includes a chapter-length analysis of the five khandas and their theological significance.

Pashaura Singh, The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority — for the textual and theological context of the khandas passages.

Trilochan Singh et al., Selections from the Sacred Writings of the Sikhs — for accessible translations of the khandas passages alongside theological commentary.

Key Takeaways

  • The five khandas (Dharam, Gyan, Saram, Karam, Sach) provide the closest thing to a systematic spiritual map in Japji Sahib, and the Garab Ganjani Teeka gives them extended philosophical attention.
  • Santokh Singh draws on Vedantic and Bhakti frameworks to elaborate the khandas but maintains the distinctively Sikh emphasis on grace as the operative power at every stage.
  • The Teeka deliberately restrains itself at the threshold of Sach Khand, acknowledging that the ultimate reality exceeds commentary — a theologically significant act of humility.
  • The soul's journey through the khandas is not the erasure of individuality but its fulfillment in alignment with the Divine will.

Homework

Read the pauris of Japji Sahib that describe the five khandas (the sections beginning with 'Dharam Khand') slowly and at least twice — once silently and once aloud. Without consulting a commentary, write a 300-word reflection on what each realm evokes for you. Then write a second paragraph of 150 words describing where you feel you currently are in that journey, and what you sense is the next step forward for you personally.

lessons.title: Hukam: Divine Order and Human Freedom
lessons.html:
Introduction

One of the most theologically charged concepts in all of Gurbani is ਹੁਕਮ (Hukam) — the divine order, will, or command. Japji Sahib engages Hukam from its very first pauri, and the Garab Ganjani Teeka treats it as one of the foundational organizing principles of Guru Nanak's theological vision. Understanding Hukam is not merely an academic exercise; it reshapes how the Sikh devotee understands their own agency, their place in the cosmos, and the nature of their relationship with the Divine.

The concept raises an ancient and urgent question: if everything operates under Hukam — if every soul, every event, every moment of suffering and every moment of grace is already within the divine order — what space remains for human freedom, responsibility, and choice? This is the classic tension between divine sovereignty and human agency, and it appears in every major religious tradition. What is remarkable about Gurbani's treatment of Hukam, and about the Garab Ganjani Teeka's elaboration of it, is the particular resolution offered — one that neither collapses into fatalism nor retreats into mere voluntarism.

This lesson examines the Teeka's reading of Hukam in detail: its philosophical definition, its relationship to the concepts of ਮਨਮੁਖ (Manmukh — self-directed) and ਗੁਰਮੁਖ (Gurmukh — Guru-directed) modes of living, and its practical implications for Sikh devotional life. We will also consider how the Nirmala tradition's philosophical resources shape Santokh Singh's interpretation.

Hukam as Cosmic Architecture

The Garab Ganjani Teeka begins its treatment of Hukam by establishing it as something larger than a divine command given on particular occasions. Hukam, for Santokh Singh, is the very structure within which existence unfolds — the laws of nature, the moral order, the grammar of causation, the patterns of karma, and the movements of grace are all expressions of a single divine ordering principle. In this sense, Hukam is less like a royal decree and more like the gravitational field that holds the cosmos together: omnipresent, inescapable, and ultimately benevolent.

The Teeka draws on the concept of ਰਜ਼ਾ (raza — divine pleasure or will, a term also used in Islamic mystical literature) and connects it to the Sanskrit concept of ऋत (rita — cosmic order) to show that Guru Nanak's use of Hukam participates in a broader South Asian and Semitic theological tradition while also transforming it. The distinctively Sikh inflection, Santokh Singh argues, is that Hukam is not simply a law that operates from outside the creation but is the living presence of the Creator within it. Hukam is how Waheguru speaks continuously to and through the created order.

This has a significant implication for how the Teeka reads suffering and injustice. If everything is within Hukam, does that mean suffering is divinely willed? Santokh Singh's answer, following Gurbani's own lead, is nuanced: the experience of suffering is real, but the ultimate significance of every experience is reframed within the context of divine purpose. Suffering does not indicate divine indifference but often signals a soul being prepared — through difficulty — to release its grip on haumai and turn toward the Divine. The Teeka does not offer a simple theodicy but a devotional reorientation: the question shifts from 'Why is this happening to me?' to 'How is this calling me toward the Divine?'

Manmukh and Gurmukh: Two Modes of Living Within Hukam

The most practically significant section of the Garab Ganjani Teeka's treatment of Hukam involves the paired concepts of ਮਨਮੁਖ (Manmukh) and ਗੁਰਮੁਖ (Gurmukh). These terms appear throughout Gurbani and are treated by the Teeka as describing not two types of people but two orientations — two ways of inhabiting the same life, the same Hukam.

The Manmukh (literally 'face toward the self' or 'self-directed') is the person who lives within Hukam but does not know it. They experience the vicissitudes of life — gain and loss, pleasure and pain — as random fortune or as the result of their own cleverness and effort. Their reference point is always the self, its preferences, its fears, its ambitions. They are not outside Hukam — nothing can be outside Hukam — but they are unaware of it, and that ignorance is itself the source of their suffering.

The Gurmukh (literally 'face toward the Guru') is the person who has turned the face of their awareness toward the Guru's teaching and, through that reorientation, has come to recognize and accept Hukam. Crucially, for Santokh Singh, this does not mean passive resignation. The Gurmukh is intensely active — in Simran, in Sevaa, in the life of the Sangat — but acts without the frantic self-assertion of haumai. Their activity is an expression of alignment with Hukam rather than a struggle against it. The Teeka describes this state through the image of the swimmer who, rather than fighting the current, learns its movement and flows with it — arriving farther and faster than any amount of desperate thrashing would allow.

Hukam and the Practice of Acceptance

The Garab Ganjani Teeka concludes its treatment of Hukam with a sustained reflection on the practical spiritual discipline of ਭਾਣਾ ਮੰਨਣਾ (bhaana mannaana — accepting the divine will). This practice, central to Sikh devotional life, is easily misunderstood as fatalistic passivity; the Teeka is at pains to distinguish it from both fatalism and from the kind of forced positivity that simply denies the reality of pain.

Santokh Singh argues that bhaana mannaana is an active, disciplined, and transformative practice. It requires the devotee to continually release the ego's insistence that things should be other than they are — not because things are always pleasant, but because the Divine will operating within all circumstances is ultimately oriented toward the soul's liberation. This release is not a single decision but a daily, sometimes moment-to-moment practice, and the Teeka is realistic about its difficulty. The devotee who finds bhaana mannaana easy has not yet understood what it asks.

The connection to Hukam is direct: to practice bhaana mannaana is to align the individual will with Hukam rather than resist it. And this alignment, the Teeka insists, is not the erasure of the individual but its liberation — the moment when the person stops spending their energy in futile resistance and begins to experience the peace that the Mool Mantar describes as a quality of the Divine itself. Santokh Singh calls this the experiential entry into what Japji Sahib means by Sach Khand: not a place one travels to, but a quality of awareness available to the Gurmukh here and now.

Key Terms

  • ਹੁਕਮ (Hukam) — Divine order, will, or command; the all-encompassing principle within which all existence unfolds according to the Garab Ganjani Teeka.
  • ਮਨਮੁਖ (Manmukh) — Self-directed; the mode of living in which the self remains the primary reference point, unaware of Hukam.
  • ਗੁਰਮੁਖ (Gurmukh) — Guru-directed; the mode of living in which awareness is oriented toward the Guru's teaching and aligned with Hukam.
  • ਭਾਣਾ ਮੰਨਣਾ (Bhaana Mannaana) — Accepting the divine will; an active spiritual discipline of releasing ego-resistance to Hukam.
  • ਰਜ਼ਾ (Raza) — Divine pleasure or will; a term with Sufi resonances used in the Teeka to illuminate the personal dimension of Hukam.
  • ਨਾਦਰ (Nadar) — Divine grace or glance; the gracious attention of the Creator that enables the soul to recognize and align with Hukam.

Discussion Questions

  1. The Garab Ganjani Teeka distinguishes between the Manmukh who is inside Hukam unknowingly and the Gurmukh who lives within Hukam consciously. Is this distinction ultimately about knowledge, practice, or something else? What does it imply about the nature of spiritual transformation?
  2. Bhaana mannaana (accepting divine will) is presented as active and transformative rather than passive. Can you think of examples — from Sikh history, or from your own experience — where this kind of acceptance required more courage than resistance would have?
  3. The Teeka reads suffering as potentially purposive within Hukam. How do you respond to this theologically? Does it resonate with or challenge your own understanding of why difficult things happen?

Further Reading

Harbans Singh, The Heritage of the Sikhs — includes accessible theological discussion of Hukam and its practical implications.

Bhai Vir Singh, Guru Nanak Chamatkar — narrative elaboration of Guru Nanak's teachings including his vision of divine order.

J.S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab — for the historical context in which Sikh theology including the doctrine of Hukam developed.

Key Takeaways

  • Hukam (ਹੁਕਮ) in the Garab Ganjani Teeka is not a series of divine commands but the very structure of existence — the living order within which all creation moves.
  • The Manmukh/Gurmukh distinction describes two modes of inhabiting Hukam: unaware resistance versus conscious alignment.
  • Bhaana mannaana (accepting divine will) is presented as an active, demanding spiritual practice — not fatalism but the disciplined release of ego-resistance.
  • The Teeka's treatment of Hukam offers a distinctive resolution to the tension between divine sovereignty and human freedom: both are real, and spiritual maturity consists in learning to act freely from within alignment with Hukam rather than against it.

Homework

Spend 15 minutes reading the opening pauris of Japji Sahib slowly, paying particular attention to wherever the concept of ਹੁਕਮ (Hukam) appears explicitly or implicitly. Then write a 350-word reflection on this question: If everything operates under divine Hukam, what role does your own effort and choice play in your spiritual life? Draw on at least one specific experience from your own life — a moment when you felt either in alignment with or in resistance to something larger than yourself.

lessons.title: Naam: The Name as Presence, Practice, and Reality
lessons.html:
Introduction

If haumai is the central diagnosis in Japji Sahib, and Hukam is the cosmic framework within which all souls live, then ਨਾਮੁ (Naam — the Divine Name) is the central medicine. Naam appears throughout Japji Sahib with a frequency and theological weight that no student of the text can ignore, and the Garab Ganjani Teeka treats it as the keystone of Guru Nanak's entire spiritual teaching. To understand what Santokh Singh means by Naam is to understand what kind of text the Teeka believes Japji Sahib to be.

The word 'naam' is deceptively simple — it means 'name' in both Sanskrit and Punjabi. But Gurbani uses it in a register that far exceeds ordinary naming. The Naam in Japji Sahib is not simply a label for the Divine but a living reality, a mode of divine self-disclosure, a vehicle of encounter, and a transformative power that operates on the devotee who engages it through ਸਿਮਰਨ (Simran — contemplative remembrance). Grasping this distinction between Naam as word and Naam as presence is essential for reading the Garab Ganjani Teeka with understanding.

This lesson traces the Teeka's theology of Naam through three dimensions: Naam as ontological reality (what the Naam is in itself), Naam as practice (how the devotee engages it), and Naam as transformation (what it does to the one who receives it). Throughout, we will attend to how Santokh Singh's Nirmala training shapes his elaboration and where it enriches or complicates the Gurbani's own formulations.

Naam as Ontological Reality

The Garab Ganjani Teeka's most philosophically ambitious claim about Naam is that it is not merely a name given by human beings to a Divine reality that exists independently of that naming. Rather, Naam is one of the primary ways in which the Divine becomes accessible to creation. The Divine in itself — as ੴ, as Nirankar — exceeds all human approach; the Naam is the bridge, the form through which the formless becomes relationally present.

Santokh Singh draws here on the Nirmala tradition's engagement with Sanskrit theories of śabda (sacred sound) — the idea, found in both Mimamsa and Vedantic philosophy, that sacred sound is not a human invention but a cosmic reality that precedes and grounds ordinary language. In this framework, the Naam is not something human devotees created to refer to God; it is a dimension of divine self-expression that human beings can tune into through practice. The Teeka reads this as consistent with Gurbani's insistence that the Naam existed before creation and will persist after it — it is co-eternal with the Divine itself.

This has significant implications for the practice of Simran. If the Naam is an ontological reality and not merely a word, then repeating it is not self-suggestion or meditation technique in the modern psychological sense — it is participatory entry into a divine reality that is already present and already active. The devotee who engages Naam through Simran is, in the Teeka's vision, aligning their own consciousness with a frequency of divine presence that pervades the cosmos. This is why Santokh Singh describes the effect of Naam practice in such strong terms: it cleanses the inner being, dissolves haumai, and progressively aligns the soul with Hukam.

Students should note that this ontological account of Naam is one of the places where the Garab Ganjani Teeka has been most debated by later Sikh scholars. Some critics argue that the Nirmala framework imports too much from Sanskrit śabda theory and risks making Naam into a kind of magical cosmic force rather than the deeply personal, relational encounter with Waheguru that Gurbani consistently emphasizes. This is a genuine tension, and the best reading of the Teeka holds both dimensions together.

Naam as Practice: The Discipline of Simran

The Garab Ganjani Teeka is not merely a philosophical treatise — it is also a practical guide, and its treatment of Naam as practice is among its most detailed and practically useful sections. Santokh Singh describes the practice of Naam Simran (ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ) with a precision that reflects deep personal familiarity with contemplative life as well as textual learning.

The Teeka distinguishes between several modes of Simran: vocal repetition (ਜਪਣਾ — reciting the Naam aloud), mental repetition (ਮਨ ਵਿੱਚ ਜਪਣਾ — reciting within the mind), and the state of ਅਜਪਾ ਜਾਪ (ajapa jaap — the prayer that recites itself, where Simran has become so deeply embedded that it continues spontaneously without deliberate effort). This progression is not a mechanical technique but a description of how the relationship between the devotee and the Naam deepens over time.

The role of the Guru in Naam practice receives particular emphasis in the Teeka. Santokh Singh follows Gurbani in insisting that Naam is not self-administered — it is received from or through the Guru. This does not mean that every act of Simran requires the physical presence of a human teacher; in the Sikh tradition, Guru Granth Sahib is the living Guru, and engaging with Gurbani is itself the form through which the Naam is transmitted. But it does mean that Simran without the Guru's grace — without the orienting influence of Gurbani and Sangat — can become merely mechanical repetition without transformative effect.

Naam as Transformation

The culminating section of the Garab Ganjani Teeka's treatment of Naam describes what it does to the devotee over time. Santokh Singh uses a rich set of images drawn from both Gurbani and the broader Indian literary tradition: Naam as medicine that heals the disease of haumai; Naam as dye that colors the consciousness permanently; Naam as light that illumines the interior darkness of the separated soul; Naam as the river in which the soul, bathing repeatedly, becomes pure.

Each of these images captures a different dimension of Naam's transformative work. As medicine, Naam addresses a specific condition — not general ignorance but the specific affliction of ego-separation from the Divine. As dye, Naam suggests permanence: the consciousness that has been 'dyed' in the Naam cannot return to its original colorless state. The Teeka is notably realistic here — it does not promise that Naam practice produces quick results or dramatic experiences, but insists that gradual, persistent engagement accumulates a transformation that ultimately cannot be reversed.

The Garab Ganjani Teeka's final word on Naam returns to grace. All of the practice, all of the Simran, all of the community life and service — these are the conditions in which grace can work, but they do not compel it. The devotee who has engaged Naam most deeply, the Teeka insists, is also the one most aware that the transformation they have undergone is not their own achievement but the gift of the One whose Naam they have been reciting. This awareness — that the Naam has been doing the work all along — is itself the sign that the medicine is working.

Key Terms

  • ਨਾਮੁ (Naam) — The Divine Name; in Gurbani, not merely a label but a living reality and vehicle of divine presence.
  • ਸਿਮਰਨ (Simran) — Contemplative remembrance or recitation of the Naam; the central devotional practice of the Sikh tradition.
  • ਅਜਪਾ ਜਾਪ (Ajapa Jaap) — The prayer that recites itself; the state of advanced Simran in which Naam awareness becomes continuous and spontaneous.
  • ਸ਼ਬਦ (Shabad) — Divine Word or sacred hymn; in the Teeka, closely related to Naam as a form of divine self-expression accessible through Gurbani.
  • ਰੰਗ (Rang) — Color or dye; used metaphorically in Gurbani and the Teeka to describe the permanent transformation of consciousness by Naam.
  • ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ (Amrit) — Nectar of immortality; a term for Naam in its life-giving and purifying dimension in Gurbani and Sikh devotional practice.

Discussion Questions

  1. The Garab Ganjani Teeka claims that Naam is an ontological reality, not merely a word. Does this claim make the practice of Simran more or less meaningful for you? What philosophical or experiential questions does it raise?
  2. Santokh Singh distinguishes between vocal Simran, mental Simran, and ajapa jaap. How do these three stages relate to each other, and what does the progression suggest about the nature of spiritual development in the Sikh tradition?
  3. The Teeka insists that Naam cannot be self-administered — it must be received through the Guru's grace. How does this shape your understanding of the role of Gurbani and Sangat in Naam practice?
  4. Compare the Teeka's account of Naam's transformative effect (as medicine, dye, light, river) with a parallel account from another tradition. What does the comparison reveal about what is distinctive in the Sikh theological vision?

Further Reading

Gurinder Singh Mann, Sikhism (Prentice Hall) — concise overview of Naam theology in the Sikh tradition with textual references.

Bhai Vir Singh, Santhya Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji — for a modern Punjabi commentary's treatment of Naam passages, useful comparison with Santokh Singh.

Christopher Shackle and Arvind Mandair (eds.), Teachings of the Sikh Gurus — for selected Gurbani passages on Naam in translation with scholarly annotation.

Key Takeaways

  • Naam in the Garab Ganjani Teeka is treated as an ontological reality — a form of divine self-disclosure — not merely a word that refers to God from the outside.
  • Santokh Singh describes a progression in Simran from vocal recitation to mental recitation to the spontaneous, continuous awareness of ajapa jaap.
  • The Teeka insists that Naam cannot be self-administered: it is received through the Guru's grace, mediated through Gurbani and Sangat.
  • Naam's transformative effect is described through multiple images (medicine, dye, light, river), each capturing a different dimension of how engagement with the Naam reshapes the devotee's inner life over time.

Homework

Choose one of the following and engage with it for 20 minutes: (a) Sit in quiet Naam Simran (ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ), silently repeating 'Waheguru' or another form of Naam that is meaningful to you. (b) Read a shabad from SGGS that speaks directly about the power or experience of Naam — select it by theme, not a specific Ang number you may not be sure of. Afterward, write a 350-word reflection: What happened in your mind, body, and awareness during this practice or reading? Where did you find it easy, and where did resistance arise? What does the experience tell you about what the Garab Ganjani Teeka means when it says the Naam is not just a label but a participatory reality?

lessons.title: The Teeka's Legacy: Reception, Critique, and Continuing Relevance
lessons.html:
Introduction

Every major text generates a history of reception — a record of how subsequent generations have read, used, debated, and transformed it. The Garab Ganjani Teeka is no exception. Since Kavi Santokh Singh completed it in the nineteenth century, it has been praised, challenged, translated, selectively appropriated, and sometimes vigorously contested. Understanding that history is not merely an academic exercise; it shapes how a modern student reads the Teeka today and what they can reasonably expect from it.

This final lesson of the course takes a step back from the Teeka's content to examine its life in the world. We will look at how the Teeka was received in the decades following its composition, how the Singh Sabha reform movement of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries complicated its status, how it has been used (and misused) in twentieth and twenty-first century Sikh education, and what a genuinely critical but respectful engagement with it might look like going forward.

Throughout the course, we have engaged the Garab Ganjani Teeka as a text worthy of serious academic and devotional attention. This lesson does not retreat from that judgment, but it asks students to hold it alongside an equally serious account of the Teeka's limits — historical, philosophical, and hermeneutical. A tradition that cannot honestly assess its own commentarial heritage is a tradition that risks being imprisoned by it rather than enriched by it.

Early Reception and the Singh Sabha Challenge

In the decades immediately following its composition, the Garab Ganjani Teeka enjoyed considerable prestige within Sikh scholarly circles, particularly among those with Nirmala training and a high valuation of Sanskrit learning. Santokh Singh's reputation as a poet of the first order — author of the massive Suraj Prakash Granth — lent his prose commentary significant authority. The Teeka was studied in the traditional educational settings of the time, where Gurbani learning proceeded through direct teacher-student transmission rather than printed books.

The Singh Sabha movement, which gained momentum in the 1870s and 1880s, changed the landscape significantly. Singh Sabha reformers were broadly critical of what they saw as the Brahmanical and Vedantic accretions that had accumulated around Sikh practice and interpretation over the preceding centuries. For many Singh Sabha scholars, the Garab Ganjani Teeka — with its Nirmala framework, its Sanskrit vocabulary, and its extensive parallels with Hindu philosophical texts — represented precisely the kind of interpretive overlay they sought to strip away in order to recover what they believed to be the authentic, distinct theology of Guru Nanak.

This critique was not entirely without merit, but it was also not entirely fair. The Singh Sabha reaction sometimes overcorrected, treating any use of Sanskrit philosophical vocabulary as evidence of corruption rather than recognizing that Guru Nanak himself used shared vocabularies of his time precisely to communicate across religious boundaries. The Garab Ganjani Teeka became a kind of contested symbol in the broader debate about Sikh identity and the boundaries of authentic Sikh interpretation — a debate that, in various forms, continues to this day.

Twentieth-Century Use and Selective Appropriation

By the twentieth century, the Garab Ganjani Teeka occupied an interesting position in Sikh literary culture: widely respected but rarely read in full, frequently cited in part, and sometimes used as a proof-text for positions its author might not have endorsed. This pattern of selective appropriation is common in the history of religious commentary — texts tend to be read in fragments, with readers gravitating toward the passages that confirm their existing views and passing quickly over those that do not.

The partial printing and distribution of the Teeka in the twentieth century meant that many Sikh readers encountered only portions of it, often already filtered through the lens of editors and publishers who had their own theological agendas. Modern students who approach the Garab Ganjani Teeka through secondary sources — summaries, quotations in other works, digital excerpts — should be aware that what they are reading may not represent the full complexity of Santokh Singh's thought. Reading the Teeka directly, even in translation, offers a very different experience from reading about it.

The twentieth century also saw new scholarly engagement with the Teeka from academic historians and theologians, both Sikh and non-Sikh. These scholars brought tools of historical criticism, comparative religion, and literary analysis to the Teeka, producing nuanced assessments that neither simply endorsed it as authoritative nor dismissed it as corrupted. This scholarly tradition — represented by figures in universities in India, North America, and the UK — provides modern students with a more rigorous framework for engaging the Teeka than either uncritical veneration or reflexive dismissal can offer.

The Teeka's Continuing Relevance

Having surveyed the Garab Ganjani Teeka's history of reception and critique, we return to the question with which this course began: what is this text for, and what can a modern student — Sikh or otherwise, scholar or devotee — reasonably expect from it? The answer, after the sustained engagement of this course, should be more textured than it was at the outset.

The Garab Ganjani Teeka remains relevant for several reasons that have nothing to do with claiming it is infallible. First, it is the most philosophically ambitious Punjabi prose commentary on Japji Sahib from the pre-modern Sikh tradition, and no student who wants to understand how Japji Sahib was read by learned Sikhs in the nineteenth century can afford to ignore it. Second, its Nirmala framework — whatever its limitations — preserves a record of the intellectual encounter between Sikh theology and the broader South Asian philosophical tradition that has historical and theological importance. Third, and perhaps most importantly for devotional readers, many of its elaborations — especially on Naam, Hukam, haumai, and the khandas — are genuinely illuminating even when read critically.

What a modern student owes the Garab Ganjani Teeka is neither uncritical acceptance nor dismissive rejection but something more demanding: engaged, critical, generous reading. This means bringing to it the same scholarly tools we would bring to any serious religious text — attention to historical context, awareness of the author's ideological commitments, sensitivity to where the text's internal logic produces genuine insight and where it strains under the weight of its own assumptions. It also means remaining open to the moments when, despite all the historical and philosophical distance, the Teeka says something about Japji Sahib that lands with the force of genuine illumination.

Key Terms

  • ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ (Singh Sabha) — The late nineteenth-century Sikh reform movement that sought to purify Sikh practice and interpretation from what it saw as Hindu accretions.
  • ਟੀਕਾ (Teeka) — Prose commentary; a genre of explanatory writing on sacred text with a long history in South Asian religious traditions.
  • ਹਰਮੇਨਿਊਟਿਕਸ (Hermeneutics) — The theory and practice of interpretation; the field of inquiry concerned with how texts are read and what makes a reading legitimate.
  • ਸੰਪ੍ਰਦਾ (Sampradaa) — Tradition or school of interpretation; refers to the lineages through which religious knowledge and interpretive methods are transmitted.
  • ਨਿਰਮਲਾ (Nirmala) — The Sikh scholarly tradition founded by Guru Gobind Singh Ji that combined Sikh and Sanskrit learning; the tradition within which Santokh Singh wrote.
  • ਵਿਆਕਰਣ (Vyaakaran) — Grammar; the technical study of language that underpins classical South Asian commentary traditions including the Garab Ganjani Teeka.

Discussion Questions

  1. The Singh Sabha movement critiqued the Garab Ganjani Teeka for importing Vedantic categories into Sikh interpretation. Was this critique fair? How would you adjudicate between the Singh Sabha position and a defense of the Nirmala approach?
  2. This course has used the Garab Ganjani Teeka as both a theological resource and an object of critical study. Do these two modes of engagement — devotional and critical — sit comfortably together for you, or do they create tension? How do you navigate that tension?
  3. If you were designing a curriculum for a contemporary Sikh educational institution, where would the Garab Ganjani Teeka fit — as a primary text, a supplementary resource, or a historical artifact? What would justify your choice?
  4. What does the history of the Teeka's reception — including the Singh Sabha critique and the twentieth-century selective appropriation — teach us about how all religious communities relate to their commentarial heritage?

Further Reading

Harjot Oberoi, The Construction of Religious Boundaries — for the Singh Sabha movement and the broader debate about Sikh identity in the colonial period.

Pashaura Singh, Life and Work of Guru Arjan — for the scholarly methodology useful for approaching classical Sikh texts with both rigor and respect.

Gurbachan Singh Talib, Japuji: The Immortal Prayer Chant — for a twentieth-century scholarly translation of Japji Sahib that can be compared with the Teeka's interpretive choices.

Key Takeaways

  • The Garab Ganjani Teeka has had a complex reception history — initially prestigious, then contested by Singh Sabha reformers, then partially rehabilitated by twentieth-century scholars.
  • The Singh Sabha critique of the Teeka's Nirmala framework raised legitimate questions but sometimes overcorrected, treating shared philosophical vocabulary as inherently corrupting.
  • Modern engagement with the Teeka requires critical generosity — neither uncritical acceptance nor dismissive rejection, but careful, contextual reading.
  • The Teeka's continuing relevance lies in its philosophical depth, its historical importance as a record of Sikh-Sanskrit intellectual encounter, and the genuine illumination it offers on key Gurbani concepts when read with appropriate critical awareness.

Homework

Having completed this course, write a 400-word personal statement addressing the following: What has studying the Garab Ganjani Teeka changed in how you approach Japji Sahib? Name one specific insight from the Teeka that you intend to carry forward into your ongoing engagement with Gurbani, and one limitation of the Teeka that you think a modern student should remain alert to. Conclude with a single question that this course has opened for you — one you intend to keep exploring.

lessons.title: What a Teeka Is and Why We Need One
lessons.summary: Introduces the teeka and the steek, and explains why a reader of Gurbani often needs help with vocabulary, grammar, and context.
lessons.html:
Full course contents
  1. What a Teeka Is and Why We Need One
  2. The Streams of Sikh Exegesis
  3. The Faridkot Wala Teeka: The First Complete Commentary
  4. Sahib Singh and the Grammatical Turn
  5. How a Teeka Treats Meaning, Grammar, and Context
  6. Using a Steek to Study a Shabad

A first definition

A ਟੀਕਾ (commentary) is a written explanation of a text. When a commentary is printed alongside the original lines, the combined work is called a ਸਟੀਕ (text-with-commentary edition). The aim of both is simple: to help a reader arrive at the ਅਰਥ (meaning) of what the Guru has written.

Why commentary helps

Gurbani draws on several older languages and a wide vocabulary. A line may use a word that is rare today, or a grammatical form whose ending changes the sense. Without help, a reader can guess wrongly. A good teeka supplies the ਪਦ ਅਰਥ (word-by-word meaning) and then a fuller ਵਿਆਖਿਆ (explanation) of the line, so the learner can read with understanding rather than only reciting (Pashaura Singh 2000).

What this course will do

This is an overview. We will look at the major streams of exegesis, two landmark commentaries, and the way commentaries handle meaning, grammar, and context. The course is neutral about the differences between schools; each tradition has served learners in its own way (Pashaura Singh and Fenech 2014).

  • Lessons 2 introduces the streams of exegesis.
  • Lessons 3 and 4 study two landmark teekas.
  • Lessons 5 and 6 turn theory into practice.
Pashaura Singh 2000; Pashaura Singh and Fenech 2014.

Homework

The word ਤੀਕਾ carries layers of meaning — linguistic, devotional, and institutional. Spend 20–30 minutes reading or listening to one short passage of Gurbani that you are familiar with, without consulting any commentary. Write down your own understanding of what the passage is saying. Then write 250 words reflecting on what questions arose, what remained unclear, and how having access to a scholarly ਤੀਕਾ might have changed your engagement. This exercise is meant to surface your own interpretive instincts before formal commentary intervenes.

lessons.title: The Streams of Sikh Exegesis
lessons.summary: Surveys the Udasi, Nirmala, Giani/Taksali, and modern grammatical/academic approaches, with a comparative table, described neutrally.
lessons.html:
Four broad streams

Sikh commentary did not come from one place. Several traditions of learning each contributed. We describe them neutrally; this is a map, not a ranking.

The ਉਦਾਸੀ (ascetic teaching order) and the ਨਿਰਮਲਾ (classically trained scholarly order) were active in early teaching and brought a wide knowledge of older texts and vocabulary to their explanations. The Giani and Taksali tradition preserved meanings through an oral chain of teachers, passing the sense of difficult lines from one generation to the next. Modern grammatical and academic approaches, associated above all with Professor Sahib Singh, set out to ground meanings in the grammar of the text itself (Grewal 1998; Pashaura Singh and Fenech 2014).

StreamMain strengthHow meaning is fixed
ਉਦਾਸੀ (ascetic order)Broad classical learningKnowledge of older texts and terms
ਨਿਰਮਲਾ (scholarly order)Formal classical scholarshipTrained reading of vocabulary and themes
Giani / TaksaliContinuity of explanationOral chain of teacher to student
Grammatical / academicConsistency and methodGrammar of the text itself

Why the streams matter to a reader
