sourceText.english: Chapter 18 God-Centered and Self-Centered People There is knowledge in diverse forms in the world, but there is only one way to acquire it. We must understand the stock of knowledge that already exists and then, if possible, add to it. The whole stock of human knowledge has advanced in the manner people acquire knowledge in a particular sphere by assimilating what already exists on the subject. One who wishes to learn music must needs receive instruction from a musician, or seek the aid of appropriate books on the subject. When we seek spiritual knowledge, we accept the guidance of a spiritual teacher. We weigh and ponder his words, and then act upon them. In acquiring knowledge of any kind, we must, of course, have faith in the teacher. This is a fundamental requirement.

courses.title: Opening the Word: Dr. Surinder Singh Kohli and Gurbani in English
courses.summary: This course studies the work of Dr. Surinder Singh Kohli, a leading academic interpreter who carried the message of Sikh scripture into clear English. Rather than reproducing his texts, the course examines how his multi-volume series Guru Granth Sahib Speaks and his other English studies of Gurbani opened the…
outcomes: Describe the place of Dr. Surinder Singh Kohli's English works within the wider effort to make Sikh scripture accessible to non-Gurmukhi readers.
Explain how Kohli's thematic method in Guru Granth Sahib Speaks differs from reading scripture in its received order.
Identify the core theological themes Kohli treats, including the divine Name, grace, death, and the afterlife.
Discuss the choices and limits a translator faces when rendering theological terms such as ਨਾਮ and ਹੁਕਮ into English.
Situate Kohli's contribution alongside the broader field of Sikh studies as surveyed in academic reference works.
Evaluate the value and the risks of approaching the Guru Granth Sahib through translation and topical study.

terms.m: The sacred utterance of the Gurus recorded in Sikh scripture; the body of revealed word that Kohli rendered into English.
The central scripture and eternal Guru of the Sikhs, the source text for Kohli's English series.
The divine Name; a central theme in Kohli's studies, often discussed as remembrance and identification with the Creator.
The divine Order or Will that governs creation; a recurring theological idea in Kohli's English expositions.
Loving remembrance and repetition of the divine Name, a practice Kohli describes when explaining devotional themes.
The script in which the Guru Granth Sahib is written; readers without it depend on translators such as Kohli.
Liberation or release, a subject treated in Kohli's volumes on death and the afterlife.
The divine Word or hymn; the unit of scripture through which the Gurus convey teaching.

references: Kohli, Surinder Singh. Guru Granth Sahib Speaks, Vol. 1: Death and Afterlife. Amritsar: Singh Brothers.
Kohli, Surinder Singh. A Critical Study of Adi Granth. Delhi: Punjabi Writers' Cooperative Industrial Society.
Kohli, Surinder Singh. Dictionary of Mythological References in Guru Granth Sahib. Amritsar: Singh Brothers.
Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014.
Kohli, Surinder Singh. The Sikh Philosophy. Amritsar: Singh Brothers.

lessons.title: The Translator as Bridge
lessons.summary: Introduces Dr. Surinder Singh Kohli and the reason his English works matter for readers outside the Gurmukhi tradition.
lessons.html:
Full course contents
  1. The Translator as Bridge
  2. Guru Granth Sahib Speaks: A Thematic Method
  3. The Divine Name and the Divine Order
  4. Death and the Afterlife in English
  5. Choices and Limits in Translation
  6. Kohli within Sikh Studies

The ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ is written in ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ, a script that most of the world cannot read. For a global audience, the meaning of the ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ must travel through a translator. Dr. Surinder Singh Kohli was one of the most active academic interpreters who did this work in English (Kohli n.d.).

This course is about Kohli and his works. We do not reproduce his texts. Instead we ask how he made scripture reachable, what themes he chose to highlight, and what a reader gains and risks when meeting the ਸ਼ਬਦ through English prose.

Kohli's best-known effort is the multi-volume series Guru Granth Sahib Speaks, which presents the scripture's teaching topic by topic. Alongside it he produced reference and study works on the same source (Kohli n.d.).

WorkKindWhat it offers the English reader
Guru Granth Sahib Speaks (series)Thematic expositionScripture arranged by subject
A Critical Study of Adi GranthAcademic studyScholarly analysis of the text
Dictionary of Mythological ReferencesReferenceExplains allusions in the hymns

The wider field of Sikh studies frames why such bridges are needed: scripture-centred faith requires careful, honest interpretation when it crosses languages (Singh and Fenech 2014).

References
Kohli, Surinder Singh. Guru Granth Sahib Speaks, Vol. 1: Death and Afterlife. Amritsar: Singh Brothers.
Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014.

Homework

Lesson 1 — The Translator as Bridge: Select any single ਸ਼ਬਦ (shabad) from the Guru Granth Sahib that is personally meaningful to you. Read Kohli's English rendering of that shabad alongside any other available English translation (by Manmohan Singh, Sant Singh Khalsa, or another scholar). Write a 300-word reflection comparing the two translations: What choices did each translator make? What is gained or lost in each version? Which moves you more, and why?

lessons.title: Guru Granth Sahib Speaks: A Thematic Method
lessons.summary: Examines how Kohli organized scripture by theme rather than by its received sequence, and what this method achieves.
lessons.html:
The ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ is arranged largely by musical measure. A new reader meeting it for the first time can find this order hard to follow. Kohli's series Guru Granth Sahib Speaks takes a different path: it gathers the teaching of the ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ under named subjects, so a reader can study one theme at a time (Kohli n.d.).

This is a translator's editorial choice. Reading by theme helps a beginner see a coherent picture of one idea. It also carries a cost: the reader sees the topic pulled out of its musical and poetic setting. A good course keeps both views in mind.

ApproachStrengthLimit
Received order (by measure)Preserves the scripture's own shapeHard for newcomers to trace a theme
Thematic order (Kohli)Clear, subject-by-subject learningRemoves hymns from their setting

Kohli's wider scholarship, such as his close study of the text, shows that the thematic series rests on careful reading rather than casual summary (Kohli n.d.). The reference field treats such organizing work as a normal and useful part of making scripture accessible (Singh and Fenech 2014).

References
Kohli, Surinder Singh. Guru Granth Sahib Speaks, Vol. 1: Death and Afterlife. Amritsar: Singh Brothers.
Kohli, Surinder Singh. A Critical Study of Adi Granth. Delhi: Punjabi Writers' Cooperative Industrial Society.
Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014.

Homework

Lesson 2 — Guru Granth Sahib Speaks: A Thematic Method: The Guru Granth Sahib is organized by ਰਾਗ (raag, melodic mode) rather than by theme. Kohli's thematic method reorganizes this experience. Spend 20–30 minutes reading a short section of the Guru Granth Sahib in its original ਰਾਗ order (any ਰਾਗ of your choice), then read a thematic passage from Kohli's work on the same topic. Journal 250 words on what each ordering reveals: what does the ਰਾਗ sequence offer that the thematic arrangement cannot, and vice versa?

lessons.title: The Divine Name and the Divine Order
lessons.summary: Looks at how Kohli's English works treat two central theological ideas: the divine Name and the divine Will.
lessons.html:
Two ideas sit at the heart of Sikh theology, and both run through Kohli's expositions. The first is ਨਾਮ, the divine Name. The second is ਹੁਕਮ, the divine Order or Will. In English study these terms are easy to flatten, so a careful interpreter explains them with care (Kohli n.d.).

When Kohli writes about the Name, he connects it to ਸਿਮਰਨ, the loving remembrance that the Gurus call the path to closeness with the Creator. He presents this not as a magic word but as a way of living turned toward the divine.

When he treats the Order, he describes how everything moves within a Will that the human mind cannot fully measure. The believer's task is to accept and align with that Will rather than resist it.

TermPlain sense in Kohli's English
ਨਾਮThe divine Name, held through remembrance
ਹੁਕਮThe divine Will that orders all of life
ਸਿਮਰਨThe practice of remembering the Name

These themes are widely recognized as central to Sikh thought in the academic literature (Singh and Fenech 2014).

References
Kohli, Surinder Singh. Guru Granth Sahib Speaks, Vol. 1: Death and Afterlife. Amritsar: Singh Brothers.
Kohli, Surinder Singh. The Sikh Philosophy. Amritsar: Singh Brothers.
Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014.

Homework

Lesson 3 — The Divine Name and the Divine Order: The concept of ਨਾਮ (Naam) is described in Gurbani as both a personal practice and a cosmic reality. Spend 15 minutes in ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ (Nam Simran) — silent or whispered repetition of ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ (Waheguru) — and then read Kohli's English discussion of Naam from his published work. Write 250 words on whether Kohli's English rendering of Naam helped you connect to the practice differently, or whether the English felt inadequate to what you experienced.

lessons.title: Death and the Afterlife in English
lessons.summary: Studies the subject of the first volume of Guru Granth Sahib Speaks and how Kohli frames death for English readers.
lessons.html:
The first volume of Guru Granth Sahib Speaks takes up death and the afterlife (Kohli n.d.). This is a fitting place to see Kohli's method at work, because death is a subject every reader meets and every tradition must address.

In the ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ, death is not the end of meaning. Kohli's exposition gathers the scripture's teaching that life and death both rest within the divine ਹੁਕਮ, and that the goal is ਮੁਕਤੀ, release from the cycle of coming and going.

For the English reader, the value of such a volume is that it collects a difficult, scattered theme into one place and explains it in plain words. We study how Kohli does this without reducing the teaching to a slogan.

IdeaHow it appears in the theme of death
ਹੁਕਮDeath falls within the divine Will
ਮੁਕਤੀThe hoped-for release beyond the cycle
ਨਾਮRemembrance as preparation in this life

The reference field confirms that liberation and the soul's destiny are long-standing concerns of Sikh scripture and scholarship (Singh and Fenech 2014).

References
Kohli, Surinder Singh. Guru Granth Sahib Speaks, Vol. 1: Death and Afterlife. Amritsar: Singh Brothers.
Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014.

Homework

Lesson 4 — Death and the Afterlife in English: Gurbani addresses the reality of death (ਮੌਤ) with remarkable directness — as a teacher rather than an enemy. Identify a passage in the Guru Granth Sahib (by topic, not fabricated Ang) that speaks about how a person of faith should relate to death. Read Kohli's English translation or commentary on this theme. Then write a 300-word personal reflection: Has your own cultural or family background shaped how you receive these teachings? Does the English translation make them more or less accessible?

lessons.title: Choices and Limits in Translation
lessons.summary: Considers the decisions and the unavoidable losses a translator faces when carrying theological terms into English.
lessons.html:
No translation is neutral. Every time a word like ਨਾਮ or ਹੁਕਮ is turned into English, the translator chooses one shade of meaning and leaves others behind. Studying Kohli means studying these choices honestly (Kohli n.d.).

Some terms have no single English match. This is why this course keeps key Sikh terms in ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ and explains them, rather than replacing them with a one-word English label. Kohli's own reference work, his dictionary of mythological references, shows how much background a reader needs to grasp a single allusion in the ਸ਼ਬਦ (Kohli n.d.).

ChallengeWhat is at stake
One word, many sensesA single English choice narrows the meaning
Cultural allusionsReaders miss references without notes
Poetic formRhythm and music are hard to carry over

Recognizing these limits is itself a mark of good scholarship, and the academic field treats translation as an interpretive act rather than a simple swap of words (Singh and Fenech 2014).

References
Kohli, Surinder Singh. Dictionary of Mythological References in Guru Granth Sahib. Amritsar: Singh Brothers.
Kohli, Surinder Singh. A Critical Study of Adi Granth. Delhi: Punjabi Writers' Cooperative Industrial Society.
Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014.

Homework

Lesson 5 — Choices and Limits in Translation: Translation always involves loss and gain. Choose one Punjabi theological term central to Sikhi — for example ਹਉਮੈ (haumai), ਸੇਵਾ (seva), ਮਾਇਆ (maya), or ਸਹਿਜ (sahaj) — and research how Kohli and at least one other translator render it in English. Write 300 words analyzing the English options available: which translation is most accurate? Which is most evocative? Which risks misunderstanding? What would you choose and why?

lessons.title: Kohli within Sikh Studies
lessons.summary: Places Kohli's contribution within the wider academic field and weighs the value of topical, translated study.
lessons.html:
Kohli was one of many scholars who worked to bring the ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ to a wider readership. To understand his place, we set his works beside the broader field of Sikh studies, which has grown into a recognized academic discipline (Singh and Fenech 2014).

His contribution has a clear shape: he made scripture usable for the English reader through thematic volumes, study works, and reference tools (Kohli n.d.). His philosophy writing tied these themes into a connected picture of Sikh thought (Kohli n.d.).

We close by weighing the approach. Topical study in translation is a doorway, not the whole house. It invites the reader in; it does not replace meeting the ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ in its own form and music.

Strength of Kohli's workReminder for the student
Makes scripture accessibleTranslation is a starting point
Organizes themes clearlyThemes still live within whole hymns
Supplies reference toolsTools support, not replace, the source

Read this way, Kohli's legacy is best honoured by using his bridges to walk toward the scripture itself.

References
Kohli, Surinder Singh. Guru Granth Sahib Speaks, Vol. 1: Death and Afterlife. Amritsar: Singh Brothers.
Kohli, Surinder Singh. The Sikh Philosophy. Amritsar: Singh Brothers.
Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014.

Homework

Lesson 6 — Kohli within Sikh Studies: Dr. Surinder Singh Kohli is one figure in a long tradition of scholars who have brought Gurbani into English. Research one other significant English-language interpreter of Sikh scripture — such as W.H. McLeod, Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, or Pashaura Singh — and compare their approach to Kohli's. Write 300 words identifying one key difference in methodology or theological emphasis and reflecting on what that difference reveals about the range of possible scholarly approaches to Gurbani.

lessons.title: The Aesthetics of Gurbani: Poetry, Raag, and the Problem of English
lessons.html:
Introduction

The Guru Granth Sahib is not a prose scripture. It is a collection of lyric poetry composed in classical musical modes called ਰਾਗ (raag), intended to be sung rather than recited or read silently. This fundamental aesthetic reality poses one of the deepest challenges any English translator faces: how to carry into another language a text whose very structure, rhythm, sound, and emotional register are constituted by music. Dr. Surinder Singh Kohli was aware of this challenge, and his treatment of Gurbani aesthetics — what he preserved, what he sacrificed, and how he reasoned about those choices — repays careful study.

This lesson examines the musical and poetic dimensions of Gurbani that underlie Kohli's English work. We consider the role of ਰਾਗ (raag) as theological statement, the function of poetic devices such as ਅਲੰਕਾਰ (alankaar, literary ornament), the relationship between meter and meaning, and the specific strategies Kohli employed to render poetry that was composed to be sung. By the end of this lesson, students should be able to articulate why translation of Gurbani is not only a linguistic problem but an aesthetic and theological one.

Understanding the aesthetics of Gurbani also illuminates debates about what counts as a faithful translation. If the music is essential to the meaning, can a prose English rendering be truly faithful at all? And if not, what obligations does that place on the translator to be transparent about the limits of the genre shift?

Raag as Theological Statement

The thirty-one ਰਾਗ (raags) in which Gurbani is composed are not merely organizational conventions or aesthetic preferences. Each raag carries a traditional emotional color (ਰਸ, ras) — a range of feeling that the performance of that raag is designed to evoke in the listener. Raag Bilaval, for instance, is associated with joy and brightness; Raag Kedara with longing and devotion; Raag Gauri with gravity and contemplation. The Gurus chose specific raags to amplify particular theological messages. A ਸ਼ਬਦ (shabad) about the pain of ਵਿਛੋੜਾ (vichhora, separation from the Divine) set in a raag of longing is not merely illustrated by the music — the music is part of the teaching.

This means that when Kohli or any other translator renders a shabad in flat prose, the emotional and devotional dimension that the raag carried is necessarily absent. A scholar reading Kohli's English version of a shabad in Raag Kedara encounters the semantic content — the ideas about longing and Divine grace — but not the affective architecture of the original. This is not a failure of translation skill; it is a structural constraint of the medium. Kohli acknowledged this constraint in his scholarly prefaces, noting that his translations were intended as intellectual guides to the meaning of Gurbani rather than devotional substitutes for singing it.

Contemporary Sikh scholars such as Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh have argued that this structural constraint should push translators toward more poetic English — toward verse that preserves at least some of the rhythmic and sonic texture of the original, even if it cannot replicate the full raag experience. Kohli's approach was more conservative, favoring precision of meaning over aesthetic experimentation. Understanding this choice illuminates much about what kind of book Kohli's translations are: scholarly resources, not devotional performances.

Poetic Devices and Their English Equivalents

Gurbani employs a sophisticated repertoire of classical Indian literary devices. ਅਨਾਫੋਰਾ (anaphora), repetition of opening words across lines, is common. ਉਪਮਾ (upama, simile) and ਰੂਪਕ (rupak, metaphor) drawn from nature, agriculture, and everyday Punjab life are woven throughout. The Gurus used imagery of the ਚਕਵੀ (chakvee, ruddy shelduck separated from her mate at night) to evoke the soul's longing for ਪਰਮਾਤਮਾ (Parmatama, the Supreme Soul). They used images of the ਵਣਜਾਰਾ (vanjara, travelling merchant) to describe the soul's journey through life. They used the image of the ਨਦੀ (nadi, river) joining the ਸਮੁੰਦਰ (samundar, ocean) to describe the merging of the individual ਆਤਮਾ (atma, soul) with the Infinite.

Kohli translated these images literally and carefully, which preserves their semantic content but can sometimes flatten their resonance for an English reader unfamiliar with the cultural world from which they come. An English reader who has never seen a chakvee, and who knows nothing of the folk poetry traditions in which this bird's nighttime separation from her mate became a symbol of longing, may read Kohli's rendering and understand the surface meaning without feeling its weight. This is not Kohli's failure — it is the irreducible distance between languages and cultures. But it does mean that Kohli's translations require supplementary cultural education to be fully received.

A thoughtful translator faces a choice: annotate extensively, domesticate the imagery (replacing the chakvee with a culturally equivalent English bird or symbol), or trust the foreign image to gradually educate the reader. Kohli, in his scholarly editions, typically chose annotation. His glosses and introductions provide much of the cultural context his English renderings alone cannot carry.

Key Terms

  • ਰਾਗ — A classical Indian musical mode, each with a specific emotional color (ras); thirty-one raags structure the Guru Granth Sahib.
  • ਰਸ — The aesthetic emotional essence or flavor that a raag or poetic work evokes in the listener.
  • ਅਲੰਕਾਰ — Classical Indian literary ornament or rhetorical device, including simile (ਉਪਮਾ) and metaphor (ਰੂਪਕ).
  • ਵਿਛੋੜਾ — Painful separation; specifically the soul's longing for reunion with the Divine, a central Gurbani theme.
  • ਚਕਵੀ — The ruddy shelduck; a classical Punjabi poetic symbol of longing, used in Gurbani for the soul separated from God.
  • ਵਣਜਾਰਾ — Travelling merchant; in Gurbani, a metaphor for the soul journeying through the world in search of the Divine.

Discussion Questions

  1. If raag is theologically essential to the meaning of Gurbani, can any prose English translation be considered fully faithful? What obligations does this limitation place on the translator and the reader?
  2. Kohli chose semantic precision over aesthetic experimentation. Do you find this the right choice for a scholarly translator? What is gained and what is sacrificed?
  3. How might a reader with no cultural familiarity with Punjab agricultural and folk imagery encounter Kohli's translated images? What responsibility does the translator have to bridge this gap?
  4. Compare Kohli's approach with Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh's more poetic rendering style. What does the comparison reveal about competing values in sacred text translation?

Further Reading

Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, The Name of My Beloved: Verses of the Sikh Gurus.

Gurnam Singh, Ragas in Guru Granth Sahib.

George A. Grierson, Linguistic Survey of India (on Punjabi poetic traditions).

Key Takeaways

  • Gurbani is fundamentally musical poetry composed for singing; the raag is not decorative but is theologically constitutive of meaning.
  • Prose English translation necessarily loses the affective and devotional architecture that the raag carries, a structural constraint Kohli acknowledged.
  • Kohli's conservative, semantically precise approach to imagery preserves meaning but places demands on the reader to supply cultural context.
  • Debates about aesthetic versus semantic faithfulness in translation reflect deeper disagreements about what scripture fundamentally is and what translation is for.

Homework

Choose a shabad from the Guru Granth Sahib set in a raag you can identify (for example, Raag Asa, Raag Gauri, or Raag Bilaval). Listen to that shabad performed in its raag by a skilled musician (recordings are widely available online). Then read Kohli's or another scholar's English prose translation of the same shabad. Write a 300-word reflection on what the music adds to your understanding that the English text alone does not convey. What does this experience reveal about the limits and possibilities of translation?

lessons.title: Kohli's Treatment of the Sikh Social Vision
lessons.html:
Introduction

Gurbani is not only a text of personal piety and individual spiritual liberation. It carries a sustained, sharply articulated social vision — a theology of equality, justice, service, and community that challenges social hierarchies and calls for the transformation of collective life. Dr. Surinder Singh Kohli's English translations and commentaries engaged directly with this social dimension, and his rendering of Gurbani's social teachings reveals important assumptions about what Sikhi means as a way of living together in the world.

This lesson examines how Kohli translated and interpreted the social teachings of Gurbani: the theology of ਸੇਵਾ (seva, selfless service), the critique of ਜਾਤ-ਪਾਤ (jaat-paat, the caste system), the vision of the ਸੰਗਤ (sangat, congregation) and ਲੰਗਰ (langar, community kitchen) as expressions of equality, and the Gurus' insistence that spiritual authenticity cannot be separated from social justice. We consider both the strengths of Kohli's approach and the places where later scholars have argued for a more radical reading.

Understanding how Gurbani's social vision is rendered in English matters enormously for global audiences encountering Sikhi for the first time. The choices a translator makes about how to render ਸਮਾਨਤਾ (samaanta, equality) and ਨਿਆਂ (niaan, justice) shape how English-speaking readers understand Sikhi's relationship to contemporary social struggles.

The Theology of Seva and Its English Rendering

ਸੇਵਾ (seva) is one of the most distinctive concepts in Sikh theology. It refers to selfless service — to the congregation, to the needy, to the Guru — as a spiritual discipline that dissolves the ego and opens the practitioner to Divine grace. The Guru Granth Sahib presents ਸੇਵਾ not as mere charity or social work but as a profoundly theological act: the self that serves others forgets itself, and in that forgetting finds the Divine. Service is thus simultaneously an ethical and a mystical practice.

Kohli generally translated ਸੇਵਾ as "service" or "selfless service," which is accurate at the semantic level. However, some scholars have noted that "service" in English carries overtones of employment, hierarchy, or even servitude that are absent from the Punjabi concept. ਸੇਵਾ in Gurbani is performed by kings for beggars, by teachers for students, by the spiritually advanced for the spiritually struggling — it inverts hierarchy rather than reinforcing it. Whether Kohli's English rendering adequately captured this inversion is a question worth examining. Where Kohli did excel was in his thematic commentary, where he explained at length the theological depth of ਸੇਵਾ and distinguished it from the philanthropic or charitable service familiar to Western readers.

Gurbani's Critique of Caste and Kohli's Engagement

The Gurus' sustained critique of ਜਾਤ-ਪਾਤ (jaat-paat, caste hierarchy) is among the most socially radical dimensions of Gurbani. Guru Nanak Sahib, Guru Ravidas Ji (whose compositions are included in the Guru Granth Sahib at Ang 345), Guru Amar Das Ji, and other Gurus repeatedly taught that caste distinctions are illusory from the perspective of the Divine, and that spiritual worth is determined by ਨਾਮ (Naam) and ਕਰਮ (karam, action) rather than by birth. The institution of ਲੰਗਰ (langar) — where all sit together as equals to eat — was explicitly designed to embody this equality in practice.

Kohli's treatment of the caste critique is notable for its directness. In his scholarly commentaries, he consistently emphasized that Gurbani's critique of caste is not merely incidental but theologically central — rooted in the teaching that all human beings share the same ਜੋਤਿ (jot, Divine Light). He translated passages affirming human equality with clarity, and his thematic arrangement helped English readers understand the sustained consistency of this critique across multiple Gurus. However, later scholars such as Pashaura Singh and Gurinder Singh Mann have argued that fully understanding this critique requires engaging with its historical context — the specific social practices in Punjab against which the Gurus were speaking — which Kohli's primarily theological framing sometimes underemphasized.

The Sangat, Langar, and the English Vocabulary of Community

The institutions of ਸੰਗਤ (sangat) and ਲੰਗਰ (langar) are the social form that Gurbani's theology of equality takes in practice. ਸੰਗਤ — the congregation gathered in the presence of the Guru — is described in Gurbani as a sacred community in which individual distinctions of caste, class, and gender are transcended. ਲੰਗਰ — the community kitchen where all eat together as equals — makes this theological claim visible and tangible in daily life. These are not peripheral institutions but central expressions of what Guru Nanak Sahib's teaching means embodied in community.

Kohli translated ਸੰਗਤ as "congregation" and ਲੰਗਰ as "community kitchen" or left it untranslated. Both choices have implications. "Congregation" is a term loaded with Christian connotations for many English readers — it suggests a gathered church community under clerical leadership, which misses the horizontal, non-hierarchical quality of ਸੰਗਤ as Gurbani describes it. Kohli's commentary, fortunately, spelled out these distinctions. His insistence that ਸੰਗਤ is defined by the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib rather than by any human religious authority is an important corrective to the congregational analogy. Later translators have experimented with leaving ਸੰਗਤ and ਲੰਗਰ untranslated, treating them as loanwords to be explained rather than domesticated — an approach Kohli's legacy has helped make possible.

Key Terms

  • ਸੇਵਾ — Selfless service to others as a spiritual discipline; inverts social hierarchy and dissolves the ego.
  • ਜਾਤ-ਪਾਤ — The caste system; a social hierarchy based on birth that Gurbani consistently critiques as spiritually false.
  • ਸੰਗਤ — The holy congregation gathered in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib; a community of spiritual equals.
  • ਲੰਗਰ — The community kitchen established by the Gurus; an institution of practical equality where all eat together regardless of status.
  • ਜੋਤਿ — The Divine Light; in Gurbani, the same Divine Light resides in all human beings, making caste distinctions spiritually meaningless.
  • ਨਿਆਂ — Justice, righteous order; a dimension of Gurbani's social vision that extends beyond personal piety to collective life.

Discussion Questions

  1. Does translating ਸੇਵਾ as "service" adequately capture its theological meaning as a hierarchy-inverting spiritual practice? What alternative English renderings might work better?
  2. Kohli emphasized the theological roots of the caste critique. Later scholars emphasized historical context. What is gained and what is lost by each approach?
  3. If you were introducing the concept of ਲੰਗਰ to an English-speaking audience with no prior knowledge of Sikhi, would you translate the word or leave it as a loanword? Why?

Further Reading

Pashaura Singh, The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority.

Gurinder Singh Mann, The Making of Sikh Scripture.

W.H. McLeod, Guru Nanak and the Sikh Religion.

Key Takeaways

  • Gurbani carries a robust social theology of equality and justice rooted in the teaching that all beings share the same Divine Light.
  • Kohli's English rendering of the social vision was theologically clear but sometimes underdeveloped in its engagement with historical context.
  • Key terms such as ਸੇਵਾ, ਸੰਗਤ, and ਲੰਗਰ resist full domestication into English and may be better treated as theological loanwords with explanatory commentary.
  • How Gurbani's social teachings are translated has direct implications for how global audiences understand Sikhi's relationship to contemporary questions of justice and equality.

Homework

Visit a gurdwara or watch a documentary about langar and seva in Sikh communities. Reflect on the gap between experiencing ਲੰਗਰ (langar) in person and reading Kohli's English description of the institution. Write 300 words on what cannot be communicated through scholarly prose about this practice, and what additional forms of documentation or translation might bridge that gap.

lessons.title: Theology of the Self (ਆਤਮਾ) in Kohli's English
lessons.html:
Introduction

Among the most philosophically complex areas of Gurbani is its teaching about the nature of the self. The Guru Granth Sahib does not present a single systematic philosophical account of human identity, but across its thousands of shabads it articulates a sophisticated and internally coherent vision of the ਆਤਮਾ (atma, soul or self), its relationship to ਹਉਮੈ (haumai, ego or self-centeredness), and its ultimate destiny in union with ਪਰਮਾਤਮਾ (Parmatama, the Supreme Soul). Dr. Surinder Singh Kohli engaged with this theological anthropology extensively, and his English renderings of Gurbani's self-theology reveal important interpretive choices that shaped how English-speaking readers came to understand Sikh thought.

This lesson examines the key dimensions of Gurbani's theology of the self: the nature of ਆਤਮਾ, the problem of ਹਉਮੈ, the concept of ਮਨ (man, mind), the aspiration of ਜੀਵਨ ਮੁਕਤੀ (jeevan mukti, liberation while living), and Kohli's strategies for rendering these concepts in English. We pay particular attention to the ways in which Gurbani's self-theology both resembles and differs from comparable teachings in Vedanta, Buddhism, and Western philosophy — and how Kohli navigated these comparisons.

Understanding Gurbani's theology of self is not merely an academic exercise. It is the theological foundation on which Sikh practice rests: if one understands what Gurbani teaches about the nature of the self and the ego, the disciplines of ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ (Nam Simran), ਕੀਰਤਨ (kirtan), and ਸੇਵਾ (seva) become intelligible as forms of self-transformation rather than mere ritual.

Haumai: The Ego That Separates

The concept of ਹਉਮੈ (haumai) is central to Gurbani's account of the human condition. Haumai is often translated as "ego," but this English word carries meanings — from Freudian psychoanalysis, from popular self-help discourse — that do not map precisely onto the Gurbani concept. In Gurbani, ਹਉਮੈ refers specifically to the habit of mind that takes the individual self as the ultimate reference point, claiming credit, asserting ownership, and separating itself from others and from the Divine. It is the state of saying "I" and "mine" in a way that forgets that all belongs to ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ (Waheguru).

Kohli translated ਹਉਮੈ as "ego" or "self-conceit" or "pride," depending on context. He also used "egotism" in some passages. Each English word captures something real: ego captures the self-referential quality; self-conceit captures the falseness; pride captures the moral dimension. But none quite captures the metaphysical dimension of ਹਉਮੈ in Gurbani — the sense that it is not merely a moral failing but an ontological error, a mistaken belief about the nature of reality. Gurbani teaches that ਹਉਮੈ is rooted in ਭਰਮ (bharam, illusion) — a failure to perceive that the Divine is in all and that the separate self is a construction rather than an ultimate reality. Kohli's commentary generally made this metaphysical dimension clear even when his translation alone could not carry it.

Atma and the Question of Individual Identity

If ਹਉਮੈ is the problem, what is its solution? Gurbani teaches that beneath the constructed ego lies the ਆਤਮਾ (atma), the true self — the Divine Light (ਜੋਤਿ, jot) that pervades all beings. When ਹਉਮੈ is dissolved through ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ (Nam Simran) and ਗੁਰ-ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ (gur-parsad, Guru's grace), the individual ਆਤਮਾ recognizes its identity with ਪਰਮਾਤਮਾ (Parmatama). This recognition is the state of ਜੀਵਨ ਮੁਕਤੀ (jeevan mukti, liberation while living) — the goal of human life as Gurbani describes it.

This teaching raises a philosophically complex question: if ਆਤਮਾ merges with ਪਰਮਾਤਮਾ, does the individual self cease to exist? Gurbani's answer is subtle. The individual soul does not annihilate into an impersonal Absolute, as in some forms of Advaita Vedanta. Rather, it enters a relationship of ਮਿਲਾਪ (milaap, loving union) with the Divine, like a river entering the ocean — which retains its nature as water while becoming something larger. This metaphor preserves individual identity while transcending the illusion of separation. Kohli's English renderings generally preserved this nuance, distinguishing Gurbani's vision from both pure monism and strict dualism.

Kohli and Comparative Philosophy

Kohli was trained in both classical Indian philosophy and Western academic traditions, and his commentaries frequently engaged in comparative analysis. He drew on parallels between ਹਉਮੈ and the Vedantic concept of ਅਹੰਕਾਰ (ahankar, ego-construction), while carefully noting that Gurbani's treatment is distinct in grounding liberation in the Guru's grace rather than in philosophical inquiry alone. He also noted resemblances between ਜੀਵਨ ਮੁਕਤੀ and Buddhist nirvana, while emphasizing that Gurbani maintains a world-affirming orientation — the liberated person does not withdraw from society but serves it more fully.

These comparative moves were valuable pedagogically, helping Western readers locate Gurbani's self-theology within a broader philosophical landscape. However, later scholars such as Arvind-Pal Singh Mandair have cautioned that too much comparative framing risks subsuming Gurbani within categories ("mysticism," "non-dualism," "liberation theology") developed in other traditions. The distinctive contribution of Gurbani's self-theology — its insistence that transformation comes through ਗੁਰ-ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ (Guru's grace) and community rather than through individual philosophical discipline alone — can be obscured when the comparative frame dominates.

Key Terms

  • ਆਤਮਾ — The soul or true self; in Gurbani, the Divine Light dwelling within the individual, identical in nature to ਪਰਮਾਤਮਾ.
  • ਹਉਮੈ — Ego-centered self-assertion; the metaphysical and moral error of taking the constructed self as ultimate reality.
  • ਮਨ — Mind; in Gurbani, the seat of spiritual struggle, capable of both deepest devotion and deepest delusion.
  • ਜੀਵਨ ਮੁਕਤੀ — Liberation while living; the state of freedom achieved when the ego is dissolved and the soul recognizes its unity with the Divine.
  • ਮਿਲਾਪ — Loving union; the relationship of the individual soul with the Divine, described in Gurbani as like a river meeting the ocean.
  • ਗੁਰ-ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ — Guru's grace; in Gurbani, the indispensable divine gift through which liberation becomes possible.

Discussion Questions

  1. Kohli translated ਹਉਮੈ variously as "ego," "self-conceit," and "egotism." Which English rendering do you find most adequate to the Gurbani concept, and what is lost in each option?
  2. Gurbani describes liberation (ਜੀਵਨ ਮੁਕਤੀ) as a state achieved while living, not after death. How does this world-affirming orientation distinguish Sikh theology from traditions that locate liberation beyond this life?
  3. Is comparative philosophical framing — connecting ਹਉਮੈ to Vedantic ਅਹੰਕਾਰ or Buddhist concepts of no-self — helpful or potentially misleading for a new reader of Gurbani? What are the risks on each side?

Further Reading

Arvind-Pal Singh Mandair, Religion and the Specter of the West: Sikhism, India, Postcoloniality, and the Politics of Translation.

Sher Singh, The Philosophy of Sikhism.

Wazir Singh, Philosophy of Sikh Religion.

Key Takeaways

  • Gurbani presents a sophisticated theology of self centered on the problem of ਹਉਮੈ (ego) and the aspiration of ਜੀਵਨ ਮੁਕਤੀ (liberation while living).
  • Kohli's English renderings of self-theological concepts were generally accurate but required supporting commentary to convey their full metaphysical depth.
  • Comparative philosophical framing is pedagogically useful but risks obscuring the distinctive features of Gurbani's self-theology, particularly its insistence on Guru's grace as the path to liberation.
  • The concept of ਮਿਲਾਪ — loving union that preserves individual identity — distinguishes Gurbani's vision from both strict monism and strict dualism, a nuance Kohli's work generally preserved.

Homework

Spend 20 minutes in quiet reflection on the concept of ਹਉਮੈ (haumai) as Gurbani describes it. Recall a moment in your own life when ego-assertion separated you from others or from a sense of deeper meaning. Then write 300 words reflecting on how Kohli's English rendering of haumai — alongside the original Punjabi concept — shapes how you understand that experience. Does the English word 'ego' capture what Gurbani is pointing to?

lessons.title: Comparative Scripture: Kohli's Gurbani alongside World Traditions
lessons.html:
Introduction

Dr. Surinder Singh Kohli worked during a period when Sikh Studies was emerging as an academic discipline and when scholars were eager to position Gurbani within global conversations about scripture, mysticism, and religious thought. One dimension of his scholarly project was explicitly comparative: he drew parallels between Gurbani's teachings and those of other traditions, including Hinduism, Islam (particularly Sufism), Christianity, and classical Indian philosophy. These comparative moves shaped how English-speaking readers — many of whom encountered Gurbani without prior knowledge of Sikhi — came to understand what Sikh scripture is and what it teaches.

This lesson examines Kohli's comparative methodology, its intellectual strengths, its methodological risks, and the debates it has generated among subsequent scholars. We consider specific examples: Kohli's treatment of the relationship between Gurbani and Sufi thought, his engagement with Vedantic parallels, and his reading of Gurbani's theology of the One in relation to the Abrahamic traditions. We also examine the critiques offered by scholars who argue that excessive comparative framing can distort rather than illuminate Gurbani's distinctive theological vision.

Engaging with comparative scripture is not merely an academic exercise. It matters for how Sikhi is represented in interfaith dialogue, religious education, and global public discourse. Understanding how Kohli navigated these comparative questions helps us think more carefully about the opportunities and limits of cross-traditional scriptural study.

Gurbani and Sufism: A Productive Comparison

Among the most frequently noted comparative relationships in Sikh studies is the one between Gurbani and the Sufi tradition of Islam. Several of the contributors to the Guru Granth Sahib — including Bhagat Farid (Baba Sheikh Farid Shakarganj, Ang 488–496) — composed within Sufi devotional frameworks. The Punjabi Sufi tradition, with its emphasis on ਇਸ਼ਕ (ishq, divine love), the ਫ਼ਕੀਰ (fakeer, renunciant mystic), and the longing of the soul for union with God, shares significant themes with Gurbani's own devotional language.

Kohli drew on these parallels to illuminate the devotional register of Gurbani for readers familiar with Rumi, Hafiz, or classical Sufi poetry. He noted that the imagery of the soul as a lover seeking the Divine Beloved — widespread in Gurbani — resonates with Sufi ਇਸ਼ਕ poetry, making Gurbani's emotional texture more accessible to readers who know that tradition. This comparative move was pedagogically valuable and historically well-grounded: the Gurus lived in a world where Sufi teachers were significant spiritual presences, and the dialogue between Sikh and Sufi thought is a real historical fact, not merely a scholarly construction.

However, Kohli was also careful — and later scholars have been even more emphatic — to mark the theological differences. Gurbani insists on ਨਿਰਗੁਣ (nirgun, the formless, attributeless Divine) alongside ਸਰਗੁਣ (sargun, the Divine as manifest in creation), in a dynamic that has no precise Sufi equivalent. Gurbani also rejects the Sufi hierarchical order of the ਪੀਰ (peer, spiritual master) as a necessary intermediary — the Guru Granth Sahib itself is the living Guru, not a human lineage of masters. These differences matter theologically and require careful marking in comparative work.

Gurbani and Vedanta: Similarities and Sharp Distinctions

Kohli's engagement with Vedantic parallels was more contested. Classical Advaita Vedanta teaches that the individual self (atman) is ultimately identical with Brahman, the universal Absolute, and that liberation consists in recognizing this identity through philosophical knowledge (jnana). Gurbani uses some similar language — it speaks of ਆਤਮਾ (atma) and ਪਰਮਾਤਮਾ (Parmatama), and it affirms the Divine Light in all — leading some early interpreters, including some within the Nirmala scholarly tradition, to read Gurbani through a broadly Vedantic lens.

Kohli drew on Vedantic parallels selectively, helping readers who came from Hindu philosophical backgrounds to find entry points into Gurbani. But he was also clear — and subsequent scholars such as Gurinder Singh Mann and Arvind-Pal Singh Mandair have been emphatic — that Gurbani's self-theology is not reducible to Vedanta. In Gurbani, liberation (ਜੀਵਨ ਮੁਕਤੀ) comes not through philosophical self-inquiry but through ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ (Nam Simran) and ਗੁਰ-ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ (Guru's grace). The role of grace makes Gurbani's soteriology fundamentally different from Advaita's emphasis on knowledge. This distinction — grace versus knowledge as the vehicle of liberation — is one of the most important theological markers separating Gurbani from Vedanta, and Kohli's best work preserved it clearly.

The Limits of Comparative Framing

Despite the pedagogical value of comparative analysis, serious methodological concerns have been raised. Arvind-Pal Singh Mandair's landmark study Religion and the Specter of the West argues that the entire project of positioning Gurbani within a comparative world religions framework risks distorting Sikh thought by forcing it into categories ("mysticism," "scripture," "religion") that were developed in Western and colonial contexts and that do not map cleanly onto Sikh self-understanding. When Kohli compared Gurbani to Sufi poetry or Vedantic philosophy, he was necessarily using a comparative grid that presupposes these are equivalent objects of the same kind — "world scriptures" or "mystical texts" — a presupposition that many Sikh thinkers would reject.

This critique does not mean comparative scholarship is worthless — it means it must be done with explicit methodological awareness, clearly marking what the comparison illuminates and what it conceals. Kohli's work at its best exemplified this awareness. His comparisons were offered as windows rather than as equivalences, and his theological commentary consistently returned to what makes Gurbani distinctive on its own terms. This practice of comparative humility is a model worth studying regardless of one's position on the methodological debate.

Key Terms

  • ਨਿਰਗੁਣ — The formless, attributeless Divine; in Gurbani, God beyond all human categories and descriptions.
  • ਸਰਗੁਣ — The Divine as manifest in creation; God encountered through the world and through the Guru's Word.
  • ਇਸ਼ਕ — Sufi concept of divine love; parallel in some respects to Gurbani's devotional register though theologically distinct.
  • ਫ਼ਕੀਰ — Sufi renunciant mystic; a figure whose presence in Punjabi spiritual culture influenced but did not determine Gurbani's imagery.
  • ਜੀਵਨ ਮੁਕਤੀ — Liberation while living; Gurbani's goal of human life, achieved through grace rather than philosophical knowledge, distinguishing it from Vedantic moksha.
  • ਗੁਰ-ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ — Guru's grace; the indispensable vehicle of liberation in Gurbani, distinguishing it from traditions that emphasize individual knowledge or effort alone.

Discussion Questions

  1. Kohli used Sufi and Vedantic parallels to make Gurbani accessible to wider audiences. At what point does accessibility shade into distortion? How can a teacher or translator navigate this line?
  2. Mandair argues that comparative world-religions frameworks distort Sikh self-understanding. Do you find this critique persuasive? What would comparative scholarship look like if it took this critique seriously?
  3. If you were introducing Gurbani to someone deeply familiar with another scripture tradition — the Hebrew Bible, the Quran, the Bhagavad Gita — what comparison would you draw, and what distinction would you immediately mark?

Further Reading

Arvind-Pal Singh Mandair, Religion and the Specter of the West: Sikhism, India, Postcoloniality, and the Politics of Translation.

Pashaura Singh, Life and Work of Guru Arjan: History, Memory, and Biography in the Sikh Tradition.

Annemarie Schimmel, Mystical Dimensions of Islam.

Key Takeaways

  • Kohli's comparative work drew on Sufi and Vedantic parallels to make Gurbani accessible, and was most successful when it marked distinctions as carefully as it noted similarities.
  • The key theological markers distinguishing Gurbani from both Sufism and Vedanta include its insistence on ਗੁਰ-ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ (Guru's grace) as the vehicle of liberation and on the living Guru Granth Sahib as the sole spiritual authority.
  • Post-colonial scholars have raised legitimate concerns about comparative world-religions frameworks imposing foreign categories on Sikh thought.
  • Comparative humility — offering comparisons as windows rather than equivalences — is a methodological virtue that Kohli's best work modeled and that students of Gurbani should practice.

Homework

Choose a teaching in Gurbani that moves you — about love, justice, the nature of God, or the human condition. Identify a parallel teaching from one other tradition you know (Christianity, Islam, Buddhism, Hinduism, or another). Write 300 words comparing the two teachings: what do they share, where do they diverge, and what does the comparison reveal about what is distinctively Sikh in Gurbani's version? Reflect on whether the comparison clarifies or risks distorting Gurbani's meaning.

lessons.title: The Reader's Experience: How English Renders Sikh Devotion
lessons.html:
Introduction

Translation is not only a transfer of meaning between languages. It is an event that happens in a reader's mind, heart, and body — and the reader's experience of a text in translation may differ profoundly from the experience of a reader in the original language. When Dr. Surinder Singh Kohli translated Gurbani into English, he was not only making arguments or conveying information. He was shaping the quality of encounter that an English-speaking reader would have with one of the most devotionally powerful scriptural traditions in the world. This lesson examines the reader's side of the translation equation.

We consider questions such as: What kind of reader did Kohli imagine when he wrote his English renderings? How does the devotional register of Gurbani — its intimacy, its grief, its joy, its awe — survive the journey into English prose? What does a reader gain from Kohli's careful scholarship that they might not get from a more devotional but less rigorous translation? And what do they lose? These questions are not merely aesthetic — they touch on fundamental issues of access, belonging, and spiritual formation for Sikhs and seekers who engage Gurbani through English.

The reader's experience of Kohli's work also raises questions about audience. Was Kohli writing primarily for Sikh readers who needed English glosses for already-familiar texts, for Western academic readers approaching Gurbani as scholars, or for global seekers with no prior background in Sikhi? Different audiences need different things from a translation, and Kohli's choices served some better than others.

The Imagined Reader and Devotional Register

Every translation implies an imagined reader — a person with specific background knowledge, spiritual needs, and affective expectations. Kohli's English translations, with their careful annotations, philological precision, and scholarly introductions, imply a reader who is educated, intellectually curious, and approaching Gurbani with questions about meaning, history, and philosophy. This imagined reader is well served by Kohli's work: they receive careful explanations of difficult terms, contextual information about the Gurus and their historical situations, and thematic guidance through a massive and complex scripture.

But Gurbani was composed for a different kind of reader — or rather, listener. The Gurus wrote for ਸੰਗਤ (sangat) gathered to sing, to weep, to laugh, to surrender in devotion. A ਸ਼ਬਦ (shabad) about the pain of separation from the Divine was not meant to be read silently at a desk; it was meant to be sung until the congregation felt that pain collectively and then felt it dissolve into ਅਨੰਦ (anand, bliss). This devotional register — the movement from longing through surrender to joy — is extremely difficult to convey in scholarly prose. Kohli's work makes the content of Gurbani available in English; it does not, and cannot, replicate the devotional event that Gurbani creates when sung in ਸੰਗਤ.

Accessibility and the Question of Who Can Encounter Gurbani

Despite these limitations, Kohli's translations have served an important function of expanding access. Before scholarly English translations were available, many second-generation Sikh diaspora children had no reliable way to understand the meaning of the Gurbani they heard sung at ਗੁਰਦੁਆਰਾ (gurdwara). Non-Punjabi spouses, interfaith families, and seekers from other backgrounds had even less access. Kohli's work, alongside that of other translators, helped make Gurbani's teachings available to these communities.

Accessibility, however, is not neutral. Making Gurbani available in English also shapes how it is received. English-speaking readers of Gurbani may engage with it primarily as a source of philosophical and ethical teaching — which it certainly is — while remaining less connected to its dimension as ਧੁਨਿ (dhuni, divine sound) that transforms through vibration and repetition. This cognitive-propositional mode of engagement is not wrong, but it is partial. Kohli was aware of this — his introductions consistently encouraged readers to engage with the musical performance tradition alongside the textual translations — but the medium of a scholarly English book cannot itself model this integration.

Emotional Truth and Scholarly Precision

The tension between emotional truth and scholarly precision is one of the deepest challenges in translating devotional literature. A rendering that is emotionally resonant but philologically loose may move the reader while misleading them; a rendering that is philologically precise but emotionally flat may inform without transforming. Kohli generally erred on the side of precision, and this choice reflected his scholarly values and his sense of responsibility to the integrity of the text.

Later translators — most notably Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh in works such as The Name of My Beloved — have attempted more poetically ambitious English renderings, arguing that emotional fidelity is as important as semantic accuracy. The debate between these approaches reflects a genuine dilemma rather than a simple error on either side. Students of Gurbani benefit from reading both Kohli's precise scholarly translations and more poetically adventurous renderings, because each illuminates dimensions of the original that the other cannot fully access.

Key Terms

  • ਅਨੰਦ — Bliss, divine joy; the state Gurbani seeks to evoke in the listener through devotional singing.
  • ਧੁਨਿ — Divine sound, vibration; the quality of Gurbani as a sonic experience that transforms through hearing and repetition.
  • ਸੰਗਤ — The congregation; the collective devotional community within which Gurbani was composed to be experienced.
  • ਵਿਛੋੜਾ — Painful separation from the Divine; a primary devotional register in Gurbani that academic prose translation struggles to convey.
  • ਗੁਰਦੁਆਰਾ — The Sikh place of worship; the institutional setting in which Gurbani is experienced as living devotional event rather than text on a page.
  • ਸ਼ਬਦ — A compositional unit in the Guru Granth Sahib; the primary form in which Gurbani is experienced devotionally.

Discussion Questions

  1. Kohli's translations served an educated, intellectually curious reader. What kind of translation would better serve a diaspora child encountering Gurbani's meaning for the first time? A spiritual seeker from another tradition?
  2. Can scholarly prose translation convey the devotional register of Gurbani, or is this a structural impossibility? What would a more devotionally adequate English rendering look like?
  3. Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh argues for emotional fidelity as a translation value alongside semantic accuracy. Do you find this compelling? What would you sacrifice in order to gain it?
  4. What responsibilities does a translator of devotional scripture have to readers who may form their primary relationship with the text through the translation rather than through the original?

Further Reading

Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, The Name of My Beloved: Verses of the Sikh Gurus.

Lawrence Venuti, The Translator's Invisibility: A History of Translation.

Trilochan Singh et al., Selections from the Sacred Writings of the Sikhs.

Key Takeaways

  • Every translation implies an imagined reader, and Kohli's implied reader was educated and intellectually curious — well-served by his scholarly approach but not the only possible audience for Gurbani in English.
  • Scholarly prose translation expands access to Gurbani's content while necessarily leaving behind its devotional register as sonic, communal, and transformative event.
  • The tension between emotional fidelity and semantic precision is a genuine dilemma, not a simple error — different translations emphasizing different values serve different readers and purposes.
  • Students gain most from reading multiple translations of the same shabads, since each approach illuminates dimensions the others cannot fully access.

Homework

Select a shabad that has personal significance to you — one you have sung, heard, or prayed with. Read Kohli's English translation of that shabad (or the closest scholarly translation available). Sit quietly for 10 minutes and reflect on the difference between your devotional experience of the shabad and what the English translation gives you. Write 300 words on what the translation captures and what it cannot. Then write one sentence about what this tells you about the limits of any translation of devotional scripture.

lessons.title: Legacy, Criticism, and the Future of Gurbani in English
lessons.html:
Introduction

Every significant scholarly project generates a legacy that is simultaneously a resource and a limitation for those who come after. Dr. Surinder Singh Kohli's contributions to Sikh Studies and to the translation and interpretation of Gurbani in English are substantial: he helped establish the discipline, produced resources that have served generations of students and scholars, and modeled a form of rigorous intellectual engagement with scripture that remained deeply respectful of its spiritual and theological dimensions. Yet his work has also attracted critical attention — not as personal attack but as the normal process by which academic disciplines advance through engagement, challenge, and revision.

This final lesson takes stock of Kohli's legacy in its full complexity. We examine the principal scholarly criticisms his work has received, the ways in which subsequent generations of Sikh scholars have built on and departed from his methods, and the current landscape of Gurbani translation and interpretation in English. We conclude by looking forward: what does the future of Gurbani in English look like, and what does Kohli's example teach us about the responsibilities and possibilities of that task?

Engaging critically with Kohli's legacy is itself an act of scholarly respect. A tradition that cannot subject its own founding figures to rigorous analysis is a tradition that cannot grow. The same intellectual courage that Kohli brought to his translations — the willingness to make difficult choices, to be transparent about limitations, and to model careful scholarly humility — is what the next generation of Sikh scholars must bring to the evaluation of his work.

Principal Criticisms of Kohli's Work

Several categories of criticism have been directed at Kohli's translations and commentaries. First, there is the question of theological framework. Some scholars, including those in the tradition of Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's lexicographical work, have argued that Kohli occasionally imported categories from classical Indian philosophy — particularly Vedanta and Sanskrit scholasticism — into his reading of Gurbani in ways that subtly distorted the ਗੁਰਮਤਿ (Gurmat) framework. When Kohli used Sanskritic philosophical terms to gloss Gurbani concepts, he risked suggesting a greater continuity between Gurbani and classical Brahmanical thought than the Gurus themselves intended. This criticism connects to a broader debate within Sikh Studies about the relationship between ਗੁਰਮਤਿ (Gurmat, the Guru's teaching) and classical Indian philosophical systems.

Second, some feminist scholars have noted that Kohli's translations did not always attend sufficiently to the gendered dimensions of Gurbani's language and imagery. Gurbani frequently uses the feminine as a theological category — the soul is often described in feminine terms as the bride longing for the Divine Husband. Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh's scholarship has demonstrated that how one translates this gendered imagery has significant implications for how readers understand Gurbani's vision of gender, the body, and spiritual identity. Kohli's translations were not blind to this dimension, but they did not foreground it with the theoretical sophistication that later feminist scholarship would bring.

Third, post-colonial scholars such as Arvind-Pal Singh Mandair have raised structural questions about whether Kohli's comparative and academic framing of Gurbani — positioning it within a global world-religions framework — inadvertently participated in a colonial project of classifying and containing Sikh thought within categories developed in Western academic institutions. This is not a personal criticism of Kohli but a systemic observation about the conditions under which Sikh Studies developed as a discipline in the twentieth century.

The Generation After Kohli

The scholars who followed Kohli built on his foundations while addressing these criticisms. Pashaura Singh's work on the textual history of the Guru Granth Sahib brought rigorous philological and historical methods that complemented and sometimes corrected Kohli's readings. Gurinder Singh Mann's scholarship on the making of Sikh scripture provided historical grounding for questions Kohli had treated more philosophically. Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh's poetic translations demonstrated that English could engage Gurbani's aesthetic dimension more fully than Kohli had attempted. Mandair's post-colonial theoretical work opened new conversations about the politics of representation and translation that Kohli could not have anticipated in his own intellectual context.

Taken together, this body of scholarship represents a discipline coming of age — building genuine expertise, engaging in rigorous self-criticism, and producing scholarship that can hold its own in the most demanding international academic conversations. Kohli's work was an essential step in making this possible, both by producing resources others could use and by demonstrating that serious intellectual engagement with Sikh thought was academically legitimate and valuable.

The Future of Gurbani in English

The future of Gurbani in English is already taking shape. Digital tools now allow scholars and learners to access multiple translations simultaneously, to search by theme or theological concept, and to listen to Gurbani being sung while reading translations — integrating devotional and scholarly dimensions of engagement in ways that print editions alone could not support. Projects at major research universities, in collaboration with Sikh community institutions, are producing new critical editions with improved historical and linguistic apparatus.

At the same time, new challenges have emerged. AI-assisted translation tools raise questions about quality control, theological accuracy, and the role of human scholarly judgment in rendering sacred text. The global reach of Gurbani through digital media has created new audiences — in Africa, Latin America, East Asia — whose first encounter with Sikh scripture is through English or through English-mediated translations into their own languages. The question of what Kohli's legacy means for these new contexts is genuinely open: the scholarly rigor he modeled remains a permanent standard; the specific cultural assumptions embedded in his work may need to be recognized and addressed as Gurbani moves into new linguistic and cultural worlds.

Key Terms

  • ਗੁਰਮਤਿ — The Guru's teaching; the distinctively Sikh theological framework that must not be reduced to or conflated with classical Indian philosophical systems.
  • ਵਿਆਕਰਣ — Grammar, philology; the systematic linguistic study that grounds rigorous scripture translation.
  • ਤੀਕਾ — Word-by-word exegetical commentary; the classical method of scriptural interpretation in the Sikh scholarly tradition.
  • ਸ਼ਾਸਤ੍ਰ-ਵਿਚਾਰ — Scriptural deliberation; the ongoing process of communal theological reflection on the meaning of Gurbani.
  • ਪੰਥ — The Sikh community as a whole; the collective body within which questions of scriptural interpretation carry communal as well as individual weight.
  • ਸੇਵਾ — In the context of scholarship: intellectual service to the community; the spirit in which Kohli and other Sikh scholars understood their academic work.

Discussion Questions

  1. Is the criticism that Kohli imported Vedantic categories into Gurbani a fundamental flaw in his work, or a correctable limitation that does not undermine his contributions? How should we evaluate a scholar's work that contains both significant achievement and specific errors?
  2. What responsibilities do contemporary Sikh scholars have toward the legacy of founders such as Kohli? Is it possible to be both critically rigorous and appropriately grateful?
  3. Digital tools and AI now make Gurbani available in multiple languages and formats in ways Kohli could not have imagined. What new opportunities and new risks does this create for the quality and integrity of Gurbani's global reception?
  4. If you were designing a new comprehensive English edition of the Guru Granth Sahib for the next generation, what would you prioritize — semantic precision, devotional resonance, feminist sensitivity, post-colonial awareness, or something else? Can these priorities be integrated?

Further Reading

Arvind-Pal Singh Mandair, Religion and the Specter of the West: Sikhism, India, Postcoloniality, and the Politics of Translation.

Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, Feminine Principle in the Sikh Vision of the Transcendent.

Pashaura Singh and Louis E. Fenech, eds., The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies.

Key Takeaways

  • Kohli's legacy is substantial and foundational — he helped establish Sikh Studies as a serious academic discipline and produced resources that continue to serve scholars and students worldwide.
  • The principal scholarly criticisms of his work — concerning theological framing, feminist dimensions, and post-colonial methodology — are serious engagements that the next generation has productively addressed.
  • Building on and departing from Kohli is itself an act of intellectual respect, continuing the tradition of rigorous, community-serving scholarship that he modeled.
  • The future of Gurbani in English is shaped by digital access, new global audiences, and emerging technologies — all of which require the same scholarly virtues of precision, humility, and devotional seriousness that Kohli exemplified at his best.

Homework

This course has traced the arc of Kohli's scholarly project — from his translation methods to his theological frameworks, his social vision, his comparative approaches, and his reception among later scholars. Write a 350-word personal assessment: What do you consider Kohli's most important contribution to the accessibility of Gurbani in English? What limitation or criticism do you find most significant? And what has this course changed or deepened in your own relationship to Gurbani — whether as a Sikh, a scholar, or a curious reader?

courses.title: Reading Dorothy Field: An Early Western Introduction to Sikhi
courses.summary: This course studies Dorothy Field's 1914 book The Religion of the Sikhs, one of the earliest short English-language introductions to Sikhi written by a Western author. We look at what the book covered, where it sits among other early English accounts such as Max Arthur Macauliffe's The Sikh Religion (1909), and how…
outcomes: Describe the purpose, audience, and structure of Dorothy Field's The Religion of the Sikhs (1914) and the Wisdom of the East series it belonged to.
Explain the main subjects an early English introduction to Sikhi typically presented, such as the lives of the Gurus, key teachings, and scripture.
Compare Field's short popular introduction with Max Arthur Macauliffe's larger multi-volume The Sikh Religion (1909).
Identify the historical and colonial context in which early Western accounts of Sikhi were written and read.
Apply critical reading skills to recognize bias, framing, and the use of sources in colonial-era works.
Evaluate how modern scholarship, such as the Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies (2014), reassesses these early texts.

terms.m: Sikhi: the faith, path, and way of life taught by the Sikh Gurus, the subject these early English books tried to explain.
Guru: the spiritual teacher and guide; in Sikhi a central term whose meaning Western writers often tried to translate for new readers.
Gurbani: the sacred words of the Gurus, the body of revealed teaching that scripture-focused accounts pointed to.
Granth: scripture or sacred volume; early writers discussed the holy book as the heart of the faith.
Panth: the Sikh community or collective body, a concept early accounts described to Western audiences.
Naam: the Divine Name; remembrance of Naam is a core practice that introductory texts highlighted.
Seva: selfless service, a value early writers noted as characteristic of Sikh life.

references: Field, Dorothy. The Religion of the Sikhs. Wisdom of the East. London: John Murray, 1914.
Macauliffe, Max Arthur. The Sikh Religion: Its Gurus, Sacred Writings and Authors. 6 vols. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1909.
Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014.
Mandair, Arvind-Pal Singh. Sikhism: A Guide for the Perplexed. London: Bloomsbury, 2013.

lessons.title: Course Overview and Contents
lessons.summary: An introduction to the course and a guide to the six lessons.
lessons.html:
Welcome

This course is about a book, not only about ਸਿੱਖੀ itself. The book is The Religion of the Sikhs by Dorothy Field, published in 1914 (Field 1914). It was one of the first short English introductions to Sikhi written for Western readers. We will study what it tried to do, how it compares to other early works, and how to read such old books with care.

Contents

LessonTitleFocus
1Course Overview and ContentsWhat the course covers
2The Book and Its SeriesField's 1914 work and Wisdom of the East
3What an Early Introduction CoveredGurus, teachings, scripture
4Field and Macauliffe ComparedTwo kinds of early English account
5Colonial ContextWho wrote, who read, and why it matters
6Reading Critically TodayModern scholarship and careful reading

How to Use This Course

Each lesson is short and uses simple English. Punjabi terms appear in their original script with a plain meaning. We stay neutral: the goal is understanding, not praise or blame.

References

Field, Dorothy. The Religion of the Sikhs. Wisdom of the East. London: John Murray, 1914.

Homework

Select one of the six existing lessons and read the corresponding section of Dorothy Field's The Religion of the Sikhs (available free on the Internet Archive). In 300–400 words, describe what surprised you most about Field's framing and what you would want a modern reader to know before opening this book.

lessons.title: The Book and Its Series
lessons.summary: Dorothy Field's 1914 book and the Wisdom of the East series.
lessons.html:
A Small Book with a Big Aim

The Religion of the Sikhs appeared in 1914 as part of the Wisdom of the East series (Field 1914). This series published short, affordable books that introduced the religions and thought of Asia to general English readers. Each volume was meant to be a friendly first step, not a deep scholarly study.

Why a Short Book Matters

Because it was brief, the book had to choose carefully what to include. It aimed to give a clear picture of ਸਿੱਖੀ to people who likely knew nothing about it. This makes it a useful window into how Sikhi was first presented to a Western public in plain language.

FeatureDescription
AuthorDorothy Field
Year1914
SeriesWisdom of the East
TypeShort popular introduction

We will not invent details about the author's life. What matters here is the book itself and the role it played as an early, accessible account.

References

Field, Dorothy. The Religion of the Sikhs. Wisdom of the East. London: John Murray, 1914.

Homework

Locate the original series listing for the Wisdom of the East series (a search of archive.org or WorldCat will return it). Identify at least three other titles in the series alongside Field's volume. In 300 words, reflect on what the choice of topics tells us about British-imperial ideas of what counted as 'Eastern wisdom' worth introducing to Western readers.

lessons.title: What an Early Introduction Covered
lessons.summary: The typical subjects of an early English account of Sikhi.
lessons.html:
Common Topics

An early English introduction to Sikhi, like Field's, would usually cover a few core subjects so that a new reader could grasp the basics (Field 1914). These often included the lives of the ਗੁਰੂ, the central teachings, and the place of scripture.

Teachings and Practice

Such books pointed to ideas like remembrance of the Divine Name, ਨਾਮ, and the value of selfless service, ਸੇਵਾ. They also described the community, the ਪੰਥ, and the importance of the sacred volume, the ਗ੍ਰੰਥ, which holds ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ.

TopicWhy Included
Lives of the GurusTo give the history and founders of the faith
Core teachingsTo explain belief in one God and ethical living
ScriptureTo show where teachings come from
CommunityTo describe Sikh life and identity

We avoid quoting specific scripture passages or page numbers here, since the focus is on the kinds of subjects these books addressed rather than on reproducing their exact words.

References

Field, Dorothy. The Religion of the Sikhs. Wisdom of the East. London: John Murray, 1914.

Homework

Field's book attempts to summarize the whole of Sikh teaching in roughly 60 pages. Choose one doctrine or practice she covers (e.g., Naam Simran, the Khalsa initiation, or the role of the Guru) and compare her treatment to a modern English-language source such as Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh's The Name of My Beloved. Write 350–400 words on what is gained and lost by a short introductory format.

lessons.title: Field and Macauliffe Compared
lessons.summary: Two different kinds of early English account.
lessons.html:
Two Books, Two Scales

Field's short 1914 volume can be set beside a much larger work: Max Arthur Macauliffe's The Sikh Religion, published in six volumes by Oxford in 1909 (Macauliffe 1909). Where Field offered a brief introduction, Macauliffe produced a long study with extensive translations.

Different Purposes

Field's book served the general reader who wanted a quick, clear picture of ਸਿੱਖੀ. Macauliffe's work served readers who wanted depth, including renderings of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ and detailed accounts of the ਗੁਰੂ tradition (Macauliffe 1909).

AspectField (1914)Macauliffe (1909)
LengthShort single volumeSix volumes
AudienceGeneral readersSerious students
DepthOverviewDetailed with translations
Series/PressWisdom of the EastOxford, Clarendon Press

Reading the two together shows that early English writing on Sikhi came in different forms, each shaped by its goals and its readers.

References

Field, Dorothy. The Religion of the Sikhs. Wisdom of the East. London: John Murray, 1914.

Macauliffe, Max Arthur. The Sikh Religion: Its Gurus, Sacred Writings and Authors. 6 vols. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1909.

Homework

Both Field and Macauliffe were non-Sikh Westerners writing for Western audiences, yet their works differ considerably in scope and method. In 400 words, compare their stated aims (as expressed in their prefaces) and evaluate which approach you find more respectful of the tradition and why.

lessons.title: Colonial Context
lessons.summary: The historical setting in which early Western accounts were written.
lessons.html:
Time and Place

Books like Field's appeared during the colonial period, when Britain ruled much of South Asia. This setting shaped who wrote about ਸਿੱਖੀ, what sources they used, and how their work was received (Field 1914).

Why Context Matters

Western authors often wrote for Western readers and drew on the sources and assumptions of their time. This does not make their work worthless, but it means we should notice the lens through which they viewed the faith, its ਗੁਰੂ tradition, and its ਪੰਥ.

FactorEffect on the Text
Colonial ruleShaped access, audience, and tone
Western readershipFramed explanations for outsiders
Available sourcesLimited what authors could draw on

Keeping this context in mind helps us read fairly: we can value the effort to explain Sikhi while staying aware of the period's limits.

References

Field, Dorothy. The Religion of the Sikhs. Wisdom of the East. London: John Murray, 1914.

Homework

Choose one specific aspect of the colonial context — for example, the 1899 Singh Sabha movement, the Gurdwara Reform Movement, or the Anand Marriage Act of 1909 — and research it using at least two sources. Write 350 words explaining how that context shapes what Field chose to include or omit.

lessons.title: Reading Critically Today
lessons.summary: How modern scholarship helps us read early texts well.
lessons.html:
A Careful Modern Reader

Today we can read Field's 1914 book with help from newer scholarship. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies (2014) gathers modern research and shows how the academic study of ਸਿੱਖੀ has grown and changed (Singh and Fenech 2014).

Skills for Reading Old Books

Good critical reading means asking: Who wrote this, and for whom? What sources did they use? What might they have missed or misunderstood? With these questions we can appreciate early accounts of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ and the ਗ੍ਰੰਥ without taking every claim at face value.

QuestionPurpose
Who is the author?Reveals viewpoint and aims
Who is the audience?Explains tone and framing
What sources are used?Tests reliability
What does modern work say?Checks and updates the account

Read this way, Field's small book remains a useful historical document: an early, sincere attempt to introduce Sikhi to the wider world, best understood alongside later and deeper scholarship (Singh and Fenech 2014).

References

Field, Dorothy. The Religion of the Sikhs. Wisdom of the East. London: John Murray, 1914.
