Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014.

Homework

Field's book is now over a century old. Identify one claim she makes that has since been revised or rejected by Sikh Studies scholarship, and one claim that has held up well. Use at least one modern academic source (e.g., an article from the Journal of Punjab Studies or a chapter from a Sikh Studies anthology). Write 400 words presenting your findings.

lessons.title: Field's Chapter I: The Ten Gurus Through a Western Lens
lessons.html:
Introduction

Dorothy Field's first chapter, titled 'The Sikh Gurus,' sets the narrative spine of her entire book. She moves chronologically through the ten Gurus, and in doing so she makes a series of interpretive choices that reveal as much about 1914 British intellectual culture as they do about Sikhi. Understanding how she constructs her account — what she emphasises, what she condenses, and what she omits — is the central skill this lecture develops.

Field was writing for an educated British general reader who had likely never encountered a Sikh text directly. Her framing therefore serves a dual purpose: it introduces the Gurus as historical figures while simultaneously arguing that Sikhism merits serious intellectual attention. This apologetic goal shapes every paragraph of the chapter, sometimes productively and sometimes at the cost of nuance.

In this lecture we examine her portraits of Guru Nanak ਗੁਰੂ ਨਾਨਕ, Guru Arjan ਗੁਰੂ ਅਰਜਨ, Guru Teg Bahadur ਗੁਰੂ ਤੇਗ ਬਹਾਦੁਰ, and Guru Gobind Singh ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ in particular detail, because Field devotes proportionally the most space to them and because her interpretive choices at each of these four figures are the most consequential for how a Western reader would have understood Sikh history.

Guru Nanak in Field's Telling

Field introduces Guru Nanak as a young man of unusual spiritual sensitivity who protests the sacred thread ceremony (janeu ਜਨੇਊ) at age nine by composing an improvised hymn. This episode is historically attested in the janam-sakhis ਜਨਮ ਸਾਖੀਆਂ, and Field uses it effectively to establish Nanak's lifelong opposition to caste hierarchy and Brahman authority. What she handles well here is the connection between Nanak's early gesture and his later theological insistence on equality before the Divine.

However, Field's Nanak is constructed primarily as a reformer reacting against existing traditions rather than as an originating voice. She writes that he 'combined the monotheistic passion of Islam with the philosophical sophistication of Hindu thought.' While this synthesis argument has some validity, it risks reducing Nanak's revelation to a derivative sum. Sikh theology insists on the direct nature of his divine experience — the encounter at the Vein river (ਵੈਣ ਨਦੀ), after which Nanak reportedly said 'There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim' — as an originating moment, not a synthesis. Field acknowledges the story but interprets it as confirmation of her synthesis thesis rather than as a claim to independent revelation.

The missionary journeys (udaasis ਉਦਾਸੀਆਂ) receive brief but accurate treatment. Field notes Nanak's travels across South Asia, the Middle East, and Central Asia with his companion Bhai Mardana ਭਾਈ ਮਰਦਾਨਾ, and she correctly emphasises the role of kirtan ਕੀਰਤਨ — devotional singing — as the medium through which Nanak's teaching spread. Her framing of Mardana as a 'minstrel' rather than a fellow traveller and devoted companion reflects a tendency to render Sikh relationships in terms legible to Western readers familiar with court musicians.

Field also emphasises Nanak's radical inclusivity toward women and lower castes, which was genuinely a distinctive feature of his teaching. This is one of the moments where her apologetic goal aligns with historical accuracy, and the resulting portrait, while simplified, is not misleading. She correctly notes that Nanak rejected gender barriers to spiritual knowledge, and she connects this to later Sikh practice of open langar ਲੰਗਰ — the community kitchen — as an institutional expression of equality.

The Middle Gurus and Institutional Development

Field's treatment of Gurus Angad through Har Rai is compressed but contains several important observations. She correctly identifies Guru Angad's ਗੁਰੂ ਅੰਗਦ development and standardisation of the Gurmukhi ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ script as a democratising act — making sacred literature accessible outside the Sanskrit-literate Brahman class. This is a sound historical observation that modern scholars have elaborated considerably. Gurumukhi was not invented from nothing, but its systematic use to record the Gurus' compositions created a distinct scriptural and literary tradition that reinforced Sikh identity.

She gives significant attention to Guru Arjan ਗੁਰੂ ਅਰਜਨ and the compilation of the Adi Granth ਆਦਿ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ (which Field calls the Granth Sahib) around 1604. Her account accurately notes that Guru Arjan included compositions not only of the Sikh Gurus but also of Hindu bhagats ਭਗਤ and Muslim saints, presenting this as evidence of Sikhi's inclusive theological vision. This is historically accurate and theologically significant: the inclusion of figures like Kabir, Namdev, Farid, and Ravidas in the scripture makes the Adi Granth a remarkably pluralistic text, and Field grasps this point even if she cannot fully articulate its theological implications.

Field's account of Guru Arjan's martyrdom in 1606 under Mughal Emperor Jahangir is factually correct. She treats it as the decisive turning point in Sikh history — the moment when a purely spiritual movement began developing martial characteristics. The phrase she uses, that the martyrdom 'brought out what was already latent,' is interpretively contested: it implies martial capacity was always present and only waiting for provocation, which some scholars find too deterministic. Nonetheless, the basic historical observation — that persecution accelerated institutional militarisation — is well-founded.

The middle Gurus also witness the development of the Akal Takht ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ by Guru Hargobind ਗੁਰੂ ਹਰਗੋਬਿੰਦ, which Field mentions but does not fully theorise. The Akal Takht as a seat of temporal authority existing alongside the Harmandir Sahib ਹਰਿਮੰਦਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ as a seat of spiritual authority represents the miri-piri ਮੀਰੀ ਪੀਰੀ doctrine — the integration of worldly and spiritual sovereignty — which is one of the most distinctive contributions of the Sikh Gurus to political theology. Field describes the two swords Guru Hargobind wore symbolically but does not develop the doctrine behind the gesture.

Guru Gobind Singh and the Khalsa

Field devotes her most sustained attention to Guru Gobind Singh ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ and the founding of the Khalsa ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ in 1699. Her account of the Vaisakhi ceremony at Anandpur Sahib ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ is largely accurate: she describes Guru Gobind Singh calling for volunteers willing to give their heads, the emergence of the Panj Pyare ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ (Five Beloved), and the preparation of amrit ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ using water stirred with a double-edged sword (khanda ਖੰਡਾ) while Gurbani was recited. She notes the revolutionary social dimension — the five came from different castes and regions — and she captures the symbolic power of Guru Gobind Singh requesting baptism from those he had just baptised, inverting the hierarchy between Guru and disciple.

Field's description of the Panj Kakars ਪੰਜ ਕਕਾਰ (the Five K's) is accurate in listing them: kes ਕੇਸ (uncut hair), kangha ਕੰਘਾ (comb), kara ਕੜਾ (steel bracelet), kachh ਕਛਹਿਰਾ (undergarment), and kirpan ਕਿਰਪਾਨ (sword). She describes the Khalsa's social transformation — drawing recruits from low-caste backgrounds and elevating them into a disciplined martial community — as 'little short of miraculous,' a phrase that reveals both her genuine admiration and her condescending surprise that non-elite South Asians could organise effectively. This kind of double-edged compliment appears throughout the chapter.

Field also records Guru Gobind Singh's declaration that after him, the Guru would be the Guru Granth Sahib ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ and the Guru Panth ਗੁਰੂ ਪੰਥ — the community of initiated Sikhs. This is the doctrine of Guruship in perpetual, living form that distinguishes Sikhism from traditions dependent on a single founding text or lineage. Field grasps its significance, noting that no individual could claim prophetic authority after Guru Gobind Singh, but she does not fully work out the theological implications of the scriptural Guru concept.

Key Terms

  • ਜਨਮ ਸਾਖੀ (Janam-sakhi) — biographical narratives of Guru Nanak's life, composed in Punjabi after his death; important sources for early Sikh history despite their hagiographic character.
  • ਉਦਾਸੀਆਂ (Udaasis) — the missionary journeys undertaken by Guru Nanak across South Asia, the Middle East, and Central Asia to spread his teachings.
  • ਮੀਰੀ ਪੀਰੀ (Miri-Piri) — the doctrine of integrated temporal and spiritual sovereignty, expressed by Guru Hargobind's wearing of two swords.
  • ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ (Panj Pyare) — the Five Beloved, the first five initiates into the Khalsa in 1699; represents diverse caste and regional backgrounds united under a single Sikh identity.
  • ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ (Amrit) — the sacred nectar used in Khalsa initiation, prepared by stirring water with a khanda while Gurbani is recited.
  • ਗੁਰੂ ਪੰਥ (Guru Panth) — the community of initiated Sikhs understood as a living embodiment of the Guru after Guru Gobind Singh's declaration in 1708.

Discussion Questions

  1. Field describes Guru Nanak's teaching as a 'synthesis' of Hindu and Islamic thought. How does this framing differ from the Sikh theological understanding of Nanak's revelation, and why does the difference matter?
  2. Field's account of the Khalsa founding emphasises its social and military dimensions. What theological dimensions does she underemphasise, and how might a Sikh theologian describe the same event?
  3. Field calls the transformation of low-caste recruits into Khalsa warriors 'little short of miraculous.' What does this phrasing reveal about her assumptions, and how would you rewrite the same observation without those assumptions?
  4. The miri-piri doctrine is one of the most distinctive contributions of Sikh political theology. Why might a Western author in 1914 find it difficult to appreciate or articulate this concept?

Further Reading

Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh — The Birth of the Khalsa: A Feminist Re-Memory of Sikh Identity

J. S. Grewal — The Sikhs of the Punjab (The New Cambridge History of India)

Pashaura Singh — The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority

Key Takeaways

  • Field's portrait of the Gurus is largely factually accurate but shaped by an apologetic goal of proving Sikhism worthy of Western intellectual respect.
  • Her 'synthesis' framing of Guru Nanak underplays the Sikh theological claim to original revelation and reduces a founding moment to a derivative sum.
  • The miri-piri doctrine, the Akal Takht, and the scriptural Guru concept receive less development than the martial and social dimensions of the Khalsa, reflecting Field's own interpretive priorities.
  • Double-edged compliments — admiration mixed with colonial surprise — appear throughout her Guru narratives and reward careful attention from critical readers.

Homework

Choose one of the ten Gurus not discussed in detail during this lecture — for example, Guru Amar Das, Guru Ram Das, or Guru Har Krishan. Using a modern academic source (such as Grewal's The Sikhs of the Punjab or the Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies), write 350–400 words on this Guru's specific contribution to Sikh theology or institutions, and briefly note whether Field mentions this Guru and how she characterises them.

lessons.title: Field's Chapter II: Religious Origins and the Synthesis Argument
lessons.html:
Introduction

Chapter II of Field's book is arguably her most intellectually ambitious. Titled 'The Religious Origins of Sikhism — Hindu Monotheism and Connection with Islam,' it attempts to situate Sikhism within the broader history of South Asian religious thought. In doing so, Field constructs what we can call the 'synthesis argument': the claim that Sikhism emerged from the convergence of Hindu monotheistic reform movements and Islamic influence on the subcontinent.

This argument was not unique to Field — it was common in early Western scholarship and even appeared in some colonial-era Indian academic writing. But Field's version is particularly clear and representative, making it an ideal text for understanding both the appeal and the limitations of the synthesis framework. The argument has been substantially challenged by later Sikh Studies scholarship, which insists on the originality of the Gurus' revelation rather than its derivativeness.

In this lecture we examine the intellectual sources Field draws on, the historical evidence she marshals, the moments where her argument is genuinely illuminating, and the points where it distorts more than it clarifies. Understanding why the synthesis argument was attractive in 1914 — and why it remains contested today — is essential for reading Field critically and for understanding the broader field of Sikh Studies.

The Hindu Monotheism Genealogy

Field opens her genealogical argument with the Rig Veda, claiming that latent monotheism was always present in Hindu thought but was suppressed by the Brahman priesthood in favour of pantheism and ritualism. She traces a tradition of protest and renewal: the bhakti ਭਗਤੀ movement's emphasis on personal devotion to a transcendent God, Buddhism's rejection of Brahman authority, and the sant tradition ਸੰਤ ਪਰੰਪਰਾ of northern India, especially figures like Kabir ਕਬੀਰ (c. 1440–1518) and Namdev ਨਾਮਦੇਵ.

This genealogy is not without merit. The sant tradition of the Doab region genuinely did precede Guru Nanak and shares with his teaching a rejection of caste hierarchy, a preference for vernacular devotion over Sanskrit ritual, and an emphasis on the unmediated relationship between the individual soul (jiv ਜੀਵ) and the Divine. Kabir's compositions, included in the Adi Granth, demonstrate that the Gurus saw value in this tradition and considered its best expressions consonant with their own teaching.

However, Field's argument oversimplifies in two directions. First, she presents the sant tradition as directly causing Sikhism rather than constituting one of several intellectual environments Guru Nanak inhabited and transformed. Second, she treats Kabir as a kind of proto-Nanak, an incomplete precursor who lacked Nanak's decisiveness. This teleological reading flattens Kabir's own originality and misrepresents the relationship between two distinct traditions that the Gurus honoured without subordinating their own revelation to them.

Field's description of the Vishnuite bhakti movement as developing 'passionate devotion to a personal God' is accurate as far as it goes, and her observation that the Brahman priesthood repeatedly absorbed or expelled reform movements is historically sound. What she misses is the crucial Sikh theological distinction between saguna ਸਗੁਣ worship (devotion directed toward a God with attributes, including incarnational forms) and nirguna ਨਿਰਗੁਣ worship (devotion to the formless, attributeless Divine). Guru Nanak's theology is firmly nirguna, which distinguishes it sharply from Vaishnava bhakti even as it shares bhakti's emotional register and vernacular medium.

The Islamic Influence Argument

Field's second genealogical strand concerns Islamic influence on Guru Nanak. She notes that Nanak studied Persian texts and had significant contact with Muslim communities, Sufi orders, and wandering faqirs ਫ਼ਕੀਰ. An early composition of Nanak's structured as an acrostic on the Persian alphabet contains language and imagery that Field identifies as purely Islamic in sentiment. She concludes that Islam supplied the 'zeal for exclusive monotheism' that distinguished Nanak from the quietistic saints who preceded him.

This argument has surface plausibility. Sufism's emphasis on loving surrender to the Divine (ishq ਇਸ਼ਕ), the concept of fana (annihilation of the ego in God), and Sufi poetry's rich imagery of the divine Beloved all find parallels in Guru Nanak's compositions. The fact that Nanak wore mixed Hindu-Muslim dress in some janam-sakhi accounts is taken by Field as evidence of his conscious attempt to transcend both traditions, drawing on each.

Modern scholarship has treated this claim carefully. There are genuine structural and thematic similarities between certain currents in Sufism and certain aspects of Gurbani. However, to claim that Islam provided Nanak's 'zeal' implies that his monotheistic conviction was borrowed rather than revealed, which Sikh tradition categorically rejects. Furthermore, the specific Sufi orders active in the Punjab during Nanak's lifetime held a variety of theological positions; treating 'Islam' as a single intellectual source oversimplifies considerably.

Field also identifies a paradox that she handles well: that political persecution by Mughal emperors progressively alienated Sikhs from Islam even as Islamic monotheism had allegedly helped form the tradition. The militarisation of the Sikh community under pressure from the Mughal state created a bitter historical enmity that Field acknowledges, and she notes the irony that Islamic influence on Sikh origins was later largely forgotten or denied within the community itself due to this historical antagonism.

Scholarly Responses to the Synthesis Argument

The synthesis argument Field articulates in 1914 was the dominant framework in Western Sikh Studies for much of the twentieth century. W. H. McLeod's influential and controversial scholarship in the 1960s and 1970s gave it a more rigorous academic form, arguing that Guru Nanak's theology was substantially shaped by the sant tradition and specifically by the nirguna bhakti current associated with Kabir and his predecessors. McLeod's work generated significant debate within the Sikh community precisely because it appeared to deny the originality of the Gurus' revelation.

Responding scholars including Gurinder Singh Mann, Pashaura Singh, and Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh have emphasised both the contextual influences on Guru Nanak and the genuinely original theological contribution that cannot be reduced to those influences. The consensus in contemporary Sikh Studies tends to acknowledge intellectual environment — the bhakti milieu, the sant tradition, the presence of Sufi thought — while insisting that the Gurus synthesised these materials in ways that produced a theologically original system rather than merely recombining existing elements.

For our purposes, the important point is that Field's version of the synthesis argument is the popular predecessor of a scholarly debate that remained active for most of the twentieth century. Reading her chapter carefully allows students to identify the argument in its simplest form, evaluate its evidence, and understand why it proved both attractive and controversial.

Key Terms

  • ਭਗਤੀ (Bhakti) — devotional movement in Hindu religious history emphasising direct, personal love for the Divine over ritual mediation; a broad tradition with many regional and theological variants.
  • ਸੰਤ ਪਰੰਪਰਾ (Sant Tradition) — the north Indian lineage of poet-saints, including Kabir and Namdev, who rejected caste, ritualism, and sectarian boundaries; an important intellectual environment for Guru Nanak.
  • ਸਗੁਣ / ਨਿਰਗੁਣ (Saguna / Nirguna) — theological categories distinguishing God-with-attributes (saguna, associated with Vaishnava bhakti) from the formless, attributeless Divine (nirguna, the emphasis of Gurbani).
  • ਫ਼ਕੀਰ (Faqir) — a Muslim or Sufi ascetic wanderer; Guru Nanak encountered and engaged with faqirs throughout his udaasis.
  • ਮਾਇਆ (Maya) — the concept of illusion or attachment that veils the soul from the Divine; borrowed from Hindu thought but given a specific meaning in Gurbani where it denotes worldly distraction from Naam.
  • ਸੰਗਤ (Sangat) — the congregation or community of Sikh worshippers; a concept that distinguishes Sikh devotion as inherently communal rather than purely individual.

Discussion Questions

  1. Field argues that Islam provided Guru Nanak with his 'zeal for exclusive monotheism.' What evidence does she offer, and what would a Sikh theologian say in response to this claim?
  2. The distinction between saguna and nirguna worship is central to understanding Sikh theology in relation to bhakti movements. Why might a Western author in 1914 miss or underplay this distinction?
  3. Field identifies a paradox in Sikh history: Islamic thought may have shaped the tradition's early development, yet political persecution created lasting antagonism toward Islam. How should historians handle this kind of historical irony?
  4. W. H. McLeod's later scholarly version of the synthesis argument was highly controversial. Why do questions about the 'origins' of a religious tradition carry such high stakes for practitioners?

Further Reading

W. H. McLeod — Guru Nanak and the Sikh Religion

Gurinder Singh Mann — The Making of Sikh Scripture

Arvind-pal Singh Mandair — Religion and the Specter of the West: Sikhism, India, Postcoloniality, and the Politics of Translation

Key Takeaways

  • Field's synthesis argument positions Sikhism as emerging from the convergence of Hindu bhakti and Islamic monotheism — an interpretation that was intellectually dominant in early Western scholarship but has been substantially critiqued.
  • The nirguna/saguna distinction is essential for understanding what separates Gurbani theology from Vaishnava bhakti, and Field's failure to develop this distinction is one of the chapter's main analytical limitations.
  • Field's observation about the historical paradox of Islamic influence followed by Mughal persecution is historically astute and anticipates later scholarly discussions.
  • The synthesis debate remained central to Sikh Studies for most of the twentieth century; Field's chapter is its popular-accessible starting point.

Homework

Read the Wikipedia article on Kabir and then read the brief introduction to Kabir's compositions in any translation of the Guru Granth Sahib (the SikhiToTheMax website provides accessible translations). In 350 words, identify two points of genuine similarity between Kabir's theology and Guru Nanak's, and one point where they differ significantly. Reflect on whether these similarities support or complicate Field's synthesis argument.

lessons.title: Field's Chapter III: Sikh Doctrine Through a Victorian Theological Framework
lessons.html:
Introduction

Chapter III, 'The Doctrines of the Sikhs,' is the theological heart of Field's book. Having established the historical narrative of the Gurus and the intellectual genealogy of the tradition, she now attempts to present Sikh beliefs systematically: the nature of God, the path to salvation, the role of the Guru, the significance of Naam, ethical requirements, and social teachings. This chapter is the most ambitious and the most revealing of Field's interpretive assumptions.

Reading Chapter III carefully requires attention to the theological frameworks Field is consciously or unconsciously applying. As a British author writing in 1914, she would have been steeped in Protestant Christianity's vocabulary — personal faith, justification, grace, the priesthood of all believers, scripture as authority — and in the comparative religion framework developed by scholars like Max Müller and Friedrich Heiler, which categorised world religions along a spectrum from 'primitive' to 'universal.' Both of these frameworks appear in her treatment of Sikh doctrine, sometimes helpfully and sometimes distortingly.

This lecture analyses her doctrinal account under three main headings: her treatment of Sikh theology and the nature of God, her account of the path to salvation and the role of Naam ਨਾਮ, and her presentation of Sikh social ethics. At each point we consider both what she gets right and what the framework she applies causes her to miss or mischaracterise.

The Theology of Ik Onkar

Field opens her doctrinal account with the Sikh affirmation of divine unity: 'There is but one God, the true' — her translation of the Mool Mantar ਮੂਲ ਮੰਤਰ, the foundational statement at the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib. She correctly identifies this as the theological centre of the tradition, and she connects it to Jewish and Islamic monotheism, positioning Sikhism within a global family of Abrahamic-style faiths. This comparative gesture was useful for her intended audience, but it also risks assimilating Sikh theology into a Western monotheist framework that does not fully capture it.

The Mool Mantar begins with ੴ (Ik Onkar), meaning 'There is One Being.' Field translates this as 'There is but one God,' which is defensible but loses something. The Gurmukhi numeral Ik (one) combined with Onkar (the primal sound, related to the Sanskrit Om) implies that divine unity is not merely a propositional claim but a sonic and experiential reality. The opening of the Guru Granth Sahib is not simply asserting monotheism in the philosophical sense — it is pointing toward the experience of divine oneness as something to be realised through practice, not merely believed as doctrine.

Field correctly notes that the Sikh conception of God involves both transcendence and immanence — God is beyond all human description (nirankar ਨਿਰੰਕਾਰ, formless) yet also the 'Ocean of Mercy' and 'Friend of Sinners.' She also correctly reports the Gurus' rejection of incarnation theology, citing Guru Gobind Singh's warning that those who call him the Supreme Being will fall into error. What she does not fully develop is the concept of Waheguru ਵਾਹੇਗੁਰੂ — the primary name of God in Sikh practice — and the specific Sikh understanding that God's 'Name' (Naam ਨਾਮ) is not merely a label but the very reality through which God is present in creation and in the human heart.

Her treatment of karma ਕਰਮ and reincarnation is respectful but somewhat mechanical. She acknowledges that Sikhism accepts these Hindu cosmological frameworks while giving them a distinct theological role: karma explains present circumstances while the future remains open to transformation through spiritual effort. This is broadly accurate, but she does not develop the specific Sikh doctrine of nadar ਨਦਰਿ — divine grace — as the power that can override karmic accumulation and liberate the soul. The interplay between human effort and divine grace is central to Sikh soteriology, and Field's emphasis on individual effort understates the grace dimension.

Naam, the Guru, and the Path to Liberation

Field's account of the path to liberation (mukti ਮੁਕਤੀ) in Sikhism is one of the most important sections of her book because it touches on what is theologically most distinctive about the tradition. She correctly identifies Naam Simran ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ — the meditative repetition and contemplation of the divine Name — as the primary spiritual practice. She notes that Waheguru is the specific name used and that its repetition, when practised with a pure heart, can result in divine union.

What Field captures well is the radical accessibility of this practice: unlike Sanskrit mantra requiring Brahman initiation, or Vedic ritual requiring caste eligibility, Naam Simran is available to all human beings regardless of birth. This democratisation of spiritual practice is one of Sikhism's most significant contributions to South Asian religious history, and Field presents it clearly and approvingly. She correctly links it to the institution of the sangat ਸੰਗਤ — the congregation — and the langar ਲੰਗਰ as communal expressions of the same egalitarian principle.

However, Field's treatment of the Guru's role is somewhat confused. She writes that 'without the Guru, man is ruined by wandering' — a genuine Gurbani teaching — and then attempts to reconcile this with Nanak's claim that God is his Guru. The resolution she offers is that the Guru-concept was democratised through the succession of human Gurus and finally transferred to the scriptural Guru. This is roughly correct but misses the Sikh theological understanding of the Guru as the divine light (jot ਜੋਤ) that passed through each of the ten human Gurus and now resides permanently in the Guru Granth Sahib. The Guru, in this understanding, is not an institution or a role but a divine reality.

Field's description of Sikh daily prayer disciplines — the Japji ਜਪੁਜੀ Sahib at dawn, evening prayers, and bedtime recitation — is accurate and shows that she had studied the tradition's practice as well as its theology. She correctly notes that Guru Nanak rejected external ritual (pilgrimage, fasting, elaborate ceremony) as insufficient substitutes for authentic inner devotion, while affirming that structured prayer supports rather than replaces direct experience of the Divine.

Social Ethics and the Reform Agenda

Field's treatment of Sikh social ethics is among the strongest sections of her book, and it is here that her sympathies are most evident. She presents Sikhism's rejection of caste (zaat-paat ਜਾਤ-ਪਾਤ), its affirmation of women's spiritual equality, and its prohibition of infanticide, widow immolation, and intoxicants as marks of a morally advanced tradition. The framing is explicitly comparative — she is positioning Sikhism favourably against both Hinduism (for its caste system and treatment of women) and Islam (for polygamy and purdah).

This comparative positioning serves her apologetic goal but has a significant cost: it constructs Sikhism's ethical merit in opposition to its neighbouring traditions rather than on its own theological terms. The rejection of caste in Sikhism is grounded in the theological claim that all human beings carry the divine light (ਅੰਸੁ ਅੰਸੁ ਕਰਿ — fragment of the Divine) within them, not merely in a reformist reaction to caste abuses. By framing the social teaching as reform rather than revelation, Field inadvertently reproduces the synthesis argument at the ethical level.

Her citation of Macauliffe's summary of Sikh ethics at the end of the chapter — which lists prohibitions and positive virtues — is historically interesting. It shows that Field was drawing directly on Macauliffe's six-volume work as her primary secondary source, and it suggests that her book functions partly as an accessible popularisation of Macauliffe's scholarship for readers who would not tackle six volumes of translated Gurbani.

Key Terms

  • ੴ / ਮੂਲ ਮੰਤਰ (Ik Onkar / Mool Mantar) — the foundational statement opening the Guru Granth Sahib, affirming divine unity; ੴ is the Gurmukhi symbol representing the One Being.
  • ਨਿਰੰਕਾਰ (Nirankar) — 'Formless One,' a key divine attribute in Gurbani affirming that God transcends physical form or human likeness.
  • ਨਦਰਿ (Nadar) — divine grace or glance of mercy; in Sikh theology, the power of God's grace can override karmic accumulation and open the soul to liberation.
  • ਮੁਕਤੀ (Mukti) — liberation from the cycle of birth and death (ਜਨਮ ਮਰਨ); the ultimate goal of Sikh spiritual practice, understood as merging with the Divine.
  • ਜਾਤ-ਪਾਤ (Zaat-Paat) — the caste system; explicitly rejected in Sikh teaching as a human-made division that contradicts the divine light in all persons.
  • ਜੋਤ (Jot) — divine light; the theological concept that the same divine light passed through each of the ten Gurus and now resides in the Guru Granth Sahib.

Discussion Questions

  1. Field translates ੴ as 'There is but one God.' What is gained and what is lost in this translation, and how might a Sikh theologian translate the same symbol differently?
  2. Field's treatment of the Guru emphasises the institutional succession but underplays the theological concept of jot (divine light). Why does this distinction matter for understanding what Sikhs mean when they say 'the Guru Granth Sahib is the living Guru'?
  3. Field praises Sikhism's social ethics largely by contrasting them with Hinduism and Islam. What are the risks of this comparative approach for understanding any tradition on its own terms?
  4. The interplay between nadar (divine grace) and individual effort in achieving mukti is a recurring tension in Sikh theology. How does Field handle this tension, and what does her handling reveal about the theological frameworks she is applying?

Further Reading

Sewa Singh Kalsi — Sikhism (Religions of the World series)

Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh — The Name of My Beloved: Verses of the Sikh Gurus

Wazir Singh — Philosophy of Sikh Religion

Key Takeaways

  • Field's theological account is built on a Protestant-Christian framework that values personal faith, scripture, and rejection of ritual mediation — a framework that maps onto Sikhi selectively and sometimes misleadingly.
  • Her treatment of Naam is accurate in outline but underplays the concept of nadar (divine grace) and the specific Sikh theological understanding of Naam as divine reality rather than mere label.
  • The jot (divine light) concept, central to understanding the Guru Granth Sahib as living Guru, is absent from her account.
  • Her social ethics section is apologetically effective but frames Sikh moral teaching as reform rather than revelation, inadvertently reproducing the synthesis argument at the ethical level.

Homework

Spend 15–20 minutes reading the Mool Mantar in Gurmukhi (available at SikhiToTheMax or iGurbani) and at least two different English translations or explanations of its meaning. In 350 words, compare Field's translation of 'There is but one God' with the translations you have found, and reflect on what theological dimensions the different translations emphasise or obscure.

lessons.title: Field's Chapter IV: Translating the Granth — Hymns in Western Hands
lessons.html:
Introduction

The final chapter of Dorothy Field's book, titled 'Hymns from the Granth Sahib, and from the Granth of the Tenth Guru,' is quantitatively the largest portion of the work — roughly half its 114 pages. Field presents a series of translated hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ and from the Dasam Granth ਦਸਮ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ, the collection attributed to Guru Gobind Singh. This choice tells us a great deal about her intellectual goals: she wants to let the texts speak, in English, for themselves, and she believes translated Gurbani can communicate Sikh theology more directly than her own prose exposition.

This lecture examines the theory and practice of translating Gurbani into English at the beginning of the twentieth century. We consider what Field was drawing on (primarily Macauliffe's translations), the theological and linguistic challenges any translator faces, the specific interpretive choices embedded in the hymn selections Field made, and what the act of presenting Gurbani in a popular English anthology meant for how Western readers would receive and understand Sikhi.

Translation is never neutral. Every choice — of vocabulary, of tone, of which hymns to include and which to omit — carries interpretive weight. Reading Field's translated hymns as documents of early Western reception, rather than as transparent windows onto Gurbani, is the critical skill this lecture develops.

The Practice of Translating Gurbani

Translating Gurbani presents challenges that are not merely linguistic but theological and philosophical. The language of the Guru Granth Sahib is a composite of Punjabi, Braj Bhasha, Sanskrit, Persian, and several regional dialects, using Gurmukhi script throughout. The compositions were set to specific musical modes (ragas ਰਾਗ), and their meaning is inseparable from their musical performance context. Furthermore, Gurbani uses paradox, imagery, and direct address in ways that resist propositional paraphrase — a hymn describing the soul's longing for the Divine does not make the same kind of argument as a theological treatise.

Field relied primarily on Macauliffe's translations, completed in his six-volume work of 1909. Macauliffe had worked with Sikh scholars, most notably Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha ਭਾਈ ਕਾਨ੍ਹ ਸਿੰਘ ਨਾਭਾ, to ensure theological accuracy, and his translations aimed to be both scholarly and readable. Field selected and in some cases slightly adapted passages from this source, and in doing so she made a second layer of interpretive choices on top of Macauliffe's first layer. The reader of Field's Chapter IV is therefore separated from the Gurmukhi original by at least two interpretive screens.

One of the most significant issues in translating Gurbani is the treatment of what scholars call the 'grammatical gender of the Divine.' In Punjabi, the Divine is sometimes addressed in masculine terms, sometimes in feminine terms, and sometimes in terms that deliberately transgress gender categories. The relationship of the human soul to God is frequently expressed through the metaphor of the bride longing for the divine Husband — a metaphor that positions every human soul, regardless of biological sex, as feminine in the presence of God. Translators working in early-twentieth-century English, where the generic masculine was standard theological usage, routinely flattened these complexities into masculine pronouns throughout.

Field's translations follow this convention. The theological significance of the bride-bridegroom metaphor — which in Gurbani carries the specific meaning that the soul (ਜੀਵ ਇਸਤ੍ਰੀ) is always in relationship with and dependent on the Divine, never self-sufficient — is substantially lost in the English rendering. Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh's feminist re-translation work, from the 1990s onward, has shown how much theological content is recoverable when this metaphor is taken seriously on its own terms.

Hymn Selection and Interpretive Agenda

The hymns Field selects from the Guru Granth Sahib are weighted heavily toward those that emphasise divine unity, moral uplift, and the rejection of ritual — themes that resonate with Protestant Christianity and with the Victorian ethical improvement discourse Field's readers would have found familiar. Hymns that emphasise the mystical union of the soul with God, the concept of Sach Khand ਸੱਚ ਖੰਡ (the Realm of Truth), or the transformative power of sangat are present but receive less prominence.

The Dasam Granth selections are interesting for a different reason. The Dasam Granth is a theologically complex and contested collection; its authorship, canonical status, and theological relationship to the Guru Granth Sahib have been subjects of ongoing debate within the Sikh community. Field presents Dasam Granth hymns attributed to Guru Gobind Singh alongside Guru Granth Sahib hymns without signalling the contested nature of the collection. For a reader in 1914 this would not have been obvious, but it represents a significant editorial decision that flattens a genuine internal debate.

The hymns Field includes from both texts do succeed in one important respect: they demonstrate that Sikh scriptural poetry operates at a high literary level. Even in translation, the imagery of divine light, the metaphors of the soul as a fish longing for water or a bird longing for its tree, and the repeated affirmations of divine mercy communicate something of the aesthetic and spiritual richness of Gurbani. This was precisely Field's goal — to show a Western readership that Sikh sacred literature deserves a place alongside the devotional poetry of any world tradition.

Translation as a Political Act in Colonial Context

The act of translating Sikh scripture into English in the early twentieth century was not merely an academic exercise — it was embedded in the politics of colonial knowledge production. Making Indian religious texts accessible to English readers served several overlapping agendas. For the Wisdom of the East series editors, it supported the goal of 'good will between East and West' on British terms. For Sikh reformers associated with the Singh Sabha ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ movement, English-language presentation of Sikh scripture was part of a broader project of defining and defending a distinct Sikh identity in the face of both colonial administration and Hindu reform movements that sought to incorporate Sikhism within a broader Hindu umbrella.

Field's translations, derived from Macauliffe's, thus participated in this politics whether she intended it or not. Macauliffe himself was explicit about his sympathies: his preface to The Sikh Religion (1909) argues that the Sikh community deserved British support and protection as a loyal and distinctive ally, and he positions his translation work as a contribution to that case. Field's popular anthology version of the same material reached a wider audience with the same implicit argument.

The concept of canon ਕੈਨਨ — which texts are authoritative, how they are bounded, and who controls interpretation — is implicated in every translation and anthology project. By presenting selected hymns as 'representative' of Sikh scripture, Field is inevitably making claims about what matters most in the tradition, claims that a practising Sikh theologian might contest. The decision to include Dasam Granth material without contextualising it is one example; the weighting toward monotheist affirmation over mystical or martial hymns is another.

Key Terms

  • ਰਾਗ (Raga) — the musical mode to which each composition in the Guru Granth Sahib is set; the organisation of the scripture by raga reflects the inseparability of devotional music and theological meaning.
  • ਜੀਵ ਇਸਤ੍ਰੀ (Jeev Istri) — 'the soul as bride'; the theological metaphor in Gurbani positioning every human soul as the bride longing for the divine Husband, regardless of the worshipper's biological gender.
  • ਸੱਚ ਖੰਡ (Sach Khand) — the Realm of Truth; the highest of five spiritual realms described in Guru Nanak's Japji Sahib, representing the state of complete union with the Divine.
  • ਦਸਮ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ (Dasam Granth) — the collection of compositions attributed to Guru Gobind Singh; its canonical status and authorship are subjects of ongoing scholarly and community debate.
  • ਭਾਈ ਕਾਨ੍ਹ ਸਿੰਘ ਨਾਭਾ (Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha) — nineteenth-century Sikh scholar and lexicographer who collaborated with Macauliffe on translations and authored the Mahan Kosh ਮਹਾਨ ਕੋਸ਼, the encyclopaedic Punjabi dictionary.
  • ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ (Singh Sabha) — Sikh reform movement founded in 1873 that emphasised distinct Sikh identity, education, and the purification of practice from non-Sikh accretions; a major institutional context for early Sikh-English translation projects.

Discussion Questions

  1. Field relies on Macauliffe's translations rather than working from the Gurmukhi original. What are the scholarly and ethical implications of this two-layer mediation for the reader of her anthology?
  2. The bride-bridegroom metaphor in Gurbani positions every human soul as feminine before God. What does Field's translation lose by defaulting to masculine pronouns throughout, and what does Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh's feminist retranslation project recover?
  3. Field includes Dasam Granth selections without noting their contested canonical status. What responsibility does a popularising author have toward internal theological debates within the tradition they are writing about?
  4. Translation projects in the colonial period often served multiple agendas simultaneously — cultural appreciation, political argument, and community self-definition. Can a translation be genuinely objective, or is all translation inherently political?

Further Reading

Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh — The Name of My Beloved: Verses of the Sikh Gurus

Gurinder Singh Mann — The Making of Sikh Scripture

Doris Jakobsh — Relocating Gender in Sikh History: Transformation, Meaning and Identity

Key Takeaways

  • Field's translated hymns are separated from the Gurmukhi original by at least two interpretive layers — Macauliffe's translation and Field's selection and adaptation — making them documents of early Western reception as much as of Gurbani itself.
  • The bride-bridegroom metaphor, central to Gurbani's soteriology, is largely lost in Field's translations due to the convention of masculine pronouns, a loss with significant theological consequences.
  • The hymn selection is weighted toward themes resonant with Protestant Christianity, reflecting Field's interpretive agenda and her intended audience.
  • Translation of scripture in colonial contexts is a political act embedded in overlapping agendas of cultural appreciation, community self-definition, and imperial knowledge production.

Homework

Visit SikhiToTheMax (sikhitothemax.com) and read the Anand Sahib, composed by Guru Amar Das. Compare the experience of reading it in Gurmukhi with the English translation provided on the same page. In 300–350 words, reflect on what is communicated by the Gurmukhi that does not come through in the English translation, and what challenges this poses for any scholar writing about Sikhism in a Western language.

lessons.title: The Wisdom of the East Series: Publishing Empire and Oriental Knowledge
lessons.html:
Introduction

Dorothy Field's The Religion of the Sikhs was published not as a standalone academic monograph but as volume 27 in the Wisdom of the East series, a collection of short popular books published by John Murray in London beginning in 1904. The series was edited by L. Cranmer-Byng and S. A. Kapadia and ran to over a hundred volumes over several decades, covering topics from Chinese poetry and Japanese art to Sufi mysticism and Hindu philosophy. Understanding the series — its editorial philosophy, its market positioning, and its ideological assumptions — is essential for understanding what kind of document Field's book actually is.

This lecture examines the Wisdom of the East series as an institutional context. We consider the series' stated aims and their ideological dimensions, the editorial choices that defined its scope and tone, the audience it was designed for and how that audience shaped content, and the place of Field's volume within the series' broader project. The series is a case study in what scholars have called 'Orientalism' — the production of knowledge about the East by and for Western consumers — and Field's book participates in this project in ways that reward careful examination.

The goal is not to dismiss the series or Field's contribution as mere propaganda, but to understand the institutional and ideological frameworks within which even well-intentioned cross-cultural scholarship operated in the early twentieth century.

The Series and Its Editorial Philosophy

The editors Cranmer-Byng and Kapadia articulated their philosophy in a brief note that appeared in each volume. They wrote that 'these books shall be the ambassadors of good-will and understanding between East and West,' and expressed the hope that deeper knowledge of 'Oriental philosophy' might foster 'that true spirit of Charity which neither despises nor fears the nations of another creed.' This language is revealing: it assumes a stable East/West binary, positions the editors as mediators between two separate civilisational spheres, and frames the project in terms of liberal tolerance rather than scholarly rigour.

The 'ambassador' metaphor is particularly interesting. Ambassadors represent one sovereign party to another; they do not claim to speak for the party they are visiting. The series editors positioned themselves as Western mediators presenting Eastern wisdom to a Western public — which means they were not facilitating genuine dialogue but rather curating a selection of non-Western thought for Western consumption. The audience for Wisdom of the East volumes was entirely assumed to be British or broadly European; there is no indication that the series imagined South Asian, East Asian, or Middle Eastern readers finding value in Western presentations of their own traditions.

The series covered an enormous geographic and cultural range, from volumes on ancient Egyptian thought to Confucian ethics to Sufi poetry to Zen Buddhism. This breadth was part of its market appeal — readers could collect a shelf of slim volumes representing the wisdom of the entire non-Western world — but it also implied a certain interchangeability of 'Eastern' traditions that flattened their enormous diversity. A series that presents Sufi poetry and Sikh theology in the same format, at the same price, with the same editorial framing, implicitly suggests that these traditions are comparable objects of Western curiosity rather than living, distinct communities with their own internal complexity.

Audience and Market Positioning

The Wisdom of the East volumes were slim — typically 100–150 pages — and inexpensive. They were designed for the educated British general reader: professionals, clergymen, teachers, and liberal-minded members of the middle class who were curious about the wider world but had neither the time nor the training for serious academic study. This market positioning had direct consequences for the content of individual volumes.

Authors in the series were required to simplify, to select, and to explain — to make unfamiliar traditions legible to readers who had no background in the relevant language, history, or religious practice. This requirement for accessibility was not in itself problematic; popular scholarship serves an important function. But in the context of the series' editorial philosophy, accessibility shaded into something else: a tendency to emphasise whatever in a given Eastern tradition resonated with Western values while minimising whatever seemed most foreign or most challenging.

In Field's case this tendency is visible in her emphasis on Sikhism's monotheism, its ethical seriousness, its rejection of idolatry and ritual, and its social reform agenda — all aspects that would have been immediately legible and appealing to an educated Protestant British reader. The more challenging aspects of Sikh theology — the specific concept of haumai ਹਉਮੈ (ego-self) as the primary spiritual obstacle, the doctrine of hukam ਹੁਕਮ (divine will or order), the complex relationship between determinism and freedom in Sikh soteriology — receive much less attention, precisely because they require more unpacking to convey to a reader without background.

The format also precluded serious scholarly apparatus. Wisdom of the East volumes typically had no footnotes, limited bibliographies, and no engagement with scholarly debate. Field's book is no exception. This makes it accessible but also means that readers had no way of knowing where claims were contested, where scholarship disagreed, or where Field was simplifying a complex picture. The authoritative tone of popular exposition — which must simplify in order to communicate — carried the risk of misleading confident readers into thinking they understood something that actually required years of study to appreciate properly.

Orientalism and Its Discontents

Edward Said's 1978 book Orientalism gave scholars a vocabulary for analysing the systematic ways in which Western writers, artists, and scholars constructed 'the East' as an object of knowledge that served Western cultural and political purposes. Said's argument was specifically about representations of the Arab and Islamic world, but scholars have applied his framework to South Asian and East Asian contexts as well, with considerable debate about its applicability and limits.

The Wisdom of the East series is a useful test case for thinking about Said's framework in the context of South Asian religious traditions. On one hand, the series clearly participates in the construction of 'Eastern wisdom' as an object of Western appreciation — it curates, simplifies, and presents non-Western traditions for a Western audience, on Western terms, in a Western format. The very category 'wisdom of the East' lumps enormously diverse traditions into a single undifferentiated category defined by its relationship to a presumed Western observer.

On the other hand, the series was not uniformly condescending or politically motivated in the way Said's harshest critics of Orientalism were. Some volumes were written by authors with genuine expertise and deep sympathy for the traditions they presented. In the Sikh context, the involvement of Macauliffe — who spent decades in Punjab, learned Punjabi, and worked closely with Sikh scholars — represents a significantly more engaged form of cross-cultural scholarship than armchair Orientalism. Field draws on this engaged scholarship and her respect for what she has read is evident throughout her text.

The more productive analytical frame may be to acknowledge that the series operated within Orientalist assumptions — the East/West binary, the curator's role of the Western author, the primarily Western audience — while recognising that individual volumes varied considerably in quality, depth, and respect for the traditions they presented. Field's book is neither the worst nor the best of the series; it is a thoughtful popular introduction shaped by the institutional and ideological constraints of its format and moment.

Key Terms

  • Orientalism — the systematic production of knowledge about 'the East' by Western scholars, artists, and writers; after Edward Said (1978), the term also carries critical connotations about the power relations embedded in such knowledge production.
  • ਹਉਮੈ (Haumai) — ego-self or self-centredness; in Sikh theology, the primary obstacle to spiritual liberation, the illusion of being a separate self apart from the Divine.
  • ਹੁਕਮ (Hukam) — divine will or order; the concept that all of creation operates according to God's command, and that aligning with hukam rather than resisting it is the path to peace.
  • Popular Scholarship — writing that translates specialist knowledge into accessible form for a general audience; distinguished from academic scholarship by its format, tone, and audience, but not necessarily by its accuracy or value.
  • Canon Formation — the process by which certain texts, authors, or ideas become established as central or authoritative within a field; relevant here because the Wisdom of the East series participated in constructing a Western canon of 'Oriental wisdom.'
  • ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ (Singh Sabha) — the Sikh reform movement of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries; its efforts to define and defend Sikh identity created the intellectual context within which Field's book was received by Sikh readers.

Discussion Questions

  1. The Wisdom of the East series positioned its volumes as 'ambassadors of good-will between East and West.' What are the limitations of the ambassador metaphor for cross-cultural intellectual exchange, and what alternative metaphor might be more appropriate?
  2. Field emphasises aspects of Sikhism most legible to Protestant British readers and gives less space to concepts like haumai and hukam. Is this a problem of bias, a problem of format, or both? Could a truly balanced popular introduction be written?
  3. Said's Orientalism framework has been both widely applied and widely contested. Does it help you understand the Wisdom of the East series, or does it overstate the degree of deliberate ideological purpose in what may have been well-intentioned cultural interest?
  4. If you were to write a short popular introduction to Sikhi for a contemporary Western audience, which aspects of the tradition would you foreground, and which would you be at risk of underemphasising? What does your answer reveal about your own assumptions?

Further Reading

Edward Said — Orientalism

Arvind-pal Singh Mandair — Religion and the Specter of the West: Sikhism, India, Postcoloniality, and the Politics of Translation

Richard King — Orientalism and Religion: Postcolonial Theory, India and 'The Mystic East'

Key Takeaways

  • The Wisdom of the East series shaped Field's book through its format requirements, its editorial philosophy, and its assumed audience, all of which pushed toward simplification and toward emphasising whatever resonated with Western liberal Protestant values.
  • The series participates in Orientalist knowledge production — constructing 'Eastern wisdom' as an object of Western appreciation — while varying considerably in the quality and integrity of individual volumes.
  • Concepts like haumai and hukam, which require substantial theological unpacking, receive less attention in Field's book partly because the series format did not support the depth they require.
  • Popular scholarship and Orientalist knowledge production are not identical; useful cross-cultural communication is possible even within institutional frameworks that carry ideological assumptions.

Homework

Browse the full list of Wisdom of the East series titles (available via WorldCat or a search of archive.org for 'Wisdom of the East series Murray'). Choose three titles from the series other than Field's and note what traditions or topics they cover. In 350 words, reflect on what the series' choices of subject and framing reveal about British assumptions in the early twentieth century about which 'Eastern' traditions were worth presenting to a Western public, and which were likely omitted or overlooked.

lessons.title: Sikh Studies After Field: A Century of Scholarly Development
lessons.html:
Introduction

Dorothy Field's The Religion of the Sikhs appeared in 1914. In the century-plus since its publication, the academic study of Sikhism has developed substantially — from early colonial-era popularisations and translations into a mature, contested, and globally active field. Understanding where Sikh Studies has gone since Field is essential for reading her book with appropriate critical distance and for appreciating which of her observations have proven durable and which have been substantially revised.

This lecture surveys the major developments in Western academic Sikh Studies from Field's time to the present, organised around three broad phases: the foundational period of translation and popular introduction (roughly 1880–1960), the academic institutionalisation period (roughly 1960–1990), and the contemporary period of critical and postcolonial Sikh Studies (1990–present). This survey is necessarily selective, but it provides the intellectual context needed to evaluate Field's contribution and its limitations.

The goal is not to dismiss Field by showing how much scholarship has advanced since 1914 — a century of scholarly development would render almost any 1914 text obsolete in some respects. The goal is to understand what questions each generation of scholars brought to the tradition, what methodological tools they employed, and how the field has responded to both internal Sikh community perspectives and broader developments in the study of religion.

Phase One: Translation, Introduction, and Apologetics (1880–1960)

The foundational period of Western Sikh Studies was dominated by two related projects: translation of Sikh scripture and popular introduction of the tradition to Western audiences. Field's book belongs squarely to this phase, as does Macauliffe's six-volume The Sikh Religion (1909), which provided the translation base that Field and many other writers drew on. Ernest Trumpp's earlier translation of the Adi Granth (1877), commissioned by the British colonial government, was the first major Western attempt at scriptural translation but was deeply flawed — Trumpp worked in isolation from Sikh scholars, misunderstood key theological concepts, and expressed contempt for what he was translating, and his work was rejected by the Sikh community as defamatory.

Macauliffe's project was explicitly a corrective to Trumpp. By working collaboratively with Sikh scholars including Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha ਭਾਈ ਕਾਨ੍ਹ ਸਿੰਘ ਨਾਭਾ and seeking community approval for his translations, Macauliffe aimed to produce a work that Sikhs themselves would recognise as accurate and respectful. His success was partial — the Sikh Educational Conference was cautious about formally endorsing his work, and subsequent scholarship has identified theological simplifications — but his six volumes remain a landmark achievement and a foundational reference.

The apologetic dimension of this phase is important. Both Macauliffe and Field were arguing, implicitly or explicitly, that Sikhism deserved Western respect and attention. For Macauliffe this had a specific political dimension: he believed the British colonial government should recognise and protect the Sikh community as a distinct and loyal ally, and his scholarship was part of that argument. For Field, writing for the Wisdom of the East series, the goal was cultural appreciation and cross-civilisational good will. Neither author was writing purely academic scholarship in the modern sense; both had audiences to persuade and arguments to make.

Other significant figures in this phase include John Malcolm, whose Sketch of the Sikhs (1812) is one of the earliest British accounts of the community, written from an administrative rather than sympathetic perspective. Joseph Davey Cunningham's A History of the Sikhs (1849) offered a more serious historical treatment but was shaped by the political context of the Anglo-Sikh Wars. These earlier works established interpretive frameworks — Sikhs as martial race, Sikhism as reformed Hinduism, the Khalsa as a specifically military institution — that Field was both drawing on and partially challenging.

Phase Two: Academic Institutionalisation and the McLeod Controversy (1960–1990)

The second phase of Western Sikh Studies is defined by the emergence of academic religious studies as a discipline and by the controversial scholarly work of W. H. McLeod ਡਬਲਯੂ ਐੱਚ ਮੈਕਲੌਡ (1932–2009), a New Zealand scholar who spent many years in Punjab and produced a body of work that remains the most discussed — and most contested — in the field's history. McLeod's Guru Nanak and the Sikh Religion (1968) applied the methods of historical-critical scholarship to the janam-sakhis and to Guru Nanak's theology, arguing that much of the hagiographic tradition could not be taken as historical fact and that Guru Nanak's theology was substantially shaped by the sant tradition.

McLeod's scholarship was rigorous by the methodological standards of academic religious studies, and it raised genuinely important historical questions. But it generated fierce controversy within the Sikh community, where many scholars and practitioners felt that applying Western historical-critical methods to sacred narratives was both methodologically inappropriate (treating religious literature as if it were secular biography) and ideologically biased (reaching conclusions that privileged Western academic frameworks over Sikh theological understanding). The debate about McLeod's work became one of the most important conversations in the field and continues to shape how Sikh Studies scholars navigate the relationship between academic method and community engagement.

This phase also saw the establishment of Sikh Studies chairs at Western universities — the first was established at the University of British Columbia in 1987 — and the development of Sikh studies as a recognised sub-field within South Asian religious studies. The growth of Sikh diaspora communities in North America, the United Kingdom, and elsewhere created both a community of Sikh scholars entering academia and a community of practitioners who were closely attentive to how their tradition was being presented in Western academic contexts.

For our purposes, the key point is that this phase raised methodological questions that Field's popular introduction format simply could not address: What counts as historical evidence about the early Gurus? How should scholars handle the relationship between hagiographic tradition and historical fact? Who has the authority to interpret Sikh scripture — the academic scholar or the practising community? These questions were invisible in 1914 but became central to the field by the 1970s.

Phase Three: Critical, Postcolonial, and Diasporic Sikh Studies (1990–Present)

The contemporary period of Sikh Studies is characterised by several major developments. Postcolonial theory, drawing on Said's Orientalism and related frameworks, has led scholars including Arvind-pal Singh Mandair, Harjot Oberoi, and Gurinder Singh Mann to examine how colonial knowledge production shaped the categories through which Sikhism was understood and how Sikh communities negotiated their identity in colonial and postcolonial contexts. Mandair's Religion and the Specter of the West argues that the very category 'religion,' applied to Sikhism, imports Western assumptions that distort the tradition's self-understanding.

Feminist Sikh Studies, associated particularly with Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, has recovered dimensions of Gurbani — especially the bride-bridegroom metaphor and the theology of the feminine — that earlier scholars marginalised or missed. This work has also examined the historical treatment of Sikh women, the patriarchal dimensions of colonial-era scholarship, and the ongoing tensions between Gurbani's egalitarian theology and patriarchal social practices within Sikh communities.

Diasporic Sikh Studies, drawing on the experiences of Sikh communities in North America, the United Kingdom, and elsewhere, has examined questions of identity, belonging, and representation in new cultural contexts. The visibility of the Sikh kirpan ਕਿਰਪਾਨ in Western public spaces, debates about Sikh representation in media and politics, and the challenges of transmitting Sikh identity across generations in diaspora communities have all become active areas of scholarly attention.

Field's book, read from the vantage point of this contemporary scholarship, appears as a thoughtful but thoroughly pre-critical document — sympathetic to the tradition it introduces, but unable to ask the methodological, postcolonial, or feminist questions that later scholarship would develop. This does not make it worthless; it makes it historically interesting as a document of its own moment and pedagogically useful as a starting point for understanding how Western knowledge of Sikhism was constructed and how that construction has been challenged and revised.

Key Terms

  • Historical-Critical Method — a set of scholarly tools for analysing ancient texts, including examination of sources, authorship, historical context, and the distinction between historical fact and theological interpretation; applied controversially to Sikh texts by McLeod and others.
  • ਡਬਲਯੂ ਐੱਚ ਮੈਕਲੌਡ (W. H. McLeod) — New Zealand scholar whose academic Sikh Studies work (1968 onward) applied historical-critical methods to Sikh texts, generating a significant and ongoing controversy about scholarly authority and community engagement.
  • Postcolonial Theory — a body of critical thought examining the lasting intellectual and cultural effects of European colonialism, particularly how colonial knowledge production shaped categories of understanding that persist after formal political independence.
  • Diaspora Studies — the academic study of communities living outside their traditional homelands; increasingly important for Sikh Studies given the size and influence of Sikh communities in North America, the UK, and elsewhere.
  • ਕਿਰਪਾਨ (Kirpan) — the ceremonial sword worn by initiated Sikhs as one of the Panj Kakars; its presence in Western public spaces has generated legal and cultural debates about religious accommodation.
  • Community Engagement — the ongoing question in Sikh Studies (and religious studies more broadly) of how academic scholarship should relate to and be accountable to the communities whose traditions it studies.

Discussion Questions

  1. McLeod's application of historical-critical methods to Sikh texts generated intense controversy. Do you think academic scholars have the right to apply their own methodological tools to any religious tradition? What responsibilities come with that right?
  2. Mandair argues that the category 'religion' imports Western assumptions that distort Sikh self-understanding. If this is true, what implications does it have for courses like this one, which presents Sikhism within a university religious studies framework?
  3. Field could not have asked postcolonial or feminist questions about her own work; these frameworks did not exist in 1914. Does this mean her book should be judged only by the standards of its own time, or are there things we can still hold her accountable for regardless of her historical moment?
  4. Diasporic Sikh communities have become major participants in Sikh Studies scholarship and in debates about how the tradition is presented. How should the relationship between diaspora community and academic scholar be structured in a field like this one?

Further Reading

Arvind-pal Singh Mandair — Religion and the Specter of the West: Sikhism, India, Postcoloniality, and the Politics of Translation

Harjot Oberoi — The Construction of Religious Boundaries: Culture, Identity, and Diversity in the Sikh Tradition

Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh — Sikhism: An Introduction

Key Takeaways

  • Western Sikh Studies has moved through three broad phases: apologetic popular introduction, academic institutionalisation with the McLeod controversy, and contemporary critical-postcolonial-feminist scholarship.
  • McLeod's work raised methodological questions about the relationship between academic scholarship and community authority that remain central to the field.
  • Postcolonial theory has shown how the category 'religion' and the broader framework of comparative religion import Western assumptions into the study of Sikhism.
  • Field's book is most productively read as a historical document of the first phase — valuable not as a guide to contemporary Sikh Studies but as evidence of how Western knowledge of Sikhism was initially constructed.

Homework

Read the Wikipedia article on W. H. McLeod and, if possible, the first few pages of the introduction to his Guru Nanak and the Sikh Religion (available on Google Books preview). In 400 words, summarise the main controversy his work generated and reflect on where you stand on the question of whether Western academics should apply historical-critical methods to Sikh sacred texts. Draw on at least one specific point from this lesson's discussion of the methodological debate.

courses.title: Reading the Dasam Granth: The Textual Scholarship of Dr. Kamalroop Singh
courses.summary: This course introduces students to the academic study of the Dasam Granth (ਦਸਮ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ) through the scholarship of Dr. Kamalroop Singh, a contemporary researcher known for his work on Sikh manuscripts and the writings attributed to Guru Gobind Singh. Students learn what the Dasam Granth is, how scholars examine its…
outcomes: Explain what the Dasam Granth is and how it differs in scope and arrangement from the Guru Granth Sahib.
Describe the methods scholars such as Dr. Kamalroop Singh use to study Sikh manuscripts and recensions.
Identify the major compositions traditionally included in the Dasam Granth and summarize their themes.
Summarize the main positions in the scholarly debate over the authorship and arrangement of the text.
Locate and cite Dr. Kamalroop Singh's published academic work using correct citation form.
