lessons.title: Course Overview and What the Dasam Granth Is
lessons.summary: An orientation to the course and a plain-language introduction to the Dasam Granth, its place in Sikh tradition, and how it relates to the Guru Granth Sahib.
lessons.html:
Course Contents

  1. Course Overview and What the Dasam Granth Is
  2. The Scholar and His Method: Dr. Kamalroop Singh
  3. Manuscripts, Recensions, and Textual Study
  4. The Major Compositions and Their Themes
  5. The Authorship and Arrangement Debate
  6. Reading Responsibly: Citation, Ethics, and Review

Welcome to this course on the academic study of the Dasam Granth (ਦਸਮ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ). The phrase means "the tenth book" and refers to a body of compositions traditionally associated with the tenth Sikh Guru, Guru Gobind Singh.

The Dasam Granth is distinct from the Guru Granth Sahib (ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ), which holds the central place of the eternal Guru in Sikh worship. The Dasam Granth is a separate collection. Some of its short compositions, such as Jaap Sahib (ਜਾਪੁ ਸਾਹਿਬ), are part of daily Sikh devotional practice and the Amrit ceremony, while other longer sections are mainly read and studied by scholars.

This course follows the scholarship of Dr. Kamalroop Singh, a contemporary researcher whose published academic work focuses on the writings attributed to Guru Gobind Singh and on Sikh manuscripts (Mann and Singh 2015). Throughout, we treat the text respectfully and present debated questions neutrally.

References

  • Singh, Gurinder Mann, and Kamalroop Singh. The Granth of Guru Gobind Singh: Essays, Lectures, and Translations. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2015.
  • Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014.

Homework

Select one composition from the Dasam Granth — such as Jaap Sahib, Tav-Prasad Savaiye, or Chaupai Sahib — and write a 350-word personal reflection describing what you knew about it before this course and what new questions the overview has raised for you. Focus on your own starting assumptions rather than definitive conclusions.

lessons.title: The Scholar and His Method: Dr. Kamalroop Singh
lessons.summary: An introduction to Dr. Kamalroop Singh as an academic scholar and the collaborative, source-based approach reflected in his published work.
lessons.html:
Dr. Kamalroop Singh is a contemporary scholar of Sikh studies whose academic work centers on the writings attributed to Guru Gobind Singh and on the study of Sikh scriptural manuscripts. His best-known academic publication is the volume he co-authored with Gurinder Singh Mann, The Granth of Guru Gobind Singh: Essays, Lectures, and Translations, published by Oxford University Press (Mann and Singh 2015).

That book combines several kinds of scholarly material: essays that situate the text historically, lectures that explain its contents, and translations that make selected compositions accessible to readers. This mix reflects a careful method that moves from primary sources outward to interpretation, rather than starting from conclusions.

His approach belongs to the broader field mapped in The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies (Singh and Fenech 2014), which surveys how scholars study Sikh scripture, history, and practice. A central principle of this scholarship is that claims about a text should be grounded in the manuscripts themselves.

Note on accuracy. This course does not invent biographical details. Where the literature is silent, we say so, and we focus on the published works that can be cited directly.

References

  • Singh, Gurinder Mann, and Kamalroop Singh. The Granth of Guru Gobind Singh: Essays, Lectures, and Translations. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2015.
  • Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014.

Homework

Research Dr. Kamalroop Singh's published work by locating at least two academic sources he has authored or co-authored (journal articles, book chapters, or the Dasam Granth volume itself). Write a 400-word summary describing his academic background, institutional affiliations, and the central arguments he advances in those sources. Reflect on how his biography shapes the questions he brings to the text.

lessons.title: Manuscripts, Recensions, and Textual Study
lessons.summary: How scholars study Sikh scripture through manuscripts, comparing recensions and using philological methods.
lessons.html:
A core part of Dr. Singh's field is the study of manuscripts, called ਬੀੜ (birh) in Punjabi. Before printing, scribes copied scripture by hand, and different copies could vary in their contents and arrangement. A particular arrangement preserved in a manuscript tradition is called a recension.

Scholars use philology — the careful study of language, script, and textual variation — to compare manuscripts, estimate their dates, and trace how a collection took shape over time. This kind of comparison is the foundation of the essays and translations in Mann and Singh (2015), and it is also surveyed in McLeod's collection of textual sources (McLeod 1990).

MethodWhat it asksWhy it matters
Manuscript comparisonHow do copies differ?Reveals variant readings and arrangements
Dating and provenanceWhen and where was it written?Helps order the tradition historically
Philological analysisWhat does the language show?Supports careful interpretation

The goal of these methods is descriptive: to understand the text as it has actually been transmitted, while leaving questions of devotion to the community.

References

  • Singh, Gurinder Mann, and Kamalroop Singh. The Granth of Guru Gobind Singh: Essays, Lectures, and Translations. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2015.
  • McLeod, W. H. Textual Sources for the Study of Sikhism. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1990.

Homework

Locate a digital or print manuscript repository — such as the Panjab Digital Library or a university special collection — and spend 30 minutes browsing historical Sikh manuscripts. Write a 350-word journal entry describing what you observed: the physical features, the scripts used, any marginal notes, and what challenges a scholar would face when working with such documents.

lessons.title: The Major Compositions and Their Themes
lessons.summary: A survey of the principal compositions traditionally included in the Dasam Granth and the themes they address.
lessons.html:
The Dasam Granth contains several distinct compositions. Among the most widely known are Jaap Sahib (ਜਾਪੁ ਸਾਹਿਬ), a devotional praise of the qualities of the Divine; Akal Ustat (ਅਕਾਲ ਉਸਤਤਿ), praise of the Timeless One; and Bachittar Natak (ਬਚਿਤ੍ਰ ਨਾਟਕ), a narrative often read as containing autobiographical material (Mann and Singh 2015).

CompositionPunjabiTheme
Jaap Sahibਜਾਪੁ ਸਾਹਿਬDevotional praise of the Divine
Akal Ustatਅਕਾਲ ਉਸਤਤਿPraise of the Timeless One
Bachittar Natakਬਚਿਤ੍ਰ ਨਾਟਕNarrative and reflective material

The collection also includes longer narrative and poetic sections that scholars analyze for their language, sources, and literary form. Rinehart's study describes the range of these contents and the questions they raise for readers (Rinehart 2011). Out of respect for the tradition, this course summarizes themes rather than reproducing or paraphrasing verses, and it does not cite specific page or Ang numbers.

References

  • Singh, Gurinder Mann, and Kamalroop Singh. The Granth of Guru Gobind Singh: Essays, Lectures, and Translations. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2015.
  • Rinehart, Robin. Debating the Dasam Granth. New York: Oxford University Press, 2011.

Homework

Choose one of the major compositions discussed in this lesson — Bachitar Natak, Chandi Charitra, or the Shastar Naam Mala — and read a brief scholarly description of it from an encyclopedia entry, a book introduction, or a peer-reviewed article. Write a 400-word comparative note identifying the themes the scholar emphasises and whether those match the framing in this lesson.

lessons.title: The Authorship and Arrangement Debate
lessons.summary: A neutral presentation of the main scholarly positions on the authorship and arrangement of the Dasam Granth.
lessons.html:
One of the most discussed topics in this field is the question of authorship and arrangement. The Dasam Granth has been the subject of long debate among scholars and within the Sikh community, and this lesson presents the main positions neutrally without endorsing any of them.

Robin Rinehart's Debating the Dasam Granth lays out the principal views and their reasoning (Rinehart 2011). In broad terms, discussions concern which compositions are attributed to Guru Gobind Singh, how the collection was assembled, and how different manuscript recensions arrange the material. Scholars draw on the manuscript evidence discussed in earlier lessons to argue their positions.

QuestionWhy it is debated
Attribution of compositionsDifferent traditions and manuscripts vary
Assembly of the collectionHistorical records are incomplete
Arrangement across recensionsManuscripts differ in order and contents

The work of Mann and Singh (2015) contributes to this conversation by presenting essays and translations grounded in source material. The general scholarly context is summarized in Mandair's guide (Mandair 2013). The aim of this course is to help students understand the debate, not to resolve it.

References

  • Rinehart, Robin. Debating the Dasam Granth. New York: Oxford University Press, 2011.
  • Singh, Gurinder Mann, and Kamalroop Singh. The Granth of Guru Gobind Singh: Essays, Lectures, and Translations. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2015.
  • Mandair, Arvind-Pal Singh. Sikhism: A Guide for the Perplexed. London: Bloomsbury, 2013.

Homework

The authorship debate around the Dasam Granth is one of the most contested topics in Sikh studies. Identify two scholars who hold different positions on the question of authorship and write a 400-word analysis comparing their core arguments. Note the type of evidence each scholar privileges — textual, historical, or theological — and reflect on what that reveals about their methodology.

lessons.title: Reading Responsibly: Citation, Ethics, and Review
lessons.summary: How to cite Dr. Singh's work correctly, engage the material ethically, and consolidate the course's main lessons.
lessons.html:
This final lesson focuses on how to use this scholarship responsibly. First, citation: academic work should be cited so that readers can check the sources. For example, an in-text reference to the co-authored volume appears as (Mann and Singh 2015), with a full entry in the reference list following Chicago style.

Second, ethics: the Dasam Granth is a sacred text for many Sikhs, and questions about it can be sensitive. Good scholarship describes the manuscript evidence, presents debates neutrally, and avoids overstating what the sources show. It also avoids inventing details, quotations, or page references that are not in the sources.

Review. Across this course we have learned what the Dasam Granth is (ਦਸਮ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ), how scholars study its manuscripts and recensions, what its major compositions address, and why authorship and arrangement are debated. We have also placed Dr. Kamalroop Singh's published work within the wider field surveyed in the Oxford Handbook (Singh and Fenech 2014).

SkillPractice
Citing sourcesUse in-text references and a full reference list
Engaging debatesPresent positions neutrally and accurately
Respecting the textSummarize themes; avoid fabricated detail

References

  • Singh, Gurinder Mann, and Kamalroop Singh. The Granth of Guru Gobind Singh: Essays, Lectures, and Translations. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2015.
  • Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014.

Homework

Academic writing in Sikh studies requires careful citation and ethical representation of living traditions. Select one scholarly article on the Dasam Granth and write a 350-word critique of its citation practices: Does it cite primary sources accurately? Does it represent community perspectives fairly? Does it distinguish between contested and settled claims? This exercise trains close critical reading of the field.

lessons.title: The Nitnem Banis and Their Scriptural Status
lessons.html:
Introduction

Among the most practically significant aspects of the Dasam Granth is its role in daily Sikh devotional life. Several compositions from the text form part of the Nitnem — the prescribed daily liturgy observed by initiated Sikhs — and yet the wider text from which these banis are drawn remains contested among scholars and within the Panth. This apparent paradox, in which selections of a text are considered non-negotiable devotional practice while the text as a whole is disputed, offers a uniquely productive entry point into the relationship between scripture, liturgy, and community authority.

This lesson focuses on the three Dasam Granth compositions included in the Amrit Sanchar (initiation ceremony) and daily Nitnem: Jaap Sahib, Tav-Prasad Savaiye, and Chaupai Sahib. We examine their textual character, their theological content, and the scholarly conversation around how these liturgical banis came to hold an undisputed place in Sikh practice even as academic debates about the broader Dasam Granth persist. Dr. Kamalroop Singh's scholarship is particularly illuminating here because he foregrounds manuscript evidence for how these texts circulated independently and together before the Dasam Granth was compiled as a single volume.

Understanding the Nitnem banis requires holding two registers simultaneously: the text as lived liturgy and the text as historical artifact. Neither register cancels the other. Rigorous textual scholarship does not diminish devotion, and devotional familiarity does not substitute for critical analysis. This dual awareness is a hallmark of responsible Sikh studies.

Jaap Sahib: The Grammar of Divine Address

Jaap Sahib opens the Amrit Sanchar recitations and is part of every initiated Sikh's morning Nitnem. It consists of a sustained litany of divine names drawn from Sanskrit, Arabic, Persian, and Braj Bhasha, constructing a vision of the Divine that transcends any single religious or linguistic tradition. The text addresses ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ (the Timeless Being) through hundreds of attributes, none of which is presented as exhaustive. This grammatical strategy — endless naming as a way of pointing beyond naming — is a sophisticated theological stance.

Textually, Jaap Sahib is among the compositions that appear in the earliest Dasam Granth manuscripts with consistent wording, lending it a degree of textual stability unusual in the broader corpus. Dr. Kamalroop Singh notes that manuscript variants in Jaap Sahib are relatively minor compared to more contested compositions, which he takes as evidence of the text's early liturgical stabilisation. Once a text enters regular recitation, the community's oral memory tends to conserve it, reducing the scope for scribal variation.

Theologically, Jaap Sahib participates in a tradition of neti-neti (not this, not that) divine description found across South Asian philosophical traditions, while simultaneously rooting itself in the Sikh understanding of the One formless Creator. The multilingual character of the divine names is not eclecticism but a deliberate theological statement: the Divine cannot be claimed by any single language, culture, or religion. Scholars who read the Dasam Granth as continuous with Guru Granth Sahib's theology point to Jaap Sahib as the clearest example of that continuity.

In practical terms, the daily recitation of Jaap Sahib functions as a discipline of re-orientation — turning the mind toward the infinite before engaging the finite concerns of the day. This functional dimension of the text is part of what liturgical scholars call the performative force of scripture: the text does something in the act of being recited, not only in the act of being read.

Tav-Prasad Savaiye and Chaupai Sahib: Critique and Refuge

Tav-Prasad Savaiye presents a strikingly sharp critique of religious formalism. Through vivid imagery drawn from classical poetry, the composition challenges the efficacy of pilgrimage, asceticism, idol worship, and mechanical ritual as paths to liberation, insisting that only ਨਾਮ (the divine Name) and loving devotion constitute genuine spiritual practice. This critique aligns closely with the theology of the Guru Granth Sahib and is often cited by scholars who argue for the theological coherence of the two canonical texts.

Chaupai Sahib, attributed to the Bachitar Natak section of the Dasam Granth, functions as a prayer of refuge and protection. Its intimate, supplicatory tone contrasts with the expansive divine-name litany of Jaap Sahib and the polemical edge of Tav-Prasad Savaiye, demonstrating the range of devotional registers within a single canonical text. Practitioners across the Panth have historically recited Chaupai Sahib in moments of difficulty, and its pastoral function is inseparable from its textual identity.

Scholarly discussions of both compositions raise the question of selection: by what authority were these particular portions of the Dasam Granth elevated to liturgical status while the rest of the text remained outside the daily Nitnem? The Sikh Rehat Maryada, standardised in 1936, codified existing practice rather than inventing it, suggesting that the liturgical status of these banis predates modern institutional authority. Dr. Kamalroop Singh traces the liturgical use of these texts in eighteenth- and nineteenth-century sources, providing historical depth to what might otherwise appear as a twentieth-century decision.

The question of liturgical selection also invites comparison with other scriptural traditions. The Christian lectionary selects portions of scripture for weekly reading; the Jewish siddur draws on Psalms and other texts in structured sequence. In each case, the community's interpretive judgment shapes how the broader textual tradition is encountered in practice. The Nitnem represents the Sikh Panth's own such judgment, with the distinctive feature that it was exercised over a text whose broader status remains a live scholarly question.

Key Terms

  • ਨਿਤਨੇਮ (Nitnem) — the prescribed daily liturgy of banis recited by initiated Sikhs, morning, evening, and night
  • ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਸੰਚਾਰ (Amrit Sanchar) — the Khalsa initiation ceremony in which the five banis are recited over amrit
  • ਜਾਪੁ ਸਾਹਿਬ (Jaap Sahib) — the opening Nitnem bani from the Dasam Granth, a multilingual litany of divine names
  • ਚੌਪਈ ਸਾਹਿਬ (Chaupai Sahib) — a bani of refuge and supplication from the Bachitar Natak section, part of the evening Nitnem
  • ਰਹਿਤ ਮਰਯਾਦਾ (Rehat Maryada) — the Sikh code of conduct, standardised in 1936, which codifies the Nitnem and Amrit Sanchar requirements
  • Performative scripture — the concept that a sacred text enacts an effect through recitation, not only through semantic content

Discussion Questions

  1. The Nitnem banis from the Dasam Granth hold an undisputed place in Sikh practice even while the broader text is contested. What does this tell us about how religious communities navigate internal textual disagreement?
  2. Jaap Sahib uses hundreds of divine names from multiple languages and traditions. How does this multilingual strategy function theologically, and what are its implications for how Sikhi understands religious diversity?
  3. Dr. Kamalroop Singh uses manuscript evidence to trace the early liturgical stabilisation of the Nitnem banis. What are the strengths and limits of using scribal consistency as an argument for early liturgical use?
  4. Compare the different emotional registers of Jaap Sahib, Tav-Prasad Savaiye, and Chaupai Sahib. What does the range of tones within a single daily liturgy suggest about the theology underlying the Nitnem?

Further Reading

  • Kamalroop Singh and Gurinder Singh Mann — Dasam Granth: The 18th Century Sikh Scripture
  • W. H. McLeod — Textual Sources for the Study of Sikhism
  • Pashaura Singh — The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority

Key Takeaways

  • Three Dasam Granth compositions — Jaap Sahib, Tav-Prasad Savaiye, and Chaupai Sahib — are integral to the Sikh daily Nitnem and Amrit Sanchar, giving the text direct liturgical significance regardless of broader debates.
  • The multilingual divine-name litany of Jaap Sahib reflects a deliberate theological stance: the Divine transcends any single language or tradition.
  • Manuscript evidence suggests the Nitnem banis were liturgically stabilised early, prior to the modern codification of the Rehat Maryada, supporting their historical rootedness in Sikh practice.
  • Holding scripture as both lived liturgy and historical artifact is a core skill in responsible Sikh studies, and the Nitnem banis offer an ideal case study for practising that dual awareness.

Homework

Attend or listen to a recording of a Nitnem recitation that includes one of the Dasam Granth banis — Jaap Sahib, Tav-Prasad Savaiye, or Chaupai Sahib. Spend 20 minutes sitting with the recitation attentively. Afterward, write a 350-word reflection on your experience: what did the language feel like in recitation versus on the page, and how does that embodied encounter inform your understanding of the text's scriptural status?

lessons.title: The Heroic Tradition: Bir Ras, Shakti, and Sikh Martial Theology
lessons.html:
Introduction

The Dasam Granth is distinctive within the world's scriptural traditions for its sustained engagement with the heroic register — what Punjabi literary tradition calls ਬੀਰ ਰਸ (bir ras), the aesthetic mood of valour. Compositions in the text invoke warrior goddesses, describe epic battles, celebrate martial virtues, and situate the Khalsa identity within a cosmic struggle between righteousness and tyranny. For some readers, this content is theologically central; for others, it requires careful contextualisation. Understanding bir ras as a literary and theological category is essential for reading the Dasam Granth with integrity.

This lesson situates the Dasam Granth's martial content within three overlapping frameworks: the classical Indian theory of aesthetic moods (rasas), the Sikh theological concept of ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ (sant-sipahi, the saint-soldier), and the historical context of the late seventeenth and early eighteenth century, when Guru Gobind Singh led the Khalsa against Mughal and hill-chieftain forces. Dr. Kamalroop Singh's scholarship insists that the martial content of the Dasam Granth is not incidental but theologically purposive, expressing a vision of divine power (ਸ਼ਕਤੀ, shakti) that is inseparable from the protection of the weak.

Modern readers sometimes find the martial content of the Dasam Granth jarring, particularly those who encounter Sikhi primarily through the more quietist registers of Guru Granth Sahib. This lesson addresses that discomfort directly, arguing that the discomfort itself is a productive site of theological reflection rather than a problem to be smoothed over.

Rasa Theory and the Literature of Valour

Classical Sanskrit literary theory, codified most influentially in Bharata's Natyashastra, describes eight (later expanded to nine) aesthetic moods or rasas that a literary work can evoke in the reader or audience. Bir ras — the heroic mood — is one of the primary rasas, characterised by energy, fearlessness, and righteous action. Guru Gobind Singh was a poet deeply trained in this tradition, and the Dasam Granth's martial compositions consciously deploy bir ras as a literary and spiritual tool.

The deployment of bir ras is not merely decorative. In the theory of rasa, aesthetic experience has a transformative function: by participating imaginatively in the hero's courage, the audience cultivates something of that courage in themselves. The recitation of martial poetry is therefore a spiritual discipline, not simply entertainment or propaganda. This understanding helps explain why Sikhs who never engage in physical combat nevertheless recite the Dasam Granth's martial banis as part of their devotional life.

Dr. Kamalroop Singh draws attention to the way Guru Gobind Singh uses classical bir ras conventions while simultaneously re-orienting them toward a Sikh theological framework. The heroic figures in the Dasam Granth are not heroes for personal glory but instruments of divine justice. Courage in the text is always coupled with surrender to ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ (Waheguru); the warrior who acts from ego rather than divine will is not celebrated but condemned.

Understanding this literary framework also helps readers navigate the goddess mythology in the Dasam Granth. Compositions like Chandi Charitra and Chandi di Var invoke the Hindu goddess Chandi (Durga) in her warrior aspect. Dr. Kamalroop Singh argues that Guru Gobind Singh uses the Chandi narrative not to endorse goddess worship but to invoke a widely understood symbol of righteous power — ਸ਼ਕਤੀ (shakti) — and redirect it toward the Sikh theological vision of the transcendent One who empowers the Khalsa.

Shakti, Justice, and the Sant-Sipahi Ideal

The concept of ਸ਼ਕਤੀ (shakti) — divine power or energy — plays a complex role in the Dasam Granth. In Hindu traditions, shakti is often personified as feminine divine energy, the active principle of the universe. The Dasam Granth engages with shakti imagery extensively, particularly in the Chandi compositions, but routes the concept through a strictly monotheistic framework. Power belongs to the One; the warrior channels that power but does not possess it independently.

The ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ (sant-sipahi) ideal — the saint-soldier who combines interior devotion with exterior readiness for righteous defence — is the Dasam Granth's most enduring theological contribution to Sikh ethics. This ideal refuses the common separation between spiritual life and political engagement. The sant-sipahi is not a warrior who prays, nor a mystic who occasionally fights, but a person whose devotional depth and martial readiness are expressions of the same underlying commitment to ਧਰਮ (dharam, righteousness).

Scholars who examine the historical context of the Dasam Granth note that Guru Gobind Singh was writing during a period of severe persecution, when the Sikh community faced existential threats from Mughal authority and local hill chieftains. The martial content of the text is not abstract philosophy but a response to concrete historical circumstances. Understanding this context does not reduce the text to mere political writing; rather, it demonstrates how theological vision and historical necessity can be woven together in a single literary project.

Contemporary Sikh communities worldwide continue to grapple with the sant-sipahi ideal in contexts far removed from seventeenth-century Punjab. Questions about when force is legitimate, how the tradition speaks to non-violent resistance, and what it means to be a Khalsa warrior in a postcolonial world are all live theological questions rooted in the Dasam Granth's bir ras tradition.

Key Terms

  • ਬੀਰ ਰਸ (Bir Ras) — the heroic aesthetic mood in classical Indian literary theory, one of the nine rasas; central to the martial compositions of the Dasam Granth
  • ਸ਼ਕਤੀ (Shakti) — divine power or energy; used in the Dasam Granth to describe the force channelled by the righteous warrior in service of the One
  • ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ (Sant-Sipahi) — the saint-soldier ideal: the person who integrates interior devotion with readiness for righteous defence
  • ਚੰਡੀ (Chandi) — the warrior goddess figure from Hindu tradition, invoked in the Dasam Granth as a symbol of divine righteous power rather than as an object of worship
  • ਧਰਮ (Dharam) — righteousness, duty, the cosmic moral order; the cause in service of which the sant-sipahi acts
  • Rasa theory — the classical South Asian literary framework describing nine aesthetic moods that literature can evoke, with a transformative function for the audience

Discussion Questions

  1. The Dasam Granth uses goddess imagery from the Hindu tradition to articulate a Sikh theological vision. Is this appropriation, translation, or something else? How should scholars and practitioners handle such cross-traditional borrowing?
  2. How does rasa theory help explain why martial poetry functions as a spiritual discipline rather than merely as warrior propaganda? What are the limits of this explanation?
  3. The sant-sipahi ideal refuses a separation between spiritual life and political engagement. What are the contemporary implications of this refusal for Sikhs living in pluralistic democratic societies?
  4. Dr. Kamalroop Singh argues that the Dasam Granth's martial content is theologically purposive rather than incidental. How does understanding historical context support or complicate this argument?

Further Reading

  • Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh — The Feminine Principle in the Sikh Vision of the Transcendent
  • Arvind-Pal Singh Mandair — Religion and the Specter of the West
  • J. S. Grewal — The Sikhs of the Punjab

Key Takeaways

  • Bir ras — the heroic aesthetic mood — is not incidental to the Dasam Granth but theologically purposive, using classical rasa theory to cultivate courage as a spiritual discipline.
  • The Dasam Granth's engagement with shakti and goddess imagery does not contradict Sikh monotheism but redirects widely understood symbols of power toward the Sikh theological framework.
  • The sant-sipahi ideal integrates interior devotion and exterior readiness for righteous defence, refusing the separation between spiritual and political life.
  • Historical context — the persecution of the Khalsa in the late seventeenth century — is essential for understanding why the Dasam Granth developed such a sustained martial register.

Homework

Identify one historical or contemporary example of a community that maintains both a martial tradition and a devotional practice — this could be from Sikh history, another religious tradition, or a secular context. Write a 400-word reflection comparing how that community navigates the tension between force and compassion, and how that comparison illuminates the bir ras tradition in the Dasam Granth.

lessons.title: The Charitropakhyan: Narrative, Allegory, and Scholarly Controversy
lessons.html:
Introduction

No section of the Dasam Granth generates more controversy, more discomfort, and more scholarly debate than the Charitropakhyan (ਚਰਿੱਤ੍ਰੋਪਾਖਿਆਨ). This extensive collection of tales — some four hundred and four narratives — depicts characters across a wide range of moral situations, including many that involve deception, sexuality, and moral ambiguity. For those who contest the Dasam Granth's authenticity, the Charitropakhyan is the most frequently cited evidence against Guru Gobind Singh's authorship. For those who affirm the text, it represents a sophisticated allegorical and didactic tradition rooted in classical South Asian narrative literature.

This lesson approaches the Charitropakhyan with scholarly care, neither dismissing its content nor accepting uncritically any particular interpretive framework. We examine the literary genre from which the text draws, the allegorical reading strategies that scholars like Dr. Kamalroop Singh have advanced, the community controversies the text has generated, and the methodological principles that should guide serious academic engagement with difficult texts.

Engaging with the Charitropakhyan well requires intellectual courage: the courage to sit with discomfort, to resist premature conclusions, and to distinguish between personal moral response to content and rigorous literary-historical analysis. Both responses are legitimate, but they belong to different registers of inquiry, and keeping them distinct is essential for good scholarship.

The Classical Narrative Tradition and the Hitopadesha Model

The Charitropakhyan belongs to a well-established South Asian genre of instructive tale collections. Works such as the Hitopadesha, the Panchatantra, and the Kathasaritsagara use morally complex narratives — often involving deception, disguise, and human weakness — to instruct readers in practical wisdom. The frame of these collections is typically didactic: a wise teacher presents cautionary tales to a pupil, and the pupil learns through narrative rather than through abstract precept.

The Charitropakhyan follows this model closely. It is framed as a series of tales told by a wise man to a king, with each narrative illustrating a teaching about human nature, desire, loyalty, and discernment. This framing device is not merely ornamental but essential to interpretation: the tales are presented as instructive examples, not as endorsements of the behaviour they depict. A story in which a character uses deception is not a recommendation of deception any more than a fable in which a fox outsmarts a crow recommends cunning as a virtue.

Dr. Kamalroop Singh situates the Charitropakhyan within this genre context and argues that reading it as a straightforward narrative — without attending to its didactic frame — is a fundamental interpretive error. He notes that the classical authors of the Panchatantra tradition were fully aware that depicting immoral behaviour in narrative does not constitute moral approval; indeed, the entire tradition depends on this distinction. The question is whether Guru Gobind Singh, trained in Sanskrit and Persian literary traditions, was operating within this same framework.

Manuscript evidence, according to Dr. Kamalroop Singh, places the Charitropakhyan within the Dasam Granth consistently across the earliest known recensions, suggesting that it was not a later addition but part of the original compilation. This does not resolve the interpretation question but it complicates any simple dismissal of the text as a later corruption.

Allegorical Readings and Community Controversy

The most sustained scholarly defence of the Charitropakhyan relies on allegorical interpretation. In this reading, the surface narrative of deception and sexuality is a vehicle for deeper teachings about the nature of maya (illusion), the treachery of ਕਾਮ (kaam, desire), and the necessity of spiritual discernment. The reader who cannot see past the surface narrative is, in a sense, experiencing the text's teaching about the seductive power of maya: they are caught by appearances just as the text's foolish characters are.

Critics of this allegorical approach argue that it is post-hoc rationalisation — a way of defending the indefensible by claiming a hidden meaning that the text itself does not clearly signal. This is a serious methodological objection. Allegorical reading is only convincing when the text provides internal signals that allegory is intended, or when there is a strong external tradition of allegorical interpretation predating the modern controversy.

Community controversies around the Charitropakhyan intensified significantly in the twentieth century, particularly following the standardisation of the Rehat Maryada in 1936 and the subsequent debates about what should constitute the Sikh canon. Some Sikh organisations and scholars have argued that the Charitropakhyan is not part of the Dasam Granth's authentic core; others defend its inclusion on both textual and theological grounds. These community debates are not merely academic: they determine which texts are read in Gurdwaras, which are taught to children, and which are considered authoritative for Sikh identity.

The scholarly task, as Dr. Kamalroop Singh frames it, is to bring manuscript evidence, genre knowledge, and comparative literary method to bear on these questions, without either capitulating to community pressure in either direction or dismissing community concerns as irrelevant to academic inquiry. The living community of interpretation is itself a scholarly resource, not merely an obstacle to objectivity.

Key Terms

  • ਚਰਿੱਤ੍ਰੋਪਾਖਿਆਨ (Charitropakhyan) — the collection of 404 tales in the Dasam Granth, often described as the most controversial section of the text
  • Hitopadesha tradition — a classical South Asian genre of instructive tale collections using morally complex narratives to teach practical wisdom
  • Allegorical reading — an interpretive method that locates the text's primary meaning at a symbolic level beneath the surface narrative
  • ਕਾਮ (Kaam) — desire or lust; one of the five vices (panj vikaar) identified in Sikh theology as obstacles to spiritual liberation
  • Didactic frame — the narrative device by which a tale collection is presented as instruction, signalling that the stories are examples rather than endorsements
  • ਮਾਇਆ (Maya) — illusion or the power of worldly entanglement; a central theological concept in Sikh thought also relevant to allegorical readings of the Charitropakhyan

Discussion Questions

  1. Allegorical interpretation is a powerful but potentially self-serving reading strategy. What internal or external evidence would make an allegorical reading of the Charitropakhyan convincing rather than merely convenient?
  2. Community controversy has shaped the Charitropakhyan debate significantly. Should scholars factor community concerns into their interpretive judgments, or should academic inquiry proceed independently? What are the risks of each approach?
  3. The Hitopadesha tradition depicts immoral behaviour to teach moral wisdom. How does understanding this genre change your reading of the Charitropakhyan? Does genre context resolve the controversy or merely reframe it?
  4. Dr. Kamalroop Singh uses manuscript consistency as evidence for the Charitropakhyan's authenticity. What other types of evidence would strengthen or weaken this argument?

Further Reading

  • Kamalroop Singh — essays on the Charitropakhyan in the Dasam Granth volume
  • Gurinder Singh Mann — The Making of Sikh Scripture
  • Harjot Oberoi — The Construction of Religious Boundaries

Key Takeaways

  • The Charitropakhyan belongs to a classical South Asian genre of instructive tale collections in which morally complex narratives serve didactic rather than endorsing purposes.
  • Allegorical readings of the Charitropakhyan are defensible but require internal textual evidence and careful methodological justification to avoid becoming mere rationalisation.
  • Manuscript evidence places the Charitropakhyan consistently within the earliest Dasam Granth recensions, complicating arguments for its later addition but not resolving the interpretive debate.
  • Community controversies around the Charitropakhyan are not merely obstacles to scholarship but important data about how living traditions negotiate difficult texts — a resource for the careful scholar.

Homework

The Charitropakhyan is the most controversial section of the Dasam Granth. Before forming a firm opinion, spend 30 minutes reading two scholarly perspectives on it — one that argues for its inclusion in the Dasam Granth canon and one that raises critical questions. Write a 400-word balanced summary of both positions, noting the type of evidence each relies upon. The goal is not to reach a verdict but to practice holding competing scholarly claims with intellectual fairness.

lessons.title: The Dasam Granth in the Eighteenth and Nineteenth Centuries: Historical Reception
lessons.html:
Introduction

The contemporary debates about the Dasam Granth can give the impression that the text has always been controversial — that from the moment of its compilation it was disputed, contested, and problematic. Historical research tells a more complex story. During the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, the text circulated, was copied, recited, and interpreted within the Sikh Panth in ways that reveal both continuity and change in its reception. Understanding this historical reception is essential for placing the modern controversy in proper perspective.

This lesson traces the Dasam Granth's history from its post-Guru compilation to the debates of the Singh Sabha reform movement in the late nineteenth and early twentieth century. Dr. Kamalroop Singh's manuscript research provides crucial evidence for this reception history, because the manuscripts themselves — where they were copied, by whom, and in what contexts — are documents of historical reception as much as they are carriers of text.

Tracing reception history requires distinguishing between the text as it existed and the text as different communities used and interpreted it. These two dimensions are always intertwined, but keeping them analytically distinct allows us to ask more precise questions: not just "what does the Dasam Granth say?" but "who read it, how, and to what purpose, in different historical moments?"

Eighteenth-Century Circulation and the Khalsa Context

The decades following Guru Gobind Singh's death in 1708 were a period of intense persecution and military conflict for the Khalsa. During this period, the texts associated with the Guru were both practically difficult to preserve and symbolically vital for community identity. The manuscript tradition shows that Dasam Granth texts circulated during this period, often in smaller collections rather than as a unified volume. Individual compositions — particularly the Nitnem banis and the Chandi narratives — appear in manuscripts that predate the compilation of the full Dasam Granth as a single volume.

The first formal compilation of the Dasam Granth as a unified text is traditionally associated with Bhai Mani Singh, a prominent scholar-Granthi in the early eighteenth century. Dr. Kamalroop Singh's manuscript research examines the evidence for and against this attribution, noting that the question of who compiled the text and on what authority is itself historically significant. The compilation of a canon is always an act of interpretation: it implies judgments about which texts belong together, in what order, and with what framing.

During the eighteenth century, the Dasam Granth was used in the Khalsa's devotional and martial life without the systematic controversies that would emerge later. The bir ras compositions were recited by warriors, the Nitnem banis were part of daily practice, and the text as a whole was treated as part of the Sikh scriptural heritage. This does not mean it was treated identically to the Guru Granth Sahib — the two texts held different statuses — but neither was it widely contested as inauthentic.

Historical sources from the eighteenth century, including Persian chronicles and early Sikh hagiographical writing, provide external testimony to the Khalsa's use of texts associated with Guru Gobind Singh. These sources do not always distinguish clearly between different compositions, but they establish that poetry attributed to the Guru was recited, revered, and functioned as a source of both devotional energy and martial inspiration during the period of the Khalsa's most severe trials.

The Singh Sabha Era and the Emergence of Controversy

The Singh Sabha movement, which emerged in the 1870s and reached its peak in the early twentieth century, was a reformist effort to clarify Sikh identity in the context of colonial modernity, missionary activity, and Hindu revivalist pressure. The movement sought to define Sikhism as a distinct religion with clear textual boundaries, rational doctrines, and institutional structures that could compete in the colonial public sphere.

It was in this Singh Sabha context that systematic controversy about the Dasam Granth intensified. Some reformers, influenced by colonial rationalist frameworks and Protestant models of religious scripture, found the Dasam Granth's mythological content, goddess imagery, and erotic narratives difficult to accommodate within a vision of Sikhism as a modern, rational monotheism. The argument that certain sections of the Dasam Granth were not authentic — that they had been inserted by later writers who did not share Guru Gobind Singh's theology — gained traction in this reformist climate.

Dr. Kamalroop Singh's scholarly contribution to this history is to point out that the reformist critique of the Dasam Granth was not simply a neutral, evidence-based reassessment of the text but was shaped by particular ideological commitments rooted in the colonial moment. This does not make the critique wrong, but it means that the historical genesis of the controversy must be understood when evaluating the arguments. Scholarship that presents the colonial-era critique as a self-evident textual discovery, without accounting for its ideological context, is doing incomplete historical work.

The early twentieth century saw the establishment of committees and institutions charged with standardising Sikh practice — culminating in the Rehat Maryada of 1936 — and these institutional processes inevitably engaged the Dasam Granth question. The decisions made during this period continue to shape how the text is received today, demonstrating that reception history is never simply past history: it is the foundation on which contemporary debates are built.

Key Terms

  • ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ (Singh Sabha) — the late nineteenth-century Sikh reform movement that sought to clarify Sikh identity and distinguish it from Hinduism and other religious traditions
  • Reception history — the scholarly study of how a text has been read, interpreted, and used by different communities across different historical periods
  • ਭਾਈ ਮਨੀ ਸਿੰਘ (Bhai Mani Singh) — eighteenth-century Sikh scholar traditionally associated with the first formal compilation of the Dasam Granth
  • Colonial modernity — the intellectual and institutional context of British India, which shaped Sikh reformist movements and their engagement with scripture
  • Canon formation — the historical process by which a religious community designates certain texts as authoritative and excludes others
  • Hagiography — biographical writing about holy persons, often blending historical information with devotional and legendary material

Discussion Questions

  1. The Singh Sabha movement's critique of the Dasam Granth was shaped by colonial-era rationalist frameworks. Does recognising the ideological context of a critique invalidate it, or simply require us to evaluate it more carefully? How do we distinguish between evidence-based and ideology-driven arguments?
  2. Reception history shows that the Dasam Granth was used without systematic controversy in the eighteenth century but became contested in the nineteenth. What does this tell us about the relationship between historical context and textual interpretation?
  3. The compilation of the Dasam Granth as a unified volume was itself an act of interpretation. What criteria might Bhai Mani Singh (or whoever compiled it) have used to decide which texts belonged in the collection?
  4. How does the Dasam Granth's reception history compare to the reception histories of other contested religious texts you know? What patterns do you notice across traditions?

Further Reading

  • Harjot Oberoi — The Construction of Religious Boundaries
  • Tony Ballantyne — Between Colonialism and Diaspora: Sikh Cultural Formations in an Imperial World
  • Pashaura Singh — Life and Work of Guru Arjan

Key Takeaways

  • The Dasam Granth circulated without systematic controversy in the eighteenth century; modern controversies intensified in the Singh Sabha era and were shaped by colonial-era reformist ideology.
  • The first formal compilation of the Dasam Granth as a unified volume was an act of interpretive canon formation, not a neutral preservation of pre-existing texts.
  • Dr. Kamalroop Singh's manuscript research reveals reception history embedded in the manuscripts themselves — where they were copied and by whom are historical documents of how the text was used.
  • Understanding the ideological contexts in which critiques of the Dasam Granth arose does not settle the textual questions but is essential for evaluating the arguments with proper historical awareness.

Homework

The Dasam Granth's reception history shows that attitudes toward the text have changed significantly across time. Identify one other religious tradition's canonical text that has experienced significant shifts in how it was received or interpreted across centuries (for example, the Song of Songs in the Hebrew Bible, or a text from the Buddhist or Islamic tradition). Write a 400-word comparative reflection on how that text's reception history illuminates the dynamics at work in the Dasam Granth debate.

lessons.title: Comparative Perspectives: The Dasam Granth Among World Religious Texts
lessons.html:
Introduction

Placing the Dasam Granth in comparative perspective — examining it alongside other sacred texts that have generated similar scholarly and community debates — is one of the most productive methods available to the student of Sikh studies. Comparative religion does not flatten differences or claim that all traditions are ultimately the same; rather, it sharpens our understanding of what is distinctive about each tradition by illuminating the structural similarities and differences that appear when texts are placed side by side.

This lesson examines the Dasam Granth through three comparative lenses: the treatment of martial and heroic content in other sacred texts, the dynamics of canon formation across religious traditions, and the relationship between scripture and living community in determining textual authority. Each comparison is designed not to reduce the Dasam Granth to a generic case but to identify what is generically shared and what is specifically Sikh about the questions this text raises.

Dr. Kamalroop Singh's scholarship is explicitly comparative in its method. His training in both South Asian manuscript traditions and Western academic religious studies allows him to bring comparative frameworks to bear on the Dasam Granth without losing sight of its particular historical and theological context. His approach models the kind of scholarly pluralism that serious comparative work requires.

Martial Content and Sacred Literature: A Comparative Survey

The Dasam Granth is not unique among the world's sacred texts in containing extensive martial content. The Hebrew Bible includes detailed accounts of warfare, commanded violence, and divine intervention in battle. The Bhagavad Gita — perhaps the most widely read text of the Hindu tradition — is set on a battlefield and contains Arjuna's crisis of conscience about killing his kinsmen, resolved by Krishna's extended teaching on righteous action. The Quran addresses the conditions and ethics of warfare across multiple surahs. The Norse Eddas celebrate warrior culture as a religious ideal.

What varies across these traditions is not the presence of martial content but the interpretive frameworks used to handle it. The Christian tradition has developed just war theory as a way of containing and regulating the martial content of its scripture. The Hindu tradition has produced elaborate allegorical readings of the Mahabharata that transform the battlefield into a metaphor for internal spiritual struggle. The Islamic tradition has developed the distinction between greater and lesser jihad — the inner spiritual struggle and the outer military effort — as an interpretive frame.

The Sikh sant-sipahi tradition, rooted in the Dasam Granth's bir ras, offers its own resolution: martial action is legitimate when undertaken in righteous defence of the weak and in surrender to divine will, and the warrior who acts from those motivations is not contradicting but fulfilling the spiritual path. Comparative analysis reveals that this is a coherent and sophisticated response to the interpretive challenge that all martial sacred texts face — not a unique problem requiring unique apology, but a recognisable religious-ethical position with parallels across the world's traditions.

The comparison also reveals what is distinctive about the Sikh response. Unlike traditions that allegorise martial content away from its literal meaning, the Dasam Granth and the Khalsa tradition it informs take the martial dimension seriously at the literal level: Sikhs have historically carried swords, maintained martial arts, and engaged in physical defence of the community. The sant-sipahi ideal is not a metaphor but a lived commitment. This literalism, combined with a robust theology of divine sanction and surrender, is arguably the most distinctive feature of the Sikh approach to martial sacred literature.

Canon, Authority, and Living Community

The dynamics of canon formation in Sikh tradition offer productive comparisons with other religious communities' negotiations of textual authority. The Christian canon was established through a series of councils and debates in the early centuries CE; texts that did not make the canonical cut — the Gospel of Thomas, the Didache — continued to circulate and influence Christian thought but lacked the institutional authority of the canonical texts. The Hebrew Bible's canon was similarly negotiated over centuries, with books like Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes accepted only after considerable debate.

The Dasam Granth's uncertain canonical status — present in Sikh practice but differently weighted than the Guru Granth Sahib — has structural analogies with the concept of deuterocanonical texts in Christianity: texts that are acknowledged as valuable and ancient but are not granted the same authority as the primary canon. This comparison does not resolve the Dasam Granth question but it normalises the existence of tiered textual authority within a single tradition and shows that navigating such tiers is a challenge that many religious communities have faced.

The role of living community in determining textual authority is another productive comparative theme. In rabbinic Judaism, the oral Torah — the living interpretive tradition — is understood to have authority alongside and continuous with the written Torah. In Shia Islam, the living Imam has historically been understood as a continuing source of authoritative interpretation alongside the Quran. In Sikhism, the ਪੰਥ (Panth, the community) holds a form of collective authority that shapes how scripture is interpreted and applied. Dr. Kamalroop Singh's attention to the Panth's reception of the Dasam Granth across history reflects this understanding: the living community's engagement with the text is itself theologically significant data, not merely sociological noise.

Key Terms

  • Comparative religion — the academic discipline that examines similarities and differences across religious traditions, traditions, texts, and practices
  • Deuterocanonical — texts acknowledged as valuable within a religious tradition but placed in a secondary canonical tier relative to primary authoritative scripture
  • Just war theory — a framework developed in Christian ethics for determining when and how military force may be legitimately used; one way of handling martial sacred content
  • ਪੰਥ (Panth) — the Sikh community or nation; in theological terms, the collective body whose consensus carries interpretive authority
  • Allegoresis — the systematic reading of texts at an allegorical level, often applied to sacred texts whose literal content is morally or theologically challenging
  • Oral Torah — in rabbinic Judaism, the body of oral interpretive tradition understood to be continuous with and authoritative alongside the written Torah

Discussion Questions

  1. Comparative religion reveals that many sacred traditions contain martial content and have developed diverse interpretive strategies to handle it. Does knowing this comparative context change how you read the Dasam Granth? Why or why not?
  2. The concept of deuterocanonical texts — valued but secondarily authoritative — appears in several religious traditions. Is this a useful framework for understanding the Dasam Granth's status relative to the Guru Granth Sahib? What are the limits of this comparison?
  3. How does the role of the ਪੰਥ (Panth) in Sikh textual authority compare to the role of living community or interpretive tradition in other religious contexts you know?
  4. Dr. Kamalroop Singh's comparative method brings frameworks from outside the Sikh tradition to bear on the Dasam Granth. What are the risks and rewards of this approach for both scholars and practitioners?

Further Reading

  • Mircea Eliade — The Sacred and the Profane
  • Jonathan Z. Smith — Imagining Religion: From Babylon to Jonestown
  • Arvind Sharma — Our Religions: The Seven World Religions Introduced by Preeminent Scholars from Each Tradition

Key Takeaways

  • The Dasam Granth is not unique in containing martial content; other major sacred texts face analogous interpretive challenges, and comparing the solutions across traditions clarifies what is shared and what is specifically Sikh.
  • The concept of tiered canonical authority — with some texts more authoritative than others — appears across religious traditions and provides a framework for understanding the Dasam Granth's relationship to the Guru Granth Sahib.
  • The role of the living Panth in shaping how the Dasam Granth is received and interpreted is theologically significant, not merely sociologically interesting, and has analogies in other traditions' concepts of community authority.
  • Comparative method, properly used, sharpens rather than erases the distinctiveness of each tradition's approach to shared challenges.

Homework

Select one sacred text from a tradition other than Sikhism — the Bhagavad Gita, the Gospel of Mark, the Quran's Surah Al-Anfal, or another text you know — that contains martial, heroic, or morally challenging content. Write a 400-word reflection comparing how that text's tradition has handled the interpretive challenges its difficult content raises, and what lessons that comparative case might offer for reading the Dasam Granth.

lessons.title: The Future of Dasam Granth Studies: Open Questions and Emerging Research
lessons.html:
Introduction

Every serious academic field is defined not only by what has been established but by what remains open, contested, and in need of further research. Dasam Granth studies is a young field by the standards of academic religious scholarship, and the work of scholars like Dr. Kamalroop Singh has opened as many questions as it has answered. This final lesson maps the open questions, emerging methodologies, and future directions that define the cutting edge of the field — and invites students to think of themselves as potential contributors to an ongoing scholarly conversation.

The course has moved from foundational questions — what is the Dasam Granth, who is Dr. Kamalroop Singh, how do manuscripts work — through advanced topics including the Nitnem banis, bir ras theology, the Charitropakhyan controversy, historical reception, and comparative perspectives. This concluding lesson synthesises those threads and asks: what comes next? What research is still needed? What methodological tools are emerging that will enable new insights? How can students at all levels contribute to advancing this scholarship?

Thinking about a field's future requires intellectual humility: the most important discoveries in any area of scholarship are often the ones no one has yet thought to look for. The student who comes to the Dasam Granth without assuming the conclusions are already settled is in the best position to contribute something genuinely new.

Open Textual and Historical Questions

Despite the significant advances in Dasam Granth manuscript research, major textual questions remain unresolved. The full census of surviving manuscripts has not yet been completed. Manuscript cataloguing in repositories across India, the UK, Canada, and the United States is ongoing, and new manuscripts — or new information about known manuscripts — continue to emerge. Dr. Kamalroop Singh himself has acknowledged that his published work represents a stage in an ongoing research process, not a final definitive account.

Specific textual questions that remain open include the precise relationship between early recensions and the standardised printed edition, the history of the ਬੀੜ (bir, volume) traditions across different regional Sikh communities, and the textual history of individual compositions within the Dasam Granth whose manuscript evidence is sparse or ambiguous. Answering these questions will require both traditional codicological skills — the close study of manuscript features — and digital humanities tools that can process large numbers of manuscripts computationally.

Historical questions about the Dasam Granth's composition and early reception are similarly open. The relationship between Guru Gobind Singh's court poets — among whom several important compositions are sometimes attributed — and the Guru himself is still debated. The social and institutional contexts in which compositions were produced and circulated, the oral traditions that preceded their inscription in manuscripts, and the political circumstances that shaped the compilation of the text all require further research in primary sources from the late seventeenth and early eighteenth century.

Interdisciplinary approaches — bringing together manuscript studies, literary history, political history, and art history (the Dasam Granth's themes appear in Pahari and Sikh visual art of the period) — will be essential for making progress on these historical questions. The boundaries of Dasam Granth studies as an academic field are themselves an open question, and future scholars will likely work across disciplinary lines in ways that current institutionalised scholarship does not fully support.

Methodological Innovations and the Digital Humanities

The digital humanities represent one of the most significant emerging methodological opportunities for Dasam Granth research. High-resolution digital imaging of manuscripts makes it possible to examine features — ink composition, paper watermarks, scribal hand characteristics — that were previously accessible only to scholars with physical access to the original documents. Digital repositories like the Panjab Digital Library have already made significant collections available online, and the scope of digital access will continue to expand.

Computational text analysis — using algorithms to identify patterns across large text collections — offers new possibilities for addressing questions about authorship, stylistic consistency, and scribal transmission. Computational stylistics has been applied to contested authorship questions in other literary contexts (Shakespeare, the Federalist Papers), and similar methods, adapted to Gurmukhi text and the particular features of Braj Bhasha and Sanskrit poetry, could contribute valuable evidence to the Dasam Granth authorship debate. These methods do not settle interpretive questions but they can constrain the range of plausible answers by providing evidence that is not available through traditional close reading.

Critical edition work — the production of scholarly editions that document manuscript variants, trace transmission history, and provide full critical apparatus — is perhaps the most urgent methodological need in the field. The absence of a complete critical edition of the Dasam Granth is a significant gap that limits research across all the questions surveyed in this course. Producing such an edition would require a collaborative international team with expertise in Gurmukhi palaeography, Braj Bhasha and Sanskrit literature, Punjabi history, and digital humanities — and sustained institutional support over many years.

The training of the next generation of scholars is itself a methodological challenge. Dasam Granth studies requires a rare combination of skills: fluency in Punjabi, Braj Bhasha, and often Sanskrit and Persian; expertise in manuscript studies; grounding in Sikh theology and history; and familiarity with contemporary methods in religious studies and literary scholarship. Building educational pathways that develop all these competencies remains an open institutional challenge for universities, Sikh organisations, and the academic field as a whole.

Key Terms

  • Codicology — the study of manuscripts as physical objects, attending to features such as material, binding, script, and layout to reconstruct the history of a document
  • Digital humanities — the application of computational and digital methods to questions in the humanities, including text analysis, manuscript digitisation, and data visualisation
  • Critical edition — a scholarly edition of a text that documents manuscript variants, reconstructs the transmission history, and provides full critical apparatus for researchers
  • Computational stylistics — the use of algorithmic analysis of linguistic and stylistic features to address questions of authorship, dating, and textual history
  • Palaeography — the study of historical scripts and handwriting, essential for reading and dating manuscripts
  • ਬੀੜ (Bir) — a volume or copy of a sacred text in the Sikh tradition; the term carries connotations of authority and completeness

Discussion Questions

  1. What do you consider the most important unresolved question in Dasam Granth studies, and what type of research would be needed to address it? What obstacles stand in the way of that research?
  2. Computational stylistics has been used to address contested authorship questions in other literary contexts. What are the specific challenges of applying such methods to the Dasam Granth, and what would a responsible application of those methods look like?
  3. The production of a critical edition of the Dasam Granth would require international collaboration across disciplinary and community lines. What institutional and community dynamics would scholars need to navigate to make such a project possible?
  4. After completing this course, how has your understanding of what it means to "read" the Dasam Granth changed? What skills or knowledge do you still need to engage with the text at the level this course has introduced?

Further Reading

  • Kamalroop Singh and Gurinder Singh Mann — Dasam Granth: The 18th Century Sikh Scripture
  • David Greetham — Textual Scholarship: An Introduction
  • Gurinder Singh Mann — Sikhism

Key Takeaways

  • Dasam Granth studies is a young and open field; significant textual, historical, and interpretive questions remain unresolved and represent genuine opportunities for future scholarly contribution.
  • Digital humanities tools — manuscript digitisation, computational stylistics, critical edition production — represent major emerging methodological opportunities for advancing research on the Dasam Granth.
  • The training of scholars with the rare combination of linguistic, manuscript, theological, and methodological skills required for this field is itself an open challenge for academic institutions and the Sikh community.
  • Engaging with open questions from a position of intellectual humility — aware of what remains unknown and committed to rigorous inquiry — is the defining characteristic of excellent scholarship in any field.

Homework

This course has covered the textual scholarship of Dr. Kamalroop Singh and the major debates in Dasam Granth studies. Write a 500-word personal scholarly statement: What questions do you still have after completing this course? What methodological tools would you need to pursue those questions further? What would you need to study next — languages, archival access, additional secondary literature — to advance your understanding? This is a forward-looking exercise in scholarly self-assessment and planning.

sourceText.english: In a few days you shall depart; understand this truth. Do not long excessively for the friends of this world. Do not be shamed; perform some virtuous deeds. Do not depart wearing the garment of condemnation. If you remain negligent, you shall suffer. Neither daughters nor sons will provide any essence or support. Repent, and do not exert your power with arrogance. The fire of hell shall burn within the grave. Many prophets, Sheikhs, kings, and lords have passed. lessons.title: Lesson 1: Introduction and Course Map
lessons.summary: An overview of Giani Gurdit Singh, his scholarly work, and the structure of this course.
lessons.html:
Welcome and Course Map

This course studies how the Punjabi scholar Giani Gurdit Singh examined the history and structure of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, the eternal Guru of the Sikhs. We approach the scripture with reverence, and we study his method: how a careful reader traces the way the ਬਾਣੀ (bani) was gathered, recorded, and arranged.

Giani Gurdit Singh was a respected writer and editor whose study, Itihaas Sri Guru Granth Sahib (Mundavani), gave special attention to the ਮੁੰਦਾਵਣੀ (Mundavani), the composition that traditionally closes the recitation of the scripture (Gurdit Singh).

Table of Contents

LessonFocus
1Introduction and course map
2Giani Gurdit Singh as scholar and editor
3How the bani was compiled: pothis, birs, and standardization
4The structure of the Granth: raag, authorship, and the close at Ang 1430
5The Mundavani: meaning, placement, and the scholarly debate
6Legacy and place within Sikh studies

How to study this course

Each lesson defines its terms, presents evidence, and asks you to think about method. Where scholars disagree, we present views neutrally and let you weigh the evidence. We do not invent quotations, page numbers, or biographical claims.

References

Gurdit Singh, Giani. Itihaas Sri Guru Granth Sahib (Mundavani). Chandigarh: Sahit Parkashan.

Homework

Lesson 1 Homework: After completing the course map overview, write a 350-word personal reflection on what it means to study ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ as an academic text without reducing its sacred character. Consider what questions you personally bring to this course and how Giani Gurdit Singh's scholarly framework might help you address them. Submit your reflection in writing before proceeding to Lesson 2.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Giani Gurdit Singh as Scholar and Editor
lessons.summary: Who Giani Gurdit Singh was as a writer, editor, and student of Sikh scripture and history.
lessons.html:
The Scholar Behind the Study

Giani Gurdit Singh is remembered as a respected Punjabi scholar, writer, and editor who devoted serious attention to Sikh history and to the text of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. His work belongs to a tradition of Punjabi scholarship that reads the scripture with devotion while also asking historical questions about how it came to be (Gurdit Singh).

His study Itihaas Sri Guru Granth Sahib (Mundavani) is notable because it brings together two concerns that are sometimes kept apart: the ਇਤਿਹਾਸ (itihaas, history) of the scripture and the close textual study of one of its compositions, the Mundavani.

What kind of scholarship is this?

To study the ਸੰਪਾਦਨ (sampadan, compilation) of a sacred text is to ask how the words we honour today were collected and arranged. This is not to doubt the scripture; it is to understand its journey. Giani Gurdit Singh's contribution is to apply careful reading and attention to sources to questions that matter to the community.

ConcernQuestion the scholar asks
History (itihaas)How was the text gathered and transmitted?
StructureHow are compositions arranged within the volume?
The MundavaniWhat does the closing composition mean and where does it sit?

We do not here invent details of his life or list page numbers from his book; instead we describe the character and aims of his scholarship as it relates to the scripture.

References

Gurdit Singh, Giani. Itihaas Sri Guru Granth Sahib (Mundavani). Chandigarh: Sahit Parkashan.

Homework

Lesson 2 Homework: Research one other Sikh scholar who produced a major critical study of ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ in the twentieth century (for example, Bhai Sahib Bhai Randhir Singh, Giani Harbans Singh, or Dr. Trilochan Singh). Write a 400-word comparison between that scholar's methodology and what you have learned so far about Giani Gurdit Singh's editorial approach, noting at least two points of similarity and two points of divergence.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: How the Bani Was Compiled
lessons.summary: Pothis, recensions, and the standardization of the text that scholars study.
lessons.html:
From Pothi to Standardized Text

Before Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji took its standardized form, the ਬਾਣੀ (bani) circulated in earlier collections. A ਪੋਥੀ (pothi) is an early manuscript volume of gathered compositions. Over time these were drawn together into a ਬੀੜ (bir/beed), a bound recension of the scripture (Gurdit Singh; Mann).

Giani Gurdit Singh's historical study attends to this process of gathering and arrangement. The wider field of Sikh studies has examined the same questions: Gurinder Singh Mann traces the making of the scripture through its manuscript stages (Mann), and Pashaura Singh studies questions of canon, meaning, and authority (Singh, The Guru Granth Sahib).

Stages of transmission (general outline)

StageFormSignificance
Early collectionsPothiCompositions recorded and preserved
CompilationBir / beedCompositions arranged into a single volume
Standardized textSri Guru Granth Sahib JiThe honoured text studied today, spanning to Ang 1430

This outline is general and well attested; we do not assign invented dates or page references. The point is method: history asks how a revered text moved from scattered sources to a single standardized volume.

References

Gurdit Singh, Giani. Itihaas Sri Guru Granth Sahib (Mundavani). Chandigarh: Sahit Parkashan. Mann, Gurinder Singh. The Making of Sikh Scripture. New York: Oxford University Press, 2001.

Homework

Lesson 3 Homework: Using only the conceptual framework discussed in this lesson (do not invent Gurbani lines), write a 350-word essay on why the process of ਬਾਣੀ compilation during the Guruship period was both a spiritual act and an editorial act. Explain how Guru Arjan Dev Ji's role as compiler shaped the devotional character of the final text. Conclude with one question you would ask Giani Gurdit Singh if you could interview him.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: The Structure of the Granth
lessons.summary: Arrangement by raag, the ordering of compositions, and the close of the text at Ang 1430.
lessons.html:
The Architecture of the Scripture

One of the most striking features of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji is its careful internal order. The text honours each leaf as an ਅੰਗ (ang), a limb of a living body rather than an ordinary page. The scripture spans to Ang 1430, and it is well attested that it closes with the Mundavani (Gurdit Singh; Singh, The Guru Granth Sahib).

Much of the body of the scripture is arranged by ਰਾਗ (raag), the musical mode under which compositions are sung. This ordering shapes how the text is read and recited, and it is part of what Giani Gurdit Singh's structural study seeks to explain.

Layers of structure

LayerOrganizing principle
OpeningFoundational compositions before the raag section
Main bodyArrangement by raag (musical mode)
ClosingCompositions after the raag section, ending with the Mundavani at the close near Ang 1430

Understanding this architecture is essential before turning to the Mundavani, because the debate about the Mundavani is partly a debate about where the closing of the scripture is marked. Giani Gurdit Singh's study takes the structure seriously as evidence (Gurdit Singh).

References

Gurdit Singh, Giani. Itihaas Sri Guru Granth Sahib (Mundavani). Chandigarh: Sahit Parkashan. Singh, Pashaura. The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2000.

Homework

Lesson 4 Homework: Draw or diagram the structural organization of ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ as described in this lesson — the ਰਾਗ divisions, the ordering of contributors, and the placement of special sections. Annotate your diagram with brief labels in Punjabi Unicode where possible. Then write a short paragraph (150–200 words) reflecting on what this structure reveals about the Gurus' theological intentions.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: The Mundavani and the Scholarly Debate
lessons.summary: The meaning and placement of the Mundavani, presented neutrally with respect for multiple views.
lessons.html:
The Closing Seal

The ਮੁੰਦਾਵਣੀ (Mundavani) is the composition that traditionally closes the recitation of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. The term is often understood to carry the sense of a seal or a closing, marking the completion of the revealed message. This much is widely accepted and central to Giani Gurdit Singh's study (Gurdit Singh).

The debate, presented neutrally

Within Sikh scholarship there has been thoughtful discussion about the precise placement and function of the Mundavani in relation to the compositions that appear around the very close of the text. Giani Gurdit Singh engaged this question carefully. Scholars such as Pashaura Singh have likewise examined questions of canon and the boundaries of the text (Singh, The Guru Granth Sahib).

We present the discussion as a matter of scholarly interpretation, not as a settled controversy with a single right answer. Different readers, working from the same reverence for the scripture, may weigh the evidence differently.

Point of inquiryWhat scholars consider
Meaning of the termThe sense of a seal or closing of the message
PlacementIts position among the compositions at the close of the text
FunctionWhat it signals about the completion of the scripture

The course does not adjudicate the debate. Following good scholarly practice and the reverence due to the scripture, it asks you to understand the questions and the evidence rather than to declare a winner.

References

Gurdit Singh, Giani. Itihaas Sri Guru Granth Sahib (Mundavani). Chandigarh: Sahit Parkashan. Singh, Pashaura. The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2000.

Homework

Lesson 5 Homework: The ਮੁੰਦਾਵਣੀ has been the subject of intense scholarly debate. Write a 400-word position paper in which you argue for one interpretation of its function — as a seal, a concluding blessing, or something else — drawing on the arguments presented in this lesson. You are not required to reach a definitive conclusion, but you must engage seriously with at least two competing scholarly views and explain why you find one more persuasive.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Legacy and Place in Sikh Studies
lessons.summary: How Giani Gurdit Singh's work fits within the broader field and why it still matters.
lessons.html:
Legacy and the Wider Field

Giani Gurdit Singh's study of the ਇਤਿਹਾਸ (itihaas) of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji belongs to a living tradition of careful scholarship on Sikh scripture. His attention to the Mundavani and to the structure of the text contributed to ongoing conversations that continue in the academy and the community (Gurdit Singh).

Later and parallel scholarship can help readers place his work. Gurinder Singh Mann's study of how the scripture was made (Mann), Pashaura Singh's work on canon and authority (Singh, The Guru Granth Sahib), and the broad survey in The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies (Singh and Fenech) together show that the questions Giani Gurdit Singh asked are central to the field.

Why it still matters

For the communityFor scholarship
Deepens reverent understanding of how the Guru's word reached usModels careful, source-based study of a sacred text
Clarifies the meaning of the closing MundavaniContributes to debates on canon and structure

Closing reflection
