To study the history of the scripture is not to lessen its sanctity but to honour the care with which it was preserved. Giani Gurdit Singh's work invites readers to hold devotion and inquiry together, treating the text that spans to Ang 1430 and closes with the Mundavani as both an eternal Guru and a profound object of study.

References

Gurdit Singh, Giani. Itihaas Sri Guru Granth Sahib (Mundavani). Chandigarh: Sahit Parkashan. Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014.

Homework

Lesson 6 Homework: Giani Gurdit Singh's legacy shapes how Sikh Studies is conducted today. Identify one area of Sikh scholarship — textual, historical, or theological — where you believe his work has opened a research question that remains unresolved. Write a 350-word research proposal sketch outlining what that question is, why it matters, and what primary sources a scholar might consult to begin addressing it.

lessons.title: Lesson 7: Raag as Theological Architecture — Why Gurbani Is Organized by Melody
lessons.html:
Table of Contents

  1. Introduction
  2. The Meaning of ਰਾਗ in Gurbani Scholarship
  3. Giani Gurdit Singh's Analysis of the Raag Framework
  4. Theological Implications of Musical Ordering
  5. Key Terms
  6. Discussion Questions
  7. Further Reading
  8. Key Takeaways
  9. Works Cited
Term (Unicode)Academic Context
ਰਾਗA melodic framework governing the emotional and devotional register of Gurbani composition.
ਗੁਰਮਤਿThe philosophical and ethical teaching of the Guru; the guiding interpretive lens.
ਸੁਰMelodic pitch; in devotional context, the tuning of the self toward the Divine.
ਕੀਰਤਨDevotional singing of Gurbani; the primary mode through which ਰਾਗ is activated.
ਅੰਗA page of ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ; used in place of the secular term "page."
ਸ਼ਬਦA hymn or sacred composition; the foundational literary unit of the Granth.

Introduction

One of the most distinctive features of ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ is that its approximately 1,430 ਅੰਗ are not organized by author, by chronology, or by theological theme alone — they are organized primarily by ਰਾਗ, the classical Indian melodic mode. This is not a decorative choice. It is a statement about how the Gurus understood the relationship between sound, consciousness, and spiritual transformation. Giani Gurdit Singh devoted considerable scholarly energy to unpacking precisely this point, arguing that the raag framework is itself a theological architecture.

This lesson examines what Giani Gurdit Singh's scholarship reveals about the raag system as an organizing principle. We explore how the thirty-one main raags of the Granth are not a neutral catalogue but a carefully curated spectrum of emotional and devotional states — from the longing of ਰਾਗ ਮਾਝ to the meditative gravity of ਰਾਗ ਭੈਰਉ. Understanding this helps students move beyond treating the Granth as a mere anthology and toward recognizing it as an integrated devotional architecture.

We will also consider the scholarly debate about whether the Gurus adapted pre-existing classical raags or transformed them into something distinctively Sikh. This debate has significant implications for how Sikh Studies situates the Granth in relation to broader South Asian musical and literary traditions. (Pashaura Singh, The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority, 2000, 87–102.)

The Meaning of ਰਾਗ in Gurbani Scholarship

In classical Indian music theory, a ਰਾਗ is not simply a scale. It is a comprehensive melodic personality — a set of ascending and descending note sequences combined with specific ornamental gestures, a characteristic mood (ਰਸ), and often a prescribed time of day or season for performance. Each raag is understood to evoke a particular emotional state in the listener. This is the classical Hindustani and Carnatic understanding that the Gurus both inherited and decisively reoriented.

Giani Gurdit Singh's scholarship, particularly in his multi-volume Itihas Sri Guru Granth Sahib, carefully traces how the Gurus accepted the classical framework of raag but subordinated its mood-evoking function to the purpose of ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ — the remembrance of the Divine Name. For the Gurus, a raag was not a performance aesthetic but a vehicle for ਸੁਰਤਿ, the attentive inner consciousness of the seeker. The raag's function is to tune the listener's inner state so that Gurbani can penetrate more deeply. (Gurdit Singh, Itihas Sri Guru Granth Sahib, vol. 3, 1990, 112–145.)

This distinction matters greatly for interpretation. Classical musicology might analyze a raag for its structural properties. Giani Gurdit Singh insists that within the Sikh context, the raag must always be read in relation to the ਸ਼ਬਦ it carries. The melody serves the word; the word carries the teaching. Separating them, or analyzing the raag in purely musicological terms, risks missing the theological point the Gurus were making.

Scholars such as Regula Qureshi have examined how raag functions in devotional contexts across South Asian traditions (Qureshi, Sufi Music of India and Pakistan, 1986, 43–67). Giani Gurdit Singh's contribution is to insist on the distinctiveness of the Sikh transformation of this framework — not dismissing the classical tradition but showing how ਗੁਰਮਤਿ redirected its energies toward liberation rather than aesthetic pleasure alone.

Giani Gurdit Singh's Analysis of the Raag Framework

Giani Gurdit Singh's analysis identifies thirty-one major ਰਾਗ in ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ, along with several sub-raags (ਰਾਗਣੀਆਂ) and mixed forms. He argues that this selection is neither arbitrary nor simply a reflection of the regional musical environment of Punjab in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Rather, the Gurus made deliberate choices about which raags to include, and the selection reflects a spectrum of devotional states — yearning, surrender, joy, grief, contemplation — that together map the complete interior journey of the Sikh seeker.

A key insight in Giani Gurdit Singh's work is his observation that the Granth opens, after the foundational ਜਪੁ ਜੀ ਸਾਹਿਬ (which has no raag designation), with ਰਾਗ ਸਿਰੀ, and that this placement is deliberate. ਰਾਗ ਸਿਰੀ is associated with gravity, longing, and the beginning of devotional engagement. The choice to open the raag section with this particular melodic personality signals to the practitioner the emotional posture with which Gurbani study should begin. (Gurdit Singh, Itihas Sri Guru Granth Sahib, vol. 3, 1990, 167.)

Giani Gurdit Singh also examines the closing raags of the main body of the Granth, noting how the sequence moves toward raags associated with peace, completion, and the dissolution of ਹਉਮੈ. This arc — from longing through transformation to peace — is not accidental. It mirrors the spiritual journey described in the ਪੰਜ ਖੰਡ (five realms of spiritual progression) articulated by Guru Nanak Dev Ji in ਜਪੁ ਜੀ ਸਾਹਿਬ. The raag system thus encodes in musical form the same spiritual map that the Granth's theology articulates in word. (Pashaura Singh, The Guru Granth Sahib, 2000, 103–118.)

Theological Implications of Musical Ordering

The theological stakes of the raag system become clearest when we consider what Giani Gurdit Singh calls the principle of ਸ਼ਬਦ-ਸੁਰ ਏਕਤਾ — the unity of sacred word and sacred sound. In ਗੁਰਮਤਿ, the Divine is described as ਸ਼ਬਦ ਗੁਰੂ — the Word as Guru. This means that how the word is sounded is not separable from what it means. The raag is not packaging for theological content; it is part of the content itself. To sing a ਸ਼ਬਦ in the wrong raag, in Giani Gurdit Singh's reading, is not merely an aesthetic error but a theological one — it alters the devotional state the composition is designed to activate. (Mandair, Religion and the Specter of the West, 2009, 287–310.)

This has significant implications for contemporary ਕੀਰਤਨ practice. Giani Gurdit Singh's scholarship has been cited by those who argue for raag-based ਕੀਰਤਨ as a theological obligation, not merely a stylistic preference. If the raag framework is theological architecture, then departing from it is not a matter of musical taste but of fidelity to the Granth's own internal logic. This debate remains live in Sikh communities worldwide, making Giani Gurdit Singh's textual scholarship directly relevant to contemporary religious practice.

Arvind-Pal Singh Mandair has noted that the question of how Gurbani is sounded connects to broader questions about Sikh identity and the relationship between ਧਰਮ and culture (Mandair, Sikhism: A Guide for the Perplexed, 2013, 145–162). Giani Gurdit Singh's work provides a textual foundation for these discussions by grounding them in careful historical and structural analysis of the Granth itself rather than in assertion or tradition alone.

Key Terms

  • ਰਾਗ — A melodic framework in classical Indian music, reoriented in Gurbani to serve devotional and theological ends.
  • ਰਾਗਣੀ — A sub-raag or feminine melodic variant assigned to certain compositions in the Granth.
  • ਸੁਰਤਿ — The attentive inner consciousness; the faculty that tunes itself to the Divine through ਕੀਰਤਨ.
  • ਕੀਰਤਨ — Devotional singing of Gurbani; the primary mode of raag activation in Sikh worship.
  • ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ — Remembrance and meditation on the Divine Name; the ultimate purpose of raag in Gurbani.
  • ਸ਼ਬਦ-ਸੁਰ ਏਕਤਾ — The unity of sacred word and sacred sound; Giani Gurdit Singh's key theological principle for the raag system.

Discussion Questions

  1. If the ਰਾਗ framework is theological rather than merely aesthetic, what criteria should a ਕੀਰਤਨੀ use when choosing how to sing a particular ਸ਼ਬਦ? How does Giani Gurdit Singh's analysis help or complicate that choice?
  2. Classical Indian musicology and ਗੁਰਮਤਿ both value ਰਾਗ but for different reasons. Where do you see genuine continuity between them, and where does Giani Gurdit Singh identify a decisive break?
  3. The debate over raag-based versus popular-tune ਕੀਰਤਨ is ongoing in Sikh communities. How does the textual and structural scholarship of Giani Gurdit Singh enter — or fail to enter — that community conversation?
  4. Giani Gurdit Singh argues that the Granth's raag sequence encodes the ਪੰਜ ਖੰਡ spiritual journey. Do you find this argument persuasive, and what would it take to test it rigorously?

Further Reading

  • Pashaura Singh — The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority (2000)
  • Regula Qureshi — Sufi Music of India and Pakistan: Sound, Context and Meaning in Qawwali (1986)
  • Gurnam Singh — A Critical Study of Kirtan in Sikhism (1997)

Key Takeaways

  • The thirty-one ਰਾਗ of ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ are a deliberate theological architecture, not a neutral musical catalogue.
  • Giani Gurdit Singh argues that the Gurus transformed the classical raag tradition so that melody serves ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ rather than aesthetic enjoyment.
  • The concept of ਸ਼ਬਦ-ਸੁਰ ਏਕਤਾ means that sound and meaning are inseparable in Gurbani; changing the raag changes the devotional act.
  • Giani Gurdit Singh's textual scholarship grounds contemporary debates about ਕੀਰਤਨ practice in historical and structural evidence.

Works Cited

Gurdit Singh, Giani. Itihas Sri Guru Granth Sahib. Vol. 3. Chandigarh: Singh Brothers, 1990.

Mandair, Arvind-Pal Singh. Religion and the Specter of the West: Sikhism, India, Postcoloniality, and the Politics of Translation. New York: Columbia University Press, 2009.

Mandair, Arvind-Pal Singh. Sikhism: A Guide for the Perplexed. London: Bloomsbury, 2013.

Pashaura Singh. The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2000.

Qureshi, Regula. Sufi Music of India and Pakistan: Sound, Context and Meaning in Qawwali. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1986.

Homework

Attend or listen to a recording of ਕੀਰਤਨ (live or archived) where the performer identifies the ਰਾਗ being sung. Write a 350-word reflection on what you noticed: Did the melodic character of the raag seem to match the devotional content of the ਸ਼ਬਦ? Did knowing the raag change how you listened? Draw on at least one concept from this lesson — such as ਸੁਰਤਿ or ਸ਼ਬਦ-ਸੁਰ ਏਕਤਾ — to frame your observation.

lessons.title: Lesson 8: The Bhagat Bani — Non-Sikh Voices in the Granth and What They Reveal
lessons.html:
Table of Contents

  1. Introduction
  2. Who Are the ਭਗਤ? Historical Identities and Traditions
  3. Giani Gurdit Singh's Criteria for Inclusion
  4. Theological Coherence Across Difference
  5. Key Terms
  6. Discussion Questions
  7. Further Reading
  8. Key Takeaways
  9. Works Cited
Term (Unicode)Academic Context
ਭਗਤ ਬਾਣੀCompositions by non-Guru devotional poets included in ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ.
ਏਕ ਓਅੰਕਾਰThe foundational affirmation: there is One Creative Being. The theological anchor for inclusion of diverse voices.
ਸਾਂਝੀਵਾਲਤਾCommonality; the Sikh principle of shared humanity and spiritual kinship across difference.
ਨਿਰਗੁਣThe formless, attributeless aspect of the Divine; emphasized by many of the ਭਗਤ poets.
ਸਰਗੁਣThe Divine with form and qualities; present alongside ਨਿਰਗੁਣ in Gurbani's theological balance.
ਪਰਮਾਤਮਾThe Supreme Soul or Ultimate Reality; the shared object of devotion across all voices in the Granth.

Introduction

ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ contains the compositions not only of the Sikh Gurus but also of fifteen devotional poets — the ਭਗਤ — drawn from Hindu, Muslim, and low-caste backgrounds across several centuries of South Asian history. Figures such as Kabir, Namdev, Ravidas, Farid, and Trilochan composed in contexts far removed from the Punjab of Guru Nanak Dev Ji's time. Their inclusion in the Granth is one of the most theologically and historically significant editorial decisions in the history of world scripture. Giani Gurdit Singh devoted sustained scholarly attention to both the historical identities of these ਭਗਤ and the principles by which Guru Arjan Dev Ji selected their compositions.

This lesson examines Giani Gurdit Singh's framework for understanding the ਭਗਤ ਬਾਣੀ. We ask: What historical persons are these poets? What theological criterion governs their inclusion? And what does the presence of their voices in the Granth reveal about the nature of ਗੁਰਮਤਿ as a philosophy that engages the world rather than withdrawing from it?

These questions are not merely historical. They bear directly on how contemporary Sikhs understand inter-religious relations, the universality of the Divine, and the scope of ਸਾਂਝੀਵਾਲਤਾ. Giani Gurdit Singh's scholarship provides a rigorous textual foundation for these discussions. (W.H. McLeod, Guru Nanak and the Sikh Religion, 1968, 152–175.)

Who Are the ਭਗਤ? Historical Identities and Traditions

The fifteen ਭਗਤ whose compositions appear in ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ span a remarkable range of time, geography, and social location. Kabir, perhaps the best-known, composed in the Varanasi region in the fifteenth century, drawing on both Hindu Vedantic thought and Islamic Sufi imagery while rejecting caste hierarchy and ritual formalism. Sheikh Farid, a thirteenth-century Sufi master of Punjab, composed in vernacular Punjabi — making him the earliest significant poet in the Granth's temporal span. Namdev, a Maharashtra cloth-printer, and Ravidas, a cobbler from Varanasi, both composed in contexts shaped by their low-caste social position and their radical devotional theology.

Giani Gurdit Singh's historical work establishes, through careful cross-referencing of hagiographical and historical sources, that these poets were not contemporaries of the Sikh Gurus in most cases. Their compositions were gathered by the Gurus — in particular by Guru Arjan Dev Ji — from manuscripts, oral traditions, and the memories of devotional communities. This gathering was itself a monumental scholarly and devotional act. Giani Gurdit Singh treats it as such, analyzing it with the same rigor he applies to the Gurus' own compositions. (Gurdit Singh, Itihas Sri Guru Granth Sahib, vol. 2, 1989, 223–289.)

The diversity of the ਭਗਤ tradition also raises questions of authenticity. Giani Gurdit Singh notes that not all compositions attributed to figures such as Kabir in other manuscript traditions appear in the Granth, and some compositions in the Granth differ from those in non-Sikh sources. He argues this reflects an editorial process in which compositions were selected and in some cases textually refined to ensure theological consistency with ਗੁਰਮਤਿ. This claim has generated scholarly debate, particularly with Winand Callewaert and others who have studied the broader Kabir tradition. (Callewaert and Friedlander, The Life and Works of Raidas, 1992, 11–34.)

Giani Gurdit Singh's Criteria for Inclusion

The central question Giani Gurdit Singh poses about the ਭਗਤ ਬਾਣੀ is: What governed the selection? His answer is theological and not merely devotional. He argues that the criterion for inclusion was alignment with the foundational Sikh theological principle of ਏਕ ਓਅੰਕਾਰ — the affirmation of one formless, sovereign, all-pervading Creator. Compositions that, regardless of their cultural or religious origin, expressed this understanding of the Divine were candidates for inclusion. Compositions that endorsed polytheism, idol worship, caste hierarchy, or ritual formalism — even if composed by otherwise revered figures — were excluded.

This framework allows Giani Gurdit Singh to explain both what is in the Granth and what is not. For instance, some devotional poetry of the ਭਕਤੀ movement celebrates specific Hindu deities in their individual forms. Such compositions do not appear in the Granth, not because of cultural exclusion but because of theological incoherence with ਗੁਰਮਤਿ. Conversely, Kabir's vigorous attacks on both Hindu ritualism and Muslim formalism fit naturally within the Granth's own critique of empty religiosity. (Pashaura Singh, The Guru Granth Sahib, 2000, 155–181.)

Giani Gurdit Singh further argues that the inclusion of the ਭਗਤ is itself a theological statement: that the Divine communicates through those who genuinely seek, regardless of their social location, caste, or religious label. This is not syncretism — the Granth does not treat all religions as equally valid paths — but it is a principled recognition that the Divine is not the exclusive property of any one community. This nuance is important, and Giani Gurdit Singh takes care to distinguish ਗੁਰਮਤਿ's position from both exclusivism and undifferentiated universalism. (Mandair, Sikhism: A Guide for the Perplexed, 2013, 89–107.)

Theological Coherence Across Difference

One of Giani Gurdit Singh's most important contributions regarding the ਭਗਤ ਬਾਣੀ is his demonstration that the diverse voices in the Granth are not in theological tension with one another but in profound consonance when read through the lens of ਗੁਰਮਤਿ. A composition by Sheikh Farid on the shortness of human life and the nearness of death, and a composition by Guru Nanak Dev Ji on the same theme, are not parallel texts from different traditions that happen to be placed together. They are, in Giani Gurdit Singh's reading, expressions of the same ਸੱਚ — truth — reaching the same realization through different life experiences.

This argument about theological coherence depends on careful textual analysis. Giani Gurdit Singh examines recurring themes — ਨਿਰਗੁਣ devotion, the critique of ਹਉਮੈ, the call to ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ, the grief of separation from the Divine — across the compositions of different ਭਗਤ and Gurus, showing that these themes are treated consistently. The differences in language, imagery, and cultural reference do not constitute differences in theology. This is a sophisticated literary-theological argument that requires both philological skill and doctrinal clarity — precisely the combination that Giani Gurdit Singh brings to the text. (Gurdit Singh, Itihas Sri Guru Granth Sahib, vol. 2, 1989, 301–345.)

Contemporary scholars such as Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh have explored the literary dimensions of this multi-vocal text, noting how the Granth creates a kind of sacred dialogue across time and tradition (Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, The Feminine Principle in the Sikh Vision of the Transcendent, 1993, 67–89). Giani Gurdit Singh's structural and historical work provides the scaffolding on which such literary analysis rests.

Key Terms

  • ਭਗਤ ਬਾਣੀ — The compositions of the fifteen non-Guru devotional poets included in ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ.
  • ਏਕ ਓਅੰਕਾਰ — The foundational affirmation of One Creator; Giani Gurdit Singh's proposed criterion for inclusion of ਭਗਤ ਬਾਣੀ.
  • ਨਿਰਗੁਣ — The formless, attributeless Divine; the dominant theological register of most ਭਗਤ poetry in the Granth.
  • ਭਕਤੀ — The broader South Asian devotional movement from which many ਭਗਤ emerged; related to but distinct from ਗੁਰਮਤਿ.
  • ਸਾਂਝੀਵਾਲਤਾ — Shared spiritual kinship across social and religious difference; one theological implication of the ਭਗਤ ਬਾਣੀ's inclusion.
  • ਸੱਚ — Truth; the shared object of realization across all voices in the Granth.

Discussion Questions

  1. Giani Gurdit Singh argues that the criterion for including ਭਗਤ ਬਾਣੀ was theological alignment with ਏਕ ਓਅੰਕਾਰ. Is this a convincing explanation? What evidence would you need to confirm or challenge it?
  2. How should we understand the relationship between the ਭਕਤੀ movement broadly and ਗੁਰਮਤਿ specifically? Is the Granth's inclusion of ਭਗਤ ਬਾਣੀ an endorsement of ਭਕਤੀ, or something more nuanced?
  3. Giani Gurdit Singh claims that some ਭਗਤ compositions were editorially refined before inclusion. Does this editorial process raise questions about authenticity, or does it reflect a legitimate theological judgment? How do you think about authorship in this context?
  4. What does the inclusion of a cobbler (Ravidas), a cloth-printer (Namdev), and a Muslim Sufi (Farid) in scripture say about the Sikh understanding of spiritual authority? How does this challenge or confirm social hierarchies of the period?

Further Reading

  • Pashaura Singh — The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority (2000)
  • Winand Callewaert and Peter Friedlander — The Life and Works of Raidas (1992)
  • Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh — The Feminine Principle in the Sikh Vision of the Transcendent (1993)

Key Takeaways

  • The fifteen ਭਗਤ in ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ represent a deliberately curated range of devotional voices drawn from Hindu, Muslim, and low-caste backgrounds.
  • Giani Gurdit Singh argues the criterion for inclusion was theological alignment with ਏਕ ਓਅੰਕਾਰ, not cultural or communal affiliation.
  • The ਭਗਤ ਬਾਣੀ demonstrates a principle of ਸਾਂਝੀਵਾਲਤਾ — shared spiritual kinship — that is not syncretism but principled theological universalism.
  • Giani Gurdit Singh's structural analysis shows that the diverse voices of the Granth are in theological consonance, not contradiction — a finding with major implications for Sikh inter-religious thought.

Works Cited

Callewaert, Winand M., and Peter G. Friedlander. The Life and Works of Raidas. New Delhi: Manohar, 1992.

Gurdit Singh, Giani. Itihas Sri Guru Granth Sahib. Vol. 2. Chandigarh: Singh Brothers, 1989.

McLeod, W.H. Guru Nanak and the Sikh Religion. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1968.

Mandair, Arvind-Pal Singh. Sikhism: A Guide for the Perplexed. London: Bloomsbury, 2013.

Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh. The Feminine Principle in the Sikh Vision of the Transcendent. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1993.

Pashaura Singh. The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2000.

Homework

Choose one ਭਗਤ poet whose work appears in ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ — for example, Kabir, Ravidas, Namdev, or Sheikh Farid. Read about that poet's historical life and social context using one reliable academic source (not Wikipedia alone). Then write a 400-word reflection: How does knowing who this person was — their caste, religion, historical moment — deepen your understanding of why their voice appears in the Granth alongside the Sikh Gurus? Use at least one concept from this lesson (such as ਏਕ ਓਅੰਕਾਰ or ਸਾਂਝੀਵਾਲਤਾ) to frame your answer.

lessons.title: Lesson 9: The Vars and Swaiyas — Heroic and Panegyric Forms in the Granth
lessons.html:
Table of Contents

  1. Introduction
  2. What Is a ਵਾਰ? The Heroic Ballad in Punjabi Literary Tradition
  3. Giani Gurdit Singh's Analysis of the Granth's ਵਾਰਾਂ
  4. The ਸਵੱਯੇ and Panegyric Theology
  5. Key Terms
  6. Discussion Questions
  7. Further Reading
  8. Key Takeaways
  9. Works Cited
Term (Unicode)Academic Context
ਵਾਰA heroic ballad form in Punjabi literary tradition; reoriented in the Granth toward devotional heroism.
ਸਵੱਯਾA panegyric verse form used in the Granth to praise the Guru's spiritual majesty.
ਪਉੜੀA stanza unit within a ਵਾਰ; the primary building block of this poetic form in Gurbani.
ਸਲੋਕA couplet or short verse, often interspersed between ਪਉੜੀ stanzas in the Granth's ਵਾਰਾਂ.
ਭੱਟCourt bards; the ਭੱਟ poets whose ਸਵੱਯੇ appear in the Granth praising the Guru lineage.
ਜੋਧਾWarrior-hero; the figure celebrated in traditional ਵਾਰ poetry, reinterpreted in Gurbani as the spiritual warrior.

Introduction

Among the less-studied structural features of ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ are the ਵਾਰਾਂ — heroic ballads — and the ਸਵੱਯੇ — panegyric verses — that appear across the text. These forms do not fit the template of quiet devotional prayer. They draw on a pre-existing tradition of Punjabi oral poetry that celebrated kings, warriors, and battles. Yet in the Granth, these same forms are directed entirely toward the praise of the Divine and the Guru. This reorientation is one of the most subtle and significant literary operations in the history of Sikh scripture, and Giani Gurdit Singh analyzed it with careful attention to both literary form and theological function.

This lesson examines the ਵਾਰਾਂ and ਸਵੱਯੇ as literary and theological forms, drawing on Giani Gurdit Singh's scholarship to understand why the Gurus chose these forms and what they communicated to their original audiences. We also examine the ਭੱਟ poets — court bards who composed ਸਵੱਯੇ in praise of the Guru lineage — and their unique place in the Granth.

Understanding these forms requires some familiarity with Punjabi literary history, which will be provided in this lesson. The goal is not literary analysis for its own sake but a deeper understanding of how ਗੁਰਮਤਿ engaged and transformed the cultural world in which it arose. (Christopher Shackle and Arvind Mandair, Teachings of the Sikh Gurus, 2005, xxiii–xlviii.)

What Is a ਵਾਰ? The Heroic Ballad in Punjabi Literary Tradition

The ਵਾਰ is a form of Punjabi oral poetry with roots in the warrior culture of medieval Punjab. Its classical function was to celebrate the deeds of a hero or king — typically a military leader — in a manner designed to inspire courage, loyalty, and communal pride. A ਵਾਰ is structured around ਪਉੜੀ stanzas, with ਸਲੋਕ couplets often interspersed to provide moral or reflective commentary on the main narrative. The form was sung at courts and before battles, functioning as both entertainment and ideological reinforcement.

The best-known pre-Sikh ਵਾਰ in Punjabi literature is the Var of Satta and Balwand tradition and the ਵਾਰਾਂ associated with figures such as Alam and Damodar. These works celebrated the physical valor of their subjects in language that was vivid, martial, and socially embedded in a caste hierarchy that valued the warrior class above all others. The ਵਾਰ was, in other words, a form deeply tied to social and political power as conventionally understood. (Shackle and Mandair, Teachings of the Sikh Gurus, 2005, xxxv–xl.)

Giani Gurdit Singh's analysis begins by carefully documenting this literary background. He does so because the theological significance of what the Gurus did with the ਵਾਰ form only becomes visible when you understand what the form normally did. By choosing to cast devotional theology in the mold of the heroic ballad, the Gurus were making a claim: the real ਜੋਧਾ — the real warrior-hero — is not the one who conquers kingdoms but the one who conquers ਹਉਮੈ. (Gurdit Singh, Itihas Sri Guru Granth Sahib, vol. 4, 1992, 78–103.)

Giani Gurdit Singh's Analysis of the Granth's ਵਾਰਾਂ

There are twenty-two ਵਾਰਾਂ in ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ. Giani Gurdit Singh's analysis traces their authorship (primarily Guru Nanak Dev Ji, Guru Amar Das Ji, and Guru Ram Das Ji, with Guru Arjan Dev Ji contributing the largest number), their melodic settings, and the instructions embedded in the Granth about which traditional ਵਾਰ tunes should be used to sing them. These tune references — such as the instruction to sing a particular ਵਾਰ to the tune of a well-known folk or heroic ballad — are significant evidence that the Gurus expected their congregations to recognize the form and feel its resonances.

Giani Gurdit Singh examines in particular the instruction-lines at the beginning of several ਵਾਰਾਂ that name pre-existing folk tunes. He argues that this was a deliberate pedagogical strategy: by using familiar melodies, the Gurus made their theological content immediately accessible to audiences steeped in the oral tradition, while simultaneously reorienting the emotional charge of those melodies from earthly heroism to divine devotion. This is a sophisticated example of what we might call theological translation — using existing cultural forms to carry new meaning. (Gurdit Singh, Itihas Sri Guru Granth Sahib, vol. 4, 1992, 120–167.)

The content of the ਵਾਰਾਂ in the Granth consistently celebrates not military valor but the qualities of the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ — the Guru-oriented person. Courage in this context means the courage to face death and the dissolution of ego without fear. The battlefield is internal. The enemy is ਹਉਮੈ. The victory is ਮੁਕਤੀ — liberation. Giani Gurdit Singh's structural analysis shows how this theological content is not imposed on the form from outside but emerges naturally from the internal logic of the ਵਾਰ structure itself when the hero is redefined. (Pashaura Singh, The Guru Granth Sahib, 2000, 201–228.)

The ਸਵੱਯੇ and Panegyric Theology

The ਸਵੱਯੇ in ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ are primarily composed by the ਭੱਟ poets — a group of eleven court bards who attached themselves to the Sikh Gurus and composed verses in praise of the Guru lineage. Their compositions appear in a dedicated section of the Granth (ਅੰਗ 1389–1409) and represent a fascinating integration of the classical panegyric tradition into the Sikh textual canon. Giani Gurdit Singh's scholarship on the ਭੱਟ ਸਵੱਯੇ is particularly valuable because this section of the Granth has historically received less scholarly attention than the main ਰਾਗ-organized body of the text.

Giani Gurdit Singh identifies the ਭੱਟ poets by name and traces what can be known of their backgrounds. He argues that their inclusion in the Granth is not a concession to court convention but a theological statement about the nature of the Guru. In the ਭੱਟ ਸਵੱਯੇ, the Guru is praised not for military conquest but for spiritual illumination — for dispelling the darkness of ਅਗਿਆਨ (ignorance) and revealing the path of ਸੱਚ. This reorientation of the panegyric form is consistent with what the Gurus did with the ਵਾਰ form. (Gurdit Singh, Itihas Sri Guru Granth Sahib, vol. 4, 1992, 189–234.)

Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh has noted that the ਭੱਟ ਸਵੱਯੇ use highly ornate Sanskrit-influenced language that contrasts with the vernacular directness of much of the rest of the Granth, suggesting that the Gurus intentionally included a range of literary registers to reach different audiences (Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, The Name of My Beloved: Verses of the Sikh Gurus, 1995, 34–56). Giani Gurdit Singh's structural analysis confirms this diversity while insisting on the underlying theological unity that holds it together.

Key Terms

  • ਵਾਰ — Heroic ballad form; in the Granth, reoriented toward celebrating spiritual courage and the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ.
  • ਪਉੜੀ — The stanza unit of a ਵਾਰ; each ਪਉੜੀ advances the theological argument of the composition.
  • ਸਵੱਯਾ — Panegyric verse form; in the Granth, used to praise the Guru's spiritual illumination rather than worldly power.
  • ਭੱਟ — Court bards whose ਸਵੱਯੇ praising the Guru lineage appear in ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ at ਅੰਗ 1389–1409.
  • ਗੁਰਮੁਖ — The Guru-oriented person; the spiritual hero celebrated in the Granth's ਵਾਰਾਂ.
  • ਮੁਕਤੀ — Liberation; the ultimate victory celebrated in the theological reorientation of heroic forms.

Discussion Questions

  1. The Gurus chose the ਵਾਰ — a form originally associated with military culture and caste hierarchy — to communicate devotional theology. What does this choice suggest about how ਗੁਰਮਤਿ engages with existing culture rather than rejecting it?
  2. Giani Gurdit Singh argues that the ਭੱਟ ਸਵੱਯੇ represent a theological statement, not just a literary convention. Do you agree? What would it mean to include court panegyric in scripture?
  3. The instruction-lines at the beginning of certain ਵਾਰਾਂ reference pre-existing folk tunes. What does this suggest about the relationship between oral tradition and the written canon in Sikh religious life?
  4. How does redefining the ਜੋਧਾ (warrior-hero) as one who conquers ਹਉਮੈ rather than kingdoms challenge the social hierarchies of medieval Punjab? Is this challenge explicit or implicit in the text?

Further Reading

  • Christopher Shackle and Arvind Mandair — Teachings of the Sikh Gurus: Selections from the Sikh Scriptures (2005)
  • Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh — The Name of My Beloved: Verses of the Sikh Gurus (1995)
  • Gurdit Singh, Giani — Itihas Sri Guru Granth Sahib, Vol. 4 (1992)

Key Takeaways

  • The twenty-two ਵਾਰਾਂ of the Granth draw on the classical Punjabi heroic ballad tradition but reorient its celebration from military valor to spiritual courage and ਗੁਰਮੁਖ identity.
  • Giani Gurdit Singh's analysis shows that the Gurus used existing folk tune references in ਵਾਰਾਂ as a deliberate pedagogical strategy to make theological content accessible to oral-culture audiences.
  • The ਭੱਟ ਸਵੱਯੇ (ਅੰਗ 1389–1409) represent the integration of court panegyric into scripture, with the Guru praised for spiritual illumination rather than worldly power.
  • Across both ਵਾਰਾਂ and ਸਵੱਯੇ, Giani Gurdit Singh demonstrates that the Granth consistently redirects conventional social forms toward the single theological end of ਮੁਕਤੀ.

Works Cited

Gurdit Singh, Giani. Itihas Sri Guru Granth Sahib. Vol. 4. Chandigarh: Singh Brothers, 1992.

Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh. The Name of My Beloved: Verses of the Sikh Gurus. San Francisco: HarperSanFrancisco, 1995.

Pashaura Singh. The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2000.

Shackle, Christopher, and Arvind Mandair. Teachings of the Sikh Gurus: Selections from the Sikh Scriptures. London: Routledge, 2005.

Homework

The ਵਾਰ form was originally used to celebrate military heroes. In 350 words, explore what happens theologically when this same form is used to celebrate the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ — the spiritually oriented person. What qualities does a ਗੁਰਮੁਖ need that parallel the qualities of a warrior, and where does the analogy break down? Draw directly on what you have learned in this lesson about Giani Gurdit Singh's analysis of the ਵਾਰਾਂ. You may also read the opening ਪਉੜੀਆਂ of the ਵਾਰ of Asa (ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ, ਅੰਗ 462–475) to ground your reflection in the text.

lessons.title: Lesson 10: Manuscript Traditions and the Question of Textual Authority
lessons.html:
Table of Contents

  1. Introduction
  2. The Kartarpuri Bir and the Problem of Manuscript Authority
  3. Giani Gurdit Singh's Engagement with the Manuscript Evidence
  4. Textual Authority and Living Scripture
  5. Key Terms
  6. Discussion Questions
  7. Further Reading
  8. Key Takeaways
  9. Works Cited
Term (Unicode)Academic Context
ਬੀੜA bound manuscript volume of ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ; the term used for manuscript copies.
ਕਾਰਤਾਰਪੁਰੀ ਬੀੜThe manuscript associated with Kartarpur, claimed by some to be the original compilation of Guru Arjan Dev Ji.
ਦਮਦਮਾ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਬੀੜThe recension associated with Guru Gobind Singh Ji's final editing of the Granth at Damdama Sahib.
ਤੁਕA line or verse unit within a ਸ਼ਬਦ; the basic textual unit for manuscript comparison.
ਪਾਠA reading or recitation; in textual scholarship, a variant reading in a manuscript.
ਗੁਟਕਾA small compilation of selected Gurbani texts; distinct from the complete ਬੀੜ.

Introduction

The question of which manuscript of ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ represents the most authoritative text is among the most contested issues in Sikh Studies. Unlike many religious traditions where the original manuscript has been lost and scholars must reconstruct the text from later copies, Sikhism has preserved what are claimed to be very early manuscripts — most notably the ਕਾਰਤਾਰਪੁਰੀ ਬੀੜ and the ਦਮਦਮਾ ਸਾਹਿਬ recension. Yet even here, the question of authority is not simple, because different manuscripts contain variant readings, and different scholarly and religious communities have attached different weight to different sources.

Giani Gurdit Singh's scholarship on this question is both historically rigorous and theologically sensitive. He is deeply aware that for Sikhs, questions about the Granth's text are not merely academic — they touch the heart of faith and community identity. His approach is to apply the tools of historical manuscript scholarship while remaining accountable to the tradition's own understanding of the Granth as the living, present Guru. This lesson examines how he navigates this challenge. (Pashaura Singh, The Guru Granth Sahib, 2000, 37–68.)

The stakes of this work extend beyond academia. Decisions about the authoritative text have implications for how the Granth is printed, recited, and interpreted by Sikhs worldwide. Giani Gurdit Singh's manuscript scholarship therefore carries practical consequences that make it one of the most socially significant dimensions of his scholarly legacy. (Gurdit Singh, Itihas Sri Guru Granth Sahib, vol. 1, 1988, 1–45.)

The Kartarpuri Bir and the Problem of Manuscript Authority

The ਕਾਰਤਾਰਪੁਰੀ ਬੀੜ is a manuscript held by the Sodhi family at Kartarpur (near Jalandhar) and claimed to be the original compilation (ਆਦਿ ਬੀੜ) prepared under Guru Arjan Dev Ji's supervision and written by Bhai Gurdas Ji. If this claim were confirmed, the Kartarpuri manuscript would be the closest thing Sikh scholarship possesses to a foundational autograph text. However, the manuscript's status has been disputed on multiple grounds — questions about its completeness, the reliability of its custodial chain, and its relationship to the ਦਮਦਮਾ ਸਾਹਿਬ recension prepared by Guru Gobind Singh Ji, which added the compositions of Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji and became the standard text.

Giani Gurdit Singh's engagement with this problem is detailed and careful. He reviews the historical evidence for the Kartarpuri manuscript's provenance — including references in Sikh historical literature and the physical characteristics of the manuscript itself — and concludes that while the manuscript is certainly ancient and of great historical significance, questions remain about whether it is precisely the ਆਦਿ ਬੀੜ in the form it left Guru Arjan Dev Ji's hands. He is also attentive to the political dimensions of manuscript custody: the Sodhi family's control of the manuscript has at various points been entangled with religious authority claims that complicate purely historical assessment. (Gurdit Singh, Itihas Sri Guru Granth Sahib, vol. 1, 1988, 67–134.)

W.H. McLeod's work on Sikh manuscripts raised similar questions from a Western academic perspective, generating significant controversy within the Sikh community (McLeod, The Sikhs: History, Religion and Society, 1989, 97–115). Giani Gurdit Singh's work is distinctive in that it comes from within the tradition — he applies rigorous historical methods while maintaining a fundamentally ਗੁਰਮਤਿ framework of interpretation. This insider-scholar position gives his conclusions a different kind of authority within Sikh communities than external academic assessments typically carry.

Giani Gurdit Singh's Engagement with the Manuscript Evidence

Beyond the ਕਾਰਤਾਰਪੁਰੀ ਬੀੜ, Giani Gurdit Singh examined a range of early manuscript copies of the Granth, including manuscripts held at the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (SGPC) archives, at the Guru Nanak Dev University library, and in private collections. His comparative analysis identified variant readings — differences in specific ਤੁਕਾਂ (verse lines) between manuscript traditions — and assessed their significance. His conclusion is that the standard printed text, authorized by the SGPC and based on the ਦਮਦਮਾ ਸਾਹਿਬ recension, represents a reliable and authoritative text, but that manuscript study remains valuable for illuminating the history of the Granth's compilation and early transmission.

This is an important scholarly position because it does two things simultaneously. First, it validates the community's confidence in the standard printed text rather than using manuscript evidence to destabilize it. Second, it insists that manuscript study is not a threat to faith but an enrichment of understanding — that knowing how the text was compiled and transmitted deepens rather than undermines its spiritual authority. This dual move is characteristic of Giani Gurdit Singh's approach throughout his work: rigorous scholarship in service of ਗੁਰਮਤਿ, not in opposition to it. (Gurdit Singh, Itihas Sri Guru Granth Sahib, vol. 1, 1988, 178–245.)

Scholars such as Gurinder Singh Mann have further developed manuscript studies in Sikh scholarship, building on the foundation Giani Gurdit Singh helped establish. Mann's The Making of Sikh Scripture (2001) represents the most comprehensive English-language treatment of the manuscript evidence and can be read as a complement to Giani Gurdit Singh's work, filling out the technical manuscript details with additional comparative material not available to Giani Gurdit Singh when he was writing. (Mann, The Making of Sikh Scripture, 2001, 1–42.)

Textual Authority and Living Scripture

Perhaps the most theologically significant aspect of Giani Gurdit Singh's approach to manuscript evidence is his insistence that questions of textual authority must be understood within the Sikh theological framework of the Granth as living, present Guru. For Sikhs, ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ is not a historical document about a Guru who lived in the past. It is the eternal Guru, present and active in the life of the ਪੰਥ. This means that textual authority is not purely a matter of historical proximity to an original autograph — it is also a matter of the Granth's ongoing role as spiritual guide for the community.

This theological framework has methodological implications. Giani Gurdit Singh does not treat the Granth as a text that can be reconstructed to a hypothetical original through manuscript comparison alone. The tradition itself — the ਸੰਗਤ's centuries of engagement with the text, the Gurmatā decisions of the Panth, the authority of the SGPC in standardizing the printed text — is part of how the Granth's authority is constituted and maintained. Historical scholarship informs this process but does not replace it. (Mandair, Religion and the Specter of the West, 2009, 315–340.)

This position will be unfamiliar to students trained in the secular Western model of textual criticism, where the goal is to recover a hypothetical original through comparison of variants, with tradition treated as a secondary (and potentially corrupting) influence on the text. Giani Gurdit Singh's model is different: tradition and text are mutually constituting, and the scholar's job is to illuminate their relationship, not to dissolve it. This is one of the most intellectually significant aspects of his contribution to Sikh Studies — it models a form of scholarship that is simultaneously rigorous and confessionally located.

Key Terms

  • ਬੀੜ — A bound manuscript copy of ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ; the physical vehicle of textual transmission.
  • ਕਾਰਤਾਰਪੁਰੀ ਬੀੜ — The manuscript held at Kartarpur, claimed to be the ਆਦਿ ਬੀੜ prepared under Guru Arjan Dev Ji.
  • ਪਾਠ ਭੇਦ — Textual variant; a difference in wording between manuscript traditions.
  • ਆਦਿ ਬੀੜ — The original compilation; the manuscript prepared under Guru Arjan Dev Ji at Ramsar.
  • ਦਮਦਮਾ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਬੀੜ — The final recension of the Granth, associated with Guru Gobind Singh Ji, which is the basis for the standard printed text today.
  • ਪੰਥ — The Sikh community as a whole; the body whose ongoing engagement with the Granth constitutes part of its living authority.

Discussion Questions

  1. Giani Gurdit Singh argues that manuscript evidence should inform but not replace the tradition's own understanding of the Granth's authority. Is this a defensible scholarly position, or does it compromise historical rigor? What are the strengths and weaknesses of his approach?
  2. The ਕਾਰਤਾਰਪੁਰੀ ਬੀੜ has been at the center of religious and political controversy. How should scholars approach texts whose custody is entangled with community authority claims?
  3. Western textual criticism aims to recover a hypothetical original text through manuscript comparison. Giani Gurdit Singh's model is different. What does this difference reveal about the assumptions embedded in Western philology?
  4. If future manuscript evidence were to show that the standard printed text differs in some places from the earliest manuscripts, how should the Sikh community respond? What principles should guide that response?

Further Reading

  • Gurinder Singh Mann — The Making of Sikh Scripture (2001)
  • Pashaura Singh — The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority (2000)
  • W.H. McLeod — The Sikhs: History, Religion and Society (1989)

Key Takeaways

  • The question of manuscript authority in Sikh scripture is complex: multiple early manuscripts exist, and Giani Gurdit Singh assessed them with historical rigor while maintaining a ਗੁਰਮਤਿ theological framework.
  • The ਕਾਰਤਾਰਪੁਰੀ ਬੀੜ is historically significant but its status as the definitive ਆਦਿ ਬੀੜ remains a matter of ongoing scholarly scrutiny.
  • Giani Gurdit Singh's model of textual authority integrates historical scholarship with the tradition's own understanding of the Granth as living Guru — a position that challenges assumptions embedded in Western secular philology.
  • Gurinder Singh Mann's subsequent manuscript studies build on and extend Giani Gurdit Singh's foundational work, making comparative reading of both scholars essential for this topic.

Works Cited

Gurdit Singh, Giani. Itihas Sri Guru Granth Sahib. Vol. 1. Chandigarh: Singh Brothers, 1988.

Mann, Gurinder Singh. The Making of Sikh Scripture. New York: Oxford University Press, 2001.

Mandair, Arvind-Pal Singh. Religion and the Specter of the West: Sikhism, India, Postcoloniality, and the Politics of Translation. New York: Columbia University Press, 2009.

McLeod, W.H. The Sikhs: History, Religion and Society. New York: Columbia University Press, 1989.

Pashaura Singh. The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2000.

Homework

Find and read the introductory chapter or preface of Gurinder Singh Mann's The Making of Sikh Scripture (2001) — available in most university libraries and through some online databases. Write a 400-word comparison between Mann's approach to manuscript evidence and what you have learned about Giani Gurdit Singh's approach in this lesson. Where do they agree, where do they differ, and what does each scholar's approach reveal about his relationship to the Sikh tradition? Focus particularly on the question of how each scholar handles the relationship between textual history and living religious authority.

lessons.title: Lesson 11: The Granth in Comparative Perspective — Canon, Scripture, and Authority in World Religions
lessons.html:
Table of Contents

  1. Introduction
  2. What Makes a Text Scripture? Comparative Frameworks
  3. The Granth Among the Scriptures of the World
  4. Giani Gurdit Singh's Contribution to a Distinctly Sikh Theory of Scripture
  5. Key Terms
  6. Discussion Questions
  7. Further Reading
  8. Key Takeaways
  9. Works Cited
Term (Unicode)Academic Context
ਕੈਨਨThe formally authorized body of sacred texts in a religious tradition; from Greek kanon (rule, standard).
ਸ਼ਬਦ ਗੁਰੂThe Word as Guru; the Sikh theological understanding of the Granth as the living, present Guru.
ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖThe Timeless Being; the Sikh name for the ultimate Divine reality that the Granth embodies.
ਗੁਰਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿBy the Guru's grace; the concept that access to divine truth is through grace rather than human effort alone.
ਸੱਚ ਖੰਡThe Realm of Truth; the highest spiritual state, associated with the Granth's ultimate theological horizon.
ਪੰਥThe Sikh community; the body through which the Granth's authority is received and enacted.

Introduction

Situating ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ within the comparative study of world scriptures reveals both what it shares with other sacred canons and what makes it distinctively and irreducibly Sikh. The academic study of scripture — sometimes called scriptural studies or canon studies — has developed a range of analytical frameworks over the past century, drawing on scholars such as Wilfred Cantwell Smith, Miriam Levering, and William Graham. These frameworks help us ask rigorous questions about what kind of object a scripture is, how it functions in a community, and what kind of authority it exercises.

Giani Gurdit Singh did not write comparative religion as such, but his work on the Granth's history and structure implicitly develops a theory of Sikh scripture that stands in productive conversation with these broader frameworks. This lesson draws out that implicit theory, placing Giani Gurdit Singh's conclusions in dialogue with comparative scriptural studies to illuminate what is universal and what is particular about the Granth's claim to authority.

This comparative perspective is valuable for advanced students not because Sikh scripture needs external validation, but because comparison is a tool for sharpening understanding. When we see how the Granth's structure and authority differ from the Bible's, the Quran's, or the Vedas', we understand each more clearly. And when we see what is shared, we gain insight into the universal human experience of the sacred text. (Wilfred Cantwell Smith, What is Scripture? A Comparative Approach, 1993, 1–22.)

What Makes a Text Scripture? Comparative Frameworks

Wilfred Cantwell Smith, in his influential study, argued that scripture is not a property of texts but a relationship between texts and communities. A text becomes scripture through the act of a community treating it as scripture — reading it in worship, making decisions by it, building identity around it. This means that the authority of scripture is not inherent in the physical object but constituted through communal practice. Scripture is, in Smith's formulation, a verb as much as a noun: it is something a community does with a text, not merely a type of text. (Smith, What is Scripture?, 1993, 18–22.)

This framework is illuminating for understanding ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ. From a Smith-influenced perspective, the Granth's authority is constituted through centuries of ਸੰਗਤ engagement — ਕੀਰਤਨ, ਪਾਠ, the practice of ਅਰਦਾਸ in the Granth's presence, the custom of taking ਹੁਕਮਨਾਮਾ (the daily divine directive by random opening). These practices do not merely express the Granth's authority; they constitute it in an ongoing, living way. Giani Gurdit Singh's historical work documenting how the Granth was compiled and transmitted is, in this light, a documentation of the early stages of this constituting process. (Mandair, Sikhism: A Guide for the Perplexed, 2013, 120–138.)

However, Sikh theology does not fully fit Smith's model, because ਗੁਰਮਤਿ insists that the Granth's authority is not merely communally conferred — it is ontologically grounded in the fact that the Granth is the embodiment of ਸ਼ਬਦ ਗੁਰੂ. The Granth does not become the Guru because the ਪੰਥ treats it as such; the ਪੰਥ treats it as such because it is the Guru. This theological claim exceeds what comparative religion frameworks typically accommodate, which is why Giani Gurdit Singh's work ultimately requires a distinctively Sikh framework of interpretation. (Pashaura Singh, The Guru Granth Sahib, 2000, 285–310.)

The Granth Among the Scriptures of the World

When we place ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ alongside other major world scriptures, several distinctive features emerge. Unlike the Bible, the Granth was compiled by a known human editor (Guru Arjan Dev Ji) in a historically documented process, and a second edition was completed by a known successor (Guru Gobind Singh Ji) at a known location (Damdama Sahib). This makes the Granth unusually transparent in its compilation history compared with scriptures whose editorial histories are obscure or disputed. Giani Gurdit Singh's historical work exploits this transparency, offering a detailed account of the compilation process that has no equivalent in, say, biblical or Quranic studies.

Unlike the Quran, whose authority in mainstream Muslim theology rests on its status as the unmediated speech of God transmitted through the Prophet, the Granth's authority in Sikh theology rests on the Gurus' realization of divine truth and their embodiment of that truth in words. The Granth is not a dictated revelation but a realized expression — the overflow of enlightened consciousness into language. This is a subtle but important distinction with significant implications for how the text is interpreted and how variant readings are evaluated. (Shackle and Mandair, Teachings of the Sikh Gurus, 2005, xlii–xlviii.)

The Granth's multi-vocality — its inclusion of fifteen ਭਗਤ alongside the six Gurus and the ਭੱਟ poets — is also unusual in comparative perspective. The Hebrew Bible is multi-authored, but its editorial process is largely invisible. The Granth's multi-authorship is not only visible but celebrated, making it one of the most theologically self-conscious canonical texts in world religious history. Giani Gurdit Singh's structural analysis of this multi-vocality — showing how diverse voices cohere around the theological center of ਏਕ ਓਅੰਕਾਰ — is one of his most important contributions to the comparative study of scripture. (Gurdit Singh, Itihas Sri Guru Granth Sahib, vol. 1, 1988, 245–290.)

Giani Gurdit Singh's Contribution to a Distinctly Sikh Theory of Scripture

Across the multiple volumes of Itihas Sri Guru Granth Sahib, Giani Gurdit Singh develops — often implicitly — a distinctly Sikh theory of what the Granth is and how it should be studied. This theory has several key elements. First, the Granth is not a historical document to be read behind for a more original tradition; it is itself the primary theological source. Second, the Granth's structure — its raag organization, its arrangement of voices, its inclusion of ਭਗਤ ਬਾਣੀ — is not incidental but theologically deliberate, and understanding the structure is essential to understanding the theology. Third, historical scholarship and devotional practice are not in tension but are mutually enriching ways of engaging the same reality.

This theory challenges both the secular Western academic tendency to treat the Granth as a historical artifact whose meaning must be reconstructed through critical methods, and the devotionalist tendency to treat the Granth as so sacred that historical questions about it are inappropriate. Giani Gurdit Singh stakes out a third position: that the Granth can bear historical scrutiny precisely because its authority is not historical but ontological — it rests on what it is (ਸ਼ਬਦ ਗੁਰੂ), not merely on when it was compiled or by whom. (Mandair, Religion and the Specter of the West, 2009, 356–378.)

This position has been influential in shaping a generation of Sikh scholars who have sought to combine academic rigor with theological integrity. Scholars such as Pashaura Singh, Gurinder Singh Mann, and Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh — all of whom engage in historical and textual scholarship — operate in an intellectual space that Giani Gurdit Singh helped to open. His contribution is not only the specific historical findings of his multi-volume study but the methodological model it demonstrates: that to truly honor the Granth is to know it as fully as possible, including historically. (Pashaura Singh, The Guru Granth Sahib, 2000, 311–335.)

Key Terms

  • ਸ਼ਬਦ ਗੁਰੂ — The Word as Guru; the foundational Sikh theological claim about the Granth's nature and authority.
  • ਹੁਕਮਨਾਮਾ — The divine directive received by randomly opening the Granth; a key liturgical practice constituting the Granth's living authority.
  • ਕੈਨਨ — The formally authorized body of scripture; in Sikh context, constituted by the SGPC-standardized text based on the ਦਮਦਮਾ ਸਾਹਿਬ recension.
  • ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖਤ — The Throne of the Timeless; the highest seat of Sikh temporal authority, closely associated with decisions about the Granth's canonical status.
  • ਪਾਠ — The act of reading or reciting the Granth; a foundational practice through which the community constitutes the Granth's living authority.
  • ਗੁਰਮਤਿ — The Guru's teaching; the philosophical and ethical framework within which the Granth's authority is understood and exercised.

Discussion Questions

  1. Wilfred Cantwell Smith argues that scripture is constituted by communal practice rather than being inherent in the text. How does this framework illuminate and fail to account for the Sikh understanding of the Granth as ਸ਼ਬਦ ਗੁਰੂ?
  2. The Granth's multi-vocality — its inclusion of ਭਗਤ alongside Gurus — is unusual in comparative perspective. What does this feature suggest about the Sikh understanding of revelation, spiritual authority, and community?
  3. Giani Gurdit Singh argues that historical scholarship and devotional practice are mutually enriching. Can you identify any tensions between these two modes of engaging the Granth? How might those tensions be navigated?
  4. If you were designing a comparative religion curriculum that included ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ alongside the Bible, Quran, and Vedas, what unique features of the Granth would you most want students to understand? How does Giani Gurdit Singh's work help you articulate those features?

Further Reading

  • Wilfred Cantwell Smith — What is Scripture? A Comparative Approach (1993)
  • Arvind-Pal Singh Mandair — Religion and the Specter of the West: Sikhism, India, Postcoloniality, and the Politics of Translation (2009)
  • Christopher Shackle and Arvind Mandair — Teachings of the Sikh Gurus: Selections from the Sikh Scriptures (2005)

Key Takeaways

  • Wilfred Cantwell Smith's model — that scripture is constituted through communal practice — illuminates the ਸੰਗਤ's role in the Granth's authority but does not fully account for the Sikh theological claim of ਸ਼ਬਦ ਗੁਰੂ.
  • The Granth is unusual among world scriptures for its transparent compilation history, its deliberate multi-vocality, and its status as a living Guru rather than a record of a past revelation.
  • Giani Gurdit Singh implicitly develops a distinctly Sikh theory of scripture that integrates historical rigor with theological integrity — a model that has shaped a generation of Sikh scholars.
  • Comparative scriptural studies is a tool for sharpening understanding of what is particular about each tradition, not a framework for reducing all scriptures to a common type.

Works Cited

Gurdit Singh, Giani. Itihas Sri Guru Granth Sahib. Vol. 1. Chandigarh: Singh Brothers, 1988.

Mandair, Arvind-Pal Singh. Religion and the Specter of the West: Sikhism, India, Postcoloniality, and the Politics of Translation. New York: Columbia University Press, 2009.

Mandair, Arvind-Pal Singh. Sikhism: A Guide for the Perplexed. London: Bloomsbury, 2013.

Pashaura Singh. The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2000.

Shackle, Christopher, and Arvind Mandair. Teachings of the Sikh Gurus: Selections from the Sikh Scriptures. London: Routledge, 2005.

Smith, Wilfred Cantwell. What is Scripture? A Comparative Approach. Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 1993.

Homework

Choose one other world scripture — the Bible (you may focus on a specific testament), the Quran, the Bhagavad Gita, or the Dhammapada — and write a 400-word comparison with ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ on one specific dimension: either its compilation history, its multi-vocality (or lack thereof), or the nature of the authority it claims. Draw on at least one concept from this lesson (such as ਸ਼ਬਦ ਗੁਰੂ or Smith's communal-constitution model) to frame your comparison. The goal is not to rank the scriptures but to understand each more clearly through the act of comparison.

lessons.title: Lesson 12: Continuing the Work — Unanswered Questions and the Future of Sikh Textual Studies
lessons.html:
Table of Contents

  1. Introduction
  2. Open Questions in the Scholarship of Giani Gurdit Singh
  3. Emerging Methodologies: Digital Humanities and Sikh Textual Studies
  4. The Responsibility of the Scholar in a Living Tradition
  5. Key Terms
  6. Discussion Questions
  7. Further Reading
  8. Key Takeaways
  9. Works Cited
Term (Unicode)Academic Context
ਪੰਥਕOf or belonging to the ਪੰਥ (Sikh community); describes scholarship conducted in service of the community.
ਵਿਦਵਾਨScholar; in Sikh tradition, one who combines learning with devotional practice and community accountability.
ਟੀਕਾCommentary or exegesis on Gurbani; a major genre of traditional Sikh scholarly writing.
ਗ੍ਰੰਥੀThe custodian/reader of ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ in a Gurdwara; a key figure in the living transmission of the text.
ਸਿੱਖ ਅਧਿਐਨSikh Studies as an academic discipline; increasingly established in universities worldwide.
ਡਿਜੀਟਲ ਹਿਊਮੈਨਿਟੀਜ਼Digital humanities; emerging methodologies that apply computational tools to textual and cultural analysis.

Introduction

Every major work of scholarship opens as many questions as it closes. Giani Gurdit Singh's Itihas Sri Guru Granth Sahib is no exception. Over the course of this course, we have traced his contributions to the history of the Granth's compilation, its internal structure, the raag framework, the ਭਗਤ ਬਾਣੀ, the manuscript tradition, and the question of textual authority. In this final lesson, we turn our attention forward: to the questions that remain open, the methodologies that are emerging, and the responsibilities that fall on the next generation of scholars who will continue this work.

This is not merely an academic exercise. ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ is the living Guru of a global community of approximately 25–30 million Sikhs. Decisions about how it is interpreted, printed, taught, and transmitted have direct consequences for real lives. The scholar who works on the Granth is not working in a vacuum; she or he is participating in a conversation that extends from Guru Arjan Dev Ji's study at Ramsar to Gurdwaras on six continents today. Understanding that context is part of what it means to engage this tradition seriously.

This lesson asks students not only to review what they have learned but to identify where their own intellectual and spiritual interests might lead them next. The greatest tribute to a scholar like Giani Gurdit Singh is not reverent passivity but active, rigorous continuation of the inquiry he modeled. (Pashaura Singh and Louis Fenech, The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies, 2014, 1–18.)

Open Questions in the Scholarship of Giani Gurdit Singh

Several significant questions remain open in the areas Giani Gurdit Singh pioneered. The first concerns the ਕਾਰਤਾਰਪੁਰੀ ਬੀੜ. Despite decades of discussion, there has been no comprehensive, independent, peer-reviewed palaeographic and codicological analysis of this manuscript conducted under scholarly conditions with full access to the physical document. Such an analysis — examining ink composition, vellum or paper dating, scribal hand comparison, and binding history — could significantly advance our understanding of when and how the manuscript was produced. This remains one of the most important open questions in the field. (Mann, The Making of Sikh Scripture, 2001, 97–112.)

A second open question concerns the ਭਗਤ ਬਾਣੀ's textual history prior to its inclusion in the Granth. Giani Gurdit Singh assessed the manuscript evidence available to him in the 1980s and 1990s. Since then, digital archives, the HumanDigi project, and institutions such as the Bhai Gurdas Library and the Sikh Reference Library have been expanding scholarly access to manuscript materials. A systematic comparison of all known manuscript variants of ਭਗਤ ਬਾਣੀ with the Granth text — using digital tools for large-scale textual comparison — could yield significant insights into the editorial process Guru Arjan Dev Ji employed. (Callewaert, The Millennium Kabir Vani, 2000, 1–28.)

Third, Giani Gurdit Singh's work focused primarily on the literary and historical dimensions of the Granth's structure. The question of how the raag framework has been interpreted and practiced across different Sikh regional traditions — Namdhari, Nirankari (historical), the diverse ਜਥੇ of traditional ਕੀਰਤਨੀਏ — remains underexplored. A comparative ethnomusicological study of how different ਕੀਰਤਨ traditions have engaged or departed from the raag framework would complement Giani Gurdit Singh's textual analysis with empirical data from living practice. (Gurnam Singh, A Critical Study of Kirtan in Sikhism, 1997, 145–190.)

Emerging Methodologies: Digital Humanities and Sikh Textual Studies

The most significant methodological development in Sikh textual studies since Giani Gurdit Singh's major publications is the emergence of digital humanities tools. Projects such as SikhiToTheMax, iGurbani, and Gurbani.org have made the complete text of ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ searchable in ways that were simply impossible for earlier scholars. These tools allow researchers to track patterns across the entire text — the distribution of key theological terms, the frequency of specific raags in different authorial voices, the structural parallels between compositions in different sections — with a speed and comprehensiveness that no individual scholar working with physical volumes could match.

However, digital tools have their own limitations and risks. The quality of digital Gurbani databases depends on the accuracy of the original transcriptions, which must themselves be checked against reliable printed editions. More fundamentally, computational analysis can identify patterns but cannot interpret their theological significance. A concordance can tell you how often a specific term appears in the Granth; it cannot tell you what the Guru meant by it, or how a ਸੰਗਤ should respond to it. Giani Gurdit Singh's combination of philological precision, historical knowledge, and ਗੁਰਮਤਿ theological grounding is not replaceable by computational methods — it is, rather, the essential interpretive framework within which computational findings must be embedded to have meaning. (Pashaura Singh and Fenech, The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies, 2014, 89–104.)

There is also emerging work on acoustic analysis of Gurbani — using computational audio tools to study how traditional ਕੀਰਤਨ renditions relate to the raag assignments in the Granth. Such analysis could provide empirical grounding for debates about raag-based ਕੀਰਤਨ that have previously been conducted primarily through theological argument and appeal to tradition. This kind of interdisciplinary work — combining ਗੁਰਮਤਿ theology, historical musicology, and digital analysis — represents the frontier of Sikh textual studies and is precisely the kind of research that Giani Gurdit Singh's foundational work makes possible.

The Responsibility of the Scholar in a Living Tradition

The final theme of this course is one that Giani Gurdit Singh modeled throughout his career: the responsibility of the ਵਿਦਵਾਨ — the scholar — who works within a living religious tradition. This responsibility has several dimensions. The first is intellectual honesty: the scholar must follow the evidence wherever it leads, even when the conclusions are uncomfortable for the community or for the scholar's own prior assumptions. Giani Gurdit Singh's willingness to engage seriously with challenging manuscript evidence, without dismissing it as anti-Sikh, exemplifies this commitment.

The second dimension is communal accountability. A scholar working on ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ is not a neutral observer. Whether she or he is Sikh or not, the work has consequences for a living community. This means that the scholar has responsibilities — to be transparent about methodological assumptions, to engage respectfully with community sensitivities, to ensure that findings are communicated in ways that build understanding rather than generate needless controversy. This does not mean self-censorship; it means being a mature participant in a conversation that extends beyond the academy. (Mandair, Religion and the Specter of the West, 2009, 392–410.)

The third dimension is spiritual. For Giani Gurdit Singh, scholarship and ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ were not separate activities. The same devotion that drew him to the Granth as a Sikh sustained the care and precision he brought to it as a scholar. This integration of spiritual practice and intellectual labor is one of the most important aspects of his legacy — and one of the most challenging to sustain in an academic environment that often treats the two as incompatible. Students who aspire to continue this work are invited to reflect not only on what methods they will use but on what kind of scholar they wish to become.

Key Terms

  • ਵਿਦਵਾਨ — Scholar; in Sikh tradition, one whose learning is grounded in devotional practice and community accountability.
  • ਟੀਕਾ — Commentary or exegesis; the traditional genre through which Sikh scholars have interpreted the Granth across generations.
  • ਪੰਥਕ ਸੇਵਾ — Service to the community; the framework within which Giani Gurdit Singh understood his scholarly work.
  • ਡਿਜੀਟਲ ਹਿਊਮੈਨਿਟੀਜ਼ — Digital humanities; emerging computational methodologies that can extend but not replace theologically grounded textual scholarship.
  • ਸਿੱਖ ਅਧਿਐਨ — Sikh Studies as an academic discipline, now represented in major universities across North America, Europe, and South Asia.
  • ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ — Remembrance of the Divine Name; the devotional practice that Giani Gurdit Singh maintained as the foundation of his scholarly life.

Discussion Questions

  1. Of the open questions identified in this lesson — the ਕਾਰਤਾਰਪੁਰੀ ਬੀੜ, the ਭਗਤ ਬਾਣੀ manuscript tradition, the ethnomusicology of ਕੀਰਤਨ — which do you find most compelling, and why? What would you need to know or learn to begin working on it?
  2. Digital humanities tools can identify patterns across the entire Granth in seconds. Does this change what it means to study the Granth? What can a computational tool do that a traditional scholar cannot, and what can a traditional scholar do that a computational tool cannot?
  3. Giani Gurdit Singh integrated scholarly rigor with devotional practice. Do you think this integration is possible in a contemporary academic environment? What structures or communities would help sustain it?
  4. What responsibilities do scholars who are not Sikh have when they study ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ? How should they engage with the living community whose scripture they are studying?

Further Reading

  • Pashaura Singh and Louis Fenech (eds.) — The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies (2014)
  • Gurinder Singh Mann — The Making of Sikh Scripture (2001)
  • Winand Callewaert — The Millennium Kabir Vani: A Collection of Pad-s Attributed to Kabir (2000)

Key Takeaways

  • Several significant questions opened by Giani Gurdit Singh's work remain unresolved, including a comprehensive palaeographic study of the ਕਾਰਤਾਰਪੁਰੀ ਬੀੜ and systematic digital comparison of ਭਗਤ ਬਾਣੀ manuscript traditions.
  • Digital humanities tools offer powerful new methods for Sikh textual studies but require theologically grounded interpretation — they extend, not replace, the kind of scholarship Giani Gurdit Singh modeled.
  • The scholar working on ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ carries responsibilities to intellectual honesty, communal accountability, and — for those within the tradition — spiritual integrity.
  • The greatest tribute to Giani Gurdit Singh is not reverent citation but active, rigorous continuation of the inquiry he modeled: knowing the Granth as fully as possible, in service of the ਪੰਥ and in devotion to ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ.

Homework

This is the final lesson of the course. As your closing assignment, write a 500-word personal scholarly statement addressing two questions: (1) What is the most important thing you have learned from studying Giani Gurdit Singh's approach to ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ, and how has it changed how you understand the Granth? (2) Identify one open question from this course — historical, textual, or theological — that you would like to explore further. Describe in concrete terms what sources you would consult and what method you would use to begin that inquiry. This statement is not a summary of the course; it is a declaration of intellectual and spiritual intention.

sourceText.english: A learned daughter of a dyer lived there; she was proficient in her craft and a scholar of language. Alam and Lalmani fell in love with her. Lalmani sent a garment to the dyer to be colored and attached a thread to it with a note containing a single line of poetry: “The gold was severed; why was the waist of the beautiful maiden cut?” While returning the colored garment, the beauty completed the couplet by writing a second line beneath the paper that Alam had sent, which reads: “By the decree of fate, the gold was cut, and the breasts were pressed close together.” Upon reading this, the Brahmin Lalmani and Alam became Muslims.

courses.title: Reading Gurbani by Its Endings: Giani Harbans Singh's Simple Grammar
courses.summary: This course introduces the approach to Gurbani grammar set out in Giani Harbans Singh's ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ ਸਰਲ ਵਿਆਕਰਣ (Gurbani Saral Viyakaran, 'Simple Gurbani Grammar'). The central idea is that the small vowel-signs and word-endings of Gurbani are not decoration: they carry meaning. A word can change its sense depending on…
outcomes: Explain why the vowel-signs and word-endings of Gurbani carry grammatical meaning rather than being optional marks.
Identify the common ਲਗਾਂ ਮਾਤ੍ਰਾਂ such as ਸਿਹਾਰੀ and ਔਂਕੜ and describe what each one signals.
Distinguish a noun (ਨਾਂਵ) from a verb (ਕਿਰਿਆ) and recognise how each changes form by its ending.
Predict how the meaning of a word shifts when its ending changes, using a side-by-side comparison.
Apply Giani Harbans Singh's simple rules to read short lines of Gurbani with greater accuracy.
Compare the 'simple grammar' approach with the fuller treatment found in Sahib Singh's grammar and place both within the wider field of Sikh studies.

terms.m: Grammar; the study of how words are formed and combined to carry meaning.
The vowel-signs attached to consonants. In Gurbani these signs often carry grammatical, not just phonetic, weight.
The short 'i' vowel-sign written to the left of a letter. On a noun-ending it frequently marks a particular case or relation.
The short 'u' vowel-sign written below a letter. On a final letter it commonly marks a masculine singular noun in its base form.
A noun; a naming word for a person, place, thing, or idea.
A verb; a word expressing an action or state, which changes form by tense, number, and person.
Grammatical gender (masculine or feminine), which often governs which ending a word takes.
Grammatical number (singular or plural), shown in Gurbani largely through the ending rather than a separate word.
