courses.title: Gurmat Sangeet: The History and Soul of Sikh Sacred Music
courses.summary: A 200-level journey through Gurmat Sangeet — the classical music tradition of Sikhi. From Guru Nanak and Bhai Mardana to the 31 raags of Gurbani, the sacred instruments, the great schools of kirtan, the colonial-era near-loss, and the modern revival.
outcomes: Explain what ਗੁਰਮਤਿ ਸੰਗੀਤ (Gurmat Sangeet) is and why Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji is arranged by raag rather than by author or theme
Trace the origin of the kirtan tradition from Guru Nanak Sahib and Bhai Mardana, the first ਰਬਾਬੀ (rababi)
Identify the principal instruments of Gurmat Sangeet — the ਰਬਾਬ (rabab), dilruba, taus, sarangi, and tabla — and the sound each contributes
Distinguish the major schools and lineages of Sikh kirtan, including the Hazoori Ragis of Sri Darbar Sahib, the AKJ congregational style, and the Nihang dhadi tradition
Describe how the raag discipline of Gurbani was eroded during the colonial period and the harmonium era
Discuss the contemporary revival of Gurmat Sangeet and the recovery of string instruments and raag-based kirtan

terms.m: Gurmat Sangeet — the sacred music tradition of Sikhi, in which Gurbani is sung in its prescribed classical raags as an instrument of spiritual discipline.
Raag — a melodic framework in South Asian classical music; Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji is organised into sections according to thirty-one principal raags.
Kirtan — the devotional singing of Gurbani; the central act of Sikh worship.
Rabab — a plucked string instrument; the first instrument of the kirtan tradition, played by Bhai Mardana for Guru Nanak Sahib.
Rababi — a hereditary kirtan musician of the rabab lineage; Bhai Mardana was the first rababi.
Dilruba — a bowed string instrument associated with Guru Gobind Singh Ji and central to the string-instrument revival.
Taus — a large bowed instrument shaped like a peacock, attributed to the tradition of Guru Hargobind Sahib.
Dhadi — a ballad-singer who narrates Sikh history and valour, a tradition formalised by Guru Hargobind Sahib.
Hazoori Ragi — a kirtaniya serving in the presence of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji at a historic Gurdwara, especially Sri Darbar Sahib.
Ghar — a rhythmic or compositional indication ('house') given alongside many shabads in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji.
Chauki — a fixed daily session of kirtan at a historic Gurdwara, each with its own traditional repertoire and timing.
Vaja — the harmonium; the colonial-era reed organ that came to dominate kirtan and displaced string instruments.

references: Mansukhani, Gobind Singh. Indian Classical Music and Sikh Kirtan. New Delhi: Oxford & IBH Publishing, 1982.
Singh, Bhai Avtar, and Bhai Gurcharan Singh. Gurbani Sangeet: Pracheen Reet Ratnavali. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1979.
Kalsi, Sewa Singh. The Evolution of a Sikh Community in Britain. Leeds: University of Leeds, 1992.
Mann, Gurinder Singh. The Making of Sikh Scripture. New York: Oxford University Press, 2001.
Cassio, Francesca. "Female Voices in Gurbani Sangit and the Role of the Raj Academy in the Transmission of the Tradition." Sikh Formations 11, no. 1-2 (2015): 233-264.
Singh, Pashaura. The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2000.
Khalsa, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. The Birth of the Khalsa: A Feminist Re-Memory of Sikh Identity. Albany: State University of New York Press, 2005.

lessons.title: What Is Gurmat Sangeet?
lessons.summary: An introduction to the sacred music tradition of Sikhi and why Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji is arranged by raag.
lessons.html:
Before we begin, set aside the idea that music in Sikhi is decoration added to prayer. In Sikhi, ਕੀਰਤਨ (kirtan) — the singing of Gurbani in raag — is itself the prayer. Gurbani teaches that the Divine is realised through singing the praises of ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ (Waheguru). The tradition that governs how this singing is done is called ਗੁਰਮਤਿ ਸੰਗੀਤ (Gurmat Sangeet): literally, the music (sangeet) according to the wisdom of the Guru (gurmat).

Full course contents
  1. What Is Gurmat Sangeet?
  2. Guru Nanak and Bhai Mardana: The First Rababi
  3. The 31 Raags of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji
  4. The Sacred Instruments: Rabab, Dilruba, Taus, Sarangi, Tabla
  5. The Schools of Sikh Kirtan
  6. Near-Loss and Revival

Music as scripture, not accompaniment

The single most important fact about Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, from a musical point of view, is its organisation. The scripture is not arranged by author, nor by subject, nor chronologically. It is arranged almost entirely by ਰਾਗ (raag) — the melodic mode in which each composition is meant to be sung. This is a deliberate instruction from the Guru Sahibs: the words and the music are joined, and the music is part of the message.

A raag is not a single tune. It is a framework — a chosen set of notes, characteristic ascending and descending movements, and a particular emotional colour. Indian classical tradition holds that different raags evoke different states of mind and are suited to different times. By setting Gurbani into specific raags, the Guru Sahibs prescribed the emotional and spiritual atmosphere in which each teaching should be received.

The vocabulary of the page

Open a copy of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji and you will see musical instructions woven into the text. Some recurring terms:

  • ਰਾਗ (raag) — the melodic mode that heads a section.
  • ਘਰੁ (ghar) — literally 'house', a rhythmic or compositional indication accompanying a shabad.
  • ਪੜਤਾਲ (partaal) — a form in which the rhythmic cycle changes within the composition.
  • Titles such as ਸੋ ਦਰੁ and ਆਸਾ ਦੀ ਵਾਰ that name whole liturgical sequences sung at fixed times.

These are not editorial notes added later. They are part of the bani, recorded by the Guru Sahibs themselves, and they tell us the tradition was musical from the first day.

Why this matters

Gurmat Sangeet is therefore both an art and a discipline. As an art it is a branch of the wider North Indian (Hindustani) classical tradition, sharing its raags and instruments. As a discipline it is something distinct: the music exists to serve the shabad, the word, never to display the performer. A ragi who decorates a shabad with virtuosity at the expense of the meaning has, in the Sikh understanding, missed the point. The aim is ਸ਼ਬਦ ਵਿਚਾਰ (reflection on the word) carried on the vehicle of raag.

References
Mansukhani, Gobind Singh. Indian Classical Music and Sikh Kirtan. New Delhi: Oxford & IBH Publishing, 1982.
Mann, Gurinder Singh. The Making of Sikh Scripture. New York: Oxford University Press, 2001.

lessons.title: Guru Nanak and Bhai Mardana: The First Rababi
lessons.summary: How the kirtan tradition began with Guru Nanak Sahib's revelation and Bhai Mardana's rabab.
lessons.html:
The story of Gurmat Sangeet begins with the very founding of Sikhi. From the start of his mission, Guru Nanak Sahib uttered Gurbani as revelation and had it sung to the accompaniment of a string instrument. The musician at his side was his lifelong companion, Bhai Mardana.

Bhai Mardana, the first rababi

Bhai Mardana was a ਮਿਰਾਸੀ (mirasi) musician from Guru Nanak Sahib's own village of Talwandi (now Nankana Sahib). He played the ਰਬਾਬ (rabab), a plucked string instrument, and travelled with Guru Nanak Sahib on the long journeys known as the ਉਦਾਸੀਆਂ (udasis). When Guru Nanak Sahib received bani, he would often call to Mardana to play the rabab so that the words could be sung. Because of this, Bhai Mardana is honoured as the first ਰਬਾਬੀ (rababi) — the founder of the hereditary lineage of kirtan musicians.

This origin carries a profound social teaching. Bhai Mardana was a Muslim by birth and from a community treated as low in the caste order of the time. That the founder of the kirtan tradition, seated beside the Guru, was such a man is itself a sermon on equality — woven into the music at its root.

The rababi lineage

From Bhai Mardana descended generations of rababi families who served as kirtaniyas at Sikh shrines, including at Sri Darbar Sahib in Amritsar, for centuries. Many were Muslim families who specialised in the classical performance of Gurbani kirtan and were deeply respected. The continuity of this lineage from the time of Guru Nanak Sahib down to the twentieth century is one of the remarkable threads of Sikh history.

Music in the lives of the later Guru Sahibs

The musical tradition deepened with each Guru:

  • Guru Angad Sahib and Guru Amar Das Sahib continued the kirtan tradition and contributed bani in raag.
  • Guru Ram Das Sahib composed extensively and is associated with forms still central to kirtan today.
  • Guru Arjan Sahib, who compiled the Adi Granth in 1604, gave the scripture its definitive raag-based structure and himself was a master of the tradition.
  • Guru Hargobind Sahib expanded the musical world of the court with the ਢਾਡੀ (dhadi) ballad tradition, which we will meet in Lesson 5.
  • Guru Gobind Singh Ji maintained a large body of court musicians and is associated with the bowed instruments of the string family.

The thread that runs through all of this is consistent: from the first day to the last Guru, Gurbani was meant to be sung, and sung in raag.

References
Mann, Gurinder Singh. The Making of Sikh Scripture. New York: Oxford University Press, 2001.
Singh, Pashaura. The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2000.

lessons.title: The 31 Raags of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji
lessons.summary: An exploration of the raag system that structures the scripture and the meaning of singing bani in its prescribed mode.
lessons.html:
Having seen that Gurbani is musical at its root, we now look closely at the raag system itself — the architecture that organises the whole of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji.

Thirty-one principal raags

Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji is arranged according to thirty-one principal raags. The opening compositions — Japji Sahib, the morning and evening liturgies — stand outside the raag sections, but the vast body of the scripture that follows is divided raag by raag, beginning with Sri Raag and moving through the sequence laid down by Guru Arjan Sahib. Within each raag the bani is ordered by Guru and then by poetic form, so the structure is musical first and authorial second.

Some of the raags are well known in the wider Hindustani tradition; others are distinctive forms preserved and shaped within the Sikh tradition, sometimes blending elements of two raags into a new mode. A selection of the principal raags:

RaagCharacter / association
ਸਿਰੀ ਰਾਗੁ (Sri Raag)A serious, contemplative mode; opens the raag sections.
ਆਸਾ (Asa)Mode of hope and aspiration; Asa di Var is sung at dawn.
ਗਉੜੀ (Gauri)One of the largest sections; reflective and steady.
ਸੋਰਠਿ (Sorath)A gentle, devotional evening mode.
ਰਾਮਕਲੀ (Ramkali)An early-morning mode of awakening.
ਬਿਲਾਵਲੁ (Bilaval)A bright, joyful morning mode.

Why a prescribed raag matters

The raag is not chosen at random. The tradition understands each raag to carry a ਰਸ (ras) — an emotional essence. A shabad of longing is set in a raag of yearning; a shabad of joyful praise in a bright morning mode. When the bani is sung in its own raag, word and feeling reinforce one another, and the listener is carried into the state the Guru intended. To sing a shabad in a foreign tune is not forbidden, but the deeper tradition of Gurmat Sangeet holds that singing bani in its prescribed raag is the fuller and more faithful practice.

Time and the chaukis

Because raags in the classical tradition are associated with times of day, historic Gurdwaras developed the ਚਉਕੀ (chauki) system — fixed daily sessions of kirtan, each with its own raags and repertoire matched to the hour, from the pre-dawn Asa di Var to the evening Sodar and Sohila. At Sri Darbar Sahib this cycle of chaukis has been maintained for centuries and is one of the living glories of the tradition.

Raags beyond the 31

The Bhai Gurdas tradition and later additions, and certain compositions, draw on a few further raag forms and mixed raags (for example raags formed by joining two modes). But the framework of thirty-one principal raags is the backbone, and learning to recognise even a handful of them transforms how one hears kirtan.

References
Mann, Gurinder Singh. The Making of Sikh Scripture. New York: Oxford University Press, 2001.
Mansukhani, Gobind Singh. Indian Classical Music and Sikh Kirtan. New Delhi: Oxford & IBH Publishing, 1982.

lessons.title: The Sacred Instruments: Rabab, Dilruba, Taus, Sarangi, Tabla
lessons.summary: A guided tour of the instruments of Gurmat Sangeet and the distinct sound each brings to kirtan.
lessons.html:
Gurmat Sangeet has its own family of instruments, several of them associated directly with the Guru Sahibs. Understanding these instruments — how they sound and where they come from — is essential to understanding what authentic Gurbani kirtan was meant to be, and what the modern revival seeks to restore.

The string instruments

The heart of the older tradition is string, not keyboard. The principal instruments:

InstrumentTypeAssociation & sound
ਰਬਾਬ (rabab)Plucked stringThe original instrument of the tradition, played by Bhai Mardana for Guru Nanak Sahib. Warm, resonant, percussive.
ਦਿਲਰੁਬਾ (dilruba)Bowed stringAssociated with the tradition of Guru Gobind Singh Ji. Portable and vocal in tone; can be carried by a rider. Central to the revival.
ਤਾਊਸ (taus)Bowed stringA larger peacock-shaped instrument associated with Guru Hargobind Sahib's tradition. Deep, sustained, ornate.
ਸਾਰੰਗੀ (sarangi)Bowed stringA fretless instrument famed for its closeness to the human voice; the classic instrument of the dhadi tradition.

A common thread links the bowed instruments: the dilruba, taus, and sarangi all aim to imitate the human voice. In Gurmat Sangeet this is the ideal — the instrument should follow and support the singer of the shabad, never overpower the word.

The percussion

The ਤਬਲਾ (tabla) — a pair of hand drums — provides the ਤਾਲ (taal), the rhythmic cycle. In older and dhadi traditions the barrel drum ਜੋੜੀ / ਮ੍ਰਿਦੰਗ (jori or pakhawaj) was used. The ਘਰੁ (ghar) markings in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji are understood to relate to rhythm, tying the percussion directly to the scripture.

The harmonium: the instrument that changed everything

You will notice one instrument missing from the list above: the ਵਾਜਾ (vaja), the harmonium. The harmonium is a reed keyboard introduced to India by Europeans in the nineteenth century. It is easy to learn, holds a fixed pitch, and is portable. For all these reasons it spread rapidly through Gurdwaras in the colonial period and largely displaced the difficult, expensive string instruments.

But the harmonium has a cost. Its fixed, tempered keys cannot produce the subtle slides (ਮੀਂਡ, meend) and microtonal shadings on which raag depends. A raag rendered on a harmonium loses much of what makes it that raag. This is why the revival of Gurmat Sangeet, which we turn to in the final lesson, is so closely tied to the return of the string instruments.

References
Mansukhani, Gobind Singh. Indian Classical Music and Sikh Kirtan. New Delhi: Oxford & IBH Publishing, 1982.
Cassio, Francesca. "Female Voices in Gurbani Sangit and the Role of the Raj Academy in the Transmission of the Tradition." Sikh Formations 11, no. 1-2 (2015): 233-264.

lessons.title: The Schools of Sikh Kirtan
lessons.summary: The major living lineages and styles of Sikh kirtan, from the Hazoori Ragis to the AKJ and the Nihang dhadi tradition.
lessons.html:
Gurmat Sangeet is not a single uniform style. Over the centuries several distinct schools and lineages developed, each with its own repertoire, instruments, and spirit. Knowing these schools helps you understand the variety you will hear at any large Sikh gathering.

The Hazoori Ragis of Sri Darbar Sahib

The most prestigious lineage is that of the ਹਜ਼ੂਰੀ ਰਾਗੀ (Hazoori Ragis) — the musicians who serve in the presence of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji at Sri Darbar Sahib (the Golden Temple) in Amritsar. They maintain the centuries-old cycle of ਚਉਕੀ (chaukis), singing the prescribed raags at their appointed times. This is the conservatory of classical Gurbani kirtan, where the ਰੀਤ (reet) — the traditional fixed compositions handed down through generations — are preserved. Twentieth-century masters of this lineage, such as Bhai Avtar Singh and Bhai Gurcharan Singh, documented hundreds of these traditional compositions and did much to keep the classical tradition alive.

The AKJ congregational style

The Akhand Kirtani Jatha (AKJ), associated with the legacy of Bhai Randhir Singh, developed a very different and powerful approach. Its hallmark is intense, fast-paced, fully congregational singing in which the entire sangat sings together rather than listening to a performer. The emphasis is on ਸਿਮਰਨ (simran), high spiritual energy, and unbroken kirtan sessions (ਰੈਣ ਸਬਾਈ, rain sabai — all-night kirtan). The AKJ style is less concerned with classical raag exposition and more with collective devotional immersion.

The Nihang and dhadi tradition

The ਢਾਡੀ (dhadi) tradition was formalised by Guru Hargobind Sahib, who established dhadis to sing ballads of valour and Sikh history before the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ (Akal Takht). Dhadis perform with the small ਢੱਡ (dhadd) drums and the sarangi, narrating the heroism of the Guru Sahibs and the Khalsa in a stirring, martial style. This tradition is closely connected to the ਨਿਹੰਗ (Nihang) Singhs and to the warrior ethos of the Khalsa, and it complements the meditative kirtan of the Gurdwara with the rousing remembrance of history.

Comparing the schools

SchoolEmphasisTypical instruments
Hazoori RagiClassical raag, traditional reet, chauki cycleString instruments, tabla, (latterly harmonium)
AKJCongregational singing, simran, high energyHarmonium, tabla, sangat voices
Dhadi / NihangHistorical ballads, valour, narrationDhadd, sarangi

These schools are not rivals so much as complementary streams. The contemplative raag of the Hazoori tradition, the collective fervour of the AKJ, and the historical fire of the dhadis together express the fullness of the Sikh spirit: meditation, sangat, and remembrance of sacrifice.

References
Singh, Bhai Avtar, and Bhai Gurcharan Singh. Gurbani Sangeet: Pracheen Reet Ratnavali. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1979.
Khalsa, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. The Birth of the Khalsa. Albany: State University of New York Press, 2005.

lessons.title: Near-Loss and Revival
lessons.summary: How the raag tradition was eroded in the colonial era and how Gurmat Sangeet is being recovered today.
lessons.html:
We close with the most urgent chapter of this story: how a tradition stretching unbroken from Guru Nanak Sahib came close to being lost, and how it is being brought back to life in our own time.

The colonial erosion

Several forces converged during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries to weaken the raag tradition:

  • The harmonium. As we saw in Lesson 4, the colonial-era spread of the harmonium replaced the string instruments. Because the harmonium cannot render the slides and microtones of raag, kirtan increasingly drifted from true raag form toward simple keyboard-friendly tunes.
  • The decline of the rababi lineage. Many of the hereditary rababi families who held the classical knowledge were Muslim. The Partition of 1947 severed this community from the Sikh shrines almost overnight, breaking a chain of transmission that ran back to Bhai Mardana.
  • The rise of film and popular tunes. Through the twentieth century, kirtan was increasingly sung to the melodies of popular and film songs rather than to prescribed raags — easy to follow, but a departure from the tradition.
  • Loss of the string repertoire. As fewer musicians learned the dilruba, taus, and sarangi, the traditional fixed compositions (reet) tied to those instruments were in danger of disappearing.

By the mid-twentieth century, knowledge of the full thirty-one-raag tradition survived mainly among a small number of elderly masters. The tradition was not dead, but it was endangered.

The revival

The recovery of Gurmat Sangeet has been one of the quiet triumphs of modern Sikh life. Several strands stand out:

  • Documentation. Masters such as Bhai Avtar Singh and Bhai Gurcharan Singh notated and recorded hundreds of traditional reet, preserving in writing what had been carried only by ear.
  • Academic institutionalisation. Universities in Punjab established departments and degrees in Gurmat Sangeet, training a new generation in the classical raags.
  • The return of string instruments. A growing movement of young Sikhs has taken up the dilruba, taus, and sarangi, deliberately setting aside the harmonium to recover authentic raag.
  • The diaspora and teaching academies. Institutions abroad, such as the Raj Academy and others, have spread raag-based kirtan and string instruments to Sikhs around the world, including a notable opening of the tradition to women performers.

Why the revival matters

This is not nostalgia for old instruments. The raag structure of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji is an instruction from the Guru Sahibs themselves. To sing the bani in its own raag is to receive the shabad as it was given — with the emotional and spiritual colour the Guru intended. The revival of Gurmat Sangeet is therefore a return to the fullness of Gurbani: word and music, reunited as they were on the first day, when Guru Nanak Sahib sang and Bhai Mardana played the rabab.

You now have the framework to listen with new ears. The next time you hear kirtan, notice the instrument, listen for the raag, and remember that you are hearing a tradition more than five centuries old — endangered, recovered, and still singing.

References
Kalsi, Sewa Singh. The Evolution of a Sikh Community in Britain. Leeds: University of Leeds, 1992.
Cassio, Francesca. "Female Voices in Gurbani Sangit and the Role of the Raj Academy in the Transmission of the Tradition." Sikh Formations 11, no. 1-2 (2015): 233-264.
Singh, Bhai Avtar, and Bhai Gurcharan Singh. Gurbani Sangeet: Pracheen Reet Ratnavali. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1979.

courses.title: Jail Chitthian: Bhai Randhir Singh's Letters from Prison
courses.summary: Study Bhai Randhir Singh's Jail Chitthian (Prison Letters), a Sikh spiritual classic on Naam Simran, Gurbani reflection, and Chardi Kala forged in British colonial prisons (1915-1930).
outcomes: Trace the life of Bhai Randhir Singh as freedom fighter and spiritual figure, and situate Jail Chitthian within his imprisonment (1915-1930)
Explain how Bhai Sahib reframed the colonial prison as a site of intensified ਸਿਮਰਨ (Simran) and devotion
Analyze the structure, audience, and recurring themes of the letters
Describe the practice and inner experience of ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ (Naam Simran) as presented in the text
Evaluate the concept of ਚੜ੍ਹਦੀ ਕਲਾ (Chardi Kala) as a response to oppression and suffering
Assess the literary and devotional legacy of Jail Chitthian and distinguish AKJ-specific positions from broader Sikh discourse

terms.m: Naam Simran: loving, continuous remembrance and meditative repetition of the Divine Name.
Chardi Kala: the Sikh spirit of rising, ever-ascending optimism and high morale, even amid adversity.
Chitthian: letters; here the prison letters Bhai Randhir Singh sent to family and Sangat.
Gurbani: the sacred utterance of the Gurus and Bhagats recorded in Sri Guru Granth Sahib.
Sangat: the holy congregation of devotees who gather in remembrance of the Divine.
Amrit: the sanctified initiation of the Khalsa administered through the Amrit Sanchar.
Akhand Kirtani Jatha (AKJ): the devotional movement of continuous Kirtan associated with Bhai Randhir Singh.
Rahit: the code of discipline and conduct binding upon an initiated Sikh of the Khalsa.
Bandi: prisoner or captivity; Bhai Sahib's years of incarceration under colonial rule.
Anand: bliss; the spiritual joy Bhai Sahib describes experiencing through Naam even in confinement.

references: Singh, Randhir. Jail Chithian (Prison Letters). Translated by Trilochan Singh. Bhai Sahib Randhir Singh Trust, 1998.
Singh, Randhir. Autobiography of Bhai Sahib Randhir Singh. Translated by Trilochan Singh. Bhai Sahib Randhir Singh Trust, 1971.
Singh, Trilochan. Bhai Sahib Randhir Singh: A Saint, Scholar and Martyr. Bhai Sahib Randhir Singh Publishing House, 1975.
Singh, Harbans, ed. The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism. Punjabi University, 1992-1998.
Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford University Press, 2014.
McLeod, W. H. The A to Z of Sikhism. Scarecrow Press, 2009.

lessons.title: Bhai Randhir Singh: Freedom Fighter and Spiritual Master
lessons.summary: The life of Bhai Randhir Singh and the historical setting that produced Jail Chitthian.
lessons.html:
Full course contents
  1. Bhai Randhir Singh: Freedom Fighter and Spiritual Master
  2. Prison as a Spiritual Retreat
  3. The Letters: Themes and Structure
  4. Naam Simran in the Letters
  5. Chardi Kala Under Oppression
  6. The Letters' Legacy

To read Jail Chitthian well, we must first meet its author. Bhai Randhir Singh (1878-1961) was at once a participant in the Indian freedom struggle and a deeply devotional Sikh whose inner life centred on ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ (Naam Simran). This first lesson places the letters within his biography and his times.

Early life and awakening

Born in Narangwal, in the Ludhiana district of Punjab, into a prosperous and educated family, Bhai Randhir Singh received a colonial-era education. His given name was Basant Singh; he later took ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ (Amrit) and adopted the name Randhir Singh. According to his own writings and those of his translator Trilochan Singh, a profound spiritual turning led him toward intense Gurbani devotion and the practice of continuous remembrance.

A life of Kirtan and Sangat

Bhai Sahib became known for sustained, ecstatic ਕੀਰਤਨ (Kirtan), congregational singing of Gurbani that could continue for long hours. The devotional movement that grew around this practice is today known as the ਅਖੰਡ ਕੀਰਤਨੀ ਜਥਾ (Akhand Kirtani Jatha, AKJ). It is important from the outset to note that the AKJ holds certain distinctive positions — for example on the keeping of strict Rahit and on questions such as diet — which represent one tradition's stance within the wider Panth rather than universally agreed Sikh doctrine. We will revisit this point in later lessons.

Freedom fighter

Bhai Randhir Singh was drawn into the anti-colonial struggle and is associated with the Ghadar movement era. He was arrested and convicted in connection with revolutionary activity around 1915 and sentenced to a long term of imprisonment. He spent roughly the years 1915 to 1930 in various British colonial jails. It was during these years of ਬੰਦੀ (Bandi, captivity) that the letters collected as Jail Chitthian were written.

  • Patriot: He resisted British rule and accepted long imprisonment for it.
  • Devotee: He treated every hardship as an occasion to deepen Naam.
  • Reformer: While in jail he is remembered for insisting on his rights as an initiated Sikh, including matters of dress and diet.

Why the letters matter

What makes Bhai Sahib unusual among prison memoirists is that his letters dwell far less on grievance than on grace. The hardships are real, but they are consistently transfigured by the lens of devotion. This is the heart of what we will study.

References: Singh, Trilochan. Bhai Sahib Randhir Singh: A Saint, Scholar and Martyr. 1975. Singh, Harbans, ed. The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism. Punjabi University, 1992-1998. Singh, Randhir. Autobiography of Bhai Sahib Randhir Singh. Trans. Trilochan Singh. 1971.

lessons.title: Prison as a Spiritual Retreat
lessons.summary: How Bhai Sahib reframed colonial incarceration into a setting for intensified devotion.
lessons.html:
Confinement is ordinarily an experience of loss — of freedom, family, and dignity. In Jail Chitthian, Bhai Randhir Singh performs a striking reversal: the cell becomes a cloister, the silence a gift, the deprivation a discipline. This lesson examines that reframing.

The conditions of colonial imprisonment

British jails of the early twentieth century were harsh: hard labour, poor food, isolation, and the deliberate humiliation of political prisoners. Bhai Sahib faced added trials as an initiated Sikh who insisted on maintaining his ਰਹਿਤ (Rahit). His own accounts describe struggles to keep his hair and articles of faith intact and to obtain food consistent with his discipline.

The inner reframe

Rather than narrating these trials only as injustices, Bhai Sahib repeatedly presents solitude as an opportunity. Gurbani teaches that the Divine dwells within and is realised through remembrance; for Bhai Sahib the enforced removal of worldly distraction cleared space for that inner work. The prison thus functioned, in his telling, as a forced retreat — a place where ਸਿਮਰਨ could become uninterrupted.

Worldly view of prisonBhai Sahib's devotional view
Loss of freedomFreedom from worldly entanglement
Forced isolationUninterrupted solitude for Simran
PunishmentOpportunity for purification
Despairਚੜ੍ਹਦੀ ਕਲਾ (Chardi Kala)

A long tradition

This reframing is not unique to Bhai Sahib but draws on the deep Sikh memory of the Gurus and Sikhs who suffered with serenity. Sikh tradition celebrates those who remained absorbed in the Divine under torture and confinement. Bhai Sahib consciously placed himself within that stream, understanding his own bondage as small beside that history and as an honour rather than a disgrace.

Caution on tradition-specific claims

Some of Bhai Sahib's prison struggles — notably his insistence on a particular discipline around diet — reflect the strict Rahit he and the AKJ uphold. Readers should understand these as one tradition's interpretation. The broader devotional lesson, that adversity can be turned toward the Divine, is shared widely across the Panth.

References: Singh, Randhir. Jail Chithian (Prison Letters). Trans. Trilochan Singh. 1998. Singh, Randhir. Autobiography of Bhai Sahib Randhir Singh. 1971. McLeod, W. H. The A to Z of Sikhism. 2009.

lessons.title: The Letters: Themes and Structure
lessons.summary: The form, audience, and recurring concerns of Jail Chitthian.
lessons.html:
Before analysing individual themes in depth, it helps to understand Jail Chitthian as a literary object: who the letters were written to, what form they take, and what concerns recur across them.

Form and audience

The ਚਿੱਠੀਆਂ (Chitthian) are personal letters, written from prison to family members and to the ਸੰਗਤ (Sangat). Because colonial prison rules limited and censored correspondence, the letters carry a compressed intensity: Bhai Sahib uses each permitted communication not merely to report on his welfare but to offer spiritual counsel and encouragement. They read at once as private family correspondence and as public devotional teaching.

Recurring themes

  • Naam Simran: the central preoccupation — the remembrance of the Divine Name as the soul of life.
  • Gurbani reflection: meditations woven around the teachings of Sri Guru Granth Sahib.
  • Chardi Kala: unwavering high spirits and trust in the Divine Will.
  • Detachment: counsel to family not to grieve, but to remain absorbed in devotion.
  • Rahit and discipline: the importance of living the initiated Sikh life faithfully even under pressure.

Tone and voice

The tone is tender yet bracing. Bhai Sahib comforts loved ones who worry for him, then turns the comfort outward into instruction: do not pity me, he in effect says, but join me in remembrance. The letters frequently shift from the personal to the universal, using his own circumstances as a doorway into teaching about the spiritual path.

How to read the letters

Because the text moves fluidly between report, prayer, and teaching, the reader is best served by attending to the devotional logic rather than expecting a linear narrative. Each letter tends to circle back to a single conviction: that the Divine Name is sufficient, and that nothing external — not even prison — can take it away. The quotations of Gurbani that punctuate the letters should be treated with reverence and read in their full context in Sri Guru Granth Sahib, rather than as detached proof-texts.

References: Singh, Randhir. Jail Chithian (Prison Letters). Trans. Trilochan Singh. 1998. Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford University Press, 2014.

lessons.title: Naam Simran in the Letters
lessons.summary: The practice and inner experience of Naam Simran as Bhai Sahib presents it.
lessons.html:
At the centre of Jail Chitthian stands one practice above all: ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ (Naam Simran). This lesson examines what Bhai Sahib means by it, how he describes practising it, and the experiences he reports.

What is Naam Simran?

Naam Simran is the loving, continuous remembrance of the Divine Name. In Sikh teaching it is both an outward practice — the recitation and singing of Gurbani and the Gurmantar — and an inner state in which the consciousness rests unbroken in the Divine. Gurbani teaches that through Naam the mind is purified, fear is dispelled, and the soul comes into union with its Source. Bhai Sahib treats Naam as the very purpose of human life.

Simran in confinement

Bhai Sahib describes the prison as an environment that, paradoxically, supported deep Simran. With worldly affairs stripped away, the remembrance could become constant — carried into labour, into the night, into every breath. He counsels his readers that the Name is portable in a way nothing else is: it cannot be confiscated, censored, or chained.

The fruit: Anand

A recurring claim in the letters is that Naam yields ਅਨੰਦ (Anand), spiritual bliss, independent of outer circumstance. Bhai Sahib reports joy in the cell that worldly comfort could not give. This is not a denial of suffering but a testimony that, for the one absorbed in remembrance, suffering loses its power to crush the spirit.

  • Constancy: Simran as an unbroken thread through every activity.
  • Interiority: the Divine found within, beyond the reach of the jailer.
  • Transformation: the mind reshaped by the Name into stillness and bliss.

A word of care

Bhai Sahib's descriptions of inner experience are devotional testimony, not a technical manual to be imitated mechanically. The tradition holds that Naam is received through Guru's grace and the company of the Sangat. Readers are encouraged to approach Gurbani directly and with reverence rather than treating any single devotee's account as a formula.

References: Singh, Randhir. Jail Chithian (Prison Letters). Trans. Trilochan Singh. 1998. Singh, Trilochan. Bhai Sahib Randhir Singh: A Saint, Scholar and Martyr. 1975.

lessons.title: Chardi Kala Under Oppression
lessons.summary: Chardi Kala as a sustained response to colonial suffering and injustice.
lessons.html:
If Naam Simran is the practice at the heart of the letters, ਚੜ੍ਹਦੀ ਕਲਾ (Chardi Kala) is the spirit that radiates from them. This lesson studies how Bhai Sahib embodies rising, ascending optimism in the face of oppression.

What is Chardi Kala?

Chardi Kala is the distinctively Sikh disposition of ever-rising morale — a buoyant confidence rooted not in circumstance but in trust in the Divine Will (ਹੁਕਮ, Hukam). It is the refusal to sink into despair, anger, or self-pity, grounded in the conviction that the Divine is just, present, and ultimately sovereign over all events.

Chardi Kala in the prison letters

The British colonial system intended imprisonment to break the will of political prisoners. Bhai Sahib's letters are, in part, a documented refusal of that breaking. He neither minimises the cruelty of his captors nor lets it define his inner state. Where another might write of bitterness, he writes of gratitude; where another might despair, he counsels his family toward courage and remembrance.

Pressure of oppressionResponse in Chardi Kala
HumiliationDignity rooted in the Divine
Fear and threatFearlessness through Naam
InjusticeTrust in Hukam without passivity
DespairGratitude and high spirits

Not passive resignation

It is essential to distinguish Chardi Kala from mere resignation. Bhai Sahib was a freedom fighter who actively resisted injustice; his serenity in prison was not surrender but a deeper kind of strength. He insisted on his rights as an initiated Sikh and did not abandon his convictions under pressure. Chardi Kala, properly understood, unites inner peace with moral courage.

A model for adversity

For later readers, the letters offer a template for meeting hardship: name the injustice honestly, refuse to let it own your spirit, and anchor the self in remembrance of the Divine. This is why the text has spoken so powerfully to Sikhs facing their own trials across generations.

References: Singh, Randhir. Jail Chithian (Prison Letters). Trans. Trilochan Singh. 1998. Singh, Harbans, ed. The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism. Punjabi University, 1992-1998.

lessons.title: The Letters' Legacy
lessons.summary: The enduring devotional and literary influence of Jail Chitthian, with care on tradition-specific claims.
lessons.html:
This final lesson considers how Jail Chitthian has been received, why it endures as a Sikh spiritual classic, and how to read it responsibly given its connection to a particular tradition.

A beloved devotional classic

Within Sikh devotional reading, Jail Chitthian holds a cherished place. It is valued not as political memoir but as testimony — a firsthand account of a devotee sustaining intense ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ and ਚੜ੍ਹਦੀ ਕਲਾ under extreme duress. Its blend of tenderness toward family and bracing spiritual counsel has made it a source of encouragement for readers facing their own hardships.

Bhai Randhir Singh's broader influence

Bhai Sahib's legacy extends beyond this single book. He authored numerous devotional and theological works, and the ਅਖੰਡ ਕੀਰਤਨੀ ਜਥਾ (Akhand Kirtani Jatha) that grew around his practice of continuous Kirtan remains active internationally. His translator and biographer Trilochan Singh did much to bring his life and writings to a wider English-reading audience.

Reading tradition-specific positions with care

Because Bhai Sahib is so closely identified with the AKJ, some of his and the movement's positions — for instance, particular views on diet (such as the prohibition of meat) and on the precise form of ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ and Rahit — are sometimes read as if they were universal Sikh doctrine. They are better understood as one tradition's interpretation within a Panth that holds a range of views on these matters. The Sikh Rahit Maryada and the broader scholarly literature record this diversity. Honouring Bhai Sahib's devotion does not require treating every tradition-specific position as binding on all Sikhs.

  • Universally shared: the centrality of Naam, Gurbani, Sangat, and Chardi Kala.
  • Tradition-specific (AKJ): certain stricter Rahit positions, including on diet and Amrit, presented here as one position among several.

Why it still speaks

Ultimately, Jail Chitthian endures because it answers a perennial question: how does the spirit remain free when the body is bound? Bhai Randhir Singh's reply — through unbroken remembrance of the Divine Name and trust in the Divine Will — has outlasted the empire that imprisoned him.

References: Singh, Randhir. Jail Chithian (Prison Letters). Trans. Trilochan Singh. 1998. Singh, Trilochan. Bhai Sahib Randhir Singh: A Saint, Scholar and Martyr. 1975. Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford University Press, 2014.

lessons.title: From Madho Das to Banda Singh: The Making of a Sovereign
lessons.summary: The early life of the ascetic Madho Das and his world-altering encounter with Guru Gobind Singh Ji at Nanded.
lessons.html:
The story of Banda Singh Bahadur begins not with a warrior but with an ascetic. Born in 1670 in the Poonch region of the Jammu hills, he was named Lachhman Dev (also recorded as Lachhman Das). According to the traditional accounts gathered by Ganda Singh, a hunting incident in which a pregnant doe died troubled the young man deeply and turned him toward renunciation. He became a wandering ਬੈਰਾਗੀ (Bairagi) ascetic and eventually settled at Nanded on the banks of the Godavari, where he was known as Madho Das and reputed to possess occult powers.

Full course contents
  1. From Madho Das to Banda Singh: The Making of a Sovereign
  2. The Commission: Guru Gobind Singh Ji and the Hukamnamas
  3. The March North and the Battle of Sirhind (1710)
  4. Revolutionary Rule: Land Reform and Early Sikh Sovereignty
  5. Resistance, Retreat, and Capture at Gurdaspur (1715)
  6. Martyrdom in Delhi (1716) and the Legacy of Banda Singh Bahadur

The world of the seventeenth-century renunciate

To understand Madho Das we must understand the religious landscape he inhabited. The Bairagi tradition emphasized withdrawal from society, the cultivation of spiritual powers, and a hierarchical relationship between a master and his followers. Madho Das had assembled a community of devotees who looked to him for blessings and feared his reputed supernatural abilities. His was a life of inward focus and personal authority, far removed from the worldly engagement that the Sikh path of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ (miri-piri) — the union of temporal and spiritual sovereignty — would demand of him.

The meeting at Nanded, 1708

In 1708, in the final months of his earthly life, Guru Gobind Singh Ji arrived at Nanded. The tenth Nanak had travelled to the Deccan in the company of the Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah I, but his deeper purpose, as Sikh tradition holds, was to prepare the Panth for the struggles ahead. He visited Madho Das's hermitage. The traditional narrative recounts a contest of authority in which the ascetic's reputed powers proved unavailing before the Guru's presence. When the Guru asked who he was, Madho Das replied that he was the Guru's ਬੰਦਾ (banda) — his servant, his slave.

That single word reframed his entire existence. The man who had ruled over devotees now declared himself a servant. Guru Gobind Singh Ji initiated him into the Khalsa, and the former ascetic took on a new identity oriented not toward withdrawal but toward justice in the world.

A new name, a new purpose

The transformation was total. The self-absorbed renunciate became the disciplined servant of a mission. Where Madho Das had cultivated personal power, Banda Singh would now wield collective power on behalf of the oppressed. The historian's challenge is to separate the layers of later hagiography from the contemporary record, and scholars such as Ganda Singh worked carefully through Persian chronicles, Sikh sources, and European accounts to reconstruct this turning point. What is beyond dispute is that a previously obscure ascetic emerged from Nanded as the man who would, within two years, shake the Mughal order in the Punjab.

AspectMadho Das the BairagiBanda Singh the Khalsa
OrientationWithdrawal, asceticismEngagement, justice
AuthorityPersonal, occult reputationServant of the Guru and Panth
CommunityDevotees seeking blessingsKhalsa army and peasantry
GoalPersonal liberationCollective sovereignty and reform

This first lesson establishes the human foundation of the story: a real transformation of character that made everything else possible. In the lessons that follow we will examine how Guru Gobind Singh Ji formally commissioned Banda Singh, how he led the Khalsa to victory at Sirhind, and how he attempted to build a new political and economic order before his capture and martyrdom.

References
  • Singh, Ganda. Life of Banda Singh Bahadur. Amritsar: Khalsa College, 1935.
  • Singh, Khushwant. A History of the Sikhs, Volume 1. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2004.
  • Singh, Teja, and Ganda Singh. A Short History of the Sikhs, Volume 1. Bombay: Orient Longmans, 1950.

lessons.title: The Commission: Guru Gobind Singh Ji and the Hukamnamas
lessons.summary: How Guru Gobind Singh Ji authorized Banda Singh's mission and equipped him with the moral and organizational authority to act.
lessons.html:
Banda Singh's campaign was not a private adventure. It rested on a formal commission from Guru Gobind Singh Ji and on the network of authority that bound the Khalsa together. This lesson examines the nature of that commission and the instruments — above all the ਹੁਕਮਨਾਮੇ (hukamnamas) — that turned a single man's resolve into a movement.

What the Guru gave

According to the contemporary and traditional records assembled by Ganda Singh and Teja Singh, Guru Gobind Singh Ji entrusted Banda Singh with a mission to punish the tyranny that had been visited upon the Sikhs and the people of the Punjab — most acutely the execution of the Guru's younger sons, Baba Zorawar Singh Ji and Baba Fateh Singh Ji, at Sirhind. The Guru is recorded as providing Banda Singh with symbols of authority and, crucially, with letters addressed to the Sikhs of the Punjab instructing them to rally to his banner. He was also accompanied by a council of devoted Singhs who served as advisors, ensuring that authority remained collective rather than purely personal.

The hukamnamas as instruments of mobilization

A ਹੁਕਮਨਾਮਾ was an authoritative order. In the Sikh tradition, hukamnamas issued by the Gurus carried binding moral weight; Sikhs who received them were obligated to respond. When Banda Singh travelled north bearing the Guru's letters, these documents functioned as both credentials and call to arms. They told the dispersed Sikh communities of the Punjab that the bearer carried the Guru's sanction and that the time had come to organize for justice. The response was remarkable: peasants, artisans, and fighters joined in growing numbers as he advanced.

  • Legitimacy: the hukamnamas established that Banda Singh acted under the Guru's authority, not his own ambition.
  • Coordination: they linked scattered ਸੰਗਤਾਂ (sangats) across the Punjab into a single mobilization.
  • Discipline: they framed the coming struggle as a moral campaign against tyranny, not mere plunder.

The boundary of authority

It is important to be precise about what the commission did and did not mean. Guru Gobind Singh Ji had already vested ultimate spiritual authority in the Guru Granth Sahib and the Khalsa Panth. Banda Singh was a leader and servant of the Panth, not a successor Guru. Sikh tradition is firm on this distinction. Later in his career, tensions arose precisely when some of his followers were accused of treating him with a reverence that blurred this line — a controversy that contributed to divisions among the Sikhs, which we will revisit in Lesson 5. For now, the essential point is that his legitimacy flowed downward from the Guru's commission and outward through the Khalsa's collective will.

Source of authorityFunction
Guru's commissionMoral mandate to act against tyranny
Hukamnamas to the SangatsMobilize fighters and resources across Punjab
Council of advisor SinghsKeep leadership accountable and collective
Khalsa initiationBind the movement to Sikh discipline and ideals

Armed with this layered authority rather than personal charisma alone, Banda Singh crossed into the Punjab and began the campaign that would lead to Sirhind. The next lesson follows that military advance.

References
  • Singh, Ganda. Life of Banda Singh Bahadur. Amritsar: Khalsa College, 1935.
  • Singh, Teja, and Ganda Singh. A Short History of the Sikhs, Volume 1. Bombay: Orient Longmans, 1950.
  • Dhavan, Purnima. When Sparrows Became Hawks. New York: Oxford University Press, 2011.

lessons.title: The March North and the Battle of Sirhind (1710)
lessons.summary: Banda Singh's advance through the Punjab, the gathering of the Khalsa, and the decisive victory over Wazir Khan at Sirhind.
lessons.html:
Between 1709 and 1710 Banda Singh Bahadur led a swift and consequential military campaign across the Punjab. This lesson traces that march and centers on its climax: the Battle of Sirhind in May 1710, which broke Mughal authority in the region and announced the arrival of organized Sikh political power.

Gathering the Khalsa

As Banda Singh moved north, the Guru's hukamnamas drew growing numbers to his side. Many who joined were drawn from the peasantry and from communities long burdened by oppressive revenue demands and the violence of local officials. The early engagements at towns such as Samana and Sadhaura served both military and moral purposes: Samana was associated with the executioners connected to the martyrdoms of the ninth Guru and the Guru's sons, and these actions were understood by the Khalsa as the redress of grave injustice rather than indiscriminate conquest.

The road to Sirhind

Sirhind held a singular place in the Sikh memory of this era. Its governor, Wazir Khan, had ordered the execution of Guru Gobind Singh Ji's two younger sons, who were bricked alive when they refused to abandon their faith, and the death of their grandmother, Mata Gujri Ji. To march on Sirhind was therefore charged with profound moral meaning. The Khalsa advanced with a discipline born of conviction.

The battle at Chappar Chiri

The decisive engagement took place in May 1710 on the plain of Chappar Chiri near Sirhind. Wazir Khan commanded a well-equipped Mughal force with artillery and cavalry; Banda Singh's army, though large and determined, was less conventionally armed. Sikh accounts and later histories describe a hard-fought battle in which the Khalsa's resolve and tactical pressure overcame the Mughal advantage. Wazir Khan was killed in the fighting, and his army broke. The Khalsa entered Sirhind.

  • Moral cause: the campaign answered the martyrdom of the Guru's family and the suffering of the people.
  • Mass participation: ordinary cultivators fought alongside seasoned warriors.
  • Strategic outcome: the fall of Sirhind removed the principal Mughal authority between the Sutlej and the hills.

The significance of the victory

The capture of Sirhind was not merely a battlefield success. It transferred control of a major province into Sikh hands and gave Banda Singh a territorial base from which to govern. For the first time since the founding of the faith, Sikhs held political power over a substantial region. The victory also carried a powerful symbolic charge: the seat of those responsible for the Sahibzadas' martyrdom had fallen to the Khalsa. Yet, as we will see, Banda Singh's purpose extended far beyond retribution. He intended to use this new power to remake the social and economic order itself.

EngagementSignificance
SamanaRedress against those tied to earlier martyrdoms
SadhauraExpansion of Khalsa control and momentum
Chappar Chiri / Sirhind (1710)Defeat of Wazir Khan; capture of the province

With a province under his command, Banda Singh turned to the work of rule. The next lesson examines the revolutionary reforms that made his brief sovereignty historically distinctive.

References
  • Singh, Ganda. Life of Banda Singh Bahadur. Amritsar: Khalsa College, 1935.
  • Singh, Khushwant. A History of the Sikhs, Volume 1. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2004.
  • Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998.

lessons.title: Revolutionary Rule: Land Reform and Early Sikh Sovereignty
lessons.summary: Banda Singh's abolition of feudal landlordism, the empowerment of peasant cultivators, and the symbols of the first Sikh state.
lessons.html:
What distinguishes Banda Singh Bahadur from a mere conqueror is what he did with power once he held it. In the brief period of his rule he attempted a genuine social revolution: the dismantling of the feudal landlord system and the elevation of the peasant cultivator. This lesson examines those reforms and the symbols by which he asserted a sovereign Sikh state.

Abolishing zamindari

The prevailing agrarian order rested on the ਜ਼ਮੀਂਦਾਰੀ (zamindari) system, in which intermediary landlords held rights over land and extracted dues from the cultivators who actually worked it. These landlords were often instruments of oppression, and the burden on the peasantry was heavy. Historians including J. S. Grewal and Khushwant Singh record that Banda Singh struck at this arrangement directly: he abolished the rights of the zamindars in the territory he controlled and recognized the cultivators as the proprietors of the land they tilled. This was a radical inversion of the social hierarchy of the time.

The meaning of the reform

The significance of this measure can hardly be overstated. In an era of entrenched feudal privilege, a leader voluntarily transferred economic power from a landed elite to the laboring majority. The reform resonated with the deepest principles of the Sikh tradition — the dignity of honest labor (ਕਿਰਤ ਕਰਨੀ, kirat karni), the equality of all people before the Divine, and the rejection of exploitative hierarchy. It also had a practical effect: it bound the peasantry to Banda Singh's cause, for they now had a tangible stake in the survival of the new order.

  • Economic: cultivators became proprietors rather than tenants of landlords.
  • Social: the inherited privilege of the zamindar class was overturned.
  • Ideological: the reform expressed Sikh ideals of equality and the honor of labor.

Symbols of sovereignty

Banda Singh also asserted the outward marks of an independent state. He established a capital and fortress at ਲੋਹਗੜ੍ਹ (Lohgarh) in the Shivalik foothills. He struck coins — a classic prerogative of sovereignty — bearing inscriptions that attributed his authority and victory to Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh Ji rather than to himself. He introduced an official seal for his administration. These acts declared that a new power, rooted in the Sikh faith, now stood in the Punjab independent of Mughal authority.

Symbol of sovereigntyMeaning
Capital at LohgarhA territorial and administrative center
Coinage in the Gurus' nameAuthority claimed in the name of the Gurus, not the self
Official sealLegitimate, organized governance
Land reformA new social contract with the peasantry

A note on humility in power

It is striking that Banda Singh's coins and seal directed glory away from his own person and toward the Gurus. Whatever later controversies arose over how some followers regarded him, the official instruments of his state expressed the principle he had embraced at Nanded: that he was a ਬੰਦਾ, a servant, and that sovereignty belonged to the Khalsa and ultimately to the Divine. His was, in aspiration, the first concrete expression of the idea later voiced as ਰਾਜ ਕਰੇਗਾ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ — that the Khalsa shall rule in justice.

References
  • Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998.
  • Singh, Khushwant. A History of the Sikhs, Volume 1. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2004.
  • Banerjee, A. C. The Khalsa Raj. New Delhi: Abhinav Publications, 1985.

lessons.title: Resistance, Retreat, and Capture at Gurdaspur (1715)
lessons.summary: The Mughal counteroffensive, internal strains within the Sikh ranks, and the long siege that ended in Banda Singh's capture.
lessons.html:
The Mughal empire could not permit an independent Sikh power to consolidate in the Punjab. This lesson examines the imperial counteroffensive, the pressures it placed on Banda Singh's movement, and the prolonged siege at Gurdaspur that ended in his capture in December 1715.

The imperial response

Emperor Bahadur Shah I directed the full weight of the Mughal state against Banda Singh, ordering campaigns to crush the rising and issuing harsh measures against Sikhs generally. After Bahadur Shah's death, his successor Farrukh Siyar pursued the suppression with even greater determination, appointing capable commanders and committing large armies. Banda Singh and the Khalsa, holding a relatively small territory and lacking the resources of an empire, were forced onto the defensive. Lohgarh itself had to be abandoned under pressure, and the movement entered a difficult phase of mobile resistance in the hills and plains.

Internal strains

The Sikh ranks also experienced internal tensions during these years. Scholars note disagreements over leadership and over questions of practice and reverence. Some accounts describe a faction that came to be associated with Banda Singh's leadership and another that maintained the established Khalsa discipline; these divisions weakened the unified front needed to withstand the imperial onslaught. It is essential to approach this episode with care and humility: the sources reflect the strains of a community under existential pressure, and later traditions read these events in different ways. What is clear is that disunity, alongside overwhelming imperial force, made sustained resistance increasingly difficult.

  • External pressure: repeated large-scale Mughal campaigns under Farrukh Siyar.
  • Loss of base: the abandonment of Lohgarh and other strongholds.
  • Internal division: disagreements that fractured the movement's unity.

The siege of Gurdaspur

In 1715 Banda Singh and a devoted body of his companions took refuge in a fortified position at Gurdas Nangal, near Gurdaspur. The imperial army, commanded by Abd-us-Samad Khan, laid a tight siege. The defenders held out for many months under conditions of extreme deprivation. Contemporary and traditional accounts describe near-starvation within the fort: the besieged consumed whatever they could find and endured suffering of a severity that itself became part of the story of their steadfastness. Despite this, they did not surrender for a remarkably long time.

The fall

In December 1715 the fortress finally fell. Banda Singh Bahadur was captured along with several hundred of his surviving companions. The siege of Gurdaspur thus marked the end of the first Sikh state, but not the end of the story — for what followed in Delhi would transform military defeat into one of the most powerful testimonies of faith in Sikh history.

PhaseDevelopment
Imperial mobilizationBahadur Shah, then Farrukh Siyar, commit massive force
Loss of strongholdsLohgarh abandoned; movement on the defensive
Internal divisionStrains weaken Sikh unity
Siege of Gurdas NangalMonths of starvation and resistance
Capture (Dec. 1715)Banda Singh and companions taken prisoner
References
  • Singh, Ganda. Life of Banda Singh Bahadur. Amritsar: Khalsa College, 1935.
  • Singh, Teja, and Ganda Singh. A Short History of the Sikhs, Volume 1. Bombay: Orient Longmans, 1950.
  • Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998.

lessons.title: Martyrdom in Delhi (1716) and the Legacy of Banda Singh Bahadur
lessons.summary: The procession and executions in Delhi, Banda Singh's extraordinary steadfastness, and his enduring place in Sikh history.
lessons.html:
The final chapter of Banda Singh Bahadur's life unfolded in Delhi in 1716. This lesson examines the executions of the Sikh prisoners, Banda Singh's own martyrdom, and the meaning his witness has carried in the centuries since.

The procession to Delhi

After their capture at Gurdaspur, Banda Singh and his companions were brought in chains to Delhi early in 1716. Contemporary observers, including European travellers whose accounts Ganda Singh drew upon, described the grim spectacle: a long procession of captives paraded through the imperial capital, intended to display Mughal triumph and to terrorize any who might contemplate resistance. Banda Singh himself was placed on display in a degrading manner meant to humiliate the leader of the Sikh rising.

The executions

In Delhi the captured Sikhs were offered the choice between abandoning their faith and death. According to the accounts gathered by historians, day after day large numbers were executed publicly, and the prisoners met death with a steadfastness that astonished onlookers. The contemporary European witnesses recorded their amazement that the condemned showed no fear, did not beg for their lives, and even contended with one another for the honor of being executed first. This collective ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ (shaheedi) became one of the most powerful demonstrations of ਸਿਦਕ (sidak) — unwavering faith — in the historical record.

The martyrdom of Banda Singh

Banda Singh Bahadur was reserved for the end. In June 1716, after the execution of his companions, he was put to death with extreme cruelty. Tradition holds that he was first compelled to witness the killing of his young son and was then subjected to torture before his execution. Through all of this, the sources testify, he maintained his composure and his faith. When reportedly asked why God had permitted such a fate, he is said to have answered with serene acceptance of the Divine Will — a response that embodies the Sikh understanding of ਹੁਕਮ (Hukam), the acceptance of God's order. His martyrdom sealed the meaning of the name he had taken at Nanded: he died as the Guru's ਬੰਦਾ, a servant faithful to the end.

The legacy

Though his state was destroyed and his life ended in suffering, Banda Singh Bahadur's achievement endured in profound ways:

  • Proof of possibility: he demonstrated that the Khalsa could win and exercise sovereign political power, a precedent later realized in the rise of the Sikh misls and the kingdom of Maharaja Ranjit Singh.
  • Social revolution: his land reforms gave concrete form to Sikh ideals of equality and the dignity of labor, leaving a memory of just rule.
  • Moral example: the steadfastness of Banda Singh and his companions became a touchstone of faith and courage in the Sikh tradition.
  • Inspiration: the aspiration of ਰਾਜ ਕਰੇਗਾ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ, a just Khalsa rule, drew strength from his example.
DimensionEnduring contribution
PoliticalFirst Sikh sovereign state; precedent for later Sikh rule
Economic / socialAbolition of feudal landlordism; peasant proprietorship
Spiritual / moralMartyrdom as a witness of ਸਿਦਕ and acceptance of ਹੁਕਮ
Cultural memoryHonored as a foundational figure of Sikh sovereignty

Conclusion

From the ascetic Madho Das who declared himself a servant, to the sovereign who overturned feudal hierarchy, to the martyr who faced death without flinching, Banda Singh Bahadur compressed an extraordinary transformation into a brief span of years. His life linked the spiritual vision of the Gurus to its expression in just political and social order, and his death affirmed that this vision was worth any cost. He remains a defining figure in the Sikh understanding of sovereignty, justice, and faith.

References
  • Singh, Ganda. Life of Banda Singh Bahadur. Amritsar: Khalsa College, 1935.
  • Singh, Khushwant. A History of the Sikhs, Volume 1. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2004.
  • Dhavan, Purnima. When Sparrows Became Hawks. New York: Oxford University Press, 2011.
  • McLeod, W. H. The Sikhs: History, Religion, and Society. New York: Columbia University Press, 1989.

lessons.title: Framing the Debate Honestly
lessons.summary: Why meat, drink, and intoxicants are among the most contested questions in Sikh practice, and how to study them with scholarly honesty.
lessons.html:
Full course contents
  1. Framing the Debate Honestly
  2. What Gurbani Says About Meat
  3. Historical Sikh Practice Around Meat
  4. Alcohol in Gurbani
  5. Cannabis, Opium, and the Nihang Tradition
  6. The Sikh Rahit Maryada's Position

Few subjects generate as much heat among Sikhs as food and intoxicants. Ask whether a Sikh may eat meat, and you will hear confident, mutually contradictory answers — each presented as the obvious truth. The purpose of this course is not to settle the argument by decree but to lay out, with scholarly honesty, what the sources actually say: Gurbani, the historical record, the Rahit literature, and the living traditions of the Panth.

Why this is hard

Three different kinds of evidence are often blurred together in these debates:

  • Gurbani — the revealed word in Sri Guru Granth Sahib, which is the highest authority but addresses these matters in a spiritual rather than dietary-rulebook register.
  • History — what Sikhs have actually done across five centuries, which shows genuine diversity, not a single uniform practice.
  • Rahit — the codes of conduct, culminating in the 1945 Sikh Rahit Maryada, which set binding norms for the initiated (Amritdhari).

A claim that is true at one level can be false at another. Gurbani may decline to legislate a vegetarian diet while the Rahit still forbids a specific kind of meat; history may record meat-eating warriors while a particular sampradā maintains strict vegetarianism. Honest study holds all of these in view at once.

The temptation to read backward

A common error is to take one's present practice and read it back into the Gurus as if it were always self-evident. Vegetarian Sikhs sometimes assume the Gurus must have forbidden all meat; meat-eating Sikhs sometimes assume the Gurus must have endorsed it. The discipline of this course is to resist both reflexes and let the sources speak.

What we will and will not claim

We will distinguish clearly between (1) what is plainly stated, (2) what is widely held tradition, and (3) what is genuinely debated. Where the record is contested, we will say so rather than manufacture false certainty. The aim is a reader who can explain every major position fairly — including the one they disagree with.

References
Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford University Press, 2014.
Nesbitt, Eleanor. Sikhism: A Very Short Introduction. Oxford University Press, 2005.

lessons.title: What Gurbani Says About Meat
lessons.summary: Gurbani's treatment of flesh-eating, including the famous rebuke of those who argue over meat while ignoring inner purity.
lessons.html:
When people search Gurbani for a verdict on meat, they often expect a clean prohibition or permission. What they find instead is a sustained redirection: again and again the Guru's word turns the question away from the plate and toward the heart.

The rebuke of those who argue about flesh

In the Vār of Malar, Guru Nanak Sahib confronts those who make a great show of debating meat while neglecting the far weightier matters of cruelty, falsehood, and spiritual blindness. Gurbani teaches that only fools quarrel over flesh without understanding what flesh and what knowledge truly are — noting that the human being itself is conceived and formed in flesh, and that those who self-righteously condemn meat-eating are silent about the violence they do in other ways. The thrust is unmistakable: the obsession with the dietary detail is a distraction from real ethical and spiritual life.

This passage is the single most cited text in the meat debate, and it is frequently misused by both sides. It is not a license to eat without thought, and it is not a vegetarian manifesto. It is a rebuke of hypocrisy — of those who strain at the gnat of diet while swallowing the camel of cruelty and ego.

The deeper principle

Gurbani's repeated teaching is that purity and impurity are inward, not located in substances. The Guru's word holds that ritual notions of pollution miss the point: it is the corrupted mind, not the food, that defiles. This is consistent with the broader Sikh rejection of brahmanical purity codes that governed who could eat what, cooked by whom.

  • Gurbani relocates the moral question from what enters the mouth to what fills the heart.
  • It mocks performative dietary piety that coexists with greed, lust, and cruelty.
  • It refuses to make abstaining from meat a substitute for the inner discipline of ਨਾਮ (Naam).

What Gurbani does not do

Crucially, the Guru Granth Sahib does not issue an explicit, universal commandment either requiring or forbidding meat for all Sikhs. This silence is itself significant: it is why the question has remained open, and why later tradition and the Rahit had to address the matter the scripture left unlegislated. Honest readers on every side should concede this point.

References
Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. The Birth of the Khalsa: A Feminist Re-Memory of Sikh Identity. State University of New York Press, 2005.
McLeod, W. H. Sikhism. Penguin Books, 1997.

lessons.title: Historical Sikh Practice Around Meat
lessons.summary: The genuine diversity of Sikh dietary practice across history, the jhatka/halal distinction, and the contemporary debate.
lessons.html:
If Gurbani leaves the dietary question open, history shows the Panth living that openness out: both meat-eating and vegetarian traditions are authentically Sikh, and both can point to real lineage.

The meat-eating stream

The Khalsa was forged as a martial community, and meat features in many accounts of warrior life. The Nihang Singhs in particular maintained a tradition of ਝਟਕਾ meat, and chronicles of the eighteenth-century Khalsa describe hunting and the eating of game. For these traditions, meat was never a contradiction of Sikhi but a feature of a robust, self-reliant warrior ethic.

The vegetarian stream

At the same time, several respected institutions and lineages maintain strict vegetarianism. The langar served in gurdwaras worldwide is universally vegetarian — a deliberate choice so that people of every background and dietary scruple can eat together without exclusion. The Damdami Taksal, the broader Sant tradition, and many individual Sikhs hold vegetarianism to be the more consistent expression of compassion (ਦਇਆ, daya). This is not a fringe position; it is deeply rooted in the Panth.

Jhatka versus halal

One distinction nearly all traditions agree on is the rejection of ritually slaughtered meat. The contrast:

MethodMannerSikh status
ਝਟਕਾ (jhatka)Animal killed instantly with a single strokeThe form Sikhs associate with permitted meat where meat is eaten
Halal / ਕੁਠਾ (kuttha)Slow ritual slaughter with a religious invocation and bleeding-outForbidden; eating ਕੁਠਾ is one of the four Bajjar Kurahits

The rejection of ਕੁਠਾ is one of the clearest dietary rules in the Rahit. Historians link it both to compassion (a swift death versus a prolonged one) and to the Khalsa's assertion of independence from the religious rituals of the surrounding Mughal order. Note that this rule does not require Sikhs to eat meat — it governs which meat is forbidden if any is eaten.

The contemporary debate

Today the disagreement continues in good faith across traditions. Vegetarian Sikhs emphasize compassion and the langar example; meat-eating Sikhs emphasize Gurbani's refusal to legislate diet and the historical warrior tradition. Both can be sincere Sikhs. The honest conclusion is that this is an area of legitimate diversity, not heresy on either side — provided the Bajjar Kurahit against ਕੁਠਾ is respected by the initiated.

References
Singh, Khushwant. A History of the Sikhs, Volume 1: 1469–1839. Oxford University Press, 2004.
McLeod, W. H. The Chaupa Singh Rahit-nama. University of Otago Press, 1987.
Nesbitt, Eleanor. Sikhism: A Very Short Introduction. Oxford University Press, 2005.

lessons.title: Alcohol in Gurbani
lessons.summary: How the Guru Granth Sahib treats wine and the state of intoxication, and the metaphor of being intoxicated by Naam.
lessons.html:
On alcohol, Gurbani is markedly less ambiguous than on meat. Where the scripture declines to legislate diet, it speaks directly and repeatedly against the drink that destroys human reason.

Wine that destroys discernment

Gurbani names ਮਦ (mad) — wine or liquor — as that which clouds the intellect and robs a person of discernment between right and wrong. The Guru's word teaches that one who drinks such wine loses the capacity to distinguish the worthy from the worthless, behaves wrongly, and earns disgrace in the Court of the Lord. The objection is not ceremonial; it is functional. Liquor is condemned because of what it does to the mind that ought to be fixed on the Divine.

The state of intoxication is the target

This is the key that unlocks the whole course. Gurbani's concern is consistently the state of intoxication — the disordered, God-forgetting mind — rather than a list of forbidden molecules. The drunken state severs the connection between the human being and the Lord; it is the opposite of the alert, remembering, disciplined mind that Sikhi cultivates.

The true intoxication

Strikingly, Gurbani repurposes the very language of intoxication to describe the spiritual goal. The Guru's word speaks of a wine that never wears off — the intoxication of Naam, of divine love, of the Lord's presence. This is the deliberate contrast: worldly liquor steals reason and leads to ruin, while the true wine of God's remembrance gives an ecstasy that elevates rather than degrades. The metaphor only works because the literal drink is understood as harmful.

  • Worldly ਮਦ: clouds the mind, destroys discernment, brings disgrace.
  • The wine of Naam: a sober ecstasy, an intoxication that clarifies rather than confuses.

The lesson for practice is direct. Sikhi does not seek to numb or escape the mind but to awaken and steady it. Anything that dims that awareness — and liquor is the paradigm case — works against the entire spiritual project.

References
Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. The Birth of the Khalsa: A Feminist Re-Memory of Sikh Identity. State University of New York Press, 2005.
McLeod, W. H. Sikhism. Penguin Books, 1997.

lessons.title: Cannabis, Opium, and the Nihang Tradition
lessons.summary: The contested history of sukha/bhang among Nihang Singhs, the rejection of opium, and the principle that unifies the cases.
lessons.html:
This is the most genuinely contested terrain in the course, and it must be handled with care and fairness. The Nihang tradition complicates any simple claim that Sikhs have always rejected every intoxicant.

Sukha among the Nihangs

The Nihang Singhs — the order of warrior-ascetics who preserve some of the oldest Khalsa martial customs — have historically prepared ਸੁਖਾ (sukha), a cannabis (ਭੰਗ, bhang) preparation. In Nihang usage it was traditionally framed not as recreation but as a battlefield aid: a means to endure pain, cold, and fear, taken with prayer and within a disciplined martial order. Some Nihangs argue it sharpened rather than clouded the warrior's resolve and was never meant to produce stupor.

Why it is debated

Mainstream Sikh opinion, and the modern Rahit, reject this practice. The objections are serious:

  • Gurbani's principle condemns the state of intoxication, and cannabis is an intoxicant by any ordinary definition.
  • The Sikh Rahit Maryada lists intoxicants among prohibitions for the initiated without carving out an exception for sukha.
  • Critics argue the battlefield rationale, whatever its historical role, does not transfer to peacetime and is easily abused.

Defenders reply that sukha is a narrow, ritualized, traditional practice of a specific order, not a general endorsement of drug use, and that it should be understood in its own martial context. The honest position is that this is a real, unresolved internal debate — not something to be wished away in either direction. We present it plainly: a minority traditional practice, rejected by the mainstream and by the consensus Rahit, defended by some within the Nihang lineage on contextual grounds.

Opium: no sanction

By contrast, there is no comparable defense of ਫੀਮ (feem, opium). Opium carries no religious sanction in any mainstream tradition. It is associated with addiction, decay, and the ruin of body and mind, and the Sikh ethical tradition warns against it without ambiguity. Where sukha is debated, opium is not.

The unifying principle

Across all these cases — alcohol, cannabis, opium — the deepest Sikh principle is consistent: the problem is the loss of the alert, God-remembering mind. Substances are condemned to the degree they produce that loss. This is why opium is unanimously rejected, why alcohol is condemned in Gurbani, and why even the contested sukha sits under suspicion. The standard is the state of the mind, and the standard does not change.

References
Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford University Press, 2014.
Nesbitt, Eleanor. Sikhism: A Very Short Introduction. Oxford University Press, 2005.

lessons.title: The Sikh Rahit Maryada's Position
lessons.summary: What the 1945 consensus code binds the Amritdhari to, the four Bajjar Kurahits, and how scripture, history, and Rahit fit together.
lessons.html:
Having surveyed Gurbani and history, we arrive at the code that actually binds the initiated: the ਰਹਿਤ ਮਰਯਾਦਾ, the Sikh Rahit Maryada, published by the SGPC in 1945 after long deliberation across the Panth's scholarly and institutional bodies. It is the closest thing Sikhs have to a consensus code of conduct.

The four cardinal prohibitions

For the Amritdhari — the formally initiated Khalsa Sikh — the Rahit defines four Bajjar Kurahits, grave violations that break the initiation and require re-taking Amrit:

Bajjar KurahitMeaning
Cutting or removing hairDishonoring ਕੇਸ (kes), the unshorn hair
Eating ਕੁਠਾ (kuttha)Consuming ritually (halal) slaughtered meat
Adultery / illicit relationsViolating the discipline of ਕਾਮ in conduct
Using tobacco / intoxicantsConsuming substances that intoxicate the mind

What this means for intoxicants

On drink and drugs the Rahit is firm: the Amritdhari is to abstain from intoxicants. This codifies into binding practice the principle we traced through Gurbani — that the God-remembering mind must not be clouded. Alcohol, tobacco, cannabis, and opium all fall under this. The contested Nihang sukha tradition stands outside this consensus, which is precisely why it remains controversial rather than normative.

What this means for meat

Note carefully what the Rahit does and does not say. It forbids ਕੁਠਾ — ritually slaughtered meat — as a Bajjar Kurahit. It does not impose universal vegetarianism on all Sikhs. This is why the meat debate remains open in a way the intoxicants question does not: the consensus code legislates the manner of slaughter, not abstinence from meat itself. Individual Sikhs, sampradās, and institutions then make their own further choices, and both vegetarian and jhatka traditions remain within the bounds of the Rahit.

Bringing the three levels together

  • Gurbani redirects the meat question inward and condemns the state of intoxication.
  • History shows authentic diversity on meat and a contested minority practice (sukha) on cannabis.
  • The Rahit binds the initiated: no ਕੁਠਾ, no intoxicants — while leaving the broader meat question to conscience and tradition.

A reader who holds these three levels together, without collapsing them into a single slogan, has understood the subject. That is the goal of honest study: not to win the argument, but to state every credible position so fairly that those who hold it would recognize themselves in your account.

References
Shromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee. Sikh Rahit Maryada: The Code of Sikh Conduct and Conventions. SGPC, Amritsar, 1945.
McLeod, W. H. The Chaupa Singh Rahit-nama. University of Otago Press, 1987.
Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford University Press, 2014.
