courses.title: Who Am I? Sikh Identity in the Diaspora
courses.summary: A course for young Sikhs growing up in Canada, the UK, US and Australia: what Sikh identity really is, cultural vs practicing Sikhi, Kes and Dastaar, peer pressure, Chardi Kala, and building your own bond with Gurbani.
outcomes: Explain why Sikh identity is fundamentally a relationship with ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ (Waheguru) and not merely an ethnicity, language, or cuisine
Distinguish between a cultural Sikh and a practicing Sikh, and locate yourself honestly without shame on that spectrum
Describe the meaning of ਕੇਸ (Kes) and the ਦਸਤਾਰ (Dastaar) and articulate why they become identity flashpoints in the diaspora
Apply the principle of ਚੜ੍ਹਦੀ ਕਲਾ (Chardi Kala) to navigate peer pressure, bullying, and code-switching
Find and build authentic Sikh community both online and offline, including ਸੰਗਤ (Sangat) and camps
Begin a personal relationship with ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ (Gurbani) regardless of how much your family practices

terms.m: Waheguru — the Sikh name for the Divine; the Wondrous Enlightener. The relationship a Sikh has with Waheguru is the core of Sikh identity.
Sikh — a learner or disciple; one who follows the Guru. The word names a way of life, not an ethnic group.
Guru — the one who brings light out of darkness; for Sikhs, the eternal Guru is Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji and Guru Khalsa Panth.
Kes — unshorn hair, kept as a gift of the Creator and one of the Five Kakaars of the Khalsa.
Dastaar — the turban; a Sikh's crown, a marker of sovereignty, dignity, and commitment, worn by Sikhs of all genders.
Chardi Kala — ever-rising spirit; relentless optimism and high spirits rooted in trust in Waheguru, even in hardship.
Sangat — the holy congregation; the community of seekers whose company shapes and strengthens a Sikh.
Gurbani — the Guru's Word; the sacred compositions within Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji and Guru-given Bani.
Khalsa — the pure, sovereign order of initiated Sikhs created by Guru Gobind Singh Ji in 1699.
Haumai — ego or self-centredness; the inner barrier Gurbani teaches us to dissolve to draw close to Waheguru.
Hukam — the Divine Order or Will; living in acceptance of and harmony with Waheguru's command.

lessons.title: Two Worlds: Being Sikh at Home and Something Else Everywhere Else
lessons.summary: Names the everyday tension of diaspora youth and reframes identity as something you build, not just inherit.
lessons.html:
If you are reading this, you may know the feeling well. At home you are a Sikh: there is Gurbani playing in the kitchen, a Nishan Sahib in the corner, Punjabi spoken at the table, langar memories from the Gurdwara. Then you step out the front door, and you become something else: a student, a teammate, an employee, often the only Sikh in the room. You learn to switch, sometimes without even noticing. This course is written for you — the young Sikh growing up in Canada, the United Kingdom, the United States, Australia, or anywhere outside Punjab.

The question in the title, Who am I?, is not a crisis to be ashamed of. It is one of the oldest and most honest spiritual questions there is. Gurbani itself opens the human heart with this exact wondering. Asking it does not make you a bad Sikh; refusing to ask it leaves your identity on autopilot, inherited but never owned.

Full course contents
  1. Two Worlds: Being Sikh at Home and Something Else Everywhere Else
  2. What Sikh Identity Actually Is: A Relationship, Not an Ethnicity
  3. Cultural Sikh or Practicing Sikh? An Honest Spectrum
  4. Kes and Dastaar: The Identity You Wear
  5. Peer Pressure, Code-Switching, and Chardi Kala
  6. Finding Your Sangat and Building Your Own Bond with Gurbani

The diaspora experience is normal, not broken

For more than a century Sikhs have lived far from Punjab — early settlers in British Columbia and California, the post-war wave to Britain, and growing communities across Australia and beyond. Today a large share of the world's Sikhs are born outside Punjab. If you feel split between two worlds, you are not a rare exception. You are part of a global generation, and the people who came before you wrestled with the same questions and built Gurdwaras, camps, and societies precisely so you would not have to do it alone.

Why "two worlds" can become one

The goal of this course is not to make you choose between being Sikh and belonging to the country you live in. That is a false choice. A grounded Sikh identity is portable: it travels with you into the classroom, the workplace, and the friendship group. The aim is to move from a borrowed identity ("I'm Sikh because my family is") to an owned one ("I'm Sikh because I have chosen this relationship with Waheguru"). When the identity is owned, the two worlds stop fighting each other.

What we will and will not do

  • We will talk honestly about peer pressure, cutting hair, the turban, racism, and feeling embarrassed — nothing is off-limits.
  • We will treat you as capable of building your own practice, even if your family is not very observant.
  • We will not shame anyone for where they are on their journey. Gurmat invites; it does not bully.
  • We will not reduce Sikhi to food, festivals, or being "Punjabi" — those are part of the culture, but they are not the heart.

How to take this course

Read one lesson at a time. After each, sit for two minutes and ask yourself the honest version of its question. Keep a note on your phone of anything that lands. By Lesson 6 you will not just know more about Sikh identity — you will have begun to build your own.

References
Nesbitt, Eleanor. Sikhism: A Very Short Introduction. 2nd ed. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2016.
Jakobsh, Doris R. Sikhism. Honolulu: University of Hawai'i Press, 2012.
Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. Sikhism: An Introduction. London: I.B. Tauris, 2011.

lessons.title: What Sikh Identity Actually Is: A Relationship, Not an Ethnicity
lessons.summary: Establishes that Sikhi is a chosen relationship with Waheguru open to anyone, distinct from Punjabi ethnicity.
lessons.html:
Many young people in the diaspora absorb a quiet misunderstanding: that being Sikh means being Punjabi — speaking the language, eating the food, having the surname. This is understandable, because culture and faith have travelled together. But it is not what the word ਸਿੱਖ (Sikh) means, and getting this clear changes everything about how you see yourself.

The word itself

The word ਸਿੱਖ comes from the idea of a learner or disciple — one who learns from the ਗੁਰੂ (Guru). A Sikh is defined not by blood or geography but by a relationship: a learner walking toward the Light. This is why Sikhi has never been an ethnic religion. From its earliest days the faith welcomed people of every background, caste, and region. The Guru Granth Sahib Ji itself includes the voices of saints from many communities and social ranks, side by side as one.

The centre: a relationship with Waheguru

At the heart of Sikh identity is a bond with ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ (Waheguru) — the One Creator. Guru Nanak Sahib Ji begins the Mool Mantar by declaring the Oneness of that Creator: ੴ (Ik Onkar), One Universal Creator. Everything else in Sikh life — honest work, sharing, service, the turban, the Khalsa — grows out of and points back to that central relationship. Gurbani teaches that the purpose of human life is to remember and merge with that One, dissolving the wall of ਹਉਮੈ (haumai), the ego.

Why this matters for diaspora youth

If Sikh identity were ethnicity, then losing the language, marrying outside the community, or not liking Bhangra would chip away at your Sikhi. But it is not ethnicity. That means:

  • You can be a complete Sikh even if your Punjabi is weak — the relationship with Waheguru is not in a single language.
  • You do not need a Punjabi face, surname, or passport to belong. Converts and Sikhs of every background are full Sikhs.
  • No one can take your Sikhi from you by mocking your accent or your food. The core is internal and chosen.

Culture, ethnicity, and faith: keeping them straight

LayerWhat it isCan you be Sikh without it?
Ethnicity (Punjabi)A people, region, and bloodlineYes — Sikhs exist of every ethnicity
Culture (food, dress, Bhangra, language)Shared customs, often beautiful, often regionalYes — culture enriches but does not define Sikhi
Faith (relationship with Waheguru, Guru, Gurbani)The core: discipleship and devotionNo — this is Sikh identity

Notice the freedom in this. You get to love and keep the parts of Punjabi culture that nourish you, let go of the parts that were only ever custom, and still stand on solid ground — because your identity is anchored in something deeper than custom.

References
Singh, Pashaura. The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2000.
Mandair, Arvind-Pal Singh. Sikhism: A Guide for the Perplexed. London: Bloomsbury, 2013.
Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. Sikhism: An Introduction. London: I.B. Tauris, 2011.

lessons.title: Cultural Sikh or Practicing Sikh? An Honest Spectrum
lessons.summary: Maps the spectrum from cultural to practicing Sikh without shame, and frames practice as a direction, not a label.
lessons.html:
Almost every diaspora Sikh has heard, or used, the phrase "I'm not really religious, I'm more of a cultural Sikh." It is worth slowing down and asking what that actually means, because the label can quietly close a door that Gurmat keeps wide open.

Two honest descriptions

A cultural Sikh usually means someone connected to Sikhi through family, festivals, food, weddings, and a general respect for the Gurus — but with little personal practice: not much Nitnem (daily prayer), occasional Gurdwara visits, limited reading of Gurbani. A practicing Sikh means someone who actively builds the relationship: doing some form of daily Simran or Nitnem, reading and trying to understand Gurbani, attending Sangat, and living the values on purpose.

These are not two boxes with a wall between them. They are two points on a single road, and almost everyone moves along it over a lifetime — sometimes forward, sometimes back, then forward again.

Why the label can trap you

Calling yourself "just cultural" can feel humble, but it can also become an excuse to never start. It can quietly say: practice is for other people, the really religious ones, not me. Gurmat does not recognise that division. The Guru's door is open to everyone, exactly as they are, today. You do not need to be "ready" or "pure enough" first. Gurbani teaches that the Divine is found by the humble seeker, not the already-perfect.

A spectrum, not a verdict

MarkerMore culturalMore practicing
Connection to GurbaniHears it, rarely reads itReads, reflects, applies it
Daily practiceLittle or noneSome Simran / Nitnem
SangatFamily events onlySeeks it out regularly
ValuesRespected in theoryPractised on purpose

The point of this table is not to grade yourself and feel bad. It is to see honestly where you are so you can take one step. Sikhi is measured by direction, not arrival.

The smallest real step

  • If you do nothing now, start with one line of Gurbani a day — read it, look up the meaning, sit with it.
  • If you already read, add one minute of Simran, quietly repeating ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ.
  • If you already do that, deepen it: understand why, not just what.

Wherever you are, you are a Sikh — a learner. Learners are, by definition, not finished. That is not a failing; it is the whole point of the word.

References
Nesbitt, Eleanor. Sikhism: A Very Short Introduction. 2nd ed. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2016.
McLeod, W. H. Sikhism. London: Penguin Books, 1997.
Jakobsh, Doris R. Sikhism. Honolulu: University of Hawai'i Press, 2012.

lessons.title: Kes and Dastaar: The Identity You Wear
lessons.summary: Explains the meaning of unshorn hair and the turban and why they become public flashpoints in the diaspora.
lessons.html:
For most parts of identity, you can choose when to reveal them. You can mention you are Sikh, or not, depending on the room. But ਕੇਸ (Kes) and the ਦਸਤਾਰ (Dastaar) are different: they speak before you do. They make your Sikhi visible and unhideable. That is exactly why they carry so much weight — and so much pressure — in the diaspora.

What Kes means

Kes is unshorn hair, kept across the whole body as a gift of the Creator. It is one of the Five Kakaars (the five articles of faith) given to the Khalsa by Guru Gobind Singh Ji in 1699. The principle behind it is acceptance: living in ਹੁਕਮ (Hukam), the Divine Order, by keeping the form the Creator gave rather than cutting and reshaping it to fit fashion. Kes is not vanity; it is the opposite — a daily, embodied trust in Waheguru.

What the Dastaar means

The Dastaar is a Sikh's crown. Historically, turbans were reserved for royalty and the elite; the Gurus gave the turban to every Sikh — including the poor and the oppressed — as a declaration that every human being is sovereign and equal in dignity. The Dastaar is worn by Sikhs of all genders. It signals commitment, responsibility, and the refusal to hide. When a Sikh wears a Dastaar, they are publicly accountable: they cannot melt into the crowd when something is wrong.

Why these become flashpoints abroad

In Punjab, a turban is ordinary. In a school in Toronto, Birmingham, California, or Melbourne, it can make you the most visible person in the building. This brings real pressures:

  • Curiosity and ignorance — endless questions, sometimes kind, sometimes mocking.
  • Bullying and racism — being singled out, having a patka pulled, being confused with groups you have nothing to do with.
  • The pressure to cut — "you'd look better," "you'd fit in," "it's just hair." The cut is often framed as freedom; in truth it is usually surrender to someone else's gaze.

Reframing the pressure

Here is the shift that helps: your Kes and Dastaar are not a burden you carry for others to judge — they are a sovereignty you carry over their judgement. Every Sikh who kept their form under pressure, from the Sahibzaade to ordinary students standing alone in a hallway, turned visibility into strength rather than shame. You are allowed to find it hard. You are also allowed to find it powerful.

The pressure saysGurmat reframes it as
"You'd fit in better."Fitting in is not the goal; standing in dignity is.
"It's just hair."It's a relationship with Hukam, lived on the body.
"People stare at you."You wear a crown; crowns are meant to be seen.

Whatever your current relationship to Kes and Dastaar — keeping, questioning, or rebuilding it — understanding their meaning lets you decide from knowledge instead of from pressure.

References
Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. Sikhism: An Introduction. London: I.B. Tauris, 2011.
Mandair, Arvind-Pal Singh. Sikhism: A Guide for the Perplexed. London: Bloomsbury, 2013.
Nesbitt, Eleanor. Sikhism: A Very Short Introduction. 2nd ed. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2016.

lessons.title: Peer Pressure, Code-Switching, and Chardi Kala
lessons.summary: Tackles fitting in, code-switching, and bullying through the Sikh principle of ever-rising spirit.
lessons.html:
Every young person code-switches — you speak one way with friends, another with family, another in an interview. That is normal and healthy. The danger for a diaspora Sikh is when code-switching quietly becomes self-erasing: hiding your Sikhi, laughing along at jokes about it, or pretending it does not matter so that you can belong. This lesson is about staying whole under pressure, using the Sikh principle of ਚੜ੍ਹਦੀ ਕਲਾ (Chardi Kala).

The pressure is real — name it honestly

Diaspora Sikh youth face pressures that are easy to minimise but heavy to live: being the only Sikh in a friend group, being asked to explain or defend things you are still figuring out, racism after global events you had nothing to do with, and the everyday pull to drink, party, or cut your hair "like everyone else." Pretending these do not exist does not help. Gurmat is not naive about hardship; it is built for it.

What Chardi Kala actually is

Chardi Kala is often translated as "high spirits" or "ever-rising spirit." It is not toxic positivity or pretending nothing hurts. It is a settled inner buoyancy rooted in trust that Waheguru's Hukam is at work even in difficulty. Sikh history is full of it: people who faced loss and even death and still rose in spirit rather than collapsing in bitterness. The Sikh Ardas remembers immense sacrifice and still ends asking for Sarbat da Bhala — the well-being of all. That is Chardi Kala: undefeated goodwill.

From code-switching to integrity

The goal is not to be loud or confrontational everywhere. It is integrity — being one person, not a hidden Sikh and a public stranger. Practical moves:

  • Decide in advance. Know your lines before the moment comes (drinking, hiding your identity, joining in mockery). Decisions made under pressure usually go the wrong way.
  • Answer questions calmly, not defensively. "It's part of my faith" is a complete, confident sentence. You do not owe anyone a debate.
  • Find one ally. One friend who respects your Sikhi changes a whole room. You do not need the crowd; you need an anchor.
  • Separate mockery from curiosity. Most questions are curiosity. Meet them with patience and you turn a flashpoint into respect.

When it is bullying or racism

Chardi Kala does not mean tolerating abuse silently. Sikhi pairs spiritual height with the duty to stand against injustice — for yourself and others. Report it, tell a trusted adult, lean on your Sangat. Standing up for your dignity is Sikhi, not a departure from it.

Reaction under pressureChardi Kala response
Hide my Sikhi to fit inStay whole; let people meet the real me
Get bitter and angry at everyoneStay rooted; act for fairness without losing goodwill
Collapse and feel ashamedRise in spirit; my dignity is not up for a vote

Chardi Kala is a muscle. Every small moment you choose integrity over hiding, it grows — and the next moment gets easier.

References
Singh, Khushwant. A History of the Sikhs, Volume 1: 1469-1839. 2nd ed. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2004.
Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. Sikhism: An Introduction. London: I.B. Tauris, 2011.
Jakobsh, Doris R. Sikhism. Honolulu: University of Hawai'i Press, 2012.

lessons.title: Finding Your Sangat and Building Your Own Bond with Gurbani
lessons.summary: Shows how to find community online and offline and start a personal relationship with Gurbani independent of family.
lessons.html:
You have seen that Sikh identity is a relationship with Waheguru, that it sits on a spectrum without shame, that Kes and Dastaar are sovereignty rather than burden, and that Chardi Kala keeps you whole under pressure. The final question is the most practical: how do I actually build this, especially if I'm starting mostly on my own? Two pillars do the heavy lifting: ਸੰਗਤ (Sangat) and ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ (Gurbani).

Why Sangat matters

Gurmat teaches that we become like the company we keep. Trying to grow a Sikh identity entirely alone, surrounded only by people who do not share it, is swimming upstream every single day. Sangat — the company of fellow seekers — does not make you weak; it makes the upstream swim survivable and even joyful. You are not meant to do this alone, and you do not have to.

Finding Sangat offline

  • The Gurdwara — go beyond family events; sit in Kirtan, eat in Pangat at langar, get to know people your age.
  • Sikh youth camps and retreats — across Canada, the UK, US, and Australia these are where many diaspora Sikhs first feel "these are my people."
  • University Sikh societies — if you are heading to university, this is one of the fastest ways to find lifelong Sangat.
  • Local Simran or Gurbani groups — small, regular, and often more sustaining than big events.

Finding Sangat online

The diaspora is spread out, and the internet is a genuine gift here. Reliable Gurbani resources, recorded Katha (explanation), Kirtan, and online courses such as this one let you build knowledge from anywhere. Online communities can connect you with Sikhs who understand your exact context. Two cautions: choose sources rooted in Gurmat rather than rumour, and let online connection lead you toward in-person Sangat, not replace it forever.

Building your own bond with Gurbani — regardless of family

This is the freedom at the centre of this whole course: your relationship with Gurbani does not depend on how much your family practices. Many young Sikhs become the most connected person in their household, and that is not disloyal — it is the Guru's door being open to you, directly.

StepWhat it looks like
1. Start small and dailyOne line or one Shabad a day, read with its meaning
2. Understand, don't just reciteUse translations and trusted Katha to grasp the message
3. Add SimranOne quiet minute of ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ, growing over time
4. Apply itCarry one idea into your day — patience, honesty, gratitude
5. Anchor in SangatShare and grow it with others, online or in person

Bringing it together: Who am I?

You began this course with a question. Here is the answer Gurmat offers: I am a Sikh — a learner — in a chosen, growing relationship with Waheguru. My identity is not my postcode, my accent, or other people's approval. I carry it whole into every room. You do not have to have it all figured out. You only have to keep walking, one Shabad and one breath at a time, in Chardi Kala.

References
Singh, Pashaura. The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2000.
Nesbitt, Eleanor. Sikhism: A Very Short Introduction. 2nd ed. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2016.
Mandair, Arvind-Pal Singh. Sikhism: A Guide for the Perplexed. London: Bloomsbury, 2013.

courses.title: Sikhs in Canada: From Komagata Maru to a Global Community
courses.summary: A history of Sikhs in Canada, from the first BC pioneers and the 1914 Komagata Maru tragedy through Ghadar activism, post-war immigration, the Air India bombing, and today's 770,000-strong community.
outcomes: Trace the arrival of the first Sikh pioneers (ਪੰਜਾਬੀ Punjabi labourers) to British Columbia in the early 1900s and the discriminatory laws they faced
Explain the events, causes, and aftermath of the 1914 Komagata Maru tragedy and its meaning for racial-exclusion policy in Canada
Describe the rise of the Ghadar Party and the link between diaspora labour, anti-colonial politics, and Sikh identity
Summarise the post-WWII immigration waves that transformed the size and shape of the Sikh-Canadian community
Discuss the 1985 Air India bombing, its victims, the failed prosecutions, and its complex legacy for the community
Evaluate the modern Sikh-Canadian community's institutions, including the ਗੁਰਦੁਆਰਾ gurdwara as a community anchor, and its growing political participation

terms.m: Gurdwara; literally 'the Guru's door,' a Sikh place of worship and community hub housing the Guru Granth Sahib
Langar; the free communal kitchen and shared meal open to all, central to gurdwara life
Ghadar; 'mutiny' or 'revolt,' the name of the early-20th-century diaspora anti-colonial movement
Punjab; the northwest South Asian homeland from which the great majority of early Sikh migrants came
Seva; selfless service to the community, a core Sikh value expressed through gurdwara and civic work
Amritdhari; an initiated Sikh who has taken Amrit and keeps the full Khalsa rehat (discipline)
Dastaar; the turban, a visible article of Sikh faith that has been central to Canadian accommodation debates

references: Johnston, Hugh. The Voyage of the Komagata Maru: The Sikh Challenge to Canada's Colour Bar. Vancouver: UBC Press, 2014.
Buchignani, Norman, Doreen M. Indra, and Ram Srivastava. Continuous Journey: A Social History of South Asians in Canada. Toronto: McClelland and Stewart, 1985.
Nayar, Kamala Elizabeth. The Sikh Diaspora in Vancouver: Three Generations amid Tradition, Modernity, and Multiculturalism. Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 2004.

Singh, Jaskaran. The Air India Bombing: A Canadian Tragedy. (Commission of Inquiry into the Investigation of the Bombing of Air India Flight 182, Report of the Honourable John C. Major.) Ottawa: Public Works and Government Services Canada, 2010.
Ramnath, Maia. Haj to Utopia: How the Ghadar Movement Charted Global Radicalism and Attempted to Overthrow the British Empire. Berkeley: University of California Press, 2011.

lessons.title: The First Pioneers: Sikhs Arrive in British Columbia
lessons.summary: How and why the earliest Sikh migrants reached Canada's west coast in the early 1900s, and the hostility they encountered.
lessons.html:
This course tells the story of one of Canada's largest and most visible faith communities. With more than 770,000 Sikhs counted in recent census data, Canada is home to one of the largest Sikh populations outside India. But that community began with a few thousand pioneers who crossed the Pacific more than a century ago, into a country that did not want them. This first lesson sets the scene.

Full course contents
  1. The First Pioneers: Sikhs Arrive in British Columbia
  2. The Komagata Maru: A Ship and a Challenge
  3. The Ghadar Party: Diaspora and Revolution
  4. Opening the Doors: Post-War Immigration Waves
  5. Air India Flight 182: Tragedy and Its Long Shadow
  6. A Global Community: Gurdwaras, Citizenship, and Power

Why they came

The first Sikhs to reach Canada arrived around 1897 and in growing numbers after 1903. Many were former soldiers of the British Indian Army who had passed through Canada on their way home from Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee, and who carried back word of work and high wages on the Pacific coast. Most came from the farming districts of central ਪੰਜਾਬ Punjab, especially the Doaba region between the Beas and Sutlej rivers, which remains the heartland of the Sikh diaspora to this day.

They found work in the resource economy of British Columbia: in sawmills and lumber camps, on the railways, and in land-clearing. They were overwhelmingly young men, intending at first to earn money and return home. Pooling wages, living frugally in shared bunkhouses, and sending remittances to Punjab, they formed the seed of a permanent community.

A hostile reception

White settler society on the coast reacted with alarm to all Asian immigration. Sikhs, alongside Chinese and Japanese migrants, were targets of an organised exclusion movement. Newspapers and politicians spoke of a "Hindoo invasion" (a careless label that lumped all South Asians together regardless of religion). In 1907 anti-Asian riots swept Vancouver.

  • In 1907, British Columbia stripped "Hindus" of the right to vote provincially, which also barred them from many professions and from the federal franchise.
  • Families were effectively prevented from joining the men, keeping the community a "bachelor society" for decades.
  • Employment, housing, and public services were routinely segregated.

The first gurdwara

Despite this, the pioneers built institutions. In 1908 they established a ਗੁਰਦੁਆਰਾ gurdwara on Second Avenue in Vancouver, one of the earliest in North America, followed soon by others in Victoria, Abbotsford, and New Westminster. The Abbotsford gurdwara (1911) is the oldest still in continuous use in Canada and is a National Historic Site. These gurdwaras were more than places of worship: they were the political, social, and welfare centres of a besieged community, the place where ਲੰਗਰ langar was served and where strategy against discriminatory laws was debated.

The "continuous journey" rule

The central legal weapon against Sikh immigration was the Continuous Journey Regulation of 1908. It barred entry to anyone who had not travelled to Canada by a "continuous journey" from their country of birth on a through ticket. Since no shipping line offered a direct, uninterrupted passage from India to Canada (the government quietly pressured the lines to ensure this), the rule shut the door on Punjabi immigration without ever naming Indians explicitly. This seemingly neutral regulation is the key to understanding the crisis that follows in Lesson 2.

References
Buchignani, Norman, Doreen M. Indra, and Ram Srivastava. Continuous Journey: A Social History of South Asians in Canada. Toronto: McClelland and Stewart, 1985.
Nayar, Kamala Elizabeth. The Sikh Diaspora in Vancouver. Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 2004.

lessons.title: The Komagata Maru: A Ship and a Challenge
lessons.summary: The 1914 voyage that deliberately tested Canada's exclusion laws, the two-month standoff in Vancouver harbour, and the deadly aftermath.
lessons.html:
In 1914 a single chartered ship turned the abstract injustice of the Continuous Journey Regulation into a human drama that the world could watch. The story of the Komagata Maru is the defining episode of early Sikh-Canadian history.

A deliberate test of the law

Gurdit Singh Sandhu, a Sikh businessman based in Singapore, chartered a Japanese steamship, the Komagata Maru, expressly to challenge the continuous-journey rule. If passengers could not travel directly from India, he reasoned, he would charter a ship to carry them directly. The vessel left Hong Kong in April 1914 and, picking up passengers at several ports, arrived in Vancouver's Burrard Inlet on 23 May 1914 carrying 376 passengers, the great majority of them Sikhs, along with a smaller number of Muslims and Hindus.

Two months in the harbour

Canadian authorities refused to let the passengers land. For two months the ship sat at anchor in Vancouver harbour, its passengers held aboard in worsening conditions, denied adequate food and water. A "Shore Committee" of local Sikhs, led by figures such as Husain Rahim and Bhag Singh, raised funds, hired lawyers, and fought a test case through the British Columbia courts. The courts ruled against the passengers, upholding the exclusion orders.

  • The passengers endured shortages of provisions deliberately used as pressure to force the ship to leave.
  • An attempt by police to board and seize the vessel was repelled by the passengers.
  • The navy cruiser HMCS Rainbow was eventually brought in to compel the ship's departure.

The forced return and the killings at Budge Budge

On 23 July 1914, after exactly two months, the Komagata Maru was escorted out of Canadian waters and forced to return across the Pacific. Only about two dozen passengers (returning residents who could prove prior domicile) had been allowed to land. The ship reached Budge Budge, near Calcutta, in late September 1914. There, British colonial authorities, suspicious that the returning passengers were radicalised, tried to force them onto a train to Punjab. In the confrontation that followed, troops opened fire. Roughly nineteen passengers were killed, and many others were arrested or interned. The course summary's phrasing that "most were killed" overstates the death toll; the precise figure was about nineteen dead, but many of the survivors faced imprisonment, internment, or surveillance for years, so the human cost extended far beyond the immediate killings.

Why it mattered

The Komagata Maru exposed the racial logic at the heart of Canadian immigration policy and of imperial citizenship. The passengers were, in law, British subjects, yet were denied entry to a British dominion purely on the grounds of race. The episode radicalised the diaspora, feeding directly into the Ghadar movement examined in Lesson 3.

Apology and memory

The injustice was formally acknowledged generations later. The Government of British Columbia apologised in 2008, and in 2016 Prime Minister Justin Trudeau delivered a full apology in the House of Commons. Memorials now stand in Vancouver's Coal Harbour and elsewhere, ensuring the episode is remembered as a foundational chapter in Canada's reckoning with its exclusionary past.

References
Johnston, Hugh. The Voyage of the Komagata Maru: The Sikh Challenge to Canada's Colour Bar. Vancouver: UBC Press, 2014.

lessons.title: The Ghadar Party: Diaspora and Revolution
lessons.summary: How exclusion and humiliation on the Pacific coast helped fuel a transnational anti-colonial movement.
lessons.html:
The same discrimination that produced the Komagata Maru crisis also radicalised the diaspora. Out of the mills and farms of the North American Pacific coast emerged the Ghadar movement, a remarkable attempt by overseas Indians to overthrow British rule.

Origins on the Pacific coast

The word ਗ਼ਦਰ ghadar means "mutiny" or "revolt." The Ghadar Party (often dated to 1913) was founded among Punjabi migrant workers and students along the west coast of the United States and Canada, with the Pacific Coast Hindustan Association based in San Francisco and a strong following in British Columbia. Its newspaper, the Ghadar, was printed in Gurmukhi, Urdu, and other languages and circulated across the global diaspora.

Who joined and why

The movement drew heavily, though not exclusively, on Sikh labourers and ex-soldiers. Several threads came together:

  • Daily experience of racism and legal exclusion in North America, which exposed the hollowness of "equal" British subjecthood.
  • The humiliation of the Komagata Maru, which became a rallying cry.
  • A tradition of martial service and sacrifice in Sikh culture, now redirected toward anti-colonial ends.
  • Secular and inclusive rhetoric: Ghadar deliberately united Sikhs, Hindus, and Muslims against a common imperial enemy.

The 1915 plan and its failure

With the outbreak of the First World War in 1914, Ghadarites saw their opportunity. Thousands left North America for India, intending to spark a mutiny in the British Indian Army and a general uprising. The plan was betrayed and crushed. The British launched mass arrests; the Lahore Conspiracy Trials that followed sentenced many Ghadarites to death or transportation for life. The uprising failed, but it left a powerful legacy of martyrdom and example.

Legacy

Though it did not free India, the Ghadar movement is remembered as a pioneering experiment in transnational, secular anti-colonialism, organised by ordinary migrant workers rather than elites. For Sikh-Canadians, it is a proud chapter linking their community to the wider Indian independence struggle and demonstrating how the diaspora experience shaped homeland politics. It is essential to note that the historical Ghadar movement of the 1910s was an anti-colonial campaign against the British Empire and should not be conflated with any later or unrelated political cause.

References
Ramnath, Maia. Haj to Utopia: How the Ghadar Movement Charted Global Radicalism. Berkeley: University of California Press, 2011.
Buchignani, Norman, Doreen M. Indra, and Ram Srivastava. Continuous Journey. Toronto: McClelland and Stewart, 1985.

lessons.title: Opening the Doors: Post-War Immigration Waves
lessons.summary: From the franchise won in 1947 to the points system of 1967, the policy changes that turned a small bachelor society into a large, family-based community.
lessons.html:
For the first half of the twentieth century the Sikh community in Canada remained tiny, aging, and male-dominated, kept that way by deliberate policy. The transformation into today's large community is the story of how, step by step, the doors were pried open after the Second World War.

Winning the vote, 1947

A turning point came in 1947, when South Asians (and Chinese Canadians) in British Columbia finally regained the right to vote, forty years after it had been stripped away. Indian independence the same year and Canada's wish to maintain good relations with Commonwealth nations both added pressure. With the franchise came eligibility for citizenship and the professions, and a small annual immigration quota was introduced for India.

Family reunification

The early post-war waves were modest but vital: they allowed the existing pioneers, many now elderly, to finally bring wives and children. The "bachelor society" slowly became a community of families. Children were born and raised in Canada, building the first truly Canadian-born Sikh generation.

The 1967 points system

The decisive change came in 1967, when Canada abolished its explicitly race-based immigration rules and adopted a "points system" that assessed applicants on skills, education, and language rather than country of origin. This, together with the official adoption of multiculturalism as policy in 1971, opened large-scale immigration from Punjab. The table below sketches the change in character of the community.

EraCharacter of Sikh immigration
1900s-1940sSmall numbers of male labourers; family migration blocked; community aging
1947-1966Franchise restored; limited quotas; family reunification begins
1967 onwardPoints system; large skilled and family migration; rapid community growth
1980s-presentEstablished community; secondary settlement beyond BC into Ontario, Alberta; refugees and continued family class

New centres of settlement

While Greater Vancouver (especially Surrey and Abbotsford) remained the historic heart, the later waves spread the community across the country. The Greater Toronto Area, particularly Brampton, became a second major hub, and significant communities grew in Calgary, Edmonton, Winnipeg, and Montreal. Each new concentration built its own ਗੁਰਦੁਆਰਾ gurdwara, and the institution of ਸੇਵਾ seva (volunteer service) knit the growing population together.

A maturing community

By the 1980s the community was large, increasingly prosperous, and Canadian-rooted, with second- and third-generation members entering business, the professions, and public life. It was at exactly this moment of growing confidence that the community was struck by the tragedy examined in the next lesson.

References
Nayar, Kamala Elizabeth. The Sikh Diaspora in Vancouver: Three Generations amid Tradition, Modernity, and Multiculturalism. Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 2004.
Buchignani, Norman, Doreen M. Indra, and Ram Srivastava. Continuous Journey. Toronto: McClelland and Stewart, 1985.

lessons.title: Air India Flight 182: Tragedy and Its Long Shadow
lessons.summary: The 1985 bombing that killed 329 people, the failed prosecutions, the public inquiry, and the painful, contested legacy for Sikh-Canadians.
lessons.html:
On 23 June 1985, Air India Flight 182 was destroyed by a bomb in mid-air off the coast of Ireland, killing all 329 people aboard. It was the deadliest act of terrorism in Canadian history, and it remains one of the most painful and complex chapters in the story of Sikhs in Canada. This lesson treats the subject with care, distinguishing between the crime, its victims, and the community as a whole.

What happened

A bomb concealed in checked baggage, loaded in Vancouver, exploded aboard Flight 182 as it approached Ireland. The same day, a second bomb intended for another Air India flight exploded prematurely at Tokyo's Narita Airport, killing two baggage handlers. The two attacks were coordinated. The 329 dead on Flight 182 were overwhelmingly Canadian citizens, including 268 Canadians and 86 children. The great majority of the victims were Canadians of Indian origin; this was, first and foremost, a mass murder of Canadians.

The context and the investigation

The bombing took place amid the turbulence of the 1980s, following the Indian Army's 1984 assault on the Darbar Sahib (Golden Temple) complex and the anti-Sikh violence that followed in Delhi, events that radicalised a militant fringe within the diaspora. The plot was attributed by investigators to extremists associated with the Babbar Khalsa group based in British Columbia. The investigation, however, was deeply flawed. Intelligence and policing failures, lost evidence (including erased surveillance tapes), and poor coordination between the RCMP and CSIS crippled the case.

The failure of justice

  • Talwinder Singh Parmar, named as the suspected mastermind, was never tried in Canada and was killed in India in 1992.
  • Inderjit Singh Reyat was the only person convicted, pleading guilty in connection with the bombs and later convicted of perjury; he served time and was eventually released.
  • In 2005, after a lengthy and costly trial, Ripudaman Singh Malik and Ajaib Singh Bagri were acquitted of mass murder, the judge citing unreliable evidence.

For the victims' families, the near-total failure to secure convictions compounded the original horror with decades of grief without justice.

The public inquiry

In 2010 the Commission of Inquiry led by retired Supreme Court Justice John C. Major delivered its report, describing the bombing as a "cascading series of errors" by Canadian institutions and a "failure" of the state to protect its citizens and prevent the attack. The government issued an official apology to the victims' families.

A contested legacy

The legacy is genuinely complex, which is why this course addresses it directly rather than avoiding it. Several truths must be held together:

  • The attack was carried out by a violent extremist fringe, not by the Sikh community, the overwhelming majority of whom were and are peaceful, law-abiding Canadians.
  • Sikh-Canadians were themselves among the victims, and the community has often felt that the tragedy was used to cast collective suspicion on all Sikhs.
  • The bombing prompted painful internal debate about extremism, homeland politics, and the responsibilities of diaspora institutions.
  • Memorials in Ireland, Ontario, British Columbia, and elsewhere now honour the 329 dead, and 23 June is recognised in Canada as a National Day of Remembrance for Victims of Terrorism.

Understanding this episode honestly, with compassion for the victims and a refusal to scapegoat a whole community, is part of the mature historical literacy this course aims to build.

References
Major, John C. Air India Flight 182: A Canadian Tragedy. Report of the Commission of Inquiry into the Investigation of the Bombing of Air India Flight 182. Ottawa: Public Works and Government Services Canada, 2010.

lessons.title: A Global Community: Gurdwaras, Citizenship, and Power
lessons.summary: The modern Sikh-Canadian community of 770,000-plus: its institutions, its rise in politics, and the gurdwara as enduring anchor.
lessons.html:
From a few thousand excluded labourers, the Sikh community in Canada has grown into one of the most established and influential Sikh populations in the world, numbering more than 770,000 according to recent census data, roughly two percent of Canada's population. This final lesson surveys the community today.

The gurdwara as anchor

The ਗੁਰਦੁਆਰਾ gurdwara remains the institutional heart of Sikh-Canadian life, just as the first one did in 1908. Canada's gurdwaras are among the largest in the diaspora, serving tens of thousands of worshippers. Beyond worship, they provide:

  • ਲੰਗਰ langar, the free meal open to all, which has fed the homeless and responded to disasters, floods, and the COVID-19 pandemic across Canada;
  • language and religious classes, seniors' programs, and youth sports;
  • settlement help for new immigrants and a base for ਸੇਵਾ seva in the wider community.

Sikh values of service have repeatedly made headlines, as when Sikh volunteers organised relief during wildfires and food drives, demonstrating the principle of ਸੇਵਾ seva toward all Canadians regardless of background.

Faith in public space

The visibility of Sikh identity, above all the ਦਸਤਾਰ dastaar (turban) worn by ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤਧਾਰੀ amritdhari and other Sikhs, has produced landmark accommodation debates and victories. Baltej Singh Dhillon became the first turbaned member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in 1990 after a national debate, and turbans and the kirpan have been accommodated in schools, courts, and the military through a series of legal and policy decisions, making Sikh articles of faith a visible and accepted part of Canadian public life.

Political participation

Sikh-Canadians have achieved a level of political representation remarkable for any minority. The community has produced numerous members of Parliament and provincial legislators, and several federal cabinet ministers. The most prominent national figure is Jagmeet Singh, who in 2017 became leader of the federal New Democratic Party (NDP), the first person from a visible-minority background to lead a major Canadian political party. A turban-wearing, kirpan-bearing Sikh leading a national party would have been unimaginable to the pioneers who lost the vote in 1907, a vivid measure of how far the community has travelled.

Then (1907)Now
Disenfranchised; barred from professionsCabinet ministers, MPs, a national party leader
"Bachelor society" of a few thousandCommunity of 770,000+ across every province
Turban a target of suspicionTurban accommodated in the RCMP, military, courts
One small gurdwara in Vancouver (1908)Hundreds of gurdwaras nationwide

Ongoing challenges

The story is not one of simple triumph. The community still confronts racism and the rise in hate incidents, and it navigates internal debates over homeland politics, generational change, and the place of tradition in a modern multicultural society. Yet the trajectory from the Komagata Maru to the present is one of extraordinary resilience.

Conclusion

The history of Sikhs in Canada is a microcosm of larger themes: the injustice of racial exclusion, the courage to challenge it, the pain of tragedy, and the patient building of community through faith and service. From a ship turned away in Vancouver harbour to a global community anchored by the Guru's door, the Sikh-Canadian story is now woven firmly into the fabric of the nation.

References
Nayar, Kamala Elizabeth. The Sikh Diaspora in Vancouver. Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 2004.
Johnston, Hugh. The Voyage of the Komagata Maru. Vancouver: UBC Press, 2014.

courses.title: Understanding Ardas: Sant Waryam Singh Ratwara Sahib's Teachings
courses.summary: An introduction to Ardas (ਅਰਦਾਸ), the Sikh prayer of supplication, drawing on Sant Waryam Singh Ratwara Sahib's katha — its history, three-part structure, and how to pray with sincerity in daily life.
outcomes: Define ਅਰਦਾਸ (Ardas) and explain its place in daily Sikh devotional life
Trace the historical development of the formal Ardas from Guru Gobind Singh Ji to the modern Rehat Maryada

lessons.title: What is Ardas? History and Structure
lessons.summary: Defines Ardas, explains its role in Sikh life, traces its historical development, and previews its three sections.
lessons.html:
Welcome to this introductory course on ਅਰਦਾਸ (Ardas), the Sikh prayer of supplication. This course follows the spirit of the katha (discourse) tradition associated with Sant Waryam Singh Ratwara Sahib, who taught that Ardas is not a recited formula but a living conversation between the devotee and Akal Purakh, the Timeless One. In this first lesson we define Ardas, locate it within daily Sikh practice, sketch its history, and preview its structure.

Full course contents
  1. What is Ardas? History and Structure
  2. Section 1 — Invoking the Gurus
  3. Section 2 — Remembering the Martyrs
  4. Section 3 — Sarbat da Bhala
  5. Doing Ardas with Full Attention
  6. Ardas in Daily Life

The meaning of the word

The word ਅਰਦਾਸ comes from the Persian arz-dasht, meaning a written petition or request submitted to a sovereign. In Sikh usage it becomes the humble petition placed before the true Sovereign, Waheguru. To make Ardas is to stand as a servant before the King of kings, acknowledging that all help and all gifts come from the Divine alone.

Ardas in daily Sikh life

A Sikh performs Ardas at many moments: at the close of daily Nitnem prayers, at the beginning and end of any seva or undertaking, during life events such as births, weddings, and deaths, and whenever the heart turns to the Guru in need or gratitude. Ardas is offered standing, with hands folded, in the presence of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji where possible. It both opens and seals devotional acts, framing every effort as something undertaken with the Guru's grace.

A brief history

The opening lines of the standard Ardas are drawn from the composition ਚੰਡੀ ਦੀ ਵਾਰ (Chandi di Var), authored by Guru Gobind Singh Ji, beginning ਪ੍ਰਿਥਮ ਭਗੌਤੀ ਸਿਮਰਿ ਕੈ. After invoking the Divine power and the Ten Gurus, the body of the Ardas grew over time to recall the sacrifices of the Sikh people. The text was given a standardized form in the twentieth century through the ਰਹਿਤ ਮਰਯਾਦਾ (Sikh Rehat Maryada) published by the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, so that Sikhs across the world share a common prayer while remaining free to add personal supplications.

The three sections

The Ardas has a clear three-part shape that this course will follow lesson by lesson:

  • Section 1 — Invoking the Gurus: remembrance of the Divine power and of the Ten Gurus and Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji.
  • Section 2 — Remembering the martyrs: recalling the ਸ਼ਹੀਦ (martyrs), the devoted, and the historic struggles and institutions of the Panth.
  • Section 3 — Sarbat da Bhala: the personal and communal petition, sealed with the prayer for ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ, the welfare of all.

Understanding this structure helps the devotee pray with awareness rather than by rote — the central theme of Sant Waryam Singh Ratwara Sahib's teaching on prayer.

References
  • Sikh Rehat Maryada: The Code of Sikh Conduct and Conventions. Amritsar: Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, 1950.
  • Singh, Kapur. Parasaraprasna: The Baisakhi of Guru Gobind Singh. Amritsar: Guru Nanak Dev University, 1989.

lessons.title: Section 1 — Invoking the Gurus
lessons.summary: Explores the opening of Ardas: remembrance of the Divine power and of the Ten Gurus and Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji.
lessons.html:
Every Ardas begins not with our requests but with remembrance. Sant Waryam Singh Ratwara Sahib emphasized that this opening tunes the heart: before asking anything, the devotee first remembers the source of all power and the lineage of the Gurus. This lesson examines that first section.

Prithm Bhagauti Simar Kai

The Ardas opens with the line ਪ੍ਰਿਥਮ ਭਗੌਤੀ ਸਿਮਰਿ ਕੈ — "First, remembering Bhagauti." The term ਭਗੌਤੀ (Bhagauti) is widely understood in this context as the Divine power itself, often imaged as the sword that destroys ego and falsehood. It is not the worship of a weapon but a remembrance of Akal Purakh's might. Beginning here establishes that the strength to live and to pray comes from God alone.

Remembering Guru Nanak and the succession

The opening then calls to mind Guru Nanak Dev Ji and the succeeding Gurus in turn — Guru Angad Dev Ji, Guru Amar Das Ji, Guru Ram Das Ji, and onward through the line. The Ardas asks for their aid (sahai) at each step. This is a remembrance of ਜੋਤਿ (jot), the one Divine light passing through the Ten Gurus, expressing the Sikh conviction that the Gurus shared a single spirit and mission.

The Ten Gurus and the Eternal Guru

The roll of the Gurus continues through Guru Arjan Dev Ji, Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji, Guru Har Rai Ji, Guru Har Krishan Ji, Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji, and Guru Gobind Singh Ji. The section then turns to Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, the eternal living Guru, and to the contemplation of the Bani (sacred word) within. In this way the worshipper places the entire Guru tradition before the mind before voicing a single need.

Element invokedWhat it signifies
ਭਗੌਤੀ (Bhagauti)The Divine power; source of all strength
The Ten GurusThe one Divine light guiding the Panth
Sri Guru Granth Sahib JiThe eternal Guru, present in the Bani

Why begin with remembrance?

Sant Waryam Singh Ratwara Sahib taught that a petition offered without first remembering the Giver is incomplete. By opening with the Divine and the Gurus, the devotee surrenders pride and acknowledges dependence on grace. The asking that follows is therefore framed by gratitude and trust, not by mere wanting.

References
  • Singh, Kapur. Parasaraprasna: The Baisakhi of Guru Gobind Singh. Amritsar: Guru Nanak Dev University, 1989.
  • Macauliffe, Max Arthur. The Sikh Religion: Its Gurus, Sacred Writings and Authors. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1909.

lessons.title: Section 2 — Remembering the Martyrs
lessons.summary: Examines the central section of Ardas that recalls the martyrs, the devoted, and the historic struggles of the Sikh Panth.
lessons.html:
The middle portion of the Ardas turns from the Gurus to those who followed them at great cost. Here the congregation remembers the ਸ਼ਹੀਦ (martyrs) and the faithful who upheld the Sikh way. Sant Waryam Singh Ratwara Sahib taught that recalling these sacrifices renews the devotee's own resolve to live by the Guru's path.

The roll of the devoted

This section asks the worshipper to call to mind the men and women of faith — those who meditated on the Divine Name, shared their earnings, served selflessly, and endured hardship. It honors the ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ (Panj Piare, the Five Beloved Ones) and the Sahibzade, the four sons of Guru Gobind Singh Ji, who gave their lives in the struggle for righteousness.

Remembering sacrifice and suffering

The Ardas recalls Sikhs who underwent extraordinary trials: those who were cut limb from limb, scalped, broken on the wheel, and yet did not abandon their faith. It remembers those who kept the discipline of the Guru "to their last breath and last hair." These are not abstractions but historical memories of the eighteenth-century persecutions and many later struggles. The recitation keeps that courage alive in communal memory.

Institutions and the collective body

The section also remembers the great Gurdwaras and historic seats of the faith, and prays for the maintenance of Sikh discipline (rehat), the choirs and standards (nishan) of the Panth, and the principle of ਦੇਗ ਤੇਗ ਫਤਹ (Deg Tegh Fateh) — provision for all through the deg (cauldron of langar) and protection through the teg (sword of justice).

Remembered in Section 2Lesson for the devotee
The Panj Piare and SahibzadeTotal devotion and willingness to sacrifice
Those who suffered for faithSteadfastness under trial
Historic Gurdwaras and the PanthBelonging to a living community

Memory as inspiration

Sant Waryam Singh Ratwara Sahib explained that this remembrance is not mourning but inspiration. By standing in the line of those who gave everything, the worshipper is lifted beyond private concerns and asked to live worthy of that inheritance. The martyrs' courage becomes a mirror in which the devotee examines their own commitment.

References
  • Sikh Rehat Maryada: The Code of Sikh Conduct and Conventions. Amritsar: Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, 1950.
  • Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. The Birth of the Khalsa: A Feminist Re-Memory of Sikh Identity. Albany: State University of New York Press, 2005.

lessons.title: Section 3 — Sarbat da Bhala
lessons.summary: Studies the closing section of Ardas: the personal petition and the universal prayer for the welfare of all.
lessons.html:
Having remembered the Gurus and the martyrs, the devotee finally voices their own needs — and then immediately widens the prayer to embrace the whole of creation. This closing movement, ending in ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ (Sarbat da Bhala), reveals the heart of Sikh ethics.

The personal petition

It is in this section that individuals and congregations may add their specific requests — for health, guidance, success in seva, or strength in difficulty. The standard text asks for gifts such as the discipline of the Guru's path, the gift of the Divine Name (ਨਾਮ, Naam), unshakeable faith, and the company of the holy. Notably, the requests are for spiritual gifts above all: the Sikh asks first for Naam and faith, and material needs are placed within that frame.

Forgiveness for errors

The Ardas humbly asks forgiveness for any mistakes made in reciting the prayer or in remembering the names — ਭੁੱਲ ਚੁੱਕ ਮਾਫ਼ ਕਰਨੀ. Sant Waryam Singh Ratwara Sahib noted that this admission of fallibility keeps the heart humble, acknowledging that even our worship is imperfect and depends on the Guru's mercy.

Sarbat da Bhala — the welfare of all

The Ardas does not end with the self. Its final aspiration is ਨਾਨਕ ਨਾਮ ਚੜ੍ਹਦੀ ਕਲਾ, ਤੇਰੇ ਭਾਣੇ ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ — through the Name may there be ever-rising spirit (Chardi Kala), and in Your will, the welfare of all. This is the moral signature of the Sikh faith: the prayer is incomplete unless it asks blessing for every being, friend and stranger alike.

MovementFocus
Personal petitionNaam, faith, and specific needs
Asking forgivenessHumility before the Guru
Sarbat da BhalaWelfare of all creation

The widening circle

The genius of the Ardas, Sant Waryam Singh Ratwara Sahib taught, is that it moves the heart from "me" to "all." One may begin praying for a personal worry, but the Guru's structure refuses to let the prayer stay self-enclosed. By ending in Sarbat da Bhala, the devotee is trained to desire for others what they desire for themselves.

References
  • Sikh Rehat Maryada: The Code of Sikh Conduct and Conventions. Amritsar: Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, 1950.
  • Mandair, Arvind-Pal Singh. Sikhism: A Guide for the Perplexed. London: Bloomsbury, 2013.

lessons.title: Doing Ardas with Full Attention
lessons.summary: Practical guidance on the inner posture of Ardas: humility, concentration, faith, and surrender to the Divine will.
lessons.html:
Sant Waryam Singh Ratwara Sahib often warned that the words of the Ardas can be spoken while the mind wanders elsewhere. The form is only the vessel; the value lies in attention. This lesson gathers his guidance on how to pray with the whole heart.

Humility — Nimrata

True Ardas begins in ਨਿਮਰਤਾ (nimrata, humility). The devotee stands as a beggar at the Guru's door, claiming nothing by right. Folded hands and a bowed head are the outward signs of an inward emptiness that makes room for grace. Gurbani teaches that the Divine dwells with the humble and turns away from the proud, so the proud heart cannot truly make Ardas.

Concentration of mind

The mind must be gathered and present. Sant Waryam Singh Ratwara Sahib advised that one should understand the meaning of what is being said rather than racing through familiar lines. When the tongue says the names of the Gurus, the mind should actually remember them; when it asks for Naam, the heart should genuinely long for it. Slowing down and feeling each phrase transforms recitation into prayer.

Faith and certainty

Ardas is offered in ਭਰੋਸਾ (bharosa, trust) that the Guru hears and answers. To pray with doubt is to weaken the prayer. The devotee should bring full confidence that nothing is impossible for Akal Purakh, while leaving the manner and timing of the answer to the Divine.

Surrender to Bhana

Crucially, sincere Ardas ends in surrender to ਭਾਣਾ (Bhana, the Divine will). We ask, but we do not demand. The closing words "ਤੇਰੇ ਭਾਣੇ" — "in Your will" — teach the devotee to accept whatever the Divine ordains as ultimately for the good. This is why a Sikh prays for Chardi Kala, rising spirits, in every circumstance, including loss.

  • Before Ardas: still the mind, recall the Guru's presence, and let go of pride.
  • During Ardas: speak slowly, mean each word, and keep the heart attentive.
  • After Ardas: accept the outcome in Bhana and live in Chardi Kala.

The fruit of attentive Ardas

When done with humility, concentration, faith, and surrender, Ardas becomes a true meeting with the Guru. The worshipper rises changed — comforted, strengthened, and more closely bound to the Divine will than before they began.

References
  • Singh, Kapur. Parasaraprasna: The Baisakhi of Guru Gobind Singh. Amritsar: Guru Nanak Dev University, 1989.
  • Singh, Jodh. Varan Bhai Gurdas: Text, Transliteration and Translation. Patiala: Vision and Venture, 1998.

lessons.title: Ardas in Daily Life
lessons.summary: Shows how to weave Ardas into everyday moments — Nitnem, life events, work, and times of joy and difficulty.
lessons.html:
Ardas is not reserved for the Gurdwara or for crises. Sant Waryam Singh Ratwara Sahib taught that the Sikh lives in a constant relationship of asking and thanking. This final lesson shows how to make Ardas a daily companion.

Ardas in Nitnem

The daily prayers (Nitnem) of morning and evening close with Ardas. After reciting the prescribed Banis, the devotee stands and offers the formal prayer, sealing the day's worship and committing the coming hours to the Guru. Making Ardas at these fixed times builds a rhythm of remembrance.

Beginning and ending tasks

It is the Sikh custom to make a short Ardas before starting any significant undertaking — a journey, a new venture, an act of seva — and again upon its completion in gratitude. This frames ordinary work as something done with the Guru's grace and returns the credit for success to the Divine rather than to the ego.

Life events and the sangat

Ardas marks the great passages of life. At the naming of a child, at the Anand Karaj (wedding), at moments of illness, and at the time of death, the sangat (congregation) gathers to make Ardas together. Communal Ardas binds individual lives into the shared life of the Panth and surrounds each person with collective prayer.

OccasionRole of Ardas
Daily NitnemSeals morning and evening worship
Starting/finishing workSeeks grace and offers thanks
Births, weddings, deathsConsecrates life's passages with the sangat
Joy and difficultyTurns every emotion toward the Guru

In joy and in sorrow

Sant Waryam Singh Ratwara Sahib stressed that Ardas belongs to good times as much as hard times. In happiness we make Ardas to give thanks and to ask that the blessing be shared in Sarbat da Bhala; in sorrow we make Ardas for strength and Chardi Kala. A life woven with Ardas is a life lived in continuous companionship with Waheguru.

Conclusion of the course

Across these six lessons we have seen that Ardas opens by remembering the Divine and the Gurus, recalls the martyrs who gave everything, voices our needs, and ends by praying for the welfare of all. Done with humility and attention, and woven into daily life, the Ardas is far more than a recitation — it is, as this tradition teaches, the breath of the Sikh's relationship with the Guru.

References
  • Sikh Rehat Maryada: The Code of Sikh Conduct and Conventions. Amritsar: Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, 1950.
  • Mandair, Arvind-Pal Singh. Sikhism: A Guide for the Perplexed. London: Bloomsbury, 2013.
