lessons.title: Reading a Gurbilas: Genre, Author, and the Problem of History
lessons.summary: Introduces the ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ as a genre, Koer Singh as author, and the historiographical questions that frame the course.
lessons.html:
ਵਿਸ਼ਾ ਸੂਚੀ (Table of Contents)

  1. Reading a Gurbilas: Genre, Author, and the Problem of History
  2. Koer Singh and His Sources: The Chain to ਭਾਈ ਮਨੀ ਸਿੰਘ
  3. The Court at ਪਾਉਂਟਾ ਸਾਹਿਬ and the ਬੱਤੀ ਕਵੀ
  4. The Poetic World: ਕਵਿ ਪਰੰਪਰਾ, Braj, and Heroic Rasa
  5. The Founding of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ: ਵਿਸਾਖੀ 1699 in Koer Singh's Telling
  6. The ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ and the Sakhi of ਭਾਈ ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰਘ
  7. The ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ Period: Battles, Sieges, and Sovereignty
  8. The ਦਸਮ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ in the Gurbilas Imagination
  9. The Sakhi of ਭਾਈ ਮਨੀ ਸਿੰਘ and the Transmission of Tradition
  10. The Gurbilas in Sikh Historiography: Reception and Critique
  11. Reading Practicum: A Critical Method for the Gurbilas

What is a ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ?

The word ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ joins ਗੁਰੂ to ਬਿਲਾਸ — 'sport,' 'play,' or 'delight.' A ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ is therefore a poem that recounts the wondrous deeds of a Guru as a kind of divine play in the world. It is not chronicle in the modern archival sense, nor hagiography of the quietist kind; it is heroic-devotional biography, written in verse, meant to be recited and to stir ਸ਼ਰਧਾ (devotion) and ਬੀਰ ਰਸ (the heroic sentiment) at once. Two great works carry the name: the Gurbilas Patshahi 6, concerning ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਹਰਿਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ, and the Gurbilas Patshahi 10 of ਕੋਇਰ ਸਿੰਘ, our subject, concerning ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ.

To read such a text well, the student must hold two truths together. First, the ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ preserves invaluable early testimony — names, places, the texture of the Guru's court, the memory of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ's founding — composed within a half-century of the events, drawing on circles close to the Guru. Second, its purpose is theological and aesthetic, not forensic; it amplifies the marvellous, frames events through ਕਵਿ convention, and is shaped by the loyalties of its patrons. The discipline of this course is to read with both eyes open: to honour the devotion and to weigh the history.

The Author and the Date

The colophon of the text places its completion around Sambat 1808, that is roughly 1751 CE, some four decades after the Guru's ਜੋਤੀ-ਜੋਤਿ at ਨਾਂਦੇੜ in 1708. ਕੋਇਰ ਸਿੰਘ identifies himself as a Sikh of the Kalal background and, crucially, claims that the substance of his narration descends from ਭਾਈ ਮਨੀ ਸਿੰਘ, the great scholar-martyr of ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤਸਰ. This claim of transmission — whether literal or a conventional gesture of authority — is itself a key object of study, taken up in the next lesson.

Why Koer Singh Matters

The Gurbilas Patshahi 10 is one of the earliest extended ਪੁਰਾਤਨ narratives devoted wholly to the tenth Guru. It stands alongside ਕਵੀ ਸੈਨਾਪਤਿ's Sri Gur Sobha (composed within living memory of the Guru), the Bansavalinama of ਕੇਸਰ ਸਿੰਘ ਛਿੱਬਰ, and the later Gurbilas of ਸੁੱਖਾ ਸਿੰਘ. Read against these, Koer Singh's work lets us see how the memory of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ was being shaped, contested, and crystallised in the volatile mid-eighteenth century, the very decades when the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ was fighting for survival and sovereignty in the Punjab.

The Editorial Foundation: Piara Singh Padam

The modern student does not approach this text raw. The standard critical edition was prepared by the scholar ਪਿਆਰਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਪਦਮ (Piara Singh Padam), published by the Bhasha Vibhag Punjab in 1968. Padam collated manuscripts, fixed the readings, supplied annotations, and wrote an introduction that remains the indispensable map of the text. His broader work on the ਦਸਮ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ and on Punjabi literary history gives him unusual authority to situate Koer Singh within ਕਵਿ ਪਰੰਪਰਾ. Throughout this course we lean on Padam's apparatus, learning from how a careful editor distinguishes the text's voice from later interpolation.

A Note on Marvels and Method

The Gurbilas, like all texts of its kind, contains episodes of the miraculous and invocations of ਚੰਡੀ as the allegory of divine martial power. The mature reader neither dismisses these as fable nor flattens them into literal report. They are the idiom in which an eighteenth-century Sikh poet expressed the conviction that the Guru's mission was the very working of ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ in history. As the tradition itself teaches in Gurbani, the world unfolds as ਹੁਕਮ — divine command — and the poet sees the Guru's life as that command made visible.

Looking Ahead

Over the lessons that follow we will move from author and sources, through the courtly and poetic world of ਪਾਉਂਟਾ, into the founding of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ, the ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ wars, the ਦਸਮ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ, and the great ਸਾਖੀਆਂ, closing with the text's reception and a hands-on method for critical reading. The aim is not merely to learn what Koer Singh says, but to learn how to read him.

lessons.title: Koer Singh and His Sources: The Chain to ਭਾਈ ਮਨੀ ਸਿੰਘ
lessons.summary: Examines Koer Singh's claimed transmission from Bhai Mani Singh and the question of sources and reliability.
lessons.html:
The Claim of Descent

At the heart of the Gurbilas Patshahi 10 lies a claim of authority: ਕੋਇਰ ਸਿੰਘ asserts that what he sets down he received in a chain reaching back to ਭਾਈ ਮਨੀ ਸਿੰਘ, and through him to the Guru's own circle. In a manuscript culture without footnotes, such a claim functions the way a citation does for us — it tells the listener why the account should be trusted. To evaluate it we must understand both the convention and the man invoked.

Who Was ਭਾਈ ਮਨੀ ਸਿੰਘ?

ਭਾਈ ਮਨੀ ਸਿੰਘ was among the most learned Sikhs of the Guru period and after — a scribe, exegete, and custodian of ਸ੍ਰੀ ਹਰਿਮੰਦਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ at ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤਸਰ. Tradition credits him with arranging compositions and with teaching a generation of Sikhs. His martyrdom under the Mughal authorities sealed his standing as a figure of unimpeachable authority. For a poet of the 1750s to root his work in ਭਾਈ ਮਨੀ ਸਿੰਘ was to wrap it in the highest possible legitimacy.

Transmission as Convention and as History

The student must resist two errors. The first is naïve acceptance: to assume that because Koer Singh names ਭਾਈ ਮਨੀ ਸਿੰਘ, every line descends verbatim from him. The second is cynical dismissal: to assume the name is mere decoration. The truth lies in disciplined uncertainty. Oral transmission in eighteenth-century Sikh circles was real and robust; ਸਾਖੀਆਂ did circulate and were remembered with care. Yet transmission also reshapes — it telescopes, harmonises, and dramatises. Piara Singh Padam, in his introduction to the critical edition, treats the ਭਾਈ ਮਨੀ ਸਿੰਘ ascription as plausible in spirit while cautioning against treating the whole text as a single authenticated dictation.

The Texture of Koer Singh's Sources

Beyond the named chain, the Gurbilas evidently draws on several streams. There is the living oral ਸਾਖੀ tradition of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ, carried by veterans and their descendants. There is the influence of contemporary and near-contemporary written works, above all ਸੈਨਾਪਤਿ's Sri Gur Sobha, with which Koer Singh shares episodes and emphases. And there is the wider ਕਵਿ ਪਰੰਪਰਾ — the stock of metres, similes, and martial imagery from Braj and Punjabi court poetry that supplies the poem's very vocabulary.

Comparing Witnesses

A core scholarly skill is the comparison of witnesses. Where Koer Singh and ਸੈਨਾਪਤਿ agree on a detail — for instance the broad shape of the ਵਿਸਾਖੀ 1699 event — we gain confidence. Where they diverge, or where Koer Singh stands alone, we mark the detail as singular and ask why. Does it serve a theological point? A patron's interest? Does it fill a narrative gap that earlier sources left open? This comparative habit, modelled across the course, is the difference between repeating the Gurbilas and reading it.

The Poet's Self-Presentation

Koer Singh frames his labour as ਸੇਵਾ — service to the Panth and to the memory of the Guru. He asks forgiveness for any failing in a manner typical of devotional poets, who present themselves as humble instruments rather than authors in the modern proprietary sense. This humility topos is not empty: it tells us the poet understood his task as preservation and praise, which in turn tells us what kinds of accuracy he prioritised. He aimed to convey the meaning and majesty of the Guru's life faithfully, even where the surface detail bends to the demands of verse.

Dating and the Mid-Century Context

The composition date of roughly 1751 places the Gurbilas in the harrowing decades after the execution of ਬੰਦਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਬਹਾਦਰ, when the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ endured campaigns of extermination yet was forging the ਮਿਸਲ order that would soon rule the Punjab. A text written then about the founding of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ is not antiquarianism; it is a community telling itself who it is in a moment of mortal danger. The historiographical pressure of that present shapes how the past is remembered — a point we return to in the final lessons.

Conclusion

Koer Singh's chain to ਭਾਈ ਮਨੀ ਸਿੰਘ is best read as a genuine but generalised claim of rootedness in the Guru's circle, mediated by decades of oral and literary transmission. Holding that claim with care — neither swallowing nor spitting it out — is the first and most important methodological move in studying the Gurbilas Patshahi 10.

lessons.title: The Court at ਪਾਉਂਟਾ ਸਾਹਿਬ and the ਬੱਤੀ ਕਵੀ
lessons.summary: Reconstructs the literary court at Paonta, the tradition of fifty-two poets, and the Guru's patronage of letters.
lessons.html:
The Founding of ਪਾਉਂਟਾ ਸਾਹਿਬ

On the bank of the ਜਮਨਾ in the Sirmaur foothills, ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ founded the town of ਪਾਉਂਟਾ in his youth, during a period of relative peace before the great Anandpur wars. The Gurbilas dwells lovingly on this place as a centre of learning and recitation. Here, the text tells us, the Guru gathered scholars, sponsored translation and original composition, and presided over a court where the sword and the pen were honoured together — an early image of the union of ਮੀਰੀ and ਪੀਰੀ that the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ would embody.

The Tradition of the ਬੱਤੀ ਕਵੀ

Sikh tradition, echoed in the Gurbilas and elsewhere, holds that fifty-two poets — the ਬੱਤੀ ਕਵੀ — graced the Guru's literary court. The number is best understood as a figure of fullness and grandeur rather than a precise census; manuscript lists vary, and not every named poet can be independently verified. Yet the tradition preserves a genuine memory: the Guru's court was a hive of literary production, attracting Braj-trained poets and translators who rendered Sanskrit and Persian heroic and ethical literature into the courtly idiom of the day.

What the Poets Did

The work of the court was various. Some poets produced ਅਨੁਵਾਦ — adaptations of classical narratives, including martial and moral tales drawn from the ਪੁਰਾਣ tradition, reframed to instil ਬੀਰ ਰਸ and ethical resolve in the Guru's Sikhs. Others composed praise-poetry and occasional verse. The aim, as the tradition presents it, was never mere ornament: literature was a tool of formation, steeling a community for the trials ahead and articulating a vision of righteous sovereignty. The Gurbilas frames the Guru as the animating intelligence of this enterprise — patron, judge, and inspiration.

ਪਾਉਂਟਾ and the Composition of the Court's Literature

Much of the literary activity associated with the tenth Guru's milieu is traditionally connected to the ਪਾਉਂਟਾ years. Whatever the precise authorship questions — debated to this day and addressed in our lesson on the ਦਸਮ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ — the Gurbilas testifies to a vivid memory of ਪਾਉਂਟਾ as the workshop where the courtly heroic literature took shape. The poet evokes recitations by torchlight, the river running below, and the Guru listening and judging the verse of his assembled ਕਵੀ.

The Battle of ਭੰਗਾਣੀ

The ਪਾਉਂਟਾ idyll was broken by the Battle of ਭੰਗਾਣੀ, fought against a coalition of hill ਰਾਜੇ. The Gurbilas narrates this first major engagement of the Guru with characteristic heroic colour, presenting it as the moment the Guru's martial destiny became manifest. The battle marks a hinge in the narrative: the world of the poets gives way to the world of the warriors, though in the Sikh vision these are never truly separate. The same court that produced verse produced the resolve that won ਭੰਗਾਣੀ.

Reading the Court Critically

How should the historian treat the ਪਾਉਂਟਾ court? The image of a brilliant literary assembly is corroborated in outline by multiple sources and by the body of literature itself. But the Gurbilas, like later tradition, tends to magnify — to round numbers up, to attribute, and to harmonise. Piara Singh Padam's scholarship on the ਦਸਮ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ and on Punjabi literary history is the surest guide here: he shows how to credit the genuine flourishing of letters at the court while resisting the temptation to take every traditional attribution at face value.

The Court as Symbol

Beyond its factual core, the ਪਾਉਂਟਾ court carries symbolic weight in the Gurbilas. It embodies the conviction that the Guru's revolution was as much intellectual and cultural as it was martial — that the making of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ required new stories, new heroes, and a new self-understanding, not only new weapons. The poets of the court were, in this vision, soldiers of the word, preparing the ground from which the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ would rise at ਵਿਸਾਖੀ 1699.

Conclusion

The court at ਪਾਉਂਟਾ, as the Gurbilas remembers it, fuses learning and valour under the Guru's patronage. The ਬੱਤੀ ਕਵੀ tradition, read with care, preserves the memory of a real and consequential literary efflorescence — one that helped forge the cultural sinews of the emerging ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ.

lessons.title: The Poetic World: ਕਵਿ ਪਰੰਪਰਾ, Braj, and Heroic Rasa
lessons.summary: Analyses the literary conventions, language, and aesthetics that shape the Gurbilas as poetry.
lessons.html:
Why the Form Matters

To read the Gurbilas Patshahi 10 as if it were a police report is to misread it utterly. It is poetry, governed by the conventions of ਕਵਿ ਪਰੰਪਰਾ — the inherited craft of metre, simile, and sentiment. Understanding these conventions is not a detour from the history; it is the precondition of extracting history responsibly. When we know how the poet is required to speak, we can tell the difference between what he reports and what the form demands he say.

The Language: Braj-Inflected Punjabi

Like much Sikh and North Indian heroic literature of the era, the Gurbilas is written in a Punjabi heavily inflected by ਬ੍ਰਜ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ, the prestige literary language of the period. Braj carried the vocabulary of courtly heroism and devotion across northern India, and a poet who wished to be taken seriously wrote in its register. The student of the Gurbilas must therefore develop an ear for this hybrid idiom, where Punjabi syntax meets Braj diction and the technical vocabulary of ਰਸ and ਛੰਦ.

ਛੰਦ: The Architecture of Metre

The poem is built in ਛੰਦ — fixed metrical forms, each with its own rhythm and mood. Martial passages favour fast, drum-like metres that mimic the clash of battle; devotional passages slow and broaden. The choice of ਛੰਦ is itself meaning: a shift in metre signals a shift in emotional register. Reading the Gurbilas in the original, one feels the narrative accelerate into combat and settle into reflection through the very pulse of the verse.

ਰਸ: The Theory of Sentiment

Classical poetics organises emotional effect through ਰਸ — aesthetic 'flavours.' The dominant ਰਸ of the Gurbilas is ਬੀਰ ਰਸ, the heroic, which the poem cultivates to forge courage in its audience. But ਬੀਰ ਰਸ is braided with ਭਗਤੀ — devotion — and at moments with the terrible and the wondrous. The Guru is at once supreme warrior and supreme ਭਗਤ, and the poem's emotional architecture is designed to make an audience feel both awe and resolve, to leave them ready to live and die for the Panth.

The Motif of ਚੰਡੀ

The courtly heroic literature of the period frequently invokes ਚੰਡੀ — the martial form of divine power that slays demons. In the Sikh literary frame this is understood allegorically: ਚੰਡੀ is the energy of righteous force, the sword-arm of ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ in the cause of ਧਰਮ, never an object of worship displacing the One. The mature reader recognises the motif as the period's idiom for divine martial agency, and reads it within the firm ਇੱਕ ਓਅੰਕਾਰ monotheism that the Sikh tradition everywhere affirms. Gurbani in the Jaap Sahib teaches that the One is beyond form yet the source of all power, and it is within that conviction that the heroic imagery must be heard.

Hyperbole and the Marvellous

Heroic poetry traffics in hyperbole: armies are numberless, blows split mountains, the hero is unconquerable. These are not lies but the grammar of praise. Likewise the marvellous episodes — portents, miraculous deliverances — belong to a worldview in which the Guru's life is the visible working of ਹੁਕਮ. The historian brackets the hyperbole to find the event beneath it, while the student of religion attends to what the hyperbole reveals about how the community understood its Guru.

From Convention to History

The practical payoff is a method. When the Gurbilas multiplies an enemy host into the hundreds of thousands, we read the figure as the metre of awe, not a muster roll. When it describes the colour of a banner, the layout of a court, the name of a Sikh, we treat the detail as more likely to preserve memory, since convention does not require it. Distinguishing the load-bearing detail from the conventional flourish is the everyday craft of reading a ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ, and it is the skill this course most wants to build.

Conclusion

The Gurbilas is a made thing, fashioned in Braj-inflected Punjabi, governed by ਛੰਦ and ਰਸ, animated by ਬੀਰ ਰਸ and ਭਗਤੀ, and decorated with the marvellous. To read its poetics is to gain the key that unlocks its history.

lessons.title: The Founding of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ: ਵਿਸਾਖੀ 1699 in Koer Singh's Telling
lessons.summary: Studies the Gurbilas narration of the creation of the Khalsa and compares it with other early sources.
lessons.html:
The Central Event

No episode is more consequential, in the Gurbilas or in Sikh history, than the founding of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ at ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ on ਵਿਸਾਖੀ in 1699. Here the Guru transformed the Sikh community into a sovereign, initiated order, bound by a common discipline and a common name. Koer Singh narrates the event with the full resources of his heroic-devotional art, and his telling is among the earliest extended accounts we possess.

The Demand for Heads

The Gurbilas recounts how the Guru, before a vast gathering, drew his sword and called for a Sikh willing to give his head. The terror and silence of the crowd, and the rising of one volunteer after another until five had offered themselves, is told with mounting intensity. These five — the ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ — drawn from different regions and social backgrounds, become the nucleus of the new order. The narrative underscores the dissolution of caste and region in the single identity of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ.

ਖੰਡੇ ਦੀ ਪਾਹੁਲ: The New Initiation

Central to the account is the preparation of ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ through the ਖੰਡੇ ਦੀ ਪਾਹੁਲ — water stirred with a double-edged sword while ਬਾਣੀ is recited, sweetened with ਪਤਾਸੇ. The Gurbilas describes the Guru administering this initiation to the five, and then, in the act that astonishes tradition, requesting initiation from them in turn — the Guru and the Khalsa made one. This reciprocity, ਆਪੇ ਗੁਰ ਚੇਲਾ, the Guru as his own disciple, is the theological heart of the episode, and the Gurbilas registers its wonder.

The New Rehat and Identity

With initiation came a discipline — the marks and obligations of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ, including the unshorn hair and the suite of identifiers that set the initiated Sikh apart. The Gurbilas presents these not as arbitrary rules but as the outward form of an inner sovereignty: the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ is to be recognisable, accountable, and proud, a standing army of the righteous answerable to the Guru alone.

Comparing the Witnesses

To read Koer Singh critically we set him beside ਕਵੀ ਸੈਨਾਪਤਿ's Sri Gur Sobha, the earliest source, and the later Rahitnama and chronicle traditions. The broad shape is shared across witnesses: the demand for heads, the five, the sword-stirred ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ, the abolition of prior distinctions. Differences lie in detail, emphasis, and the degree of the marvellous. Where Koer Singh elaborates a scene beyond what earlier sources attest, we mark the elaboration and weigh its purpose — usually the heightening of devotion and drama.

The Theology of ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ

The Gurbilas does not merely report the five; it invests them with theological meaning. They are the proof that ordinary Sikhs, offering themselves wholly, become vessels of the Guru's authority — so much so that the Guru kneels to receive ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ from their hands. In Sikh practice this flowers into the principle that the ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ embody the Guru's collective presence. Koer Singh's account is an early literary witness to this conviction taking narrative form.

History and Memory

The historian asks what we can firmly know. That a decisive initiation creating the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ occurred at ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ at ਵਿਸਾਖੀ 1699 is among the best-attested events of the Guru period, anchored by ਸੈਨਾਪਤਿ's near-contemporary witness. The precise choreography — the order of dialogue, the exact words — is where memory and art shape the telling. Koer Singh's value is that he preserves, within a half-century, the community's vivid sense of what had happened and what it meant, even as he renders it in heroic verse.

Conclusion

In Koer Singh's telling, ਵਿਸਾਖੀ 1699 is the axis on which Sikh history turns: the moment the community becomes the sovereign ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ, caste dissolved, the Guru and disciple made one. Reading his account against the earliest witnesses lets us honour both its devotional power and its historical core.

lessons.title: The ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ and the Sakhi of ਭਾਈ ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰਘ
lessons.summary: Focuses on the Five Beloved Ones in the Gurbilas, especially Bhai Daya Singh, and the meaning of their sakhis.
lessons.html:
The Five and the First

The ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ — the Five Beloved Ones who rose at the Guru's call — are the living foundation stones of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ. Tradition names them and remembers their origins in different regions and walks of life, a deliberate cross-section of humanity reborn as one. First among them in the order of offering is ਭਾਈ ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰ�​ਘ, and the Gurbilas, like the wider tradition, accords him a special place. This lesson studies how Koer Singh and the ਸਾਖੀ tradition present him and his companions.

ਭਾਈ ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰਘ in the Narrative

ਭਾਈ ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰਘ is remembered as the first to answer the Guru's demand for a head — the one who, when others hesitated, stepped forward without condition. The Gurbilas frames this act as the supreme expression of ਸ਼ਰਧਾ and surrender. In the devotional logic of the text, his willingness to die is precisely what makes him fit to live as ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ; the giving of the head is the giving of the ego, ਹਉਮੈ, the inner sacrifice that the outward drama enacts.

The Sakhi as a Form

A ਸਾਖੀ is more than an anecdote; the word means 'testimony,' and each ਸਾਖੀ bears witness to a truth about the Guru and the Sikh way. The ਸਾਖੀਆਂ of the ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ are didactic: they teach what devotion looks like, what the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ demands, and how an ordinary person becomes extraordinary through surrender. Reading them, we attend not only to what happened but to what the community wished its members to learn.

The Later Role of ਭਾਈ ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰਘ

Tradition remembers ਭਾਈ ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰਘ as a trusted companion of the Guru in the years after 1699, including in the perilous period following the evacuation of ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ. He is associated in tradition with the conveying of the ਜ਼ਫ਼ਰਨਾਮਾ, the Guru's defiant epistle to the Mughal emperor — a connection that, whatever its precise historicity, expresses his standing as one entrusted with the gravest missions. The Gurbilas and allied sources thus carry him from the founding scene into the heart of the Guru's later struggle.

Equality and the Dissolution of Caste

A central meaning the ਸਾਖੀਆਂ of the five carry is the abolition of caste within the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ. The five came from varied backgrounds, and in receiving ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ from one bowl they became kin, sharing a single new name and a single discipline. The Gurbilas registers this as a marvel of the Guru's design: the making of a casteless ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ-brotherhood is itself one of the wonders the poem celebrates. This realises in social form the Gurbani teaching that all are children of the One Light.

Reading the Sakhi Critically

The critical reader treats the ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ ਸਾਖੀਆਂ on two levels. At the level of event, the existence of five initiates who became the founding cadre of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ is well attested; their names and origins are preserved with consistency across the tradition. At the level of detail, the dialogues and the precise sequence are shaped by didactic and devotional aims, and later tellings tend to embellish. Distinguishing the firm core — five beloved, drawn from across society, made one — from the embroidered surface is the discipline.

The Enduring Institution

The ਸਾਖੀ of ਭਾਈ ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰਘ and his companions is not a closed chapter but the charter of a living institution. To this day the ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ act in the Guru's name — administering ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ, making collective decisions, embodying the Guru's continuing presence in the ਸੰਗਤ. Koer Singh's telling stands near the headwaters of this institution's self-understanding, which is part of why his account repays close study.

Conclusion

In the Gurbilas, ਭਾਈ ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰਘ stands as the archetype of the surrendered Sikh, first to offer his head and first among the ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ. His ਸਾਖੀ, read as testimony rather than mere anecdote, opens the deepest meanings of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ: surrender of ਹਉਮੈ, the dissolution of caste, and the elevation of the devoted Sikh to share the Guru's own authority.

lessons.title: The ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ Period: Battles, Sieges, and Sovereignty
lessons.summary: Covers the Gurbilas account of the Anandpur years, the sieges, and the theology of righteous war.
lessons.html:
ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ as Capital of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ

After 1699, ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ became the fortified seat of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ, ringed by strongholds and humming with the life of a sovereign community. The Gurbilas presents the city as the visible sign of the Guru's ਮੀਰੀ — temporal authority joined to the ਪੀਰੀ of spiritual sovereignty. It was a court, a garrison, and a centre of ਸੰਗਤ all at once, and its very existence challenged both the hill ਰਾਜੇ and the imperial power.

The Cycle of Battles

The Gurbilas narrates a sequence of engagements as the hill chiefs, and later Mughal forces, moved against ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ. The poem renders these in full heroic register — the marshalling of armies, the duels of champions, the valour of named Sikhs. The historian reads through the hyperbole to a real and sustained military pressure on the Guru's seat across the years following the founding of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ, culminating in the great siege and the eventual, negotiated and then betrayed, evacuation.

The Theology of ਧਰਮ ਯੁੱਧ

For the Gurbilas, the wars of ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ are not mere politics but ਧਰਮ ਯੁੱਧ — righteous struggle. The Guru fights not for conquest but to defend ਧਰਮ against oppression. This frames the violence within a moral theology familiar from the wider tradition: the sword is taken up only when all else has failed, in defence of the defenceless and the faith. The Gurbani-rooted conviction that the cause is righteous transforms the battlefield into an arena of ਸੇਵਾ and witness. As the tradition teaches, when other means fail it is just to take the sword in hand.

The Heroism of the Sikhs

The Gurbilas lavishes attention on the courage of individual Sikhs — their refusal to flee, their joy in facing death for the Guru. These portraits serve the poem's formative purpose: an audience hearing them in the dangerous 1750s was being taught how to be ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ in their own time of persecution. The remembered valour of ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ became a living model for a ਪੰਥ then fighting for survival.

The Siege and Evacuation

The climactic siege of ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ, with its hunger and hardship, and the eventual evacuation under oaths that were then broken, looms in the tradition as a passage of supreme trial. The Gurbilas registers the suffering and the steadfastness, and sets the stage for the later sacrifices — the loss of the Guru's sons and mother — that the wider tradition mourns and venerates. Koer Singh's treatment, composed when the wounds of persecution were fresh, carries a charged immediacy.

Reading the Battle Narratives

Methodologically, the battle sections demand the firmest critical hand. Numbers are conventional; single combats are stylised; outcomes are framed to vindicate the Guru's cause. Yet beneath the convention lie real events — real sieges, real losses, real defiance — corroborated in outline by other sources. The skill is to extract the durable historical structure (sustained conflict, specific named participants and places, the fact and broad sequence of the sieges) while reading the heroic surface as the period's way of honouring it.

Sovereignty Without a State

The deepest theme of the ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ narrative is sovereignty. The ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ claimed a sovereignty answerable only to ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ, refusing submission to unjust earthly power. This claim — not territorial ambition but the assertion of a free and righteous community under God — is what made ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ intolerable to its enemies and luminous to the tradition. The Gurbilas is, among other things, an extended meditation on what such sovereignty costs and what it means.

Conclusion

The ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ period in the Gurbilas is the crucible in which the newly founded ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ is tested by war. Read critically, the battle narratives yield a real history of siege and sacrifice; read theologically, they articulate a vision of ਧਰਮ ਯੁੱਧ and God-grounded sovereignty that has shaped Sikh self-understanding ever since.

lessons.title: The ਦਸਮ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ in the Gurbilas Imagination
lessons.summary: Examines how the Gurbilas relates to the literature of the tenth Guru's court and the Dasam Granth.
lessons.html:
The Court and Its Literature

The literary court reconstructed in earlier lessons was the matrix from which the body of literature associated with the tenth Guru emerged — the corpus that came to be gathered as the ਦਸਮ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ. The Gurbilas does not present itself as scripture, but it breathes the same air: its heroic idiom, its invocations of divine martial power, and its devotional framing all belong to the world that produced the court literature. This lesson studies that relationship and the scholarly questions it raises.

What the ਦਸਮ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ Contains

The ਦਸਮ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ is a varied collection. It includes devotional compositions of the highest standing in Sikh practice — the ਜਾਪੁ ਸਾਹਿਬ recited daily and used in the ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ceremony, and other ਬਾਣੀ central to ਨਿਤਨੇਮ and ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ initiation. It also contains long heroic and narrative works, including martial retellings and the autobiographical ਬਚਿਤ੍ਰ ਨਾਟਕ, as well as the Persian ਜ਼ਫ਼ਰਨਾਮਾ. The Gurbilas's world is continuous with this literature, and understanding the corpus illuminates the poem.

The Question of Composition and Compilation

The authorship and compilation of the ਦਸਮ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ have been debated by scholars and within the Panth for generations. Some compositions are universally received as the Guru's own ਬਾਣੀ; others, especially the long narrative sections, are the subject of scholarly discussion regarding the role of court poets and later compilation. Piara Singh Padam devoted a major study, ਦਸਮ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਦਰਸ਼ਨ, to mapping these questions. The student of the Gurbilas need not resolve the debate but must know its contours, because the Gurbilas inherits and reflects the court's literary practices.

The Role of ਭਾਈ ਮਨੀ ਸਿੰ�​ਘ Again

Tradition connects ਭਾਈ ਮਨੀ ਸਿੰਘ with the gathering and arrangement of the tenth Guru's compositions after the Guru's passing. This is the same figure to whom Koer Singh traces his own narration. The convergence is instructive: in the mid-eighteenth-century Sikh imagination, ਭਾਈ ਮਨੀ ਸਿੰਘ stands as the great mediator between the Guru's court and the later Panth — the one through whom both the scripture and the story are believed to flow. The Gurbilas's claim of descent thus places it within a recognised channel of transmission.

Heroic Literature as Formation

The narrative and martial literature of the court, like the Gurbilas itself, was understood as formative — designed to instil ਬੀਰ ਰਸ and moral resolve. The retellings of righteous struggle against tyranny were never antiquarian exercises; they equipped a community for its own struggles. The ਚੰਡੀ motif, read allegorically as the power of ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ against oppression, runs through both the court literature and the Gurbilas, binding them in a shared imaginative project.

The Gurbilas as a Witness to the Corpus

For the historian of the ਦਸਮ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ, early narratives like the Gurbilas are valuable witnesses to how the corpus and its court of origin were remembered within decades of the Guru. They attest to the centrality of the literary court, the names and roles associated with it, and the devotional uses of the compositions. Read alongside ਸੈਨਾਪਤਿ and the Rahitnama tradition, the Gurbilas helps triangulate the early reception of the tenth Guru's literature.

A Caution on Conflation

The student must not conflate the Gurbilas with the ਦਸਮ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ. The Gurbilas is a biography about the Guru, composed by ਕੋਇਰ ਸਿੰਘ; the ਦਸਮ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ is the corpus of and around the Guru's own court. They are kin, not the same. Keeping the distinction sharp protects against the common error of treating later devotional biography as if it carried scriptural authority, and it sharpens our appreciation of each on its own terms.

Conclusion

The Gurbilas Patshahi 10 and the ਦਸਮ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ arise from one world — the literary, martial, devotional court of the tenth Guru. Studying their relationship, guided by Padam's ਦਸਮ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਦਰਸ਼ਨ, enriches our reading of the Gurbilas while teaching us to keep biography and scripture properly distinct.

lessons.title: The Sakhi of ਭਾਈ ਮਨੀ ਸਿੰਘ and the Transmission of Tradition
lessons.summary: Studies the figure of Bhai Mani Singh in the Gurbilas and his role as transmitter and martyr.
lessons.html:
The Pivotal Figure

We return, near the close of the course, to the figure who frames the whole text: ਭਾਈ ਮਨੀ ਸਿੰਘ. He is at once a character within the tradition the Gurbilas narrates and the claimed source of that narration. To study his ਸਾਖੀ is therefore to study how the Sikh tradition understood its own transmission — how the memory of the Guru passed from the court into the keeping of the Panth.

Scholar and Custodian

ਭਾਈ ਮਨੀ ਸਿੰਘ is remembered as a Sikh of deep learning, entrusted with the care of ਸ੍ਰੀ ਹਰਿਮੰਦਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ and with the teaching of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ. Tradition associates him with the preservation and arrangement of the tenth Guru's compositions and with the instruction of countless Sikhs in the meaning of the ਬਾਣੀ. He embodies the ideal of the Sikh as scholar-servant — ਵਿਦਵਾਨ and ਸੇਵਕ together — whose learning is always in the service of the Panth.

The Martyrdom

ਭਾਈ ਮਨੀ ਸਿੰਘ's life ended in martyrdom under Mughal authority, a death the tradition remembers as supremely steadfast. The ਸਾਖੀ of his martyrdom became a touchstone of ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ resolve in the persecuted decades when Koer Singh wrote. To invoke ਭਾਈ ਮਨੀ ਸਿੰਘ as one's source was thus to invoke not only learning but the authority of a martyr — the highest seal the tradition could set on a narrative.

Transmission as Sacred Trust

The Sikh tradition treats the transmission of the Guru's memory as a sacred trust, a ਸੇਵਾ continuous with the keeping of the ਬਾਣੀ. ਭਾਈ ਮਨੀ ਸਿੰਘ stands as the archetype of the faithful transmitter, the one through whom the living water of the Guru's word and example flows to later generations. Koer Singh's claim to stand in this line is a claim to participate in that sacred trust — and an obligation to transmit faithfully.

The Sakhi and Its Lessons

Read as testimony, the ਸਾਖੀ of ਭਾਈ ਮਨੀ ਸਿੰਘ teaches several truths the Gurbilas wishes to impart: that learning and courage are one; that fidelity to the Guru may demand the ultimate price; and that the preservation of the Guru's word is itself a form of devotion equal to the battlefield. In a community under threat, these lessons were not abstract but urgent — a curriculum for survival with honour.

Critical Perspective on the Transmission Claim

The scholar holds the transmission claim with the same disciplined care urged throughout this course. That ਭਾਈ ਮਨੀ ਸਿੰਘ was a real and central figure is beyond doubt; that traditions genuinely flowed through such custodians is highly probable; that every detail in Koer Singh descends unaltered from him is not demonstrable. The claim authenticates the spirit and rootedness of the work more than it guarantees its every particular. Recognising this is the mark of a reader who respects both faith and evidence.

The Web of Transmission

Beyond any single figure, the Gurbilas reveals a whole web of transmission — court poets, veteran Sikhs, custodians of shrines, reciters of ਸਾਖੀਆਂ — through which the Guru's memory travelled the dangerous decades to reach the page. ਭਾਈ ਮਨੀ ਸਿੰਘ is the most luminous node in this web, but he stands for a wider community of memory. Studying him, we glimpse the human machinery by which a tradition keeps itself alive across persecution and time.

Conclusion

The ਸਾਖੀ of ਭਾਈ ਮਨੀ ਸਿੰਘ binds the Gurbilas to its claimed origin and to the Sikh ideal of faithful transmission. Scholar, custodian, and martyr, he is both a subject of the tradition and its conduit — and through him Koer Singh links his poem to the very heart of the Panth's memory.

lessons.title: The Gurbilas in Sikh Historiography: Reception and Critique
lessons.summary: Situates the Gurbilas among Sikh historical writings and surveys its reception, influence, and scholarly critique.
lessons.html:
A Place Among the Sources

Having read the Gurbilas from within, we now step back to place it in the landscape of Sikh historiography. It belongs to a family of early ਪੁਰਾਤਨ texts on the tenth Guru that includes ਸੈਨਾਪਤਿ's Sri Gur Sobha, the Bansavalinama of ਕੇਸਰ ਸਿੰਘ ਛਿੱਬਰ, the Gurbilas of ਸੁੱਖਾ ਸਿੰਘ, and the later, sweeping Suraj Prakash of ਕਵੀ ਸੰਤੋਖ ਸਿੰਘ. Each refracts the Guru's life through its own moment and aims; together they form the deposit from which all later Sikh history is built.

The Gurbilas and Sri Gur Sobha

The closest and most important comparison is with ਸੈਨਾਪਤਿ's Sri Gur Sobha, which is earlier and closer to the events. Where Koer Singh and ਸੈਨਾਪਤਿ overlap, we gain a measure of the stable core of tradition; where they diverge, we see how memory developed in the intervening years. Generally, ਸੈਨਾਪਤਿ is leaner and Koer Singh more elaborated and devotional, a difference that itself charts the growth of the heroic-devotional mode across the first half of the eighteenth century.

Influence on Later Tradition

The Gurbilas Patshahi 10 fed into the broad stream of Sikh historical memory. Its episodes, emphases, and turns of phrase echo in later works and in the popular ਸਾਖੀ tradition. ਕਵੀ ਸੰਤੋਖ ਸਿੰਘ's monumental Suraj Prakash, the great nineteenth-century synthesis, drew on this earlier body of writing. Thus Koer Singh, though less famous than some successors, helped set the channels through which the tenth Guru's life would be remembered and retold for generations.

The Modern Critical Turn

Modern scholarship, from the early twentieth century onward, brought historical-critical methods to bear on these texts. Scholars learned to distinguish the ਪੁਰਾਤਨ sources by date and reliability, to compare witnesses, and to read devotional amplification as such. ਪਿਆਰਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਪਦਮ's critical edition of the Gurbilas Patshahi 10 is itself a monument of this turn: by establishing the text, annotating it, and dating it, Padam made responsible study possible and modelled the editorial virtues this course has tried to teach.

Contested Reliability

The Gurbilas's reliability has been debated. Some scholars have flagged anachronisms, the influence of later sectarian interests, and the conventional amplifications of the heroic genre. Others have emphasised the genuine early testimony it preserves and the value of its window onto mid-century Sikh self-understanding. The judicious position, and the one this course commends, treats the Gurbilas as a precious but mediated witness — neither infallible record nor mere legend, but a source to be read with the comparative and critical care we have practised throughout.

Why the Debate Matters

These are not idle academic disputes. How one reads the Gurbilas shapes how one understands the founding of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ, the character of the Guru's court, and the development of Sikh tradition. Because such texts inform devotional practice and communal identity, the stakes of reading them well are high. The discipline of source criticism is, in this field, a form of ਸੇਵਾ — a service to truth and to the integrity of the tradition's memory.

The Gurbilas Today

For the contemporary student, the Gurbilas Patshahi 10 remains a primary gateway into the world of ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ as it was remembered by the generation that followed him. Read with Padam's edition in hand and the comparative sources at one's side, it rewards the labour richly, offering not only events but the very texture of how an embattled Panth understood its Guru and itself.

Conclusion

Within Sikh historiography the Gurbilas stands as an early, influential, and contested witness to the tenth Guru's life. Situating it among its peers, and reading it with the critical apparatus that Padam and modern scholarship provide, lets us draw on its riches without naïveté.

lessons.title: Reading Practicum: A Critical Method for the Gurbilas
lessons.summary: A capstone practicum consolidating a step-by-step critical method for reading the Gurbilas, closing with the Works Cited.
lessons.html:
From Knowledge to Skill

This capstone lesson turns everything we have learned into a portable method — a set of moves a student can apply to any passage of the Gurbilas Patshahi 10, or indeed to any ਪੁਰਾਤਨ text. The goal is not to memorise conclusions but to internalise a way of reading that honours both ਸ਼ਰਧਾ and scholarship.

Step One: Identify the Genre and Purpose

Begin by naming what the passage is doing. Is it heroic narrative, devotional praise, didactic ਸਾਖੀ, or a marvel? Each mode has its own conventions and its own relationship to fact. A battle scene multiplies and stylises; a ਸਾਖੀ teaches a lesson; a praise passage exalts. Knowing the mode tells you what kind of accuracy to expect and where the load-bearing detail is likely to lie.

Step Two: Read the Poetics

Attend to the ਛੰਦ and the ਰਸ. Notice when the metre quickens into ਬੀਰ ਰਸ or broadens into devotion. Mark the conventional flourishes — the numberless armies, the world-splitting blows, the invocations of ਚੰਡੀ as allegory of divine force. Bracketing these as the grammar of praise clears the field so that the reportable substance can emerge.

Step Three: Compare the Witnesses

Set the passage beside the parallel accounts — above all ਸੈਨਾਪਤਿ's Sri Gur Sobha, and where relevant the Bansavalinama and later chronicles. Note agreements, which strengthen confidence, and divergences, which demand explanation. Ask of every Koer-Singh-only detail: does it serve devotion, a patron, or a narrative need? Singular detail is not automatically false, but it carries a lighter evidentiary weight until corroborated.

Step Four: Consult the Apparatus

Turn to Piara Singh Padam's critical edition. Check his readings, his notes on variants, and his judgements about interpolation and dating. A responsible reading of the Gurbilas is always a reading-with-Padam, leaning on the editor who established the text. Where Padam flags a problem, the student should slow down and weigh it.

Step Five: Distinguish Core from Embellishment

Now separate the durable historical core — names, places, the broad shape and sequence of events, well-attested institutions like the ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ and ਖੰਡੇ ਦੀ ਪਾਹੁਲ — from the embellished surface of dialogue, number, and marvel. Hold the core with confidence; hold the surface as meaningful testimony to how the community remembered and what it valued, without mistaking it for forensic report.

Step Six: Read for Theology and Formation

Finally, ask what the passage was meant to do to its audience. The Gurbilas was composed to forge ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ in a time of persecution — to instil courage, devotion, and identity. Reading for this formative purpose recovers the text's deepest meaning, which no amount of source-criticism alone can reach. The historian and the devotee meet here: in attending to what the tradition wished its members to become.

A Worked Illustration

Take the founding of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ. Genre: foundational heroic-devotional narrative. Poetics: rising intensity, the terror-and-wonder of the demand for heads. Comparison: corroborated in core by ਸੈਨਾਪਤਿ. Apparatus: Padam's text and notes. Core versus embellishment: the five, the sword-stirred ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ, the dissolution of caste are core; the exact words and choreography are shaped by art. Formation: the passage teaches surrender of ਹਉਮੈ and the birth of a sovereign, casteless brotherhood. Six steps, and the passage opens fully.

The Reader's Disposition

Above all, the method requires a disposition: reverence without credulity, criticism without contempt. The Gurbilas is a treasure of the Panth and a document of its history. To read it well is to give it both the love and the rigour it deserves — and in doing so to practise a ਸੇਵਾ of memory worthy of the tradition it carries.

ਹਵਾਲੇ (Works Cited)

  • Padam, Piara Singh, ed. Gurbilas Patshahi 10 by Koer Singh. Patiala: Bhasha Vibhag Punjab, 1968.
  • Padam, Piara Singh. Dasam Granth Darshan. Patiala: Kalam Mandir, 1990.
  • Singh, Ganda, ed. Kavi Sainapati Rachit Sri Gur Sobha. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1967.
  • Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. The New Cambridge History of India. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1990.
  • McLeod, W. H. The Chaupa Singh Rahit-Nama. Dunedin: University of Otago Press, 1987.
  • Fenech, Louis E. The Sikh Zafar-namah of Guru Gobind Singh: A Discursive Blade in the Heart of the Mughal Empire. New York: Oxford University Press, 2013.
  • Fenech, Louis E., and W. H. McLeod. Historical Dictionary of Sikhism. 3rd ed. Lanham, MD: Rowman and Littlefield, 2014.
  • Mann, Gurinder Singh. The Making of Sikh Scripture. New York: Oxford University Press, 2001.
  • Dhavan, Purnima. When Sparrows Became Hawks: The Making of the Sikh Warrior Tradition, 1699-1799. New York: Oxford University Press, 2011.
  • Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014.

courses.title: Sri Nanak Prakash: Theological Biography of Guru Nanak
courses.source: Sri Nanak Prakash by Kavi Santokh Singh
courses.summary: An advanced study of ਸ੍ਰੀ ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼, the early nineteenth-century poetic life of Guru Nanak composed by ਕਵੀ ਸੰਤੋਖ ਸਿੰਘ. The course examines the work's ਬ੍ਰਜ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ poetics, its relationship to the later ਸੂਰਜ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼, its theological framework of Guru Nanak as the ਜੋਤਿ incarnate, its major ਸਾਖੀਆਂ drawn from the ਜਨਮਸਾਖੀ tradition, and its enduring place in Sikh hagiography and the wider ਨਿਰਮਲਾ scholarly milieu.
outcomes: Trace the composition, dating, and patronage of ਸ੍ਰੀ ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ and situate it within ਕਵੀ ਸੰਤੋਖ ਸਿੰਘ's larger literary project
Analyze the work's ਬ੍ਰਜ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ poetic structure, its division into ਪੂਰਬਾਰਧ and ਉੱਤਰਾਰਧ, and the function of ਅਧਿਆਇ and ਛੰਦ
Explain the theological construction of Guru Nanak as ਜੋਤਿ-incarnate and the doctrine of ਗੁਰੂ continuity it advances
Interpret major ਸਾਖੀਆਂ and assess how Santokh Singh adapts the ਜਨਮਸਾਖੀ tradition
Evaluate the relationship between ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ and the later ਸੂਰਜ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ within Sikh historiography
Critically appraise the ਨਿਰਮਲਾ and Vedantic interpretive lens and modern scholarly responses to it

terms.m: The divine Light or radiance; in Sri Nanak Prakash, Guru Nanak is presented as this Light taking human form, embodying the eternal divine luminosity.
Genre of narrative birth-and-life accounts of Guru Nanak; Santokh Singh draws on this earlier tradition (especially Bala and Puratan strands) for his episodes.
The literary Braj dialect of Hindi used as the prestige medium of North Indian devotional and courtly poetry; the language in which Santokh Singh composed.
A narrative episode or testimony recounting an event from the Guru's life that carries doctrinal or moral instruction.
Chapter; the structural unit into which Sri Nanak Prakash is divided, grouped under larger sections.
Metrical verse form; the prosodic units (such as ਦੋਹਰਾ and ਚੌਪਈ) through which the narrative is versified.
The first or 'earlier half' of Sri Nanak Prakash, covering the Guru's birth through the early period of his mission.
The 'latter half' of the work, narrating the udasis (travels) and final years at Kartarpur.
The scholarly Sikh order, learned in Sanskrit and Vedanta, to which Santokh Singh belonged and whose interpretive idiom shapes the text.
The later, monumental Gur Pratap Suraj Granth covering all ten Gurus; Nanak Prakash is often read as its precursor and was later folded into the larger cycle as its opening Rashi.
The great preaching journeys of Guru Nanak across India and beyond; a major narrative arc of the Uttararadh.
The invocatory benediction opening the poem, in which the poet salutes the divine and the Gurus before beginning the narrative.
Descent or manifestation of the divine; a contested term Santokh Singh deploys, drawing on Puranic idiom to frame Guru Nanak's advent.
The Sikh community and path established through Guru Nanak's teaching and continued by his successors.
