lessons.title: Course Introduction and the Place of Sri Nanak Prakash
lessons.summary: Orientation to the course, the author, and why this poetic biography matters.
lessons.html:
ਵਿਸ਼ਾ ਸੂਚੀ (Table of Contents)

  1. Course Introduction and the Place of Sri Nanak Prakash
  2. Kavi Santokh Singh: Life, the Nirmala Milieu, and Literary Career
  3. Dating, Patronage, and the Manuscript Tradition
  4. Braj Bhasha and Poetic Architecture: Adhiai, Chhand, and Structure
  5. The Mangalacharan: Invocation and Theological Frame
  6. Guru Nanak as ਜੋਤਿ: The Theology of Light Incarnate
  7. The Janamsakhi Inheritance: Sources Behind the Sakhis
  8. Major Sakhis of the Purbaradh: Birth, Childhood, and Sultanpur
  9. The Udasis: Travels of the Uttararadh and Their Meaning
  10. From Nanak Prakash to Suraj Prakash: One Work, Two Horizons
  11. The Nirmala-Vedantic Lens and Modern Scholarly Debate
  12. Legacy, Reception, and Reading Nanak Prakash Today

Why Study a Nineteenth-Century Poem?

The work known as ਸ੍ਰੀ ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ stands among the most influential poetic accounts of the life of Guru Nanak ever composed. Written by the Nirmala scholar-poet ਕਵੀ ਸੰਤੋਖ ਸਿੰਘ in the early nineteenth century, it gathers the inherited stream of the ਜਨਮਸਾਖੀ tradition and recasts it in elevated ਬ੍ਰਜ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ verse, framed by a sophisticated theological vision. For more than a century after its composition it shaped how learned Sikhs, kathakars (expounders), and ordinary devotees imagined the first Guru's life.

This course treats ਸ੍ਰੀ ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ not as a naive collection of pious stories but as a deliberate work of theological biography: a text that argues, through narrative and verse, a particular claim about who Guru Nanak was. That central claim is that Guru Nanak is the ਜੋਤਿ, the divine Light, descended into the world to redeem the age. Understanding how Santokh Singh builds and sustains this claim is the heart of our study.

What This Work Is — and Is Not

It is important from the outset to fix the identity of the text. ਸ੍ਰੀ ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ is the earlier and shorter of Santokh Singh's two great hagiographical projects. It is devoted entirely to Guru Nanak. The later, vastly larger ਸੂਰਜ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ — formally the Gur Pratap Suraj Granth — covers the lives of all the Gurus from Guru Angad through Guru Gobind Singh. In the eventual editorial arrangement of the complete cycle, ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ came to function as the opening portion, so that the two works together form a continuous Guru-biography. We will examine that relationship carefully in Lesson 10, because it bears directly on how the poet understood his own task.

The poem is organized into two halves: the ਪੂਰਬਾਰਧ, covering birth through the early mission, and the ਉੱਤਰਾਰਧ, covering the great journeys and the final years at Kartarpur. Each half is subdivided into chapters, the ਅਧਿਆਇ, and the narrative is carried in a variety of metrical forms, the ਛੰਦ. This architecture is not incidental; it reflects the conventions of Indic narrative poetry that Santokh Singh inherited and consciously deployed.

The Interpretive Stakes

Santokh Singh wrote as a member of the ਨਿਰਮਲਾ order, a body of Sikhs trained in Sanskrit learning and Vedantic philosophy. This formation left a deep mark on his idiom. He frequently reaches for Puranic vocabulary, including the language of ਅਵਤਾਰ, to express the advent of Guru Nanak. Modern scholars have debated vigorously whether this idiom faithfully renders Guru Nanak's own theology — which insists on the formless ਨਿਰੰਕਾਰ and resists incarnationism — or whether it overlays a Brahmanical frame upon a tradition that had defined itself against precisely that frame. This tension is one of the recurring themes of the course, and we will not resolve it prematurely; we will instead learn to read the text with the tension in view.

Our guide in this study is the scholarship of ਰਤਨ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੱਗੀ, whose critical editions and monographs on Santokh Singh remain foundational. Where his readings are contested, we will note the counter-arguments of scholars such as W. H. McLeod, J. S. Grewal, and Harjot Oberoi.

How to Approach the Material

  • Read each ਸਾਖੀ first as story, then as argument: ask what theological claim the episode advances.
  • Attend to the verse forms; the choice of ਛੰਦ often signals shifts in register from narration to devotional climax.
  • Keep the distinction between hagiography and history active. A statement that Guru Nanak said or did something in ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ is evidence of nineteenth-century Sikh belief, which may or may not coincide with verifiable sixteenth-century fact.

By the end of this course you should be able to read a passage of ਸ੍ਰੀ ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼, identify its place in the structure, recognize its source in the earlier tradition, and articulate the theological work it performs. We begin in the next lesson with the poet himself.

lessons.title: Kavi Santokh Singh: Life, the Nirmala Milieu, and Literary Career
lessons.summary: The biography and intellectual formation of the poet.
lessons.html:
The Poet's Origins

ਕਵੀ ਸੰਤੋਖ ਸਿੰਘ (commonly dated circa 1787 to circa 1843) was born in the village of Noor, near Amritsar, into a Sikh family of the Brar lineage. From an early age he was drawn into the world of letters, studying under the renowned scholar ਗਿਆਨੀ ਸੰਤ ਸਿੰਘ at Amritsar. It was here that he absorbed the dual inheritance that would define his life's work: on one hand the Sikh scriptural and ਜਨਮਸਾਖੀ tradition, and on the other the Sanskritic learning — grammar, poetics, and Vedanta — cultivated by the ਨਿਰਮਲਾ scholars.

The Nirmala Formation

The ਨਿਰਮਲਾ order traced its origins, by its own account, to Sikhs sent by Guru Gobind Singh to study Sanskrit at Varanasi. By the time of Santokh Singh the order had become the principal vehicle of learned, text-based Sikh scholarship, maintaining akharas and deras where Sanskrit grammar, the Puranas, and Vedantic commentary were taught alongside Gurbani. To belong to this milieu was to think in a particular register: to treat the Sikh tradition as continuous with, and expressible through, the categories of classical Indian thought.

This is the single most important fact for reading ਸ੍ਰੀ ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼. When Santokh Singh describes Guru Nanak's advent, he reaches naturally for the vocabulary of cosmic descent and divine play that he had learned from the Puranas. When he expounds the Guru's teaching, he tends to read it as a form of non-dual Vedanta. Rattan Singh Jaggi, the foremost modern authority on the poet, stresses that this is not a distortion imposed cynically but the honest idiom of a deeply learned devotee for whom Sanskrit categories were simply the available language of theology.

A Career of Patronage

Like most poets of his era, Santokh Singh worked under patronage. He spent time at various Sikh courts and establishments, and his major works were composed with the support of sympathetic patrons. His literary output was substantial and ranged across translation, devotional poetry, and hagiography. Among his works, beyond ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ and the ਸੂਰਜ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼, are renderings and adaptations of classical materials that demonstrate his command of ਬ੍ਰਜ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ and his fluency in Indic poetics.

His later years were spent at Kaithal under the patronage of the local ruling family, and it was there that he completed his monumental ਸੂਰਜ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼. The ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼, the subject of our course, belongs to an earlier phase and represents the poet's first sustained engagement with the project of Guru-biography.

The Poet's Self-Understanding

Throughout his work Santokh Singh presents himself with humility as a servant transmitting the glory of the Gurus rather than as an originator. In the conventional manner of Indic poets he invokes blessing and disclaims personal merit, attributing whatever eloquence the verse possesses to the grace of the Guru. Yet beneath this humility lies a confident scholarly ambition: to produce a comprehensive, theologically coherent, poetically elevated account of the Guru's life that would supersede the scattered and sometimes contradictory ਜਨਮਸਾਖੀ manuscripts then in circulation.

Why the Author Matters for the Text

A central methodological lesson of this course is that we cannot read ਸ੍ਰੀ ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ as an anonymous deposit of tradition. It is a shaped, authored work, and its shape reflects its author's training and convictions. Where the older ਜਨਮਸਾਖੀਆਂ are often loose and episodic, Santokh Singh imposes structure, theological coherence, and a unifying vision. He selects, harmonizes, expands, and interprets. He resolves contradictions in his sources by choosing one version or by synthesizing. He frequently supplies theological commentary that the bare episode does not require, turning narrative into doctrine.

Understanding the poet therefore equips us to distinguish, in the text, between what Santokh Singh inherited and what he contributed. The inherited material connects ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ to the wider tradition; the contributions reveal the particular theological biography that Santokh Singh wished to write. In the lessons that follow we will repeatedly return to this distinction. We turn next to the questions of dating, patronage, and the manuscript record that anchor the work in time.

lessons.title: Dating, Patronage, and the Manuscript Tradition
lessons.summary: When the work was composed, under whose patronage, and how it was transmitted.
lessons.html:
Fixing the Date

Indic poets routinely embed the date of composition in their texts using the ਬਿਕ੍ਰਮੀ (Vikrami) calendar, often encoded in a chronogram. ਸ੍ਰੀ ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ follows this convention. Scholars, following the analysis of ਰਤਨ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੱਗੀ, place the completion of the work in the early nineteenth century, in the second decade of the 1800s by the common era reckoning. This dating places it within the lifetime of Maharaja Ranjit Singh and during the consolidation of Sikh political power in the Punjab — a context of relative confidence and patronage for Sikh letters.

The precise year matters because it sets ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ before the later and larger ਸੂਰਜ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼, which Santokh Singh completed roughly two decades afterward. The earlier work is thus the product of the poet's maturity but not his final phase, and comparison of the two reveals development in his theological emphasis and poetic technique.

Patronage and Social Setting

The production of a long poetic work required material support: the poet needed sustenance, scribes, and an audience. ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ was composed within the network of Sikh patronage that flourished under sympathetic chiefs and establishments. The poem was intended for recitation and exposition. Sikh ਕਥਾ (homiletic exposition) drew heavily on such texts; a kathakar would recite a passage and then expound it for a congregation. This performative destination shaped the work: its verses are crafted to be heard, its episodes structured to deliver instruction, and its theological climaxes positioned for devotional effect.

The Manuscript and Print Tradition

Before the age of print, ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ circulated in manuscript. Copies were made by scribes attached to deras and akharas, and as with any hand-copied text, variants accumulated. The establishment of a reliable text therefore became a scholarly task. In the early twentieth century the great Sikh scholar ਭਾਈ ਵੀਰ ਸਿੰਘ undertook the editing of Santokh Singh's corpus, producing the standard printed edition of the combined ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ and ਸੂਰਜ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ through the Khalsa Samachar press at Amritsar. Vir Singh supplied annotations, glosses on difficult ਬ੍ਰਜ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ vocabulary, and editorial apparatus that made the work accessible to a modern readership.

Later, ਰਤਨ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੱਗੀ produced further critical scholarship, including detailed studies of the language, sources, and structure of the works. For the modern student, the Vir Singh edition remains the textual foundation, while Jaggi's monographs provide the critical scholarly apparatus.

Editorial Arrangement and the Two Works

An important editorial fact concerns how ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ relates to the larger cycle. Because Santokh Singh's two hagiographical works together cover all ten Gurus, later editors and the tradition itself came to treat them as a single continuous biography, with ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ as the opening section. In the conventional arrangement of the complete Suraj Granth cycle, the material is divided into large sections sometimes called ਰਾਸਿ (Ras), and the life of Guru Nanak constitutes the first of these. This is why one will sometimes see ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ referred to as if it were a part of the Suraj Granth: editorially it became one, even though it was composed as a freestanding work years earlier.

Methodological Caution

For the historian, the relatively late date of ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ — some three centuries after Guru Nanak — is decisive. The work is a primary source not for the sixteenth century but for the early nineteenth: it tells us authoritatively what learned Sikhs of Santokh Singh's circle believed about Guru Nanak and how they wished his life to be understood. J. S. Grewal and W. H. McLeod have both emphasized that the hagiographical sources must be read for the theology and the imaginative world they encode, not mined naively for biographical fact. We will adopt that discipline throughout.

With the work fixed in time, transmitted through manuscript to the Vir Singh edition, and situated in its world of patronage and performance, we can turn to the poem itself. The next lesson examines its language and its architecture.

lessons.title: Braj Bhasha and Poetic Architecture: Adhiai, Chhand, and Structure
lessons.summary: The language and formal structure of the poem.
lessons.html:
The Choice of Braj Bhasha

ਸ੍ਰੀ ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ is composed in ਬ੍ਰਜ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ, the literary dialect that served across North India as the prestige medium for devotional and courtly poetry from the sixteenth century onward. This choice was deliberate and significant. Although Santokh Singh was a Punjabi writing for a Punjabi Sikh audience, he reached for ਬ੍ਰਜ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ because it was the recognized vehicle of serious narrative and devotional verse in the wider Indic world. Writing in it placed his work within a respected literary tradition and signaled its ambition.

The consequence for the modern reader is that the language is not straightforward Punjabi. It is dense with Sanskritic vocabulary, Braj grammatical forms, and conventional poetic diction. This is precisely why editions such as that of ਭਾਈ ਵੀਰ ਸਿੰਘ supply extensive glosses, and why the linguistic studies of ਰਤਨ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੱਗੀ are essential aids. Reading the poem well requires patience with its idiom.

The Larger Architecture

The work is divided into two great halves. The ਪੂਰਬਾਰਧ, the earlier half, narrates the events from Guru Nanak's birth through his childhood, marriage, employment at Sultanpur, and the foundational experience of his divine commission. The ਉੱਤਰਾਰਧ, the latter half, follows the great journeys, the ਉਦਾਸੀਆਂ, and culminates in the establishment of the community at Kartarpur and the passing of the Guru. This bipartite structure mirrors a natural division in the Guru's life between formation and mission.

The Chapter Unit: Adhiai

Within each half the narrative is organized into chapters, the ਅਧਿਆਇ. Each ਅਧਿਆਇ typically treats a coherent episode or a connected cluster of events, opening with a transitional or invocatory verse and closing with a colophon. This chaptering imposes order on material that, in the older ਜਨਮਸਾਖੀਆਂ, was often loosely strung together. By segmenting the life into discrete chapters, Santokh Singh makes the work navigable, suitable for serial recitation, and rhetorically shaped, so that each chapter can build to its own devotional or doctrinal point.

The Metrical Units: Chhand

The narrative is carried in a variety of metrical forms, collectively the ਛੰਦ. The poet moves between meters such as the ਦੋਹਰਾ (a two-line couplet) and the ਚੌਪਈ (a four-line quatrain), among others. These are the standard meters of Indic narrative poetry. The ਦੋਹਰਾ, compact and epigrammatic, frequently carries summary statements, transitions, or pointed doctrinal assertions. The ਚੌਪਈ, more expansive, carries the flow of narration. The alternation between meters gives the verse its rhythm and allows the poet to modulate between brisk storytelling and lingering devotional reflection.

Attending to the ਛੰਦ is not a merely technical exercise. The shift to a particular meter often signals a shift in register. When the narrative reaches a moment of theological intensity — the manifestation of the ਜੋਤਿ, a revelation, a miracle — the poet frequently marks it with a change of meter or a heightening of diction. The form, in other words, participates in the meaning.

Conventions of Narrative Poetry

Santokh Singh works within a rich set of inherited conventions. Each major section opens with a ਮੰਗਲਾਚਰਣ, an invocatory benediction. Episodes are introduced with formulaic phrases. Descriptions of natural beauty, of cities, and of the Guru's radiance employ the stock imagery of classical poetics. Dialogue is set within frame formulas. These conventions are not signs of unoriginality; they are the grammar of the genre, and a skilled poet works expressively within them, much as a composer works within a musical form.

Structure as Argument

The architecture of ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ is itself part of its theological argument. By framing the whole with invocation, by ordering the episodes into a coherent progression, and by marking theological climaxes with formal intensification, the poet shapes the reader's experience toward a single conclusion: that the life narrated is the manifestation in time of the eternal ਜੋਤਿ. We will see this most clearly in the opening invocation, the ਮੰਗਲਾਚਰਣ, which is the subject of our next lesson. There the poet states his theological frame before a single episode is told, so that the entire narrative unfolds under the sign of that frame.

Before proceeding, the student should practice reading a short passage aloud, attending to the meter and the recurrence of formulaic openings. The aural dimension of the poem — its destination in recitation and ਕਥਾ — is inseparable from its meaning.

lessons.title: The Mangalacharan: Invocation and Theological Frame
lessons.summary: How the opening invocation establishes the poem's theological vision.
lessons.html:
The Function of the Mangalacharan

Every major work of Indic devotional poetry opens with a ਮੰਗਲਾਚਰਣ, an invocatory benediction in which the poet salutes the divine, seeks blessing for the undertaking, and disclaims personal merit. Far from being a mere formality, the ਮੰਗਲਾਚਰਣ is where a poet declares the theological coordinates of everything that follows. To read the opening of ਸ੍ਰੀ ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ attentively is therefore to grasp in advance the interpretive key to the whole.

Saluting the Formless and the Manifest

Santokh Singh's invocation moves characteristically between two registers. On one hand he salutes the supreme reality in terms that echo Gurbani's insistence on the formless: the ਨਿਰੰਕਾਰ, beyond attribute and image, the one ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ who is without beginning. On the other hand he prepares to narrate that same reality entering the world as Guru Nanak. The invocation thus holds together the formless source and its manifestation — a tension that the entire poem will work to reconcile.

The poet salutes the Gurus in succession and seeks their grace upon his labor. He presents himself, in the conventional posture, as utterly unworthy, his verse possible only by the Guru's favor. The language is one of devotion and self-effacement, but it carries a confident claim: that to narrate the life of Guru Nanak is to narrate the descent of the divine itself.

The Theological Claim Stated at the Outset

The decisive feature of the ਮੰਗਲਾਚਰਣ is that it states the work's central thesis before any episode is told. Guru Nanak is presented not merely as a great teacher or saint but as the ਜੋਤਿ, the divine Light, taking human form to redeem a darkened age. Santokh Singh draws here on a current of thought already present in earlier Sikh tradition — the ਜਨਮਸਾਖੀਆਂ likewise portray the Guru's birth as cosmically significant, attended by light and rejoicing in the heavens — but he sharpens and systematizes it. The advent of Guru Nanak is figured as the dispelling of darkness, the rising of light upon a world sunk in ignorance.

As Gurbani in the ਆਸਾ ਕੀ ਵਾਰ tradition and the compositions of the Gurus themselves teach, the true Guru is the one who reveals the divine Name and dispels the darkness of ignorance. Santokh Singh takes this theological commonplace and renders it as the governing image of his biography. The very title — ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼, meaning light or illumination — encodes the thesis. The life of Guru Nanak is the ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼, the illumination, of the world.

The Puranic Idiom and Its Risks

In framing the advent of Guru Nanak, Santokh Singh reaches for the vocabulary of cosmic descent familiar from the Puranas, including the language of ਅਵਤਾਰ. This is where the ਨਿਰਮਲਾ formation of the poet is most visible and most consequential. The Puranic frame says that when unrighteousness prevails, the divine descends to restore order. Mapping Guru Nanak onto this pattern makes his advent intelligible within classical Indian thought.

Yet this move is theologically delicate. The Guru's own bani resists incarnationism; the divine is ਨਿਰੰਕਾਰ, formless, and is not said to take birth as the gods of the Puranas are said to do. Modern scholars, prominently W. H. McLeod and Harjot Oberoi, have pointed to exactly this idiom as evidence of the Brahmanizing or Vedanticizing tendency of the ਨਿਰਮਲਾ tradition. Defenders, following the more sympathetic reading of ਰਤਨ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੱਗੀ, argue that Santokh Singh uses the ਅਵਤਾਰ idiom loosely and devotionally, as the available poetic language for divine manifestation, without committing to the full metaphysics of Puranic incarnation. We will examine this debate in depth in Lesson 11. For now, the student should simply register that the tension is present from the very first verses.

Reading the Frame Forward

Because the ਮੰਗਲਾਚਰਣ states the thesis, every subsequent episode should be read as its demonstration. When the child Nanak astonishes his teacher, when the young man disappears into the river and returns commissioned, when he confronts the powerful and the proud on his journeys, each ਸਾਖੀ functions as evidence that the ਜੋਤਿ is at work in the world. The invocation tells us what to look for; the narrative shows it to us. This is why a careful reading of the opening repays the effort: it hands us the lens through which the poet intends his entire work to be seen.

In the next lesson we develop the central theological theme — Guru Nanak as the ਜੋਤਿ incarnate — in full, examining how the image of light governs the poem and how it connects to the Sikh doctrine of the one Light passing through the succession of Gurus.

lessons.title: Guru Nanak as ਜੋਤਿ: The Theology of Light Incarnate
lessons.summary: The central theological theme of divine Light and Guru continuity.
lessons.html:
The Governing Image

The single most important theological idea in ਸ੍ਰੀ ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ is that Guru Nanak is the ਜੋਤਿ, the divine Light, made manifest in human form. The title of the work proclaims it: ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ means illumination. Across the poem, the imagery of light recurs — the darkness of the age, the rising of the sun, the dispelling of ignorance, the radiance of the Guru's presence. To understand the work theologically is to understand how this image of light organizes everything.

The Scriptural Root of the Doctrine

The theology of the divine ਜੋਤਿ is not Santokh Singh's invention. It is rooted in Sikh scripture itself. Gurbani in the compositions of the Gurus teaches that the same divine Light dwells within all creation — that the one Light pervades all beings. More specifically, the Sikh tradition holds that a single divine Light passed through the succession of the ten Gurus: the body changed but the Light, and the office, remained one. This doctrine of the one ਜੋਤਿ passing from Guru to Guru is foundational to Sikh self-understanding and is affirmed within the scriptural tradition itself.

Santokh Singh takes this established doctrine and makes it the spine of his biography of the first Guru. If the one Light passed through all ten Gurus, then with Guru Nanak that Light first entered the world. His advent is therefore the original ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼, the first shining-forth of the divine Light in the line of the Gurus. The poet's task, as he understands it, is to narrate that first shining-forth.

Light Against Darkness

The poem repeatedly frames the world before Guru Nanak as sunk in darkness — moral, spiritual, and religious. Falsehood prevails, true devotion is forgotten, and humanity wanders in ignorance of the divine Name. Into this darkness the ਜੋਤਿ descends. The structural logic is that of dawn: the rising of light upon a benighted world. As Gurbani in the ਜਪੁ and elsewhere teaches that the dispelling of the darkness of ignorance comes through the Guru's grace and the divine Name, so Santokh Singh renders the whole life of Guru Nanak as that dispelling enacted in history.

This is why the miracles and confrontations of the narrative matter theologically. Each time the Guru reveals truth to the deluded, humbles the proud, or awakens the sleeping conscience of an individual or a community, the episode dramatizes light overcoming darkness. The ਸਾਖੀਆਂ are not random anecdotes; they are repeated enactments of the central image.

The Tension with Formlessness

Here we must hold two truths together. Sikh theology insists that the supreme reality is ਨਿਰੰਕਾਰ, formless, beyond birth and death. How then can the formless be said to take form as Guru Nanak? Santokh Singh negotiates this by way of the doctrine of manifestation: the formless does not cease to be formless, but its Light becomes manifest through the Guru. The Guru is the locus where the formless becomes accessible, where the unmanifest ਜੋਤਿ shines into the world of form. This is subtly but importantly different from the Puranic ਅਵਤਾਰ, in which a deity literally takes bodily birth. The sympathetic reading, advanced by ਰਤਨ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੱਗੀ, holds that Santokh Singh intends manifestation, not incarnation in the full Puranic sense — though his Puranic vocabulary sometimes blurs the line.

The Guru as Mediator of Grace

Closely tied to the theology of light is the role of the Guru as the channel of divine grace. In Sikh thought the ਗੁਰੂ is the indispensable guide who reveals the ਸ਼ਬਦ, the divine Word, and through it grants liberation. By presenting Guru Nanak as the ਜੋਤਿ, Santokh Singh underscores that to encounter Guru Nanak is to encounter the divine itself reaching toward humanity. The biography is thus also a soteriology: it shows how the Light, by entering the world, opens the path of liberation for those who turn toward it.

Why This Matters

The theology of ਜੋਤਿ is what raises ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ above a mere chronicle. Santokh Singh is not content to record what Guru Nanak did; he wants to reveal who Guru Nanak is. The answer, sustained through every chapter, is that he is the divine Light made manifest, the first ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ in the line of the Gurus, the dawn that ends the long night of the age. Every subsequent lesson — the sources of the ਸਾਖੀਆਂ, the episodes of birth and travel, the relationship to the ਸੂਰਜ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ — should be read in the light, quite literally, of this central claim. We turn next to the inherited tradition from which Santokh Singh drew his episodes.

lessons.title: The Janamsakhi Inheritance: Sources Behind the Sakhis
lessons.summary: The earlier narrative tradition Santokh Singh drew upon and transformed.
lessons.html:
The Stream Behind the Poem

Santokh Singh did not invent the episodes of Guru Nanak's life. He inherited them from a rich and complex narrative tradition known collectively as the ਜਨਮਸਾਖੀਆਂ — the birth-and-life accounts of the Guru that had circulated, grown, and diversified for more than two centuries before he wrote. Understanding ਸ੍ਰੀ ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ requires understanding this inheritance, because much of the poet's artistry lies in how he selects from, harmonizes, and reinterprets it.

The Major Janamsakhi Traditions

Modern scholarship, above all the foundational work of W. H. McLeod in his study of the early Sikh tradition, has distinguished several major strands of ਜਨਮਸਾਖੀ. The ਪੁਰਾਤਨ (Puratan) tradition, preserved in early manuscripts, presents a relatively austere and structurally coherent account organized around the Guru's journeys to the four directions. The ਬਾਲਾ (Bala) tradition, attributed to a companion named Bhai Bala, became enormously popular and is marked by abundant detail and a strong devotional flavor, though scholars have questioned its historical reliability. The ਮਿਹਰਬਾਨ (Miharban) tradition, associated with a collateral branch of the Guru's family, is more exegetical, weaving extended commentary on Gurbani into the narrative frame.

These traditions overlap, contradict, and supplement one another. The same episode may appear in different forms across them; some episodes are unique to one strand. By Santokh Singh's time this material formed a vast, somewhat unruly reservoir of story. His task was to draw from it a single, ordered, theologically coherent narrative.

How Santokh Singh Used His Sources

Santokh Singh's method was that of a learned synthesizer. Where his sources offered multiple versions of an episode, he selected, combined, or reconciled them. Where they were terse, he expanded, supplying poetic description, dialogue, and theological reflection. Where they were merely narrative, he added interpretation, drawing out the doctrinal meaning of the event. ਰਤਨ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੱਗੀ's source-critical studies trace these operations in detail, showing how the poet transformed the raw material of the ਜਨਮਸਾਖੀਆਂ into elevated ਬ੍ਰਜ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ verse governed by his theology of ਜੋਤਿ.

One characteristic effect of this transformation is harmonization. The older traditions disagree on chronology, on which companions accompanied the Guru, and on the details of episodes. Santokh Singh tends to smooth these disagreements, producing a continuous and consistent life-story. The gain is coherence and devotional power; the cost, from the historian's standpoint, is that genuine variation and uncertainty are concealed beneath a confident surface.

The Question of Historicity

It is essential for the advanced student to keep the historiographical issue clearly in view. The ਜਨਮਸਾਖੀਆਂ are hagiography, not biography in the modern sense. They were composed to edify and to proclaim the Guru's greatness, not to satisfy a documentary standard of evidence. W. H. McLeod's analysis demonstrated that many episodes bear the marks of legend, of borrowing from wider Indian narrative motifs, and of accretion over time. J. S. Grewal, in his study of Guru Nanak in history, likewise distinguished sharply between what can be cautiously affirmed about the historical Guru and the much larger body of hagiographical tradition.

Santokh Singh stands at the far end of this developmental process. He inherited the tradition in its mature, elaborated form and gave it its most polished poetic expression. ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ is therefore evidence of the tradition's culmination, not of its origins. To read it well is to read it as the crowning literary achievement of the ਜਨਮਸਾਖੀ tradition, transformed by the theological and poetic sensibility of a ਨਿਰਮਲਾ scholar.

Continuity and Innovation

Yet we should not overstate the gap between Santokh Singh and his sources. In its deepest commitments his work is continuous with the tradition: the older ਜਨਮਸਾਖੀਆਂ already proclaim the Guru's divinity, already attend his birth with cosmic signs, already present his life as the manifestation of grace. Santokh Singh systematizes and elevates what was already there. His innovation is one of form, coherence, and theological articulation rather than of basic content. He is the tradition's interpreter, not its inventor.

With the sources in view, we can now turn to the episodes themselves. In the next two lessons we examine the major ਸਾਖੀਆਂ of the two halves of the poem — first the birth and early life of the ਪੂਰਬਾਰਧ, then the great journeys of the ਉੱਤਰਾਰਧ — reading each not only as story but as the enactment of the theology of light.

lessons.title: Major Sakhis of the Purbaradh: Birth, Childhood, and Sultanpur
lessons.summary: The key episodes of the first half of the poem and their meaning.
lessons.html:
The Birth Narrative

The ਪੂਰਬਾਰਧ opens with the birth of Guru Nanak, and Santokh Singh invests this event with cosmic significance. Following the inherited tradition, he presents the birth not as an ordinary human event but as the entry of the ਜੋਤਿ into the world. The heavens rejoice; the night of the age gives way to dawn; creation senses the advent of its redeemer. The poet's imagery of light, established in the ਮੰਗਲਾਚਰਣ, here finds its first concrete narrative occasion. The newborn is the ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ promised in the invocation.

This treatment exemplifies how Santokh Singh works. The bare fact of birth is taken from tradition; the cosmic framing, the heightened diction, and the explicit theological reading are the poet's elaboration. The reader is left in no doubt that an extraordinary advent has occurred.

The Childhood Episodes

The poem then recounts episodes of the Guru's childhood that display his precocious spiritual insight and his estrangement from worldly convention. A recurring pattern in these ਸਾਖੀਆਂ is that conventional authorities — teachers, elders, employers — fail to comprehend the child, who already perceives a deeper truth. In the well-known episode of the schooling, the boy confounds his teacher by revealing the futility of mere worldly learning compared with knowledge of the divine. The lesson is theological: the ਜੋਤਿ does not need to be taught; it is the source of true teaching.

Another cluster of childhood episodes concerns the Guru's apparent disregard for profit and convention, which troubles his father. When set to tend cattle or to conduct trade, the young Nanak acts according to a higher logic. The most celebrated of these is the episode often called the true bargain, ਸੱਚਾ ਸੌਦਾ, in which the Guru, given money to invest in trade, spends it instead on feeding the hungry and the holy, declaring this the only truly profitable transaction. The episode dramatizes the inversion of worldly and spiritual values that runs throughout the Guru's teaching: the true commerce is the service of others and the remembrance of the divine.

Marriage and Sultanpur

The narrative follows the Guru into adulthood, marriage, and employment. Santokh Singh recounts the Guru's move to Sultanpur, where, through the help of his sister ਬੇਬੇ ਨਾਨਕੀ and his brother-in-law, he takes service in the local administration, managing a storehouse. The Sultanpur period is crucial because it sets the stage for the foundational event of the Guru's life. Even while engaged in worldly duty, the Guru is depicted as scrupulously honest and inwardly absorbed in the divine.

The River and the Commission

The pivotal ਸਾਖੀ of the ਪੂਰਬਾਰਧ is the episode at the river ਵੇਈਂ. The Guru enters the water and disappears; those who search believe him drowned. After three days he reappears, transformed and commissioned. In the inherited tradition this is the moment of divine encounter — the Guru is taken into the divine presence, given the cup of the Name, and sent forth to proclaim it. His first utterance upon returning, as the tradition preserves it, is the proclamation that establishes his universal mission: that there is no Hindu and no Muslim in the ultimate reckoning, only humanity before the one divine.

Santokh Singh narrates this event as the decisive manifestation of the Guru's purpose. The hidden ਜੋਤਿ now becomes openly active in the world; the period of preparation ends and the mission begins. The episode functions as the hinge of the whole poem, marking the transition from the formation of the ਪੂਰਬਾਰਧ to the mission of the ਉੱਤਰਾਰਧ.

Reading the Purbaradh Theologically

Across these episodes a single argument is advanced. From birth, the Guru is shown to be other than ordinary; through childhood and youth, his actions reveal a wisdom and a value-system that come from beyond the world; at the river, the latent ਜੋਤਿ is openly commissioned. The ਪੂਰਬਾਰਧ is thus a sustained demonstration of the thesis stated in the invocation: that the divine Light has entered the world in the person of Guru Nanak. Each ਸਾਖੀ contributes a facet of that demonstration.

The student should notice how Santokh Singh selects episodes that serve this theological purpose and frames even the most homely incidents — a schoolroom, a herd of cattle, a sum of money — as occasions for the manifestation of divine truth. Nothing in the narrative is merely biographical; everything is made to bear theological weight. With the formation of the Guru complete and his mission commissioned, we follow him in the next lesson onto the great journeys of the ਉੱਤਰਾਰਧ.

lessons.title: The Udasis: Travels of the Uttararadh and Their Meaning
lessons.summary: The great journeys of Guru Nanak and their theological function.
lessons.html:
The Mission Begins

The ਉੱਤਰਾਰਧ is structured around the ਉਦਾਸੀਆਂ, the great journeys on which Guru Nanak set out after his commission at Sultanpur. In the inherited tradition these travels carry the Guru across the length and breadth of India and beyond — to the south, to the north into the Himalayas, to the east, and to the west as far as the centers of Islamic pilgrimage. The journeys are accompanied by the faithful companion ਭਾਈ ਮਰਦਾਨਾ, the Muslim minstrel whose rebab accompanies the Guru's singing of the divine Word.

The figure of ਭਾਈ ਮਰਦਾਨਾ is theologically significant in itself. That the Guru's lifelong companion was a Muslim of humble background embodies the universalism proclaimed at the river: the divine mission transcends the boundaries of religion and caste. Throughout the ਉਦਾਸੀ narratives, Mardana's presence keeps this universalism before the reader.

The Pattern of the Travel Episodes

The travel ਸਾਖੀਆਂ follow a recognizable pattern. The Guru arrives at a place — a city, a center of pilgrimage, a gathering of holy men or of the powerful. There he encounters a form of error: empty ritualism, pride, hypocrisy, cruelty, or false renunciation. Through word and deed, often through a memorable act or a pointed utterance, he exposes the error and reveals the truth. Those who are receptive are transformed; the proud are humbled. Then the Guru moves on.

This pattern is the narrative engine of the ਉੱਤਰਾਰਧ, and it directly serves the theology of ਜੋਤਿ. Each episode is another enactment of light dispelling darkness. The darkness takes many forms — the dead ritualism of pilgrimage, the arrogance of the powerful, the self-deception of false ascetics — but in every case the Guru's presence reveals it for what it is and points beyond it to the living truth of the divine Name.

Representative Episodes

Among the most celebrated travel ਸਾਖੀਆਂ that Santokh Singh narrates are several that have become emblematic of the Guru's teaching. At a great center of Hindu pilgrimage, the Guru is shown challenging the practice of offering water to the sun for departed ancestors, throwing water in the opposite direction toward his fields and thereby exposing the logic of the ritual through a memorable demonstration. At a Muslim setting, when reproached for the direction in which he lay, the Guru responds that the divine is present in every direction, dissolving the assumption that the sacred can be confined to a single point on the compass.

In encounters with assemblies of yogis and ascetics, the Guru is depicted in extended dialogue, affirming the path of the householder devoted to the divine Name over the path of world-renouncing austerity. These dialogues allow Santokh Singh to expound, in the Guru's voice, the core of Sikh teaching: that liberation is found not in flight from the world but in living truthfully within it while remembering the divine.

The Theological Geography

The sweep of the journeys is itself meaningful. By carrying the Guru to the four directions and to the heart of every major religious tradition of his world, the narrative makes a universal claim. The ਜੋਤਿ is not the possession of one region or one community; it shines for all. The Guru's mission is to the whole of humanity. This universalizing geography is one of the most enduring features of the inherited tradition, and Santokh Singh renders it with full force.

Return to Kartarpur

The ਉੱਤਰਾਰਧ culminates in the Guru's return and the founding of the community at Kartarpur. Here the wandering teacher becomes the settled founder of a ਪੰਥ. He establishes the disciplines that will define the community: the gathering of the faithful, the singing of the divine Word, the institution of the common kitchen where all eat together without distinction of caste, and the daily life of honest labor, sharing, and remembrance. The final episodes narrate the appointment of the successor — the passing of the ਜੋਤਿ to Guru Angad — and the Guru's own passing.

The appointment of the successor is theologically decisive, for it inaugurates the doctrine of the one Light passing through the succession of Gurus. With Guru Nanak's passing the ਜੋਤਿ does not depart from the world; it continues in the line of the Gurus. Thus the close of ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ opens directly onto the larger story that the ਸੂਰਜ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ will tell. That relationship between the two works is the subject of our next lesson.

lessons.title: From Nanak Prakash to Suraj Prakash: One Work, Two Horizons
lessons.summary: The relationship between the two great hagiographies of Santokh Singh.
lessons.html:
Two Works, One Vision

Santokh Singh composed two great hagiographical works. ਸ੍ਰੀ ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼, the earlier and shorter, is devoted entirely to Guru Nanak. ਸੂਰਜ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ — formally the Gur Pratap Suraj Granth — is the vastly larger work covering the lives of the remaining nine Gurus, from Guru Angad to Guru Gobind Singh. Together they constitute a complete poetic biography of the ten Gurus, and the tradition came to read them as a single continuous account, with ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ as the opening section.

The Solar Architecture

The relationship between the two titles is itself illuminating. The word ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ means light or illumination, and ਸੂਰਜ means sun. The combined cycle is built on a sustained solar metaphor. The complete ਸੂਰਜ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ is organized into large divisions that the poet names with the vocabulary of the sun's daily and seasonal course — sections evoking the rising, the seasons, and the phases of solar movement. The life of each Guru is figured as a phase in the shining of a single sun. Within this scheme, Guru Nanak is the dawn: the first rising of the light that will traverse the whole sky of the ten Gurus.

This is why ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ fits so naturally as the opening of the larger cycle. Its theology of ਜੋਤਿ — the divine Light first manifest in Guru Nanak — is precisely the premise on which the solar architecture of the ਸੂਰਜ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ depends. The one Light that rises with Guru Nanak passes through each successive Guru, just as one sun moves through the hours of the day. The doctrine of the single ਜੋਤਿ passing through the Gurus is the conceptual link that joins the two works into one.

Differences Between the Works

Despite their unity of vision, the two works differ in important ways. ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ was composed earlier and is the product of the poet's first sustained engagement with Guru-biography. The ਸੂਰਜ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼, completed some two decades later under the patronage at Kaithal, is far more massive, more encyclopedic in its detail, and in places more elaborate in its theological and philosophical digression. Scholars including ਰਤਨ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੱਗੀ have noted development in the poet's technique and emphasis between the two works.

There is also a difference in the available source material. For the life of Guru Nanak, Santokh Singh drew on the rich and elaborated ਜਨਮਸਾਖੀ tradition. For the later Gurus, especially those whose lives were more fully documented and historically proximate, he drew on a different body of sources — historical traditions, the ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ literature, and other accounts. This affects the texture of the two works: the life of Guru Nanak is more saturated with legend and miracle, while portions of the later cycle engage more directly with political and military history.

Editorial Unification

As noted in an earlier lesson, the editorial tradition — culminating in the edition of ਭਾਈ ਵੀਰ ਸਿੰਘ — treated the two works as one continuous cycle. In the conventional arrangement, the material is divided into large sections, and the life of Guru Nanak constitutes the opening section of the whole. This editorial unification reflects the genuine continuity of conception between the works while sometimes obscuring the fact that ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ was composed as a freestanding poem years before its companion.

Why the Relationship Matters

For the student of ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼, understanding its relationship to the ਸੂਰਜ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ accomplishes two things. First, it reveals the larger theological design within which the life of Guru Nanak is set: not an isolated biography but the opening movement of a unified account of the divine Light's journey through all ten Gurus. Second, it guards against a common confusion. Because the two works were editorially merged, ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ is sometimes spoken of as simply a part of the Suraj Granth. The student should now be able to hold both truths: that it was composed as an independent work, and that it functions within the tradition as the first chapter of a greater whole.

Having situated ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ within Santokh Singh's larger project, we turn in the next lesson to the most contested question raised by his work: the ਨਿਰਮਲਾ and Vedantic lens through which he interpreted the Guru, and the vigorous modern debate it has provoked.

lessons.title: The Nirmala-Vedantic Lens and Modern Scholarly Debate
lessons.summary: The interpretive controversy surrounding Santokh Singh's reading of Guru Nanak.
lessons.html:
The Heart of the Controversy

No serious study of ਸ੍ਰੀ ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ can avoid the central interpretive controversy that surrounds it. Santokh Singh wrote as a ਨਿਰਮਲਾ scholar, trained in Sanskrit and Vedanta, and his reading of Guru Nanak bears the deep imprint of that training. He interprets the Guru's teaching through the categories of non-dual Vedanta and frames the Guru's advent in the Puranic idiom of ਅਵਤਾਰ. The question that modern scholarship has debated with great intensity is whether this interpretive lens faithfully renders Guru Nanak's own theology or distorts it.

The Case for Distortion

One influential line of scholarship argues that the ਨਿਰਮਲਾ reading represents a Brahmanizing overlay upon a tradition that had originally defined itself against Brahmanical categories. On this view, Guru Nanak's bani is radically critical of ritualism, caste, and the authority of the Brahmanical scriptures, and it insists on a formless divine that does not take birth. To read this teaching through Vedanta and to frame the Guru's advent as an ਅਵਤਾਰ is, the argument runs, to assimilate the Sikh tradition back into the very Brahmanical framework it had transcended.

Harjot Oberoi, in his study of the construction of religious boundaries, situated the ਨਿਰਮਲਾ and ਉਦਾਸੀ scholarship within a broader nineteenth-century religious world in which the boundaries between Sikh, Hindu, and other traditions were fluid and porous. The later ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ reform movement, which sought to define a sharply distinct Sikh identity, would react precisely against this fluidity. W. H. McLeod, for his part, treated the hagiographical and ਨਿਰਮਲਾ traditions critically, distinguishing their theological constructions from the historical Guru and from the Guru's own bani.

The Case for Continuity

Against this, a more sympathetic reading — associated with scholars including ਰਤਨ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੱਗੀ — argues that Santokh Singh's use of Sanskritic and Puranic vocabulary should not be read as a metaphysical commitment to Brahmanical doctrine. On this view, the poet employed the available learned idiom of his time, the prestige language of theology and poetry, as a vehicle for genuinely Sikh content. When he calls the Guru's advent an ਅਵਤਾਰ, he means divine manifestation in a loose, devotional sense, not the literal bodily incarnation of a Puranic deity. His underlying theology, this reading holds, remains faithful to the Sikh insistence on the formless ਨਿਰੰਕਾਰ and the unique mediating role of the Guru.

This debate cannot be settled by a simple verdict, and the advanced student should resist the temptation to do so. The honest position is that Santokh Singh's text genuinely contains both impulses. It affirms the formless divine and the distinctiveness of the Guru's mission; it also reaches habitually for Brahmanical and Vedantic categories. The text is a site where these impulses meet, and its richness lies partly in that meeting.

The Historical Context of the Debate

It is important to understand why this controversy carries such weight. The decades after Santokh Singh saw the rise of the ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ movement, which undertook to purify Sikh practice and self-understanding of what it regarded as Brahmanical accretions. From this reforming standpoint, the ਨਿਰਮਲਾ scholarship of the early nineteenth century, including Santokh Singh's, came to be viewed with suspicion as having blurred the boundaries of Sikh identity. The modern scholarly debate is in part a continuation of this earlier internal Sikh argument about what constitutes authentic Sikh theology.

At the same time, it would be anachronistic to judge Santokh Singh by the standards of a movement that arose after him. He wrote within his own intellectual world, in good faith, as a devoted Sikh employing the learned tools available to him. The ਨਿਰਮਲਾ idiom was not, in his time, experienced as a betrayal of the tradition; it was the natural language of Sikh learning.

Reading with the Tension in View

The mature way to read ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ is therefore neither to dismiss it as Brahmanized distortion nor to deny the presence of the Vedantic and Puranic lens. It is to read it as a profound and beautiful work that interprets Guru Nanak through the categories of its author's formation, and to remain alert to where those categories illuminate the Guru's teaching and where they may pull against it. This double awareness — appreciation joined to critical discernment — is the disposition this course aims to cultivate. In the final lesson we consider the work's legacy and how to read it responsibly today.

lessons.title: Legacy, Reception, and Reading Nanak Prakash Today
lessons.summary: The enduring influence of the work and guidance for responsible reading.
lessons.html:
An Enduring Influence

For more than a century after its composition, ਸ੍ਰੀ ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ shaped the Sikh imagination of Guru Nanak's life. Together with its companion ਸੂਰਜ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼, it became the principal source for ਕਥਾ, the homiletic exposition delivered in gurdwaras and gatherings. Generations of kathakars drew their episodes, their phrasing, and their theological framing from Santokh Singh's verse. When ordinary Sikhs pictured the birth, the childhood, the river commission, and the great journeys of the Guru, they were very often picturing them as Santokh Singh had rendered them.

This influence makes the work historically important quite apart from its literary merit. To study ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ is to study one of the principal channels through which the image of Guru Nanak reached the modern Sikh community. Even where later scholarship has questioned the historicity of particular episodes, the cultural and devotional impact of the poem is undeniable.

The Editorial Legacy of Vir Singh

The modern reception of the work is inseparable from the editorial labor of ਭਾਈ ਵੀਰ ਸਿੰਘ. His annotated edition, produced in the early twentieth century, made the dense ਬ੍ਰਜ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ text accessible to a wide readership through glosses, explanations, and editorial apparatus. Vir Singh, himself a leading figure of the Sikh literary renaissance, treated Santokh Singh's work with deep respect while bringing modern editorial standards to bear. His edition remains the standard text and the gateway through which most readers approach the poem.

The Critical Legacy of Jaggi

The scholarly study of the work was placed on rigorous foundations by ਰਤਨ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੱਗੀ, whose monographs on the life and writings of Santokh Singh and on the ਸੂਰਜ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ remain indispensable. Jaggi's source-critical, linguistic, and structural analyses allow the modern student to read the poem with scholarly precision: to identify its sources, to follow its architecture, and to assess its theological claims. Alongside Jaggi, the wider field of Sikh studies — the work of J. S. Grewal, W. H. McLeod, Gurinder Singh Mann, Harjot Oberoi, and others — provides the critical context within which the work must now be read.

How to Read the Work Responsibly

The responsible modern reader of ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ holds several commitments together. First, genre awareness: the work is theological biography, hagiography in the best sense, and must be read for the faith it expresses and the meaning it constructs, not mined naively for historical fact. Second, source awareness: the episodes derive from the ਜਨਮਸਾਖੀ tradition, transformed by the poet's selection and interpretation. Third, theological awareness: the governing claim is that Guru Nanak is the ਜੋਤਿ incarnate, and every episode serves that claim. Fourth, critical awareness: the ਨਿਰਮਲਾ and Vedantic lens shapes the interpretation in ways that have been vigorously debated.

With these commitments in place, the work becomes neither an infallible record nor a discredited relic, but a rich and rewarding object of study: a masterwork of Sikh devotional poetry, a culmination of the ਜਨਮਸਾਖੀ tradition, and a window onto the theological imagination of early nineteenth-century Sikhism.

The Work's Place in Sikh Letters

Finally, ਸ੍ਰੀ ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ deserves recognition as a literary achievement in its own right. The skill with which Santokh Singh deploys the resources of ਬ੍ਰਜ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ, the architecture of ਅਧਿਆਇ and ਛੰਦ, the sustained image of light, and the integration of narrative and theology mark him as one of the major poets of the Sikh tradition. His work stands at the meeting point of the Sikh and the wider Indic literary worlds, drawing on both to create something that is distinctively its own.

This course has aimed to equip you to read that achievement with both appreciation and discernment — to honor the devotion and artistry of the poet while bringing to bear the critical tools of modern scholarship. The student who completes it should be able to take up a passage of ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼, locate it within the structure and the tradition, identify the theological work it performs, and assess it within the ongoing scholarly conversation. That is the mark of an advanced reader of this remarkable text.

  • Jaggi, Rattan Singh. Kavi Santokh Singh: Jiwan te Rachna. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1968.
  • Jaggi, Rattan Singh. Gur Pratap Suraj Granth: Adhiain. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1990.
  • Mann, Gurinder Singh. The Making of Sikh Scripture. New York: Oxford University Press, 2001.
  • McLeod, W. H. Early Sikh Tradition: A Study of the Janam-sakhis. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1980.
  • Oberoi, Harjot. The Construction of Religious Boundaries: Culture, Identity and Diversity in the Sikh Tradition. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1994.

quiz.q: What is the central theological claim that ਸ੍ਰੀ ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ advances about Guru Nanak through its narrative and its very title?
options: That Guru Nanak was primarily a social reformer opposed to Mughal rule
That Guru Nanak is the ਜੋਤਿ, the divine Light, made manifest in human form
That Guru Nanak compiled the entire Guru Granth Sahib himself
That Guru Nanak rejected all earlier Indian religious vocabulary

quiz.q: How does ਸ੍ਰੀ ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ relate to the later ਸੂਰਜ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ (Gur Pratap Suraj Granth)?
options: It is an unrelated work by a different author
It was composed earlier and devoted to Guru Nanak, later treated editorially as the opening section of the combined cycle
It is a prose summary of the Suraj Granth
It contradicts the theology of the Suraj Granth

quiz.q: In what language did ਕਵੀ ਸੰਤੋਖ ਸਿੰਘ compose the work, and why is this significant?
options: Modern standard Punjabi, to reach the common people
Persian, because of Mughal patronage
ਬ੍ਰਜ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ, the prestige medium of North Indian devotional and narrative poetry
Sanskrit, to exclude lay readers

quiz.q: What body of earlier tradition supplied Santokh Singh with the episodes (ਸਾਖੀਆਂ) of Guru Nanak's life?
options: The ਜਨਮਸਾਖੀ tradition, including the Puratan, Bala, and Miharban strands
The Mughal court chronicles
The Vedas and Upanishads directly
Contemporary British colonial records

quiz.q: What is the core of the modern scholarly debate surrounding Santokh Singh's interpretation of Guru Nanak?
options: Whether the work was actually written by Santokh Singh at all
Whether his ਨਿਰਮਲਾ-Vedantic and Puranic idiom faithfully renders Guru Nanak's theology or overlays a Brahmanical frame upon it
Whether Guru Nanak ever traveled outside Punjab
Whether the work was composed in verse or prose

quiz.q: Which pivotal episode of the ਪੂਰਬਾਰਧ marks the Guru's divine commission and the transition to his public mission?
options: The founding of Kartarpur
The schooling episode with his teacher
The disappearance into and return from the river ਵੇਈਂ at Sultanpur
The appointment of Guru Angad

courses.title: Gurbilas Patshahi 6: Guru Hargobind Ji and Miri-Piri
courses.summary: An advanced study of the Gurbilas Patshahi 6, the early Sikh verse-chronicle (ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ) celebrating the reign of Guru Hargobind Ji, the sixth Nanak. The course examines the text as a literary and historical source for the doctrine of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ — the union of temporal and spiritual sovereignty — the founding of the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ, the militarisation of the Panth, the four battles against Mughal forces, the Guru's imprisonment in Gwalior, his relations with Emperor Jahangir, and the development of Amritsar and the Kartarpur period. Students engage critically with questions of authorship, dating, and the place of ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ literature within the wider corpus of Sikh historiography.
outcomes: Explain the genre of ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ literature and locate Gurbilas Patshahi 6 within the development of Sikh historical writing, including the scholarly debates over its authorship and date.
Analyse the doctrine of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ as articulated through the imagery of the two swords and the founding of the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ, and assess how the text theologises Sikh sovereignty.
Reconstruct the principal military engagements of Guru Hargobind Ji's reign as narrated in the text and evaluate their reliability against other primary sources.
Interpret the Guru's imprisonment at Gwalior and his relations with Emperor Jahangir as presented in the chronicle and in Mughal sources.
Assess the role of Amritsar, the ਲੋਹਗੜ੍ਹ fort, and the Kartarpur period in the institutional consolidation of the Panth.
Evaluate the historiographical value and limitations of Gurbilas Patshahi 6 as a source for seventeenth-century Sikh history.

terms.m: "The play/glory of the Guru" — a genre of Sikh verse-chronicle, mostly composed in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, celebrating the martial and miraculous deeds of a particular Guru, especially the sixth and tenth.
The doctrine of the union of temporal authority (ਮੀਰੀ, from Persian mir, commander) and spiritual authority (ਪੀਰੀ, from pir, saint) embodied by Guru Hargobind Ji wearing two swords.
The "Throne of the Timeless One," raised by Guru Hargobind Ji at Amritsar in 1606 as the seat of Sikh temporal sovereignty, standing opposite the ਹਰਿਮੰਦਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ.
The ideal of the "saint-soldier" — one who unites inward devotion with the readiness to wield the sword in defence of righteousness, modelled by the sixth Guru.
The "iron fortress" built by Guru Hargobind Ji at Amritsar — the first Sikh fort, symbol of the Panth's new military posture.
The Timeless Being, the formless Divine of Gurmat, in whose sovereignty the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ and Sikh temporal authority are grounded.
The Sikh community as a corporate body and path; under Guru Hargobind Ji it took on an explicitly martial and politically self-conscious character.
The great war-drum sounded at the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ — an emblem of sovereignty, since the right to beat a drum was a royal prerogative under Mughal custom.
Local representatives who collected offerings (ਦਸਵੰਧ) for the Guru; their network funded Amritsar's growth and the gathering of horses and arms.
"Cauldron and sword" — the twin emblems of charitable provision and just force, encapsulating the Mughal-era Sikh ideal of sovereignty rooted in service and protection.
Poet; the author of the Gurbilas is conventionally named Sohan Kavi, whose identity and date remain contested among scholars.
The central Sikh shrine at Amritsar, completed under Guru Arjan; the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ was raised facing it, pairing devotion with sovereignty.

references: Padam, Piara Singh. Sri Guru Granth Sahib de Lekhak. Patiala: Kalam Mandir, 1990.

McLeod, W. H. Sikhs of the Khalsa: A History of the Khalsa Rahit. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2003.

lessons.title: Introduction: The Genre of Gurbilas and the Reign of the Sixth Guru
lessons.summary: An orientation to ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ literature, the place of Gurbilas Patshahi 6 within Sikh historiography, and the course as a whole.
lessons.html:
ਵਿਸ਼ਾ ਸੂਚੀ (Table of Contents)

  1. Introduction: The Genre of Gurbilas and the Reign of the Sixth Guru
  2. Authorship, Dating, and the Manuscript Tradition of the Text
  3. From Martyrdom to Militancy: The Succession of Guru Hargobind Ji
  4. The Two Swords: The Doctrine of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ
  5. Raising the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ and the Architecture of Sovereignty
  6. The Militarisation of the ਪੰਥ: Horses, Arms, and the ਲੋਹਗੜ੍ਹ
  7. Imprisonment at Gwalior and Relations with Jahangir
  8. The Four Battles: Amritsar, Lahira, and Kartarpur
  9. Amritsar, the ਮਸੰਦ Network, and Institutional Consolidation
  10. The Kartarpur Years and the Passing of the Guru
  11. Gurbilas Patshahi 6 as a Historical Source: Method and Critique
  12. Legacy: ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ in Later Sikh Thought and Practice

What is a ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ?

The word ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ joins gur ("of the Guru") with bilas ("play," "sport," or "glory"). As a genre it designates a class of Sikh verse-chronicles, composed largely in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, that narrate the deeds of a particular Guru in heightened, celebratory, and frequently miraculous terms. The two most famous specimens are the Gurbilas Patshahi 6, concerning Guru Hargobind Ji, and the various Gurbilas Patshahi 10 texts concerning Guru Gobind Singh Ji. Unlike the earlier ਜਨਮਸਾਖੀ tradition, which centres on the life and word of Guru Nanak, the ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ foregrounds martial valour, the establishment of sovereignty, and the divine sanction behind the Guru's resort to arms.

This shift in emphasis is itself a historical datum. The genre arose during a period when the Panth was contending with Mughal and later Afghan power, and it reads the seventeenth-century reign of the sixth Guru through the militant self-understanding of a later age. For the student of history, the ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ is therefore a double document: it tells us something about the events it narrates, and a great deal about the community that produced and cherished it.

Why the Sixth Guru?

Guru Hargobind Ji (Guru from 1606 to 1644) occupies a hinge position in Sikh history. He inherited the gaddi at the age of eleven in the immediate aftermath of the martyrdom of his father, Guru Arjan Dev Ji, under Emperor Jahangir. Tradition holds that, at his installation, he asked for two swords rather than the customary ਸੇਲੀ (woollen cord of renunciation) worn by his predecessors. This gesture — whether understood literally or as a later theologisation — inaugurated the doctrine of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ, the union of temporal and spiritual authority, and the ideal of the ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ, the saint-soldier.

The Gurbilas Patshahi 6 is our most extended narrative source for this transformation. It dwells on the founding of the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ, the construction of the ਲੋਹਗੜ੍ਹ fort, the gathering of horses and arms through the ਮਸੰਦ network, the Guru's imprisonment at Gwalior, his complicated rapport with Jahangir, and the four pitched battles he fought against imperial detachments. Gurbani in the bani of the Gurus already speaks of the sovereign who is fearless and without enmity; the text translates that theology into a story of kingship and arms.

The Shape of This Course

Over twelve lessons we will move from genre and authorship, through the doctrinal core of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ, into the military and institutional history the text narrates, and finally to a critical assessment of its value as a source. Three questions will recur throughout. First, how does the text theologise sovereignty — that is, how does it ground worldly power in ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ, the Timeless One? Second, how reliable is its narration when measured against Mughal chronicles such as Jahangir's own Tuzuk and against other Sikh sources? Third, what does the text's later composition tell us about the memory and identity of the Panth?

A word on method. This course treats the Gurbilas as a primary source to be read closely and critically, not as a devotional text to be either accepted whole or dismissed. We will quote it in ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ where its language is load-bearing, and we will read it alongside the scholarship of historians such as J. S. Grewal, Ganda Singh, and our nominal professor for this course, the great Punjabi literary historian Piara Singh Padam, who did pioneering work on the dating and authenticity of ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ texts. By the end you should be able to use this chronicle as a working historian uses any source: with sympathy, with rigour, and with a clear sense of its horizon.

A Note on Sovereignty and Service

The seventeenth-century Sikh ideal is compactly captured in the later formula ਦੇਗ ਤੇਗ — "cauldron and sword." The ਦੇਗ is the cauldron of ਲੰਗਰ, the free kitchen that feeds all without distinction; the ਤੇਗ is the sword that defends the weak and upholds justice. Guru Hargobind Ji's reign is the moment at which these two became inseparable in Sikh self-understanding, and the Gurbilas Patshahi 6 is the literary monument to that fusion.

lessons.title: Authorship, Dating, and the Manuscript Tradition of the Text
lessons.summary: The scholarly debates over who wrote Gurbilas Patshahi 6, when, and how the manuscript tradition shapes our reading.
lessons.html:
The Problem of Authorship

The Gurbilas Patshahi 6 is conventionally attributed to a poet named ਸੋਹਨ ਕਵੀ (Sohan Kavi), who states in the colophon-like verses of the work that he completed it in the early nineteenth century. Yet almost everything about this attribution has been contested, and the question of authorship is the necessary starting point for any critical use of the text. A chronicle that purports to describe events of the early seventeenth century but is composed two centuries later cannot be read as an eyewitness record; it must be read as the crystallisation of a long oral and written tradition, refracted through the concerns of its own age.

The literary historian Piara Singh Padam, after whom this course is named, devoted careful attention to the ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ corpus. His work emphasised that these texts belong to a recognisable Braj-influenced Punjabi poetic idiom and that their internal dating must be tested against language, metre, and the manuscripts that survive. The ਕਵੀ tradition of Sikh court poetry, in which a poet composes in elaborate metres to glorify a patron or a sacred subject, supplies the formal conventions within which the Gurbilas operates.

Internal Evidence and Its Limits

The text itself offers chronological markers, genealogies of transmission, and occasional claims about its sources. Scholars have debated whether the Sohan named in the work is the original author of a seventeenth-century core that was later expanded, or whether the entire composition is a nineteenth-century production drawing on earlier materials. The presence of episodes that align with the militant, sovereignty-conscious mood of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries — the period of Sikh political ascendancy in the Punjab — has led several historians to read the text as much for what it reveals about that later moment as for what it reports about the sixth Guru.

This is not a counsel of despair. Historians routinely use late sources for early events, provided they discipline their reading. The key is to distinguish layers: a probable core of remembered fact (the founding of the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ, the battles, the Gwalior imprisonment, all corroborated elsewhere) from the elaborations, miracle accounts, and speeches that the genre supplies.

The Manuscript Tradition

Like most pre-print Punjabi works, the Gurbilas survives in multiple manuscript recensions that differ in length, ordering, and detail. The printed edition prepared by Gyani Inder Singh Gill and others made the text widely accessible but also fixed one version of a fluid tradition. A responsible reading attends to the fact that the text we hold is an editorial settlement of variant witnesses. Where manuscripts disagree, the modern reader inherits the editor's choices.

Three methodological principles follow. First, corroboration: a claim in the Gurbilas gains weight when independent sources — Mughal records, other Sikh chronicles such as those of the Bhatt vahis or the later Suraj Prakash of Santokh Singh — agree. Second, tendency-criticism: where the text's narration serves an obvious theological or political purpose, we weigh that interest. Third, plausibility: speeches and inner thoughts attributed to historical figures are conventions of the genre, not transcripts.

The Gurbilas Within the Corpus of Sikh Historiography

It helps to situate the text on a timeline of Sikh historical writing. The earliest layer is the ਜਨਮਸਾਖੀ literature on Guru Nanak. Then come the Bhatt vahis and contemporary administrative traces. The ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ texts form a middle period of devotional-martial chronicle, followed by the great nineteenth-century syntheses such as Santokh Singh's Gur Pratap Suraj Granth and, later still, Giani Gian Singh's Twarikh Guru Khalsa. The Gurbilas Patshahi 6 thus stands at a transitional point: more historically ambitious than the saakhi, less critical than the modern academic histories.

For our purposes the upshot is clear. The Gurbilas Patshahi 6 is indispensable because it preserves, in extended narrative form, the Panth's memory of how the sixth Guru transformed the community — but it must be used as a memory-text, read with the tools of source criticism. Throughout this course we will hold its testimony against the wider record, neither swallowing nor discarding it. As the historian J. S. Grewal has insisted, the social and political transformation of the Sikh community under Guru Hargobind Ji is well attested in its outline even where its details are coloured by later devotion.

lessons.title: From Martyrdom to Militancy: The Succession of Guru Hargobind Ji
lessons.summary: The martyrdom of Guru Arjan Dev Ji and the installation of the eleven-year-old Guru Hargobind, marking the turn toward sovereignty.
lessons.html:
The Martyrdom of Guru Arjan Dev Ji

The reign of Guru Hargobind Ji begins, in every telling, with a death. In 1606 his father, Guru Arjan Dev Ji, the fifth Nanak and compiler of the ਆਦਿ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ, was tortured to death at Lahore under the order of Emperor Jahangir. The emperor's own memoir, the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, records his decision to have the Guru put to death and his estates confiscated, complaining that too many people, Hindu and Muslim alike, were being drawn to the Guru's path. This is one of the rare moments where a Mughal source directly corroborates the Sikh narrative of persecution.

The Gurbilas, like the wider tradition, presents this martyrdom as the decisive provocation. The fifth Guru, it is held, instructed his son to sit fully armed upon his throne and to maintain an army to the best of his ability. Whether or not these precise words were spoken, they encapsulate the meaning the community drew from the event: the path of pure devotion now required the means of self-defence. Gurbani in the compositions of Guru Arjan teaches a serene acceptance of the Divine Will even in suffering, and it is against that backdrop of ਭਾਣਾ (acceptance of the Divine Order) that the turn to arms must be understood — not as a repudiation of the spiritual path but as its protection.

The Installation of an Eleven-Year-Old Guru

Guru Hargobind Ji was a child of about eleven when he assumed the gaddi. The Gurbilas dwells on the famous departure from custom at the installation ceremony. Where his predecessors had received the ਸੇਲੀ ਟੋਪੀ — the woollen cord and cap of the renunciant — the young Guru is said to have asked Baba Buddha Ji, the venerable Sikh who performed the ceremony, to gird him instead with a sword. According to the tradition he then donned a second sword, declaring one to be the emblem of ਮੀਰੀ (temporal authority) and the other of ਪੀਰੀ (spiritual authority).

This is the foundational scene of the doctrine we will study in the next lesson. For now, note its narrative function in the text: it transforms a moment of grief and vulnerability — a boy succeeding a martyred father in the shadow of imperial power — into an assertion of sovereignty. The Gurbilas converts loss into legitimacy.

Continuity and Change

It would be a mistake to read the sixth Guru's reign as a rupture with everything before. The institutional foundations he built upon — the ਮਸੰਦ network of representatives, the centrality of Amritsar with its ਹਰਿਮੰਦਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ, the practice of ਦਸਵੰਧ (the tithe of one-tenth), and above all the authority of the ਆਦਿ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ — were the legacy of Guru Arjan. The new Guru added a martial and political dimension without abandoning the spiritual and devotional core. The continuity of ਨਾਮ (the Divine Name), ਸੇਵਾ (selfless service), and ਸੰਗਤ (the congregation) is essential to understanding why the Sikhs did not become merely a soldiery but remained a religious community under arms.

The Logic of Sovereignty

Why did the response to persecution take the form of sovereignty rather than mere armed self-defence? The answer lies in the Sikh theology of ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ as the only true King. If the Timeless One is sovereign, then the worldly ruler who persecutes the devout is a usurper of a kind, and the Guru's assumption of royal symbols — the throne, the parasol, the war-drum — is not rebellion but the visible reflection of divine kingship in the world. The Gurbilas develops this logic in narrative form. As we shall see when we examine the founding of the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ, the sixth Guru did not claim to be a king like other kings; he claimed to embody, in the temporal realm, the sovereignty that belongs to ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ alone. The martyrdom of the fifth Guru thus becomes, in the structure of the text, the seed from which the doctrine of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ grows.

lessons.title: The Two Swords: The Doctrine of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ
lessons.summary: A close analysis of the doctrine of temporal and spiritual sovereignty embodied in the two swords of Guru Hargobind Ji.
lessons.html:
The Meaning of the Two Swords

The central doctrine the Gurbilas Patshahi 6 dramatises is ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ. The terms are of Persian origin: ਮੀਰੀ derives from mir, a commander or prince, and denotes temporal, political, worldly authority; ਪੀਰੀ derives from pir, a spiritual master or saint, and denotes spiritual authority. By wearing two swords, one for each, Guru Hargobind Ji declared that these two domains, which the surrounding political and religious culture tended to keep separate, were in the Guru united in a single person and a single mission.

This was a genuinely novel synthesis. In the Mughal order, the emperor held temporal power while spiritual authority was vested in the ulama and the Sufi pirs; in much of the Indic tradition, the renunciant who sought liberation withdrew from worldly power altogether. The Sikh claim was that the householder-devotee could and must hold both — that the pursuit of ਨਾਮ and the responsibility for justice in the world are not opposites but a single calling. This is the doctrinal root of the ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ, the saint-soldier.

The Theological Ground

The doctrine is not an opportunistic militarisation; it has deep roots in Gurmat. Gurbani in the bani of the earlier Gurus already affirms that ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ is the true Sovereign, that worldly kingship is a shadow held in trust, and that the devotee must live fearlessly and without enmity while standing for righteousness. Guru Nanak Sahib's searing critique of the tyranny of rulers — his witness against the violence of Babar's invasions — establishes that the Guru's voice does not retreat from the political sphere but judges it. The sixth Guru's two swords give institutional form to a prophetic stance that was present from the beginning.

Crucially, ਮੀਰੀ is subordinate to and in service of ਪੀਰੀ. The sword of temporal power is not an end in itself; it exists to protect the conditions in which devotion and justice can flourish. This ordering distinguishes Sikh sovereignty from mere conquest. The later formula ਦੇਗ ਤੇਗ ਫ਼ਤਹ — "victory to the cauldron and the sword" — preserves the same priority: provision and protection together, with force always at the service of compassion and justice.

How the Gurbilas Stages the Doctrine

The Gurbilas does not present ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ as an abstract proposition; it embodies it in scenes. The installation with two swords, the building of the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ facing the ਹਰਿਮੰਦਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ, the morning gathering for ਕੀਰਤਨ at the temple and the afternoon court of justice and martial display at the throne — these paired images render the doctrine visible. The text presents the Guru holding court (ਦਰਬਾਰ), hearing petitions, dispensing justice, receiving gifts of horses and weapons, and patronising bards who sang of heroism (ਵਾਰਾਂ). Each of these is the temporal sword in action, always anchored to the spiritual sword that legitimises it.

The Pairing of ਹਰਿਮੰਦਰ and ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ

The architecture of Amritsar itself preaches the doctrine. The ਹਰਿਮੰਦਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ, set low and approached by descending steps, signifies humility before the Divine — the realm of ਪੀਰੀ. The ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ, raised on a high platform directly facing it, signifies the throne of temporal sovereignty — the realm of ਮੀਰੀ. The worshipper who stands between them stands at the meeting-point of the two swords. We will examine the founding and meaning of the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ in the next lesson, but it is worth pausing here on the deliberateness of the design: the two centres face one another, neither swallowing the other, a built theology of balance.

Why the Doctrine Mattered

The doctrine of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ supplied the Panth with a durable answer to the problem of how a religious community should relate to political power. It refused both quietist withdrawal and unprincipled rebellion. It authorised the use of force, but only in defence of justice and the freedom to worship, and only under spiritual discipline.
