When, generations later, Guru Gobind Singh Ji created the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ and the Sikhs took up arms against tyranny, they were drawing on the synthesis that the sixth Guru first embodied and that the Gurbilas Patshahi 6 records and celebrates.

lessons.title: Raising the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ and the Architecture of Sovereignty
lessons.summary: The founding of the Akal Takhat in 1606 as the seat of Sikh temporal authority and its symbolic meaning.
lessons.html:
The Founding of the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ

In 1606, shortly after assuming the gaddi, Guru Hargobind Ji raised a platform at Amritsar, directly facing the ਹਰਿਮੰਦਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ, which he called the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ — the Throne of the Timeless One. The Gurbilas Patshahi 6 narrates its construction with the participation of revered Sikhs such as Baba Buddha Ji and Bhai Gurdas Ji. The name is itself a theological statement: ਤਖ਼ਤ is the Persian-Indic word for a royal throne, and to prefix it with ਅਕਾਲ (Timeless, beyond death) is to declare that the only sovereignty the Sikhs acknowledge as ultimate is that of ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ.

A Counter-Court to the Mughal Throne

The significance of the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ can hardly be overstated. By raising a throne, the Guru asserted a sovereignty parallel to and independent of the imperial throne at Delhi and Agra. The Gurbilas reports the adoption of royal insignia that, under Mughal protocol, were the jealously guarded prerogatives of kingship: the ਛਤ੍ਰ (royal parasol), the ਚੌਰ (whisk), and above all the ਨਗਾਰਾ, the great war-drum. The right to beat a drum and to hold court were marks of a ruler; their assumption by the Guru was a public claim to sovereign status.

Yet this was not a claim to ordinary kingship. The Guru held no land grant from the emperor, levied no land tax, and ruled no territory in the administrative sense. His was a sovereignty of conscience and community — the sovereignty of the ਪੰਥ as a self-governing body owing ultimate allegiance to ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ alone. The ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ became the seat from which the temporal affairs of the community were directed: justice dispensed, disputes resolved, the martial spirit cultivated.

The Daily Rhythm of the Two Centres

The tradition preserves a vivid picture of the Guru's daily routine that perfectly enacts the doctrine of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ. In the morning the Guru attended the ਹਰਿਮੰਦਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ for ਕੀਰਤਨ and the devotional life of the ਸੰਗਤ; in the afternoon and evening he held court at the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ, where bards sang ballads of heroism, wrestlers and warriors displayed their skill, petitioners brought their grievances, and the Guru received tribute of arms and horses. The same person, the same day, encompassed both worship and rule.

The Gurbilas also records the institution of the ਢਾਡੀ — minstrels who sang martial ballads (ਵਾਰਾਂ) at the throne, kindling courage and recalling the deeds of heroes. Where the ਹਰਿਮੰਦਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ resounded with hymns of divine love, the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ resounded with songs of valour. The two musics together expressed the whole Sikh ideal.

The ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ as Institution

The throne the sixth Guru raised did not remain merely a building; it became an enduring institution of Sikh self-governance. In later centuries the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ would be the place from which the ਸਰਬੱਤ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ (the assembly of the whole Khalsa) issued its collective decisions (ਗੁਰਮਤਾ), and from which the highest authority of the Panth would speak. The seed of all this was planted in 1606. The Gurbilas Patshahi 6, by narrating the founding in detail, helped fix in the community's memory the meaning and dignity of this institution.

Reading the Founding Critically

As historians we should note that the precise ceremonial details the Gurbilas supplies — the speeches, the exact insignia, the order of events — bear the marks of the genre and of later institutional development read back into the founding moment. What is well grounded is the core fact: that Guru Hargobind Ji established at Amritsar a seat of temporal authority facing the central shrine, and that this act crystallised the doctrine of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ in stone and protocol. The historian J. S. Grewal treats this institutional innovation as one of the most consequential developments of the early seventeenth-century Panth, and the Gurbilas is our richest narrative window onto it, provided we read it with the source-critical discipline established in Lesson 2.

lessons.title: The Militarisation of the ਪੰਥ: Horses, Arms, and the ਲੋਹਗੜ੍ਹ
lessons.summary: How Guru Hargobind Ji gathered arms, horses, and fighting men and built the first Sikh fort.
lessons.html:
A Community Under Arms

The most visible change of the sixth Guru's reign was the transformation of the ਪੰਥ into a community capable of bearing arms. The Gurbilas Patshahi 6 describes the Guru issuing a call, through the ਮਸੰਦ network, for offerings to be made not only in cash but in the form of horses and weapons, and for young men of spirit to come to Amritsar to serve. Where earlier the ਦਸਵੰਧ had funded ਲੰਗਰ and the building of shrines, now a portion supported a standing body of retainers and the means of war.

The text speaks of the gathering of fine horses, of armouries, and of a bodyguard of devoted Sikhs. Tradition records that the Guru maintained a force of several hundred mounted soldiers and that warriors from the Majha and Doaba regions of the Punjab, and from further afield, came to enlist. The famous Pathan warrior Painda Khan, raised in the Guru's service, is one of the figures the tradition remembers — a reminder that the Guru's following crossed communal lines.

The Building of the ਲੋਹਗੜ੍ਹ

To defend Amritsar, Guru Hargobind Ji constructed a fort, the ਲੋਹਗੜ੍ਹ — the "iron fortress." The Gurbilas narrates its building as a deliberate act of preparedness. The fort was the first Sikh military structure of its kind and a concrete sign that the Panth now reckoned with the possibility of armed conflict. Its very name, joining ਲੋਹ (iron) with ਗੜ੍ਹ (fort), broadcasts the new martial identity; iron would become a recurring emblem of Sikh strength, later enshrined in the ਸਰਬਲੋਹ (all-iron) ideal.

The construction of a fort at Amritsar did not go unnoticed by the Mughal administration. A religious community gathering horses, arms, and fighting men, building fortifications, and beating a war-drum near the imperial heartland of the Punjab was bound to attract suspicion. The military preparations of these years form part of the background to the Guru's later imprisonment at Gwalior and to the battles that would follow.

The Economy of Arms

It is worth dwelling on the institutional mechanics. The ਮਸੰਦ were the Guru's appointed agents in the regions, gathering the offerings of the ਸੰਗਤ and conveying them to the centre. This network, inherited from Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan, was the financial backbone that made militarisation possible without the Guru holding any territorial revenue. The Gurbilas shows the masand network being redirected, at least in part, from purely devotional purposes toward the support of a martial establishment. This continuity of institutions across a change of function is exactly the kind of detail the working historian prizes, because it shows how a religious movement could mobilise material resources for defence.

Discipline and Restraint

The militarisation of the Panth was not a turn to aggression. The tradition is emphatic that the Guru's forces were maintained for defence and for the protection of the weak, not for conquest or plunder. The sixth Guru fought, as we shall see, only when attacked, and the Sikh ideal that emerges is of arms held under spiritual discipline — the ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ who fights without hatred and refrains from cruelty even in battle. Gurbani in the wider Sikh tradition teaches that one should raise the sword only when all other means have failed; this principle of force as a last resort governs the way the Gurbilas presents the Guru's campaigns.

The Significance of the Transformation

The arming of the Panth under Guru Hargobind Ji is the practical correlate of the doctrine of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ. A throne without the means to defend justice would be an empty symbol; the horses, the arms, the fort, and the soldiers gave the temporal sword its edge. At the same time, the persistence of ਕੀਰਤਨ, ਲੰਗਰ, and the authority of the ਆਦਿ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ensured that the community remained, in its self-understanding, a fellowship of devotees and not a mere warband. The Gurbilas Patshahi 6 captures this dual character with particular vividness, and it is one of the reasons the text remains a central source for the study of the Panth's transformation in the seventeenth century.

lessons.title: Imprisonment at Gwalior and Relations with Jahangir
lessons.summary: The Guru's confinement in Gwalior fort, the tradition of Bandi Chhor, and the complex relationship with Emperor Jahangir.
lessons.html:
The Summons and the Imprisonment

One of the most celebrated episodes the Gurbilas Patshahi 6 narrates is the imprisonment of Guru Hargobind Ji in the fortress of Gwalior. The circumstances reflect the suspicion with which the Mughal court regarded the Guru's growing temporal power. According to the tradition, Emperor Jahangir, troubled by reports of the Guru's military preparations — and perhaps also by the unpaid fine that had been levied against the house of the Guru after the martyrdom of Guru Arjan — summoned the Guru and ordered him confined in the great hill-fort of Gwalior, where other princes and political detainees were held.

The length of the confinement is given variously in different accounts. What the tradition agrees upon is that the Guru bore the imprisonment with composure, that he ministered to fellow prisoners, and that his release became the occasion for one of the most cherished memories of the Panth.

The Tradition of ਬੰਦੀ ਛੋੜ

The Guru is remembered as ਬੰਦੀ ਛੋੜ — "the Liberator of Prisoners." The tradition holds that when Jahangir ordered the Guru's release, the Guru refused to leave unless the other princes confined with him were also freed. The emperor, it is said, agreed that as many could leave as could hold on to the Guru's cloak; the Guru had a special garment made with many tassels, and so a number of detained rajas walked free clutching its hems. Whatever the historical kernel of this account, its meaning in the tradition is profound: the Guru's own freedom is incomplete so long as others remain in chains. The episode is commemorated, in popular Sikh observance, in close connection with the autumn festival of lights, when the Guru's return to Amritsar is recalled.

The story crystallises the ethical core of ਮੀਰੀ: temporal power exercised for the liberation of the oppressed. The Guru does not seek his own advantage from the emperor but uses the moment to free the captive. This is sovereignty in the service of ਪੀਰੀ.

The Ambiguous Rapport with Jahangir

The relationship between Guru Hargobind Ji and Jahangir is more complex than a simple opposition of persecutor and persecuted. After the Gwalior episode, the sources suggest a period of relative accommodation. Jahangir's own memoir mentions the Guru, and the tradition records meetings, even hunting expeditions, between the two. It seems that, for a time, the emperor was satisfied that the Guru posed no immediate political threat, and the Guru was able to consolidate the Panth without open conflict.

This phase of accommodation is historically important. It reminds us that the militarisation of the Panth did not entail perpetual war, and that the Mughal state was not monolithically hostile. The decisive turn to armed conflict came largely after Jahangir's death, under the more rigid policies associated with the reign of Shah Jahan, when the four battles of the Guru's reign were fought.

Reading the Episode Critically

The Gwalior imprisonment is well attested in outline; the fortress was indeed a place of political confinement under the Mughals, and the Guru's detention there is consistent with the imperial concern over his temporal claims. The miraculous and ceremonial elaborations — the precise number of liberated princes, the tasselled cloak, the supernatural signs — belong to the devotional texture of the Gurbilas and the broader tradition. The historian distinguishes the plausible core (confinement at Gwalior, release, the persona of ਬੰਦੀ ਛੋੜ) from the legendary detail, while recognising that the legend itself carries the community's enduring interpretation of the event.

The Meaning for the Doctrine of Sovereignty

The Gwalior episode advances the text's argument about ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ in two ways. First, it shows the Guru as a figure the empire must reckon with — a sovereign power, not a quietist sect. Second, it shows the moral content of that sovereignty: the Guru uses his standing not for self-aggrandisement but to liberate the captive. In the figure of ਬੰਦੀ ਛੋੜ, temporal authority and spiritual compassion are perfectly fused, and the Gurbilas Patshahi 6 offers this as the model of true kingship under ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ.

lessons.title: The Four Battles: Amritsar, Lahira, and Kartarpur
lessons.summary: The military engagements of Guru Hargobind Ji's reign as narrated in the Gurbilas and assessed against the wider record.
lessons.html:
From Accommodation to Conflict

Guru Hargobind Ji is remembered as the first Guru to fight pitched battles, and the Gurbilas Patshahi 6 narrates these engagements at length. Tradition counts four principal battles, fought largely in the later part of his reign, after the death of Jahangir, when relations with the Mughal state under Shah Jahan deteriorated. The text presents each as a defensive action forced upon the Guru, consistent with the principle that arms are taken up only when justice and survival demand.

The Battle of Amritsar

The first major engagement is the battle fought at or near Amritsar. The tradition attributes its outbreak to imperial provocation — in some accounts a dispute over a hawk or a horse seized from the Guru, in others a punitive expedition sent against the growing Sikh power. A Mughal force advanced on Amritsar; the Guru's Sikhs, fighting from the ਲੋਹਗੜ੍ਹ and the town, repelled it. The Gurbilas records acts of individual heroism and the participation of revered Sikhs. The defence of Amritsar demonstrated that the militarisation of the Panth had produced a force capable of withstanding imperial arms.

The Battle of Lahira (Mehraj)

A second battle was fought in the Malwa region, near Mehraj, in the area associated with Lahira. The tradition again presents the conflict as provoked — a dispute over horses intended for the Guru that were seized by imperial officers. The Sikhs gave battle and prevailed. The engagement is significant for extending the Guru's reputation and influence into the Malwa tract, a region that would later become a heartland of Sikh power.

The Battle of Kartarpur

Among the most dramatic episodes the Gurbilas narrates is the battle of Kartarpur, in the Jalandhar Doab. Here the tradition recounts the tragic turning of the Pathan Painda Khan, once raised in the Guru's own household, who took up arms against his master. The Gurbilas describes the Guru's grief at having to fight a man he had nurtured. In the climactic combat the Guru is said to have prevailed over Painda Khan and, in a gesture that the tradition treasures, to have shielded the dying man's face from the sun and urged him to remember the Divine in his last moments. The episode encapsulates the ideal of the ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ — victorious in battle yet without hatred, compassionate even toward a treacherous foe.

Assessing the Military Narrative

How reliable is the Gurbilas as a record of these battles? The general fact that Guru Hargobind Ji fought several defensive engagements against Mughal detachments is accepted by historians and is consistent with the political situation under Shah Jahan. The specific causes the tradition assigns — disputes over hawks and horses — may telescope more complex tensions over the Guru's temporal power into memorable anecdotes. The numbers of combatants, the speeches, and the miraculous interventions reflect the conventions of the ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ genre. As ever, the historian reads for the well-attested core (the occurrence and broad outcome of the battles, the defensive posture, the locations) while bracketing the embellishments.

The Theology of the Battles

For the text itself, the battles are not merely military events but demonstrations of the doctrine of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ in action. The Guru fights only when attacked; he fights to defend the community and the freedom to worship; he fights without hatred and shows mercy to the fallen. The repeated victories are read as signs of divine favour, the temporal sword vindicated because it serves the spiritual one. After the battle of Kartarpur the Guru withdrew from the western Punjab to the Shivalik foothills, and it is to that final, more peaceful phase of his life that we turn in the next lesson. The Gurbilas thus uses the cycle of battles to argue that the militant turn was righteous, defensive, and crowned with the favour of ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ.

lessons.title: Amritsar, the ਮਸੰਦ Network, and Institutional Consolidation
lessons.summary: The development of Amritsar as a Sikh capital and the institutional structures that sustained the Panth.
lessons.html:
Amritsar as the Centre of the Panth

Behind the dramatic episodes of battle and imprisonment lies a quieter but equally consequential story: the consolidation of Amritsar as the spiritual and political centre of the ਪੰਥ. Founded by Guru Ram Das and developed by Guru Arjan with the completion of the ਹਰਿਮੰਦਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ and the compilation of the ਆਦਿ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ, Amritsar became under Guru Hargobind Ji a true capital — a place of pilgrimage, governance, trade, and arms. The raising of the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ and the building of the ਲੋਹਗੜ੍ਹ completed the picture of a city that was at once a holy place and a seat of sovereignty.

The ਮਸੰਦ Network

The institutional sinew of the Panth in this period was the ਮਸੰਦ system. The masands were the Guru's appointed deputies in the various regions where Sikhs lived. They organised local ਸੰਗਤ, collected the ਦਸਵੰਧ, conveyed offerings to Amritsar, and represented the Guru's authority at a distance. Under Guru Hargobind Ji this network sustained not only the devotional life of scattered communities but also, as we have seen, the gathering of horses, arms, and fighting men. The masand system allowed the Panth to function as a coordinated body across a wide territory without holding a contiguous state.

It should be noted that the masand system, so vital in this era, would in later generations become corrupted, and Guru Gobind Singh Ji would ultimately abolish it. But in the seventeenth century it was the indispensable instrument of the Panth's cohesion and material strength, and the Gurbilas presupposes its functioning throughout.

The ਆਦਿ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ and the Continuity of Devotion

Amid the militarisation, the devotional core of Sikh life remained central. The ਆਦਿ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ, compiled by Guru Arjan, was installed in the ਹਰਿਮੰਦਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ and was the spiritual authority around which the community's life revolved. Daily ਕੀਰਤਨ, the institution of ਲੰਗਰ, and the gathering of the ਸੰਗਤ continued without interruption. The genius of the sixth Guru's reign was to add the temporal dimension without diminishing the spiritual; the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ never eclipsed the ਹਰਿਮੰਦਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ but stood beside it.

Travel and the Widening of the Panth

The Gurbilas and the wider tradition record the Guru's travels beyond the Punjab plains, including journeys toward the east and a significant presence in the Shivalik hill country, where he would eventually establish himself at Kiratpur. These travels widened the reach of the Panth and planted Sikh communities in new regions. The cultivation of relations with hill rajas and the founding of new centres laid groundwork that would matter for the later history of the Gurus, especially the tenth Guru's long sojourn in the same hill country.

Sovereignty Without a State

It is worth reflecting on the distinctive character of the sovereignty the Panth claimed in this period. The Guru held no recognised kingdom, levied no land revenue, and governed no province in the administrative sense. Yet through the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ, the ਮਸੰਦ network, the war-drum, the fort, and the army, the Panth functioned as a sovereign community — a body that governed its own affairs, dispensed its own justice, defended itself by arms, and owed ultimate allegiance to ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ rather than to the emperor. This is a sovereignty grounded in conscience and community rather than territory, and it is one of the most original contributions of Sikh political thought. The Gurbilas Patshahi 6, in narrating the institutional life of Amritsar under the sixth Guru, gives us our fullest picture of how such a sovereignty actually worked.

lessons.title: The Kartarpur Years and the Passing of the Guru
lessons.summary: The Guru's withdrawal to the Shivalik foothills, the founding of Kiratpur, and the transmission of Guruship.
lessons.html:
Withdrawal to the Hills

After the cycle of battles in the plains, Guru Hargobind Ji withdrew to the Shivalik foothills, eventually settling at Kiratpur in the region of the upper Sutlej. This move marked the final phase of his long reign — a period of relative peace, of teaching, and of preparation for the succession. The withdrawal should not be read as defeat; rather, it reflected a strategic and spiritual choice to establish the Panth in new ground, away from the immediate pressure of the imperial heartland, in country where Sikh communities could grow.

The Founding of Kiratpur

Kiratpur, founded with the cooperation of the local hill authorities, became the new centre of the Guru's activity. Here the devotional and teaching life of the Panth continued. The hill country would remain associated with the Gurus for generations: the seventh Guru, Guru Har Rai Ji, and the eighth, Guru Har Krishan Ji, would be connected with this region, and the tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh Ji, would later make nearby Anandpur the great centre of the Khalsa. The sixth Guru's establishment in the Shivaliks thus had long consequences.

Family, Succession, and Loss

The Gurbilas and the tradition record the Guru's family life and the sorrows that attended it. Guru Hargobind Ji outlived several of his sons. Significantly, he passed over the line of his eldest surviving sons and designated his grandson, the young Har Rai, as his successor. This choice reflected the Sikh principle that Guruship passes not by primogeniture but by spiritual fitness — the same principle by which the sixth Guru himself, and his predecessors, had been chosen. One of his sons, Tegh Bahadur, would later become the ninth Guru and a martyr for religious freedom, and through him the line would continue to Guru Gobind Singh Ji.

The Passing of the Sixth Guru

Guru Hargobind Ji passed away at Kiratpur in 1644, after a reign of some thirty-eight years. The Gurbilas Patshahi 6 brings its narrative to a close with the Guru's final instructions and the installation of Guru Har Rai Ji. The text presents the passing not as an end but as a transmission — the light passing on, the mission continuing. The doctrine of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ, the institution of the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ, the martial discipline of the ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ, and the sovereign self-understanding of the Panth were the legacy he bequeathed.

The Achievement of the Reign

Viewed as a whole, the reign of the sixth Guru accomplished a transformation whose consequences run through the whole subsequent history of the Sikhs. He inherited a community that was already a distinct religious fellowship with its own scripture, shrine, and institutions, and he gave it a temporal and political dimension without sacrificing its spiritual identity. The union of the two swords, the throne facing the temple, the cauldron and the sword — these became the permanent grammar of Sikh life. When Guru Gobind Singh Ji created the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ in 1699, and when the Sikhs later established their own state in the Punjab, they were realising possibilities that the sixth Guru had opened.

The Text at Its Close

As a literary work, the Gurbilas Patshahi 6 ends by celebrating the completeness of the Guru's mission. As a historical source, it leaves us with a rich, if devotionally coloured, account of one of the most consequential reigns in Sikh history. In our final two lessons we will step back to assess the text as a source and to trace the afterlife of the doctrine of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ in later Sikh thought and practice, so that the student may carry forward both a knowledge of the events and a critical command of the source that transmits them.

lessons.title: Gurbilas Patshahi 6 as a Historical Source: Method and Critique
lessons.summary: A methodological reflection on how to use the Gurbilas as a historical source, its strengths, biases, and limits.
lessons.html:
The Source-Critical Task

Having traced the narrative of the sixth Guru's reign as the Gurbilas Patshahi 6 presents it, we now turn to the discipline of using such a text responsibly. Every historical source has a horizon — a perspective shaped by when, by whom, and for what purpose it was composed. The Gurbilas was composed long after the events it narrates, within a devotional and martial tradition, and in the elaborate idiom of ਕਵੀ court poetry. To use it as history is to read it with these conditions in view.

Strengths of the Source

The Gurbilas has real and distinctive strengths. First, it preserves, in extended and coherent narrative form, the Panth's memory of a formative reign for which contemporary documentation is sparse. Second, it gives us the community's own interpretation of the meaning of these events — how the Sikhs themselves understood the turn to sovereignty and arms. This interpretive testimony is itself a primary historical datum: it tells us what the doctrine of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ meant to those who lived by it. Third, in its outline of institutions — the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ, the ਲੋਹਗੜ੍ਹ, the ਮਸੰਦ network, the army — it preserves information that can be cross-checked and is broadly corroborated.

Biases and Limits

The text's limits are equally real. As a devotional chronicle it is committed to glorifying its subject; it presents the Guru's actions as always righteous and divinely favoured. As a product of a later, militant age, it may project the sovereignty-consciousness of that age back onto the early seventeenth century, sharpening edges that were softer in their own time. As a work of the ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ genre, it freely includes miraculous interventions, set speeches, and inner thoughts that are literary conventions rather than recoverable facts. And as a single editorial settlement of a fluid manuscript tradition, the text we read is one version among several.

The Method of Corroboration

The historian's chief tool is corroboration across independent sources. For the sixth Guru's reign we can set the Gurbilas alongside: the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, which independently attests the martyrdom of Guru Arjan and the imperial concern over the Sikh movement; the Bhatt vahis and other contemporary administrative traces; later Sikh works such as Santokh Singh's Gur Pratap Suraj Granth and Giani Gian Singh's Twarikh Guru Khalsa; and the modern critical scholarship of historians such as J. S. Grewal, Ganda Singh, Hari Ram Gupta, and the literary studies of Piara Singh Padam. Where these converge with the Gurbilas, our confidence rises; where they diverge or are silent, we hold the Gurbilas's testimony more lightly.

Distinguishing Layers

A practical method is to read the text in layers. The institutional and political core — the founding of the throne, the building of the fort, the imprisonment at Gwalior, the occurrence of the battles, the withdrawal to the hills — is well grounded and corroborable. The dramatic and ceremonial detail — exact numbers, speeches, the tasselled cloak, the precise sequence of events — is the working of memory and genre. The miraculous element is the language of devotion. The skilled reader holds all three in view without collapsing them into one another, neither treating the whole as literal report nor dismissing the whole as legend.

The Value of Memory-Texts

Finally, it is worth defending the positive value of a source like the Gurbilas against a narrow positivism that would discard everything not independently documented. The community's memory and interpretation of its own past are part of history, not a distraction from it. The way the Sikhs remembered Guru Hargobind Ji — as the Guru of the two swords, the ਬੰਦੀ ਛੋੜ, the saint-soldier who fought without hatred — shaped the identity and the actions of generations. To study the Gurbilas Patshahi 6 critically is therefore to study not only what happened in the seventeenth century but how a people understood themselves and were thereby moved to act. That double yield is the reward of disciplined historical reading.

lessons.title: Legacy: ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ in Later Sikh Thought and Practice
lessons.summary: The afterlife of the doctrine of Miri-Piri in the Khalsa, Sikh political thought, and the modern Panth, with works cited.
lessons.html:
The Doctrine Carried Forward

The synthesis that Guru Hargobind Ji embodied did not remain confined to his own reign; it became a permanent and defining feature of Sikh thought and practice. The doctrine of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ, the institution of the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ, and the ideal of the ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ shaped the whole subsequent history of the Panth. In this final lesson we trace that legacy and reflect on the enduring meaning of the text we have studied.

The Khalsa of Guru Gobind Singh Ji

The most direct heir of the sixth Guru's synthesis is the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ, created by Guru Gobind Singh Ji in 1699. The Khalsa institutionalised, for the whole community, the ideal of the saint-soldier that the sixth Guru had embodied in his own person. The amritdhari Sikh, bearing the ਕਿਰਪਾਨ and bound by the ਰਹਿਤ, lives out the union of devotion and the readiness to defend justice. The later Khalsa watchword ਦੇਗ ਤੇਗ ਫ਼ਤਹ — "victory to the cauldron and the sword" — is the doctrine of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ compressed into a battle-cry, and the all-iron ideal of ਸਰਬਲੋਹ echoes the iron of the ਲੋਹਗੜ੍ਹ.

The ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ as Living Institution

The throne the sixth Guru raised became the supreme temporal institution of the Panth. From the eighteenth century, the ਸਰਬੱਤ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ gathered at the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ to deliberate and to pass binding resolutions, the ਗੁਰਮਤਾ. Through the perilous decades of persecution and the rise of the Sikh misls, and into the era of Sikh rule under Maharaja Ranjit Singh, the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ remained the symbolic and often the actual centre of Sikh collective authority. It continues to occupy that place in the life of the Panth today.

Sikh Political Thought

The doctrine of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ gave Sikh tradition a distinctive answer to the perennial question of the relation between religion and political power. Against both the quietism that withdraws from the world and the secularism that severs faith from public life, the Sikh ideal insists that spiritual devotion and the responsibility for justice in the world belong together, with the temporal always in the service of the spiritual. This conviction has informed Sikh political engagement from the seventeenth century to the present, including movements for justice and self-determination in the modern era. The slogan ਰਾਜ ਕਰੇਗਾ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ — "the Khalsa shall rule" — expresses the durable Sikh aspiration to a just sovereignty grounded in the will of ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ.

Why the Gurbilas Patshahi 6 Still Matters

For the student of Sikh history, the Gurbilas Patshahi 6 remains an essential text precisely because it stands at the source of this living tradition. It is the most extended narrative monument to the reign in which the union of the two swords was forged. Read critically, with attention to its genre, its date, and its devotional purpose, it yields both a rich account of formative events and an invaluable window onto how the Panth understood its own turn to sovereignty. The text teaches us, as much by how it tells its story as by what it tells, what ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ has meant to the Sikhs.

Concluding Reflection

We began this course with the genre of ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ and the problem of using a late, devotional, poetic text as history. We end with an appreciation of why such a text is indispensable. The reign of Guru Hargobind Ji transformed the Sikh community, and the Gurbilas Patshahi 6 is the literary form in which that transformation was remembered and transmitted. To master this text is to grasp both a pivotal chapter of seventeenth-century history and the doctrinal foundation — the union of ਮੀਰੀ and ਪੀਰੀ, of cauldron and sword, of throne and temple — on which the later Khalsa and the modern Panth were built.

ਹਵਾਲੇ (Works Cited)

  • Padam, Piara Singh. Sri Guru Granth Sahib de Lekhak. Patiala: Kalam Mandir, 1990.
  • Sohan Kavi. Gurbilas Patshahi Chhevin. Edited by Gyani Inder Singh Gill. Amritsar: Khalsa Samachar, 1968.
  • Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Rev. ed. The New Cambridge History of India II.3. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998.
  • McLeod, W. H. Sikhs of the Khalsa: A History of the Khalsa Rahit. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2003.
  • Singh, Ganda. A Bibliography of the Punjab. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1966.
  • Fauja Singh, ed. Guru Tegh Bahadur: Martyr and Teacher. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1975.
  • Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014.
  • Dhillon, Balwant Singh. Early Sikh Tradition: A Study of the Janamsakhis. Amritsar: Singh Brothers, 1999.
  • Gupta, Hari Ram. History of the Sikhs. Vol. 1, The Sikh Gurus, 1469–1708. New Delhi: Munshiram Manoharlal, 1984.

quiz.q: What does the term ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ designate as a genre of Sikh literature?
options: A verse-chronicle celebrating the martial and miraculous deeds of a particular Guru, mostly composed in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries
A legal code governing the conduct of the Khalsa
The earliest biographies of Guru Nanak focused on his spiritual journeys
A collection of hymns added to the Adi Granth

quiz.q: What did the two swords worn by Guru Hargobind Ji at his installation symbolise?
options: Victory over the Mughals in two great battles
The union of temporal authority (ਮੀਰੀ) and spiritual authority (ਪੀਰੀ)
The defence of the eastern and western frontiers of the Punjab
The two earlier martyrdoms in Sikh history

quiz.q: What is the significance of the name ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ?
options: It means the throne built by Emperor Jahangir for the Guru
It refers to the war-drum sounded at Amritsar
It means the Throne of the Timeless One, asserting that ultimate sovereignty belongs to ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ alone
It was a fortress in the Shivalik hills

quiz.q: Why is Guru Hargobind Ji remembered with the title ਬੰਦੀ ਛੋੜ?
options: He built the iron fortress at Amritsar
He compiled the Adi Granth while imprisoned
He refused to leave Gwalior unless the other princes confined with him were also freed
He abolished the corrupt masand system

quiz.q: According to the lessons, how should a historian best use the Gurbilas Patshahi 6 as a source?
options: Accept its entire account as literal eyewitness testimony
Reject it completely because it was composed long after the events
Read it in layers, distinguishing a corroborable institutional core from genre conventions and miraculous elaboration
Use it only for its poetic value, never for historical content

quiz.q: Which Mughal source independently corroborates the Sikh narrative of Guru Arjan Dev Ji's martyrdom?
options: The Ain-i-Akbari of Abul Fazl
The Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, the memoir of Emperor Jahangir
The Akbarnama
The Padshahnama of Shah Jahan

courses.title: Suraj Prakash: Guru Gobind Singh Ji — The Warrior-Saint
courses.source: Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth, Rut 6-12 by Kavi Santokh Singh
courses.summary: An advanced textual and historical seminar on the portions of Kavi Santokh Singh's monumental Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth (1843) that narrate the life of the tenth Master, ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ. Reading the relevant Ruts of the Suraj Prakash alongside primary contemporary sources — the ਬਚਿੱਤ੍ਰ ਨਾਟਕ, the ਜ਼ਫ਼ਰਨਾਮਾ, the rehatnamas, and the Bhatt vahis — students examine the Guru's birth at Patna, the Paonta years and the literary darbar of fifty-two poets, the founding of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ in 1699, the battles of Bhangani, Nadaun, and the Anandpur sieges, the evacuation and shaheedis at Chamkaur and Sirhind, the composition of the ਜ਼ਫ਼ਰਨਾਮਾ, the southern journey, and the conferral of eternal Guruship upon ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ. The course foregrounds the figure of the ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ and trains students to read Braj-inflected nineteenth-century Sikh hagiography critically, distinguishing kavi convention from historical kernel.
outcomes: Situate Kavi Santokh Singh's ਸੂਰਜ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ within the genre of Sikh hagiographical literature and explain its sources, language, and prosodic structure of Ruts and Ainsus.
Reconstruct the chronology of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ's life from birth at Patna (1666) to joti-jot at Nanded (1708) using both the Suraj Prakash and corroborating primary sources.
Analyze the theological meaning of the ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ ideal and the doctrine of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ as embodied in the Guru's life.
Explain the creation of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ in 1699, the role of the ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ, and the institution of ਖੰਡੇ ਦੀ ਪਾਹੁਲ.
Critically read the Guru's battles — Bhangani, Nadaun, Anandpur — as narrated in the Suraj Prakash against the ਬਚਿੱਤ੍ਰ ਨਾਟਕ.
Interpret the shaheedis of the ਸਾਹਿਬਜ਼ਾਦੇ at Chamkaur and Sirhind and their place in Sikh collective memory.
Read and contextualize the ਜ਼ਫ਼ਰਨਾਮਾ as an epistle of moral victory addressed to Aurangzeb.
Explain the doctrinal significance of the command conferring eternal Guruship upon ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ.

terms.m: The 'Light of the Sun' — popular title of Kavi Santokh Singh's Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth, a vast verse hagiography of the ten Gurus completed in 1843, organized into seasons (Rut) and sub-sections (Ainsu).
The 'saint-soldier' — the integrated ideal of spiritual devotion and martial readiness exemplified by Guru Gobind Singh Ji and demanded of the Khalsa.
The order of initiated, sovereign Sikhs created by Guru Gobind Singh Ji at Anandpur on Vaisakhi 1699; 'the pure' and the Guru's own.
The 'nectar of the double-edged sword' — the Khalsa initiation rite (amrit) instituted in 1699, prepared by stirring water and patasas with a khanda while reciting the five banis.
The 'Five Beloved Ones' — the first five Sikhs who offered their heads at the 1699 Vaisakhi and were initiated as the nucleus of the Khalsa.
The doctrine of combined temporal (ਮੀਰੀ) and spiritual (ਪੀਰੀ) authority, symbolized by Guru Hargobind Sahib's two swords and fully realized in Guru Gobind Singh Ji.
The 'Epistle of Victory' — Guru Gobind Singh Ji's Persian letter in verse to Emperor Aurangzeb, indicting his treachery and asserting righteous resistance.
The 'Wondrous Drama' — an autobiographical composition attributed to Guru Gobind Singh Ji within the Dasam Granth corpus, narrating his previous birth, mission, and early battles.
The four sons of Guru Gobind Singh Ji — Baba Ajit Singh, Baba Jujhar Singh, Baba Zorawar Singh, and Baba Fateh Singh — all of whom attained martyrdom.
Chamkaur Sahib — the mud fortress where Guru Gobind Singh Ji and forty Singhs withstood the Mughal-hill army; site of the shaheedis of the two elder Sahibzade in December 1705.
'Giver of the entire family' — an epithet of Guru Gobind Singh Ji, who sacrificed his father, mother, and all four sons for Dharam.
'Season' — the major structural division of the Suraj Prakash; the life of Guru Gobind Singh Ji spans the later Ruts of the Granth.
'Light merging into Light' — the term for a Guru's passing from the physical form, used for Guru Gobind Singh Ji's departure at Nanded in 1708.
The 'path' or community — the collective body of the Khalsa, invested by the Guru with corporate authority as Guru Panth.

references: Santokh Singh, Kavi. Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth. Edited by Bhai Vir Singh. 14 vols. Amritsar: Khalsa Samachar, 1926–1935.
Jaggi, Rattan Singh. Dasam Granth da Kartritav. Patiala: Punjabi University Press, 1966.
Jaggi, Rattan Singh, ed. Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth: Path Sampadan ate Adhyan. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1990.
Grewal, J. S. Guru Gobind Singh (1666–1708): Master of the White Hawk. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2019.
Singh, Ganda. Life of Banda Singh Bahadur. Amritsar: Khalsa College, 1935.
McLeod, W. H. The Chaupa Singh Rahit-nama. Dunedin: University of Otago Press, 1987.
Singh, Harbans, ed. The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism. 4 vols. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1992–1998.
Fenech, Louis E. The Sikh Zafar-namah of Guru Gobind Singh: A Discursive Blade in the Heart of the Mughal Empire. New York: Oxford University Press, 2013.
Singh, Gurmukh. Historical Sikh Shrines. Amritsar: Singh Brothers, 1998.
Dhavan, Purnima. When Sparrows Became Hawks: The Making of the Sikh Warrior Tradition, 1699–1799. New York: Oxford University Press, 2011.

lessons.title: The Suraj Prakash and the Hagiography of the Tenth Master
lessons.summary: An orientation to Kavi Santokh Singh's text, its language and structure, and the methodology of reading nineteenth-century Sikh hagiography.
lessons.html:
ਵਿਸ਼ਾ ਸੂਚੀ (Table of Contents)

  1. The Suraj Prakash and the Hagiography of the Tenth Master
  2. Birth at Patna and the Childhood of ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਰਾਏ
  3. Anandpur, the Martyrdom of the Ninth Nanak, and the Boy Guru
  4. The Paonta Years and the Darbar of Fifty-Two Poets
  5. The Battle of Bhangani and the First Test of Arms
  6. Nadaun, the Hill Rajas, and the Years of Preparation
  7. The Creation of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ — Vaisakhi 1699
  8. The Sieges of Anandpur and the Evacuation
  9. Chamkaur Sahib and the Shaheedis of the ਸਾਹਿਬਜ਼ਾਦੇ
  10. Sirhind, the Younger Sahibzade, and the Cold Tower
  11. The ਜ਼ਫ਼ਰਨਾਮਾ — The Epistle of Victory
  12. The Southern Journey and the Command to ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ

A Granth as Vast as the Sun

Few works in the Sikh literary tradition rival the scale and influence of Kavi Santokh Singh's Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth, known affectionately across the ਪੰਥ as the ਸੂਰਜ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼, the 'Light of the Sun.' Completed in 1843 under the patronage of Raja Udai Singh of Kaithal, the Granth narrates in over fifty thousand verses the lives of all ten Gurus, building upon the poet's earlier Nanak Prakash. Where the Nanak Prakash illumined the first Master, the larger Suraj Prakash carries the narrative from ਗੁਰੂ ਅੰਗਦ ਸਾਹਿਬ through ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ. This course concerns the later ਰੁੱਤ — the 'seasons' into which the work is divided — that recount the life of the tenth Nanak.

Structure and Prosody

Santokh Singh organized his Granth using a calendrical metaphor. The major divisions are called ਰੁੱਤ (seasons), each subdivided into ਅੰਸੂ (rays, literally 'sunbeams'), so that the reader passes through the seasons of the Guru's life as one passes through a solar year. The poetry is composed in the Braj Bhasha literary idiom favoured by the courtly poets of North India, dense with Sanskrit tatsama vocabulary, alankaras (figures of speech), and a wide variety of chhand (metres). For the modern student this presents a genuine challenge: the language is neither colloquial Punjabi nor the Sant Bhasha of Gurbani, and reading it requires patience and, ideally, the steel-bound ਟੀਕਾ (commentary) of Bhai Vir Singh, whose fourteen-volume annotated edition (1926–1935) remains the scholarly standard.

Reading Hagiography Critically

The Suraj Prakash is hagiography, not chronicle. It was composed roughly a century and a half after the events it describes, drawing on the ਜਨਮ ਸਾਖੀ tradition, the ਗੁਰ ਬਿਲਾਸ literature, oral memory, and the poet's own devotional vision. Professor Rattan Singh Jaggi, whose critical edition and study of the text anchors this course, insists that the student must learn to distinguish three layers: the historical kernel, the conventions of the kavi (poet) who embellishes with miracle and metaphor, and the theological message the poet wishes to convey. To dismiss the text as 'mere legend' is as great an error as to read it as a court transcript. The Granth's value lies precisely in how a devout nineteenth-century Sikh imagination remembered and interpreted the Guru.

The Figure of the ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ

The organizing theological idea of the entire narrative is the ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ, the saint-soldier. In ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ the contemplative and the martial are not two roles uneasily joined but a single integrated way of being. This realizes the doctrine of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ — the union of temporal and spiritual sovereignty first dramatized by ਗੁਰੂ ਹਰਿਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਾਹਿਬ with his two swords. As we read the Suraj Prakash, we will watch Santokh Singh repeatedly frame the Guru's wars not as conquest but as ਧਰਮ ਯੁੱਧ, righteous struggle undertaken only when, as the Guru himself wrote in the ਜ਼ਫ਼ਰਨਾਮਾ, all other means have failed. The Guru's own words in the ਬਚਿੱਤ੍ਰ ਨਾਟਕ declare the purpose of his coming: ਧਰਮ ਚਲਾਵਨ ਸੰਤ ਉਬਾਰਨ। ਦੁਸਟ ਸਭਨ ਕੋ ਮੂਲ ਉਪਾਰਨ — 'To spread Dharam, to deliver the saints, and to uproot all the wicked.'

The Plan of This Course

Over twelve lessons we move season by season through the Guru's life. We will read selected passages of the Suraj Prakash in Gurmukhi alongside corroborating primary sources — the ਬਚਿੱਤ੍ਰ ਨਾਟਕ, the ਜ਼ਫ਼ਰਨਾਮਾ, the rehatnamas of Bhai Nand Lal and Chaupa Singh, and the Bhatt vahis whose dated entries help anchor the chronology. The aim is not merely to retell a beloved story but to equip the advanced student to handle Sikh hagiographical sources with the discipline of a historian and the reverence of a Sikh.

lessons.title: Birth at Patna and the Childhood of ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਰਾਏ
lessons.summary: The Guru's birth at Patna in 1666, the prophecies surrounding it, his childhood years in Bihar, and the journey back to the Punjab.
lessons.html:
The Light Rises in the East

The Suraj Prakash places the birth of the future tenth Master in the eastern city of Patna, in the region of Bihar, where ਗੁਰੂ ਤੇਗ ਬਹਾਦਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ had left his family while travelling east on his great preaching tour. According to the traditional reckoning the child who would be named ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਰਾਏ was born to Mata Gujri in late December 1666 (Poh, Samvat 1723). Santokh Singh, in keeping with the conventions of sacred biography, surrounds the birth with luminous portents: the heavens rejoice, holy men sense the arrival of a great soul, and the Muslim faqir Bhikhan Shah of Thaska is said to have turned his prayer toward the east, recognizing that a divine light had descended there.

The Story of Bhikhan Shah

The episode of Bhikhan Shah is among the most beloved in the Patna narrative and repays careful reading as hagiography. The faqir, drawn to Patna, is brought before the infant. To test whether the child belongs to the Hindus or the Muslims, he sets before him two vessels of sweets, one representing each community. The infant places his hands upon both. Santokh Singh reads this as a sign of the Guru's universal mission — that he comes for all of humanity, not for one community against another. Whatever the historicity of the precise event, the meaning the poet draws from it is consonant with the Guru's later life and with the Gurmat teaching of ਏਕ ਪਿਤਾ ਏਕਸ ਕੇ ਹਮ ਬਾਰਿਕ — 'One is the Father, and we are all His children.'

Childhood in Bihar

The young ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਰਾਏ spent his early years in Patna, where the Takht Sri Patna Sahib now stands. The Sakhis preserve memories of a spirited, charismatic child who organized his playmates into two armies and staged mock battles, who possessed a striking presence, and who was beloved of the local sangat. Whether or not we read these as literal recollections, they encode the Sikh community's sense that the martial and the leaderly were native to him from the beginning. The Suraj Prakash dwells on his beauty, his intelligence, and the devotion he inspired, employing the standard repertoire of the kavi to communicate his exceptional nature.

The Return to the Punjab

When ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਰਾਏ was a young boy, the family was summoned back to the Punjab. The Guru-father, having returned from his eastern travels, established the family at the newly founded town of ਚੱਕ ਨਾਨਕੀ in the Shivalik foothills — the settlement that would grow into ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ. The journey westward across the breadth of northern India is narrated by Santokh Singh with attention to the sangats the family encountered along the way, reinforcing the geographic spread of the early Panth from Bihar to the Punjab.

Historical Anchoring

Here the advanced student must hold the hagiographic and the documentary together. The Bhatt vahis — the genealogical day-books kept by the Bhatt bards who attended the Gurus — provide dated entries that scholars such as Giani Garja Singh used to anchor the chronology of the Guru's life, including the family's movements. Where the Suraj Prakash gives us the devotional meaning of the birth and childhood, these terse documentary sources give us the skeleton of dates and places. Professor Jaggi's method, which we adopt, is to read the two registers in counterpoint: the vahi tells us when and where; Santokh Singh tells us what the Panth understood it to mean.

The Meaning of the Name

The name ਗੋਬਿੰਦ — a name of the Divine, the 'Lord of the earth' — was itself read as significant by the tradition. The child bearing the Creator's name was destined, in the poet's telling, to become ਸਰਬੰਸਦਾਨੀ, the one who would give his entire lineage for ਧਰਮ. From the eastern light at Patna the narrative now turns westward and darkward, toward the supreme sacrifice of the ninth Master that would place the Guruship upon a child's shoulders.

lessons.title: Anandpur, the Martyrdom of the Ninth Nanak, and the Boy Guru
lessons.summary: The shaheedi of Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib in Delhi, the response of the nine-year-old Gobind Rai, and the meaning of a martyrdom for the freedom of conscience.
lessons.html:
The Supreme Sacrifice at Delhi

The central event that shapes the early Guruship of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ is the martyrdom of his father, ਗੁਰੂ ਤੇਗ ਬਹਾਦਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ, in Delhi in 1675. The Suraj Prakash, following the tradition, narrates how a delegation of Kashmiri Pandits, persecuted under the religious policy of Aurangzeb and threatened with forced conversion, came to ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ to seek the Guru's protection. The ninth Master sat in contemplation of how the crisis might be met.

'A Great Soul Must Offer Himself'

It is here that the tradition places one of the most extraordinary moments in Sikh history. The young ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਰਾਏ, then about nine years of age, observing his father's grave reflection, asked the cause. When told that the suffering could be relieved only by the sacrifice of a truly great soul, the boy is said to have replied that no one was greater than his own father. ਗੁਰੂ ਤੇਗ ਬਹਾਦਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ embraced this response and resolved to give his life. Santokh Singh treats this not as a child's naivety but as the early flowering of the ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ spirit — the willingness to face death for the freedom of another's faith.

The Martyrdom for Freedom of Conscience

The Guru travelled to Delhi, where, after the torture and execution of his companions Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das, and Bhai Dyala, he was beheaded at Chandni Chowk for refusing to abandon his faith and for defending the right of others — the Hindu Pandits — to keep theirs. This is the martyrdom that ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ would later commemorate in the ਬਚਿੱਤ੍ਰ ਨਾਟਕ in lines the tradition holds in deepest reverence: Gurbani in the ਬਚਿੱਤ੍ਰ ਨਾਟਕ teaches that the ninth Master 'broke the potsherd of his body on the head of the king of Delhi and departed to the abode of the Lord' — ਠੀਕਰ ਫੋਰਿ ਦਿਲੀਸ ਸਿਰਿ ਪ੍ਰਭ ਪੁਰਿ ਕੀਯਾ ਪਯਾਨ — declaring that no one had ever performed such a deed as ਤੇਗ ਬਹਾਦਰ.

The Body Recovered

The Suraj Prakash recounts the recovery of the Guru's severed head by Bhai Jaita, a devoted Sikh of the Mazhabi community, who carried it through great danger to ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ. There the boy Guru received it, embraced Bhai Jaita, and is traditionally said to have honoured him with the words ਰੰਘਰੇਟਾ ਗੁਰੂ ਕਾ ਬੇਟਾ — 'the Ranghreta is the Guru's own son.' The body was cremated in Delhi by Bhai Lakhi Shah Vanjara, who burned his own house to conceal the act. These episodes, beyond their historical content, communicate a profound message: the new Guru's authority rested on a community that crossed every line of caste and status.

The Investiture of the Boy Guru

At nine years of age, ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਰਾਏ was installed as the tenth Nanak. The Suraj Prakash describes the Guru-gaddi ceremony, the application of the tilak, and the gathering of the sangat. The tradition is keenly aware of the poignancy: a child now bore the full weight of Guruship in a hostile age, his father's blood freshly spilled by the empire. Yet the poet stresses the continuity of the one ਜੋਤਿ, the single divine light passing from Guru to Guru. The body changes; the light is one.

The Formative Wound

For the advanced student, this lesson is pivotal because it explains the trajectory of everything that follows. The martyrdom of ਗੁਰੂ ਤੇਗ ਬਹਾਦਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ taught the young Guru that spiritual truth without the power to defend the defenceless leaves the innocent at the mercy of tyranny. The decision, decades later, to create an armed and initiated ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ flows directly from this wound. The contemplative father had given his head so that others might keep their faith; the son would build a community that could no longer be slaughtered without resistance. The saint had been martyred; the Guru would now also make soldiers.

lessons.title: The Paonta Years and the Darbar of Fifty-Two Poets
lessons.summary: The Guru's years at Paonta Sahib on the Yamuna, his literary court of fifty-two poets, and the great project of translation and composition.
lessons.html:
The Court on the Yamuna

Among the most luminous chapters of the Suraj Prakash are those treating the Guru's years at ਪਾਉਂਟਾ ਸਾਹਿਬ, the town he founded on the banks of the Yamuna in the territory of the Raja of Sirmaur. Here, in the 1680s, ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ established not only a strategic settlement but a flourishing literary darbar. The Paonta years reveal the Guru as patron of letters and poet in his own right — the ਪੀਰੀ dimension of his sovereignty expressed through the cultivation of the word.

The ਬਾਵੰਜਾ ਕਵੀ

Tradition remembers a court of fifty-two poets — the ਬਾਵੰਜਾ ਕਵੀ — gathered around the Guru at Paonta. Among the names preserved are Sainapati, author of the Gur Sobha; Nand Lal Goya, the Persian master whose ghazals breathe ਪ੍ਰੇਮ ਭਗਤੀ; and the poets engaged in rendering classical Sanskrit and Puranic narratives into the vernacular. The Suraj Prakash celebrates the intellectual ferment of this court, where kirtan, poetic recitation, and learned discussion filled the days. The historicity of the precise number fifty-two is a matter of scholarly caution, but the existence of a substantial literary establishment under the Guru's patronage is well attested.

The Project of Translation

A central purpose of the Paonta darbar, as the tradition presents it, was to make the heroic and ethical literature of the classical tradition available to the common people in a language they could understand, infusing it with the spirit of ਬੀਰ ਰਸ — the heroic sentiment — to prepare the community for the struggles ahead. The Guru commissioned renderings of works such as portions of the Mahabharata and tales of the goddess's victories over demons, not as objects of worship but as vehicles of moral courage. This must be understood within Gurmat: the Guru's own devotion was directed wholly to the ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ, the Timeless One beyond birth and death, whom he praised in the ਜਾਪੁ ਸਾਹਿਬ as ਨਮਸਤੰ ਅਕਾਲੇ — 'salutation to the Deathless.'

The Guru's Own Compositions

Paonta is associated in the tradition with the composition of several of the Guru's own banis. The ਜਾਪੁ ਸਾਹਿਬ, with its thunderous litany of the Divine's attributes and negations, and the ਅਕਾਲ ਉਸਤਤਿ, the praise of the Timeless, articulate a theology of a God who is utterly transcendent, without form, caste, lineage, or enemy, yet present in all. The Guru's poetry fuses the ਭਗਤੀ devotion of his predecessors with a martial grandeur suited to the age. Gurbani in the ਜਾਪੁ ਸਾਹਿਬ teaches the worshipper to bow before the One who is ਚੱਕ੍ਰ ਚਿਹਨ ਅਰੁ ਬਰਨ ਜਾਤਿ ਅਰੁ ਪਾਤਿ ਨਹਿਨ ਜਿਹ — 'without mark or sign, without colour, caste, or lineage.'

Music and the Sound of the Court

Santokh Singh also conveys the soundscape of Paonta: the kirtan of the rababis, the recitation of the poets, and the martial music of the nagara and ranjit nagara that the Guru introduced as instruments of sovereignty. The drum that announced the Guru's darbar was itself an assertion of ਮੀਰੀ — the sound of an independent court that bowed to no emperor. This integration of the aesthetic and the political is characteristic of the Guru's vision.

The Gathering Storm

Yet Paonta was not destined to remain a peaceful seat of letters. The Guru's growing prestige, his maintenance of armed retainers, and the alarm of the surrounding hill rajas at his independence soon drew the community into open conflict. The very martial spirit cultivated through the ਬੀਰ ਰਸ poetry of the darbar would shortly be tested on the battlefield of Bhangani, only a few miles from Paonta itself. The lesson for the student is the seamlessness of the Guru's life: the court of poets and the field of battle were not opposites but two faces of the ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ. The pen that wrote the ਜਾਪੁ ਸਾਹਿਬ and the sword that would be drawn at Bhangani served one and the same ਧਰਮ.

lessons.title: The Battle of Bhangani and the First Test of Arms
lessons.summary: The first major battle of the Guru's life against a confederacy of hill rajas in 1688, narrated in the Suraj Prakash and the Bachittar Natak.
lessons.html:
The First Battle

The Suraj Prakash and the autobiographical ਬਚਿੱਤ੍ਰ ਨਾਟਕ converge on the Battle of Bhangani as the inaugural armed conflict of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ's life, fought near Paonta around 1688. For the historian this battle is invaluable because we possess the Guru's own first-person account in the ਬਚਿੱਤ੍ਰ ਨਾਟਕ — a rare instance where a primary autobiographical source can be set beside Santokh Singh's later retelling.

The Causes of Conflict

The hill rajas of the Shivalik region, nominally subordinate to the Mughal empire, grew uneasy at the Guru's rising power, his armed following, and his refusal to render the customary deference. The immediate trigger, as the sources present it, involved the rajas' demand for tribute or their alarm at the Guru's establishment at Paonta within Raja Medni Prakash's domain. A confederacy under Raja Bhim Chand of Kahlur and his allies, reinforced by Pathan mercenaries, moved against the Guru. Crucially, a body of Pathan soldiers in the Guru's own pay deserted to the enemy on the eve of battle — a betrayal the Guru records with sorrow.

The Account in the ਬਚਿੱਤ੍ਰ ਨਾਟਕ

The Guru's own narration in the ਬਚਿੱਤ੍ਰ ਨਾਟਕ is vivid and immediate, naming the warriors who fell and rose, the arrows that flew, and the valour of his companions such as the masand Kirpal and his cousin Sango Shah, who attained martyrdom in the fighting. The Guru attributes the victory not to himself but to the grace of the ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ. Gurbani in the ਬਚਿੱਤ੍ਰ ਨਾਟਕ teaches that 'by the grace of the Lord the battle was won' and that the enemy fled the field, while the Guru's small force, against odds, held firm. This theological framing — victory as divine gift, not personal glory — is essential to the Sikh reading of the Guru's wars.

Santokh Singh's Retelling

Santokh Singh, writing a century and a half later, amplifies the heroic register. He develops the characters, heightens the drama of single combats, and deploys the full machinery of ਬੀਰ ਰਸ poetry — the clash of weapons, the flowing of blood likened to rivers, the heroism of named Sikhs. The advanced student should compare the two accounts attentively. Where the ਬਚਿੱਤ੍ਰ ਨਾਟਕ is terse and devotional, the Suraj Prakash is expansive and dramatic. Neither is a neutral chronicle; both serve to teach. But the kernel of fact — a confederacy of hill rajas, a Pathan desertion, the martyrdom of the Guru's kinsmen, and a hard-won Sikh victory — is common to both.

The Meaning of a Defensive War

The Sikh tradition is emphatic that Bhangani was a defensive battle, forced upon the Guru by the aggression of others. This frames the entire ethics of the Guru's warfare, later crystallized in the ਜ਼ਫ਼ਰਨਾਮਾ couplet that the sword may rightly be raised only when all peaceful means are exhausted. At Bhangani the Guru did not march out to conquer; he defended his settlement and his community against an attacking host. The victory established his reputation as a formidable leader and, paradoxically, prepared the ground for a temporary reconciliation with Bhim Chand.

Aftermath and the Return to Anandpur

In the wake of Bhangani the Guru left Paonta and returned to the family seat at ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ, which would remain the centre of his activity for the next decade and a half. The hill region had learned to respect his arms. Yet the structural tension — between a sovereign Guru building an independent power and the surrounding rajas and the empire beyond them — was unresolved. Bhangani was the first of many trials of the ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ. The next would come at Nadaun, where, in a striking reversal, the Guru would fight alongside the very hill rajas who had opposed him, against the forces of the Mughal governor.

lessons.title: Nadaun, the Hill Rajas, and the Years of Preparation
lessons.summary: The Battle of Nadaun against Mughal forces, the shifting alliances of the hill rajas, and the long period of consolidation at Anandpur before 1699.
lessons.html:
A War Beside Former Enemies

The Battle of Nadaun, fought around 1691 on the banks of the Beas, presents the student with the tangled politics of the Shivalik hills. Here ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ fought not against the hill rajas but in alliance with them — chiefly with Raja Bhim Chand of Kahlur, his former adversary at Bhangani — against the army of the Mughal commander Alif Khan, who had been sent to enforce the payment of arrears of tribute that the rajas had withheld.

The Course of the Battle

The ਬਚਿੱਤ੍ਰ ਨਾਟਕ again gives the Guru's own account. Alif Khan besieged the fort of Nadaun, held by Raja Bhim Chand's ally. The Guru's forces and the hill rajas' levies engaged the Mughal army in fierce fighting along the river. The Guru describes the action of his musketeers and the rout of Alif Khan's forces, who fled the field by night. Once more the Guru ascribes the outcome to the ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ. The victory demonstrated that the Guru's military skill could be decisive even against imperial troops.

The Unreliability of the Hill Rajas

Yet Nadaun also taught a hard lesson about the hill rajas. No sooner was the immediate threat lifted than the rajas reverted to their old jealousies, and several soon made their peace with the Mughal authorities, agreeing to pay the very tribute they had fought to avoid. The Guru, who had shed Sikh blood to aid them, found himself once again isolated. Santokh Singh and the broader tradition read the rajas' conduct as a study in the faithlessness of those who serve self-interest rather than ਧਰਮ. The contrast with the loyalty the Guru would soon demand of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ is pointed: a community bound by initiation and principle, not by the shifting calculations of petty kings.

The Years of Preparation at Anandpur

The decade between Nadaun and the founding of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ in 1699 was, in the Suraj Prakash's telling, a period of intense consolidation at ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ. The Guru fortified the town with a ring of forts — Anandgarh, Lohgarh, Keshgarh, Fatehgarh, and Holgarh — whose very names proclaimed a martial purpose. He maintained stables of horses, manufactured arms, and trained his Sikhs in the use of weapons. The sangat continued to gather, bringing offerings, and the Guru's darbar combined the spiritual and the martial as it had at Paonta.

The Problem of the Masands

This period also saw the Guru's growing concern with the corruption of the ਮਸੰਦ system. The masands, originally appointed deputies to collect offerings and tend the local sangats, had in many cases become exploitative, withholding funds and lording over the Sikhs. The Guru's eventual decision to abolish the masand system and have the Sikhs relate to him directly was part of a broader restructuring of the community that would culminate in the creation of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ. The corrupt intermediary would be replaced by a direct bond between the Guru and the initiated Sikh.

The Spiritual Preparation

It would be a grave distortion to read these years as merely military preparation. Santokh Singh stresses that the Guru's darbar remained saturated with kirtan, katha, and the recitation of Gurbani. The community was being prepared spiritually as much as martially, for the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ the Guru envisioned would be defined first by devotion to the ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ and only then by the readiness to bear arms. The years of preparation were the gathering of the in-breath before the great utterance of 1699. The student should hold in mind the totality of this preparation — forts and stables, but also kirtan and Naam — as the necessary background to the revolutionary Vaisakhi that was to come.

lessons.title: The Creation of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ — Vaisakhi 1699
lessons.summary: The founding of the Khalsa at Anandpur on Vaisakhi 1699, the institution of Khande di Pahul, the Panj Piare, and the new identity of the Sikh.
lessons.html:
The Day the Panth Was Reborn

No episode in the Suraj Prakash carries greater weight than the founding of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ at ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ on Vaisakhi of 1699. Santokh Singh narrates the event with all the gravity it deserves, for here the Guru transformed the Sikh community into a sovereign, initiated order with a distinct identity and a binding discipline.

The Demand for a Head

The Guru had summoned the sangat from across the land to gather at ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ for the festival. Before the vast assembly, with a drawn sword, he made a startling demand: he asked for a Sikh willing to give his head. A hush of fear fell over the crowd. Then ਭਾਈ ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰਘ rose and offered himself. The Guru led him into a tent; a sound was heard, and the Guru emerged with a bloodied sword to ask for a second head. One by one, four more rose — ਭਾਈ ਧਰਮ ਸਿੰਘ, ਭਾਈ ਹਿੰਮਤ ਸਿੰਘ, ਭਾਈ ਮੋਹਕਮ ਸਿੰਘ, and ਭਾਈ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਸਿੰਘ — each prepared to die at the Guru's word. The tradition holds that the Guru then revealed all five alive, robed in new garments, having tested the community to find those of perfect devotion.

The ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ

These five became the ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ, the Five Beloved Ones, the nucleus of the new order. Their composition is itself a sermon: they came from different regions and different castes, yet were made one in the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ, eating from one vessel, bound by one discipline. The Guru thus enacted in the most dramatic possible way the Gurmat teaching that ਮਾਨਸ ਕੀ ਜਾਤਿ ਸਭੈ ਏਕੈ ਪਹਿਚਾਨਬੋ — that the whole human race is to be recognized as one. Caste, the deepest fracture of Indian society, was dissolved in the ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ.

ਖੰਡੇ ਦੀ ਪਾਹੁਲ

The Guru then instituted the rite of ਖੰਡੇ ਦੀ ਪਾਹੁਲ, the nectar of the double-edged sword. Water and patasas were placed in an iron vessel and stirred with a ਖੰਡਾ while the five banis were recited; Mata Sahib Devan, the tradition holds, added the patasas, infusing sweetness into the steel. The initiated were given the name ਸਿੰਘ (lion) and bound to the ਰਹਿਤ — the discipline of the ਪੰਜ ਕਕਾਰ (kes, kangha, kara, kachhera, kirpan), abstention from the four cardinal transgressions, and a life of Naam, daan, and ishnan. In a gesture without parallel, the Guru then knelt before the ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ and begged to be initiated by them, becoming himself ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ — the disciple of his own disciples. ਆਪੇ ਗੁਰ ਚੇਲਾ — he was at once Guru and disciple.

The Theology of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ

The word ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ, drawn from the Persian, signified land held directly by the sovereign without intermediary — and so the Sikh of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ belonged directly to the Guru and to the ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ, with no masand between. The Guru declared the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ to be his own very form. The tradition preserves his words: ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ ਮੇਰੋ ਰੂਪ ਹੈ ਖ਼ਾਸ — 'The Khalsa is my own special form.' The Sikh was now to be ਨਿਰਭਉ ਅਤੇ ਨਿਰਵੈਰ — fearless and without enmity — a saint in devotion and a soldier in the defence of righteousness.

The Revolution Assessed

For the historian, the founding of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ is a watershed: it gave the Sikhs a corporate identity, a code of conduct, an egalitarian membership, and a martial readiness, transforming a religious community into a self-governing order capable of resisting empire. Purnima Dhavan's study of the making of the Sikh warrior tradition traces the long consequences of this day across the eighteenth century. Santokh Singh, for his part, reads it as the fulfilment of the divine mission for which the Guru took birth — the gathering of the saints, the spreading of ਧਰਮ, and the uprooting of tyranny. The boy who had received his martyred father's head at Anandpur had now forged a community that could no longer be slaughtered in silence.

lessons.title: The Sieges of Anandpur and the Evacuation
lessons.summary: The repeated Mughal-hill confederacy sieges of Anandpur, the long blockade, the broken oaths of safe passage, and the desperate evacuation of December 1705.
lessons.html:
The Gathering of the Hosts

The creation of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ alarmed both the hill rajas and the Mughal empire, and the years following 1699 saw ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ subjected to repeated assault. The Suraj Prakash narrates a series of engagements as the confederacy of hill rajas, unable to tolerate the Guru's growing power and the egalitarian threat the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ posed to caste hierarchy, combined against him and eventually called upon the imperial forces of the Mughal governors of Sirhind and Lahore.

The Battles Around Anandpur

The fortified town, ringed by its forts, withstood several attacks. The tradition recounts episodes of great valour — the Sikhs sallying out to break sieges, the use of the forts' defences, and individual feats of arms. One celebrated incident involves the Guru's stratagem against a war elephant sent to batter down the gate of Lohgarh, met by ਭਾਈ ਬਚਿੱਤਰ ਸਿੰਘ with the ਨਾਗਣੀ ਬਰਛਾ. Whatever embellishment the kavi adds, these narratives communicate the ferocity of the struggle and the resolve of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ to hold their ground.

The Long Blockade

By 1705 the enemy adopted the strategy of blockade rather than assault, ringing ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ and cutting off supplies in an attempt to starve the garrison into surrender. The Suraj Prakash dwells on the privations of the siege: the exhaustion of provisions, the suffering of the Sikhs, and the testing of their faith. It is in this context that the tradition places the episode of the ਚਾਲੀ ਮੁਕਤੇ — the forty Sikhs who, overcome by hunger and hardship, signed a ਬੇਦਾਵਾ (a disclaimer renouncing the Guru) and departed, only to return later and attain martyrdom and liberation at Muktsar.

The False Oaths

The besiegers, unable to take the town by force, resorted to solemn oaths of safe passage. The Suraj Prakash records that the hill rajas swore upon the cow and the Mughal commanders upon the Qur'an that if the Guru evacuated ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ, his people would be allowed to depart unharmed. After much deliberation, and at the urging of his mother and the Sikhs, the Guru agreed to leave. The Guru himself, in the ਜ਼ਫ਼ਰਨਾਮਾ, would later indict the perjury of those who swore by their holy book and then broke their word: he reminds Aurangzeb that an oath upon the Qur'an, once given, must be kept.

The Evacuation and the Betrayal at the Sarsa

In the bitter cold of December 1705, the Guru and his household and the remaining Sikhs evacuated ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ by night. No sooner had they left the protection of the forts than the enemy, oaths forgotten, fell upon them. At the rain-swollen ਸਰਸਾ river, in darkness and confusion, the column was attacked and scattered. Here occurred the great separation of the Guru's family — the vichhora. Mata Gujri and the two younger ਸਾਹਿਬਜ਼ਾਦੇ, ਬਾਬਾ ਜ਼ੋਰਾਵਰ ਸਿੰਘ and ਬਾਬਾ ਫਤਹਿ ਸਿੰਘ, became separated from the Guru and were taken by the family's former cook Gangu toward Sirhind. The Guru, with his two elder sons and a remnant of Sikhs, pressed on toward Chamkaur. Precious manuscripts and possessions were lost in the flooded river.

The Faithlessness of Power

Santokh Singh frames the betrayal at the Sarsa as the culmination of the lesson begun at Nadaun: those who serve worldly power keep faith only as long as it suits them. The sworn oaths upon cow and Qur'an were worth nothing once the Guru was exposed. Against this faithlessness the poet sets the steadfastness of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ, who would now, in the days to come at Chamkaur and Sirhind, demonstrate a loyalty unto death that no oath could compel and no torture could break. The evacuation had begun the darkest and most sacred passage of the Guru's life.

lessons.title: Chamkaur Sahib and the Shaheedis of the ਸਾਹਿਬਜ਼ਾਦੇ
lessons.summary: The siege of the mud fortress at Chamkaur, the martyrdoms of Baba Ajit Singh and Baba Jujhar Singh, and the command of the Panj Piare to the Guru.
lessons.html:
Forty Against an Empire

The episode of ਚਮਕੌਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ is among the most exalted in the entire Suraj Prakash, and indeed in all Sikh history. Pursued from the Sarsa, ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ reached the small town of Chamkaur with his two elder sons — ਬਾਬਾ ਅਜੀਤ ਸਿੰਘ and ਬਾਬਾ ਜੁਝਾਰ ਸਿੰਘ — and roughly forty exhausted Sikhs. There they took shelter in a fortified mud haveli, the ਕੱਚੀ ਗੜ੍ਹੀ, and prepared to face the vast pursuing army of the Mughals and the hill rajas.

The Battle at the Garhi

The Suraj Prakash recounts how, at dawn, the enemy host surrounded the little fortress. The Sikhs, though outnumbered by overwhelming odds, sold their lives dearly. From the walls and the upper storey they loosed arrows and musket-fire; when the enemy pressed close, parties of Singhs sallied out to fight hand to hand until they fell. Santokh Singh narrates the successive sorties, naming the martyrs, in the full heroic register of ਬੀਰ ਰਸ. The defenders, the tradition holds, exacted a fearful price for every life they gave.

The Martyrdom of the Elder ਸਾਹਿਬਜ਼ਾਦੇ

The most poignant passages narrate the martyrdoms of the Guru's own sons. ਬਾਬਾ ਅਜੀਤ ਸਿੰਘ, the eldest, about seventeen years of age, sought his father's permission to go out and fight. The Guru, far from restraining him, embraced him and sent him to the field, where he fought with great valour until he attained ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ. Then ਬਾਬਾ ਜੁਝਾਰ ਸਿੰਘ, only about fourteen, asked the same leave, and the Guru sent his second son after the first, watching from the garhi as the boy gave his life in battle. The Sikh tradition holds that the Guru, far from weeping, gave thanks to the ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ that what was His had been returned to Him. This is the supreme expression of the Guru as ਸਰਬੰਸਦਾਨੀ — the giver of his entire lineage.

The ਗੁਰਮਤਾ of the ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ

As the night wore on and the defenders dwindled to a handful, the surviving Sikhs took a momentous step. Invoking the authority the Guru himself had vested in the ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ, five Singhs constituted themselves as the embodied ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ and commanded the Guru to leave the garhi and preserve himself for the Panth. Here the Suraj Prakash dramatizes one of the most extraordinary doctrines in Sikhism: that the Guru, having bowed before the ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ at the founding of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ, was bound to obey their collective command. The Guru accepted the ਗੁਰਮਤਾ. He could not be ordered as a man, but he had made the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ his own form, and he honoured its authority.

The Departure from Chamkaur

In the darkness the Guru left the garhi, clapping his hands and challenging the besiegers openly so that none could later say he had fled in stealth. With a small number of companions he passed through the encircling army and into the wilderness of the Machhiwara forest, while ਭਾਈ ਸੰਗਤ ਸਿੰਘ, who resembled the Guru and wore his aigrette, remained to deceive the enemy and attain martyrdom. The remaining defenders fought to the last. ਚਮਕੌਰ stands in Sikh memory as the place where forty held off an empire and where two of the Guru's sons watered the field with their blood.

The Meaning of Chamkaur

For the advanced student, Chamkaur is the supreme demonstration of the ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ and of the doctrine of the Guru-Panth. The Guru's willingness to send his own sons to martyrdom, and his submission to the command of the ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ, together teach that in the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ no one — not even the Guru's own family, not even the Guru's own person — stands above the Panth and its ਧਰਮ. The tradition's phrase captures it: what is the wonder if a thousand fight one, when the Guru, the True King, watches over the few? Chamkaur was not a defeat but, in the Sikh reckoning, a victory of spirit over numbers, of ਧਰਮ over tyranny.

lessons.title: Sirhind, the Younger Sahibzade, and the Cold Tower
lessons.summary: The betrayal of Gangu, the martyrdom of the two younger Sahibzade bricked alive at Sirhind, and the passing of Mata Gujri.
lessons.html:
The Younger Sons and the Cold Tower

While the elder ਸਾਹਿਬਜ਼ਾਦੇ attained martyrdom in open battle at ਚਮਕੌਰ, the two younger sons of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ met a fate that the Sikh conscience has never ceased to mourn and to honour. The Suraj Prakash narrates the parallel tragedy at Sirhind with restrained sorrow and theological depth.

The Betrayal of Gangu

Separated from the Guru at the ਸਰਸਾ, ਮਾਤਾ ਗੁਜਰੀ and the two small boys — ਬਾਬਾ ਜ਼ੋਰਾਵਰ ਸਿੰਘ, about nine, and ਬਾਬਾ ਫਤਹਿ ਸਿੰਘ, about seven — fell into the company of Gangu, a former Brahmin cook of the household. He took them to his village, where, tempted by the reward offered for the Guru's family and by greed for their valuables, he betrayed them to the Mughal officials of Morinda, who delivered them to the ਸੂਬਾ of Sirhind, Wazir Khan.

The Court of Wazir Khan

The Suraj Prakash recounts how the two children were brought before the governor's court at Sirhind and confined, with their grandmother, in the ਠੰਡਾ ਬੁਰਜ — the cold tower — exposed to the bitter December cold. Day after day the boys were brought before Wazir Khan and pressed to abandon their faith and accept Islam in exchange for their lives, riches, and honour. The tradition preserves the children's fearless reply: they were the grandsons of ਗੁਰੂ ਤੇਗ ਬਹਾਦਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ and the sons of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ, and they would never forsake the ਧਰਮ of their grandfather and father for any inducement or threat. The motif of the unbroken child-witness is central to the poet's purpose: faith is not the property of the strong and the grown, but burns brightest in the innocent.

The Martyrdom

When neither persuasion nor menace could move them, the children were condemned. The Suraj Prakash and the wider tradition relate that the two Sahibzade were bricked up alive within a wall. The qazi who pronounced the sentence is remembered with infamy; the Pathan nawab Sher Muhammad Khan of Malerkotla, who raised a cry against the killing of innocents — the ਹਾਅ ਦਾ ਨਾਅਰਾ — is remembered with honour, for he protested that the children bore no part in their father's quarrel. The boys attained ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ, the youngest martyrs in the Sikh tradition. Their grandmother, ਮਾਤਾ ਗੁਜਰੀ, hearing of their martyrdom, also passed away in the cold tower, completing the sacrifice of three generations.

The Theological Weight
