  6. Vaar 2: Guru Angad Dev Ji and the Gift of ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ
  7. Vaar 3: Guru Amar Das Ji, ਸੰਗਤ and ਪੰਗਤ
  8. Vaar 4: Guru Ram Das Ji and the Founding of ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤਸਰ
  9. Vaar 5: Guru Arjan Dev Ji and the Compilation of the Adi Granth
  10. Vaar 6: Guru Hargobind Sahib and ਮੀਰੀ ਪੀਰੀ
  11. Conclusion: The Vaars as Theology and as History

Who was Bhai Gurdas Ji?

Bhai Gurdas Ji (c. 1551–1636) stands at the very centre of early Sikh letters. A close relative of the house of the Gurus, he served four Gurus — from Guru Ram Das Ji to Guru Hargobind Sahib — as a missionary, scribe, theologian, and steward of the young community. When Guru Arjan Dev Ji set down the ਆਦਿ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ (Adi Granth) in 1604, it was the hand of Bhai Gurdas Ji that wrote the volume at the Guru's dictation. No figure of the period is closer to the textual and institutional birth of Sikhi.

Yet Bhai Gurdas Ji is remembered above all as a poet. His two great bodies of work are the ਕਬਿੱਤ ਸਵਈਏ (Kabitt Savaiye), composed in Braj, and the forty ਵਾਰਾਂ (Vaars) composed in Punjabi. This course studies the first six of those Vaars. Although his writing is not part of Sri Guru Granth Sahib, it occupies a singular place of honour: by long tradition, Guru Arjan Dev Ji called the Vaars the ਕੁੰਜੀ — the key — to the Granth, and they are the only non-scriptural compositions formally permitted to be sung as ਕੀਰਤਨ within the ਗੁਰਦੁਆਰਾ.

Why the Vaars are called the key

The honorific "key" is precise. The language of Sri Guru Granth Sahib is dense, multilingual, and metaphorically charged. Bhai Gurdas Ji, writing as a contemporary who had heard the Gurus teach and who knew the living idiom of the Sikhs, restates the central doctrines of Gurmat in patient, expository Punjabi. Where Gurbani compresses, the Vaars unfold. Where Gurbani sings, the Vaars explain. A student who learns the vocabulary of the Vaars — ਗੁਰਮੁਖਿ and ਮਨਮੁਖਿ, ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ, ਹੁਕਮੁ, ਨਾਮੁ — comes to the Granth already fluent in its conceptual world.

There is a second sense in which the Vaars are a key. They preserve the earliest connected narrative of Sikh sacred history. The opening Vaar tells how and why Guru Nanak Sahib came; later Vaars carry the story forward through the succession of the Gurus. Because Bhai Gurdas Ji wrote within living memory of these events, modern historians treat the Vaars as a primary source — with care, for the Vaars are devotional literature, not chronicle, and their purpose is to evoke faith rather than to date events.

The shape of this course

We read Vaars 1 through 6 as a continuous account of the ਪੰਥ taking form. Vaar 1 is the longest and most theologically ambitious: it moves from the creation of the cosmos by ਨਿਰੰਕਾਰ (the Formless), through the moral collapse of the age, to the appearance of Guru Nanak Sahib as the answer to a suffering world's cry. Vaars 2 through 6 follow the institution-building of the next five Gurus — the script and schooling of Guru Angad Dev Ji, the congregational order of Guru Amar Das Ji, the sacred city of Guru Ram Das Ji, the canon of Guru Arjan Dev Ji, and the sovereignty of Guru Hargobind Sahib.

Throughout, we hold two readings together. The theological reading asks what the Vaars teach about God, the Guru, and the liberated life. The historical reading asks what they tell us about how a real community in sixteenth- and seventeenth-century Punjab came into being. Bhai Gurdas Ji himself does not separate these; for him the rise of the Panth is the working out of a divine purpose in time.

A note on Professor Bhai Jodh Singh

This course is taught under the name of Bhai Jodh Singh (1882–1981), the eminent Sikh scholar, first principal of Khalsa College and later first Vice-Chancellor of Punjabi University, Patiala. Bhai Jodh Singh produced a careful edition, transliteration, and translation of the Vaars and wrote extensively on their doctrine; his work remains a standard reference for the academic study of Bhai Gurdas Ji. Where this course paraphrases the sense of a pauri, it follows the interpretive tradition that his scholarship helped to stabilise.

How to study the Vaars

Read slowly. A Vaar is built to be sung and absorbed line by line, not skimmed. In each lesson you will meet selected pauris in Gurmukhi with an English rendering. Do not treat the translation as a substitute for the original — let it return you to the Gurmukhi. Keep the glossary of terms beside you, and notice how the same handful of words — ਗੁਰਮੁਖਿ, ਚਰਨ ਕਮਲ, ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ — recur and accumulate meaning across the six Vaars. By the end you should be able to hear in a single pauri the whole argument of the work.

lessons.title: The Form of the Vaar: Poetry, Prosody, and the Pauri
lessons.html:
From battlefield ballad to spiritual instruction

To read Bhai Gurdas Ji well we must first understand the form he chose. The ਵਾਰ is one of the oldest genres of Punjabi verse. In its original setting a Vaar was a heroic ballad — a ਢਾਡੀ (bard) would sing of battles, of the courage of warriors and the disgrace of cowards, often to the beat of the ਢੱਡ drum, rousing listeners to valour. The Vaar was the poetry of the war camp.

The Gurus and Bhai Gurdas Ji took this charged martial form and turned it inward and upward. The battle becomes the struggle of the soul against the five thieves; the hero becomes the ਗੁਰਮੁਖਿ; the coward becomes the ਮਨਮੁਖਿ; the king to be served is ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ. This transformation is itself a theological statement: the energies of worldly heroism are not denied but redirected toward the conquest of the self. Long before the Khalsa was instituted, the very form of the Vaar anticipated the Sikh ideal in which spiritual discipline and heroic courage are one.

The architecture of a Vaar

Each of Bhai Gurdas Ji's forty Vaars is a self-contained poem on a theme, and each is built of numbered stanzas called ਪਉੜੀਆਂ (pauris). The word ਪਉੜੀ means a "step" or a rung of a ladder, and the image is exact: the pauris of a Vaar mount an argument step by step, so that the reader climbs from a first statement to a culminating insight. Vaar 1, the longest, has forty-nine pauris; the Vaars we study in this course range across many stanzas each.

Within a pauri, Bhai Gurdas Ji typically opens with a series of images or examples drawn from nature, craft, or common life — the lotus in muddy water, the swan that separates milk from water, the philosopher's stone that turns iron to gold — and then turns, in the closing line, to apply the figure to the spiritual life. This movement from ਦ੍ਰਿਸ਼ਟਾਂਤ (illustration) to ਸਿੱਧਾਂਤ (doctrine) is the signature rhythm of his style. Learning to anticipate the turn is the first skill of reading the Vaars.

The texture of the language

Bhai Gurdas Ji writes a supple, idiomatic Punjabi, far more accessible than the high, compressed registers of much of Gurbani. This accessibility is deliberate and is part of why the Vaars function as a ਕੁੰਜੀ. He explains, repeats, and accumulates; he is content to make a point three ways so that it lodges. The poetry is rich in ਅਲੰਕਾਰ (figures of speech) — simile, metaphor, and especially the extended analogy that fills a whole pauri.

Consider the celebrated image with which the tradition associates his praise of the holy congregation:

ਚੰਦਨ ਵਾਸੁ ਵਨਾਸਪਤਿ ਚੰਦਨੁ ਹੋਇ ਨ ਚੰਦਨੁ ਵਾਸੁ ॥

— Vaaran Bhai Gurdas Ji

"By the fragrance of the sandal the surrounding forest becomes sandal — though the sandal asks nothing in return." The figure is botanical and homely, but its target is the ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ: company with the holy transforms the ordinary person as the scent of sandalwood transfigures a whole grove. The whole method of the Vaars is here — a picture from the world made to carry a teaching about the self.

Vaar and the oral tradition

Because the Vaar was sung, its sound matters as much as its sense. The pauris are metrically shaped for the breath and the voice; they were meant to be heard in ਸੰਗਤ. This is the deepest reason the Vaars alone, among non-scriptural works, may be sung as ਕੀਰਤਨ in the ਗੁਰਦੁਆਰਾ: they were composed within and for the congregational life they describe. When you read a pauri silently, try to hear it aloud, in the cadence of a ਢਾਡੀ before a gathered sangat. The form is not a container for the meaning; in the Vaar, the form is part of the meaning.

A discipline of reading

For the lessons that follow, adopt three habits. First, identify in each pauri the illustration and the doctrine, and watch for the turn between them. Second, keep a running list of recurring images — sandal, swan, lotus, the philosopher's stone, the lotus feet (ਚਰਨ ਕਮਲ) of the Guru — and notice how Bhai Gurdas Ji reuses them as a shared vocabulary across Vaars. Third, read every quoted pauri first in Gurmukhi, aloud if you can, before reading the English. The translation is a bridge back to the original, never a replacement for it. With these habits in place, we are ready to enter Vaar 1.

lessons.title: Vaar 1, Part One: Creation, the Fallen World, and the Cry for a Guru
lessons.html:
The Formless before form

Vaar 1 opens not with history but with metaphysics. Before there was a Panth, before there were Gurus or Sikhs, before there was a world, there was ਨਿਰੰਕਾਰ — the Formless One, ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ, alone and self-existent. Bhai Gurdas Ji begins his account of the Sikh story at the very beginning of all things because his claim is large: the coming of Guru Nanak Sahib is not an accident of Punjabi history but a movement within the divine purpose for the whole creation.

The Vaar describes, in its early pauris, how the One assumed the play of creation. From the Formless came ਓਅੰਕਾਰ, and from the creative Word unfolded the worlds, the elements, and all living kinds. This is the same cosmology the Sikh hears in the ਜਪੁਜੀ ਸਾਹਿਬ: a God who is at once ਨਿਰਗੁਣ (without attributes) and ਸਰਗੁਣ (manifest in creation), whose ਹੁਕਮੁ (command) orders all that is. Bhai Gurdas Ji is careful to keep both truths in view — God remains formless even as the worlds pour forth.

The descent of the age

Having set the cosmic stage, Vaar 1 turns to the condition of the world into which Guru Nanak Sahib would come. Here Bhai Gurdas Ji paints a dark and famous picture of a humanity that has lost its way. He surveys the religious landscape of his inherited world and finds it fractured: the ਚਾਰ ਵਰਨ (four castes) divided against one another, the ਛਿਅ ਘਰ (six schools) of Hindu philosophy quarrelling, the many sects each insisting on its own path, and beneath the disputes a general forgetfulness of the One.

He describes the ਕਲਿਜੁਗ (the dark age) as a season in which truth has thinned and ਹਉਮੈ (egotism) has thickened. Ritual has replaced devotion; the powerful oppress the weak; the very teachers of religion are blind. The tradition preserves his stark verdict on this age in lines such as:

ਕਲਿ ਆਈ ਕੁਤੇ ਮੁਹੀ ਖਾਜੁ ਹੋਆ ਮੁਰਦਾਰੁ ਗੁਸਾਈ ॥

— Vaaran Bhai Gurdas Ji

"The dark age came with the face of a dog; people fed, O Lord, on carrion." The image is deliberately repulsive: an age that devours what it should never touch, a humanity that has lost the instinct for what is pure. Bhai Gurdas Ji is not merely complaining; he is building a case. A world in this condition cannot heal itself. It can only cry out.

The cry of the earth

The most moving movement of this part of Vaar 1 is the depiction of creation itself appealing for rescue. The earth, suffering under the weight of injustice and ignorance, raises a cry to ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ. This motif — the petition of a groaning world — frames the whole drama of Guru Nanak Sahib's coming as response. The Guru does not arrive into an indifferent world to start a new sect; he is sent, in answer to a need that has reached the throne of the Formless.

This is a crucial theological move, and it is worth dwelling on. By framing the Guru's advent as the answer to a cosmic petition, Bhai Gurdas Ji elevates the local event of one teacher's birth in Talwandi into an act of divine mercy on the scale of the whole creation. The Sikh story begins, in his telling, with the compassion of God for a world that can no longer save itself.

Why this matters for the Panth

It might seem that a lesson on creation and the dark age belongs to cosmology rather than to the formation of the Panth. But Bhai Gurdas Ji's design is exact. The ਪੰਥ that Vaars 2 through 6 will describe — its script, its congregations, its city, its scripture, its sovereignty — is presented as the institutional shape of the rescue announced here. Every later development is, for him, the unfolding of the mercy that first stirred when the earth cried out. To understand why the Panth had to take the particular form it did, one must first feel the depth of the world's need as Vaar 1 portrays it.

In the next lesson we meet the answer to that cry: the mission of Guru Nanak Sahib, the ਉਦਾਸੀਆਂ that carried his message across the world, and the new society he began to gather.

lessons.title: Vaar 1, Part Two: The Mission of Guru Nanak Sahib and the Udasian
lessons.html:
"A wail of mercy arose"

If the first part of Vaar 1 is the cry of the world, the second is the answer. Bhai Gurdas Ji marks the coming of Guru Nanak Sahib with one of the most quoted lines in all of Sikh literature:

ਸੁਣੀ ਪੁਕਾਰਿ ਦਾਤਾਰ ਪ੍ਰਭੁ ਗੁਰੁ ਨਾਨਕ ਜਗ ਮਾਹਿ ਪਠਾਇਆ ॥

— Vaaran Bhai Gurdas Ji

"The Benefactor Lord heard the cry, and sent Guru Nanak into the world." Everything that the earlier pauris built — the suffering of creation, the petition of the earth — resolves in this single sentence. The Guru is ਪਠਾਇਆ, "sent": his coming is an act of God's own initiative.

The Vaar continues with the immediate transformation his coming works. The tradition cherishes the lines that describe the lifting of the age's darkness:

ਸਤਿਗੁਰੁ ਨਾਨਕੁ ਪ੍ਰਗਟਿਆ ਮਿਟੀ ਧੁੰਧੁ ਜਗਿ ਚਾਨਣੁ ਹੋਆ ॥

— Vaaran Bhai Gurdas Ji

"Satguru Nanak appeared; the fog lifted and light spread through the world." The image answers the carrion-eating darkness of the previous lesson point for point: where there was ਧੁੰਧੁ (fog) there is now ਚਾਨਣੁ (light). The Vaar even reaches for cosmic scale — as the sun rises the stars hide and the darkness flees; as the lion comes the deer scatter — to convey that a new order has begun.

The four journeys

Bhai Gurdas Ji is also our earliest connected source for the ਉਦਾਸੀਆਂ, the great preaching journeys of Guru Nanak Sahib. According to the tradition the Vaars helped to fix, the Guru travelled in the four directions, carrying the message of the One Name to centres of religious authority both within and beyond India. The Vaar describes him reaching ਮੱਕਾ (Mecca), ਮਦੀਨਾ, ਬਗਦਾਦ, and the great pilgrimage sites of the Indian subcontinent.

The purpose of the udasian, as the Vaar presents them, is dialogue and correction. Guru Nanak Sahib does not destroy other paths; he converses with their custodians — the ਪੀਰ and ਕਾਜ਼ੀ, the ਪੰਡਿਤ and ਜੋਗੀ — and turns each conversation toward the living truth they have forgotten. Bhai Gurdas Ji's account of the encounter at Mecca, where the Guru is rebuked for sleeping with his feet toward the ਕਾਅਬਾ and replies by asking that his feet be turned wherever God is not, became one of the defining stories of the tradition. The lesson is the omnipresence of ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ: no direction is sacred against the rest, because God is in every direction.

The encounter with the Siddhas

Among the most theologically important episodes the Vaar records is Guru Nanak Sahib's dialogue with the ਸਿੱਧ yogis in the mountains — the substance of which the Granth itself preserves in the ਸਿਧ ਗੋਸਟਿ. The Siddhas, withdrawn from the world into ascetic isolation, challenge the Guru's path. His answer defines the Sikh way against world-renouncing asceticism: liberation is to be found within the world, in the householder's life of honest work, remembrance, and sharing, not in flight from it. The ਗੁਰਮੁਖਿ lives in the marketplace and the home, "unstained as the lotus in muddy water." This refusal of ਉਦਾਸੀ renunciation in the ascetic sense — even as the Guru undertakes his own udasi journeys — is foundational for everything the Panth will become.

A new society in seed

Two features of the udasian deserve emphasis for our theme. First, the journeys establish the universality of the message: Guru Nanak Sahib's truth is not for one region or community but is carried deliberately to the centres of every major tradition, Hindu and Muslim alike. The Panth that will form is, in principle, a path for all humanity, not a sect of Punjab. Second, the method of dialogue rather than denunciation models the posture the community will inherit: the ਗੁਰਮੁਖਿ engages the world to correct and uplift it, not to flee or condemn it. Bhai Gurdas Ji's account of the udasian is thus already an account of the spirit of the Panth.

The Vaar does not leave Guru Nanak Sahib as a wandering preacher. It shows him, at the end of his travels, settling at ਕਰਤਾਰਪੁਰ on the bank of the Ravi and gathering a community around the daily disciplines that would become the marks of the Panth: ਨਾਮੁ (the divine Name), ਦਾਨੁ (charity and sharing), and ਇਸ਼ਨਾਨੁ (cleanliness of body and mind). Here the morning ਜਪੁਜੀ and the evening ਸੋਦਰੁ were sung, the ਲੰਗਰ was kept, and the first ਸੰਗਤ took shape. The seed of every institution that Vaars 2 through 6 will describe is planted at Kartarpur. The next lesson follows that seed into its first great act of growth: the choosing of a successor and the founding of a continuing line.

lessons.title: Vaar 1, Part Three: The Succession and the Birth of the Panth
lessons.html:
The problem of continuity

A teacher dies and his teaching scatters; a movement built on one charismatic figure rarely survives him. Bhai Gurdas Ji understood this danger, and the closing movement of Vaar 1 addresses it directly. The genius of the Sikh tradition — and the reason it became a ਪੰਥ rather than a memory — is that Guru Nanak Sahib did not leave his work to chance. He chose a successor and transmitted to him the same light he himself had carried.

The Vaar describes the testing of the disciples and the choosing of Bhai Lehna, who would become Guru Angad Dev Ji. What is decisive in the account is the nature of the transfer. The Guruship does not pass to a son by blood, nor to the most learned, but to the most surrendered — to the one whose obedience and ਸੇਵਾ have made him perfectly transparent to the Guru's will. Bhai Gurdas Ji frames the succession with the famous image of one lamp lighting another:

ਜੋਤੀ ਜੋਤਿ ਮਿਲਾਇ ਕੈ ਸਤਿਗੁਰ ਨਾਨਕ ਰੂਪੁ ਵਟਾਇਆ ॥

— Vaaran Bhai Gurdas Ji

"Merging light into light, Satguru Nanak changed his form." The ਜੋਤਿ (light) is one; only the ਰੂਪੁ (form, body) changes. This is the doctrine of the single eternal Guruship taking successive human bodies — the theological heart of how the Sikh tradition understands its own continuity. The ten Gurus are one light in ten lamps.

Why succession is a doctrine, not an administrative fact

It would be easy to read the choosing of a successor as mere organisation — a founder arranging his estate. Bhai Gurdas Ji forbids that reading. For him the succession is the means by which the rescue announced at the start of the Vaar is made durable. The mercy that sent Guru Nanak Sahib does not withdraw at his passing; it continues, embodied, through the line of Gurus. The ਪੰਥ is possible only because the Guruship is continuous. Every institution that follows — script, congregation, city, scripture, sovereignty — rests on this foundation of unbroken light.

This is also why later Sikh thought could speak of the Guruship passing, after the ten human Gurus, to the ਸ਼ਬਦ (the Word) enshrined in Sri Guru Granth Sahib and to the ਪੰਥ itself. The principle that the Guruship is a light independent of any one body was established here, in the very first succession, and Vaar 1 is our earliest devotional articulation of it.

The contrast figures: rivals and the unworthy

Bhai Gurdas Ji's account of the succession is sharpened by its shadows. He is candid about the ਮਨਮੁਖ rivals who claimed authority they had not been given — including, in the wider tradition the Vaars reflect, the disappointed kin who set themselves up against the chosen Guru. By naming the false claimants, Bhai Gurdas Ji clarifies the true principle: legitimacy in the Panth flows not from blood, ambition, or learning, but from ਗੁਰਮੁਖਤਾ — total orientation to the Guru. The ਮਨਮੁਖਿ grasps at the Guruship and is empty; the ਗੁਰਮੁਖਿ renounces all claim and is filled.

The Panth defined

By the end of Vaar 1 the essential elements of the Sikh community are in place: a God who sends, a Guru who is sent, a message of ਨਾਮੁ, ਦਾਨੁ, and ਇਸ਼ਨਾਨੁ, a gathered ਸੰਗਤ, and a continuous Guruship that guarantees the message will outlast any single life. This is the ਪੰਥ in seed. The remaining five Vaars in our course show that seed unfolding into the great institutions of Sikhi.

It is worth pausing to appreciate the architecture of the whole Vaar. It begins with the Formless before creation and ends with a living community walking the Guru's path in history. The arc is from ਨਿਰੰਕਾਰ to ਪੰਥ — from God's hidden being to God's visible work in the world. For Bhai Gurdas Ji these are not two stories but one: the Panth is what the mercy of the Formless looks like when it takes shape in time. With this whole vision before us, we turn in the next lesson to Vaar 2 and the first of the institution-builders, Guru Angad Dev Ji.

lessons.title: Vaar 2: Guru Angad Dev Ji and the Gift of Gurmukhi
lessons.html:
The Guru who served before he led

Vaar 2 takes up the second Guru, Guru Angad Dev Ji (1504–1552), and Bhai Gurdas Ji's portrait turns on a single virtue: ਸੇਵਾ. Before Bhai Lehna became Guru Angad, he was the disciple whose obedience was without limit. The Vaar recalls how he would rise in the cold of night at the Guru's word, carry mud-soaked grass on his own head without complaint, and step without hesitation into whatever the Guru asked. His Guruship is presented as the fruit of this surrender. The lesson Bhai Gurdas Ji draws is one of the deepest in the Vaars: authority in the Panth is earned by service, and the one fit to be served is the one who has most fully served.

This is why Guru Nanak Sahib named him ਅੰਗਦ — "of my own limb," part of my own body. The ਗੁਰਮੁਖਿ becomes so transparent to the Guru's will that no distance remains between them. The image of one lamp lighting another from Vaar 1 here finds its first living embodiment.

The standardising of Gurmukhi

The institution most associated with Guru Angad Dev Ji is the ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ script. The Guru gave the Sikhs a refined and standardised script in which to write the language of Gurbani — the script whose very name, "from the mouth of the Guru," declares its purpose. This was an act of enormous and lasting consequence for the formation of the Panth, and we should be clear about why.

First, a distinct script gave the young community a distinct identity. The Sikhs would not read their scripture in the ਦੇਵਨਾਗਰੀ of the Brahmin nor in the ਫ਼ਾਰਸੀ script of the Muslim administration, but in a script of their own, tied to their own teaching. Second, and more profoundly, ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ was an instrument of equality. The sacred languages of the inherited order were guarded by priestly classes; literacy in them was a privilege of caste. By giving ordinary Punjabis a simple script for their own tongue, Guru Angad Dev Ji put the scripture within reach of the ਆਮ (common) Sikh — the farmer, the labourer, the woman — and broke the monopoly of the learned over the word of God.

Schools, children, and the body

Bhai Gurdas Ji's Guru Angad is a builder of healthy community. The Guru established centres where children were taught ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ, turning the script into a programme of mass education. He encouraged ਮੱਲ ਅਖਾੜੇ (wrestling arenas), tending the body alongside the spirit — an early sign of the integrated, world-affirming ethic that would culminate in the ਮੀਰੀ ਪੀਰੀ of Vaar 6. The ਲੰਗਰ begun by Guru Nanak Sahib was carried forward and strengthened, with Mata Khivi Ji's care for the ਲੰਗਰ celebrated in the Sikh tradition. Here the Panth becomes not merely a circle of disciples but an ordered society with its own institutions of learning, nourishment, and discipline.

The Gurmukh as the model citizen of the Panth

Vaar 2 is also where the figure of the ਗੁਰਮੁਖਿ receives some of Bhai Gurdas Ji's most extended treatment. Across its pauris he draws the portrait of the ideal Sikh: humble as the earth that bears all feet, patient as the tree that gives shade even to the one who throws stones at it, fragrant as sandal that perfumes the axe that cuts it. The ਗੁਰਮੁਖਿ does not retaliate, does not boast, does not grasp. The tradition preserves the simple measure of this life:

ਗੁਰਮੁਖਿ ਸੁਖ ਫਲੁ ਪਿਰਮ ਰਸੁ ਚਰਣ ਕਮਲ ਮਕਰੰਦ ਲੁਭਾਏ ॥

— Vaaran Bhai Gurdas Ji

"The fruit of bliss for the Gurmukh is the nectar of love; the bee of the soul is drawn to the pollen of the Guru's lotus feet." The ਚਰਨ ਕਮਲ — the lotus feet of the Guru — is the recurring image of the disciple's humble refuge. To be a ਗੁਰਮੁਖਿ is to be the bee who has found this flower and asks for nothing else.

From identity to institution

With Vaar 2 we watch the Panth acquire the second of its great supports. Vaar 1 gave it a mission and a continuous Guruship; Vaar 2 gives it a script, a system of education, and a refined portrait of the ideal member. The community now has the means to read its own scripture, to teach its own children, and to recognise its own saint. In the next lesson, Guru Amar Das Ji will give it the institutions of congregation and common table that bind these individuals into a single egalitarian body.

lessons.title: Vaar 3: Guru Amar Das Ji, Sangat and Pangat
lessons.html:
The seeker who came late and gave the most

Vaar 3 turns to the third Guru, Guru Amar Das Ji (1479–1574), and Bhai Gurdas Ji again finds the meaning of a Guruship in the quality of a service. Guru Amar Das came to the Guru late in life and served Guru Angad Dev Ji with a devotion that became legendary — most famously by carrying water from the river each dawn for the Guru's bath, in all weathers and into great age. The Vaar makes this ਸੇਵਾ the ground of his elevation: he who carried water for the Guru would be given the spring of ਨਾਮੁ to pour out for the whole world.

Bhai Gurdas Ji's repeated insistence that each Guru first served is not incidental. It is a structural argument about the Panth: the community is built by service, and its leaders are made by it. The chain — Guru Angad serving Guru Nanak, Guru Amar Das serving Guru Angad — is the visible proof that the ਜੋਤਿ passes through surrender.

Sangat and Pangat: the twin institutions of equality

The contribution most identified with Guru Amar Das Ji, and the heart of Vaar 3's relevance to our theme, is the consolidation of ਸੰਗਤ (the congregation) and ਪੰਗਤ (the row of common dining). These two institutions, taken together, gave the Panth its enduring social form.

The ਸੰਗਤ is the gathering of Sikhs to remember the Name and hear the Word. Guru Amar Das Ji organised the growing community by establishing the system of ਮੰਜੀ — twenty-two seats of spiritual authority across the regions, each a centre for local sangats. He thus turned a single congregation into a network, allowing the Panth to grow beyond the reach of one place. Bhai Gurdas Ji's praise of the ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ as the workshop of liberation belongs here: it is in the company of the holy that the ਮਨਮੁਖਿ is remade into the ਗੁਰਮੁਖਿ.

The ਪੰਗਤ is the institution of the common table. Guru Amar Das Ji made it a rule that all who came to see him must first sit together in a single row and eat from the one ਲੰਗਰ — ਪਹਿਲੇ ਪੰਗਤ ਪਾਛੇ ਸੰਗਤ, "first the row, then the audience." The ਪੰਗਤ is a theology made edible: by requiring king and labourer, Brahmin and outcaste, to sit at the same level and share the same food, it enacts the truth that all are equal before ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ. The tradition records that even the emperor Akbar sat in the ਪੰਗਤ before he could meet the Guru.

The attack on caste and on the degradation of women

Bhai Gurdas Ji's Guru Amar Das is a reformer of the social order. The ਪੰਗਤ is itself an assault on ਜਾਤ-ਪਾਤ (caste hierarchy), but the Guru went further. He spoke against the cruelties inflicted on women — against ਸਤੀ (the burning of widows), against the seclusion of the ਪਰਦਾ, and against the contempt heaped on widows — and affirmed the dignity and remarriage of women. The Vaars' vision of a community in which the ਗੁਰਮੁਖਿ may be anyone, of any birth or sex, finds in Guru Amar Das Ji its concrete social legislation.

The making of sacred occasion and place

Guru Amar Das Ji also gave the Panth its own rhythm of gathering, establishing the centre at ਗੋਇੰਦਵਾਲ with its ਬਾਉਲੀ (stepped well) as a place of pilgrimage for the Sikhs, and encouraging the community to assemble on its own occasions rather than at the festivals of the inherited tradition. Step by step the Panth is acquiring everything a distinct people needs: its own script (Vaar 2), its own congregational network and common table (Vaar 3), and soon its own sacred city and scripture.

The sangat as the body of the Guru

The deepest teaching of Vaar 3 is that the ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ is not merely a useful organisation but a sacred reality — the very place where the Guru is present and liberation is found. Bhai Gurdas Ji can speak of the holy congregation as the visible form of the Guru in the world. To sit in true ਸੰਗਤ and ਪੰਗਤ is already to be in the Guru's presence. This is why the institutions of Guru Amar Das Ji are so central to the formation of the Panth: they are not scaffolding around the spiritual life but its actual dwelling-place. In the next lesson the community gains a permanent centre of its own, as Guru Ram Das Ji founds Amritsar.

lessons.title: Vaar 4: Guru Ram Das Ji and the Founding of Amritsar
lessons.html:
The Guru of devotion

Vaar 4 brings us to the fourth Guru, Guru Ram Das Ji (1534–1581), and Bhai Gurdas Ji's portrait is suffused with the language of ਪ੍ਰੇਮ (love) and ਭਗਤੀ (devotion). If Guru Angad Dev Ji is remembered for the script and Guru Amar Das Ji for the congregation, Guru Ram Das Ji is the Guru of the longing heart and the gathered city. Bhai Gurdas Ji, who himself entered the service of the Gurus in this period and was a relative of Guru Amar Das Ji's family, writes of Guru Ram Das Ji with the warmth of one who knew the household closely.

As with each Guru before him, the Vaar locates his greatness first in ਸੇਵਾ. Jetha — the future Guru Ram Das — served Guru Amar Das Ji with such complete devotion that he became the chosen one, and the Guruship passed to him as the lamp passes its flame. Once again the principle holds: the ਜੋਤਿ flows through surrender, not blood.

The digging of the sacred pool

The act for which Vaar 4 is remembered in the history of the Panth is the founding of ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤਸਰ — the "pool of nectar." Guru Ram Das Ji acquired land and began the excavation of the great ਸਰੋਵਰ (tank) that would become the spiritual centre of the Sikh world. Around this pool a town arose, first called ਰਾਮਦਾਸਪੁਰ after the Guru, which grew into the city of ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤਸਰ.

The significance for the formation of the Panth is hard to overstate. Until now the centre of the community had moved with the Guru — Kartarpur, Khadur, Goindwal. With the founding of Amritsar the Panth acquired a permanent centre of its own, a place that did not depend on the residence of any one Guru. This was a city built by the Sikhs, for the Sikhs, around an institution of the Sikhs. The community that began as a circle of disciples around a wandering teacher now had a homeland and a heart.

A city of honest trades

Guru Ram Das Ji designed Amritsar to be a working, prosperous town, inviting traders and craftsmen of many kinds to settle there — a ਬਾਜ਼ਾਰ as well as a ਸਰੋਵਰ. This is the Sikh ethic of ਕਿਰਤ (honest labour) made into urban policy: the sacred pool and the bustling market stand side by side, expressing the refusal — first heard in Guru Nanak Sahib's reply to the Siddhas — to separate the spiritual life from the life of work and the world. Amritsar is the householder's ideal built in brick.

The Lavan and the shaping of Sikh life

Guru Ram Das Ji's gift to the inner life of the Panth was as great as his gift of a city. He composed the ਲਾਵਾਂ (Lavan), the four hymns that became the heart of the Sikh marriage rite, the ਅਨੰਦ ਕਾਰਜ. In the ਲਾਵਾਂ the union of husband and wife is made a figure for the soul's union with ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ: the four circlings are four stages of the spiritual journey, from the start of duty to final merging in the Beloved. Through this composition Guru Ram Das Ji gave the Panth its own sacred ceremony of marriage — another institution by which the community marked its life with its own forms rather than borrowing them.

Gurbani in the ਲਾਵਾਂ teaches that the householder's love, rightly lived, is itself a path to the divine — that one need not leave home and family to reach ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ, but may find the Beloved within the bonds of an honest life. This is the same world-affirming vision that runs through every Vaar.

The Panth acquires a home

With Vaar 4 the pattern of formation reaches a new stage. The Panth now has its mission and Guruship (Vaar 1), its script and education (Vaar 2), its congregation and common table (Vaar 3), and now its permanent sacred city and its own rites of life (Vaar 4). What remains is the gathering of the Word itself into a single scripture, and the assumption of worldly authority to defend the community. These are the achievements of the next two Gurus, and the subjects of our final two Vaars.

lessons.title: Vaar 5: Guru Arjan Dev Ji and the Compilation of the Adi Granth
lessons.html:
The Guru who gathered the Word

Vaar 5 brings us to the fifth Guru, Guru Arjan Dev Ji (1563–1606), and to the achievement that, more than any other, gave the Panth its enduring centre of authority: the compilation of the ਆਦਿ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ. Bhai Gurdas Ji writes of this Guru with particular closeness, for he was himself the scribe who, at Guru Arjan Dev Ji's dictation, wrote the great volume in his own hand. No commentator on the formation of the Panth speaks from nearer the event.

Guru Arjan Dev Ji is presented in the tradition as the Guru in whom the work of the previous four reaches its fullness — the river fed by every preceding stream. His Guruship is the maturity of the Panth: it now has its city, and it will now have its scripture and, soon after, its sword.

The making of the canon

The compilation of the ਆਦਿ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ in 1604 was an act of immense theological and historical consequence. Guru Arjan Dev Ji gathered the compositions of the preceding Gurus, added his own, and — in a gesture of breathtaking inclusiveness — set alongside them the hymns of the ਭਗਤ (the Bhakti and Sufi saints) such as ਕਬੀਰ, ਫ਼ਰੀਦ, ਨਾਮਦੇਵ, and ਰਵਿਦਾਸ, regardless of their caste or creed. The Word of a low-caste ਚਮਾਰ and a Muslim Sufi was placed in the same volume as the Word of the Gurus, because for Sikhi the test is truth, not birth.

This act of compilation did several things at once for the Panth. It fixed an authoritative text against the corruptions and forgeries that rivals were already circulating. It gave the community a single, shared scripture — a centre that would, after the tenth Guru, become the eternal Guru itself, ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ. And it enshrined in the very structure of the scripture the egalitarian theology that the earlier Vaars had described, by admitting the ਭਗਤ as equals before the Word.

The seat of the Word: Harmandir Sahib

Guru Arjan Dev Ji completed the work of Guru Ram Das Ji at Amritsar by building the ਹਰਿਮੰਦਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ in the midst of the sacred ਸਰੋਵਰ, and there, in 1604, he installed the newly compiled ਆਦਿ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ. The symbolism of the building completes the symbolism of the city. The ਹਰਿਮੰਦਰ was built low, descending to its threshold rather than rising above the worshipper, and opened on four sides — a sign that it was open to all four castes and all four directions, to the whole of humanity. The scripture of equality was housed in an architecture of equality, at the centre of a city of honest trades. Every thread of the Panth's formation is here drawn together.

The price of the Word: the first martyrdom

Vaar 5's Guru Arjan Dev Ji is also the first ਸ਼ਹੀਦ (martyr) of the Sikh tradition. The rise of a self-confident community with its own scripture, city, and authority drew the suspicion of the Mughal state, and in 1606 Guru Arjan Dev Ji was tortured and gave his life rather than alter a word of the truth. His martyrdom is the hinge of Sikh history. It demonstrated that the Panth would hold to its scripture and its principles to the death — and it made unavoidable the next development, the taking up of temporal power for the defence of the community. The ਆਦਿ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ and the martyrdom together are the two faces of Vaar 5: the Word, and the willingness to die for it.

Scripture as the spine of the Panth

The deepest meaning of Vaar 5 for our theme is that with the ਆਦਿ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ the Panth received a centre of authority that no death could destroy. A community gathered around a living Guru is vulnerable to the loss of that Guru; a community gathered around an authoritative scripture endures. In compiling the Granth, Guru Arjan Dev Ji prepared the Panth for the day when the Guruship would pass from human form to the eternal Word. The institution-building of the earlier Vaars — script, congregation, city — finds its spine here, in the gathered ਸ਼ਬਦ. In our final Vaar, the Panth that holds this Word will take up the sword to defend it.

lessons.title: Vaar 6: Guru Hargobind Sahib and Miri-Piri
lessons.html:
The sword answers the Word

Vaar 6 brings us to the sixth Guru, Guru Hargobind Sahib (1595–1644), and to the doctrine that completes the Panth's formation: ਮੀਰੀ ਪੀਰੀ, the union of temporal and spiritual sovereignty. The martyrdom of his father, Guru Arjan Dev Ji, stands behind this whole Vaar. A community whose Guru could be tortured to death by the state could no longer be defended by piety alone. Guru Hargobind Sahib answered the murder of the Word with the taking up of the sword — not to abandon the spiritual path, but to give it the power to survive.

This is the meaning of the two swords the Guru is said to have girded on at his accession: ਮੀਰੀ, the sword of temporal authority, and ਪੀਰੀ, the sword of spiritual authority. He wore both at once, declaring in a single gesture that the Sikh path embraces the whole of life — the inner kingdom of the soul and the outer kingdom of justice. The ਗੁਰਮੁਖਿ of the earlier Vaars, humble as the earth and patient as the tree, is now also the ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ — saint and soldier in one.

The seat of temporal authority: the Akal Takht

Opposite the ਹਰਿਮੰਦਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ, the seat of the Word, Guru Hargobind Sahib raised the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ — the "throne of the Timeless." Here the architecture of the Panth reaches its final form. The ਹਰਿਮੰਦਰ, low in the pool, is the seat of ਪੀਰੀ, of devotion and the Word; the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ, raised high before it, is the seat of ਮੀਰੀ, of justice and the community's worldly decisions. From the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ the Guru received petitions, dispensed justice, and built the community's capacity to govern and defend itself. The two buildings facing each other across the ਸਰੋਵਰ are ਮੀਰੀ ਪੀਰੀ written in stone.

What miri-piri does not mean

It is important to read ਮੀਰੀ ਪੀਰੀ correctly. It is not the worldly ambition that the Vaars everywhere condemn in the ਮਨਮੁਖਿ. The Guru did not take up the sword for conquest or wealth, and the tradition is careful to record that the wars of Guru Hargobind Sahib were defensive. ਮੀਰੀ is power held in service of ਪੀਰੀ — temporal authority placed entirely at the disposal of righteousness, exercised to protect the weak and to keep the community free to remember the Name. The sword is taken up precisely so that the ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ of Vaar 3 and the ਆਦਿ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ of Vaar 5 cannot be destroyed by tyranny. Power, in this doctrine, is the servant of devotion, never its master.

The world-affirming arc completed

Seen against the whole sweep of Vaars 1 through 6, ਮੀਰੀ ਪੀਰੀ is not a sudden departure but the natural completion of a vision present from the start. Guru Nanak Sahib had already refused the world-renouncing path of the ਸਿੱਧ, insisting that liberation is found within the world of work and family. Guru Angad Dev Ji tended the body in the wrestling arena; Guru Amar Das Ji reformed the social order; Guru Ram Das Ji built a city of honest trades; Guru Arjan Dev Ji gave the Word and then his life for it. ਮੀਰੀ ਪੀਰੀ is the logical end of this world-engaging path: a spirituality that takes full responsibility for the world must, in the face of tyranny, also take up the means to defend justice. The ਪੰਥ that began as the answer to a suffering world's cry now stands fully equipped to act in that world.

The Panth complete in form

With Vaar 6 the formation of the Panth as Bhai Gurdas Ji narrates it is complete. Trace the arc one last time: a divine mission and continuous Guruship (Vaar 1); a script and a system of learning (Vaar 2); a congregation and a common table (Vaar 3); a sacred city and the rites of life (Vaar 4); a scripture and the first martyrdom (Vaar 5); and now sovereignty, the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ, and the ideal of the ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ (Vaar 6). The community that began as a cry from the earth now possesses everything a people needs to endure in history: identity, institutions, a homeland, a canon, and the power to defend them. In our concluding lesson we step back to weigh the Vaars as a whole, both as theology and as history.

lessons.title: Conclusion: The Vaars as Theology and as History
lessons.html:
One argument across six Vaars

Having read Vaars 1 through 6, we can now see that they are not six separate poems but a single sustained argument about the formation of the ਪੰਥ. The argument begins with God and ends with a sovereign community, and every step is presented as the unfolding of a single divine mercy. Bhai Gurdas Ji's design is theological at its root: the Panth is what happens when the compassion of ਨਿਰੰਕਾਰ, stirred by a suffering world, takes shape in time through a line of Gurus.

This is why the institutional achievements of the Gurus — script, congregation, city, scripture, sovereignty — are never, for Bhai Gurdas Ji, merely practical. Each is a sacrament of the original mercy. The ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ script is mercy made legible; the ਪੰਗਤ is mercy made edible; ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤਸਰ is mercy made a home; the ਆਦਿ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ is mercy made permanent; ਮੀਰੀ ਪੀਰੀ is mercy made able to defend itself. To study the formation of the Panth through these Vaars is to watch a single act of divine love articulate itself into a living people.

The Vaars as a historical source

Modern scholarship treats Bhai Gurdas Ji's Vaars as a primary source of the first importance for early Sikh history — but a source that must be read for what it is. Historians such as J. S. Grewal and W. H. McLeod have shown that the Vaars are our earliest connected Sikh account of the ਉਦਾਸੀਆਂ of Guru Nanak Sahib and of the succession of the Gurus, written within living memory of the events. Bhai Gurdas Ji knew several of the Gurus personally; his testimony is close to the source.

At the same time, the Vaars are devotional literature, not chronicle. Their purpose is to evoke and confirm faith, not to record dates and disputes with the neutrality of a modern historian. Bhai Gurdas Ji writes as a believer celebrating the work of God, and he selects, shapes, and heightens his material to that end. The careful student therefore reads the Vaars alongside other sources — the ਜਨਮਸਾਖੀ literature, the Granth itself, later chronicles, and the work of modern scholars — using each to test and illuminate the others. The Vaars tell us, with unmatched immediacy, how the early Panth understood its own formation; that understanding is itself a historical fact of the first order.

Why these Vaars remain the key

Guru Arjan Dev Ji's traditional honorific, the ਕੁੰਜੀ, holds true to the end. Having read Vaars 1 through 6, a student approaches Sri Guru Granth Sahib with the conceptual world of Gurmat already in hand: the relation of ਨਿਰਗੁਣ and ਸਰਗੁਣ, the meaning of ਹੁਕਮੁ and ਨਾਮੁ, the contrast of ਗੁਰਮੁਖਿ and ਮਨਮੁਖਿ, the centrality of the ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ, and the doctrine of the one light in successive forms. The Vaars do not replace the Granth; they prepare the reader for it. They are the threshold across which the student steps into the scripture.

From study to practice

Bhai Gurdas Ji would not have wished his Vaars to be studied only as theology or history. They were composed to be sung in ਸੰਗਤ and lived in the body. Their final purpose is the formation not only of the Panth but of the ਗੁਰਮੁਖਿ — the individual Sikh oriented wholly to the Guru. The humility of the earth, the patience of the tree, the fragrance of the sandal, the bee drawn to the ਚਰਨ ਕਮਲ of the Guru: these are not decorations but instructions. The student who has followed the formation of the Panth across six Vaars is invited, at the last, to become a small part of that formation — to take up in their own life the ਸੇਵਾ that made each Guru, the ਸੰਗਤ and ਪੰਗਤ that bound the community, and the integrity of the ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ who holds the inner and outer kingdoms as one.

This is where the course ends and where the practice begins: in the recognition that the ਪੰਥ Bhai Gurdas Ji describes is not a finished monument of the past but a living path that each generation of ਗੁਰਮੁਖ continues to walk.

quiz.q: By long tradition, what honorific did Guru Arjan Dev Ji give to the Vaars of Bhai Gurdas Ji?
options: The crown of the Granth
The key (kunji) to Sri Guru Granth Sahib
The shadow of the Gurus
The first Janamsakhi

quiz.q: In Vaar 1, how does Bhai Gurdas Ji frame the coming of Guru Nanak Sahib?
options: As a chance event in Punjabi history with no larger meaning
As the founding of one more sect among many
As the divine response to the cry of a suffering world
As a reform internal to a single existing tradition

quiz.q: The image of one lamp lighting another (jot milai jot) in Vaar 1 expresses which doctrine?
options: That the Guruship passes only through blood relation
That each Guru taught a different message
That the one eternal Guru-light takes successive human forms while the body changes
That the Guruship ended with Guru Nanak Sahib

quiz.q: Which pair of institutions, consolidated under Guru Amar Das Ji, enacts the equality of all before Akal Purakh?
options: Sangat and Pangat (congregation and the common row of dining)
Miri and Piri
Udasi and Janamsakhi
Manji and Masand taxation

quiz.q: What was the most consequential achievement associated with Guru Arjan Dev Ji in Vaar 5?
options: The standardising of the Gurmukhi script
The compilation of the Adi Granth, including the hymns of the Bhagats
The founding of the sacred pool at Amritsar
The raising of the Akal Takht

quiz.q: How does the course correctly characterise the doctrine of Miri-Piri under Guru Hargobind Sahib?
options: A turn to worldly conquest and the pursuit of wealth
The abandonment of the spiritual path in favour of politics
Temporal power (miri) held entirely in the service of spiritual authority (piri) to defend justice
A rejection of the world-affirming ethic of the earlier Gurus

courses.title: Naam Simran: The Practice of Divine Remembrance
courses.source: Gurbani — Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji
courses.summary: An academically rigorous, devotionally grounded study of ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ (the remembrance of the Divine Name) as taught throughout Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. The course moves from the theology of ਨਾਮ through its disciplines—ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਵੇਲਾ, ਅਜਪਾ ਜਾਪ, and the ਗੁਰਮੰਤ੍ਰ—to the obstacles of ਹਉਮੈ and the ਪੰਜ ਵਿਕਾਰ, the inner experience of ਅਨਹਦ ਸ਼ਬਦ, and the integration of remembrance into daily life. Throughout, students engage directly with Gurbani at its original Ang references.
outcomes: Define ਨਾਮ theologically and distinguish mechanical recitation from absorbed ਸਿਮਰਨ.
Explain the Gurmat teaching on ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਵੇਲਾ and the disciplines of ਨਾਮ ਜਪਣਾ.
Analyse the role of the ਗੁਰੂ and ਸ਼ਬਦ in transmitting ਨਾਮ.
Identify the obstacles of ਹਉਮੈ and the ਪੰਜ ਵਿਕਾਰ and how Gurbani dissolves them.
Describe the nature of ਮਨ and the experience of ਅਨਹਦ ਸ਼ਬਦ.
Integrate ਨਾਮ into ਕਿਰਤ ਕਰਨੀ and cultivate a lifelong practice oriented toward ਨਦਰਿ.

terms.m: Remembrance; the continuous, loving recollection of the Divine within the mind and heart.
The Divine Name; the living, creative essence and presence of God that pervades all creation.
The mind; the inner faculty of thought and desire that must be stilled and turned toward the Divine.
Egotism; the self-centred 'I-am-ness' that separates the soul from God.
The ambrosial hour before dawn, the time most fit for remembrance and meditation.
The unrepeated repetition; remembrance that continues effortlessly without conscious utterance.
The word given by the Guru; the sacred formula ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ through which the Sikh remembers.
The unstruck sound; the inner celestial melody heard in the deepest states of remembrance.
The Word; the divine vibration and teaching of the Guru that conveys ਨਾਮ.
The Guru; the enlightener who reveals the Divine Name and dispels darkness.
The five thieves—ਕਾਮ (lust), ਕ੍ਰੋਧ (anger), ਲੋਭ (greed), ਮੋਹ (attachment), ਅਹੰਕਾਰ (pride).
The Glance of Grace; the Divine look of mercy by which remembrance bears fruit.
Honest labour; earning one's living through righteous work while remembering God.
The holy congregation; the company of the devout where ਨਾਮ is sung and absorbed.
The state of effortless equipoise and inner peace attained through remembrance.
Loving awareness or consciousness directed toward the Divine in meditation.

  4. Methods of ਸਿਮਰਨ
  5. The Role of the ਗੁਰੂ
  6. Obstacles: ਹਉਮੈ and the ਪੰਜ ਵਿਕਾਰ
  7. ਸਿਮਰਨ and the ਮਨ
  8. ਅਨਹਦ ਸ਼ਬਦ: The Unstruck Sound
  9. ਸਿਮਰਨ in Daily Life
  10. Building a Lifelong Practice (ਨਦਰਿ)

Orientation

This course is an inquiry into the central spiritual discipline of the Sikh path: ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ, the loving remembrance of the Divine Name. Before we can practise it, we must understand what is meant by ਨਾਮ and what is meant by ਸਿਮਰਨ. Neither term translates cleanly into a single English word, and the imprecision of translation is itself a lesson: the realities pointed to here are experiential, not merely conceptual.

The Meaning of ਨਾਮ

In Gurbani, ਨਾਮ is far more than a label or a sound. It is the living essence and creative presence of the Divine, the vibration by which all things are sustained. Guru Arjan Dev Ji declares that the entire cosmos rests upon the Name:

ਨਾਮ ਕੇ ਧਾਰੇ ਸਗਲੇ ਜੰਤ ॥ ਨਾਮ ਕੇ ਧਾਰੇ ਖੰਡ ਬ੍ਰਹਮੰਡ ॥

By the Name all beings are sustained; by the Name the continents and universes are upheld.

Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, Ang 284

To remember ਨਾਮ is therefore not to recall an abstraction but to attune the self to the foundational reality of existence. The Name is not arbitrary; it is the way the unmanifest ਨਿਰਗੁਣ becomes available to the human heart.

Recitation versus Absorption

A crucial distinction governs this entire course: the difference between mechanical recitation and inward absorption. One may move the tongue, count beads, or repeat words a thousand times and remain spiritually unchanged. Gurbani is blunt about this. The opening of Japji Sahib dismisses every outward technique that does not touch the inner self:

ਸੋਚੈ ਸੋਚਿ ਨ ਹੋਵਈ ਜੇ ਸੋਚੀ ਲਖ ਵਾਰ ॥

By thinking and contriving, He cannot be conceived, even by thinking hundreds of thousands of times.

Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, Ang 1

Outward purifications, fasts, and clever reasoning all fail; what remains is the alignment of the will with the Divine Will, the ਹੁਕਮ, through remembrance. Thus ਸਿਮਰਨ is not the quantity of words but the quality of presence. The Punjabi root of ਸਿਮਰਨ conveys 'to hold in mind continuously,' and Gurmat refines this into loving, attentive, surrendered recollection that gradually saturates the ਮਨ.

The Goal of Remembrance

Why remember at all? Because the human condition, in Gurmat diagnosis, is one of forgetfulness. The soul, originally a 'ray of the Divine Light' (ਜੋਤਿ), has fallen into the sleep of ਹਉਮੈ and identification with the perishable. ਸਿਮਰਨ is the medicine that awakens it. Guru Arjan Dev Ji teaches that the very act of meditating on the Name brings the mind to bloom:

ਨਾਮੁ ਜਪਤ ਮਨੁ ਭਈ ਪਰਸੰਨ ॥

Meditating on the Name, the mind becomes blissful.

Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, Ang 265

This single line, drawn from Sukhmani Sahib, names the experiential fruit we will study repeatedly: ਪਰਸੰਨਤਾ, a settled inner gladness that does not depend on circumstance.

How This Course Proceeds

We begin with theology (Lesson 2), establishing what Gurbani actually commands regarding the Name. We then study the temporal foundation of practice in ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਵੇਲਾ (Lesson 3) and the concrete methods of remembrance (Lesson 4). Because no one walks this path alone, Lesson 5 examines the indispensable role of the ਗੁਰੂ. We then turn to obstacles—ਹਉਮੈ and the ਪੰਜ ਵਿਕਾਰ (Lesson 6)—and to the psychology of the ਮਨ (Lesson 7). The inner journey culminates in the experience of ਅਨਹਦ ਸ਼ਬਦ (Lesson 8). Finally we ground all of this in ordinary life (Lesson 9) and in a sustainable lifelong practice oriented toward grace, ਨਦਰਿ (Lesson 10). Throughout, you are asked to read Gurbani directly, at the Ang references provided, rather than to accept summary alone.

Homework

Spend 15 minutes reading Japji Sahib (Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, Ang 1), slowly, in whatever language is most native to you. After reading, sit in silence for 5 minutes with the words settling in your mind. Journal for 10 minutes about a single phrase that struck you—not what it means intellectually, but what it stirred in your heart.

lessons.title: The Theology of ਨਾਮ
lessons.summary: Gurbani's command to remember: ਨਾਮੁ ਜਪਹੁ, ਨਾਮੁ ਸੁਣਹੁ, and the fruit of remembrance.
lessons.html:
The Name as Command and Gift

Gurmat theology does not present remembrance as an optional devotional ornament. It presents ਨਾਮ as both the supreme command and the supreme gift. The repeated imperatives of Gurbani—ਨਾਮੁ ਜਪਹੁ (meditate on the Name) and ਨਾਮੁ ਸੁਣਹੁ (listen to the Name)—frame the whole spiritual life.

The Name and Purification

Why is the Name commanded? Because, as we saw in Lesson 1, no external act cleanses the inner self. The famous line of Japji Sahib establishes the principle negatively, and the rest of the Bani supplies the positive answer: only the Name purifies. Guru Ram Das Ji teaches that without it the human being remains polluted regardless of outward observance, while the one who remembers is washed clean from within.

Listening and Speaking the Name

Gurbani distinguishes complementary modes. To 'listen,' ਸੁਣਿਆ, is to receive the Name; the four stanzas of Japji Sahib beginning ਸੁਣਿਆ describe how mere listening transforms one into a knower, a sage, a fearless soul. To 'meditate' or 'utter,' ਜਪਿਆ, is to actively give voice and attention. The two are not opposed: the devotee speaks the Name until speaking dissolves into listening to the Name resounding within.

The Fruit: ਮਨ ਭਈ ਪਰਸੰਨ

The most quoted promise of Sukhmani Sahib distils the entire theology of remembrance into a single experiential claim:

ਨਾਮੁ ਜਪਤ ਮਨੁ ਭਈ ਪਰਸੰਨ ॥

Meditating on the Name, the mind becomes blissful.

Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, Ang 265

Notice that the bliss is located in the ਮਨ, the mind itself, not in external reward. The theology here is therapeutic: remembrance heals the very organ of suffering. Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji affirms the same enduring sufficiency of the Name:

ਹਰਿ ਕਾ ਨਾਮੁ ਸਦਾ ਸੁਖਦਾਈ ॥

The Name of the Lord is forever the giver of peace.

Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, Ang 727

This is not a temporary consolation but a 'forever' (ਸਦਾ) condition: the peace of the Name does not expire with circumstance.

The Name as the Whole of Religion

In Gurmat, the Name effectively contains all other virtues. Guru Arjan Dev Ji repeatedly states that charity, pilgrimage, austerity, and ritual are surpassed by remembrance; indeed they are fulfilled within it. This is why ਨਾਮ is called the essence of all ਧਰਮ. The devotee who has the Name lacks nothing; the one without it, however accomplished outwardly, remains spiritually empty. The historical testimony of the ਭਗਤ (the devotees whose hymns are enshrined in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji) reinforces this: Bhagat Kabir Ji, Bhagat Namdev Ji, and others reached the Divine not through caste or ritual but through the Name alone.

The Universality of the Name

Crucially, the theology of ਨਾਮ is universal. It is not the property of one community. Because the Name is the sustaining vibration of all creation, it is available to every being who turns toward it. Guru Nanak Dev Ji's travels and dialogues consistently affirmed that the door of the Name is open to all—householder and renunciate, learned and unlettered. This universality will matter greatly when, in Lesson 9, we study how remembrance integrates with ordinary working life rather than requiring withdrawal from it.

Having established what the Name is and why it is commanded, we now ask when remembrance is best practised—the subject of the next lesson.

Homework

Read one shabad from Sukhmani Sahib (Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, Ang 262–296) where Guru Arjan Dev Ji speaks of ਨਾਮ ਜਪਣਾ. Then spend 20 minutes in remembrance (vocal or silent, as you prefer), using the ਗੁਰਮੰਤ੍ਰ or the phrase that resonated. Notice what emerges: calm, resistance, clarity, drowsiness. Record your observation without judgment.

lessons.title: The Foundation: ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਵੇਲਾ
lessons.summary: The primacy of the ambrosial pre-dawn hour for remembrance.
lessons.html:
The Ambrosial Hour

If ਨਾਮ is the substance of the spiritual life, ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਵੇਲਾ is its appointed season. The term combines ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ (ambrosia, the nectar of immortality) with ਵੇਲਾ (time): the nectar-time, the hours before dawn when the world is still and the mind is least disturbed.

The Command of Japji Sahib

The locus classicus is found early in Japji Sahib, where Guru Nanak Dev Ji instructs the seeker on how true greatness is obtained:

ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਵੇਲਾ ਸਚੁ ਨਾਉ ਵਡਿਆਈ ਵੀਚਾਰੁ ॥

In the ambrosial hour of the early morning, contemplate the True Name and reflect on His greatness.

Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, Ang 2

The verse is directive, not merely descriptive. It tells the disciple when and what: in the ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਵੇਲਾ, dwell upon the ਸਚੁ ਨਾਉ, the True Name. The discipline of rising early is thus woven into the very structure of Sikh practice and is enshrined in the Sikh code of conduct.

Why the Pre-Dawn Hours?

Several reasons converge. First, the external silence of the night supports inner silence; the noise of the day has not yet begun, and the ਮਨ is more easily gathered. Second, the rested mind, fresh from sleep, is less agitated by the ਪੰਜ ਵਿਕਾਰ. Third, the act of choosing remembrance over comfort—leaving a warm bed for the cold dark—is itself a small surrender of ਹਉਮੈ, a daily renunciation that strengthens the will. The early hour is therefore not arbitrary ritual but a psychologically and spiritually optimal condition.

The Discipline of Rising

Gurbani repeatedly honours those who rise to remember and gently warns those who sleep through the nectar-time. Guru Ram Das Ji describes the daily rhythm of the ਗੁਰਸਿਖ, the Guru-oriented soul: rising in the ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਵੇਲਾ, bathing, remembering the Name, and joining the ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤ. This is not asceticism for its own sake but the establishment of a container in which remembrance can deepen over years.

From Discipline to Continuity

It is essential to understand that the ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਵੇਲਾ is a beginning, not a boundary. The morning practice is meant to set a tone that carries through the day. The remembrance kindled in the silent hours is then sustained, in lower intensity, through work and family life (Lesson 9). The morning is the tuning of the instrument; the day is the music. One does not tune once and never play, nor play an untuned instrument. Thus the ambrosial hour and daily life form a single continuous discipline.

Inner Ambrosia

There is a deeper, esoteric reading of ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਵੇਲਾ. For the advanced practitioner, the 'ambrosial time' is also an inner state—the moment when the ਮਨ becomes still enough that the nectar of the Name begins to flow within, independent of the clock. Guru Amar Das Ji and others speak of tasting ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ within. Yet this inner ambrosia is reached precisely by faithfulness to the outer discipline. The literal and the mystical readings reinforce rather than replace one another, which is characteristic of Gurbani's layered teaching.

With the when established, we turn to the how: the concrete methods of ਸਿਮਰਨ.

Homework

Choose one morning this week to wake even 15 minutes earlier than usual and sit in ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਵੇਲਾ, the pre-dawn quiet. Read one passage from Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji and sit in remembrance. Afterward, journal about what the early hour offered compared to your usual practice time.

lessons.title: Methods of ਸਿਮਰਨ
lessons.summary: Vocal and silent remembrance, the breath, and the ਗੁਰਮੰਤ੍ਰ ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ.
lessons.html:
From Words to Wordlessness

Gurmat offers a graduated path of remembrance, moving from audible utterance toward silent, breath-borne, and finally effortless recollection. These are not competing techniques but stages on a single continuum.

Vocal Remembrance: ਨਾਮ ਜਪਣਾ

The most accessible method is to recite the Name aloud or in a low murmur, especially the ਗੁਰਮੰਤ੍ਰ given by the Guru: ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ. Vocal repetition occupies the tongue and ears, drawing scattered attention to a single point. Bhagat Kabir Ji and Bhagat Namdev Ji both testify to the power of simple, repeated utterance of the Name to absorb the heart. The audible practice is the doorway; it should never be despised as elementary, for it carries even the advanced through dry seasons.

Whispered and Mental Remembrance

As steadiness grows, the practice moves inward—from the tongue to the whisper to the silent mental repetition within the ਮਨ. Here the Name is held in awareness without external sound. This requires more concentration and so is cultivated gradually. The aim is that the Name should sound in the mind as naturally as the heartbeat, present beneath all other thoughts.

Remembrance with the Breath

A central Gurmat discipline is to wed the Name to the breath, remembering with each inhalation and exhalation so that no breath is wasted. Guru Arjan Dev Ji praises the one who does not let a single breath pass without the Name:

ਸਾਸਿ ਸਾਸਿ ਸਿਮਰਹੁ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ॥

With each and every breath, remember the Lord of the Universe.

Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, Ang 295

To remember ਸਾਸਿ ਸਾਸਿ, breath by breath, is to weave ਸਿਮਰਨ into the most involuntary rhythm of the body, so that even sleep and labour do not wholly interrupt it.

ਅਜਪਾ ਜਾਪ: The Unrepeated Repetition

The culmination of method is ਅਜਪਾ ਜਾਪ—the 'unrepeated repetition.' Here the seeker no longer consciously utters the Name; the Name repeats itself within, continuously, without effort. The practitioner has become a vessel through which remembrance flows. This is the natural ripening of disciplined practice, not a technique one can force. Guru Nanak Dev Ji and Guru Arjan Dev Ji describe this state as one in which the Name vibrates ceaselessly, the tongue at rest while the heart sings.

The Place of the ਮਾਲਾ

Many practitioners use a ਮਾਲਾ (rosary) to support vocal ਸਿਮਰਨ, giving the hands an anchor while the mind attends to the Name. Gurbani, however, locates the true rosary within: the real counting is the breath, and the real beads are the qualities of the heart. The outer aid is welcomed but never mistaken for the inner reality. As always, Gurmat permits supports while warning against attachment to them.

Quality over Quantity

Across all methods one principle governs: the worth of remembrance lies in attention and love, not in numerical count. A single utterance with full presence outweighs ten thousand distracted ones. This is why the ਗੁਰੂ is indispensable—only the Guru's grace converts mechanical repetition into living remembrance, which is the subject of our next lesson.

Homework

Practise one method of ਸਿਮਰਨ from Lesson 4 (vocal, whispered, breath-borne, or a combination) for five consecutive days, 15–20 minutes each. Note which method feels most natural and where resistance arises. After five days, write briefly about what you're learning about your own ਮਨ.

lessons.title: The Role of the ਗੁਰੂ
lessons.summary: How the ਸ਼ਬਦ transmits ਨਾਮ and the ਗੁਰੂ-disciple relationship.
lessons.html:
No Remembrance Without the Guru

A defining feature of Gurmat is that ਨਾਮ is not self-generated. The mind, clouded by ਹਉਮੈ, cannot by its own power lay hold of the Divine. It requires the ਗੁਰੂ—the enlightener who reveals the Name and plants it within the heart. Guru Nanak Dev Ji states plainly that without the Guru the Name is not obtained.

The ਸ਼ਬਦ as the Living Guru

For Sikhs, the ਗੁਰੂ is fundamentally the ਸ਼ਬਦ, the divine Word now enshrined in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. The Word is not a text to be merely read but a vibration to be absorbed. Guru Ram Das Ji and Guru Amar Das Ji teach that the Name dwells within the ਸ਼ਬਦ and is transmitted through it. When the disciple immerses in Gurbani, the ਸ਼ਬਦ conveys the very ਨਾਮ it speaks of. The relationship to the ਗੁਰੂ is itself a discipline of love (ਪ੍ਰੇਮ), not mere study; the disciple who loves the True Guru enshrines the Name within the heart.

The ਗੁਰੂ Dispels Darkness

The word ਗੁਰੂ is traditionally understood as that which dispels darkness and gives light. The disciple comes in the darkness of forgetfulness; the Guru's ਸ਼ਬਦ kindles the lamp of awareness. Without this light, the seeker's own efforts at remembrance grope blindly. With it, even the simplest practice becomes luminous. This is why Gurbani insists that the Name is a gift of the Guru's grace and not a possession one can seize.

The ਗੁਰਮੰਤ੍ਰ as Transmission

The ਗੁਰਮੰਤ੍ਰ—the word ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ conferred by the Guru—is the concrete vehicle of this transmission. It is not a private invention but a received gift, carrying the authority and grace of the Guru lineage. When the disciple takes ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ and receives the ਗੁਰਮੰਤ੍ਰ, a living link is formed; the remembrance that follows is thus rooted in relationship, not in technique alone.

The ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤ as the Guru's Field

The Guru's grace also flows through the ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤ, the holy congregation. In the company of the devout, the Name is sung, heard, and amplified; the individual's faltering remembrance is carried by the collective. Guru Arjan Dev Ji teaches that the highest of all deeds is to join the ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤ and there to repeat the Name of God. The congregation is, in effect, an extension of the Guru—a field in which ਨਾਮ grows more readily than in isolation.

The Guru as Boat and Bridge

Gurbani offers many images for the necessity of the Guru. The Guru is the boat that carries the soul across the terrifying world-ocean of birth and death; the Guru is the ladder, the bridge, the raft. None of these images is incidental. They all insist that the human being, by unaided effort, cannot cross the gulf that egotism has opened. The disciple who tries to reach the Divine by personal cleverness only deepens the very pride that separates. It is the Guru who carries, and the disciple who is carried. To remember this is itself a humbling that prepares the heart for the Name.

Surrender and Grace

The disciple's part is surrender (ਸਮਰਪਣ): to offer the ਮਨ to the ਗੁਰੂ and let it be reshaped. This surrender is not a single dramatic gesture but a daily, repeated yielding—each time the self-will rises, it is again laid down before the Guru. The Guru's part is grace, freely and constantly given. Where these two meet, ਨਾਮ takes root and begins to grow of its own accord. The disciple learns, over years, that even the desire to remember was itself a gift of the Guru, so that gratitude rather than pride becomes the natural posture of the awakened heart. This dynamic of surrender and grace will return in the final lesson, where we study the progression from human effort to the Divine Glance of ਨਦਰਿ. But first we must confront what obstructs remembrance.

Homework

Visit a ਗੁਰਦੁਆਰਾ (Sikh gurdwara) if you have access, or listen to recorded ਕੀਰਤਨ for at least 45 minutes. Sit with the intention of listening to the ਸ਼ਬਦ as the Guru's voice. After, reflect on how the collective and the music affected your sense of the ਗੁਰੂ's presence.

lessons.title: Obstacles: ਹਉਮੈ and the ਪੰਜ ਵਿਕਾਰ
lessons.summary: Egotism and the five thieves, and how Gurbani dissolves them through ਨਾਮ.
lessons.html:
The Inner Enemies of Remembrance

If ਨਾਮ is medicine, we must understand the disease. Gurmat names two interlocking maladies that obstruct remembrance: ਹਉਮੈ (egotism) and the ਪੰਜ ਵਿਕਾਰ (the five thieves) that egotism breeds.

ਹਉਮੈ: The Root Affliction

ਹਉਮੈ is the self-centred sense of 'I' and 'mine,' the illusion that one is a separate, self-sufficient agent rather than a ray of the Divine. It is the original wall between the soul and God. Guru Nanak Dev Ji and Guru Amar Das Ji diagnose it as the deepest sickness of the human condition:

ਹਉਮੈ ਦੀਰਘ ਰੋਗੁ ਹੈ ਦਾਰੂ ਭੀ ਇਸੁ ਮਾਹਿ ॥

Egotism is a chronic disease, but within it also lies its own remedy.

Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, Ang 466

The remedy 'within the disease' is the Name received by grace: when the ਮਨ surrenders its self-assertion in remembrance, ਹਉਮੈ dissolves. ਸਿਮਰਨ and ਹਉਮੈ cannot finally occupy the same heart; as the Name grows, the ego shrinks.

The Five Thieves

From ਹਉਮੈ spring the ਪੰਜ ਵਿਕਾਰ: ਕਾਮ (lust), ਕ੍ਰੋਧ (anger), ਲੋਭ (greed), ਮੋਹ (attachment), and ਅਹੰਕਾਰ (pride). They are called thieves because they steal the wealth of the Name from the heart, scattering attention and inflaming desire. Each, left unchecked, makes remembrance nearly impossible, for the agitated ਮਨ cannot hold still upon the Divine.

How Gurbani Addresses Them

Gurmat does not prescribe violent suppression of the vices, which only feeds ਹਉਮੈ. Instead it prescribes substitution and transformation. The five thieves are subdued not by force but by filling the heart with the Name so that they find no room. Guru Arjan Dev Ji teaches that in the company of the holy and through remembrance, lust, anger, and the rest are conquered. The positive virtues—contentment, compassion, humility—grow naturally as their counterweights when ਨਾਮ fills the inner space.

ਮਾਇਆ and Forgetfulness

Underlying both ਹਉਮੈ and the vices is ਮਾਇਆ, the illusory attachment to the transient world that masks the Divine. ਮਾਇਆ induces forgetfulness; forgetfulness empowers the thieves. Remembrance reverses the chain: as the soul recalls its source, the spell of ਮਾਇਆ weakens, the thieves lose their grip, and ਹਉਮੈ is dissolved in surrender.

The Vices as Misdirected Energy

It is important to grasp that Gurmat does not regard the energies behind the vices as evil in themselves. Desire, when turned toward the Divine, becomes longing for union; anger, when turned against injustice, becomes righteous courage; attachment, when directed to the Guru and the holy congregation, becomes love. The thieves are simply these native energies pointed in the wrong direction, toward the perishable self rather than the eternal source. Remembrance does not annihilate the human being's vitality; it reorients it. This is why the awakened devotee is not a lifeless ascetic but a person of great warmth, courage, and love—the same energies, now redeemed and made fruitful.

The Struggle Is Real but Winnable

Gurbani is honest that this is a lifelong battle, not a single victory. The vices return; the ego reasserts itself even in those far advanced on the path, and Gurbani warns against the subtle pride that can creep into the heart of one who imagines the battle finished. Yet the teaching is unwaveringly hopeful: the disease carries its own cure, and grace is always available to the one who keeps turning back to the Name. There is no failure except the failure to begin again. The next lesson examines the battlefield itself—the nature of the ਮਨ—and how it may be won.

Homework

Spend 20 minutes sitting with the teaching on ਹਉਮੈ and the ਪੰਜ ਵਿਕਾਰ. Honestly examine one instance this week where you felt ego-assertion or the pull of one of the five thieves. Rather than judge yourself, reflect on what Gurbani teaches: where would remembrance have shifted your response? Write 150–200 words on this moment and what it taught you.

lessons.title: ਸਿਮਰਨ and the ਮਨ
lessons.summary: The nature of the mind in Gurbani; mastering the ਮਨ rather than being ruled by it.
lessons.html:
The Nature of the ਮਨ

The whole drama of ਸਿਮਰਨ unfolds within the ਮਨ, the mind. Gurbani treats the ਮਨ with remarkable psychological subtlety: it is at once the seat of bondage and the very thing to be liberated, the wild horse and the field of harvest.

The Restless Mind

By nature the unrefined ਮਨ is restless, fickle, and driven by the senses. It chases pleasure, recoils from pain, and rarely rests. Guru Nanak Dev Ji and Bhagat Kabir Ji compare it to a runaway elephant, a fish out of water, a bird flitting from branch to branch. This restlessness is the immediate obstacle to remembrance: a mind that will not settle cannot hold the Name.

The Mind as Divine in Origin

Yet Gurbani makes a startling claim: the ਮਨ is not essentially evil. In its origin it is of divine substance. Guru Amar Das Ji addresses the mind directly as a spark of the Divine Light:

ਮਨ ਤੂੰ ਜੋਤਿ ਸਰੂਪੁ ਹੈ ਆਪਣਾ ਮੂਲੁ ਪਛਾਣੁ ॥

O my mind, you are the embodiment of the Divine Light—recognise your own origin.

Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, Ang 441

This verse reframes the entire task. The goal is not to destroy the ਮਨ but to awaken it to its true nature. The mind that has forgotten its source behaves like a thief; the mind that remembers becomes a saint. ਸਿਮਰਨ is precisely this act of reminding the mind who it is.

Mastery, Not Suppression

Gurmat psychology rejects both indulgence and brutal suppression. The mind cannot be beaten into stillness; force only strengthens ਹਉਮੈ. Instead the ਮਨ is won through love—given a higher object of desire, the Name, that gradually displaces lower cravings. Guru Nanak Dev Ji's famous teaching that one who conquers the mind conquers the world (ਮਨਿ ਜੀਤੈ ਜਗੁ ਜੀਤੁ) locates the entire spiritual conquest within. To master the ਮਨ is to master everything.

The Mind Turned Toward the Guru: ਗੁਰਮੁਖ

Gurbani contrasts the ਮਨਮੁਖ (the self-willed, mind-following person) with the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ (the Guru-oriented person). The ਮਨਮੁਖ is ruled by the restless mind and its desires; the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ has turned the mind to face the Guru, so that the mind now serves remembrance rather than sabotaging it. This reorientation is the practical fruit of the relationship studied in Lesson 5.

The Mind and the Senses

Gurbani also analyses how the ਮਨ is fed and scattered through the five senses, which run outward toward their objects and drag awareness with them. The eye runs to beauty, the ear to praise and slander, the tongue to taste, and through these gates the mind is perpetually pulled outward and dispersed. Remembrance works in the opposite direction: it gathers the scattered awareness, ਸੁਰਤਿ, and turns it inward and upward toward the source. The practitioner does not destroy the senses but masters them, so that they serve the remembering mind rather than enslave it. This inward gathering of awareness is the practical heart of meditation.

Stilling the Waters

As remembrance deepens, the agitated waters of the ਮਨ grow calm, and in that calm the Divine is reflected as the moon in still water. A turbulent pond reflects nothing clearly; only when it is still does it mirror the sky. So the still mind alone can reflect the Divine. This stillness is ਸਹਜ, the equipoise of one who is no longer tossed by hope and fear, gain and loss, praise and blame. From this stillness, in the next lesson, arises the most subtle fruit of remembrance: the hearing of the ਅਨਹਦ ਸ਼ਬਦ, the unstruck sound.

lessons.title: ਅਨਹਦ ਸ਼ਬਦ: The Unstruck Sound
lessons.summary: The inner celestial melody described by Bhagat Kabir Ji and Guru Nanak Dev Ji.
lessons.html:
The Sound That No Hand Strikes

At the deepest reaches of remembrance, Gurbani describes an inner experience: the ਅਨਹਦ ਸ਼ਬਦ, literally the 'unstruck sound.' Ordinary sound is produced by striking—a string, a drum, vocal cords. The ਅਨਹਦ ਸ਼ਬਦ is the celestial vibration that requires no striking, the eternal resonance of the Divine heard within the stilled ਮਨ.

The Joy of ਅਨੰਦ ਸਾਹਿਬ

Guru Amar Das Ji's ਅਨੰਦ ਸਾਹਿਬ opens with the announcement of this inner bliss, which is inseparable from the inner music:

ਅਨੰਦੁ ਭਇਆ ਮੇਰੀ ਮਾਏ ਸਤਿਗੁਰੂ ਮੈ ਪਾਇਆ ॥

I am in bliss, O my mother, for I have found my True Guru.

Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, Ang 917

Later in the same composition Guru Amar Das Ji describes the divine melodies (ਅਨਹਦ ਸਬਦ) resounding in the home of the self, where the mind, having found its Guru, hears the unstruck strains of celestial music. This bliss, ਅਨੰਦ, is not an emotion stirred by external cause but the native condition of the soul reunited with its source.

Bhagat Kabir Ji and the Inner Sky

The ਭਗਤ tradition, especially Bhagat Kabir Ji, speaks vividly of this inner journey. Kabir Ji describes the opening of the 'tenth gate' (ਦਸਮ ਦੁਆਰ), an inner aperture beyond the nine bodily openings, through which the practitioner enters the inner sky and hears the unstruck sound. There, he says, the lotus blooms upside-down and nectar rains; the metaphors point to a complete inversion of ordinary consciousness, in which the soul drinks the ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ of the Name.

Guru Nanak Dev Ji and Listening

In Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak Dev Ji devotes four stanzas to ਸੁਣਿਆ—listening. To truly 'listen' is ultimately to hear the ਅਨਹਦ ਸ਼ਬਦ, the Name resounding through all creation and within the heart. The progression from vocal ਸਿਮਰਨ to silent remembrance to ਅਜਪਾ ਜਾਪ (Lesson 4) finds its consummation here, where the practitioner no longer makes the sound but receives it.

A Fruit, Not a Goal

It is vital to read these descriptions correctly. The ਅਨਹਦ ਸ਼ਬਦ is not a trophy to be hunted; the seeker who chases inner experiences feeds ਹਉਮੈ and obstructs the very state desired. Gurbani presents these experiences as natural by-products of faithful remembrance and grace, never as the aim itself. The aim remains union with the Divine and the dissolution of ego; the inner music is the sign, not the substance, of that union.

The Music That Is Already Sounding

One further point preserves us from a common misunderstanding. Gurbani does not teach that the ਅਨਹਦ ਸ਼ਬਦ is created by the practitioner's meditation, as though the seeker manufactures an inner sound. Rather, the celestial music is already and eternally sounding throughout creation and within the heart; the practice of remembrance simply quiets the noise of the restless mind enough that this ever-present melody can at last be heard. The sun does not begin to shine when the clouds part; it was always shining, and the clouds merely hid it. So the unstruck sound is the perpetual song of the Divine, hidden only by the agitation of the ਮਨ. Remembrance removes the veil; it does not produce the light behind it.

Returning to Earth

The one who hears the unstruck sound is not thereby removed from the world. Indeed, the highest stage in Gurmat is not perpetual trance but the ability to carry this inner stillness into active life—to hear the divine melody while working, serving, and living among others. The mystic who withdraws permanently into inner absorption has, in Gurmat's estimation, not reached the summit; the summit is the integration of the inner and the outer in a single undivided life. This integration is the subject of our next lesson.

lessons.title: ਸਿਮਰਨ in Daily Life
