lessons.title: The Royal Commission: Faridkot and the Birth of a Teeka
lessons.summary: How a princely state became the patron of the first complete commentary on the Guru Granth Sahib.
lessons.html:
ਵਿਸ਼ਾ ਸੂਚੀ (Table of Contents)

  1. The Royal Commission: Faridkot and the Birth of a Teeka
  2. The Scholars: ਗਿਆਨੀ ਬਦਨ ਸਿੰਘ and the Editorial Committee
  3. The ਨਿਰਮਲਾ Tradition of Learning
  4. The Nine-Volume Architecture of the Printed Teeka
  5. Method: ਪਦ ਅਰਥ, ਅਨ੍ਵੈ and ਭਾਵਾਰਥ
  6. The Language of the Commentary: ਬ੍ਰਜ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ
  7. Doctrine and the ਵੇਦਾਂਤ Lens
  8. The ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ Critique and the Reform Controversy
  9. Comparing the Teekas: ਗਰਬ ਗੰਜਨੀ, ਸ਼ਬਦਾਰਥ and ਦਰਪਣ
  10. The Seven-Language Digital Editions on the Sikh Archive
  11. Reading the Teeka Today: A Practical Method

A Kingdom and a Book

In the closing decades of the nineteenth century, the small princely state of ਫਰੀਦਕੋਟ in the Malwa region of Punjab undertook a project of extraordinary ambition: to produce the first complete, written ਟੀਕਾ — a running commentary — on the whole of the ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ. Earlier commentators had glossed individual ਬਾਣੀਆਂ such as ਜਪੁਜੀ ਸਾਹਿਬ or selected ਸ਼ਬਦ, but no scholar or institution had yet attempted a sustained, ਅੰਗ-by-ਅੰਗ exposition of the entire scripture. The work that emerged from Faridkot — known popularly as the ਫਰੀਦਕੋਟ ਵਾਲਾ ਟੀਕਾ — became, for a generation of readers, the standard reference commentary of the Sikh tradition.

The Patron: ਰਾਜਾ ਬਿਕ੍ਰਮ ਸਿੰਘ

The driving force behind the project was ਰਾਜਾ ਬਿਕ੍ਰਮ ਸਿੰਘ, who ruled Faridkot in the second half of the nineteenth century. Like several of the Sikh princely houses of the Malwa, Faridkot combined loyalty to the colonial paramount power with active patronage of Sikh and Hindu religious scholarship. The Raja was himself a man of letters who maintained a court of ਗਿਆਨੀ scholars, ਨਿਰਮਲਾ ascetics and ਪੰਡਿਤ pandits. Patronage of religious learning was, for a princely ruler, both an act of piety and an assertion of legitimacy: a king who could underwrite the definitive commentary on the Guru's word placed his throne under the canopy of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ. The expense of assembling scholars, lodging them for years, providing manuscripts, and finally underwriting printing was considerable, and only a state treasury could sustain it.

Why a Complete Commentary Was Needed

By the 1880s the conditions that made such a project both possible and urgent had ripened. Lithographic and movable-type printing had reached Punjab, making it feasible to circulate a long prose work cheaply and uniformly. At the same time, Christian missionary critiques, the rise of the ਆਰੀਆ ਸਮਾਜ, and internal debates about the meaning of Sikh scripture created a demand for an authoritative, accessible exposition. A ਟੀਕਾ answered a deeply practical need: the language of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ draws on Sant Bhasha, Sahaskriti, Persian, regional dialects and technical philosophical vocabulary, and an ordinary reader required help to cross those linguistic thresholds. As Gurbani in ਜਪੁਜੀ ਸਾਹਿਬ teaches, the seeker is told ਸੁਣਿਐ and ਮੰਨੈ — to listen and to internalize — but listening fruitfully presupposes understanding, and understanding, for many, required a commentary.

Faridkot as a Centre of Learning

Faridkot was not an arbitrary location. The Malwa princely states had become refuges for the ਨਿਰਮਲਾ and ਉਦਾਸੀ scholarly orders after the turbulence of the eighteenth century. These orders carried a tradition of Sanskrit grammar, ਵੇਦਾਂਤ philosophy and the Indic sciences of exegesis. The court at Faridkot drew on this reservoir of expertise. The decision to base the project there reflected the convergence of three resources rarely found together: royal money, a community of trained scholars, and access to authoritative ਬੀੜਾਂ — manuscript copies of the Guru Granth Sahib — against which readings could be checked.

The Shape of the Project

The commission was conceived not as the work of a single author but as a collaborative, committee-reviewed enterprise. A lead scholar would draft the commentary, but his work was to be examined and corrected by a panel of learned men before it was sanctioned. This editorial structure — closer to the production of a modern scholarly edition than to the solitary labours of a single ਗਿਆਨੀ — is one of the most distinctive features of the Faridkot project, and it lends the Teeka a quasi-official character. When later readers speak of the Teeka as the 'official' or 'royal' commentary, they are pointing to precisely this process of collective sanction under princely authority. The remaining lessons of this course examine the scholars who carried out that labour, the method they devised, the doctrinal world they inhabited, and the long afterlife of their book.

lessons.title: The Scholars: ਗਿਆਨੀ ਬਦਨ ਸਿੰਘ and the Editorial Committee
lessons.summary: The team of scholars who drafted, reviewed and sanctioned the commentary.
lessons.html:
The Lead Author

The principal author of the ਫਰੀਦਕੋਟ ਵਾਲਾ ਟੀਕਾ is generally identified as ਗਿਆਨੀ ਬਦਨ ਸਿੰਘ of the Sekhwan tradition of Gurmat learning. A ਗਿਆਨੀ in this period was not merely a reader of scripture but a trained exegete who had passed through the ਸੰਪ੍ਰਦਾਇ — the chain of teacher-to-pupil transmission — in which the meanings of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ were handed down orally alongside the techniques of Sanskrit grammar and ਵੇਦਾਂਤ. ਗਿਆਨੀ ਬਦਨ ਸਿੰਘ brought to the work both this inherited oral exegesis and the literary competence to render it in sustained written prose. His task was monumental: to gloss every ਸ਼ਬਦ, ਸਲੋਕ and ਪਉੜੀ of a scripture running to many hundreds of ਅੰਗ.

The Earlier Groundwork

The Faridkot Teeka did not arise from nothing. It built upon an existing body of ਨਿਰਮਲਾ exegesis, much of it associated with ਪੰਡਿਤ ਤਾਰਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਨਰੋਤਮ, one of the most learned Sikh scholars of the nineteenth century. ਤਾਰਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਨਰੋਤਮ had produced earlier commentarial and reference works, and the intellectual framework he represented — a confident synthesis of Gurbani with classical Indic learning — supplied the scaffolding on which the Faridkot scholars built. Understanding the Teeka therefore requires seeing it as the culmination of a school rather than the invention of a single mind.

The Committee and Its Function

What distinguished the Faridkot project from a private ਟੀਕਾ was its editorial committee. ਰਾਜਾ ਬਿਕ੍ਰਮ ਸਿੰਘ convened a panel of scholars whose responsibility was to examine the draft commentary, to test its readings against authoritative ਬੀੜਾਂ, and to debate contested interpretations before sanctioning them. This process served two ends. First, it improved accuracy: a single commentator might miss a sense or err in grammar, but a committee could catch and correct. Second, it conferred authority: a reading sanctioned by an assembly of learned men under royal auspices carried more weight than one offered by an individual. In this sense the Teeka aspired to a collective, almost conciliar, voice.

The Discipline of Cross-Checking

The scholars worked at a moment when the textual stabilization of the Guru Granth Sahib was itself a live concern. As Gurinder Singh Mann has shown in The Making of Sikh Scripture, the textual history of the Granth involved real variation among early manuscripts. The Faridkot committee, working with the ਬੀੜਾਂ available to them, had to make choices about readings, and their commentary embeds those choices. For the modern student this is doubly valuable: the Teeka is both an interpretation of meaning and a witness to how a particular nineteenth-century scholarly community read its text.

The Labour of Years

A complete commentary on the Guru Granth Sahib is the work of years, not months. The scholars proceeded composition by composition, beginning with the foundational ਬਾਣੀਆਂ and moving through the ਰਾਗ sections. Each verse demanded that the commentator supply the meanings of difficult words, untangle the syntax, and then state the intended sense. Where ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ alludes to Indic mythology, to ਪੁਰਾਣਕ narratives or to Sufi imagery, the commentator was expected to explain the allusion. Where a verse admitted of more than one reading, the committee weighed the alternatives. The cumulative result was a reference work of immense density.

The Question of Authorship

Scholars have debated how much of the finished Teeka should be credited to ਗਿਆਨੀ ਬਦਨ ਸਿੰਘ alone and how much to the committee and to the earlier ਨਿਰਮਲਾ tradition. The honest answer is that the work is genuinely composite. It is best understood as the deposit of a whole ਸੰਪ੍ਰਦਾਇ, fixed in print at a particular moment, under a particular patron, by an identifiable lead scholar and his reviewers. Recognizing this composite character guards the student against two errors: treating the Teeka as the private opinion of one man, and treating it as an anonymous, timeless authority. It is neither. It is the considered, collective, datable reading of a specific school of Sikh learning — and that is precisely what makes it so valuable a historical witness.

lessons.title: The ਨਿਰਮਲਾ Tradition of Learning
lessons.summary: The scholarly order whose Sanskritic and Vedantic training shaped the commentary.
lessons.html:
Who Were the ਨਿਰਮਲਾ?

To read the ਫਰੀਦਕੋਟ ਵਾਲਾ ਟੀਕਾ intelligently one must understand the ਨਿਰਮਲਾ order from which its scholars came. The ਨਿਰਮਲਾ ('the unblemished ones') were a learned Sikh order whose origins tradition traces to the time of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ, who is said to have sent Sikhs to study Sanskrit and the classical Indic sciences at ਕਾਸ਼ੀ (Banaras). Whether or not every detail of that origin narrative is historically secure, by the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries the ਨਿਰਮਲਾ had become the principal carriers of textual and philosophical learning within the Sikh world.

A Curriculum of Sanskrit and ਵੇਦਾਂਤ

The ਨਿਰਮਲਾ curriculum was built on Sanskrit grammar (ਵਿਆਕਰਣ), logic (ਨ੍ਯਾਯ), and above all ਵੇਦਾਂਤ — the non-dualist philosophy of the Upanishads as systematized in the Advaita tradition. A ਨਿਰਮਲਾ scholar read ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ with this classical apparatus in hand. When the Guru's word spoke of the one reality pervading all things, the ਨਿਰਮਲਾ exegete naturally reached for the vocabulary of ਬ੍ਰਹਮ and ਆਤਮਾ, of ਮਾਇਆ and ਅਵਿਦਿਆ, to articulate its meaning. This was not perceived as importing an alien system; it was experienced as using the most refined available philosophical language to honour the depth of the scripture.

The Strengths of the Tradition

The ਨਿਰਮਲਾ approach brought real strengths to exegesis. Its practitioners possessed genuine command of the Sanskrit and Sahaskriti vocabulary that pervades ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ, and of the ਪੁਰਾਣਕ and ਵੇਦਾਂਤਕ allusions the Gurus deployed. They could explain a recondite term, identify a mythological reference, and place a verse within a larger conceptual order. For a scripture as linguistically and intellectually demanding as the Guru Granth Sahib, this learning was indispensable, and much of it remains valid regardless of one's view of the wider Vedantic frame.

The Tension Within

Yet the ਨਿਰਮਲਾ frame also generated tension. Critics — especially the later ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ reformers — argued that reading ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ through ਵੇਦਾਂਤ risked subordinating the distinctive teaching of the Gurus to a pre-existing system. Where ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ proclaims a God who is at once transcendent and personally devotional, the strict Advaitin tends toward an impersonal absolute. Where the Gurus affirm the reality and worth of the created world and of householder life, classical ਵੇਦਾਂਤ can tilt toward viewing the world as ਮਾਇਆ in the sense of illusion. The ਨਿਰਮਲਾ commentators were aware of these tensions and often negotiated them with subtlety, but the gravitational pull of their training is visible throughout the Faridkot Teeka.

Orality and Transmission

The ਨਿਰਮਲਾ also preserved the ਸੰਪ੍ਰਦਾਇ — the living chain of oral interpretation. Meanings were not invented afresh by each commentator; they were received from a teacher and handed on to pupils, tested in the ਕਥਾ (discourse) tradition where a scholar would expound ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ before an audience. The Faridkot Teeka is in large part this oral exegesis committed to writing. Its glosses often preserve interpretations that had circulated for generations in the ਕਥਾ tradition, which is why the work has documentary value even where its philosophical frame is contested.

Why This Matters for the Reader

For the modern student, recognizing the ਨਿਰਮਲਾ character of the Teeka is the single most important interpretive key. It explains the work's vocabulary, its reflexes, its strengths and its blind spots. A reader who knows that the commentary thinks in ਵੇਦਾਂਤਕ categories can benefit fully from its linguistic and allusive learning while reading its doctrinal conclusions critically — neither dismissing the Teeka as 'corrupted' nor accepting its frame uncritically as the plain sense of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ. This balanced posture, which the later lessons develop, is the mark of a mature student of the commentarial tradition.

lessons.title: The Nine-Volume Architecture of the Printed Teeka
lessons.summary: How the commentary was organized, printed and distributed as a multi-volume set.
lessons.html:
From Manuscript to Print

The ਫਰੀਦਕੋਟ ਵਾਲਾ ਟੀਕਾ is most familiar to readers in its printed form, issued as a multi-volume set that in its standard editions runs to roughly nine volumes. The move from the labour of composition to a printed series was itself a significant act. Printing fixed the text, multiplied it, and placed a once-rare scholarly resource within reach of ਗੁਰਦੁਆਰੇ, schools and individual readers across Punjab. The physical bulk of the set — thousands of pages across multiple volumes — testifies to the scope of the undertaking: a complete commentary on the Guru Granth Sahib cannot be small.

The Organizing Principle: ਅੰਗ by ਅੰਗ

The Teeka follows the order of the Guru Granth Sahib itself, proceeding ਅੰਗ by ਅੰਗ — folio by folio — from the ਮੂਲ ਮੰਤਰ and ਜਪੁਜੀ ਸਾਹਿਬ at the beginning, through the ਰਾਗ sections in their canonical sequence, to the closing ਸਲੋਕ and the ਮੁੰਦਾਵਣੀ. Within each ਰਾਗ the commentary follows the Gurus and ਭਗਤ in the order the Granth itself preserves. This strict adherence to the scripture's own architecture is deliberate: the Teeka presents itself not as an independent treatise but as a humble companion that walks beside the text, never departing from its sequence.

The Layout of the Page

On the page, the typical arrangement places the original ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ verse first, followed by the commentary beneath or alongside it. The commentary itself moves through recognizable stages for each unit of text: the difficult words are glossed, the syntax is clarified, and the intended sense is stated. Cross-references to parallel verses and to ਪੁਰਾਣਕ or ਵੇਦਾਂਤਕ sources appear where the commentator judges them illuminating. The reader can thus hold the Guru's word and its explanation in a single field of vision — the defining convenience of the ਟੀਕਾ genre.

Volume Divisions

The division into volumes follows practical considerations of length, breaking the continuous commentary at convenient points in the scripture's progression. The early volumes carry the foundational ਬਾਣੀਆਂ and the opening ਰਾਗ; the middle volumes cover the great body of the ਰਾਗ sections; the final volumes complete the later ਰਾਗ and the concluding compositions. Because the divisions are editorial rather than doctrinal, different printings have sometimes apportioned the material slightly differently, but the nine-volume shape is the form in which the work is most widely known and cited.

Apparatus and Front Matter

Beyond the running commentary, the printed editions typically carry introductory material: prefatory notes on the project's origins, on the patron, and on the principles of interpretation followed. This front matter is itself a valuable historical source, for it tells us how the scholars and their patron wished the work to be understood. It frames the Teeka as an act of ਸੇਵਾ — service to the ਪੰਥ — undertaken so that ordinary devotees might grasp the meaning of the Guru's word.

Circulation and Reception

Once printed, the Teeka circulated widely and quickly became the reference commentary for ਕਥਾਵਾਚਕ (expounders), for ਗਿਆਨੀ in training, and for educated lay readers. For decades it had no rival as a complete commentary, and even after newer ਟੀਕੇ appeared in the twentieth century, the Faridkot work retained its authority among traditionalists and its interest among scholars. Its very ubiquity is part of its historical importance: when we ask how the Guru Granth Sahib was understood by literate Sikhs in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, the Faridkot Teeka is among our most direct and comprehensive witnesses.

The Material Object as Evidence

Finally, the physical set deserves attention as an object. Its size, its typography, its lithographed or typeset pages, and its distribution network all belong to the story of print modernity in colonial Punjab. The Teeka is not only a text to be read for its meanings; it is an artifact of a moment when Sikh scholarship, princely patronage and the printing press converged to produce something genuinely new — a complete, fixed, reproducible commentary on the entire scripture.

lessons.title: Method: ਪਦ ਅਰਥ, ਅਨ੍ਵੈ and ਭਾਵਾਰਥ
lessons.summary: The three-stage exegetical procedure that structures every entry in the commentary.
lessons.html:
A Disciplined Procedure

What gives the ਫਰੀਦਕੋਟ ਵਾਲਾ ਟੀਕਾ its scholarly character is not only its completeness but the disciplined, repeatable procedure by which it treats each verse. The commentary characteristically moves through three stages — ਪਦ ਅਰਥ, ਅਨ੍ਵੈ and ਭਾਵਾਰਥ — a sequence inherited from classical Indic exegesis and adapted to ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ. Understanding this method is the practical key to using the Teeka, because once a reader recognizes the stages, the dense commentary becomes navigable.

ਪਦ ਅਰਥ: The Meaning of Words

The first stage is ਪਦ ਅਰਥ — word-meaning. Here the commentator glosses the individual words of the verse, supplying for each difficult term its meaning. Because ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ draws on Sant Bhasha, Sahaskriti, Persian, Arabic and regional dialects, this glossing is genuinely necessary work. A single line may contain a Persian word, a Sanskrit-derived term and a colloquial Punjabi form, and the reader needs each unlocked. This layer of the Teeka remains its most durable and least controversial contribution: the glosses are the fruit of generations of ਸੰਪ੍ਰਦਾਇ learning, and even readers who reject the commentary's philosophy often consult its ਪਦ ਅਰਥ.

ਅਨ੍ਵੈ: Untangling the Syntax

The second stage is ਅਨ੍ਵੈ — the re-ordering of the verse into prose syntax. ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ is poetry, and its word order is shaped by metre, rhyme and rhetorical effect; the grammatical relations among its words are not always apparent on the surface. In the ਅਨ੍ਵੈ stage the commentator rearranges the words into their logical prose order, making explicit which word governs which, what is subject and what is object, where a clause begins and ends. This is the same operation a Sanskrit commentator performs when he supplies the ਅਨ੍ਵਯ of a verse, and it is indispensable for verses whose syntax is compressed or inverted.

ਭਾਵਾਰਥ: The Intended Sense

The third stage is ਭਾਵਾਰਥ — the inner or intended sense. Having established what the words mean and how they fit together grammatically, the commentator now states what the verse teaches. This is the interpretive heart of the Teeka, and it is also where the commentator's ਨਿਰਮਲਾ and ਵੇਦਾਂਤਕ frame is most visible. The ਭਾਵਾਰਥ may expand a terse verse into a paragraph of explanation, may connect it to a wider doctrine, may resolve an apparent difficulty, or may draw a devotional or ethical lesson. It is here, too, that the reader must be most alert, for the ਭਾਵਾਰਥ carries the commentator's judgments, not merely the text's words.

An Illustrative Pattern

Consider how the method works in principle. The opening of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ teaches, in the words of the ਮੂਲ ਮੰਤਰ, of the One whose name is true — ੴ ਸਤਿ ਨਾਮੁ — 'There is One reality; Truth is its Name.' A Teeka entry on such a phrase would first gloss each term (ਪਦ ਅਰਥ): the numeral and ਓਅੰਕਾਰ, the word ਸਤਿ, the word ਨਾਮੁ. It would then state the grammatical relation among them (ਅਨ੍ਵੈ). Finally, in the ਭਾਵਾਰਥ, it would expound the doctrine of the one non-dual reality, here drawing on its ਵੇਦਾਂਤਕ resources. The student can see in this how the neutral, philological early stages give way to the interpretively-loaded final stage.

The Value of Recognizing the Stages

For the user of the Teeka, separating these layers is an act of critical hygiene. The ਪਦ ਅਰਥ and ਅਨ੍ਵੈ are largely matters of language and grammar, and the commentary's authority there rests on genuine learning. The ਭਾਵਾਰਥ is where interpretation enters, and there the reader should weigh the commentary against other ਟੀਕੇ, against the wider witness of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ, and against the teaching of the ਪੰਥ. A reader who confuses the layers — taking a contestable ਭਾਵਾਰਥ for an established word-meaning — misuses the Teeka. A reader who distinguishes them extracts its lasting value while exercising appropriate judgment over its conclusions.

A Bridge to Later Commentaries

This three-stage method did not die with the Faridkot Teeka. It became the template that later commentators inherited and refined. When ਪ੍ਰੋਫੈਸਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਸਿੰਘ later produced his grammar-based ਦਰਪਣ, he was in part reforming the ਅਨ੍ਵੈ and ਪਦ ਅਰਥ stages with stricter philological rigour. Thus the Faridkot method is not only a tool for reading this particular work but a window onto the whole subsequent history of Gurbani exegesis.

lessons.title: The Language of the Commentary: ਬ੍ਰਜ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ
lessons.summary: Why the Teeka was written in literary Braj and what that choice reveals.
lessons.html:
A Commentary in ਬ੍ਰਜ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ

One of the features that most surprises the first-time reader of the ਫਰੀਦਕੋਟ ਵਾਲਾ ਟੀਕਾ is its language. The commentary is written not in modern colloquial Punjabi but in ਬ੍ਰਜ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ — the literary Braj idiom of north India — written in the ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ script. To understand why, and to read the Teeka fluently, one must appreciate the linguistic world of nineteenth-century Sikh scholarship.

The Prestige of Braj

In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, ਬ੍ਰਜ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ was the prestige literary language of much of north India for devotional and learned composition. Sikh poets and scholars of the period — including those of the Sikh courts and the ਨਿਰਮਲਾ and ਉਦਾਸੀ orders — composed extensively in Braj. Much of the ਦਸਮ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ literature and a great deal of the poetic and commentarial output of the period uses Braj. For a scholar undertaking a learned commentary, Braj was the natural register: it carried prestige, it was supple enough for philosophical prose, and it was widely understood by the educated class for whom such a work was first intended.

Braj and the Vocabulary of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ

There was also an internal logic to the choice. The vocabulary of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ overlaps substantially with the Sant Bhasha and Sahaskriti that feed into literary Braj. A commentary in Braj could mirror and extend the scripture's own idiom, explaining a Braj-inflected verse in a closely related learned Braj prose. The continuity between the language of the text and the language of the commentary made the exposition feel organic rather than translated.

The Cost to Later Readers

What was an asset in 1883 became, for many, an obstacle by the twentieth century. As standardized modern Punjabi rose to become the literary and educational language of Sikhs, the Braj of the Faridkot Teeka grew less accessible. A reader fluent in contemporary Punjabi may stumble over Braj grammatical forms, vocabulary and idioms. This linguistic distance is one reason later twentieth-century commentaries — written in accessible modern Punjabi — gradually displaced the Faridkot Teeka for everyday use, even as it retained its scholarly prestige. The seven-language digital editions discussed later in this course are in part a response to exactly this problem of access.

Script and Sound

It is worth stressing that the Teeka is written in ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ script throughout, even though its language is Braj. This combination — Braj language in Gurmukhi letters — is characteristic of a large body of Sikh literature of the period. The student must therefore learn to read Gurmukhi not only for Punjabi but for Braj, recognizing that the same script encodes a different grammar and lexicon. Forms that look almost-Punjabi but behave differently are the signature of this register, and attentiveness to them prevents misreading.

A Window onto a Plural Linguistic Past

For the historian, the Braj of the Teeka is not a defect but a document. It reminds us that the Sikh literary and scholarly world of the nineteenth century was multilingual and that the boundaries later drawn around 'Punjabi' Sikh identity were not yet fixed. The choice of Braj situates the Faridkot scholars within a pan-north-Indian republic of letters, in conversation with Hindu and Sufi learned traditions that shared the same literary medium. To read the Teeka is thus to enter a linguistic landscape broader than the one modern readers inhabit, and that breadth is part of its instruction.

Reading Braj Today

Practically, the modern student approaching the Teeka in Braj should keep a few habits in mind: read aloud, since the sound often clarifies forms the eye finds strange; watch for Braj verbal and case endings that differ from Punjabi; and use the parallel-language digital editions to triangulate meaning when a passage resists. With patience the Braj becomes legible, and the reward is direct access to one of the foundational documents of Sikh exegetical tradition in the very words its authors chose.

lessons.title: Doctrine and the ਵੇਦਾਂਤ Lens
lessons.summary: The theological commitments of the commentary and where they shape interpretation.
lessons.html:
Reading Through ਵੇਦਾਂਤ

The most consequential and most debated feature of the ਫਰੀਦਕੋਟ ਵਾਲਾ ਟੀਕਾ is its doctrinal orientation. Composed by scholars steeped in the ਨਿਰਮਲਾ curriculum, the commentary characteristically reads ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ through the lens of ਵੇਦਾਂਤ — and particularly the non-dualist Advaita tradition. This lesson examines what that means concretely, where it illuminates and where it strains, so that the student can read the Teeka's ਭਾਵਾਰਥ with informed judgment.

The Non-Dual Absolute

At the heart of the Advaitin reading is the conviction that ultimate reality is one, non-dual, and that the apparent multiplicity of the world is, in some sense, a play upon that one reality. When ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ proclaims that the One pervades all — that, as the Gurus teach, the Creator dwells within the creation — the ਵੇਦਾਂਤਕ commentator hears the language of ਬ੍ਰਹਮ, the absolute, and of the identity of the individual self (ਆਤਮਾ) with that absolute. Much of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ's language of immanence lends itself readily to this reading, and here the Teeka often expounds the text with genuine depth.

ਮਾਇਆ and the Status of the World

The strain appears most clearly around the concept of ਮਾਇਆ. In strict Advaita, ਮਾਇਆ tends toward the meaning of cosmic illusion — that which veils the sole reality of ਬ੍ਰਹਮ. ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ certainly warns against attachment to ਮਾਇਆ, but the Gurus also affirm the reality and the moral seriousness of the created world and of householder life. Where the Advaitin frame can devalue the world as illusion, the Gurus' teaching insists that the world is the field of righteous action and devotion. A ਵੇਦਾਂਤਕ ਭਾਵਾਰਥ may therefore tilt a verse toward world-negation in a way that careful readers, then and now, have questioned.

The Personal and the Impersonal

A second tension concerns the nature of the divine. ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ addresses a God who is at once beyond all attributes (ਨਿਰਗੁਣ) and intimately personal, the beloved ਪ੍ਰੀਤਮ to whom the devotee sings in longing love. Classical Advaita inclines toward an impersonal absolute, with personal devotion as a lower, provisional stage. The Faridkot commentary negotiates this, but its frame can subordinate the passionate ਭਗਤੀ of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ to a higher impersonal realization, whereas the Gurus hold the personal and the transcendent together without ranking one beneath the other.

Where the Lens Illuminates

It would be a serious error to dismiss the Teeka's doctrine wholesale. The ਵੇਦਾਂਤਕ learning of its authors equipped them to handle the abstract metaphysical passages of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ with a sophistication few others could match. Their command of the technical vocabulary of consciousness, of the relation between the one and the many, and of the stages of spiritual realization frequently yields illuminating exposition. The point is not that ਵੇਦਾਂਤ is irrelevant to ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ — the Gurus engaged Indic thought deeply — but that it must be one interlocutor among others, not the sole frame.

The Gurus' Own Engagement with Indic Thought

Indeed, ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ itself engages, adopts and transforms the vocabulary of ਵੇਦਾਂਤ, ਯੋਗ and ਭਗਤੀ. The Gurus did not write in a vacuum; they took up the religious vocabulary of their world and bent it to their own teaching. The ਨਿਰਮਲਾ commentators were therefore not simply imposing an alien grid; they were extending a conversation the Gurus had begun. The critical question is always whether a given ਭਾਵਾਰਥ honours the Gurus' transformation of the inherited vocabulary or flattens it back into its source system.

A Posture for the Student

The mature student of the Faridkot Teeka, then, neither accepts its ਵੇਦਾਂਤਕ conclusions as the plain meaning of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ nor rejects the work as 'Brahmanized' and worthless. Both reflexes are lazy. The disciplined posture is to receive the Teeka's enormous philological and allusive learning gratefully, to read its ਭਾਵਾਰਥ as one learned interpretation among several, and to test its doctrine against the full witness of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ and the teaching of the ਪੰਥ. This is exactly the critical stance that the ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ reformers, in their own way, demanded — and to their critique the next lesson turns.

lessons.title: The ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ Critique and the Reform Controversy
lessons.summary: How the reform movement challenged the Teeka's Vedantic frame and what was at stake.
lessons.html:
A Changing Climate

Within a generation of the Faridkot Teeka's appearance, the religious climate of Punjab shifted decisively. The ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ movement, born in the 1870s and gathering force into the early twentieth century, set out to define a distinct Sikh identity, purified of what its leaders regarded as accreted Hindu and Brahmanical influence. This reforming impulse inevitably turned a critical eye on the ਨਿਰਮਲਾ exegesis that the Faridkot Teeka embodied.

The Heart of the Critique

The ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ critique of the Teeka tradition can be stated simply: by reading ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ through ਵੇਦਾਂਤ, the ਨਿਰਮਲਾ commentators had, in the reformers' view, subordinated the Gurus' distinctive revelation to a pre-existing Brahmanical philosophy. Where the Faridkot ਭਾਵਾਰਥ explained a verse in terms of ਬ੍ਰਹਮ and ਮਾਇਆ as illusion, the reformers heard the muffling of the Gurus' own voice. The slogan that captured the era — that the Sikhs were neither Hindu nor Muslim but followers of a distinct path — implied that Sikh scripture demanded interpretation on its own terms.

Harjot Oberoi and the Historical Picture

The historian Harjot Oberoi, in The Construction of Religious Boundaries, has shown how the ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ reformers worked to replace a fluid, plural 'Sanatan' Sikh world — in which ਨਿਰਮਲਾ and ਉਦਾਸੀ scholars, Hindu practices and Sikh devotion coexisted — with a sharply bounded Sikh identity. The Faridkot Teeka belongs squarely to that older, plural world. Reading the controversy through Oberoi's lens, we see that the dispute over the Teeka was never merely about the meaning of particular verses; it was about the very boundaries of Sikh tradition.

The Reformist Alternative

The reformers did not merely criticize; they produced alternatives. The drive for commentaries written in accessible modern Punjabi, grounded in Gurbani's own internal logic rather than in imported ਵੇਦਾਂਤ, gathered momentum. This impulse would culminate in the twentieth century in works like the ਸ਼ਬਦਾਰਥ produced under reformist auspices and, supremely, in the grammar-based ਦਰਪਣ of ਪ੍ਰੋਫੈਸਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਸਿੰਘ, who sought to anchor interpretation in the rigorous grammar of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ rather than in any external philosophy. These works defined themselves in part against the ਨਿਰਮਲਾ tradition the Faridkot Teeka represented.

What the Critique Got Right

The reform critique identified something real. The Faridkot ਭਾਵਾਰਥ does at times read ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ in ways that flatten its distinctive teaching into ਵੇਦਾਂਤਕ commonplace, and the reformers were right to insist that the Gurus' word be heard in its own register. Their demand for accessible language and for interpretation disciplined by the text's own grammar was a genuine advance, and Sikh exegesis is the richer for it.

What the Critique Risked Missing

Yet the reform critique also carried risks. In its zeal to purify, it could undervalue the genuine learning of the ਨਿਰਮਲਾ scholars and could project a later, sharply-bounded identity backward onto a more plural past. The Faridkot Teeka's command of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ's Sanskritic vocabulary and its ਪੁਰਾਣਕ allusions is a real asset that a too-thorough rejection of the ਨਿਰਮਲਾ tradition would squander. The Gurus themselves engaged Indic thought; a Sikh exegesis that refused all such engagement would impoverish itself.

The Settled Verdict

The settled scholarly verdict today is balanced. The Faridkot Teeka is honoured as a landmark — the first complete commentary, a monument of nineteenth-century Sikh learning, an indispensable historical witness and a treasury of philological glosses. At the same time its ਵੇਦਾਂਤਕ ਭਾਵਾਰਥ is read critically, in the light of the reform tradition's legitimate insistence that ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ be interpreted on its own terms. The student who holds both judgments together — gratitude for the learning, critical distance from the frame — has grasped the place of the Teeka in Sikh intellectual history.

lessons.title: Comparing the Teekas: ਗਰਬ ਗੰਜਨੀ, ਸ਼ਬਦਾਰਥ and ਦਰਪਣ
lessons.summary: Situating the Faridkot Teeka within the wider tradition of Gurbani commentary.
lessons.html:
The Faridkot Teeka in Company

No commentary stands alone, and the ਫਰੀਦਕੋਟ ਵਾਲਾ ਟੀਕਾ is best understood in conversation with the other great ਟੀਕੇ of the tradition. This lesson sets it beside three landmarks — the ਗਰਬ ਗੰਜਨੀ ਟੀਕਾ that preceded it, and the ਸ਼ਬਦਾਰਥ and ਦਰਪਣ that followed — to clarify what is distinctive about each.

The ਗਰਬ ਗੰਜਨੀ ਟੀਕਾ

The ਗਰਬ ਗੰਜਨੀ ਟੀਕਾ, a commentary on ਜਪੁਜੀ ਸਾਹਿਬ associated with the milieu of the nineteenth-century scholar-poet tradition, exemplifies the pre-Faridkot situation: rich commentary existed, but it was partial, focused on individual ਬਾਣੀਆਂ rather than the whole Granth. Its very name — 'the destroyer of pride' — signals its polemical, doctrinally assertive character. Comparing it with the Faridkot Teeka shows the difference between a focused commentary on one composition and a comprehensive commentary on the entire scripture. The Faridkot project's ambition was precisely to do for the whole Granth what works like the ਗਰਬ ਗੰਜਨੀ had done for single ਬਾਣੀਆਂ.

The ਸ਼ਬਦਾਰਥ

The ਸ਼ਬਦਾਰਥ ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ, produced in the twentieth century under the auspices of the ਸ਼੍ਰੋਮਣੀ ਗੁਰਦੁਆਰਾ ਪ੍ਰਬੰਧਕ ਕਮੇਟੀ, represents a different model. Concise, written in accessible Punjabi, and designed for wide devotional use, it offers brief word-meanings and a short paraphrase rather than the expansive ਵੇਦਾਂਤਕ exposition of the Faridkot Teeka. Where the Faridkot work expounds at length and within a philosophical frame, the ਸ਼ਬਦਾਰਥ aims at clarity and economy for the ordinary reader. The contrast reveals two different visions of what a commentary is for: deep scholarly exposition versus accessible devotional aid.

The ਦਰਪਣ of ਪ੍ਰੋਫੈਸਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਸਿੰਘ

The ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਦਰਪਣ of ਪ੍ਰੋਫੈਸਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਸਿੰਘ, completed in the mid-twentieth century, marks the methodological turning point. ਸਾਹਿਬ ਸਿੰਘ grounded his ਟੀਕਾ in a systematic grammar of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ that he himself worked out, insisting that the meaning of a verse must be controlled by its grammar — by the case endings, verb forms and syntactic relations of the actual words. This was, in effect, a disciplining of the ਅਨ੍ਵੈ and ਪਦ ਅਰਥ stages with new rigour, and a deliberate move away from interpretation driven by external ਵੇਦਾਂਤ. The ਦਰਪਣ thus represents the reformist alternative brought to full scholarly maturity, and it has become the most widely consulted modern commentary.

What the Comparison Teaches

Setting these works side by side yields several lessons. First, the Faridkot Teeka's distinctive contribution is its combination of completeness with deep, learned, ਵੇਦਾਂਤ-informed exposition — it is the great monument of the ਨਿਰਮਲਾ exegetical tradition applied to the whole Granth. Second, the later works each correct or supplement it: the ਸ਼ਬਦਾਰਥ in accessibility, the ਦਰਪਣ in grammatical discipline and doctrinal independence. Third, none of the later works renders the Faridkot Teeka obsolete, because each pursues different aims; the serious student consults them together, triangulating among them.

A Method of Comparative Reading

The practical upshot is a method. To interpret a difficult ਸ਼ਬਦ responsibly, the student reads it in several commentaries at once: the Faridkot Teeka for its rich exposition and allusive learning, the ਦਰਪਣ for its grammatical control, the ਸ਼ਬਦਾਰਥ for its concise clarity, and any focused commentary on that particular ਬਾਣੀ. Where the commentaries agree, confidence rises; where they diverge, the divergence itself is instructive, exposing the interpretive choices and frames at work. This comparative discipline is the antidote to dependence on any single authority.

The Continuing Conversation

The history of Gurbani ਟੀਕਾ is best seen not as a succession in which each work replaces the last, but as a cumulative conversation across generations. The Faridkot scholars heard the partial commentaries before them and aspired to completeness; the reformers heard the Faridkot Teeka and demanded textual discipline; ਸਾਹਿਬ ਸਿੰਘ heard the reformers and built a grammar. Each contributed something lasting. To read the Faridkot Teeka comparatively is to take one's place in that long conversation — the proper posture of a student of the tradition.

lessons.title: The Seven-Language Digital Editions on the Sikh Archive
lessons.summary: How the Teeka has been digitized and made available across seven languages for modern study.
lessons.html:
From Rare Volumes to Open Access

For most of its life the ਫਰੀਦਕੋਟ ਵਾਲਾ ਟੀਕਾ was a rare and unwieldy resource: nine bulky volumes in ਬ੍ਰਜ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ, held in a limited number of libraries and ਗੁਰਦੁਆਰੇ, accessible only to those who could reach the volumes and read the language. The digital era has transformed this situation. Through digitization initiatives such as those gathered on the Sikh Archive, the Teeka has been made openly available, and — crucially — rendered across multiple languages so that readers who cannot navigate the original Braj can still benefit from its learning.

The Seven-Language Approach

The distinctive feature of the modern digital edition is its multilingual presentation, with the commentary made available across seven languages. This typically means that alongside the original ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ text and the Braj commentary, a reader can access the material rendered into other scripts and languages — serving the global ਸਿੱਖ ਪੰਥ, whose members read Punjabi in different scripts and who live in communities where English, Hindi and other languages predominate. The seven-language design directly addresses the access problem created by the original's Braj idiom: a reader in the diaspora who cannot parse nineteenth-century Braj can still reach the substance of the gloss.

Why Multilingual Access Matters

The theological stakes of access are real. ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ teaches that understanding the Guru's word is integral to the spiritual path; a commentary locked behind a linguistic barrier serves only a few. By rendering the Faridkot Teeka across seven languages, the digital edition extends the original scholars' purpose — to make the meaning of the Guru's word available to devotees — to a global, multilingual community the nineteenth-century compilers could scarcely have imagined. In this sense the digital project is faithful to the Teeka's founding intention even as it transcends the Teeka's original limits.

Searchability and Cross-Reference

Digital form brings more than translation. A digitized, searchable Teeka allows the student to find every place the commentary discusses a given word or concept, to jump directly to the commentary on a particular ਅੰਗ or ਸ਼ਬਦ, and to place the Faridkot gloss beside other commentaries on the same verse. What once required pulling volumes from a shelf and turning hundreds of pages can now be done in seconds. This radically lowers the cost of the comparative reading method commended in the previous lesson, putting serious exegetical study within reach of any motivated learner.

Cautions in Using Digital Editions

The student should, however, use digital and translated editions with appropriate care. Translation is itself interpretation: a rendering of the Braj commentary into another language embeds choices, and a careless translation may smooth over the very ਵੇਦਾਂਤਕ nuances that make the Teeka distinctive — or, conversely, may sharpen them. Whenever a point of weight rests on the Teeka's wording, the serious student returns to the original ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ-Braj text, using the translations as aids rather than substitutes. The digital edition is a gateway, not a replacement for the original.

The Archive as a Scholarly Ecosystem

The placement of the Faridkot Teeka within a larger Sikh Archive is itself significant. There the Teeka sits alongside other ਟੀਕੇ, manuscripts, and scholarly resources, so that the comparative reading method becomes natural rather than laborious. The Archive functions as a digital ਸੰਪ੍ਰਦਾਇ — a gathered tradition of texts and commentaries through which the student can move freely. For the history of Sikh exegesis this is a development of the first importance: the resources that once defined an elite scholarly formation are now open to all.

A New Chapter in the Teeka's Life

The digital, multilingual edition is thus best understood as a new chapter in the long life of the Faridkot Teeka rather than a mere convenience. Each era has received the commentary anew: the print era fixed and multiplied it; the reform era critiqued it; the modern scholarly era contextualized it; and now the digital era has made it globally and multilingually accessible. The student who reads the Teeka on the Sikh Archive participates in this latest chapter, and bears the corresponding responsibility to read it well — gratefully, comparatively and critically.

lessons.title: Reading the Teeka Today: A Practical Method
lessons.summary: A disciplined workflow for using the Faridkot Teeka in serious Gurbani study.
lessons.html:
Putting It All Together

This final lesson gathers the course into a practical method for using the ਫਰੀਦਕੋਟ ਵਾਲਾ ਟੀਕਾ in serious study of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ. The aim is neither uncritical reverence nor dismissive suspicion, but disciplined use — extracting the Teeka's genuine learning while exercising sound judgment over its interpretive frame.

Step One: Establish the Text

Begin with the ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ verse itself. Read it slowly in the original ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ, attending to its sound, its metre and its place within the ਸ਼ਬਦ and the ਰਾਗ. Before consulting any commentary, form a provisional sense of the verse on your own. This guards against simply absorbing the commentator's reading without first wrestling with the text — a discipline ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ itself commends, since the Gurus call the seeker to reflect (ਵੀਚਾਰ) on the word, not merely to receive opinions about it.

Step Two: Mine the ਪਦ ਅਰਥ

Turn to the Teeka's word-meanings. This is the commentary's most durable contribution, and even readers who reject its philosophy consult it here. Note how it glosses each difficult term, recognizing that these glosses carry the accumulated learning of the ਨਿਰਮਲਾ ਸੰਪ੍ਰਦਾਇ. Where a word draws on Sanskrit, Persian or a ਪੁਰਾਣਕ allusion, the Teeka will often unlock it. Record the glosses, but cross-check them against at least one other commentary, since even learned glosses can reflect interpretive bias.

Step Three: Follow the ਅਨ੍ਵੈ

Use the Teeka's syntactic re-ordering to clarify the grammar of the verse. Where the poetry inverts or compresses the word order, the ਅਨ੍ਵੈ shows the logical relations. Here especially it is wise to compare the Faridkot reading with the grammatically rigorous ਦਰਪਣ of ਪ੍ਰੋਫੈਸਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਸਿੰਘ, since disagreements over syntax often signal deeper interpretive forks.

Step Four: Weigh the ਭਾਵਾਰਥ Critically

Now read the Teeka's statement of the intended sense — and read it as one learned interpretation, not as the verdict of the text. Ask: does this ਭਾਵਾਰਥ honour the distinctive teaching of the Gurus, or does it flatten the verse into ਵੇਦਾਂਤਕ commonplace? Does it respect ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ's affirmation of the world and of personal devotion, or does it tilt toward world-negation and an impersonal absolute? Test the reading against the wider witness of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ, against other commentaries, and against the teaching of the ਪੰਥ. This critical weighing is the heart of responsible use.

Step Five: Read Comparatively

Never rely on the Faridkot Teeka alone. Set it beside the ਦਰਪਣ for grammatical control, the ਸ਼ਬਦਾਰਥ for concise clarity, and any focused commentary on the particular ਬਾਣੀ. Where the commentaries converge, your confidence is warranted; where they diverge, study the divergence, for it exposes the interpretive choices at stake. The seven-language digital editions on the Sikh Archive make this comparative reading practical, since the texts can be placed side by side and searched.

Step Six: Situate Historically

Finally, remember what the Teeka is: the considered, collective reading of a particular ਨਿਰਮਲਾ school, fixed in print under princely patronage in the late nineteenth century. Read its ਭਾਵਾਰਥ as a window onto how that learned community understood the Guru's word, valuable precisely as a dated, situated witness. This historical awareness prevents both the error of treating the Teeka as timeless authority and the error of dismissing it as mere distortion.

The Reward of Disciplined Use

A student who follows this method gains a great deal. From the Teeka's ਪਦ ਅਰਥ and ਅਨ੍ਵੈ come philological and grammatical riches; from its ਭਾਵਾਰਥ, a sophisticated if contestable interpretation to think with and against; from its history, a vivid sense of how ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ was read by a confident, learned community a century and a half ago. The ਫਰੀਦਕੋਟ ਵਾਲਾ ਟੀਕਾ is not the last word on the Guru Granth Sahib — no commentary is — but it is an indispensable companion on the path of ਵੀਚਾਰ, and the disciplined reader who knows how to use it is the richer for its company.

ਹਵਾਲੇ (Works Cited)

  • Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Rev. ed. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998.
  • Mandair, Arvind-Pal Singh. Sikhism: A Guide for the Perplexed. London: Bloomsbury, 2013.
  • Mann, Gurinder Singh. The Making of Sikh Scripture. New York: Oxford University Press, 2001.
  • Mann, Gurinder Singh, and Kamalroop Singh. The Granth of Guru Gobind Singh: Essays, Lectures, and Translations. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2015.
  • Nripinder Singh. The Sikh Moral Tradition. New Delhi: Manohar, 1990.
  • Oberoi, Harjot. The Construction of Religious Boundaries: Culture, Identity, and Diversity in the Sikh Tradition. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1994.
  • Padam, Piara Singh. Sri Guru Granth Sahib de Tikakar. Patiala: Kalam Mandir, 1990.
  • Pashaura Singh. The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2000.
  • Taran Singh. Gurbani dian Viakhia Pranalian. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1980.
