Over the following ten weeks four major engagements were fought — Mudki (18 December), Ferozeshah (21–22 December), Aliwal (28 January 1846), and Sobraon (10 February 1846). They were among the bloodiest the Company had ever fought in India.

At Ferozeshah, British accounts record that the issue hung in the balance through a freezing night, with Governor-General Hardinge reportedly preparing to surrender his sword. What turned these battles was less British superiority of arms than the conduct of the Sikh high command. The commanders Lal Singh and Tej Singh, both tied to the ਡੋਗਰਾ faction and in secret communication with the British, repeatedly failed to press advantages, withdrew at decisive moments, and left their own troops exposed. At Sobraon, Tej Singh is alleged to have fled across the river and ordered the pontoon bridge destroyed behind him, drowning the retreating ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ in the Sutlej. The valor of the soldiery — what the historian J. S. Grewal calls the genuine fighting spirit of the Panth — was squandered by the calculated treachery of its generals.

The Treaty of Lahore

The defeated durbar sued for peace. The Treaty of Lahore was signed on 9 March 1846. Its terms were designed not to extinguish the Sikh state outright — the Company was not yet ready to govern so large and martial a province directly — but to render it harmless and dependent. The key provisions were severe:

  • The Jullundur Doab, the rich tract between the Beas and the Sutlej, was ceded outright to the Company.
  • An indemnity of one and a half crore of rupees was imposed. Unable to pay in full, the durbar ceded the hill territories between the Beas and the Indus, including Kashmir, in lieu of one crore.
  • The ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ army was to be drastically reduced — to twenty thousand infantry and twelve thousand cavalry — stripping the state of the very force that had made it formidable.
  • The young Duleep Singh was recognized as Maharaja under the regency of Jind Kaur, but British control was inserted into the heart of the administration.

Kashmir and the Reward of Treachery

The disposal of Kashmir is one of the most revealing episodes of the settlement. By a separate Treaty of Amritsar concluded a week later, on 16 March 1846, the British sold Kashmir and its dependencies to Gulab Singh ਡੋਗਰਾ for seventy-five lakh rupees. Gulab Singh, who had held back his forces during the war, was thus rewarded with a kingdom carved out of the body of the Sikh state he had helped to betray. For many Sikhs this transaction crystallized the bitterness of the defeat: the heartland had been dismembered and a traitor enthroned over the spoils, all under the seal of the conqueror.

The Treaty of Bhairowal and Creeping Annexation

Within months the fiction of Sikh self-rule was further hollowed out. By the Treaty of Bhairowal, signed on 16 December 1846, a British Resident was installed at Lahore with sweeping powers over every branch of the administration, and a British garrison was stationed in the capital until Duleep Singh came of age in 1854. Maharani Jind Kaur, whose influence the British feared as a focus of Sikh loyalty, was stripped of authority and, soon after, removed from Lahore and pensioned off — later imprisoned at Sheikhupura and exiled. The historian Khushwant Singh notes that this calculated humiliation of the queen-mother, a figure of deep reverence among the soldiery, did much to inflame the resentment that would erupt in the second war.

A Protectorate in All But Name

By the close of 1846 the ਸਰਕਾਰ-ਏ-ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ had become a protectorate. Its army was gutted, its richest provinces gone, its treasury drained, its queen-regent disgraced, and its capital occupied. Yet the Sikh state still existed on paper, and this very ambiguity — sovereign in name, subject in fact — was unstable. The British Resident Henry Lawrence and his assistants administered Punjab as if it were already theirs, dispossessing chiefs, reassigning ਜਾਗੀਰ (revenue grants), and disbanding troops. The accumulated grievances of dispossessed sardars, unpaid soldiers, and a humiliated court would, within two years, ignite a second and final war. The Treaty of Lahore had not pacified Punjab; it had merely deferred the reckoning, and ensured that when revolt came it would be answered not with another treaty but with outright annexation. We turn to that revolt and its consequences in the next lesson.

lessons.title: The Second Anglo-Sikh War and the Annexation of Punjab
lessons.summary: The revolt at Multan, the battles of Chillianwala and Gujrat, and Lord Dalhousie's proclamation of annexation in March 1849.
lessons.html:
The Spark at Multan

The settlement of 1846 had created a province seething with dispossessed men. The flashpoint came at Multan in April 1848, when Mulraj, the dewan (governor) of the city, who had been pressured to resign and accept a reduced position, rose against the British arrangement. Two British officers sent to take over, Vans Agnew and Lieutenant Anderson, were murdered. The Resident at Lahore treated the affair at first as a local mutiny rather than a national rising, and Governor-General Lord Dalhousie deliberately allowed the revolt to spread before moving in force — a posture many historians read as a calculated wish to manufacture the pretext for total conquest.

The rising indeed spread. Sikh sardars who had lost their estates, soldiers cashiered from the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ, and chiefs across the province rallied to the cause. The most significant defection was that of Sher Singh Attariwala, a commander dispatched by the British-controlled durbar to suppress Mulraj, who instead went over to the rebels with his troops. His father Chattar Singh raised the Hazara region. What had begun as a local mutiny became a war of Sikh national resistance, fought under the old banner of the Panth.

Chillianwala and Gujrat

The major engagements of the Second Anglo-Sikh War were ferocious. At Ramnagar and then at Chillianwala on 13 January 1849, the Sikh forces under Sher Singh inflicted heavy losses on the army of Lord Gough; the British lost several guns and the regimental colours of more than one unit, and the battle was at best a costly draw that sent a shock through Britain. The historian Khushwant Singh observes that Chillianwala demonstrated, once more, that when the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ fought free of treacherous high command, it was a match for any army in Asia.

The decisive blow fell at Gujrat on 21 February 1849. Here, in what was called the 'Battle of the Guns', British artillery superiority — reinforced and reorganized after Chillianwala — broke the Sikh formations. The defeated Sikh army surrendered at Rawalpindi. There is a famous and poignant account, recorded in British and Sikh memory alike, of the disbanded ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ soldiers laying down their arms; one veteran is said to have declared, 'ਅੱਜ ਰਣਜੀਤ ਸਿੰਘ ਮਰ ਗਿਆ' — 'Today Ranjit Singh has died' — meaning that with the surrender of the army the soul of the Sikh state itself had finally expired.

The Proclamation of Annexation

Lord Dalhousie, an unapologetic expansionist, had no intention of restoring even the fiction of Sikh rule. On 29 March 1849 he proclaimed the annexation of ਪੰਜਾਬ to British India. The ten-year-old Maharaja Duleep Singh was made to sign away his sovereignty. The terms were total and personal:

  • The Maharaja resigned for himself and his heirs all right, title, and claim to the sovereignty of Punjab.
  • All state property was confiscated to the Company toward the costs of the war.
  • The famous ਕੋਹਿਨੂਰ diamond, long the symbol of Punjab's sovereignty, was surrendered to Queen Victoria.
  • Duleep Singh was granted a pension and removed from Punjab; he was later converted to Christianity, taken to England, and lived out a tragic, dispossessed life as a ward of the Empire.

The Meaning of 1849

The annexation of 1849 was an epochal rupture. For the first time since Guru Gobind Singh instituted the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ, the Sikhs were a people without political sovereignty in their own land. Harnik Deol, in her study of religion and nationalism in Punjab, identifies this loss of sovereignty as the foundational trauma around which modern Sikh political identity would be reconstructed. The state was gone, but the Panth — the religious and social body of the Sikhs — remained, and it was through religious institutions, reform movements, and eventually mass politics that the energy once embodied in the ਸਰਕਾਰ-ਏ-ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ would be channeled anew.

The British, for their part, were now masters of a vast, martial, and recently hostile province on the most sensitive frontier of their empire. How they chose to govern it — co-opting its soldiers, restructuring its land, and patronizing select strands of its religious life — would profoundly shape the trajectory of Sikh history for the next century. We turn to that colonial reconstruction in the next two lessons.

lessons.title: Colonial Restructuring: Land, Canals, and the Punjab School
lessons.summary: How the British remade annexed Punjab through the 'Punjab School' of paternalist administration, land settlement, and the canal colonies.
lessons.html:
The Board of Administration and the 'Punjab School'

Annexed ਪੰਜਾਬ was placed under a Board of Administration headed initially by the brothers Henry and John Lawrence. The system of governance they devised — informal, paternalist, militarized, and personally interventionist — became famous as the 'Punjab School' or 'Punjab tradition' of administration. Its officers, men like Robert Montgomery, John Nicholson, and Herbert Edwardes, governed through direct contact with the peasantry rather than through elaborate codes, riding circuit, settling disputes summarily, and cultivating the loyalty of landholders and headmen. The province was deliberately governed as a frontier under a 'non-regulation' regime that concentrated authority in the district officer.

This style was not benevolent in intent so much as strategic. Having just conquered a martial people, the British sought to bind the rural elites and the soldiery to the new order before resentment could organize. As the historian Tai Yong Tan argues in his study of the colonial 'garrison state', Punjab was administered from the start with an eye to its function as the chief recruiting ground and strategic glacis of the Indian Army. Stability, loyalty, and a steady supply of soldiers were the governing priorities.

Land Settlement and the Reordering of Rural Society

At the heart of the new regime lay the land settlement. British settlement officers surveyed the province, fixed proprietary rights, recorded them in the ਜਮਾਬੰਦੀ (revenue records), and assessed the land revenue. This was a transformation of immense consequence. Where the older ਸਰਕਾਰ-ਏ-ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ had collected a share of the produce through intermediaries in a flexible, customary fashion, the British imposed a fixed cash demand on legally defined proprietors. The effect was to freeze and sharpen rural hierarchies, to convert customary tenures into alienable property, and to expose the peasant to the money-lender and the market.

The colonial state was acutely aware that this exposure could destabilize the very rural order it depended on. Indebtedness among the peasant 'agriculturist' castes — who were also the prime recruits for the army — threatened to pass their lands into the hands of urban 'non-agriculturist' money-lending castes. The state's eventual response, the Punjab Land Alienation Act of 1900, prohibited the permanent transfer of land from designated agricultural tribes to non-agricultural ones. Richard Fox and other historians read this Act as a striking instance of the colonial construction of social categories: the state defined who was an 'agricultural tribe', and in doing so reinforced caste and community identities for its own administrative and military convenience.

The Canal Colonies

The most ambitious colonial intervention was the network of canal colonies established from the 1880s onward in the arid western doabs of ਪੰਜਾਬ. By cutting vast irrigation canals from the rivers, the British turned millions of acres of waste and pasture into some of the most productive agricultural land in the subcontinent. These newly watered tracts — Chenab Colony (Lyallpur), Jhelum Colony, and others — were settled with hand-picked colonists drawn largely from the central Punjab districts that supplied the army.

The allotment of canal land was a deliberate instrument of patronage and control. Grants were given to demobilized soldiers, to families with men in service, and to loyal yeomen, binding the most martial sections of the population ever more tightly to the colonial state through land and water. The economy of central and western Punjab was reoriented toward commercial agriculture — wheat and cotton for the imperial market. The prosperity this generated was real, but it was a prosperity engineered to produce loyalty and recruits. As Tan argues, the canal colonies fused the agrarian and military structures of the province into a single system: land rewarded service, and service secured land.

The Capital of Empire's Sword-Arm

The cumulative effect of these measures — paternalist administration, fixed land settlement, protective tribal legislation, and the canal colonies — was to make ਪੰਜਾਬ into what scholars have called the 'sword-arm of British India'. The province was governed less as an ordinary administrative unit than as a vast military estate, its society engineered to be stable, prosperous in a controlled way, and inexhaustibly recruitable. This restructuring had profound consequences for the Sikhs, who, as a martial rural community concentrated in the central districts, were drawn into the heart of the colonial military system. How the British turned the conquered ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ into the model soldier of their own army — and what that did to Sikh identity — is the subject of our next lesson.

lessons.title: The Manufacture of the Martial Race and the Sikh Soldier
lessons.summary: The colonial theory of 'martial races', the recruitment of Sikhs into the Indian Army, and the enforced maintenance of Khalsa identity in the ranks.
lessons.html:
From Enemy to Instrument

One of the most remarkable inversions in modern Sikh history is that within a generation of the annexation, the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ that had fought the British at Sobraon and Chillianwala had become the backbone of the British Indian Army. The men who had been the empire's most dangerous enemy became its most trusted soldiers. Understanding this transformation is essential to grasping both the prosperity and the predicament of the Sikhs under colonial rule.

The Theory of Martial Races

After the great rebellion of 1857, British military thinking crystallized around the doctrine of 'martial races'. According to this pseudo-scientific theory, the peoples of India were divided into those who were inherently warlike — hardy, loyal, and fit for soldiering — and those who were not. The Sikhs of central ਪੰਜਾਬ, along with Punjabi Muslims, Dogras, Gurkhas, and Pathans, were classified as a premier martial race. The supposed criteria were a blend of climate, caste, physique, and a record of loyalty; in practice, as Richard Fox argues incisively in Lions of the Punjab, the category was a colonial construction that produced the reality it claimed merely to describe.

The army recruited heavily and almost exclusively from these designated communities, especially from the Jat Sikhs of the central districts. Military service brought pay, pension, land grants in the canal colonies, and prestige. A whole rural economy and culture came to revolve around the regiment. The Sikhs, perhaps a small fraction of India's population, came to supply a strikingly disproportionate share of its army.

The Colonial Enforcement of ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ Identity

Here lies one of the most consequential paradoxes of the period. The British did not recruit Sikhs and assimilate them into a generic soldiery; on the contrary, they insisted that Sikh recruits maintain the full external discipline of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ. Recruits were required to keep ਕੇਸ (unshorn hair), to wear the ਪੰਜ ਕਕਾਰ (the five articles of faith), and to be formally initiated through ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ in the regimental gurdwara, with the ਗ੍ਰੰਥੀ and the ceremony supervised under army auspices. The British believed, as Harjot Oberoi and Richard Fox both emphasize, that a Sikh soldier who observed the full ਰਹਿਤ (code of discipline) made a better, braver, and more cohesive fighting man.

The unintended consequence was momentous. The colonial army became an engine for standardizing and reinforcing a distinct, orthodox ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ identity at precisely the moment when, in civilian Punjabi society, the boundaries between Sikh and Hindu practice were often blurred and fluid. The soldier returning to his village in canal-colony Punjab carried with him a sharpened, regiment-disciplined sense of what it meant to be a Sikh. In this way the army's recruitment policy ran parallel to, and reinforced, the reformist project of the ਤੱਤ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ that we will study later: both, for very different reasons, insisted on a pure and bounded Sikh identity.

The Price of Loyalty

The bargain had two faces. On one side, military service made the Sikh peasantry of central Punjab relatively prosperous, integrated, and proud; the Sikh soldier earned a reputation across the empire — from China to East Africa to the trenches of France — for discipline and courage. On the other side, this prosperity was purchased at the price of political dependence. The community's elites were bound to the colonial state by the threads of pension, land, and patronage. The instinct of the dominant Sikh leadership through the later nineteenth century was therefore loyalism, not resistance — a loyalism dramatically displayed during the 1857 rebellion, which we examine next.

The Seeds of Future Tension

Yet the very identity the army cultivated would, in time, turn against colonial control. When the British were perceived to have insulted or interfered with the religious discipline of the Sikh soldier — as in disputes over the right to keep articles of faith, or later in the corruption of the gurdwaras that soldiers held sacred — the loyalty so carefully cultivated could curdle into grievance. The disciplined, religiously self-conscious ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ that the army helped to forge would supply both the manpower and the moral fervor of the resistance movements of the early twentieth century, from the ਗ਼ਦਰ Party to the Gurdwara Reform Movement. The colonial state, in manufacturing the loyal martial Sikh, had also helped to manufacture the conditions of its own future challenge. We turn first to the great test of that loyalty in 1857.

lessons.title: The Paradox of 1857: Sikh Loyalism and the Great Rebellion
lessons.summary: Why most Sikhs supported the British during the 1857 uprising, and the long consequences of that choice for Sikh-British relations.
lessons.html:
The Rebellion and the Punjab Frontier

In May 1857 the sepoy regiments of the Bengal Army rose in revolt at Meerut and Delhi, igniting the great rebellion that the British called the Mutiny and Indian nationalists would later remember as the First War of Independence. The rebellion swept across the Gangetic plain, but in the recently annexed ਪੰਜਾਬ it failed to take hold — and, crucially, the Sikhs of Punjab not only abstained from the revolt but actively assisted the British in crushing it. This is one of the most studied and morally complex episodes in Sikh history.

Why Did the Sikhs Not Rebel?

The reasons are several and interlocking. First, the rebellion was led principally by the high-caste Hindu and Muslim sepoys of the Bengal Army and rallied symbolically around the restoration of the Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar in Delhi. For the Sikhs, the memory of Mughal persecution — the martyrdoms of the Gurus, the long struggle of the eighteenth century — was vivid and bitter. The prospect of a restored Mughal throne held no appeal; it evoked the very tyranny against which the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ had been forged. As J. S. Grewal observes, the symbolism of the revolt actively alienated Sikh sentiment.

Second, the wounds of 1849 were fresh, but the Bengal sepoys who now rebelled had themselves been part of the army of conquest that had annexed Punjab only eight years earlier. There was little instinctive solidarity between the defeated ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ and the very Purbia (eastern) soldiers who had helped subdue them. Some Sikhs saw in the crisis an opportunity to settle old scores against the Bengal Army.

Third, and most importantly for the long run, the British had by 1857 already begun to cultivate the Sikh rural elite through the patronage system described in earlier lessons. Sardars and chiefs who had been confirmed in their estates, and a peasantry being drawn into military service, had material reasons to back the new masters. The 'Punjab School' administrators, led by John Lawrence, acted with decisive energy: they disarmed the suspect Bengal regiments stationed in Punjab and raised new levies of Sikhs, Punjabi Muslims, and Pathans to march on Delhi.

The Siege of Delhi and the Reward of Loyalty

Punjabi troops, including substantial Sikh contingents, played a central role in the assault and recapture of Delhi in September 1857 and in the relief of besieged garrisons. Their contribution was widely credited by the British with saving their position in northern India. The reward was correspondingly large. After the rebellion, the Bengal Army was thoroughly reorganized and the British turned decisively toward ਪੰਜਾਬ and the northwest as their preferred recruiting ground. The doctrine of martial races, examined in the previous lesson, was in significant part a rationalization of the lesson the British drew from 1857: trust the Punjabis, who stood by us; distrust the Purbias, who rose against us.

The Long Shadow of the Choice

The Sikh role in 1857 had profound and ambivalent consequences. In the short and medium term it cemented the bargain of loyalism: privileged recruitment, canal-colony land, official patronage of Sikh religious institutions, and a reputation as the most reliable soldiers of the Raj. For a community stripped of its state only eight years before, this was a path back to prosperity and a kind of collective dignity within the imperial order.

Yet the choice also bound the Sikhs to a colonial state whose interests would, in the twentieth century, diverge sharply from their own. Indian nationalists of later generations would sometimes reproach the Sikhs for their role in 1857, and Sikh leaders themselves would grow uneasy at the memory as the freedom movement gathered force. Harnik Deol's analysis is useful here: she stresses that Sikh political identity in the colonial period was shaped by a continual negotiation between accommodation with the state and the assertion of a distinct community interest. The loyalism of 1857 represented the pole of accommodation; the resistance movements that followed — Namdhari, ਗ਼ਦਰ, Akali — represented the assertion of distinctness, often against the same state the community had once served.

From Loyalty to Reform

It would be a mistake, however, to imagine that loyalism meant quiescence. Even as the dominant Sikh elite cleaved to the British, currents of religious reform and, in places, outright resistance were stirring in Punjabi society. The first of these, the Namdhari or ਕੂਕਾ movement, arose in the very decades after 1857 and offered a startling counterpoint to elite loyalism — combining intense spiritual revival with social reform and, ultimately, anti-colonial defiance. To these early reform movements we now turn.

lessons.title: Early Reform: The Nirankari and Namdhari (ਕੂਕਾ) Movements
lessons.summary: The first nineteenth-century movements to purify Sikh practice — Baba Dyal's Nirankaris and Baba Ram Singh's Namdharis — and the 1872 Malerkotla tragedy.
lessons.html:
A Tradition in Need of Renewal

By the mid-nineteenth century, many observers within and outside the Panth perceived that Sikh religious life had drifted far from the teachings of the Gurus. The shrines were often controlled by hereditary ਮਹੰਤ and ਪੁਜਾਰੀ who had introduced idol-worship, Brahminical ritual, caste exclusion, and superstition into spaces dedicated to the formless ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ. The collapse of Sikh political power after 1849 removed the institutional patronage that had sustained a degree of orthodoxy under the ਸਰਕਾਰ-ਏ-ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ. Into this vacuum stepped a series of reform movements that sought to recall the Sikhs to the pure devotion of ਨਾਮ (the divine Name) and the authority of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ.

The Nirankari Movement

The earliest of these was the Nirankari movement founded by Baba Dyal Das (1783–1855) in the Rawalpindi region. The very name ਨਿਰੰਕਾਰੀ derives from ਨਿਰੰਕਾਰ, the 'Formless One', and announces the movement's central thrust: a return to the worship of the formless ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ and a rejection of idolatry and the worship of living gurus or images. Baba Dyal preached against the encrustation of Hindu ritual upon Sikh practice and called the community back to ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ (remembrance of the divine Name) and the teachings of ਗੁਰੂ ਨਾਨਕ.

The Nirankaris are especially significant for their insistence on distinctively Sikh life-cycle rites. They sought to replace Brahmin-officiated, Hindu-style ceremonies of birth, marriage, and death with rites grounded in ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ. The Nirankari emphasis on the ਅਨੰਦ marriage ceremony — a Sikh rite of marriage solemnized around the ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ — anticipated by decades the reformist agenda later carried into law as the Anand Marriage Act of 1909. In this sense the Nirankaris were pioneers of the broader project, fulfilled by the ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ, of distinguishing Sikh practice from Hindu custom.

The Namdhari or ਕੂਕਾ Movement

More dramatic, and more politically charged, was the Namdhari movement. Its founding figure was Baba Ram Singh (1816–1885) of Bhaini Sahib, who had served in the army of Ranjit Singh before turning to spiritual reform. The Namdharis became popularly known as ਕੂਕਾ — from ਕੂਕ, the loud cry or ecstatic utterance into which their devotees would burst during fervent congregational singing of the divine Name. Baba Ram Singh stressed an intense, disciplined devotion to ਨਾਮ, a strict ethical code, vegetarianism, simplicity in marriage and ceremony, the rejection of caste, and the wearing of white homespun.

Reform as Resistance

What distinguished the Namdharis from the broadly loyalist temper of the Sikh elite was their developing anti-colonial edge. Baba Ram Singh advocated a program that prefigured later nationalist methods: the boycott of British goods, government schools, courts, and the colonial postal system, and the use of an alternative Namdhari postal and administrative network. This early ਸਵਦੇਸ਼ੀ-like withdrawal from the institutions of the Raj made the movement deeply suspect to the colonial authorities, who placed Baba Ram Singh under surveillance and restriction.

The Malerkotla Tragedy of 1872

The crisis came over the issue of cow protection. In January 1872 a band of Namdharis, enraged by the slaughter of cattle, attacked the Muslim ruler of Malerkotla. The colonial authorities responded with ferocious and summary violence. The Deputy Commissioner of Ludhiana, J. L. Cowan, without proper trial, had some sixty-five captured ਕੂਕਾ blown from the mouths of cannon — a deliberately terrifying mode of execution. Baba Ram Singh, though he had not authorized the attack, was arrested and deported to Rangoon in Burma, where he remained in exile until his death in 1885.

The Malerkotla executions stand as one of the earliest mass colonial atrocities against Sikhs and a stark foreshadowing of ਜਲ੍ਹਿਆਂਵਾਲਾ ਬਾਗ਼ nearly half a century later. The Namdharis are remembered in Sikh and Indian nationalist memory as among the first to defy British rule directly, even as their theological innovations — notably the doctrine of a living guru in the line of Baba Ram Singh — set them apart from the mainstream ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ.

The Significance of the Early Movements

The Nirankari and Namdhari movements together demonstrate that the impulse to reform, purify, and distinguish Sikh practice from surrounding Hindu custom long predated the more famous ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ. They established the key reformist themes — the formless ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ, distinctively Sikh life-cycle rites, the rejection of caste and Brahminical ritual, and devotion to ਨਾਮ — that the Singh Sabha would systematize and carry to the whole community. And in the Namdhari case, they showed that religious revival and anti-colonial resistance could fuse into a single movement. It was the ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ, however, that would harness the printing press, modern education, and organizational sophistication to remake Sikh identity on a mass scale. To that revival we now turn.

lessons.title: The ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ Revival and the Contest over Sikh Identity
lessons.summary: The founding of the Singh Sabha in 1873, the threat of conversion, and the modernizing program of education, print, and reform.
lessons.html:
The Crisis of the 1870s

The ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ (Singh Sabha) movement was born in ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤਸਰ in 1873 out of a sense of acute crisis. Several pressures converged. Christian missionaries, well funded and active across ਪੰਜਾਬ, were making conversions, and in a notorious episode several Sikh students at the Amritsar mission school were on the verge of, or did, convert to Christianity. Hindu revivalist movements were also asserting themselves. The Arya Samaj, founded by Swami Dayananda and arriving in Punjab in the 1870s, preached a militant, reformed Hinduism and, in its more aggressive moods, claimed the Sikhs as a sect of Hindus and launched ਸ਼ੁੱਧੀ (purification/reconversion) campaigns. Kenneth Jones, in his study of the Arya Samaj in Punjab, shows how this competitive religious environment forced every community to define and defend its boundaries.

For thoughtful Sikhs, the danger was existential. Without modern schools, printed scripture and literature, a defined creed, and organized institutions, the Panth seemed liable to be absorbed — by Christianity from without, by a resurgent Hinduism from within, and by the simple drift of an unreformed, ritual-laden popular practice. The ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ was the Sikh response to this multi-front challenge.

The Amritsar and Lahore Sabhas

The first Singh Sabha was founded at Amritsar in 1873 under the leadership of established figures such as Sir Khem Singh Bedi (a descendant of ਗੁਰੂ ਨਾਨਕ), Baba Sir Khem Singh and Kanwar Bikrama Singh, and the scholar Giani Gian Singh among others. This Amritsar body was led largely by aristocrats, ਸੋਢੀ and ਬੇਦੀ lineages, and traditionalists, and it took a conservative, accommodating view of Sikh tradition — what would come to be called ਸਨਾਤਨ ਸਿੱਖੀ.

In 1879 a second and more dynamic body, the Lahore Singh Sabha, was founded under the leadership of Professor Gurmukh Singh, Giani Ditt Singh, and Bhai Jawahir Singh. The Lahore Sabha attracted the rising professional and educated classes and adopted a far more radical, reformist stance, insisting on a Sikhism sharply distinct from Hinduism. This faction became the ਤੱਤ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ, the 'pure Khalsa', whose contest with the Sanatan party we will examine in detail in the next lesson.

The Program of Reform

Whatever their differences, the Singh Sabhas pursued a broadly modernizing program with extraordinary energy. Its principal instruments were three:

  • Education. The movement founded schools and, supremely, Khalsa College at Amritsar in 1892, which became the intellectual flagship of Sikh modernity. A network of Khalsa schools spread education in Gurmukhi, Sikh history, and modern subjects to a generation of Sikhs.
  • Print. The Singh Sabha seized upon the printing press as no Sikh movement before it. Newspapers and journals such as the Khalsa Akhbar and the Khalsa Samachar, tracts, standardized editions of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ, catechisms, and historical works poured from reformist presses, creating for the first time a mass print public among Sikhs.
  • Institutional organization. Local Singh Sabhas multiplied across Punjab and were eventually coordinated through umbrella bodies, culminating in the Chief Khalsa Diwan, founded in 1902, which became the central representative organization of the reformist Sikhs in the early twentieth century.

Reforming Ritual and Defining the Creed

The reformers worked to purge what they regarded as un-Sikh accretions: idol images in gurdwaras (including, controversially, idols installed within the precincts of the Darbar Sahib complex), Brahmin officiants, caste discrimination in the ਲੰਗਰ and at worship, and Hindu-style life-cycle rites. They promoted the ਅਨੰਦ marriage and campaigned successfully for its legal recognition in the Anand Marriage Act of 1909. They sought to standardize the ਰਹਿਤ ਮਰਯਾਦਾ (code of conduct) and to fix a normative account of Sikh belief and practice. Bhai Vir Singh, the towering literary figure of the movement, produced a vast body of devotional poetry, fiction, and exegesis that gave the reformed Sikh identity emotional and aesthetic depth.

The Construction of Modern Sikh Identity

Harjot Oberoi's influential interpretation, set out in The Construction of Religious Boundaries, frames the Singh Sabha as the moment when a fluid, pluralistic 'Sanatan' Sikh world — in which Sikh, Hindu, and folk practices freely mingled — was replaced by a sharply bounded, systematized, and exclusive Sikh identity. Whether one accepts Oberoi's strong thesis or reads the reformers as recovering an authentic Khalsa orthodoxy, there is no doubt that the Singh Sabha transformed what it meant to be a Sikh. The crucial battle in that transformation was fought between the two wings of the movement — the ਤੱਤ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ and the defenders of ਸਨਾਤਨ ਸਿੱਖੀ — over the most basic question of all: were the Sikhs Hindus, or a distinct people? To that contest we now turn.

lessons.title: ਤੱਤ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ versus ਸਨਾਤਨ ਸਿੱਖੀ: Defining the Boundaries
lessons.summary: The internal struggle within the Singh Sabha over Sikh identity, culminating in the victory of the Tat Khalsa and the slogan 'We are not Hindus'.
lessons.html:
Two Visions of the Panth

The ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ was never a single mind. Within it two fundamentally opposed visions of Sikh identity contended for nearly four decades. The outcome of their struggle determined the shape of modern Sikhism. On one side stood ਸਨਾਤਨ ਸਿੱਖੀ; on the other, the ਤੱਤ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ.

ਸਨਾਤਨ ਸਿੱਖੀ: The Pluralist Tradition

The Sanatan vision, associated above all with the Amritsar Singh Sabha and aristocratic custodians like Khem Singh Bedi, understood Sikhism as an inclusive, capacious tradition continuous with the wider Indic religious world. In this view, the Sikhs were not sharply separate from Hindus; the Gurus stood within a broad ਸਨ�ਾਤਨ (eternal, traditional) dharma. The Sanatan world accommodated a plurality of practice: veneration of living holy men and the hereditary descendants of the Gurus, the presence of images and the worship of various deities alongside ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ, the authority of Brahmin pandits and ਪੁਜਾਰੀ in ritual, caste distinctions, and a fluid spectrum of identities in which a person might be Sikh and Hindu at once. As Harjot Oberoi documents, this was in fact how a great many Punjabis actually lived their religion in the nineteenth century.

ਤੱਤ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ: The Essential Khalsa

The ਤੱਤ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ — the term means the 'pure' or 'essential' Khalsa — rejected this pluralism root and branch. Centered in the Lahore Singh Sabha and led by men like Professor Gurmukh Singh and Giani Ditt Singh (himself of low-caste origin, which sharpened his hostility to caste and Brahminical privilege), the Tat Khalsa insisted that Sikhism was a wholly distinct religion, founded by ਗੁਰੂ ਨਾਨਕ and perfected by ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ in the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ, owing nothing to and sharing nothing essential with Hinduism. Their program demanded:

  • The removal of idols and Brahmin officiants from gurdwaras and the exclusive authority of ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ.
  • The abolition of caste within the Panth and the full inclusion of all in ਸੰਗਤ and ਪੰਗਤ.
  • Distinctly Sikh life-cycle rites, free of Hindu and Brahminical forms.
  • A standardized ਰਹਿਤ ਮਰਯਾਦਾ binding on all Sikhs.
  • The rejection of the worship of living gurus and hereditary holy men.

'ਹਮ ਹਿੰਦੂ ਨਹੀਂ' — We Are Not Hindus

The decisive intellectual blow was struck by Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha, the great scholar and lexicographer, whose tract Ham Hindu Nahin ('We Are Not Hindus'), first published in 1898, argued systematically that the Sikhs constituted a separate religion and people with their own scripture, Gurus, history, and code of conduct. The very title became a slogan of the age. Bhai Kahn Singh's later monumental encyclopaedia, the Gurushabad Ratnakar Mahankosh, would give the reformed tradition a vast scholarly foundation. The argument that the Sikhs were a distinct ਕੌਮ (community/nation) had profound implications: it underwrote separate Sikh legal status, separate political representation, and, ultimately, a distinct Sikh national consciousness.

The Triumph of the Tat Khalsa

By the early twentieth century the ਤੱਤ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ had effectively won. Several forces favored it. The colonial army, as we have seen, enforced ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ orthodoxy among its Sikh recruits, reinforcing the bounded identity the reformers preached. The competitive pressure of the Arya Samaj's ਸ਼ੁੱਧੀ campaigns and its claim that Sikhs were Hindus drove home the need for a defensible separate identity. The print and educational apparatus of the movement disseminated the reformist creed to a mass public. And the social composition of the rising professional and Jat peasant classes favored the egalitarian, anti-caste, anti-aristocratic Tat Khalsa over the hierarchical Sanatan order.

The Stakes and the Critique

The victory of the ਤੱਤ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ produced the systematized, bounded Sikhism that is largely normative today — its standardized rites, its insistence on the exclusive authority of ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ, its rejection of caste and idolatry, its self-understanding as a distinct ਕੌਮ. Oberoi's provocative argument is that this was less a recovery of original purity than the construction of a new kind of religious boundary, suited to the conditions of colonial modernity — the census, competitive communalism, print, and the politics of representation. Critics of Oberoi, including many traditional Sikh scholars, respond that the Tat Khalsa recovered the authentic teaching of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ from genuine corruption.

Whatever one's judgment, the consequence is clear. By winning the argument over identity, the ਤੱਤ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ created the self-conscious, organized, distinct community that would, within a few years, mobilize politically — first in the radicalism of the ਗ਼ਦਰ Party, then in the great non-violent struggle for the gurdwaras. The reform of identity made possible the politics of resistance. To that resistance, in its revolutionary form, we now turn.

lessons.title: The ਗ਼ਦਰ Party and Transnational Sikh Radicalism
lessons.summary: The emigration of Punjabi Sikhs to North America, the racism they faced, the Komagata Maru, and the founding of the revolutionary Ghadar Party in 1913.
lessons.html:
The Punjabi Diaspora on the Pacific

In the first decade of the twentieth century, thousands of Punjabis — overwhelmingly Sikhs from the central districts, many of them ex-soldiers — emigrated across the Pacific to the western coast of North America. They labored in the lumber mills of British Columbia, the railways of the Pacific Northwest, and the farms of California's Central Valley. They had been drawn abroad by the same forces of agrarian pressure and military mobility that the colonial transformation of ਪੰਜਾਬ had set in motion. Ironically, men who had served the Empire as soldiers now found themselves, as immigrants, subjected to systematic racial exclusion.

Racism and Political Awakening

On the Pacific coast these Punjabis met virulent discrimination: the 'Asiatic Exclusion' agitation, riots, denial of citizenship and the franchise, restrictions on immigration designed explicitly to keep out Indians, and the constant indignity of being treated as an inferior race. The contrast was sharp and radicalizing. As subjects of the British Crown they had been told they were partners in the Empire; as immigrants they discovered that the Empire offered them no protection against the racism of its own settler dominions. Many concluded that their humiliation abroad flowed directly from their subjection at home — that only a free India could command respect for its people anywhere. As the historian Maia Ramnath argues in Haj to Utopia, the Ghadar movement was forged in this crucible of diaspora, racism, and global radical currents.

The Founding of the ਗ਼ਦਰ Party

Out of this ferment, the ਗ਼ਦਰ Party was founded in 1913, with its headquarters — the 'Yugantar Ashram' — in San Francisco. Its leading figures included the scholar-revolutionary Lala Har Dayal as its first organizing intellect, and Sikh leaders such as Baba Sohan Singh Bhakna, the party's first president, and Pandit Kanshi Ram as treasurer. The word ਗ਼ਦਰ means 'mutiny' or 'revolt', consciously invoking the rebellion of 1857. The party's organ, the newspaper Ghadar, was printed in Urdu, Gurmukhi, and other languages and smuggled across the world to Punjabi communities from California to Shanghai to Punjab itself.

The Ideology of Ghadar

The ਗ਼ਦਰ Party was strikingly modern and secular in its political vision, even though its rank and file was overwhelmingly Sikh. It preached the violent overthrow of British rule and the establishment of a free, republican, and secular India in which Hindus, Muslims, and Sikhs would be equal citizens. It was anti-imperialist, egalitarian, and internationalist, drawing on the wider currents of global anarchism, socialism, and anti-colonial revolt that Ramnath traces. Its poetry — the famous Ghadar di Gunj ('Echoes of Mutiny'), much of it in Punjabi — fused the martial idiom of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ with revolutionary republicanism, summoning the memory of the Gurus and the eighteenth-century ਸ਼ਹੀਦ (martyrs) to the cause of national liberation.

The Komagata Maru

A galvanizing event was the voyage of the Komagata Maru in 1914. A Japanese steamship chartered by the Sikh entrepreneur Gurdit Singh, it carried some 376 Punjabi passengers — mostly Sikhs — to Vancouver in a deliberate challenge to Canada's exclusionary immigration laws. The ship was refused entry, held in the harbor for two months under appalling conditions, and finally forced to return. When it reached Budge Budge near Calcutta, the colonial authorities attempted to detain and disperse the passengers; in the ensuing confrontation, police fired on them, killing several. The Komagata Maru affair became a searing symbol of imperial racism and turned many returning emigrants decisively toward the ਗ਼ਦਰ cause.

The Failed Uprising of 1915

The outbreak of the First World War in 1914 seemed to the Ghadarites the appointed hour. Thousands returned to ਪੰਜਾਬ intending to subvert the Indian Army — heavily Sikh, and now drawn down by the war — and to ignite a general military uprising, planned for February 1915. But the conspiracy was riddled with British informers. The colonial intelligence apparatus, forewarned, struck first: the planned mutinies in the Punjab garrisons were pre-empted, the leaders rounded up, and the rising crushed before it could begin. In the Lahore Conspiracy Trials that followed, scores of Ghadarites were tried; many were hanged and many more imprisoned or sent to the penal colony in the Andaman Islands. Baba Sohan Singh Bhakna and other leaders endured long imprisonment.

The Legacy of Ghadar

Though it failed as an insurrection, the ਗ਼ਦਰ Party left a profound legacy. It demonstrated that the loyalist bargain forged after 1849 and 1857 was breaking down; that Sikhs, even ex-soldiers, could turn the martial energies cultivated by the Empire against the Empire itself. It planted the seeds of revolutionary and left nationalism in Punjab that would later feed the Babbar Akali and Kirti movements and figures like Bhagat Singh. And it forced the colonial state, already nervous, to view Punjab — its 'sword-arm' — with new suspicion. That suspicion, and the repressive wartime apparatus it produced, set the stage for the catastrophe of 1919, to which we now turn.

lessons.title: ਜਲ੍ਹਿਆਂਵਾਲਾ ਬਾਗ਼ and the Rupture of 1919
lessons.summary: The Rowlatt Act, the Vaisakhi massacre at Jallianwala Bagh on 13 April 1919, and the shattering of Sikh and Indian faith in British rule.
lessons.html:
The Wartime State and the Rowlatt Act

The First World War strained ਪੰਜਾਬ to the limit. As the chief recruiting ground of the army, the province poured its young men into the trenches of France, the campaigns of Mesopotamia, and the battlefields of East Africa; Sikhs served and died in numbers vastly disproportionate to their share of the population. Recruitment was driven hard, often coercively, by a colonial administration under Lieutenant-Governor Michael O'Dwyer that brooked no dissent. Wartime also brought inflation, requisition, disease — the influenza pandemic of 1918–19 was devastating — and the bitter memory of the ਗ਼ਦਰ repression. Expectation of post-war reform ran high.

Instead came repression. In March 1919 the government enacted the Rowlatt Act, extending the wartime emergency powers of detention without trial into peacetime. To Indians who had sacrificed so much for the Empire and anticipated a loosening of control, the Act was a betrayal. Mohandas Gandhi called for a nationwide ਸਤਿਆਗ੍ਰਹ (non-violent resistance) and ਹੜਤਾਲ (strike). Protest swept the country, and ਪੰਜਾਬ, with its accumulated grievances, was especially restive.

The Crisis in ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤਸਰ

In ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤਸਰ, the spiritual capital of the Sikhs, tension mounted in early April 1919. Two popular local leaders, Dr. Saifuddin Kitchlew (a Muslim) and Dr. Satyapal (a Hindu), symbols of Hindu-Muslim-Sikh unity, were arrested and deported on 10 April. Crowds protesting their arrest were fired upon; in the ensuing disorder some Europeans were killed and property destroyed. The administration, gripped by fear of another 1857 or 1915, resolved on a policy of exemplary terror. Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer was given military command of the city, and a ban on public assemblies was proclaimed — though it was poorly publicized and unknown to many.

The Massacre

On 13 April 1919 — ਵੈਸਾਖੀ, the most sacred day in the Sikh calendar, the very anniversary of the founding of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ in 1699 — thousands gathered in the ਜਲ੍ਹਿਆਂਵਾਲਾ ਬਾਗ਼, a walled garden near the Darbar Sahib. Many were pilgrims who had come to the holy city for the festival and to the cattle fair, with no knowledge of the assembly ban; others had gathered to protest peacefully. The Bagh was an enclosed space with high walls and only a few narrow exits.

General Dyer arrived with a detachment of troops, blocked the main entrance with his men and armoured cars, and without warning ordered them to open fire on the dense, trapped, unarmed crowd. The firing continued for some ten minutes, until the ammunition — some 1,650 rounds — was nearly exhausted. Dyer directed fire at the exits where people pressed to escape and at those who flung themselves into the well in the Bagh to avoid the bullets. Official British figures admitted 379 dead and over 1,100 wounded; Indian estimates ran far higher, to a thousand or more killed. Dyer later told the Hunter Commission that he had fired not merely to disperse the crowd but to produce a 'moral effect' throughout ਪੰਜਾਬ — a calculated act of terror.

Martial Law and 'Crawling'

The massacre was followed by the imposition of brutal martial law across the province under O'Dwyer's authority. Public floggings, mass arrests, the bombing of crowds from aircraft elsewhere in Punjab, and the notorious 'crawling order' — by which Indians were forced to crawl on their bellies along the lane where a European woman had been assaulted — deepened the humiliation and rage. The full extent of the atrocities was for a time concealed by censorship.

The Rupture

When the truth emerged, it shattered whatever remained of Indian faith in British justice and British rule. The poet Rabindranath Tagore renounced his knighthood in protest. Gandhi, who had believed in reform within the Empire, was moved decisively toward non-cooperation; he would soon declare that cooperation with so satanic a government was sinful. For the Sikhs the wound was peculiarly deep: the massacre had occurred in their holiest city, on their holiest day, beside their holiest shrine.

The community's outrage was compounded by an act of collaboration that became a rallying cry of reform. The ਮਹੰਤ-controlled management and the ਪੁਜਾਰੀ of the Akal Takht, the supreme temporal seat of the Sikhs, honored General Dyer — the butcher of ਜਲ੍ਹਿਆਂਵਾਲਾ ਬਾਗ਼ — with a ਸਿਰੋਪਾ (robe of honor) and declared him an honorary Sikh. This obscene episode crystallized for reformist Sikhs the necessity of wresting their sacred institutions from the corrupt, colonially compliant custodians who controlled them. As Harnik Deol observes, the convergence of colonial atrocity and the manifest corruption of the shrine establishment fused religious reform and political resistance into a single mass movement. The massacre of 1919 thus did not only mark the end of an era of faith in the Raj; it lit the fuse of the Gurdwara Reform Movement, to which our final lesson turns.

lessons.title: From Reform to Institution: The ਅਕਾਲੀ ਦਲ and the SGPC
lessons.summary: The culmination of seventy years of reform and resistance in the Gurdwara Reform Movement, the founding of the SGPC and the Shiromani Akali Dal, and the Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925.
lessons.html:
The Logic of Culmination

The seven decades traced in this course — from the fall of the ਸਰਕਾਰ-ਏ-ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ in 1849 to the trauma of 1919 — converged at last upon a single great struggle: the campaign to liberate the Sikh shrines from corrupt hereditary custodians and to vest their control in the democratic body of the Panth. This Gurdwara Reform Movement, and the institutions it created, represent the institutional culmination of everything that came before: the loss of sovereignty, the colonial restructuring of Punjab, the disciplining of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ in the army, the reform of identity by the ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ, and the radicalization wrought by ਗ਼ਦਰ and ਜਲ੍ਹਿਆਂਵਾਲਾ ਬਾਗ਼.

The Problem of the ਮਹੰਤ

By the early twentieth century most of the historic gurdwaras, including the great shrines of ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤਸਰ and Nankana Sahib, were controlled by hereditary ਮਹੰਤ. Over generations these custodians had come to treat the shrines and their vast endowed lands as private property. Many had introduced practices the ਤੱਤ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ regarded as abominations — idol worship, Brahminical ritual, the exclusion of low-caste Sikhs — and some led personally corrupt and dissolute lives off the offerings of the faithful. Worst of all, as the honoring of General Dyer at the Akal Takht had shown, the ਪੁਜਾਰੀ and ਮਹੰਤ establishment was politically compliant with the colonial state that had massacred Sikhs at ਜਲ੍ਹਿਆਂਵਾਲਾ ਬਾਗ਼. The shrines were administered, in effect, under the protection of the Raj.

The Founding of the SGPC and the ਅਕਾਲੀ ਦਲ

The reformers moved to seize control. On 15 November 1920 a representative assembly of Sikhs founded the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (SGPC) — the Supreme Gurdwara Management Committee — to administer the historic shrines on behalf of the whole Panth on democratic, reformed principles. Almost simultaneously, in December 1920, the Shiromani ਅਕਾਲੀ ਦਲ was organized as the political and activist arm of the movement, coordinating the bands of volunteers — the ਅਕਾਲੀ ਜਥੇ — who would actually carry out the campaign. The term ਅਕਾਲੀ, evoking the ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ and the fearless Akali-Nihangs of old, signaled a self-consciously militant yet disciplined movement of reform.

The Method of Non-Violent ਮੋਰਚਾ

The genius of the Akali movement was its adoption of disciplined non-violence — ਅਹਿੰਸਾ in the service of the Panth. The Akalis launched a series of ਮੋਰਚਾ (organized agitations) to take over individual gurdwaras, sending jathas of volunteers who courted arrest and endured beatings without retaliation, bound by a vow of non-violence taken before ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ. Several of these campaigns became epics of sacrifice:

  • Nankana Sahib (February 1921). At the very birthplace of ਗੁਰੂ ਨਾਨਕ, the mahant and his hired men massacred a peaceful jatha of reformers — well over a hundred Sikhs — and burned their bodies. The atrocity shocked the Panth and the nation and immensely strengthened the movement.
  • The Keys Affair (1921). A dispute over control of the keys of the Toshakhana (treasury) of the Darbar Sahib became a constitutional test of who controlled the shrine; the government's eventual surrender of the keys to the SGPC was hailed by Gandhi as the first decisive victory in India's freedom struggle.
  • Guru ka Bagh (1922). Thousands of Akali volunteers submitted to systematic, brutal beatings by police without raising a hand, in a display of non-violent endurance that drew worldwide attention and admiration.
  • Jaito (1923–24). A long and bloody ਮੋਰਚਾ over the deposition of the ruler of Nabha, in which jathas marching to complete an ਅਖੰਡ ਪਾਠ were fired upon.

The Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925

The sustained sacrifice of thousands of Akalis — many imprisoned, many killed — at last compelled the colonial government to concede. The Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925 transferred legal control of the historic gurdwaras of ਪੰਜਾਬ to the SGPC, an elected body representative of the Sikh community. This was a landmark achievement. For the first time, the central religious institutions of the Sikhs were placed under the democratic, collective control of the Panth, ending generations of hereditary and colonially protected mismanagement. The SGPC became, and remains, the principal religious-administrative body of the Sikhs — sometimes called a 'Sikh parliament' — and the ਅਕਾਲੀ ਦਲ became the enduring vehicle of Sikh political life.

The Meaning of the Whole Arc

Here our course reaches its natural close. Consider the journey: in 1849 the Sikhs lost their sovereign state and became subjects of a foreign empire. Through seventy years they were restructured, recruited, reformed, and radicalized. And by 1925 they had forged, out of religious reform and non-violent resistance, a set of durable national institutions — the SGPC and the ਅਕਾਲੀ ਦਲ — that gave the stateless Panth a democratic political and religious organization of its own. Harnik Deol's central insight illuminates the whole arc: deprived of a state, the Sikhs reconstituted their collective identity and agency through religion, and in doing so fused faith and politics into the distinctive form of modern Sikh nationalism. The energy once embodied in the ਸਰਕਾਰ-ਏ-ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ had found new institutional vessels. The story of British annexation and Sikh resistance is thus not merely a tale of conquest and defeat, but of a people who, having lost a kingdom, built a nation.

ਹਵਾਲੇ (Works Cited)

  • Deol, Harnik. Religion and Nationalism in India: The Case of the Punjab. London: Routledge, 2000.
  • Oberoi, Harjot. The Construction of Religious Boundaries: Culture, Identity and Diversity in the Sikh Tradition. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1994.
  • Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Rev. ed. The New Cambridge History of India II.3. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998.
  • Singh, Khushwant. A History of the Sikhs, Volume 2: 1839–2004. 2nd ed. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2004.
  • Fox, Richard G. Lions of the Punjab: Culture in the Making. Berkeley: University of California Press, 1985.
  • Jones, Kenneth W. Arya Dharm: Hindu Consciousness in 19th-Century Punjab. Berkeley: University of California Press, 1976.
  • Ramnath, Maia. Haj to Utopia: How the Ghadar Movement Charted Global Radicalism and Attempted to Overthrow the British Empire. Berkeley: University of California Press, 2011.
  • Sahni, Ruchi Ram, and Ganda Singh, ed. Struggle for Reform in Sikh Shrines. Amritsar: Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, 1965.
  • Tan, Tai Yong. The Garrison State: The Military, Government and Society in Colonial Punjab, 1849–1947. New Delhi: Sage, 2005.
  • Singh, Mohinder. The Akali Movement. Delhi: Macmillan, 1978.

quiz.q: What was the principal cause of Sikh military defeat in the First Anglo-Sikh War (1845–46), according to historians such as Khushwant Singh?
options: The numerical inferiority of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ army
The betrayal of the Sikh soldiery by treacherous commanders allied to the ਡੋਗਰਾ faction
The absence of any artillery in the Sikh forces
A lack of religious motivation among the troops

quiz.q: By the Treaty of Amritsar of March 1846, what became of Kashmir?
options: It was retained by Maharaja Duleep Singh's durbar
It was annexed directly into British India
It was sold by the British to Gulab Singh ਡੋਗਰਾ for seventy-five lakh rupees
It was granted independence under a local council

quiz.q: Why did most Sikhs support the British rather than join the rebellion of 1857?
options: Because the rebellion threatened to restore Mughal rule, and the British had begun cultivating the Sikh rural elite
Because the Gurus had commanded loyalty to the British Crown
Because the rebels promised to restore the ਸਰਕਾਰ-ਏ-ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ
Because the Sikhs were forbidden to bear arms

quiz.q: What was the central claim of the ਤੱਤ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ wing of the ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ, expressed in Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's famous tract?
options: That Sikhs should return to the worship of hereditary living gurus
That the Sikhs were a sect within the broad ਸਨਾਤਨ tradition
That the Sikhs were a wholly distinct religion and people — 'We Are Not Hindus'
That gurdwaras should remain under the control of Brahmin officiants

quiz.q: The ਗ਼ਦਰ Party, founded in 1913 in San Francisco, is best characterized as:
options: A loyalist organization seeking greater Sikh recruitment into the British army
A revolutionary, secular, republican movement seeking the violent overthrow of British rule
A religious reform body focused only on gurdwara ritual
A constitutional party seeking dominion status within the Empire

quiz.q: What legislative outcome marked the culmination of the Gurdwara Reform Movement?
options: The Rowlatt Act of 1919
The Anand Marriage Act of 1909
The Punjab Land Alienation Act of 1900
The Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925, which vested control of the shrines in the SGPC

courses.title: The Historical Rehatnamas: Codes of Sikh Conduct
courses.source: Rehatnamas, compiled by Piara Singh Padam
courses.summary: A scholarly survey of the historical ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ — the early codes of Sikh conduct attributed to the Khalsa era. This course examines the ਚੌਪਾ ਸਿੰਘ, ਦੇਸਾ ਸਿੰਘ, ਪ੍ਰਹਿਲਾਦ ਰਾਇ, ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ, ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰਘ and related ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ, their disputed dates, the textual and authenticity debates surrounding them, what they reveal about eighteenth-century Sikh practice, the contradictions among them, and the central methodological problem of distinguishing genuine Guru-era injunctions from later sectarian and Brahmanical additions — culminating in how these texts were sifted to produce the modern ਸਿੱਖ ਰਹਿਤ ਮਰਯਾਦਾ.
outcomes: Identify the major historical ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ, their attributed authors, and their approximate dates of composition
Analyze the textual-critical debates over the authenticity, interpolation, and dating of each ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ
Explain what the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ collectively reveal about eighteenth-century Khalsa belief and practice
Compare and contrast the contradictory injunctions found across different ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ
Evaluate the methodological problem of separating genuine ਗੁਰੂ-era ਰਹਿਤ from later ਬ੍ਰਾਹਮਣਵਾਦੀ and sectarian accretions
Trace how the historical ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ were critically sifted to produce the modern ਸਿੱਖ ਰਹਿਤ ਮਰਯਾਦਾ (1945)

terms.m: A written code of conduct or 'manual of discipline' for the Khalsa Sikh, setting out injunctions on belief, ritual, diet, dress, and social conduct. Plural: ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ.
The disciplined Khalsa way of life — the body of conduct, observances, and prohibitions that define a Sikh's daily living and identity.
The order of initiated Sikhs instituted by Guru Gobind Singh in 1699; the collective body whose conduct the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ seek to regulate.
A religious penalty or fine imposed by the Panth for a breach of ਰਹਿਤ; one who incurs it is a ਤਨਖਾਹੀਆ.
A cardinal transgression of the ਰਹਿਤ (such as cutting hair, ਕੁੱਠਾ meat, adultery, tobacco) that breaks one's status as an Amritdhari and requires re-initiation.
The initiatory 'nectar' of the double-edged sword (ਖੰਡੇ ਦੀ ਪਾਹੁਲ) by which a person enters the Khalsa; central to every ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ.
Brahmanical ritualism and caste ideology; many later interpolations in the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ reflect its intrusion, which modern critics sought to strip away.
Authenticity — the central scholarly question of which injunctions genuinely derive from the Guru period and which are later additions.
Interpolation; text inserted into a manuscript by a later hand, a pervasive problem in the transmission of the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ.
The collective Sikh community as a corporate body with the authority to enforce ਰਹਿਤ and impose ਤਨਖਾਹ.
A binding resolution passed by the Panth in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib; the mechanism by which Panthic decisions on conduct were ratified.
Meat of an animal slaughtered by the slow ritual (halal) method, prohibited to the Khalsa; one of the four cardinal ਕੁਰਹਿਤ.
The modern, Panthically-approved Code of Conduct (finalized 1945 by the SGPC) that critically distilled the diverse historical ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ into a single authoritative document.
The older term for Sikh initiation; ਚਰਨ ਪਾਹੁਲ (foot-nectar) in the early period and ਖੰਡੇ ਦੀ ਪਾਹੁਲ (sword-nectar) after 1699.

references: Padam, Piara Singh, ed. Rahitname. Patiala: Kalam Mandir, 1974.
McLeod, W. H., trans. and ed. The Chaupa Singh Rahit-nama. Dunedin: University of Otago Press, 1987.
McLeod, W. H. Sikhs of the Khalsa: A History of the Khalsa Rahit. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2003.
McLeod, W. H., trans. Prem Sumarag: The Testimony of a Sanatan Sikh. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2006.
Singh, Ganda. Hukamname. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1967.
Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Rev. ed. The New Cambridge History of India II.3. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998.
Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. The Birth of the Khalsa: A Feminist Re-Memory of Sikh Identity. Albany: State University of New York Press, 2005.
Oberoi, Harjot. The Construction of Religious Boundaries: Culture, Identity and Diversity in the Sikh Tradition. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1994.
Mann, Gurinder Singh, and Kamalroop Singh. The Granth of Guru Gobind Singh: Essays, Lectures, and Translations. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2015.
Fenech, Louis E., and W. H. McLeod. Historical Dictionary of Sikhism. 3rd ed. Lanham: Rowman & Littlefield, 2014.

lessons.title: Introduction: What Is a ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ?
lessons.summary: Defines the genre of the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ, situates it within the formation of Khalsa identity, and lays out the central problems of dating and authenticity that the course addresses.
lessons.html:
ਵਿਸ਼ਾ ਸੂਚੀ (Table of Contents)

  1. Introduction: What Is a ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ?
  2. The ਤਨਖਾਹਨਾਮਾ and Bhai Nand Lal's Verse Rehat
  3. The ਚੌਪਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ: The Great Compendium
  4. The ਦੇਸਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ: Verse Discipline of the Eighteenth Century
  5. The ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰਘ and ਪ੍ਰਹਿਲਾਦ ਰਾਇ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ
  6. The ਸਾਖੀ ਰਹਿਤ and the ਪ੍ਰੇਮ ਸੁਮਾਰਗ
  7. The Problem of ਅੰਤਰ-ਪਾਠ: Interpolation and Brahmanical Accretion
  8. Contradictions Across the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ
  9. What the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ Reveal About Eighteenth-Century Sikh Practice
  10. The Four ਕੁਰਹਿਤ, ਤਨਖਾਹ, and the Disciplinary Order of the ਪੰਥ
  11. From Manuscript to ਮਰਯਾਦਾ: Sifting the Tradition
  12. Conclusion: Reading the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ Critically

The Genre and Its Stakes

A ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ is, at its simplest, a written code of conduct for the Khalsa Sikh — a manual that prescribes what a Sikh must do, must believe, must avoid, and must look like. Yet behind that plain definition lies one of the most contested bodies of literature in the Sikh tradition. The ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ are our principal documentary windows into how the eighteenth-century Khalsa understood its own ਰਹਿਤ — its disciplined way of life — and yet almost every one of them is dogged by questions of date, authorship, and authenticity. To study them is to study not only the rules themselves but the very problem of how a tradition transmits and polices its identity through time.

The word ਰਹਿਤ derives from the sense of 'living' or 'keeping' — the manner in which a Sikh lives. A ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ (literally a 'document of ਰਹਿਤ') is therefore a textualization of that lived discipline. The genre emerges in the wake of the founding of the ਖਾਲਸਾ by Guru Gobind Singh at Anandpur in 1699, when the community's boundary-markers — uncut hair, the ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ initiation, the prohibition of ਕੁੱਠਾ meat, the rejection of caste — acquired sudden urgency. The ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ are the attempt of the early Khalsa to fix that boundary in writing.

The Authorial Attributions

The texts come down to us under the names of figures said to have been close to the Tenth Guru: Bhai Nand Lal Goya, the poet of the Guru's court; ਚੌਪਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਛਿੱਬਰ, said to have been the Guru's tutor and attendant; ਦੇਸਾ ਸਿੰਘ; ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰਘ, identified with one of the ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ; ਪ੍ਰਹਿਲਾਦ ਰਾਇ (or ਪ੍ਰਹਿਲਾਦ ਸਿੰਘ); and others. These attributions lend the texts the authority of eyewitness proximity to the Guru. But as the scholar Piara Singh Padam — whose 1974 compilation ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ remains the indispensable critical edition — repeatedly cautioned, an attribution is not a date. A text bearing ਚੌਪਾ ਸਿੰਘ's name may contain a genuine eighteenth-century core overlaid with material from many later hands.

The Two Great Questions

This course is organized around two questions that the historian W. H. McLeod placed at the centre of his life's work on the ਖਾਲਸਾ ਰਹਿਤ. First, the question of ਪ੍ਰਮਾਣਿਕਤਾ (authenticity): which injunctions genuinely descend from the Guru period, and which are later additions? Second, the question of ਅੰਤਰ-ਪਾਠ (interpolation): how do we detect the seams where a later copyist inserted his own concerns — often Brahmanical caste ideology or sectarian polemic — into an older text? As Gurbani in the ਆਨੰਦ ਸਾਹਿਬ teaches that the seeker must test what is true and discard what is false, so the student of the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ must learn to weigh each line.

We will proceed text by text, then thematically. By the end you will be able to name the major ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ, situate them in time, articulate the debates over each, map their contradictions, and understand how the modern ਸਿੱਖ ਰਹਿਤ ਮਰਯਾਦਾ of 1945 emerged as a critical distillation of this turbulent inheritance. The aim is not to dismiss the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ as forgeries — they are precious historical evidence — but to read them with the discernment the ਪੰਥ itself eventually applied.

A Note on Method

Throughout, we treat the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ as historical sources rather than as timeless scripture. The Guru Granth Sahib alone holds scriptural authority in Sikhi; the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ are subordinate, human documents that interpret and apply the Guru's teaching to lived discipline. This distinction — between revealed ਬਾਣੀ and prescriptive ਰਹਿਤ — is itself a key to the critical method, for it licenses us to question a ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ wherever it contradicts ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ.

lessons.title: The ਤਨਖਾਹਨਾਮਾ and Bhai Nand Lal's Verse Rehat
lessons.summary: Examines the earliest layer of rehat literature attributed to Bhai Nand Lal, including the ਤਨਖਾਹਨਾਮਾ and the prose ਪ੍ਰਸ਼ਨ-ਉੱਤਰ, and the debates over their genuineness.
lessons.html:
The Poet of the Guru's Court

Bhai Nand Lal Goya (ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ) was among the most celebrated literary figures associated with Guru Gobind Singh. A Persian poet of extraordinary refinement, his ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ and ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀਨਾਮਾ are devotional masterpieces in Persian. Yet attached to his name in the Punjabi tradition are two short ਰਹਿਤ texts: the ਤਨਖਾਹਨਾਮਾ (a verse 'document of penances') and the ਪ੍ਰਸ਼ਨ-ਉੱਤਰ or ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ in prose, cast as a dialogue between the Guru and his disciple. These represent, for many scholars, the earliest stratum of the rehat genre.

The ਤਨਖਾਹਨਾਮਾ

The ਤਨਖਾਹਨਾਮਾ is structured around the concept of ਤਨਖਾਹ — the religious penalty incurred by one who breaks the discipline. It is most famous for a single resounding couplet that has become a touchstone of Sikh aspiration. Gurbani-style verse in the ਤਨਖਾਹਨਾਮਾ teaches:

ਰਾਜ ਕਰੇਗਾ ਖਾਲਸਾ ਆਕੀ ਰਹੈ ਨ ਕੋਇ ॥

'The ਖਾਲਸਾ shall rule; no rebel shall remain. Those who endure, broken and scattered, shall in the end return and find refuge.'

— Ardas (Sikh daily prayer, traditional)

This couplet, recited at the close of ਅਰਦਾਸ in many traditions, is itself a case study in the problems of the genre: its language and triumphalist political vision have led several scholars to suspect that it postdates Bhai Nand Lal and reflects the rising confidence of the Khalsa during the eighteenth-century struggle against Mughal and Afghan power. The verse may be authentically old, but 'old' here may mean the mid-eighteenth century rather than the Guru's own lifetime.

The Prose ਪ੍ਰਸ਼ਨ-ਉੱਤਰ

The prose ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ attributed to Nand Lal takes the form of the Guru answering his Sikh's questions about correct conduct. It is brief, devotional in tone, and notably light on the elaborate ritual prescriptions and caste anxieties that crowd the longer texts. Piara Singh Padam regarded its restraint as a mark of relative antiquity — the further a text drifts from the Guru period, he argued, the more encrusted it tends to become with later social concern. The Nand Lal material foregrounds inner devotion: ਨਾਮ, ਸਿਮਰਨ, service, and loyalty to the Guru, with the outward marks treated as expressions of that inner state.

The Authenticity Debate

Whether Bhai Nand Lal actually composed these Punjabi ਰਹਿਤ texts is genuinely uncertain. Nand Lal was a Persian poet; the Punjabi verse and prose under his name are stylistically a world apart from his signed ਦੀਵਾਨ. Three positions exist in the scholarship. The traditional view accepts the attribution and treats the texts as direct testimony of the Guru's instruction. A sceptical view, associated with the textual-critical approach of W. H. McLeod, treats the attribution as an honorific later affixed to anonymous rehat material to lend it authority. A mediating view — closest to Padam's — holds that a genuine kernel of remembered instruction may underlie the texts even if the present wording was shaped by later transmission.

Why This Layer Matters

The Nand Lal material matters because it shows the rehat tradition in a relatively unencumbered form, dominated by ਨਾਮ and devotion rather than by the dense ritual law that would accumulate later. It thus serves as a baseline. When we turn to the vast ਚੌਪਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ in the next lesson, the contrast will be instructive: where Nand Lal is spare, ਚੌਪਾ ਸਿੰਘ is encyclopaedic, and that very encyclopaedism is one of the clues that much of it belongs to a later, more anxious phase of Khalsa self-definition. As ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ in the ਜਪੁ ਜੀ teaches that disciplined conduct without inner truth is empty, the Nand Lal texts hold the inner and outer together — a balance later ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ would sometimes lose.

lessons.title: The ਚੌਪਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ: The Great Compendium
lessons.summary: A detailed study of the longest and most complex rehatnama, attributed to Chaupa Singh Chhibbar, its Chhibbar-Brahman bias, and its layered composition.
lessons.html:
The Longest of the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ

The ਚੌਪਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ is by far the most substantial of the historical codes — a sprawling prose compendium running to many hundreds of injunctions, intermixed with ਸਾਖੀਆਂ (anecdotes), genealogical material, and theological reflection. It is attributed to ਚੌਪਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਛਿੱਬਰ, said to have been a tutor and trusted attendant of Guru Gobind Singh in his youth, and a member of the ਛਿੱਬਰ family of Brahman-descended Sikhs who served the Gurus across generations. W. H. McLeod devoted an entire critical volume to it — The Chaupa Singh Rahit-nama (1987) — establishing it as the richest single source for eighteenth-century Khalsa norms and, simultaneously, the clearest case study in textual layering.

A Layered Text

McLeod's analysis distinguished several strata within the work. There is an older core that may indeed reach back toward the early eighteenth century; there are expansions reflecting the embattled mid-century; and there are passages whose preoccupations are unmistakably those of the ਛਿੱਬਰ family itself. The text repeatedly elevates the status of Brahmans and of the ਛਿੱਬਰ lineage, prescribing deference to them in ways that sit awkwardly with the Khalsa's egalitarian charter. This is the celebrated 'ਛਿੱਬਰ bias' — a vivid example of how a ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ can become a vehicle for the social interests of its transmitters.

What It Prescribes

For all its biases, the ਚੌਪਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ is a treasure-house of detail. It specifies the daily ਨਿਤਨੇਮ (regimen of prayers), the conduct of ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ initiation, dietary prohibitions including ਕੁੱਠਾ meat and tobacco, rules of dress and the bearing of arms, the treatment of women and family, comportment toward the Guru Granth Sahib, and an elaborate apparatus of ਤਨਖਾਹ for breaches. It insists, in a representative passage, that a Sikh must keep the hair intact, bear arms, rise in the last watch of the night to bathe and recite ਬਾਣੀ, and shun the company of the ਪੰਜ ਮੇਲ (the five reprobate groups). The text in the ਚੌਪਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ teaches that 'the Sikh of the Guru who abandons the ਰਹਿਤ abandons the Guru' — a stark insistence on the inseparability of identity and discipline.

The Brahmanical Problem

The ਚੌਪਾ ਸਿੰਘ text is where the intrusion of ਬ੍ਰਾਹਮਣਵਾਦ becomes most visible and most troubling. Alongside Khalsa injunctions sit prescriptions that look like imported Hindu ritual: deference to Brahmans, concern with caste purity, ritual observances around birth and death that ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ explicitly rejects. Modern Tat Khalsa reformers of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries seized upon precisely these passages as proof that the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ had been corrupted, and they used the contradiction with ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ as the lever for purification. The ਚੌਪਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ thus became Exhibit A in the reformist case for a critically purified code.

Its Evidentiary Value

Yet precisely because it is so detailed and so evidently a composite, the ਚੌਪਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ is invaluable. It preserves, embedded within its later accretions, a great deal of genuine early Khalsa practice. The historian's task is to read it stratigraphically — like an archaeologist reading layers of soil — distinguishing the egalitarian Khalsa core from the ਛਿੱਬਰ overlay. Padam and McLeod, working from different angles, agreed that the text cannot be taken at face value as the Guru's literal words, but that no source tells us more about how an eighteenth-century Sikh household actually understood the ਰਹਿਤ. As ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ teaches that gold must be tested in fire, the ਚੌਪਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ must be tested against the Guru's own word before its injunctions are accepted.

Dating

The consensus places the text's core in the first half of the eighteenth century, with substantial expansion through the century and a stabilized manuscript tradition by its later decades. Colophons in some manuscripts give dates, but these record the act of copying, not of original composition — a distinction the student must keep constantly in view when reading any ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ.

lessons.title: The ਦੇਸਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ: Verse Discipline of the Eighteenth Century
lessons.summary: Studies the verse rehatnama attributed to Desa Singh, its systematic treatment of daily discipline and the five Ks, and its place in the maturing Khalsa.
lessons.html:
A Code in Verse

Where the ਚੌਪਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ is sprawling prose, the ਦੇਸਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ is composed in disciplined Braj-inflected Punjabi verse. It is attributed to ਦੇਸਾ ਸਿੰਘ, of whom little firm is known; tradition links him to the circle around the Tenth Guru, but the text's developed and systematic character points most scholars toward a later eighteenth-century date, when the Khalsa's institutions had matured and its self-image as a martial brotherhood was fully formed.

Structure and Content

The ਦੇਸਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ is notable for the orderliness with which it lays out the Khalsa's daily life. It treats the ਨਿਤਨੇਮ, the bearing and care of arms, the discipline of the ਕੇਸ (uncut hair), the maintenance of the five articles of faith, conduct in battle, charity, honest livelihood, and the avoidance of the cardinal transgressions. It dwells with particular feeling on the ਖਾਲਸਾ as a sovereign, God-belonging order. A representative passage in the ਦੇਸਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ teaches that the true Sikh keeps weapons ever at hand, recites the Guru's ਬਾਣੀ at the appointed watches, gives a tenth of his earnings (ਦਸਵੰਧ), and never bows his head before any but the Guru and Akal Purakh.

The Martial Ideal

This ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ crystallizes the ideal of the ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ — the saint-soldier who unites devotion with martial readiness. Its insistence on always bearing arms, on courage in the face of death, and on the sovereignty of the Khalsa reflects the lived reality of the mid-to-late eighteenth century, when Sikhs were fighting for survival and then for territory across the Punjab. The text's confidence is the confidence of a community that has passed through persecution and emerged ascendant. This historical fit is itself an argument for its date: the ਦੇਸਾ ਸਿੰਚ vision belongs to the era of the ਮਿਸਲਾਂ rather than to the besieged Anandpur of 1699.

Relation to the ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰਘ Tradition

The ਦੇਸਾ ਸਿੰਘ and ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ share considerable material and are sometimes transmitted together or confused in the manuscript tradition. This overlap is itself instructive: the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ did not circulate as fixed, sealed books but as living texts that scribes copied, combined, abridged, and expanded. A line found in ਦੇਸਾ ਸਿੰਘ may reappear, slightly altered, in ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰਘ, and the question of priority is often unanswerable. Piara Singh Padam, in collating the manuscripts for his critical edition, mapped these overlaps carefully, and his apparatus remains the starting point for any serious comparison.

Comparative Restraint on Caste

The ਦੇਸਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ is, on the whole, less encumbered with the explicit Brahmanical material that burdens the ਚੌਪਾ ਸਿੰਘ text. Its emphasis falls on martial-devotional discipline rather than on ritual purity and caste deference. This does not make it 'earlier' in a simple sense — its martial confidence points later — but it does illustrate that the intrusion of ਬ੍ਰਾਹਮਣਵਾਦ was uneven across the tradition, concentrated in particular transmission streams (notably the ਛਿੱਬਰ line) rather than uniform across all ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ.

Reading Verse Critically

The verse form of the ਦੇਸਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ has consequences for its transmission. Verse is more resistant to casual interpolation than prose, because inserted lines must scan and rhyme; this gives the verse ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ a somewhat greater textual stability. But verse also invites memorization and performance, which means variants arise through recitation as well as copying. The student should therefore read the ਦੇਸਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ as a relatively coherent late-eighteenth-century statement of the matured Khalsa ideal — valuable precisely because it shows us the ਰਹਿਤ as a confident, self-governing community understood it, rather than as a beleaguered sect.
