lessons.title: The ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰਘ and ਪ੍ਰਹਿਲਾਦ ਰਾਇ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ
lessons.summary: Surveys two further codes — that attributed to Bhai Daya Singh of the Panj Piare and the short Prahlad Rai text — and their distinctive emphases and problems.
lessons.html:
Two Shorter but Significant Codes

Beyond the great compendia stand a cluster of shorter ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ that have nonetheless exercised wide influence. Two of the most important are the ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ and the ਪ੍ਰਹਿਲਾਦ ਰਾਇ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ. Each is bound up with a name of high authority in the Khalsa imagination, and each contributes distinctive material to the composite picture of eighteenth-century discipline.

The ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ

This text is attributed to ਭਾਈ ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰਘ — by tradition the first of the ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ, the five beloved ones who rose to offer their heads at the founding of the ਖਾਲਸਾ in 1699. No attribution could carry greater weight, for ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰਘ stood at the very inception of the order. The text combines prose and verse and treats the full range of Khalsa concerns: initiation, the cardinal prohibitions, the ਨਿਤਨੇਮ, the bearing of the ਕਿਰਪਾਨ, conduct toward the Guru Granth Sahib and the ਸੰਗਤ, and the schedule of ਤਨਖਾਹ. Its prestige made it one of the most widely copied and cited ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ, and many of its formulations fed directly into later codifications.

Yet the very weight of the ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰਘ attribution made the text a magnet for interpolation. A scribe wishing to lend authority to a favoured injunction had every incentive to insert it into a ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰਘ manuscript. As Piara Singh Padam observed, the more authoritative the name, the more the text attracted later additions — a paradox at the heart of rehat transmission. The ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ in its received form therefore cannot be read as the literal testimony of the historical ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰਘ, however much its core may preserve genuinely early material.

The ਪ੍ਰਹਿਲਾਦ ਰਾਇ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ

Shorter and more enigmatic is the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ attributed to ਪ੍ਰਹਿਲਾਦ ਰਾਇ (also given as ਪ੍ਰਹਿਲਾਦ ਸਿੰਘ). It is a compact verse text, and like the ਤਨਖਾਹਨਾਮਾ it is remembered chiefly for a few resonant lines rather than for systematic coverage. It is one of the texts that articulates the doctrine of the Guru's continuing presence in the ਖਾਲਸਾ and in the ਸ਼ਬਦ — the teaching that after the Tenth Guru, authority passes to the ਸ਼ਬਦ-ਗੁਰੂ and the corporate ਪੰਥ. This makes the ਪ੍ਰਹਿਲਾਦ ਰਾਇ text doctrinally important out of proportion to its length, for it preserves an early articulation of the doctrine of ਗੁਰੂ ਪੰਥ and ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ.

The Doctrine of Guruship

The ਪ੍ਰਹਿਲਾਦ ਰਾਇ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ teaches, in substance, that the Guru is to be sought in the assembled ਖਾਲਸਾ and in the revealed word — a teaching consonant with the well-attested injunction of Guru Gobind Singh that the Sikhs were thenceforth to recognize the Guru Granth Sahib as Guru. The presence of this doctrine in a ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ shows that the codes were not merely lists of dos and don'ts but also vehicles for the community's foundational theology of authority. Conduct and doctrine were woven together: to keep the ਰਹਿਤ was to acknowledge where the Guru now resided.

Manuscript Confusion

These shorter texts present acute problems of identification. Because they are brief and were often copied alongside other ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ in composite manuscripts, lines migrate between them, and the same verse may be attributed to ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰਘ in one manuscript and to ਪ੍ਰਹਿਲਾਦ ਰਾਇ in another. Disentangling them requires the patient collation that Padam undertook. The lesson for the student is that 'the ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ' or 'the ਪ੍ਰਹਿਲਾਦ ਰਾਇ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ' is less a single fixed book than a label attached to a fluid cluster of material — a reminder that the rehat tradition was oral and scribal as much as it was literary, and that fixity is something the modern editor imposes, not something the tradition itself possessed.

lessons.title: The ਸਾਖੀ ਰਹਿਤ and the ਪ੍ਰੇਮ ਸੁਮਾਰਗ
lessons.summary: Examines anecdote-based rehat texts and the contested Prem Sumarag, a code reflecting a 'Sanatan' vision of Sikh society and its debated dating.
lessons.html:
Beyond the Named Codes

The rehat tradition includes texts that do not fit neatly into the pattern of the named ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ. Two important examples are the ਸਾਖੀ ਰਹਿਤ literature and the remarkable ਪ੍ਰੇਮ ਸੁਮਾਰਗ. Both extend our picture of how eighteenth-century Sikhs imagined the disciplined life, and both sharpen the problems of dating and authenticity.

The ਸਾਖੀ ਰਹਿਤ

Some rehat material is embedded in or framed by ਸਾਖੀਆਂ — narrative anecdotes about the Guru and his Sikhs. The so-called ਸਾਖੀ ਰਹਿਤ presents injunctions through stories: the Guru is shown instructing a Sikh in a particular situation, and the moral is the rule. This narrative form has consequences for authenticity. On one hand, the story-frame can preserve memory vividly; on the other, it is highly susceptible to embellishment, since a good story invites elaboration. The ਚੌਪਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ itself is shot through with such ਸਾਖੀਆਂ, showing that the boundary between rehat-as-law and rehat-as-narrative was porous.

The ਪ੍ਰੇਮ ਸੁਮਾਰਗ

The ਪ੍ਰੇਮ ਸੁਮਾਰਗ (the 'Excellent Path of Love') is among the most fascinating and contested texts in the broader rehat tradition. It is not a ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ of the short prescriptive kind but an extended manual prescribing a complete pattern of life for a Sikh society — covering not only initiation and prohibition but marriage rites, the conduct of rulers, the treatment of women, inheritance, and the ordering of a whole community. W. H. McLeod translated it under the telling subtitle The Testimony of a Sanatan Sikh, signalling his view that it expresses a 'Sanatan' (traditionalist, Hindu-inflected) vision of the Khalsa rather than the reformed Tat Khalsa ideal.

The Dating Controversy

The ਪ੍ਰੇਮ ਸੁਮਾਰਗ is a flashpoint precisely because of its date. Traditional opinion has sometimes placed it in or near the Guru period, treating its detailed social vision as an authentic Guru-era blueprint. McLeod and other critical scholars argued for a substantially later date — likely the later eighteenth or even early nineteenth century — on the grounds that its developed social legislation and its particular ritual concerns fit a settled, ruling Sikh society rather than the embattled early Khalsa. The text prescribes, for instance, distinctive Sikh life-cycle rites that look like deliberate alternatives to Brahmanical ones, suggesting a community engaged in self-conscious boundary-construction of a sort more characteristic of the late period.

A Window onto an Alternative Vision

Whatever its date, the ਪ੍ਰੇਮ ਸੁਮਾਰਗ is precious because it shows that the rehat tradition contained more than one vision of Sikh society. It imagines an entire ਖਾਲਸਾ social order, complete with its own jurisprudence and ceremony. Harjot Oberoi, in his study of the construction of religious boundaries, drew on such texts to argue that eighteenth and nineteenth-century Sikh society was internally diverse, accommodating practices that later reformers would reject. The ਪ੍ਰੇਮ ਸੁਮਾਰਗ thus stands as evidence against any assumption that 'the ਰਹਿਤ' was ever singular and fixed; it was a field of competing articulations.

Method and Caution

For the student, the ਪ੍ਰੇਮ ਸੁਮਾਰਗ and the ਸਾਖੀ ਰਹਿਤ teach a crucial methodological lesson: the rehat literature is generically diverse, and its texts must be dated and weighed individually, not lumped together. A short prescriptive verse code, a narrative ਸਾਖੀ collection, and an extended social manual are different kinds of documents with different relationships to the Guru period. As ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ teaches the seeker to discriminate the real from the counterfeit, the historian must discriminate among the genres and strata of the rehat corpus before drawing any conclusion about 'what the Khalsa believed.'

lessons.title: The Problem of ਅੰਤਰ-ਪਾਠ: Interpolation and Brahmanical Accretion
lessons.summary: A methodological lesson on how interpolations entered the rehatnamas, how scholars detect them, and the special problem of Brahmanical material contradicting Gurbani.
lessons.html:
The Central Methodological Problem

Every previous lesson has gestured toward it; now we confront it directly. The single greatest obstacle to using the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ as historical sources is ਅੰਤਰ-ਪਾਠ — interpolation, the insertion of later material into an older text. Because the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ were copied by hand over generations, and because each carried the authority of a name from the Guru's circle, they were uniquely vulnerable to having later concerns smuggled into them. Learning to detect interpolation is the core analytical skill of this course.

How Interpolation Happens

Interpolation in the rehat tradition arose from several pressures. A scribe with a sectarian allegiance might insert injunctions favouring his ਡੇਰਾ or lineage — as the ਛਿੱਬਰ family did in the ਚੌਪਾ ਸਿੰਘ tradition. A copyist anxious about a contemporary controversy might add a rule addressing it and attribute it to the Guru. Brahmanical ritual specialists serving Sikh households might fold in caste-purity observances and life-cycle rites drawn from their own tradition. And the sheer prestige of names like ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰਘ acted as a magnet, since an injunction gained authority the moment it appeared in such a text. The result is that the received ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ are palimpsests, with genuine early material and later accretion layered together.

The Brahmanical Accretion

The most consequential category of interpolation is ਬ੍ਰਾਹਮਣਵਾਦ — Brahmanical ritualism and caste ideology. ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ is unambiguous in rejecting caste hierarchy, idol-worship, ritual purity rules, pilgrimage as a means of salvation, and the mediating authority of Brahmans. The ਜਪੁ ਜੀ and countless ਸ਼ਬਦ teach that all are equal before Akal Purakh and that liberation comes through ਨਾਮ, not ritual. Yet several ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ — above all the ਚੌਪਾ ਸਿੰਘ text — contain injunctions prescribing exactly such Brahmanical observances. This is the smoking gun of interpolation: where a ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ contradicts the explicit teaching of the Guru Granth Sahib, the historian has strong grounds to suspect a later, non-Guru hand.

The Criterion of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ

This gives us our single most powerful analytical tool, one the Tat Khalsa reformers themselves wielded decisively. The Guru Granth Sahib is the supreme authority; the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ are subordinate human documents. Therefore any rehat injunction that contradicts ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ must be rejected as inauthentic, whatever name it travels under. This criterion does not depend on dating the manuscript; it depends only on comparing the injunction with the Guru's own word. It was precisely this principle that allowed the compilers of the modern ਸਿੱਖ ਰਹਿਤ ਮਰਯਾਦਾ to strip out the Brahmanical material while retaining the genuine Khalsa core.

Other Detection Methods

Beyond the criterion of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ, scholars use several techniques. Linguistic analysis can flag passages whose vocabulary or style differs from their surroundings, suggesting a later hand. Manuscript collation — comparing many copies — reveals which passages are present in the oldest witnesses and which appear only in later ones; a line absent from early manuscripts and present only in late ones is probably interpolated. Internal contradiction is another clue: where a text both prescribes and forbids the same thing, the layers have not been fully harmonized. And historical anachronism — a reference to circumstances that did not exist in the Guru period — betrays later composition, as with the triumphalist political vision of some passages.

The Danger of Over-Correction

A caution is in order. The reformist impulse to purge 'Brahmanical' material, while methodologically sound in principle, can be applied too aggressively, dismissing as 'interpolation' anything that does not fit a modern ideal. The careful historian distinguishes between injunctions that genuinely contradict ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ — which should indeed be rejected — and injunctions that are merely unfamiliar or inconvenient to modern sensibilities, which deserve to be understood in their historical context before being judged. The goal is critical understanding, not the manufacture of a sanitized past. As ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ teaches discernment between truth and falsehood, the historian must exercise that same discernment evenly, neither credulous nor reflexively dismissive.

lessons.title: Contradictions Across the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ
lessons.summary: Catalogues and analyzes the substantive contradictions among the codes and what they reveal about the contested, evolving nature of Khalsa discipline.
lessons.html:
A Tradition That Disagrees With Itself

If the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ spoke with one voice, the historian's task would be simple. They do not. The codes contradict one another on matters large and small, and these contradictions are among the most revealing features of the corpus, for they show the ਰਹਿਤ not as a fixed deposit handed down intact but as a contested, evolving body of practice over which different communities and periods disagreed.

Diet and the Question of Meat

One of the most persistent areas of disagreement concerns diet. All the major ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ agree in forbidding ਕੁੱਠਾ — meat slaughtered by the slow ritual (halal) method — which is a cardinal ਕੁਰਹਿਤ. But on the broader question of meat-eating itself the texts diverge. Some permit the eating of ਝਟਕਾ meat (from an animal killed with a single blow); others lean toward vegetarianism; and particular ਡੇਰਾ and ਸੰਪ੍ਰਦਾਇ traditions read the rehat to mandate abstinence from all meat. This divergence has fuelled centuries of debate and persists in the ਪੰਥ today. The contradiction shows that the early Khalsa did not hold a single settled position, and that the prohibition that unites all the codes is specifically of ਕੁੱਠਾ, not of meat as such.

Caste and Social Hierarchy

The codes diverge sharply on caste. The ਚੌਪਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ, with its ਛਿੱਬਰ bias, preserves caste deference and Brahmanical privilege; other ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ, closer to the egalitarian charter of the ਖਾਲਸਾ, insist that ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ dissolves caste and that all initiated Sikhs are kin. This is not a trivial inconsistency: it goes to the heart of what the Khalsa is. The contradiction reflects a real social struggle within eighteenth-century Sikh society between the egalitarian thrust of the Guru's teaching and the gravitational pull of the surrounding caste order.

Ritual and Life-Cycle Rites

The texts disagree on how far Sikhs should adopt distinctive rites versus retain customary (often Brahmanical) ones for birth, marriage, and death. The ਪ੍ਰੇਮ ਸੁਮਾਰਗ prescribes elaborate distinctively-Sikh ceremonies; other texts are silent or accommodate inherited practice. This spread reflects the gradual and uneven process by which the community built its own ritual repertoire to replace the Brahmanical one — a process not complete in the eighteenth century and still being negotiated in the reform era.

The Status of Authority After the Tenth Guru

Even on the foundational question of where authority resides after Guru Gobind Singh, the emphasis varies. Texts like the ਪ੍ਰਹਿਲਾਦ ਰਾਇ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ stress the doctrine of ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ and ਗੁਰੂ ਪੰਥ; others foreground the personal continuity of charismatic teachers or lineages. These differences map onto the broader tension between the corporate, egalitarian model of authority and the lineage-based models favoured by particular ਡੇਰੇ.

Reading Contradiction Constructively

How should the student read these contradictions? Not as embarrassments to be explained away, but as data. Each contradiction is a fossil of a real disagreement, a trace of the diversity that Harjot Oberoi and J. S. Grewal have shown characterized eighteenth and nineteenth-century Sikh society. The contradictions also vindicate the criterion of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ: when the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ disagree, the way to adjudicate is to ask which position accords with the Guru Granth Sahib. On caste, on the rejection of empty ritual, on equality, ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ speaks clearly, and the codes that align with it carry the weight of the Guru's own authority. The contradictions, in other words, are not only a problem; they are an invitation to read the rehat tradition in the light of ਬਾਣੀ, which is exactly what the ਪੰਥ ultimately did.

lessons.title: What the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ Reveal About Eighteenth-Century Sikh Practice
lessons.summary: Synthesizes the codes as social-historical evidence for how the eighteenth-century Khalsa actually lived, worshipped, ate, dressed, and organized itself.
lessons.html:
The ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ as Social History

Having learned to read the codes critically, we can now ask what, taken together and read with discernment, they reveal about how the eighteenth-century Khalsa actually lived. Even where individual injunctions are interpolated or contested, the corpus as a whole is an irreplaceable record of the lived ਰਹਿਤ of a community in formation. Read as social history rather than as law, the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ illuminate worship, diet, dress, gender, livelihood, and corporate organization.

The Rhythm of Worship

The codes are unanimous that the Sikh's day was structured by ਬਾਣੀ. The ਨਿਤਨੇਮ — rising in the ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਵੇਲਾ (the ambrosial last watch of night) to bathe and recite the morning ਬਾਣੀਆਂ, with prescribed prayers at evening and night — appears across the corpus. This testifies that disciplined daily devotion was the spine of Khalsa life, not an optional extra. The centrality of ਸਿਮਰਨ and the recitation of the Guru's word marks the rehat as fundamentally devotional, the outward discipline serving an inner relationship with Akal Purakh.

The Marks of the Body

The codes converge on the bodily markers of Khalsa identity: uncut ਕੇਸ, the bearing of the ਕਿਰਪਾਨ, and the maintenance of the articles of faith. The insistence on ਕੇਸ as inviolable — cutting the hair being a cardinal ਕੁਰਹਿਤ — runs through the whole tradition and shows how central the visible, unaltered body was to Khalsa self-understanding. The constant readiness to bear arms reflects the martial reality of the age and the ideal of the ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ.

Diet and Prohibition

On diet, the codes reveal a community defining itself partly by what it would not consume: ਕੁੱਠਾ meat, tobacco, and intoxicants. The prohibition of tobacco is especially revealing as a boundary-marker distinguishing the Khalsa from surrounding Muslim and Hindu populations. The four cardinal ਕੁਰਹਿਤ — violating the ਕੇਸ, eating ਕੁੱਠਾ, illicit sexual relations, and using tobacco — emerge from the codes as the non-negotiable core, the breaches that unmade one's Khalsa status.

Gender and the Household

The codes give us glimpses, often problematic, of the eighteenth-century Sikh household and the place of women within it. Some passages reflect patriarchal and caste-bound assumptions of the surrounding society; others, especially where they echo ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ, affirm the dignity and inclusion of women in ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ and ਸੰਗਤ. Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh's feminist re-reading of Khalsa identity draws attention to how the founding vision of the ਖਾਲਸਾ exceeded the patriarchal limits that later transmission sometimes imposed, and the rehat corpus, read against ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ, supports this recovery.

Livelihood and Charity

The codes prescribe honest livelihood (ਕਿਰਤ) and the giving of ਦਸਵੰਧ, the tenth part of one's earnings, to the ਪੰਥ. They forbid theft, gambling, and dishonest gain. This economic ethic — earn honestly, share with the community, serve — is one of the most consistent and least interpolated strands of the tradition, and it aligns closely with ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ's teaching of ਕਿਰਤ ਕਰੋ, ਨਾਮ ਜਪੋ, ਵੰਡ ਛਕੋ (earn by honest work, remember the Name, share with others).

Corporate Organization

Finally, the codes reveal a community organized as a corporate body — the ਪੰਥ — with the authority to admit through ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ, to discipline through ਤਨਖਾਹ, and to decide collectively through the ਗੁਰਮਤਾ passed in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib. This is the institutional substance of the rehat: not merely private piety but a self-governing order. J. S. Grewal's account of eighteenth-century Sikh history shows how this corporate self-organization underpinned the Khalsa's survival and rise to power, and the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ are the constitutional documents, however contested, of that order.

lessons.title: The Four ਕੁਰਹਿਤ, ਤਨਖਾਹ, and the Disciplinary Order of the ਪੰਥ
lessons.summary: Focuses on the disciplinary machinery of the rehat — the cardinal transgressions, the system of penalties, and the corporate authority that enforced them.
lessons.html:
Discipline as the Engine of Identity

A code of conduct is only as real as its enforcement. The ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ are not merely aspirational; they describe a working disciplinary system through which the ਪੰਥ defined, maintained, and policed Khalsa identity. This lesson examines that machinery: the cardinal transgressions (ਕੁਰਹਿਤ), the system of penalties (ਤਨਖਾਹ), and the corporate authority that administered them.

The Four ਕੁਰਹਿਤ

At the heart of the disciplinary system stand the cardinal transgressions, the ਕੁਰਹਿਤ, whose commission breaks one's status as an Amritdhari and requires re-initiation. Though the codes vary in detail, the four that crystallized as the core are: dishonouring the ਕੇਸ (cutting or removing the hair); eating ਕੁੱਠਾ (ritually slaughtered meat); ਪਰ-ਇਸਤ੍ਰੀ ਗਮਨ (illicit sexual relations, adultery); and the use of ਤਮਾਕੂ (tobacco). These are categorically different from lesser infractions. A ਕੁਰਹਿਤ is not merely a fault to be penanced; it severs the bond of ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ, and restoration requires taking ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ again. The codes thus distinguish a hierarchy of gravity: the apostatizing ਕੁਰਹਿਤ on one hand, and the many lesser breaches that incur ਤਨਖਾਹ on the other.

The System of ਤਨਖਾਹ

ਤਨਖਾਹ is the religious penalty imposed by the ਪੰਥ for a breach of ਰਹਿਤ. The very name of the ਤਨਖਾਹਨਾਮਾ — the earliest layer we studied — signals how central this concept was. One who incurs it is a ਤਨਖਾਹੀਆ, a defaulter, who must present himself before the ਸੰਗਤ, confess, and accept the penalty — typically seva (service), a financial contribution, or recitation of ਬਾਣੀ — to be restored to good standing. Crucially, ਤਨਖਾਹ is not punitive in a vindictive sense; it is reintegrative, a mechanism for restoring the erring Sikh to the community rather than expelling him. This reflects the ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ teaching that the door of grace remains open to the repentant.

The Authority of the ਪੰਥ

Who imposes ਤਨਖਾਹ? Not a priesthood — Sikhi has none — but the ਪੰਥ itself, the corporate community, acting through the ਸੰਗਤ assembled in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib. The codes presuppose this corporate authority. The ਖਾਲਸਾ governs its own conduct collectively; the assembled Sikhs adjudicate breaches and pronounce penalties. This is one of the most distinctive features of the rehat order and one of the clearest points of continuity between the eighteenth-century codes and the modern ਪੰਥ. The Akal Takht and the institution of the ਹੁਕਮਨਾਮਾ extend this corporate disciplinary authority into the present.

The ਗੁਰਮਤਾ

The supreme expression of corporate authority is the ਗੁਰਮਤਾ — a binding resolution passed by the ਪੰਥ in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib. Through the ਗੁਰਮਤਾ the community could resolve disputes, set policy, and ratify decisions about conduct. The historical ਹੁਕਮਨਾਮੇ collected by Ganda Singh show this corporate decision-making in action across the eighteenth century. The ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ and the ਹੁਕਮਨਾਮੇ thus complement one another: the former lay out standing rules, the latter record specific corporate decisions, and both presuppose the same underlying authority of the ਪੰਥ under the Guru.

The ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ

In matters of ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ and serious discipline, the codes assign a special role to the ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ — five initiated Sikhs of good standing who act on behalf of the ਪੰਥ. This institution, born at the founding of the ਖਾਲਸਾ in 1699, embodies the principle that authority resides in the collective rather than the individual. The five administer ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ, hear confessions of ਕੁਰਹਿਤ, and pronounce restoration. The continuity of this institution from the rehat literature to present practice is among the strongest threads linking the eighteenth-century codes to the living ਪੰਥ.

Discipline and Grace

It is essential to read this disciplinary order in the light of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ's spirit. The machinery of ਕੁਰਹਿਤ and ਤਨਖਾਹ is not legalism for its own sake; it serves the formation of the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ, the God-oriented person. The ਆਸਾ ਦੀ ਵਾਰ teaches that outward observance without inner truth is hollow. The disciplinary system of the rehat is meant to support, not replace, the inward journey of ਨਾਮ and ਸਿਮਰਨ — a balance the best of the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ keep, and the loss of which the worst interpolations represent.

lessons.title: From Manuscript to ਮਰਯਾਦਾ: Sifting the Tradition
lessons.summary: Traces how the diverse historical rehatnamas were critically sifted by the Singh Sabha reformers and the SGPC to produce the modern Sikh Rahit Maryada of 1945.
lessons.html:
The Reformist Reckoning

By the late nineteenth century the contradictions and accretions of the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ had become a pressing practical problem. The ਪੰਥ possessed not one code but a dozen, mutually inconsistent and shot through with material that contradicted ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ. The story of how this turbulent inheritance was sifted into the single authoritative ਸਿੱਖ ਰਹਿਤ ਮਰਯਾਦਾ of 1945 is the culmination of our course and a model of critical tradition-building.

The ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ Movement

The reckoning began with the ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ movement, which arose from the 1870s onward to defend and define Sikh identity in the colonial era. Its dominant Tat Khalsa wing held that authentic Sikhi must be recovered by stripping away the ਬ੍ਰਾਹਮਣਵਾਦੀ accretions that had crept into practice and into the rehat texts. Their criterion was exactly the one we identified earlier: ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ. Wherever a ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ prescribed caste deference, idol-worship, Brahmanical ritual, or anything else the Guru Granth Sahib rejected, the reformers judged it a corruption to be discarded. Harjot Oberoi has documented how this reformist project deliberately narrowed the diverse, fluid Sikh practice of the earlier period into a sharply defined boundary.

Scholarly Recovery

The reform also stimulated scholarly recovery of the rehat texts themselves. The labour of collecting, collating, and editing the scattered manuscripts — work that would culminate decades later in Piara Singh Padam's authoritative 1974 ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ — gave the ਪੰਥ access to its own rehat tradition in a critically organized form for the first time. Only by laying the texts side by side could their contradictions be mapped and their common core discerned. This philological recovery was the indispensable foundation for the codifying work that followed.

The Drafting of the ਸਿੱਖ ਰਹਿਤ ਮਰਯਾਦਾ

The decisive institutional step came through the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (SGPC), established in 1925 as the corporate body governing the historic Gurdwaras. The SGPC convened scholars and representatives to draft a single, Panthically-approved code. The process was deliberative and slow, extending over two decades, precisely because the aim was consensus across a diverse ਪੰਥ. The result, finalized in 1945, was the ਸਿੱਖ ਰਹਿਤ ਮਰਯਾਦਾ — a relatively concise document that distilled the genuine core of the historical ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ while omitting their contradictions and Brahmanical accretions.

What Was Kept and What Was Set Aside

The modern code retained the substance that the historical texts held in common and that accorded with ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ: the ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ initiation by the ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ, the five articles of faith, the ਨਿਤਨੇਮ, the four cardinal ਕੁਰਹਿਤ, the rejection of caste and idol-worship, honest livelihood and ਦਸਵੰਧ, and the corporate authority of the ਪੰਥ. It set aside the ਛਿੱਬਰ caste material, the Brahmanical life-cycle rites, the triumphalist political glosses, and the mutually contradictory dietary maximalisms — adjudicating, for instance, the meat question by prohibiting ਕੁੱਠਾ while leaving the broader matter to individual conscience.

A Living, Contested Settlement

The ਸਿੱਖ ਰਹਿਤ ਮਰਯਾਦਾ is authoritative but not uncontested. Some ਸੰਪ੍ਰਦਾਇ and ਡੇਰੇ — the Nihangs, the Namdharis, the Akhand Kirtani Jatha and others — maintain rehat practices that diverge from it on particular points, often appealing to specific historical ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ to justify their usages. This continuing diversity is not a failure of the codifying project but a reminder that the rehat tradition was always plural. The ਮਰਯਾਦਾ provides a Panthic centre of gravity without erasing the historical texts from which it was drawn.

The Achievement

The achievement of the 1945 code lies in its method as much as its content. It demonstrated that a tradition could face its own documentary diversity honestly — acknowledging contradiction and accretion — and resolve it not by fiat but by the disciplined application of a principled criterion (ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ) through corporate, consensual process (the ਪੰਥ acting through the SGPC). In this the modern ਮਰਯਾਦਾ is the heir not only of the content of the historical ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ but of their deepest logic: that the conduct of the ਖਾਲਸਾ is decided by the community under the Guru.

lessons.title: Conclusion: Reading the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ Critically
lessons.summary: Draws together the course's methods and findings, articulates a mature critical posture toward the rehat tradition, and closes with the Works Cited.
lessons.html:
What We Have Learned

We began by asking what a ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ is and discovered that the answer is inseparable from the problem of how a tradition transmits and polices its identity across time. Through twelve lessons we have surveyed the major historical codes — the ਤਨਖਾਹਨਾਮਾ and Nand Lal material, the great ਚੌਪਾ ਸਿੰਘ compendium, the verse discipline of ਦੇਸਾ ਸਿੰਘ, the prestigious ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰਘ text, the doctrinally weighty ਪ੍ਰਹਿਲਾਦ ਰਾਇ, the narrative ਸਾਖੀ ਰਹਿਤ, and the contested ਪ੍ਰੇਮ ਸੁਮਾਰਗ — and we have built a method for reading them.

The Critical Posture

That method rests on a few principles worth restating. First, attribution is not date: a text bearing the name of a figure from the Guru's circle may nonetheless contain material from many later hands. Second, the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ are palimpsests, layered through generations of copying, and must be read stratigraphically. Third, the supreme criterion for adjudicating rehat injunctions is ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ: where a code contradicts the Guru Granth Sahib, the code yields. Fourth, contradiction across the corpus is not an embarrassment but evidence of a real, diverse, evolving tradition. Fifth, the codes are most valuable not as literal law but as social-historical testimony to how the eighteenth-century Khalsa lived its ਰਹਿਤ.

Neither Credulity Nor Cynicism

The mature student of the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ steers between two errors. The first is credulity — treating every injunction as the Guru's literal command, which collapses under the weight of contradiction and interpolation. The second is cynicism — dismissing the whole corpus as forgery, which throws away an irreplaceable record of Khalsa formation. The right posture is critical reverence: honouring the texts as precious witnesses to the community's self-understanding, while reading them with the discernment that the ਪੰਥ itself ultimately exercised in producing the ਸਿੱਖ ਰਹਿਤ ਮਰਯਾਦਾ.

The Continuing Relevance

This is not antiquarianism. The questions the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ raise — what is the genuine ਰਹਿਤ, how is it to be known, who has authority to define it, how does a community distinguish the Guru's teaching from later accretion — are live questions in the ਪੰਥ today. Debates over diet, over the boundaries of identity, over the authority of various ਸੰਪ੍ਰਦਾਇ all reach back into the rehat literature. To read these texts critically is therefore to equip oneself for the living conversation of the ਪੰਥ, not merely to survey a closed chapter of the past.

A Final Word on ਬਾਣੀ and ਰਹਿਤ

The deepest lesson of the rehat tradition is its own subordination to ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ. The codes themselves, at their best, point beyond the outward discipline to the inner life of ਨਾਮ and ਸਿਮਰਨ that the discipline is meant to serve. The ਆਸਾ ਦੀ ਵਾਰ teaches that outward observance without inner truth is empty, and the ਜਪੁ ਜੀ that conduct must be grounded in the realization of the divine Will (ਹੁਕਮ). The ਰਹਿਤ, rightly understood, is the disciplined body of a devotion whose soul is ਬਾਣੀ. To study the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ critically is, in the end, to be returned to the Guru Granth Sahib as the measure of all things — which is precisely where the rehat tradition itself, in its wisest moments and in its modern codification, directs us.

ਹਵਾਲੇ (Works Cited)

  • Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Rev. ed. The New Cambridge History of India II.3. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998.
  • Mann, Gurinder Singh, and Kamalroop Singh. The Granth of Guru Gobind Singh: Essays, Lectures, and Translations. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2015.
  • McLeod, W. H., trans. and ed. The Chaupa Singh Rahit-nama. Dunedin: University of Otago Press, 1987.
  • McLeod, W. H., trans. Prem Sumarag: The Testimony of a Sanatan Sikh. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2006.
  • McLeod, W. H. Sikhs of the Khalsa: A History of the Khalsa Rahit. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2003.
  • Oberoi, Harjot. The Construction of Religious Boundaries: Culture, Identity and Diversity in the Sikh Tradition. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1994.
  • Padam, Piara Singh, ed. Rahitname. Patiala: Kalam Mandir, 1974.

quiz.q: What is the central methodological problem the course identifies in using the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ as historical sources?
options: That they were all written in Persian rather than Punjabi
That distinguishing genuine Guru-era injunctions from later ਅੰਤਰ-ਪਾਠ (interpolations) is extremely difficult
That none of them mention the ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ initiation
That they were all composed after the year 1900

quiz.q: What is the supreme criterion the course proposes for adjudicating whether a rehat injunction is authentic?
options: The age of the oldest surviving manuscript alone
Whether the injunction accords with ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ (the Guru Granth Sahib)
The number of ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ that repeat it
The authority of the ਛਿੱਬਰ family

quiz.q: The ਚੌਪਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ is especially noted by scholars for which distinctive bias?
options: A pro-Mughal political stance
An elevation of Brahmans and the ਛਿੱਬਰ lineage reflecting Brahmanical accretion
A strict prohibition of all reading of ਬਾਣੀ
A rejection of the ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ initiation

quiz.q: What does the term ਤਨਖਾਹ refer to in the rehat tradition?
options: A salary paid to Sikh soldiers by the ਮਿਸਲਾਂ
A reintegrative religious penalty imposed by the ਪੰਥ for a breach of ਰਹਿਤ
The double-edged sword used in initiation
A pilgrimage required of every Amritdhari

quiz.q: On the question of diet, what do all the major ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ agree upon, even though they disagree about meat-eating generally?
options: That all Sikhs must be strictly vegetarian
That ਕੁੱਠਾ (ritually/halal slaughtered) meat is forbidden as a cardinal ਕੁਰਹਿਤ
That only fish may be eaten
That meat may be eaten only during festivals

quiz.q: How did the modern ਸਿੱਖ ਰਹਿਤ ਮਰਯਾਦਾ (finalized 1945) emerge from the historical ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ?
options: A single ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ was adopted unchanged as the official code
The SGPC and Singh Sabha reformers critically sifted the codes, keeping the ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ-consonant core and discarding contradictions and Brahmanical accretions
The British colonial government imposed it on the ਪੰਥ
All the historical ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ were destroyed and a new code invented with no historical basis

courses.title: ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ: Seat of Sikh Sovereignty
courses.summary: A comprehensive intermediate course on ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ, the supreme temporal seat of the Sikh Panth founded by Guru Hargobind Ji in 1609 facing ਹਰਿਮੰਦਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ. The course traces the doctrine of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ, the institution of the five ਤਖ਼ਤ, the tradition of ਹੁਕਮਨਾਮੇ and ਗੁਰਮਤਾ, the governance of the Panth through ਸਰਬੱਤ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ during the ਮਿਸਲ period, the trauma of 1984, and contemporary debates over Panthic authority. Students examine the architectural and theological symbolism of the Takhat, its relationship to the ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ–ਗੁਰੂ ਪੰਥ doctrine, and its evolving role as the conscience and sovereign voice of the Khalsa.
outcomes: Explain the doctrine of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ and how Guru Hargobind Ji embodied temporal and spiritual sovereignty in the founding of ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ in 1609.
Identify the five ਤਖ਼ਤ of the Sikh Panth, their historical origins, and their distinct jurisdictions.
Analyze the function of ਹੁਕਮਨਾਮੇ, ਗੁਰਮਤਾ, and ਸਰਬੱਤ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ as instruments of collective Panthic governance.
Describe the role of ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ during the ਮਿਸਲ period and the rise of Sikh political power in eighteenth-century Punjab.
Critically evaluate the events of 1984 and Operation Bluestar and their lasting impact on the institution and the Sikh psyche.
Assess contemporary controversies over the authority, autonomy, and reform of ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ in the modern era.

terms.m: The Throne of the Timeless One; the supreme temporal seat of Sikh authority founded in 1609, situated directly opposite Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar.
The twin doctrine of temporal (worldly/political) and spiritual sovereignty, symbolized by the two swords worn by Guru Hargobind Ji.
Throne or seat of authority; in Sikh tradition, one of the five supreme seats of Panthic governance and decision-making.
An edict or order of command; an authoritative directive issued from a Takhat to the Sikh Panth, carrying binding moral and Panthic force.
A resolution adopted in the presence of Sri Guru Granth Sahib by the collective Panth; a binding Panthic decision on matters affecting the whole community.
The grand assembly of the entire Khalsa Panth, historically convened at Akal Takhat to deliberate and pass collective resolutions.
The custodian or leader who presides over a Takhat and articulates its directives on behalf of the Panth.
An autonomous Sikh confederacy or fighting band of the eighteenth century; the Misls collectively governed Punjab and gathered under Akal Takhat.
The collective army of the Khalsa during the eighteenth century, organized under Panthic discipline and the authority of Akal Takhat.
The doctrine that the collective Khalsa Panth, guided by Sri Guru Granth Sahib, embodies the Guru's authority in temporal matters.
The path or community; the collective body of the Sikh nation as a religio-political whole.
A religious penance or fine imposed by a Takhat upon one who has breached the Rehat or Panthic discipline.
The Timeless, Deathless Being; God in Sikh theology, whose sovereignty the Akal Takhat represents on earth.
The Takhat at Anandpur Sahib marking the birthplace of the Khalsa in 1699; one of the five Takhats.
